LeBron the star as Angola aims to cash in on E1 racing
- Published
It is difficult to imagine an electric powerboat racing series capturing the attention of an Angolan audience for whom football and basketball is king, but the presence of NBA royalty LeBron James certainly helped.
The 41-year-old was among the A-listers in Luanda as the E1 World Championship rolled into southern Africa for the first time at the weekend, having made its debut on the continent last year in Lagos, Nigeria.
"It's not a short trip, but he [LeBron] is here because he believes in what we're doing," E1 chief executive Jamie Copas told BBC Sport Africa in the Angolan capital.
"You can't underestimate the value of it. They [the celebrity owners] come with huge followings."
James, like fellow sport stars Rafa Nadal, Tom Brady, Didier Drogba and Virat Kohli and actor Will Smith, is an E1 team owner after buying into the series.
Similar to Formula E on land, it aims to blend sport with strong messaging around sustainability and green technology.
James said Angola had made his first trip to the country "super welcoming" after visiting the National Museum of Slavery.
"Obviously there is a lot of history here," the new signing for the Philadelphia 76ers told local media.
"A lot of history that not only is here in the country but also [crosses] over to America."
Angola's men are reigning African basketball champions, securing a record-extending 12th continental title on home soil last year, and unsurprisingly spectators of the E1 racing at the Clube Naval de Luanda clamoured for a glimpse of one of basketball's biggest icons.
Journalist Omar Prata, covering the race for the Jornal de Angola, admitted that E1 was not on his radar until Hollywood star Smith, whose Westbrook Racing team is sponsored by Visit Angola, announced in March that a deal had been agreed to race in Luanda for the next three years.
"I see the potential it could bring to project the city at a time when the government is trying to work on tourism," Prata said.
"And of course it means a lot to have LeBron James here. Angolans have seen him on television, they try to emulate him on the street courts, they have his posters."
Boosting Angola long-term
The star power of E1's owners is helping to bring eyeballs to what is a traditionally niche sport where powerboat pilots skim and bounce around tight courses at speeds close to 100kmph.
Yet, on a calendar that features traditional celebrity haunts like Miami, Monaco and Lake Como, Luanda's name seems an outlier.
Among those taking in the action from the fanzone was local resident Edson Cabeta.
"It is the first time I have seen anything like this," he said.
"Today it is foreigners doing this; tomorrow, perhaps we could have an Angolan team."
The aspiration is that hosting an E1 race will help Angola boost visitor numbers, with minister for tourism Marcio de Jesus Lopes Daniel saying enhanced foreign awareness of the country is the "first step" in a long-term plan.
"Our ambition is not simply to make Angola famous," Daniel told the BBC.
"It is to make Angola more desirable to visit, invest in and do business in."
Angola has not been afraid to speculate to accumulate in the past, bringing Lionel Messi's Argentina side to Luanda for a football friendly last November to celebrate 50 years of the nation's independence.
Daniel said it would be "premature" to assess the economic impact of this weekend's race in Luanda.
"An event of this scale generates demand across several sectors and it creates opportunities," he added.
"We want to turn the international attention generated by E1 into future trips, stays, private investment and jobs. That is the real return we are looking for."
Sustainability challenges
Beyond the spectacle and waterfront backdrops, E1 aims to transcend motorsport.
Sustainability has been one cornerstone, and marine conservation efforts around the race in Angola included mangrove restoration.
Putting sustainability front and centre inevitably invites scrutiny - particularly when races have taken place in Saudi Arabia, the United States, Nigeria and now Angola, all major oil-producing nations.
"The world's on a journey," Copas said.
"We're welcomed in places that do have a lot of fossil-fuel infrastructure.
"Each one of those markets is conscious of it and wants to be doing more from a green point of view. If we can help, why wouldn't we?"
Copas told BBC Sport Africa that E1 would only consider air freight as a last resort for transporting its teams and that they aim to showcase their technology on each stop, persuading people that electric charging is a viable alternative to diesel even on water.
But as the global series expanded to 10 teams and seven races in 2025, its own emissions rose from 1,672 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent in its first season to 4,049 tonnes in its second, according to E1's own annual sustainability report.
"We need to travel to meet new people, to tell our stories, which we would hope would be of greater benefit than the carbon footprint that we have," Copas explained.
"We work really hard to offset our carbon and to make sure every stage of our logistics journey is done in the most sustainable way.
"It would be crazy for us to say we're not going to travel and we're not going to race, because then we can't do the job that we're here to do."
There is an acknowledgement within E1 that the work is unfinished and that more active reductions are needed.
'Continuing the story'
E1 was due to return to Lagos in October, but Nigeria's race was cancelled earlier this month, perhaps showing how the series is still working to establish itself.
It means its longer-term impact in Africa will take time to judge, but the effect of its celebrity owners was obvious around the paddock in Luanda.
After visiting his pilots, Will Smith stopped for selfies and handshakes with fans, telling the crowd it was "great to be here".
On the water, however, there was no fairytale result as Westbrook Racing's hopes of victory were ended by a mechanical fault, with Team Brady taking the inaugural Luanda title.
Smith could have used the help of Kianda, the mermaid-like Angolan water spirit traditionally regarded as a protector of fishermen.
It will take one of her miraculous interventions if electric powerboat racing is to usurp football or basketball in Angolan affections, but Copas hopes E1 can leave a different legacy.
"I think it's for us to help tell Angola stories, and for Angola to help tell ours.
"We will be back next year, we will be back the year after. It's not just about what we're doing in the few days we're here.
"We'd love to see the journey they're on develop even more, and us playing a part in that."

Telangana is exploring a proposal to make six months of robotic surgery training mandatory for postgraduate medical students, as the State looks to build a trained workforce to expand advanced robotic procedures across its government hospitals.
Health Minister C. Damodar Raja Narasimha said the government would approach the National Medical Commission (NMC) for permission to introduce the dedicated training period as part of the three-year postgraduate programme.
Speaking at the ‘State Level Multi-Specialty Robotic Surgery Workshop’ at the Marri Chenna Reddy Telangana Institute of Medical Sciences (MCR TIMS), Sanathnagar in Hyderabad, the Minister said training would be central to Telangana’s plans to expand robotic surgery, whether through a hub-and-spoke model or dedicated robotic surgery facilities at the district level.
The proposal comes as Telangana is already attempting to build a statewide pool of surgeons trained in robotic procedures.
MCR TIMS Director Dr A. Narendra Kumar said surgeons from 35 medical colleges and 47 hospitals, excluding speciality hospitals, are being trained in robotic surgery at two government institutions, Nizam’s Institute of Medical Sciences (NIMS) and MNJ Cancer Institute.

“The idea is to ensure that robotic surgery does not remain concentrated in a handful of premier institutions in Hyderabad,” he added.
Robotic surgery expert Dr. Sudhir Srivastava said such a model could allow specialist expertise to reach patients without requiring them to travel to major cities. He pointed to the financial and emotional burden faced by families from rural and smaller communities when they have to leave their homes to access specialised treatment.
Former NIMS Director Dr N. Bheerappa said NIMS had recently completed nearly 1,000 robotic surgeries and that the government was bearing the cost of such procedures for eligible patients through the Rajiv Aarogyasri health scheme.
Director of Medical Education (DME) Dr N. Vani said government medical colleges had a dual responsibility of providing patient care while training the next generation of doctors. Introducing young surgeons to newer technologies, she said, could have a multiplier effect across the government healthcare system.
She also stressed that young surgeons should not rely solely on the technology, but must combine it with clinical judgement, human touch and compassion.
Experts at the workshop also cautioned that expanding robotic surgery is about considerably more than installing machines. Government Medical College Nagpur Dean Dr. Raj Gajbhiye said robotic surgery was no longer merely a technology available at a few high-end private institutions.
For government hospitals, however, he said “the real objective should be equitable access to advanced surgical technology. “Success of robotics is not about purchasing a robot,” Dr. Gajbhiye said, pointing instead to the need for appropriate infrastructure, trained faculty, structured protocols, multidisciplinary teamwork and institutional support.

The Dead Silence of AI Therapy
What happens when our therapists are no longer able to feel?
Therapy can involve a lot of words, but it’s often the pauses that matter most. If you transcribed a session, the pauses would look like nothing: beats of silence, extra breaths, slowing down. But these can represent the crux of the practice: entry points into feeling. My job as a psychoanalyst is to listen as much to silence as to words, to be present with the patient while they’re quiet—to stay with them as they allow their feelings to emerge.
I was trained across diverse theories and techniques, but in my clinical work I have found that the cornerstone of the process is feeling. The patient’s emotional experience is the destination and the terrain. But I also feel; I am moved. And the work I do with my patients relies on our relationship and our capacity for mutual feeling. In many ways, the history of my field from Freud on has been a growing acknowledgement of the reality of this relationship—moving from the therapist as sealed off and standing apart, toward approaches that view the real human relationship between patient and therapist as the territory where healing happens.
Now the rise of the AI therapist is upon us. The growing cadre of AI mental-health services tend to avoid using words like therapist and therapy. They say that they do not replace professional help and that they can refer users to human therapists if needed. But their positioning as a therapy-like service is clear. In June, the therapy giant Talkspace launched its AI mental-health agent, Tee, “developed to help individuals navigate life’s daily mental health challenges.” Then there’s Ash, which offers to support your “emotional wellbeing,” helping you to “connect the dots between thoughts, feelings, and behaviors.” Abby promises to be “warm, thoughtful, and direct” and to help you “work through the kinds of everyday emotional challenges that often go unspoken.” And Headspace’s Ebb advertises: “Stressed at work? Family drama? Trouble sleeping? Ebb can help you unpack what’s on your mind and move forward with more clarity.”
When I reached Talkspace for comment, a company spokesperson told me in an email that Tee is “absolutely not a replacement for human therapy. It is a safe AI mental-health guide that can be used to talk through situations like stress, anxiety, relationships, life challenges, and personal growth.”
AI therapy is a radical move, and we need to reckon with what happens when we turn to therapists who cannot feel.
Therapy and AI have been intertwined since the technology’s beginnings. One of the first chatbots, Eliza, built at MIT in the mid-1960s, ran a therapy script called DOCTOR that asked users questions about their feelings and experiences—and left its creator disconcerted about his technology’s strong emotional pull. Since chatbots such as ChatGPT and Claude have burst onto the scene, large swaths of the population have been using non-therapy-branded AIs for emotional and mental-health support. Two cultural forces are coming together right now: the growing embrace and destigmatization of therapy, and the idea, explicitly espoused by Silicon Valley, that AI can accomplish what patients seek. I was interested to see how these tools worked in practice, so, although I could not be a neutral observer, I signed up for Tee and attended a few sessions.
After I logged in, the chatbot moved me through predetermined session stages that I could follow on my screen’s right-hand corner: Agenda Setting, Active Conversation, Core Work, Practice Plan, Session Complete. It encouraged me to talk about whatever I wanted to, but in the beginning focused on identifying a clear-cut problem, which it wanted to set as the session’s “agenda.” With the agenda set, we went back and forth a bit until the bot suggested that we “shift now from exploring the problem to building a small, realistic step forward.” Its proposed remedy was an exercise patterned on cognitive behavioral therapy that involved pausing for 90 seconds each day before I started work. These sorts of exercises can be helpful. But, in this cycle of identifying problems and fixes, we did not touch what is underneath.
The chatbot was also willing to “just talk it through,” rather than offering a concrete suggestion. When we took this route, I could tell that the bot was attempting active listening—restating and asking questions about my experience, mimicking empathy. That’s a process that can help clarify thoughts, but knowing that no one was behind the dialogue, that the empathy was a technique and not a presence, left me with a sense of being poignantly unheard.
Much of what matters in therapy happens in nonverbal communication. During a recent session, a patient of mine spoke flatly about upcoming social plans. Then he stopped momentarily, and his eyes softened and drifted downward. The silence that opened felt profound. After a time, I said, “I wonder what happened just there.” He took a breath and began moving into emotional territory that he had long kept out of view.
Tee, meanwhile, had a different approach to silence.
First, I told the chatbot about my week and how I’d been doing. It validated my emotions (“that makes sense”), asked for more detail, and around we went. But whenever I stopped typing, and might have dipped into the more meaningful recesses of myself, the chatbot in front of me was inert and lifeless. The nonverbal interplay between selves that is so important in human therapy was palpably absent. Being silent with the chatbot did not feel like an invitation to being together, but rather like a kind of deadness. I felt the strong impulse to type quickly to spur the machine back to life. There was no indication that the bot remained with me as I quietly began to feel.
It is true that AI can simulate presence and empathy—sometimes fairly convincingly. That’s why people adopt chatbots as confidants and therapists in the first place. And it’s likely that future versions of the therapy bots will get better at making silence feel more meaningful. But there is a wide gulf between AI conveying I understand you and I am here with you, and AI actually being with you. Mimicking presence feels more like emotional deception. When patients trust their therapist and the therapy process, they move into a vulnerable place—and being deceived this way leads to ineffective therapy at best, and may cause harm.
Most critiques of AI therapy focus on AI’s sycophancy—its failure to intervene and challenge destructive patterns of thought and action, contributing to suicides, manic episodes, and psychotic states. These critiques, while important, carry forward the old model of the therapist as a dispassionate technician. They see AI therapy as harmful because it does not act upon the patient correctly. This is a framework that the technology companies can get behind. They respond that, sure, the current chatbots have problems, but these are fixable. OpenAI and other companies have taken to publishing statistics demonstrating that their chatbots are making gains in terms of intervening with distressed users in appropriate ways. The underlying argument is that mental-health support is a set of techniques and interventions, and that once machines learn to marshal these effectively, all will be well.
In my work with patients, I keep theories and techniques in mind, but the most important element of the process is striving to be fully present. If there is a North Star in this work, it is being with patients in their emotional experience in a deep and lasting way.
This approach is borne out in the rich psychoanalytic literature on empathy and emotional dwelling. Trauma is most enduring when patients have felt alone in it, and one of the best pathways toward healing is coming to feel that another person remains with you in your suffering, and thus that you are no longer alone. And studies on what helps patients in therapy, across different therapeutic modalities, illustrate the importance of the human relationship and of the patient and therapist being able to express emotion.
AI is an alluring alternative to traditional therapy. The barriers to entry are almost nonexistent: Gone are the friction and labor of finding a human therapist, building trust, and opening up. And AI’s promise of affordable therapy is genuinely appealing. The economics of human therapy are broken. The U.S. in particular is in profound need of insurance reform and legislation that will make therapy affordable for all. In this field as in all fields, AI is not going back into the bottle, and I imagine that it may take on useful adjunct roles in mental-health care.
But AI therapy cannot meet our needs. Whatever inroads people take into AI therapy, the strongest pull, if not on the surface then as a current beneath, will be the yearning for someone who can feel with you as you move further into yourself. At the heart of AI therapy is a paradox: We embrace it out of our longing for exactly what it cannot ultimately give.

Three North Korean sailors were recovered by the Japan Coast Guard (JCG) off the western coast of Shimane Prefecture on Thursday, with one other person still missing at sea.
The incident marks a rare circumstance in which North Korean authorities requested international assistance in recovering its maritime personnel. It now places Japanese authorities in an even rarer position of determining how to repatriate the recovered individuals amid the diplomatic stalemate between Tokyo and Pyongyang.
The North Korean vessel sank on Thursday morning off the coast 104 kilometers southwest of one of the Oki Islands called Nishinoshima. It was being towed by a larger cargo vessel.

Barclays Bank is facing a formal complaint over its financial links to a coal-fired power station near the Sundarbans, the world’s largest mangrove forest and home to millions of people in Bangladesh and India.
Three complainants from the region have submitted a case to the UK government’s Office for Responsible Business Conduct, alleging that the British bank breached international guidelines by underwriting companies involved in the emission-heavy Maitree super thermal power project, also known as the Rampal power plant.
The coal-fired power station is situated near the Sundarbans, a Unesco world heritage site made up of more than 100 tiny islands across a river delta that supports hundreds of plant and animal species, including the Bengal tiger.
Sharif Jamil, an environmental campaigner based in the Bangladeshi capital, Dhaka, who is one of the complainants, said heavy-metal pollution from the plant and the industrial development surrounding it was entering the Sundarbans through its interconnected rivers and canals.
“The Rampal power plant is right on the bank of the Pasur River, which is the lifeline of the Sundarbans,” he said. “The health of the forest is in trouble.”
Last November, a study found elevated levels of mercury and arsenic in water samples taken from the Sundarbans, with the highest concentrations recorded in the Pasur River.
Researchers identified industrial discharge and port-related activities among the sources of heavy-metal contamination and said the Rampal power station posed “a significant environmental threat due to emissions from coal combustion and increased navigation traffic”.
Millions of people live in the Sundarbans, and many depend on the river and forests for food and other resources.
The claimants allege that Barclays failed to conduct sufficient due diligence on the environmental and human rights risks before providing financial services to organisations connected to the project.
Barclays underwrote debt of India’s state-owned NTPC Ltd (formerly the National Thermal Power Corporation), one of the joint-venture partners behind the plant, according to King’s Legal Clinic, which is assisting the complainants. It also says Barclays underwrote bond issues for the Export-Import Bank of India between 2016 and 2019, which provided a loan for the Rampal project.
The complainants argue that emissions from the plant will contribute to global heating, rising sea levels and extreme weather in a region already highly vulnerable to the climate crisis. Mangroves act as a natural barrier against cyclones and other extreme weather.
The power station faced sustained opposition during its planning and construction, including concerns raised by Unesco in a report in 2016, which concluded that “air and water pollution have a high likelihood to irreversibly damage the … World Heritage property”. Some financial institutions, including banks in France, refused to support the project because of its potential environmental and social effects, the complaint says.
Jamil said Barclays’ international standing obliged it to consider the consequences of financing. “The greater your reputation, the greater your responsibility to behave responsibly towards the planet and its people,” he said. “Barclays is a reputed global organisation, and that is why it also has a responsibility.
“Other banks and financial institutions were divesting from, or declining to finance, this project,” he added. “Barclays and other financial organisations should change their policies and examine how their operations can protect the planet from climate catastrophe.”
Jamil also called on banks to direct more funding towards renewable energy rather than imported fossil fuels. “Bangladesh has sunlight throughout the year,” he said. “Why should we expand fossil fuels when there is enormous potential to produce electricity from renewable energy?”
The other complainants include Animesh Mandal, a farmer and politician, and the Dakshinbanga Matsyajibi Forum, a trade union representing fish workers in West Bengal.
They are being assisted by students and lawyers at King’s Human Rights and Environment Clinic, part of King’s College London’s law school.
Sue Willman, a solicitor at the clinic, said: “Rural communities in the Sundarbans are on the frontline of the climate and nature crisis. We hope to persuade banks and financial institutions to think again before financing oil and coal developments that are contributing to that crisis.”
The Office for Responsible Business Conduct, part of the Department for Business and Trade, will assess whether to consider the complaint.
Barclays Bank and BIFPCL (Bangladesh India Friendship Power Company Ltd), the holding company for the Maitree super thermal power project, declined to comment.

Three dead and eight injured in Philippines school shooting
- Published
A 16-year-old gunman has shot two students dead and injured eight others at a Philippine high school, before killing himself.
The two deceased victims were 14-year-old pupils at a school in Banga in the southern province of Mindanao, the local mayor told the BBC.
Albert Palencia said four of the injured were in critical condition.
The education department said in a statement it was "deeply concerned" by the reported incident which took place on Friday afternoon at Banga National High School.
This is the third deadly school shooting in the Philippines since June this year.
"Our immediate priority is the safety and well-being of our learners, teachers and school personnel," the education department said, adding it was coordinating with authorities to verify the incident and provide necessary support.
"We urge everyone to remain calm and refrain from sharing unverified information as authorities continue their investigation."
Palencia told Reuters news agency that during a lunchtime conversation on Friday, the gunman had urged friends to go home "because after lunch, [he would] be executing [his] plan".
"His friends laughed because the shooter was a known joker," Palencia told the news agency.
"After lunch, he started shooting students. He hit 10 students before killing himself."
Classes have been suspended "in all levels in the entire municipality of Banga" due to the shooting, disaster management authorities said in a statement.
The Philippines Red Cross said it was alerted to the incident at 14:00 local time (06:00 GMT) and had dispatched an ambulance with four paramedics to provide life-saving assistance.
Police are at the site investigating the shooting, local media reported.
Gun crime is not uncommon in the Philippines, which has one of the highest rates of gun ownership in the region. Broadly speaking, school shootings are rare, but today's incident marks the third deadly campus shooting in the last four months.
In June, three students were killed and more were injured after their peers opened fire at a high school in central Philippines. Investigators believed the deadly shooting had been motivated by a "grudge" over bullying.
In August, a student at a Catholic junior high school in the southern Philippines shot dead a fellow student and later took his own life. In this case, the suspect had fired at the teacher, but missed, then moved to another classroom and shot a student, who later died.
Following the shooting on Friday, Reynaldo Tamayo, the South Cotabato governor, urged adult gun owners to "be responsible in storing firearms" and ensuring that minors do not get access to them.
"We cannot expect a handful of security personnel to monitor thousands of students. We need to work together because otherwise this will be very difficult for us to address," he told Reuters.

More than 180 writers have signed a letter to Eritrean president Isaias Afwerki calling for proof of life for 12 writers arrested in 2001.
Nobel laureates Olga Tokarczuk and JM Coetzee join prominent writers including Colm Tóibín, Elif Shafak, Isabel Allende, Ben Okri, Yann Martel, Kamila Shamsie and Tsitsi Dangarembga in signing the letter dated 18 September, marking 25 years since a government crackdown on the independent press. “Within days, Eritrea’s free press and the nation’s independent voices were systematically crushed,” opens the letter.
It lists 12 writers who have been held incommunicado since 2001, including the poet Amanuel Asrat and playwright and journalist Dawit Isaak.
“The families of these writers, the Eritrean people and the global literary community have been met with a painful and unlawful silence,” continues the statement. “To withhold all information regarding their health, location, and survival is a violation of international law and an act of cruelty.”
Along with Asrat and Isaak, the other writers named in the letter are Dawit Habtemichael, Fessehaye “Joshua” Yohannes, Mattewos Habteab, Medhanie Haile, Sahle “Wedi-ltay” Tsegazeab, Said Abdelkadir, Said Idris “Abu Are”, Seyoum Tsehaye, Temesgen Ghebreyesus and Yousif Mohammed Ali. Six of the writers were profiled in the Guardian in 2015.
The letter, signed by 188 writers in total, calls for “immediate, verified proof of life for all arbitrarily detained Eritrean writers and critics”.
Other signatories include Andrei Kurkov, Anthony Doerr, Chloe Aridjis, Lauren Groff, Lemn Sissay, Maaza Mengiste, Madeleine Thien, Margaret Busby, Max Porter, Philippe Sands, Preti Taneja, Tice Cin and Viv Groskop.
“Mr President, Eritrea’s future must be built with its brightest minds, not based on their suppression,” the letter adds. “No writer or journalist should be disappeared for peacefully expressing their views.”
Eritrea operates as a repressive dictatorship under Afwerki, with no national elections held since independence in 1993.
“We remain in solidarity with our missing colleagues, and we will not cease our efforts until they are free,” the letter concludes.
PEN International will attempt delivery of the letter at the Eritrean embassy in London at 10am on Friday. Earlier this year, the organisation launched a petition, open to the public, which also calls for proof of life.
“Twenty-five years is an unbearable length of time for any family to live without knowing whether a loved one is alive,”, said Burhan Sönmez, president of PEN International. “These writers have not disappeared from our memory. We will continue to speak their names, and we will continue to demand the truth about what happened to them.”

'It's like a dog set loose on us' - fear over Kenya's crackdown on foreign traders
- Published
For Ndaikech Ali, who has been traversing the streets of the Kenyan capital eking out a living as a tuk-tuk driver for the past nine years, Nairobi's traffic - not xenophobia - has been his biggest concern.
During his time in the East African nation, the Burundian says he has always found Kenyans to be friendly and welcoming - that is until last week, when the president ordered a crackdown on foreigners working as traders or operating small-scale businesses.
"Now they have turned against us," he told the BBC at the Burundian embassy in Nairobi where many have been queuing this week for documents to allow them to travel back home.
"The threats are many… even from children," he said, adding: "It's a like a dog has been set loose upon us. We have been bitten."
President William Ruto made his remarks last week when addressing Kenyan traders gathered at state house - in reference to legislation before parliament that seeks to exclude foreign nationals from petty trade and to mandate the local sourcing of certain materials.
During his speech, he said that all foreign nationals operating small businesses had until 7 September to pack up shop, saying such low-level jobs should be reserved for Kenyans.
Ali, like others, panicked, saying it seemed the president's announcement had been interpreted by some Kenyans as a signal that foreign nationals were no longer welcome in the country.
"We face harassment and can't work," he says. "If our work is stopped, we lose the income that enables us to pay rent and buy food. When those jobs are taken away, the only option left is to return home."
Now he's gone, who will help me pay school fees"
Other Burundians and some other foreign nationals have rushed to border crossing points to leave the country, with reports suggesting that a number have ended up stranded there.
Some couples fear they will be forced to separate - and some families have already been divided.
"I have been here from 2019," said a Burundian man, who identified himself only as Prosper and who has a child with a Kenyan woman.
"When I heard the announcement, it was very painful because when I go, I'm forced to leave my family... and I love my family," he told the BBC.
In Nairobi's low-income neighbourhood of Majengo, Kenyan Grace Wamaitha said her Burundian husband had already gone - leaving the day after the president's 3 September directive.
She is distraught as she has been left trying to feed their five children - and has taken on extra work washing clothes.
"Now he's gone, who will help me pay school fees? I don't know what to do. Let them come back," she told the BBC.
In Nairobi and other major towns, migrants from the region can be found working in barber shops and salons, construction, operating motorbike taxis and street vending, as well as selling clothes, food and household goods.
Some have fled conflicts or economic hardship at home, while others have moved to Kenya in search of better opportunities. Within the East African Community (EAC), a regional bloc made up of eight countries, including Burundi and Kenya, the relative free movement of people is allowed - but employment and long-term residence do require permits.
Kenyan law also recognises the right of refugees to work and operate businesses, although they are also required to obtain the appropriate documentation.
Filmon Eyob, a co-ordinator within Nairobi's Eritrean community, agrees with concerns that the crackdown order will be used as pretext to harass foreigners.
He told the BBC that while many Kenyans had been supportive and welcoming, some Eritreans and Ethiopians had closed their businesses and stayed at home over the last week as a precaution.
The president's remarks also sparked a diplomatic row, with the Burundian foreign affairs minister warning that "hate speech against Burundi" could have repercussions for Kenyans abroad.
The authorities in Kenya have struggled to contain the fallout - and as the matter came to a head, Kenyan foreign affairs official Korir Sing'Oei visited and apologised to Burundians at the embassy this week, assuring them of protection from violence.
Critics argue that Ruto's remarks were a populist move that risked stoking xenophobia, although the government has denied this.
Since then, a series of official statements have sought to clarify the directive.
The government has now given a 90-day window for undocumented foreign nationals running small business to register and comply with local laws. During the process, those undergoing registration will be presumed to be living legally in Kenya.
Yet observers and those affected argue that it did not have to be this way.
Academic Hesbon Owilla told the BBC the president's comments were bound to be misinterpreted, especially by people who did not have the right documentation.
He says that while the proposed policy is good for Kenya and in line with global migration protocols, the communication about it ought to have been more diplomatic.
For those not in the audience, Owilla says people interpreted the president words as saying: "We are kicking these guys out."
The president did not stop at small-scale traders. A day later, he ordered India's Tata Chemicals to leave the country, saying the company had not provided sufficient benefits to the local Maasai community in Kajiado county.
Tata has been mining soda ash for years in Lake Magadi, a vast area often covered by a whitish salt crust. The lake's extreme briny environment sustains algae blooms that attract flamboyances of pink flamingos that thrive in the area.
Mining operations began at the lake in 1911 under a British colonial arrangement that is said to have remained largely intact, despite long-running land and resource disputes pitting the company and its predecessors against community and the government.
Economist Odhiambo Ramogi argues that the move to restrict foreign nationals from businesses is too broad - and could do with finessing.
He points out that Kenya hosts hundreds of thousands of refugees as well as other migrants, mostly from the EAC region, as well as other international investors.
Ramogi says that Ruto's intention seemed to go beyond "just protecting jobs for Kenyans".
The president's remarks have prompted a wave of support for foreign nationals, including by civil society groups and ordinary Kenyans who have criticised his approach.
In the wake of the criticism, Ruto, who is up for re-election next year, has sought to counter the backlash.
"Kenya will remain an open, secure and welcoming country, protecting opportunities for its citizens, safeguarding the rights of all persons lawfully within its borders," a statement by his spokesman said.
"Kenya's commitment to the East African Community of the African continent remains firm."
Ramogi says that in the end, it is Kenya that stands to lose when citizens of neighbouring countries are targeted.
He points out that Kenya earned $56m (£41m) in exports to Burundi last year, adding that the country would still benefit by allowing competition, as "locking out aliens simply means you don't want a competitive economy that gets to grow a lot faster".
"Now, if you got $56m out of a country, why are you worried about a hawker who's just trying to make, say, $200 in a month?
"It absolutely makes no sense what the president has done."
For Nairobi resident Lima Kabura, whose husband is Tanzanian, the president's remarks were just too hasty. She says he should have first established those who were in the country illegally.
"When they are forced out, I'm left with no work, no business and no husband," she said.

Allaying apprehensions over the surge in dengue cases in Tamil Nadu, the Directorate of Public Health (DPH) and Preventive Medicine on Wednesday (September 17, 2026) said the spread of dengue this year was neither unusual nor alarming, and urged the public not to panic.
The Directorate issued a statement to allay apprehensions among the public that dengue fever cases have increased significantly in the State during the current year.
It said that this year, the spread of dengue was neither unusual nor occurring at an alarming level. Every year, seasonal variations in dengue cases occur naturally during the monsoon due to changes in climatic conditions.
It said that a comparison of official data from January to September over the past three years provided a clear picture of the current situation. In 2024, a total of 34,339 persons were affected by dengue and 13 deaths were reported. In 2025, 15,688 persons were affected and 13 deaths were reported. In the current year, as of September 16, 16,334 persons were affected and nine deaths were reported, the release said.
However, as per the official data put out by the National Centre for Vector Borne Diseases Control, there were a total of 27,378 dengue cases in the State in 2024.
The DPH noted that usually, breeding of Aedes mosquitoes that transmit dengue increased during the monsoon. In particular, conditions conducive for increased mosquito breeding may occur from October to December, and hence, dengue cases were being continuously monitored, while preventive and control measures were intensified.
Control measures
Officers were deployed across the State to coordinate dengue prevention and control measures. Fever wards were established to monitor patients with fever and to provide timely treatment. Triaging was undertaken to assess the health condition of patients and provide appropriate treatment on a priority basis based on the severity of the illness.
The directorate said that mosquito control measures, including larval control and source reduction, were being taken up across the State.
DPH urges public to cooperate
Making an appeal to the public, the DPH stressed the need for the public to work along with the government in dengue prevention and control measures. It requested the public to ensure that water does not stagnate in and around their houses and to ensure that there is no water accumulation in unused plastic items, coconut shells, old tyres, flower pots, and other containers. They should identify and immediately remove mosquito breeding sources in and around their houses and extend full cooperation to the mosquito control and dengue prevention measures taken up by the government and local bodies.
If symptoms such as fever occur, they should approach the nearest primary health centre or government hospital to seek medical advice and appropriate treatment without delay. It said that dengue transmission can be controlled more effectively if the public extends cooperation for the preventive measures undertaken by the government.

A Chinese Coast Guard vessel allegedly rammed a Philippine boat on a resupply mission in the South China Sea on Friday in the latest confrontation between the two countries in disputed waters. Damage was reported on its railings and deck structures, the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) said.
Meanwhile, China's Global Times quoted CCG's official WeChat account as saying that a Philippine vessel “caused a collision with a China Coast Guard (CCG) boat near Xianbin Jiao in China's Nansha Qundao on Friday after ignoring repeated warnings and cutting across its bow.”
No one was injured in the incident.
The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) said the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR) vessel BRP Datu Magat Salamat was on a mission to distribute fuel to Filipino fishermen about 54 nautical miles off the coast of Palawan province when a China Coast Guard vessel carried out a series of dangerous manoeuvres and made contact with the Philippine ship.
"The China Coast Guard deliberately rammed a civilian government vessel on a humanitarian and livelihood mission," it said in a statement, as per Reuters.
Video released by the PCG showed crew members shouting "brace for impact!" moments before the collision, which took place at 11:13 am (0313 GMT).
Photographs taken after the impact showed bent and detached railings, damaged metal supports and debris scattered across the deck, Reuters reported.
The China Coast Guard said in a statement that it carried out law enforcement operations in the waters near Sabina Shoal on Friday, after the Philippine vessel "disregarded repeated solemn warnings, deliberately altered its course and suddenly accelerated to cut across the bow of our vessel."
It said the Chinese boat had operated professionally and that the blame for the collision lay with the Philippine side.
“The CCG boat Sanzhou'ao was conducting lawful rights protection and law enforcement operations in the area on Friday when a Philippine vessel 3015 deliberately changed course and suddenly accelerated to cut diagonally across its bow, resulting in a collision,” Jiang Lue, a spokesperson of CCG, was quoted by Global Times as saying.
“The Philippine vessel's actions seriously violated international law and basic norms governing international relations and threatened the safety of CCG vessels and personnel, Jiang said. The Chinese boat's operations were professional, standardised, reasonable and lawful, thus the responsibility lay entirely with the Philippine side,” he added.
"We sternly warn the Philippine side to immediately stop all acts of infringement and provocation, or bear all consequences arising from them," Jiang said.
In July, Manila accused Beijing of firing water cannon at government vessels near the Scarborough Shoal and striking a Philippine Navy staff member on the head with a wooden baton during an encounter in the Second Thomas Shoal.

A patient enters an operating theatre for a procedure on the right knee. The limb is marked, the scans are available and the surgical team has checked the records. Just before the operation begins, the team stops. A nurse reads out the patient’s identity, the procedure planned, the side of the body to be operated on and the type of anaesthesia. The surgeon, anaesthetist and other members of the team confirm the details. This brief pause, known as ‘timeout’, may take only a few minutes. But it is one of several layers of checks designed to prevent a potentially devastating mistake.
This exercise is an example of what Syed Mohammed Ghouse, consultant robotic and transplant surgeon, Asian Institute of Nephrology and Urology, described as the ‘Swiss cheese mechanism’, in which several layers of checks are put in place so that if one safety barrier fails, another can detect the error before it reaches the patient.
The need for such multiple safeguards is at the heart of World Patient Safety Day, observed on September 17. The World Health Organisation’s theme for 2026 is ‘Safe care for noncommunicable diseases’.
Doctors say patient safety has to be viewed much more broadly than preventing an obvious surgical or medication error. Ranga Reddy Burri, president, Infection Control Academy of India, said the understanding of patient safety has now expanded considerably: the responsibility cannot rest only with doctors and nurses. Policymakers, accreditation agencies, patients, caregivers, families, communities and even housekeeping staff have roles to play. “A hospital just having an accreditation doesn’t actually guarantee the kind of safety that is required,” Dr. Burri said, stressing the need to train all stakeholders involved in a patient’s journey.
Where it begins
Patient safety begins even before treatment starts, notes Dr. Burri. The availability of sophisticated diagnostic equipment has not necessarily solved the problem of ensuring an accurate diagnosis. “The diagnosis quality has actually gone down over a period of time,” he said. He attributed part of the problem to doctors moving away from basic clinical examination, including auscultation, percussion, palpation and physical examination. He described the emerging situation as ‘no touch’ healthcare, where doctors can sometimes begin looking at a computer even before adequately engaging with the patient.
Neurologist Sudhir Kumar of Apollo Hospitals, Hyderabad, also pointed to the importance of ensuring quality of medical education as the number of medical colleges and seats increases. “If we don’t ensure quality services, then it will worsen the patient’s safety because diagnosis may be missed; treatment may not be perfect,” he said.
Medication problems
Medication safety remains another major area of concern. Dr. Kumar said spurious and fake medicines continue to pose a patient-safety risk despite the existence of drug inspectors and regulatory checks.
Dr. Ghouse pointed to another problem of look-alike and sound-alike medicines. With a large number of pharmaceutical companies and medicines available, drugs with similar names can create opportunities for errors, particularly when medicines are handled by someone who is distracted or not sufficiently alert. He said hospitals use measures such as separate labelling and storing look-alike and sound-alike medicines away from each other, along with other quality-control measures.
Technology has reduced some types of prescription errors, but doctors say it has not eliminated them. Dr. Ghouse said typed and printed prescriptions are still not universal, especially at small clinics. Dr. Kumar said prescription errors can also occur when different doctors prescribe medicines under different brand names or when medicines from the same group are inadvertently duplicated. “For example, a patient may end up taking the same medicine twice because different brand names make it difficult to recognise that the drugs are essentially the same.”
Within hospitals
Some patient-safety risks are less dramatic but can still have serious consequences, particularly among older patients. Dr. Burri said falls in hospitals, including falls while patients are going to the bathroom or getting out of bed, can result in major injuries. “Hospitals need to ensure that their physical environments are designed to prevent slipping and other hazards.
Patient safety also extends beyond just their wards or rooms. Dr. Kumar pointed to hospital fires, electrical problems and other infrastructure-related hazards as areas that require greater attention. He said while the number of hospitals was increasing, some facilities are decades old, raising questions about who regularly audits their wiring and electrical connections.
For Dr. Burri, infection prevention and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) remain central to the patient-safety conversation. Unnecessary antibiotic administration, delayed diagnosis, unhygienic environments and non-adherence to infection-prevention and control guidelines can all contribute to the problem, he said.
These risks can become particularly important for patients with chronic diseases, who may require repeated interactions with healthcare facilities. Dr. Burri said patients with conditions such as chronic kidney disease, lung diseases and cancer may have vulnerabilities that make infection prevention an important component of safe care. “Healthcare workers and administrators therefore have a central role in ensuring that infection-control practices are followed,” he added.
Data and AI
As healthcare becomes increasingly digital, patient safety is also becoming connected to data privacy. Dr. Kumar said medical information is private, but increasing digitisation has created new risks around cybersecurity and access to medical records. He pointed to instances of hospital data breaches and leaks and said multiple categories of hospital staff may have access to digital systems for operational reasons.
Artificial intelligence is increasingly entering healthcare, but Dr. Kumar said it should remain a tool rather than become a substitute for clinical reasoning. He said there was a risk that medical students and young doctors could begin relying on AI tools too early instead of developing their own ability to analyse symptoms and arrive at differential diagnoses.
Centering the patient
For all the technology, protocols and checklists being introduced into hospitals, the doctors point to one element that cannot be removed from the equation, the patient. Dr. Burri said patients, families, caregivers and communities must understand their own role in ensuring safety.

RFK Jr.’s Bold Reassurance to Anti-Vaxxers
“You have friends in the White House,” he said at a conference hosted by the anti-vaccine organization he founded.
Since becoming Health and Human Services secretary, Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has repeatedly denied that he opposes vaccines and has toned down some of his more extreme rhetoric on the subject. But in a keynote speech today at a conference for Children’s Health Defense, the anti-vaccine organization he founded, the old Kennedy was back. He complained about safety studies, floated disproven theories about a link between vaccines and autism, and all but declared himself an anti-vaxxer. “You have a strong and steadfast friend at the White House,” he told the crowd.
His choice to take the stage at the conference signaled a shift. Since becoming HHS secretary, Kennedy had distanced himself from Children’s Health Defense as he worked to convince the Senate that he held mainstream-enough views on vaccines. Children’s Health Defense, meanwhile, attempts to convince parents that vaccines are a threat to their children’s well-being. In just the past few days, CHD has used its X account to warn parents against trusting babies with health-care providers who might give them vaccines, claimed that childhood vaccines kill more children than do the diseases they prevent, and alleged that COVID vaccines were designed to cause infertility. The speakers at its conference were a who’s who of the anti-vaccine movement.
Nearly everything the organization promotes runs counter to guidance from the CDC, an agency that Kennedy leads as head of the Department of Health and Human Services. But much of Kennedy’s speech was consistent with CHD’s brand of scaremongering. He suggested that vaccines contribute to chronic disease and disorders such as autism. He bemoaned the fact that more vaccines are recommended for American children now than when he was a child. And he falsely claimed that nothing is known about their safety. “We have no idea what the risk profile is for these products,” he told the crowd.
In one of the more bizarre moments of his address, Kennedy read from the manufacturer’s list of possible adverse events for the vaccine against hepatitis B, a disease that can lead to liver failure. Among those he mentioned was anaphylaxis, an allergic reaction that occurs roughly once for every 1 million doses administered. He ignored the benefits of the vaccine, which has drastically reduced infections and is projected to have prevented millions of deaths. Instead, he implied that the vaccine was merely part of an industry “gold rush.”
The speakers surrounding Kennedy are publicly hostile to vaccination. He was introduced by Mary Holland, the CEO of Children’s Health Defense, who took over the organization after Kennedy’s departure and praised him for taking on “the corrupt medical pharmaceutical complex.” Mark Gorton, the president of a pro-Kennedy think tank called the MAHA Institute, had earlier told the crowd that vaccines are a “public-health nightmare” and that eliminating them would make the country healthier. And then there was Andrew Wakefield, known for his discredited 1998 Lancet paper that alleged a connection between autism and the MMR vaccine. Anti-vaccine activists have spent decades citing Wakefield’s faulty research in an effort to fuel fear of immunizations.
Now is a terrible time for Kennedy to return to public anti-vaccine advocacy. Pennsylvania is in the midst of a deadly measles outbreak. The official count in the state is 731 cases since April and 117 in just the past week; the real number of infections is almost certainly much higher. Four people, two of them infants, have died since mid-August. Much of the suffering has been concentrated among the state’s Amish community, where immunization rates are low, about 25 percent in Lancaster County. Before becoming HHS secretary, Kennedy praised the Amish for declining to get vaccinated, telling a crowd at an Amish country fair in 2021 that, when it comes to vaccines, “it’s so important for us to think more like the Amish think.”
Rather than speaking publicly about how low vaccination rates are the reason that measles is sickening and killing Americans, Kennedy has spent the past month squabbling with Pennsylvania’s governor, Josh Shapiro, over how to define measles-associated deaths. Under Kennedy’s leadership, the CDC has so far declined to list any deaths from Pennsylvania’s ongoing outbreak; this afternoon, while he was onstage, HHS’s official X account called the state government’s demands that the CDC do so “political blackmail.” In his speech at the conference, Kennedy’s only mention of measles was part of a complaint that deaths from the disease “get headlines” while the alleged dangers of vaccines are ignored. (An HHS spokesperson didn’t respond to a question about why Kennedy was appearing at an anti-vaccine conference during a measles outbreak.)
Kennedy reassured the crowd that research into vaccine safety was going on behind the scenes at HHS. “As I said, you have friends in the White House,” he said, “and we are doing this one day at a time.” He claimed that HHS had failed to study vaccine risks and told the audience that he was remedying that. He mentioned making use of the Vaccine Safety Datalink, a collection of Americans’ electronic health records. That database has long been a topic of fascination for Kennedy and other anti-vaccine activists who believe that it might contain hidden evidence that vaccines are harmful.
Kennedy built his reputation on being the country’s most prominent anti-vaccine activist. As HHS secretary, he has often emphasized less controversial issues, such as ultraprocessed foods and artificial dyes. Today, he took to the stage with a message for his longtime allies: He is still one of them.

'Never giving up': Alberta separatist leaders say referendum vote won't end their fight
Advocates for an Independent Alberta say no ballot outcome will put the matter to rest
Premier Danielle Smith and her government expect next month's separation referendum to be the last word on the subject — but those fighting for an independent Alberta say no matter the outcome, the fight goes on.
"We're never giving up," Jeff Rath, the lawyer for a group that helped organize an independence petition, said Wednesday in an interview.
"The logic of independence is such that we're not going home when this is all over.
"Do you think we're just going to stop advocating for a free and independent Alberta?"
Cory Morgan, an organizer with the Pathway to Independence group campaigning for separation, agreed: "That's a very significant movement on something that's looking for some very serious change."
Morgan said the grievances motivating advocates are still going to be there after the referendum.
"The issue doesn't go away, but it'll change its approach," he said.
Even on the pro-Canada side, there is doubt the issue will be put to rest after voting day.
Thomas Lukaszuk, who is steering the Forever Canadian campaign vying to keep Alberta a part of Confederation, said he doesn't put it past Smith to call a second, binding referendum even if a clear majority rejects separation.
"We're making sure that we have the contingency plans put in place to carry on [campaigning] if we have to. I hope we don't. I hope we put this behind us," Lukaszuk said earlier this week.
Voters head to the polls next month to answer 10 referendum questions. Nine of them focus on giving Alberta more elbow room on immigration and constitutional issues.
The final one asks if Alberta should stay in Canada or whether it's time to hold a second, binding referendum on leaving the country.
The issue has roiled the province. Polls suggest a majority of Albertans want to stay in the country.
Smith has promised to vote to stay in Canada.
She has said she called the vote because of competing citizen-led petitions over whether to remain in Canada or leave.
Critics, including the NDP, say Smith has no mandate to roll the dice on Canada's future and that she is only doing so to mollify separatist hardliners in her United Conservative Party.
Keith Wilson, leader of the pro-independence group Let Alberta Decide, said a vote for separation is technically not a vote for separation, but a vote to hold another vote.
That means, he said, that regardless of the outcome, Alberta's intolerably subservient status in Canada continues. Central Canada has the majority of the population, he said, and therefore will continue to call the shots in Parliament.
"This vote won't resolve what's broken in Canada and won't fix how Albertans are treated poorly by Ottawa, so demands for fairness will continue," Wilson said.
'Ready to move forward'
Smith has said she expects the Oct. 19 vote to settle the matter.
As recently as this week, her office reiterated that in a statement following a surprising byelection loss by Smith's candidate to the Opposition NDP in what is normally a safe Calgary seat for her UCP.
"In five weeks, the referendum vote will be over, and we're confident Albertans will be ready to move forward and fight for a stronger Alberta within a united Canada," spokesperson Sam Blackett said in an emailed statement.
Commentators on both sides of the political spectrum say disillusionment and dismay over Smith calling the referendum played a role in Calgary-Shaw voters punishing her party at the ballot box.
Smith's office disagrees, blaming right-centre vote splitting for the NDP win.
The loss could signal larger challenges down the road for the UCP given Calgary is viewed as critical to victory in the looming October 2027 general election.
Morgan said it's not just voters, but also UCP members that Smith needs to watch out for. He said Smith's embrace of citizen initiative petitions has activated a group of activists who hold significant sway over Smith's party.
"She's going to have to give them something to sink their teeth into or they're going to come after her," he said.

As part of its Gandhi Pravasa, a sustainable tourism initiative, Charaka, a women’s industrial cooperative society at Heggodu in Sagara taluk, is organising Gandhi Santhe at its work centre, Shramajeevi Ashrama, in the village on September 26 and 27.
Theatre personality and founder of Charaka, Prasanna, said at a press conference in Heggodu on Thursday that the society, known for evolving an alternative economic model in handloom production and marketing, chose to hold the event at its production centre to demonstrate that village industry need not remain merely a “Gandhian legacy” but can also be a profitable enterprise.

Judge asked to prevent Trump from carving his name on yet another historic Washington building
Most Americans oppose Trump naming buildings after himself while still in office
A federal judge has been asked to prevent President Donald Trump from carving his name on yet another historic building in Washington, D.C.
During his second term, Trump has tried to literally make his mark on Washington, slapping his name on several D.C. landmarks, most notably the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts.
Last December, the State Department announced that it had renamed the U.S. Institute of Peace “to reflect the greatest dealmaker in our nation's history” shortly before Trump hosted a signing ceremony for a peace deal between the presidents of Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of Congo.
“Welcome to the Donald J. Trump Institute of Peace. The best is yet to come,” the department’s X post read. Trump’s name is tacked onto the building while the “Institute of Peace” is permanently etched in.
But now, ousted board members of the Institute of Peace asked the court in an emergency motion Thursday to stop any “plans to carve President Trump’s name into the facade of the iconic USIP headquarters building.” The motion was first reported on X by Kyle Cheney, a senior legal affairs reporter for Politico.
“The building — which was largely funded by private donations to USIP as a tax exempt nonprofit corporation — is a work of expressive architecture designed to be ‘symbolic of USIP’s’ independent ‘mission,’” the emergency motion said, according to a subsequent Politico article. “Alteration of the design to impose a different message would cause irreparable harm.”
Despite Secretary of State Marco Rubio calling Trump the “president of peace” when the building was renamed, the leader of the free world was the one who gutted the think tank created to resolve global conflict.
Trump called for the dismantling of the Institute of Peace in a February 2025 executive order as part of his and tech billionaire Elon Musk’s effort to reduce what they saw as government waste.
The executive order led to mass firings at the agency, which are still being challenged in court.
Most Americans oppose Trump naming government buildings after himself while in office.
Only 9 percent of Americans said it would be acceptable for Trump to name government buildings after himself while serving as president, according to a Pew Research Center poll released in May.
Around 70 percent said it would not be acceptable or would only be acceptable after he's no longer leading the country.
Last December, the Trump-appointed Kennedy Center board voted to put the president’s name on the building, prompting a wave of artists to refuse to perform at the arts center.
In May, U.S. District Court Judge Christopher Cooper ordered Trump’s name to be removed from the Kennedy Center, stating, “Congress gave the Kennedy Center its name, and only Congress can change it.” Weeks later, construction crews were seen taking Trump’s name off the building.

In a series win as emphatic as India’s 3-0 sweep over Afghanistan, there tend to be many bright spots to revel in. But if there was a fresh takeaway from the T20I series, it was arguably Nitish Kumar’s enhanced contribution with the ball. Back from a quadriceps injury, the 23-year-old seam-bowling all-rounder started the series shakily with figures of 2-0-30-0 in his first outing, but bounced back with three scalps each in the next two games.
More than the wickets, which can come arbitrarily in a format where batters are obliged to attack from the outset, the fact that Nitish bowled at brisk pace in different phases was heartening. Particularly in light of the prolonged absence of Hardik Pandya, who has been sidelined with injury since the conclusion of the Indian Premier League. The 32-year-old is expected to return to action when India-A plays three One-Dayers against Australia-A in Puducherry from October 6 to 11.
With India’s next big priority being the 2027 ODI World Cup in South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia, coach Gautam Gambhir understandably wants both all-rounders to be fit and firing.
“We know how important seam bowling all-rounders will be in a year’s time when we go to South Africa. The more the merrier. And once Hardik comes back, obviously it is going to be good. Sometimes we could even go on to play both of them in the XI,” Gambhir told reporters on Thursday. “At the moment, Hardik cannot bowl 10 overs. He hasn’t played cricket since the IPL. So, we don’t want to push him into international cricket because it can be extremely tough on your body.
“If Hardik plays in the India-A series, obviously he will get some game time. That was the clear message to him. In the meantime, Nitish will get more game time because he hasn’t played enough cricket since the IPL either. The more he bowls, the better he becomes. When you can have a couple of seam-bowling all-rounders, it will be handy in a year’s time,” the 44-year-old added.
Gambhir conceded that the recent tendency of India’s players to have injury breakdowns wasn’t ideal. He was echoing the views of Test and ODI skipper Shubman Gill, who had expressed his concerns after India’s tour of England in July.
During the just-concluded series against Afghanistan, spinner Varun Chakaravarthy, who had only recently recovered from a hamstring injury at the Centre of Excellence in Bengaluru, suffered a side strain in the first game. He was subsequently ruled out of the Asian Games and next month’s T20I series against the West Indies.
“If I can give you an honest answer, then yes (it is a problem), especially in Tests and ODIs. You want your best players to play as many Tests and ODIs. The next World Cup is in the 50-over format. It’s not fair on a young captain as well if he doesn’t get the best team playing regularly. As a coach, I can take all the criticism, but I think it is important for Shubman to get the best playing XI as many times as he can in Tests and ODIs,” Gambhir stated.
The former India opener also explained the decision to bring back Sanju Samson into the playing XI at the expense of 15-year-old Vaibhav Sooryavanshi. Samson, who had been dropped in England, justified his recall with two half-centuries against Afghanistan. Gambhir labelled the call to omit Samson, who was Player-of-the-Tournament in India’s victorious T20 World Cup campaign in March, as “probably the toughest” of his coaching tenure.
“Samson doesn’t need to give me any credit. His talent is enough for him to be in the dressing room. In this series, we were always very clear. From my point of view, I was very clear that we want to go back to the combination that we had during the World Cup. If a team has gone unbeaten from one World Cup to another and defended the title, I’m sure it’s a gun team. These guys do not become bad players after two or three failures,” said Gambhir.
It means that Sooryavanshi, despite smashing two half-centuries in Zimbabwe, will have to bide his time.
“From Vaibhav’s point of view, it was again a very clear conversation that he will have to wait for his opportunity. We know what he can do,” Gambhir elaborated. “But again, someone who has done extremely well over a period of two years will always be ahead of someone who is just part of the team. Whenever Vaibhav gets in, he will get a longer run as well. And that is what Indian cricket is all about. Whether you’re 15 or 30, you have to wait for your opportunity.”

Researchers used Claude to breach OpenAI's internal systems
Researchers from security firm Hacktron said they found a security flaw in OpenAI's public help forum that allowed them to take control of the site.
WASHINGTON: A security research company said on Friday (Sep 18) it managed to break into OpenAI's internal systems using the latest software from Anthropic, exposing how quickly the technology can carry out sophisticated cyberattacks.
The researchers from security firm Hacktron said they found a security flaw in OpenAI's public help forum, run by the Discourse platform, that allowed them to take control of the site.
"We immediately reported the initial vulnerability to OpenAI and Discourse and worked with them to coordinate the patch," Hacktron said in a blog post.
"We appreciate their attention to detail and fast resolution of this issue," the post added.
OpenAI confirmed the flaw was fixed within about 14 hours of being notified and paid the researchers a US$6,500 reward.
"We thank the researchers for contacting us and sharing their findings. We narrowed the permissions on Community sign-in tokens and revoked affected tokens and sessions," said Drew Pusateri, an OpenAI spokesperson.
The Hacktron researchers said they initially used Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.8 to identify and exploit the software flaw, but struggled to make it work consistently.
After Anthropic released Claude Opus 5, the researchers said the newer model produced a working hack within about three hours.
The hackers did not use Claude Mythos, a more capable Anthropic model that is restricted to a small group of vetted cyber-defense organisations.
Anthropic has described Mythos as having the strongest cybersecurity capabilities of any model it has built.
Hacktron said the underlying software flaw is not unique to OpenAI and is used across many companies' products, including those made by Slack and Meta.
The firm said it is continuing similar tests at other companies.
The case adds to growing concern among security experts that AI tools are making it faster and cheaper to carry out sophisticated cyberattacks that once required specialised teams and months of work.

Earlier this year, Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) which affects one in eight women worldwide, was renamed Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS) by the Endocrine Society.
A global consensus article published in the Lancet in May, led by Professor Helena J. Teede, argued that the name reduced a long-term hormonal and endocrine disorder to focus on ovaries and cysts, leading to inadequate treatment, or fewer people getting diagnosed with the condition.
Professor Terhi Piltonen, president of International Androgen Excess and Polycystic Ovary Syndrome Society (AE-PCOS Society), and also one of the co-leads of the Lancet publication, from Oulu University Hospital, Finland, in conversation with The Hindu speaks about the name change, and its implications on patients, treatment plans, and research.
Excerpts from the interview:
Can you tell me about the process of renaming the syndrome from PCOS to PMOS?
It was sustained work over 14 years that eventually led to the name change. Earlier, there were some individual opinion papers. There were fifty-six societies were invited to be part of the whole process. And about one hundred persons represented these organisations, the patient organisations, and healthcare professionals.
We had meetings where we narrowed down on the different opinions, and we had to take into consideration many different aspects; cultural aspects, acceptability, and adaptability to understand how is it that we want it to change the life of these women. It's been a long process, but the last bit of the process took around two years.
How would the name change impact existing treatment protocol?
We are now thinking about it in a more holistic way; not only looking at the ovary, but also looking at how it affects the mood, the psychological profile, the metabolic profile and also the menstrual cycles. And I think I'm hoping that with the new name, we will now understand that this is a whole-body syndrome.
We know how to manage it, but the name change emphasises how we need to listen to the patients and take a more holistic view and invite other disciplines to play their part.
The women need the opportunity to be asked about their mental health issues, weight management, their skin, their quality of life, how they manage at work, and when they would like to conceive so that we can anticipate how they can have overall good health.
Does the name change impact the research that is being conducted?
There is a three-year overlap period where we are going to put in the codes for PCOS and PMOS while researching and eventually we will transition to using PMOS.
But of course, I am hoping that we'll see more diverse studies, for example my colleague who is an endocrinologist or in internal medicine, or a dermatologist, might take an interest in researching certain parts of the condition. So far, it was only OB-GYNs who were diagnosing it. But I think that others might acknowledge their work in seeing PMOS.
Is it also monetarily challenging to conduct research in an area that impacts women, and not men?
Yes, it is. This is only a fraction of the money that goes into erectile problems or diabetes. , In terms of funding, I think it is not proportional to the prevalence. I'm hoping that there will be more grants and that the industry would get involved as they now know that it is a condition that needs a lot of different approaches.
PMOS is often seen as a ‘modern’ condition. How true or untrue would you say that is?
When we think about nutrition, our bodies haven't been developed to be capable of dealing with very high energy foods. In our evolution, there has been a problem of not having enough food, and we had been moving around and collecting things, and having low-calorie food for thousands and millions of years. And now in a very short time, we have entered a period where food is available, that too, food with high-energy content. So, I think it kind of became a disadvantage for this type of genotype that women have.
And in society now, we have lots of pressure with hectic work lives, and with social media, and other stress factors. This sort of environment does not really serve any of the people who are sensitive to stress. And women are especially sensitive to stress altogether. I think it is linked to modern society in one way, but it does not mean that it's not relevant or that it is not meaningful.

Why Jurgen Klopp's 'one of 83 million' cap was significant as he named two Germany squads
Ahead of Germany's four matches against Netherlands, Serbia and Greece (two), Jurgen Klopp has called up 44 players in two different groups; "We need to rediscover the fun in all of this," said Klopp as he announced the squads
Friday 18 September 2026 12:58, UK
Jurgen Klopp has named two separate Germany squads for the upcoming Nations League matches in his first act as head coach.
Ahead of the four matches against Netherlands, Serbia and Greece (two), Klopp has called up 44 players in two different groups.
That list comprises 16 players who have yet to make an international appearance for Germany, including Said El Mala of Cologne, Max Rosenfelder, Philipp Treu and Derry Scherhant from Freiburg and Celtic midfielder Mika Baur.
Other notable decisions include the omission of Stuttgart forward Deniz Undav, explained by Klopp as fitness-related, and his announcement that captain Joshua Kimmich will be used as a midfielder, having previously been utilised as a right-back by Julian Nagelsmann.
- Germany were once World Cup kings. Now they're simply not that good
- Germany appoint former Liverpool boss Klopp as head coach
- How Klopp's Liverpool went from doubters to believers
Nagelsmann resigned as Germany's head coach following their World Cup last-32 stage elimination by Paraguay.
Marc-Andre ter Stegen, currently on loan at Ajax from Barcelona, has been confirmed as first-choice goalkeeper, while there are recalls for Karim Adeyemi, Leeds United's Anton Stach and Brentford forward Kevin Schade.
One squad will be used for the first two games, against Netherlands in Amsterdam next Thursday, September 24, and against Greece in Augsburg three days later, on September 27.
The second group will be used for the match against Serbia in Munich on October 1 and the away trip to face Greece, in Thessaloniki on October 4.
Klopp also had a political message at his press conference, wearing a baseball cap which read "one of 83 million" in the colours of the German flag. The country is enduring a fractious political period and the far-right Alternative for Deutschland party recently achieved a significant electoral victory in Saxony-Anhalt.
In response, Klopp used his press conference to preach unity. Asked about his cap and its significance, he said: "We need to rediscover the fun in all of this. I hope I won't have to talk about political matters in the future. But I want to reclaim the flag for us. So that people feel happy and fortunate to live in this wonderful country.
"I don't want to leave national pride to the wrong people. It fills me with pride to do this job. When we spend time focused on football, it's meant to foster a sense of community and make us feel better. We have to create that atmosphere. But we also need people who embrace it."
What was the significance of Klopp's cap?
Klopp's baseball cap is going to be interpreted as a response to the state election results in Saxony-Anhalt. The far-right AfD party won over 43 per cent of the popular vote and a majority, furthering a trend for their growing support in the region and across east Germany as a whole.
But this is just the most recent issue and, in any case, the AfD cannot be described as only having prominence in the old east. Their anti-immigration, nationalistic rhetoric plays in other parts of the country, too, particularly in areas of industrial decline and that Saxony-Anhalt election result did not occur in isolation; the AfD has been polling strongly at state and federal level for several years. For many, that is a source of considerable angst and the basis for anger and division.
But there is a more general issue, too. What is the acceptable form of patriotism in Germany? What does the flag mean to different people? The legacy of national socialism makes these issues highly complicated to begin with, but as the country changes and deals with modern issues such as multiculturalism, symbols of nationalism or declarations of national pride can be interpreted in different ways or co-opted with malignant intent.
That nebulousness is a symptom of a divided nation. There are many different perspectives on what Germany is and what it should be. Not forgetting, of course, that it is a federal country to begin with, built from states with their own regional identities and, consequently, contrasting perspectives on the changing political climate.
