Furniture and appliance rental startup RentoMojo made a strong stock market debut, with its shares listing at a premium of nearly 19% over the IPO issue price. The stock listed at ₹482.45 on the NSE, a premium of 19.42% over its issue price of ₹404. On the BSE, RentoMojo opened at ₹480, up 18.81% from the issue price. The shares gained further following the listing and touched a high of ₹500 on the BSE. At 10:10 IST, the stock was trading at ₹500, up 23.76% over the issue price and 4.15% from its BSE opening price. The company’s market capitalisation stood at ₹5,205.74 Cr ($543 Mn). This was about 30% higher than the valuation of approximately ₹4,006 Cr sought by the startup at the upper end of its IPO price band of ₹384-₹404. The strong listing followed robust demand for RentoMojo’s ₹1,256 Cr IPO, which closed with an overall subscription of 72.88X. Ahead of the public issue, RentoMojo raised ₹376.1 Cr from 41 anchor investors by allotting 93.1 Lakh shares at ₹404 apiece. RentoMojo’s public issue comprised a fresh issue worth ₹150 Cr and an OFS of up to 2.74 Cr shares worth ₹1,105.6 Cr. The OFS delivered sizeable cash-outs for RentoMojo’s early investors. Accel India pocketed around ₹317 Cr by selling 78.47 Lakh shares, clocking an 8.6X gross return. Cofounder and CEO Geetansh Bamania received ₹34.31 Cr from selling 8.49 Lakh shares. Meanwhile, Rajeev Chitrabhanu HUF and Nazara Technologies founder Nitish Mittersain recorded gross returns of 265.97X and 152.45X, respectively, on the shares they sold through the OFS. Accel, Edelweiss and ValueQuest retained substantial stakes in RentoMojo following the IPO, while IDG Ventures India Fund III, GMO Payment Gateway, GMO GFF and some other shareholders exited the startup completely. Founded in 2014 by Bamania and Ajay Nain, RentoMojo operates a subscription-based platform for renting furniture, appliances and other household products. As of March 2026, the startup had about 2.5 Lakh live subscribers and 8.5 Lakh live items across its furniture and appliance portfolio. RentoMojo’s operating revenue jumped 45.5% to ₹387 Cr in FY26 from ₹266 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Its profit after tax surged nearly 142% YoY to ₹104.3 Cr, although this included a tax credit of ₹36.6 Cr. The company’s EBITDA rose 38% YoY to ₹163.5 Cr in FY26, while its EBITDA margin narrowed to 41.5% from 43.6%. It generated around ₹170 Cr in operating cash flow during the year, while incremental capital expenditure stood at about ₹175 Cr as the startup expanded its rental inventory. RentoMojo competes with the likes of Furlenco, Rentickle and Cityfurnish. With its market debut, RentoMojo has become India’s first listed furniture and appliance rental startup.

As Carney's popularity soars, Conservatives weigh what to do about their own leader
Sources say there is no strong appetite to oust Pierre Poilievre
A number of Conservative MPs have soured on Pierre Poilievre as leader, but despite this growing angst, his position is relatively secure because there is no strong appetite to oust him and choose someone new right now, according to party and caucus sources who spoke to CBC News.
Last year, Poilievre was on the cusp of leading his party to the largest Conservative government in a generation only to fall short when the Liberals replaced an unpopular incumbent with a leader offering a new vision.
He has struggled to recover ever since, facing accusations from some critics that he's yesterday's man, and poorly placed to deal with the issue of our time: an increasingly hostile U.S. government determined to wreck Canada economically.
Poilievre earned plaudits for a series of pro-Canada interviews on U.S. television last week, but he hasn't said if he supports the government's retaliatory tariffs on American products. He says he wants to wait for an "analysis" of the expected economic costs before taking a position.
His lines about this fight have largely focused on trying to cajole the government to bring Parliament back sooner than planned and reveal a failed trade deal that negotiators say is protected by confidentiality clauses.
Sources speaking to CBC News on the sidelines of the party's caucus retreat in Penticton, B.C., describe caucus morale as low because the U.S. dispute dominates the news cycle, putting their leader and the team at a disadvantage.
One MP said Canadians simply "don't want to hear from us right now," and their relevance is in question.
Poilievre has made a career out of fiercely opposing Liberal policies he says have ruined this country. That sort of rhetoric doesn't sell as well as it used to given the current patriotic climate, this MP said.
CBC News has agreed not to name the sources so they can speak freely about internal dynamics.
But at least one MP, Jamil Jivani, who has said Canadians have thrown "an anti-America hissy fit" and that the government is overreacting to the trade war, publicly suggested he wants his leader to take a harder line.
- As Poilievre tours U.S., Conservative MP bemoans lack of 'alternative to the Liberals'
- Conservatives seek relevance, unity in B.C. gathering ahead of Parliament's return
During Poilievre's U.S. media tour, which was largely deferential to Carney, Jivani, a close friend of Vice-President JD Vance, said: "You have people who should be offering an alternative to the Liberals instead going out there to appease people in positions of power."
In this context, the party's poll numbers have fallen further. The recent performance in federal byelections — losing one seat and considerable support in two others — has only increased the sense of doom among some Conservatives.
"I think you have to be quite honest, this is not the position that we want to be in at this juncture — there’s no question about that," Conservative deputy leader Melissa Lantsman told reporters after meeting with her caucus mates in the B.C. interior.
Lantsman said that given the underperformance, the party will make some "changes" to the Conservative playbook this fall.
What's unlikely to change is the leader. While some MPs say behind closed doors that they are decidedly done with Poilievre, most don't want to take the next step and trigger a Reform Act ousting, like the one parliamentarians used to remove the last leader, Erin O'Toole, sources said.
Such a move could split the party, as some of the more stridently populist members might revolt against what could be perceived as an elite-driven coup, said one MP.
Conservative MP Michael Barrett said the party base strongly supported Poilievre at his leadership review in January — Poilievre won a commanding 88 per cent of the vote — so the caucus will stick with him.
When asked if Poilievre is the best person to lead the party right now, Barrett deferred to the grassroots.
"The Conservative membership made a very strong decision this year for Mr. Poilievre to lead our party. And that's the direction that we've taken," he said in an interview.
Two senior Conservatives said replacing Poilievre now would just needlessly burn through another leader given the perception that the Liberals would likely win if there's another election sometime soon.
These Conservatives posited that it's better to let Poilievre lead the party into another election, potentially lose and then resign to trigger a new leadership process. That would be less divisive than trying to remove a leader who has a strong and vocal online following, especially one who sailed through a recent leadership review, these sources said.
Another ex-campaign staffer close to Poilievre said even if a Reform Act ouster prompted the leadership selection process, Poilievre could always run again and win — given few people have expressed serious interest in the job.
While he came up short, Poilievre did lead his party to a respectable showing in the last campaign, taking 41 per cent of the vote and 144 seats, a figure that has since been whittled down by floor-crossings and defections.
Poilievre could reassure skeptical members that while things aren't looking good now, they can change on a dime in politics, this ex-campaign staffer said.
Plus, given the divisions in caucus over how to handle the U.S., as well as other longstanding divides on social issues, Poilievre is best placed to hold this disparate group together, the staffer said.
Chad Rogers, a longtime Conservative and a partner at the public affairs firm Crestview Strategy, said all is not lost for Poilievre.
Rogers said he is old enough to remember when some pundits claimed former prime minister Paul Martin would win a "super majority" in 2004, leaving the unpopular Stephen Harper on the Opposition benches for years.
That never panned out — Martin limped to a minority, and Harper eventually won and governed for nearly a decade.
Carney's aura could also wear off as it did for that Liberal leader some 20 years ago, Rogers said. Poilievre is struggling to punch through now, but that might not always be the case, he said.
He said Poilievre's plan to go all-in on affordability concerns during this fall sitting of Parliament could bear fruit, given that voters consistently tell pollsters it's a major issue for them.
"I don't know that I would want to be an incumbent premier or prime minister anywhere in Canada with the inflation numbers, the debt numbers. There are a number of bills soon coming due to pay," he said.
"I think as a Conservative, I have a medium-term optimism that Canadians are about to hire us back to clean up the economy."
MP Michelle Rempel Garner said Poilievre's understanding of what average Canadians are going through in an economy wracked by higher prices makes him a good leader for this moment.
"I'm proud to serve under his leadership this fall," she said.

Across medicine, doctors are increasingly using artificial intelligence models to predict patient risk, from sepsis to falls to death. Often embedded directly into electronic health records, these predictions can be easy to incorporate into care — and their performance can be easily taken for granted.
James Deardorff, a geriatrician and assistant professor in the division of geriatrics at the University of California San Francisco, has developed several models that aim to make predictions for older adults, from mortality to the need for nursing home care. In geriatrics, he says, it’s important for clinicians to be aware of both the performance of an algorithm — including in subgroups like older patients — and how to responsibly use its output.
This month, Deardorff penned a commentary on a large analysis of Epic’s proprietary end-of-life prediction model published in JAMA Network Open, highlighting how a model can contribute to a poor outcome even if it’s accurate. If a patient’s one-year mortality prediction is used to prompt an open-ended conversation about the goals of care, he and his co-author wrote, there are few downsides. But if it’s used to inform a higher-stakes decision like transplant priority, the impacts could be profound.

“The hardest day on Obsession was the easiest day on Anything But Ghosts.”
Curry Barker shared with us the following earlier last weekend at Deadline’s TIFF DGA panel about his next horror movie with Focus Features and Blumhouse Atomic Monster.
Unlike his half-billion grossing Obsession, Barker says that on Anything But Ghosts, “We had a 130-page script and we had 26 days to shoot it. I’m also starring in it and directing and I’m the lead character. I have more lines than anyone in the movie.”
Talk about stress.
Watch on Deadline
“Zach Kregger just told me, ‘You have to cut 30 pages’ and I probably should have listened to him. So, did my manager; he told me that, too.”
“But I didn’t cut a single page because I wanted to shoot all of it,” says Barker who was at TIFF for the one-year anniversary of the Obsession premiere, “It was the hardest thing I’ve ever done and we were compromising shots left and right off the shot list. Gone. Just like coverage was going out the windows. It was crazy.”
Barker also spoke to us about how he cracked the idea for Obsession, a movie that has pulled in everyone from Gen Z to their ’50s, with couples leaving the cinema and either taking Bear (Michael Johnston) or Nikki’s (Inde Navarrette) side.
“I think it’s really interesting that we as humans can fixate and obsess over something. And turning that into a place of danger and horror was really interesting to me,” he said.
	
“I had already had this idea for a while of maybe a woman obsessed with a man or a man obsessed with a woman. And I actually hadn’t cracked exactly how I wanted to, like, figure that out. And then once I figured out the wish element of it, I was like, oh my God, my obsession idea. I could make it like a wish gone wrong thing.”
“I discovered that when I watched some of these wish gone wrong movies nobody really talked about how uncomfortable it is. Some of these wishes — what would it actually be like if you wished for someone to love you back, would it be them actually loving you? Or would it be an entity that loves you and what does that actually look like? And how does a person respond to that?”
Still the half billion success has shocked the director.
“I knew that there was going to be parts that were relatable, because I always told Inde to play it like a real person and not to play into this possessed demon, but to just play it as a jealous girlfriend.”
And the response he’s gotten?
“Sometimes people are like, ‘Dude, this is just like my girlfriend.’ I’m like, ‘Which part?’ They’re like, ‘The whole movie!'”
As far as one of the boldest directs he pulled off on the set of the $750K costing Obsession, was that Barker only had one take for the scene where Nikki bashes her head through the car window. The first prop window shattered in the art department’s hands because “it’s made of candy,” says Barker.
“We literally just had one piece of glass. I was like, ‘Alright, Inde, you got to ram your head into this window!'”
“That was crazy. If that didn’t work out, we would have actually been screwed for the day and we didn’t have the budget to come back the next day.”
Anything But Ghosts was also written by Barker. He costars with longtime collaborator and Obsession star Cooper Tomlinson. The movie follows ghosthunters who are hucksters. Barker has said that the pic takes place in the same universe as Obsession. Aaron Paul and Bryce Dallas Howard co-star. The movie doesn’t have a release date yet.

Will even one of the U.N.'s 17 'sustainable development goals' be met by 2030?
By any standards, it was an eye-popping to-do list.
No poverty. Zero hunger. Quality education for all. Gender equality. Clean water and sanitation. Reduced inequalities. Peace, justice and strong Institutions.
In September 2015, these were just some of the 17 goals that global leaders set for themselves to accomplish in the next fifteen years. The United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals, broken down into 169 targets, were meant to transform the world by 2030.
A decade later, that deadline is closing in, but the world is nowhere near achieving much of what it promised. According to the U.N.'slatest assessment report"
- Just 15% of the targets for which sufficient data are available are on track.
- 21% are making moderate progress
- 32% are making marginal progress
- 17% are stagnant.
- And 15% have alarmingly slipped far below where they stood in 2015.
These numbers raise big questions. Were these goals just too unrealistic and ambitious in the first place? Can the world expect to tick some of those boxes before the deadline? And if none of the goals are met, is the enterprise a failure?
While none of the SDGs goals are literally impossible to achieve, many require rates of progress that would be "historically unprecedented" — far beyond what even the fastest-improving countries have previously achieved, says Charles Kenny, senior fellow at the Center for Global Development, a think-tank in Washington, D.C. "In order to meet them, we'd have to see incredibly dramatic global policy change," he says.
Zero poverty, for instance, is a great goal to have, he says. "There is no moral excuse for [extreme poverty] at all. On the other hand, given the global system and political realities, the idea that we were going to get to zero by 2030 was really optimistic."
There's no point in blaming the goal, experts say, when the actions of the global community don't match up. "I don't want to let governments off the hook," Kenny says. "These SDGs were agreements between the planet's leaders." But he points out: "the heads of countries that signed these goals then went back home and didn't do any of the things that might have helped speed it up."
Wealthier countries could have accelerated progress by increasing development aid, expanding trade opportunities, increasing private investment in poorer countries, and allowing greater migration, Kenny says. Instead, several of these trends have either stalled or moved in the opposite direction.
But Kenny cautions that judging progress solely by whether countries are on track to meet those ambitious targets can obscure how much has actually changed. "One of the problems with setting really ambitious goals is you can be off track and yet making big progress," he says.
What's working?
This is especially true with some of the health goals, says Thoai Ngo, Professor and Chair of Population and Family Health at Columbia Mailman School of Public Health, New York. "We do continue to see child mortality fall year after year, and life expectancy increase. We see more and more kids going to school. There is a lot of progress," he says.
Some goals, such as gender equality, have had a domino effect, says Ngo. "We've managed to keep more girls in school, which has helped prevent child marriage and has improved the health of women in general."
"In my view, the goals worked where money, technology and political will lined up," says Paul Spiegel, director of the Johns Hopkins Center for Humanitarian Health. Since 2015, he notes, roughly a billion people have gained access to safe drinking water, and 1.2 billion have decent sanitation. Electricity now reaches 92% of the world and 74% are connected to the internet. New HIV infections have fallen by 30%, and AIDS-related deaths by 35%. The proportion of births attended by a trained health professional is on track to reach 90%. "For the first time, more than half of humanity has some form of social protection [such as a pension, cash assistance, maternity or disability benefits, unemployment support or health coverage]," he says.
The goals have provided a universal direction of where we want to get, they have inspired new partnerships and collaborations among different sectors, they have facilitated data collection and measurement, says Shirin Malekpour, associate professor of sustainability governance at Monash University in Melbourne, Australia. "I see all of the above as facilitators of change," she says.
Inadequate or ... more than adequate?
Measuring the SDGs solely by how many targets have been met may miss what the goals were intended to achieve, says Sakiko Fukuda-Parr, professor emerita of international affairs at The New School, New York. "It means that our actions have been inadequate to actually live up to our aspirations," she says. "But that doesn't mean we shouldn't have goals at all. It helps to think about these and to make an effort to take action."
On a visit to Okayama in Japan this month, she was struck by how universities and the wider community had embraced the goals as a framework for sustainable development.
In 2018, Japan designated Okayama an"SDGs Future City," recognizing its effort to put the sustainable development goals into practice in everyday life by building sustainable businesses and healthier communities and by encouraging greater citizen participation in community initiatives and decision-making. Schools, universities, nonprofits, businesses and local governments now work together to translate the broad goals into community action. "I think at that community level, the SDGs have been extraordinarily successful in bringing like-minded people together," she says. "It's not just a numerical scorecard but a political and social catalyst."
Crises don't help
Meanwhile, the world scene hasn't helped. Repeated global crises have put pressure on the SDGs.
"There has been one crisis after another, and some of these are global crises, like the COVID pandemic or the effects of certain wars leading to inflation and critical materials becoming much more expensive. Climate change, of course, has affected each region differently," says Andrew Shepherd, senior research associate at ODI Global, a think tank, and director of the Chronic Poverty Advisory Network in the U.K.
"While people have escaped poverty, other people have fallen into poverty. Or some of the people who've escaped poverty have fallen back into poverty as a result of these crises," he says.
Shepherd argues that policymakers need to anticipate crises better and focus more on preventing people from slipping back into extreme poverty, especially the large number whose lives are better but remain highly vulnerable to economic shocks. It can be much harder for governments and the international community to create economic growth that is genuinely inclusive and reaches those most often left behind, such as women, people with disabilities and other marginalized folk, he says.
For this, governments need a lot of foresight. "There isn't enough attention given to the resources and support for people to recover from crises," Shepherd says. He says governments and international agencies are generally better at responding to emergencies than at helping people recover from them. Support often tapers off quickly once the immediate crisis passes, he says, even though households may remain financially vulnerable for years.
What protects people?
Giving poorer people better access to loans and financial services can help, Shepherd says, but it can also create new problems. Microfinance has made it easier for many low-income families to borrow money, but without strong safeguards, people can end up taking on more debt than they can repay.
He points to Bangladesh, where microfinance first became widely established and where over-borrowing is now a concern. "Microfinance is definitely part of the solution," he says, adding that digital finance has also helped more people gain access to financial services. "But there are still some risks there which need to be addressed and governments should focus more on this."'
Health insurance, he says, offers another kind of protection. Rwanda's community-based health insurance system called the Mutuelles de Santé, developed in the late 1990s, is worth emulating, he says. Premiums are linked to income. Under the current system, those in the poorest category pay nothing because the government covers the entire premium, and people in higher income categories contribute increasingly larger amounts. Such systems, Shepherd says, can help prevent an unexpected illness from wiping out a family's savings or pushing people back below the poverty line.
That preventive approach is particularly relevant to the SDGs' pledge to "leave no one behind," he says.
Another area where the world could focus on more would be on environmental goals, says Ngo. "We need to invest more in climate resilience, increasing [disease] surveillance, community infrastructure, strengthening food, agriculture and social systems. Our ecosystems and biodiversity continue to be lost. War and conflict are wiping out our gains."
Although the narrower measure of chronic hunger has recently improved, 2.1 billion people experienced moderate or severe food insecurity in 2025 —527 million more than in 2015. In conflict-ridden Western Asian countries like Palestine, Yemen and Syria , undernourishment is still increasing, says Ngo. Forced displacement reached 117 million people by mid-2025, while civilian conflict deaths remain well above post-2015 levels. The number of refugees relative to the global population hasmore than doubled since 2015.
The global risk of species extinction continues to worsen. More than48,600 species are now threatened, facing extinction.
We're also consuming more resources than ever before, with record levels of e-waste and hazardous waste, moving in theopposite direction of sustainable development objectives.
Collective policies can make a difference, says Kenny. Governments, and people working together make it worthwhile to strive toward these goals, even if many remain unmet, he says. "There's still much reason for hope."

Actor Nawazuddin Siddiqui found himself at the receiving end of comedian Samay Raina’s sharp humour during his appearance on India’s Got Latent Season 2. The actor, who joined the show’s latest episode alongside Bhuvan Bam, Mukesh Chhabra and Kaustubh Agarwal, was repeatedly teased by Samay about his film Thamma.
The horror-comedy, which starred Ayushmann Khurrana and Rashmika Mandanna in the lead roles, received mixed-to-negative reactions after its release. During the episode, Samay did not miss the opportunity to bring up the film while interacting with Nawazuddin.
Samay Raina roasts Nawazuddin Siddiqui
Samay directly asked the actor, “Sir, why did you do Thamma? Why did you even make it?” Nawazuddin paused before asking, “Thamma?” After another pause, he responded, “Well, it got made. It’s done.”
The comedian continued the joke by asking, “Sir, we can say such things, na?” Nawazuddin replied, “I mean, sure. You already said it anyway. What more could you say?”
Samay then joked, “No, no, I should ask for permission.” Nawazuddin played along and said, “You really should.”
The conversation soon moved to Nawazuddin’s acclaimed work in Sacred Games. Praising the series, Samay said, “But Sacred Games was amazing. Genuinely. Everyone loves Sacred Games,” before adding, “In that one, Nawaz sir did drugs, drank alcohol, slept with prostitutes, and then he showed up on set.”
Nawazuddin responded with a joke of his own: “I came prepared the same way today.”
Samay then told him, “Please choose your words wisely. People in this seat have said some outrageous things,” seemingly referring to the controversy surrounding an earlier episode featuring Ranveer Allahbadia, also known as Beer Biceps.
Samay brings Thamma back into the conversation
Later in the episode, Samay asked Nawazuddin to help a contestant learn how to act so he could ask a female contestant out on a date. Nawazuddin admitted, “I get scared in such situations.”
When Samay asked, “You know how to act, right?” Nawazuddin replied, “Yeah, I can act.”
Samay immediately brought Thamma back into the conversation and asked, “So, what went wrong with Thamma?”
The question left the panel and audience laughing. Nawazuddin responded, “Come on, man. I will act like I did in Thamma then.” Samay quickly added, “No, not the Thamma one, please.”
Thamma was directed by Aditya Sarpotdar and was reportedly made on a budget of around Rs 125 crore and earned Rs 187.59 crore at the box office.

On 15 September 2026, an Indian Navy vessel and a Pakistani naval vessel came into contact in the North Arabian Sea. India said the Pakistani vessel approached at high speed and manoeuvred unsafely while the Indian vessel was on a routine surveillance mission, and summoned Pakistan’s Chargé d’Affaires on 16 September to protest. Pakistan gave a different account, saying the incident occurred during its SEASPARK-26 naval exercise and alleging that the Indian vessel carried out aggressive manoeuvres near the Pakistani ship.
In this context, a video is being shared on social media (here, here) with the claim that it shows the collision between a Pakistani naval vessel and an Indian Navy warship on 15 September 2026. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows the collision between a Pakistani naval vessel and an Indian Navy warship on 15 September 2026.
Fact: The video does not show the collision between an Indian Navy warship and a Pakistani naval vessel on 15 September 2026. It shows a 2011 incident involving PNS Babur and INS Godavari during an escort mission for the merchant vessel MV Suez. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to the same clip (archived) uploaded on a YouTube channel named “mix” on 16 October 2014. The video was titled “Pakistan Navy Ship BABUR VS Indian Navy Ship”, and its description stated that it showed a Pakistan Navy ship and an Indian Navy ship in the Gulf of Aden during the rescue of the merchant vessel MV Suez. This confirms that the video predates the recent collision by over a decade.
Using these clues, we searched for relevant keywords and found a 2011 NDTV report showing similar footage from another angle. According to the report, the collision occurred on 16 June 2011 when the Pakistani warship PNS Babur rammed into the rear of the Indian frigate INS Godavari while attempting to overtake it during an escort mission for the merchant vessel MV Suez. The report stated that PNS Babur, caught in INS Godavari’s wake in heavy sea conditions, scraped against the frigate and damaged its helicopter deck. It also showed footage recorded from the deck of PNS Babur, capturing crew members celebrating after the collision.
A press release issued by India’s Ministry of External Affairs on 18 June 2011 confirmed that India had formally protested Pakistan’s conduct, stating that PNS Babur’s risky manoeuvres jeopardised the safety of INS Godavari and its crew and violated international maritime safety regulations and the 1991 India-Pakistan agreement on advance notice of military exercises.
To sum up, this viral video shows a 2011 Pakistan-India naval collision, not the September 2026 incident.

A clinical trial by doctors at a private medical college hospital in Chickballapur near Bengaluru has found that a dual stellate ganglion block (SGB) procedure may help reduce anxiety symptoms in patients who do not respond to standard treatment.
The study, published in the July-August 2026 issue of Pain Physician, an open-access journal, involved 63 patients with moderate to severe treatment-resistant anxiety. The researchers found that those who underwent the procedure had a significantly greater reduction in anxiety symptoms than those who received a sham procedure.
What the study involved
Led by G. Niraj, senior consultant, anaesthesiology, and a multidisciplinary team of pain medicine physicians, psychiatrists, and clinical psychologists at the Sri Madhusudan Sai Institute of Medical Sciences and Research (SMSIMSR) in Chickballapur, the randomised controlled trial evaluated dual SGB specifically for treatment-resistant anxiety.
The study focused on patients whose anxiety had persisted despite standard treatment. Treatment-resistant anxiety was defined as failure to respond to at least one first-line medication and one first-line psychotherapy, each given for at least eight weeks. Most patients in the study had tried several medications. Forty-six of the 63 participants had tried at least two medications.
The study involved 63 patients, of whom 42 received the dual SGB procedure and 21 received the sham treatment. The patients were followed for 12 weeks.
What is the procedure?
A stellate ganglion block involves injecting a local anaesthetic and steroid mixture into a group of nerves in the neck under ultrasound guidance. These nerves are part of the sympathetic nervous system, which controls the body’s ‘fight-or-flight’ response.
The procedure was performed on both sides of the neck, with the second block given between 24 hours and seven days after the first. The researchers said that reducing excessive activity in the sympathetic nervous system may help ease some symptoms of anxiety.
“Persistent anxiety is not just in the head. The body’s stress alarm can remain stuck in the ‘on’ position. Our research helps to reset this stress response, offering hope to people whose anxiety has not responded to standard treatments,” Dr. Niraj said.
He stressed that SGB was not intended to replace psychological therapy or medication. “It provides another valuable option for patients with poorly controlled anxiety,” he said.
The procedure was generally well tolerated by the patients in the study. None of the adverse events reported in the SGB group was serious. Temporary hoarseness lasting one to three hours was reported by 14 patients, while one patient experienced numbness in an upper limb that resolved within six hours.
Future potential
Dr. Niraj and his colleagues said the findings could have implications for mental healthcare in both rural and urban areas, particularly where access to long-term psychological therapy is limited. The researchers said a clinic-based intervention, when used appropriately alongside existing mental health treatment, could provide a valuable option for patients with difficult-to-treat anxiety.
The researchers cautioned that the findings need to be confirmed through larger studies. The trial was conducted at a single centre and followed patients for only 12 weeks. Further research is needed to determine how long the benefits last and to better understand the mechanism through which SGB may help reduce anxiety.

Tens of thousands flee as Iran-backed rebels draw Yemen into the wider war
The lightning advance of the Iran-backed Houthi rebels has forced tens of thousands of people to flee their homes in Yemen
CAIRO -- As Houthi rebels closed in, Eshraq Abdel Gelil and her husband fled their home, walking through the mountains before catching a ride to a nearby city. Four months pregnant, she feared another miscarriage.
They are among more than 125,000 people who have fled as the Iran-backed rebels have advanced down the Red Sea coast to a key maritime chokepoint. The offensive, linked to the wider Iran war, has threatened Saudi oil exports, pushed up global fuel prices and rattled markets.
The cost has been far greater for Yemenis caught in the crossfire. Many have fled their homes with only what they could carry. The Arab world’s poorest country was pushed to the brink of famine in an earlier phase of the civil war, which killed an estimated 150,000 people.
A Saudi-led blockade, along with the Houthis’ repressive rule and detention of U.N. and aid workers, has made life miserable in the now-expanding territory under rebel control. Yemen’s Saudi-backed government, weak and fragmented, has struggled to push them back.
Abdel Gelil is now sheltering with family in the southwestern city of Taiz, while others are sleeping in the streets or erecting makeshift tents out of plastic.
Her husband, Mohamed Thabet, said the latest fighting was “extremely fierce” and more intense than a battle in 2017 that had also forced him to flee. “There was shelling and shrapnel near the house,” he said.
They walked for 5 kilometers (3 miles) before taking a vehicle for around 60 kilometers (37 miles) on mountain roads.
When they arrived in Taiz, a doctor told them that the baby had moved lower in the womb. Abdel Gelil miscarried at the same point in a previous pregnancy.
“My wife cried from the shock and was very fearful,” Thabet said.
Now they are packed into a home with extended family. They can only afford to eat twice a day, and they worry that Abdel Gelil is not getting enough nutrients for her and the baby.
Thabet also worries about his sister, who hasn't been able to afford her diabetes medication for over a month. She and her two daughters, 8 and 13, have a blood condition that makes them susceptible to anemia, he said.
The civil war dates back to 2014, when the Houthis seized much of northern Yemen, including the capital, Sanaa. Saudi Arabia intervened the following year in support of Yemen's internationally recognized government. A 2022 ceasefire largely halted the fighting.
Hostilities erupted again in July, when the Houthis renewed attacks on Saudi Arabia in what the rebels said was an attempt to lift the blockade. The attacks on Saudi Arabia's oil industry came as the U.S. was having some success in reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
The fighting in Yemen has killed eight civilians and wounded another 32, according to the U.N. humanitarian office, which says an estimated 125,000 people have fled their homes. The U.N. children's agency, known as UNICEF, says the displaced include more than 57,000 children.
“This is one of the most fast-moving and volatile displacement waves Yemen has seen in years,” said Obia Achieng, a UNICEF representative in Yemen. “Families are fleeing with little or no warning, often at night, carrying only what they can grab.”
“The situation is particularly concerning because it comes on top of an already severe humanitarian crisis,” Achieng added.
Before the latest fighting, the U.N. had warned that around 5 million Yemenis were experiencing “crisis or worse levels of acute food insecurity.”
Milena Murr, of Prosper Global, a humanitarian group previously known as Mercy Corps, said some people arriving in Taiz had walked for over 16 hours, arriving at displacement camps exhausted, dehydrated and with some of the children appearing malnourished.
Iman Abdullahi, country director for CARE, another aid group, said there's an urgent need for food, maternal and newborn healthcare, hygiene supplies, private latrines and mental health support.
“One woman had to wash her only clothes and remain inside her tent until they dried because she had nothing else to wear. Another was forced to flee just two weeks after giving birth,” he said.
Nashwan Ahmed Said was stitching together a tent from plastic wheat sacks. He said this is the third time he's been displaced since the start of the war.
“We are in such a state! We have no home, no toilet, no food and nothing to drink,” he said.
Arwa Ahmed, who was displaced with her five children, said she and her family ate nothing but rice for days.
“We need everything. We need tents, we need food and all the essentials, because we were displaced and took nothing with us,” she said.

A Chinese optical engineer is the winner of this year’s Small World in Motion competition, sponsored by Nikon. Ning Xu of Tsinghua University in Beijing beat out 346 other video entries from 40 different countries with his super-resolution video (above) of the abnormal beating of cilia in the airways of a child with a rare genetic respiratory disorder.
Founded in 2011, the Nikon Small World in Motion competition is a spinoff of the company’s Small World Photomicrography Competition, which has been around since 1974. Both are meant “to showcase the beauty and complexity of things seen through the light microscope”—one through still photographs, the other through photovideography, taking advantage of all the technological advances that now allow users to make movies or time-lapse images through the microscope.
Primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD) is a genetic disorder that adversely affects the tiny hairlike structures that line the lungs, among other areas. Their wavelike motion helps move around germs, mucus, dust, and other irritants so the body can dispel them via coughing or sneezing. In people born with PCD, there is something wrong with those cilia, so those irritants build up, causing respiratory infections, among other complications. The cilia might be the wrong size, the wrong shape, or missing altogether. They might move abnormally or not move at all.

In response to a new European Union law, AI platforms are implementing new schemes for watermarking the content they generate. Anthropic recently disclosed its future Claude models will use SynthID-Text, an approach Google created and released as open source. It uses a secret key that subtly changes the process a model uses for choosing the next word in a sentence. Whereas a top next word choice might be “cloudy,” the key might change it to “overcast.” Anyone who knows the key can determine if it was generated by the platform using it.
New research shows that SynthID-Text can change not just word selection but also the tools a model invokes and the chances it will adhere to or disregard safety guardrails it has been trained to follow. The threat can become greater in the face of an adversarial prompt, in which an attacker attempts to cause a model to carry out a harmful action, such as revealing a password or other sensitive information. Instructions that normally wouldn’t be followed will, in some cases, be performed once the watermarking is deployed. The finding underscores the need for developers to thoroughly test how their LLMs and agents behave when watermarking is in place.
Changing safety behavior
“As compared to the same models without watermarking, it is definitely going to change their behavior, especially when we place it under adversarial conditions, or we make these models call tools when they’re powering an agent,” Andrea Siposova, an AI security researcher at Lasso Security, told Ars. “Watermarking is made to not be perceptible to a reader, but we know that when we are changing anything about what the model is generating, it is going to cause some tradeoffs, it’s going to show up somewhere.”
Watermarking works by embedding a signal that allows output to be identified as AI generated, something known as provenance. SynthID takes the normal sampling process and adds a random seed generator, sampling algorithm, and scoring function to it. Instead of the process using an arbitrary random number generator for next-word selection, the watermarking uses a secret key. While the word selection is still random, people with knowledge of the key can check the sequence of words to determine the likelihood that the key was used.
A key feature of SynthID is something known as tournament sampling. Similar to a sports game, SynthID evaluates large numbers of next-word token candidates. It uses a secret key to assign them probability scores. A pair of tokens competes in a round. The one with the higher hidden score wins and advances to the next round. The process continues until a final winning token is determined. More about tournament sampling can be found here and here.
Siposova tested the “non-distortionary” configuration of SynthID-Text through Hugging Face’s unmodified SynthIDTextWatermarkLogitsProcessor. She fed harmful prompts into six open-weight models and compared the responses when the watermarking was used and when it wasn’t. The experiment revealed that the watermarking changed responses to harmful requests, particularly when they were made using prompt-injection techniques.
“Watermarking changes refusal behavior on bare harmful requests, but the effect is more pronounced when the same requests are paired with the prompt-injection technique,” Siposova wrote. “On several models, watermarking then makes the model more likely to answer harmful requests that it would otherwise refuse.”
The changes have important safety consequences because they influence not only the LLM responses but also subsequent actions of AI agents relying on the model.
“At the model level, this can change safety behavior, including whether the model refuses a harmful request and whether that refusal holds under prompt injection,” the researcher wrote. “At the agent level, the same sampled tokens can determine which tool is called and what arguments are passed to it. Prompt injection connects these two settings because a weakened refusal becomes more consequential when the model can also act through tools. Such a watermarking procedure can therefore affect both what the model says and what an agent does. We call this behavioral effect sampling drift.”
Also interesting: Model responses behaved differently depending on which secret key was used.
There are limitations to the research. It doesn’t test how Claude model responses change under the watermarking. Instead, it tests a half-dozen open-weight models, so the researcher has access to token sampling that could be enabled and disabled during tournament sampling while keeping other settings fixed. The experiments also tested the Hugging Face implementation of SynthID-Text tournament sampling and not the specific implementation Claude models will use.
Still, the results show that at least some forms of the watermarking approach may affect model and agent safety. It will be important for red-team hacking exercises to stress-test their platforms to ensure they perform as expected when SynthID is deployed.

Singapore Airlines named world’s best airline for 2026
This is the sixth time the national carrier has claimed the world’s best airline title, having last done so in 2023.
SINGAPORE: Singapore Airlines (SIA) was named the world’s best airline at the 2026 Skytrax World Airline Awards in London on Friday (Sep 18).
This is the sixth time the national carrier has claimed the world’s best airline title, having last done so in 2023.
Qatar Airways, last year’s top airline, took second place in 2026, with Cathay Pacific Airways coming in third. All Nippon Airways ranked fourth while Turkish Airlines rounded out the top five.
SIA also won the awards for world’s best economy class, world’s best economy class onboard catering and best airline in Asia, and took second place in the world’s best cabin crew category.
“We are grateful to our customers for their trust and support, and we are committed to delivering an exceptional, world-class travel experience every time they fly with us,” said SIA group CEO Goh Choon Phong.
“This award is a testament to the dedication and professionalism of our people, who continually strive to uphold SIA’s renowned standards for service and operational excellence.”
SIA’s low-cost subsidiary Scoot, meanwhile, was named best long-haul low-cost airline for the sixth consecutive year.
The budget carrier also came in second in the world’s best low-cost airlines category after Malaysia’s AirAsia and ahead of Spain’s Vueling Airlines.
“This recognition validates Scoot’s commitment to providing our customers with comfortable, reliable and seamless travel experiences,” said Scoot CEO Leslie Thng.
“Scoot will continue to innovate, strengthen our operational resilience, and enhance the customer experience as we reinforce our position as a leading low-cost carrier.”
The awards were based on a survey of over 24.8 million travellers globally, who rated over 300 airlines between September 2025 and August 2026.
Introduced in 1999, the awards are described as the Oscars of the aviation industry, according to their organiser Skytrax.
“We congratulate the Singapore Airlines Group on the major achievement of being named the world’s best airline 2026 for Singapore Airlines, and the best long-haul low-cost airline for Scoot,” said Skytrax CEO Edward Plaisted.
“These successes highlight the level of product and service excellence they are providing to customers and should be a source of great pride and motivation for the management and staff in the group.”
Singapore Airlines and Scoot carried a record total of 42.4 million passengers in the 2025 to 2026 financial year, 7.7 per cent more than the 39.4 million they served in the previous financial year.
However, the group also reported a net loss of S$76 million in the first quarter of 2026, as a 78.5 per cent increase in net fuel costs due to the turmoil in the Middle East and a larger share of losses from Air India weighed on results.
Supply chain constraints have also led to SIA delaying its rollout of new first and business class seats on its Airbus A350s to the first quarter of 2027, later than the initially announced second quarter of 2026.

- GTA 6 is locked at 30 FPS at launch, as revealed in Rockstar's hands-on preview.

Will GTA 6 Have a 60 FPS Performance Mode?
No, GTA 6 is currently targeting 30 FPS on consoles at launch. Rockstar Games told creators who saw the GTA 6 preview that the game is running at only 30 FPS during development. At the time of writing, there is no confirmation about 60 FPS support for GTA 6 on PS5 or Xbox Series X|S.

Russians begin voting in parliamentary election in shadow of war
Kremlin’s United Russia party set to maintain a tight grip on the Duma alongside a handful of Putin-aligned groups
Polling stations opened Friday in Russia’s Far East, kicking off a three-day election that President Vladimir Putin’s party is all but guaranteed to win in the fifth year of war with Ukraine.
It will be Russia’s first parliamentary election since Moscow sent troops to Ukraine in February 2022. The conflict has since killed hundreds of thousands.
Only parties that support Putin and the Kremlin’s dragging military campaign have been registered to run. Moscow has also organised voting in occupied Ukraine.
While few in Russia doubt Putin’s United Russia party would sail to victory again, the vote is an opportunity for the Kremlin to gauge public support for the Ukraine war, the effects of which have hit home more than ever this year.

Patricio Guzmán, the film-maker who chronicled Chile’s bloody 1970s political strife and its subsequent social and political turmoil in films such as The Battle of Chile and Nostalgia for the Light, has died aged 85. According to Chilean news outlet Emol, Guzmán died on Tuesday in Paris after a cardiorespiratory arrest.
Guzmán’s chief preoccupation throughout his career was the carnage unleashed by Augusto Pinochet’s coup in 1973 against Salvador Allende, Chile’s elected president. He later told the Guardian: “I’m a film-maker who was very marked by the ways of the dictator. It has remained with me for ever. I cannot leave it behind.” However, he resisted the idea that he was an activist, political film-maker, adding: “I’m not a sociologist. Neither am I a politician. I make films that are metaphorical and poetic; I interpret reality through my own personal way of looking.”
Born in Chile in 1941, Guzmán initially worked in advertising before studying film, first in Chile and then in Madrid. On his return to Chile, Guzmán responded to the febrile political atmosphere after Allende’s election in 1970, eventually completing the mammoth Battle of Chile documentary that chronicled Pinochet’s ultimately successful attempt to overthrow Allende, resulting in the latter’s suicide. Guzmán did not shrink from the brutality of the period, even including footage shot by camera operator Leonardo Henrichsen as he is shot dead by the soldier he is filming.
Guzmán was helped in the endeavour by French film-maker Chris Marker, who supplied film stock and connections that proved vital to make the film. Guzmán himself was arrested but eventually released, but the film’s cinematographer Jorge Müller was not so lucky – along with his girlfriend Carmen Bueno, he was arrested, tortured and “disappeared” in 1974.
Guzmán completed The Battle of Chile outside the country, releasing each of its three parts – The Insurrection of the Bourgeoisie (1975), The Coup d’État (1976) and Popular Power (1979) – through the rest of the 70s. Described by the Guardian as “an outstandingly photographed example of a newsreel film that captures the drama and volatility of the period”, it has continued to attract acclaim since then. Guzmán revisited the film in the mid-90s with Chile, Obstinate Memory, in which he returned to the country after a quarter-century of exile. In 2001 he completed The Pinochet Case, after the Chilean former dictator was arrested in London in 1998.
The director moved on to more metaphysical subjects with a trilogy of films starting in 2010: Nostalgia for the Light, The Pearl Button and The Cordillera of Dreams. They sought to explore Chile’s traumatic past by absorbing the country’s magnificent natural landscapes. His final film, My Imaginary Country, was premiered in 2022 and covered Chile’s dramatic 2019 street protests.

On Friday, a day before the opening ceremony of the Asian Games in Nagoya, India’s national flag was officially raised alongside those of the other nations competing in the continental tournament at Garden Pier on the shores of Ise Bay in southern Japan. This practice is an age-old tradition of these continental games.
But there’s more than a bit of history here already. Moored alongside the pier is the icebreaker ship Fuji, which carried out Japan’s Antarctic expeditions from 1965 and is now on display as a museum vessel.
A little further inland, right next to where the Indian flag was raised, stands a larger-than-life bronze statue, now blue with patina, of two Sakhalin Huskies named Taro and Jiro. The two were among a group of 15 dogs that accompanied Japan’s first Antarctic expedition, carried out by Fuji’s predecessor, Soya, in 1958.
When severe weather conditions forced the crew to evacuate their base on East Ongul Island, the dogs were left behind, chained and with only a few days’ supply of food. No one expected them to survive. However, when another expedition returned almost a year later, Taro and Jiro were found alive. They had broken free from their chains and survived the Antarctic winter.
Their story became a national sensation, and the pair came to symbolise endurance and survival against the odds. Statues of the dogs can be found in several places in Japan, but one of the famous ones is here in Nagoya, beside the Fuji.
Cut to the present day, there is an altogether less heroic version of being left to fend for oneself playing out elsewhere in Nagoya this week.
Inauspicious start
The last few days have seen visuals you wouldn’t normally associate with a major sporting event in Japan: scenes of chaos and dysfunction.
Multiple videos and photographs of athletes arriving from across Asia and then stuck at Nagoya airport waiting for accommodation have done the rounds on social media. Some have complained of waiting for hours for transport from the airport to their rooms. There were also instances of male and female athletes mistakenly put up in the same rooms. Later, when incessant rains hit Nagoya, a Korean basketball player posted a photograph of a soaked floor with the caption: “Save me!”
“Disaster in the making,” read some of the online chatter. “If India had done something like this, we’d never hear the end of it,” said others.
ALSO READ | Room crunch had left 30-35 Indian athletes in a spot: Chef de Mission Sahdev Yadav
Much of the gripe has centred on the nature of the accommodation itself. The Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games are the first without a designated Games Village. Instead, around 3,000 athletes and coaches have been put up in temporary container-style housing at the pier. Another 4,000 are bunked up in the Costa Serena, a cruise ship docked at Kinjofuto Pier, some 10 kilometres away. The rest have been booked into hotels across Aichi Prefecture and Tokyo, closer to where events are being held.
There’s of course no denying that athletes have been affected.
“Mismanagement is there,” admits Sahdev Yadav, the Chef de Mission of the Indian contingent. “There was a delay in getting the accreditation cards made for people in the cruise ship. There were also some issues in the transport,” Yadav said.
Making matters worse was the fact that, at least initially, volunteers weren’t familiar with all the procedures for admitting athletes, said deputy Chef de Mission and former international shooter Anjali Bhagwat.
“Initially, we were not sure about the processes and the volunteers weren’t aware either. It was taking several hours to make the passes that allowed athletes to travel to the cruise ship or their hotels. But eventually we got that down to a few minutes. All this took a couple of days to settle down. Athletes in the sports disciplines that arrived first, like wushu and shooting, faced problems because of this,” Bhagwat said.
Yadav said the Indian team ended up booking 18 hotel rooms on its own and planned to book another 10, just to be safe. “We had to book because they (organisers) said they had a shortage of rooms and more athletes had come than they expected. But that’s not the case. The number of players who had been invoiced, only that many players are here. When they cut their names, we booked our own hotels,” he said.
Lack of a Games village
But while Yadav insisted that India had not sent more athletes than had been invited, it’s clear that organisers weren’t expecting nearly as many overall to turn up. The local organising committee maintains that the accommodation issue arose because they were expecting 15,000 athletes and officials for the Games, only for the numbers to increase. Last week, the Local Organising Committee in Nagoya admitted that at least 17,000 athletes and officials were likely to come.
These numbers aren’t outsized by themselves. China hosted about the same in the Hangzhou edition three years ago. But while China had the resources to conduct the event within a small radius and host all athletes and coaches in a dedicated Village, Japan has tried to keep the budget manageable by avoiding the construction of a designated residential facility.
The decision to dispense with the traditional Village was defended by the Olympic Council of Asia (OCA) on Friday. OCA Director General Husain Al-Musallam said that organisers had to take into account the circumstances of the host country and what would happen to the infrastructure after the Games.
“We wish that we have an athlete village, number one. But, number two, we also have to be flexible,” Al-Musallam said.
He pointed to the post-Games use of Villages at previous editions, including Doha in 2006, where the one there was converted into a medical centre, and Hangzhou, where the accommodation was subsequently sold to the public.
Mohammad Tayyab Ikram, chairman of the Aichi-Nagoya 2026 Asian Games Coordination Committee, said organisers did not want to leave a “white elephant” behind after the Games and described the container accommodation and cruise ship as alternatives developed after discussions with the OCA.
ALSO READ | Asian Games 2026: Manu Bhaker, Tajinderpal Singh Toor named India’s flagbearers for Opening Ceremony
It is possible that the local organising committee might have found it easier to manage a more modestly budgeted Games while avoiding some of the opening-day hiccups if it had not had to accommodate so many athletes and officials. But Al-Musallam said capping the number of entrants was not an option.
“I am a supporter of increasing the number of athletes, not to decrease athletes. If we have to choose between the expense of the Games and the athletes, I will support the athletes,” he said.
Al-Musallam said he expected things to fall into place after the initial troubles, and so far that does appear to be happening. The same sentiment has been expressed by officials, including those from India.
“Everyone has got accommodation. There’s no problem from our end. There was some trouble at the start but these are such big Games and something always happens in these events. Our job isn’t to find fault but to try and ensure that there isn’t any issue for our athletes. We have done that. Now everything is fine. There is no one without accommodation. Transport is fine and the buses are working too. Everyone is going to their training and returning. Everyone is waiting for the Games to begin,” Yadav said.
Yadav says the discussion he wants to focus on now is the team’s performance at the Asian Games. Having crossed the 100-medal mark in Hangzhou, he is hopeful the squad can achieve something similar this time as well.
Perhaps there is some inspiration to be taken from Taro and Jiro themselves. Much like some of the athletes here in Nagoya, they found themselves in an unfortunate situation they would rather not have been in. But they made the most of it and, against all odds, emerged as heroes.

'Not a catastrophe' - Carrick dismisses Man Utd job fears
- Published
Manchester United boss Michael Carrick says it would be "ridiculous" to start thinking how long he has left in the job after "two or three" bad results.
His side visit Fulham on Sunday after an awful week.
After United lost at home to a Manchester City side reduced to 10 men after 23 minutes, Brighton became the first side to come from two goals down to win at Old Trafford in 50 years in their Carabao Cup tie.
United supporters responded to the midweek setback with boos and by chanting against their team.
Carrick said in the aftermath he was "not bothered" by the pressure - a sentiment he reinforced as he spoke to the media before the Fulham trip.
"I know the club, I know the role, I know what's expected here in terms of playing to a certain standard and achieving certain things on the pitch," he added.
"I get all that.
"In terms of future and ownership and how long I've got in the job, that's totally not in my thinking. It's ridiculous to think that way in the position I'm in, that's just not on the radar.
"It's two or three games. It's two or three games too many because I really hate losing, but that doesn't mean the world caves in. In some minds it does, it can't for us."
There has been no sense from senior figures inside United that Carrick's position is under threat. They are more focused on the perceived under performance of so many players given the 12 games out of 17 that were won under the 45-year-old over the second half of last season.
By contrast, they have two victories from six games so far, against newly promoted Ipswich - when they had to come from behind - and Azerbaijan champions Sabah FK in the Champions League.
"It's not a catastrophe or a disaster," said Carrick. "It's not the end of the world."
Yet it is the measure of the noise around a club of United's size that is often feels that way.
Carrick accepted issues at Old Trafford are frequently amplified, so they look to be bigger than they actually are.
Despite this, he loves his job - and the club he served with such distinction as a player, and began his coaching career.
"There's great feelings, and there's obviously disappointments, and sometimes the smaller disappointments lead to being a little bit bigger," he added. "It's just part of coping and being at this great football club.
"I wouldn't want to be anywhere else, genuinely.
"It's the best place for me to be, in part because of the times when it's maybe not going to plan. Sometimes they are best times to work your way through, to find out a few things and come out an awful lot stronger."
Externally, the inquests have tended to focus around recruitment - or lack of it, specifically at left-back - United's finances and debt levels, Carrick's relative inexperience and, other than assistant boss Steve Holland, that of his coaches.
"It's not a blame game," said Carrick, who revealed Luke Shaw and new signing Carlos Baleba "have a chance" of being fit for the Craven Cottage meeting.
"We all search for things to look at and point at, or whatever reason it may be and find a blame. Blame me. No problem. I will take the responsibility.
"But it's not about blaming people. It's about us, it's about us finding solutions and being better. That's as a whole football club."

He alleged that stones and eggs were also hurled at his vehicle as the crowd moved towards him.
Bittu further alleged that the local police failed to act and, instead, directed the attackers towards his convoy.

BITTU’S STERN WARNING TO BHAGWANT MANN

From depression after Chelsea injury to playing non-league at 37
- Published
Sam Hutchinson played under both Jose Mourinho and Carlo Ancelotti at Chelsea, set up a goal for Frank Lampard, and was in Munich on the historic night they won the Champions League for the first time in 2012.
His time at Chelsea, however, was "filled with regret and what might have been" after a chronic knee injury so nearly ended his career before it had properly started.
A product of Chelsea's youth system, Hutchinson was a promising defender on the fringes of the first team when he was diagnosed with a chondral defect (a hole in his right knee) after suffering a serious injury during a reserve game at Aston Villa.
Having joined Chelsea as a seven-year-old, made his first-team debut at 17 under Mourinho and captained England at Under-19s level, Hutchinson took the gut-wrenching decision to retire at the age of 21 in 2010 after struggling to recover.
A period of depression followed for the young player, who had been identified by Mourinho as a bright prospect.
"I had already played for the first team and Mourinho had said some encouraging things about me in interviews," he says.
"Then the injury happened and everything fell apart. I was just a kid.
"After I retired I was in a bad place with dark thoughts."
Hutchinson sought help for his depression.
"Unless you get help, you never know how bad you are," he tells BBC Sport.
"Even telling this story, it's like therapy.
"It's like the old saying - a problem shared is a problem halved. That's true about mental health. If you're suffering in silence, it's not going to help."
After receiving treatment at the Priory, and with his damaged knee finally fixed, Hutchinson came out of retirement in December 2011 to re-sign for Chelsea.
More injuries followed but despite being limited to six senior Chelsea appearances, he has gone on to have a fulfilling career.
Hutchinson played 200-plus games in the Championship, most notably for Sheffield Wednesday, where fans remember him fondly.
In addition to overseas spells in the Netherlands with Vitesse Arnhem and in Cyprus with Pafos, he has also turned out for Nottingham Forest, Reading and AFC Wimbledon.
Sixteen years after fearing his career was over for good, the father-of-three is still playing the game he loves at the age of 37.
This summer Hutchinson signed a two-year contract with non-league Farnham Town - after surviving a major health scare.
'Thank us later for saving your life'
Monday, 26 May 2025. A date etched in the memories of AFC Wimbledon fans after their side won promotion to League One by beating Walsall at Wembley in the play-off final.
It was Hutchinson's winner at Grimsby three weeks earlier that ensured the Dons made the play-offs.
He did not know it at the time but the defender-turned-midfielder would not start another game for 11 months after scoring at Blundell Park.
"Throughout the first half my chest was getting increasingly tighter and I was in so much pain," recalls Hutchinson about that game at Grimsby.
"I felt dizzy and my hands started sweating.
"I was rapidly going downhill but then our centre-back won a great header, the keeper tipped it on to the bar, and it dropped down to me to tap over the line."
While AFC Wimbledon's travelling fans celebrated the goal wildly, Hutchinson felt so unwell his only thoughts were finishing the game and making it home to his wife and three children.
It would be several days, however, before he returned to the family home in Ascot.
On the journey back to London, his condition deteriorated to such an extent that a decision was taken to divert the team coach to a hospital in Nottingham so he could receive treatment.
After tests Hutchinson was quickly transferred to a nearby cardiac unit.
"I was put me in the back of an ambulance and I remember hearing the blues and twos," he recalls.
"My blood levels had spiked so much, I was in a really bad way. A couple of the paramedics knew who I was because I had played for Nottingham Forest a few years earlier.
"They said: 'You can thank us later for saving your life.' I was told I'd had a heart attack."
Hutchinson spent the next five days in hospital and had successful heart surgery.
"A branch of an artery was blocked 75%. I had an angiogram, external and had a stent put in by a specialist. The one thing that the professor - who had looked after both Tom Lockyer and Christian Eriksen – said was my situation was nothing like theirs.
"It was a blockage and it was all fixed, there was no need for a defibrillator to be fitted."
John Terry, his former Chelsea team-mate, was among those who reached out to Hutchinson during his recovery, while the player was well enough to visit Wembley to watch AFC Wimbledon win promotion.
A month later the Dons announced he had signed a one-year contract extension after being given the all-clear to train again.
However, Hutchinson was limited to just a handful of appearances in 2025-26 and in May - 12 months after that game at Grimsby - it was announced he would be leaving at the age of 36.
"Sam played a pivotal role in getting us over the line, not only with that iconic goal at Grimsby but his performances leading up to that," said an AFC Wimbledon statement, external announcing his departue.
Some may have decided it was the perfect time to retire from playing after what he had been through.
Hutchinson, though, had other ideas.
1 of 4
'I need heart surgery when I stop playing'
It's the opening day of the National League South season and Surrey-based Farnham Town are at home to AFC Totton in their first ever game in the sixth tier of English football.
Three years ago, Farnham struggled to attract crowds of 400 playing in the ninth-tier Combined Counties League.
But three straight promotions,, external together with Hutchinson's arrival in the summer, have caused a stir in the historic market town and there are 1,178 at the 2,200-capacity Memorial Ground to witness his debut, which ends in a 1-0 defeat.
Hutchinson has since gone on to help the part-timers win four of their first eight games and on Saturday will line up for Farnham at Cirencester Town in the second qualifying round of the FA Cup (15:00 BST).
"I'm loving it," he says about playing non-league 19 years after Mourinho sent him on for his Chelsea debut in the 89th minute against Everton on the final day of the 2006-07 Premier League season.
"Part-time football suits me after all that I've been through with my health.
"I have to go back every six months for tests and I have been told I will need further heart surgery when I finally stop playing football.
"But the specialists are happy for me to carry on for now."
It is 16 years since Hutchinson set up a goal for Lampard in Chelsea's 7-0 demolition of Stoke City at Stamford Bridge in 2010; 14 years since he flew to Munich with Roberto di Matteo's squad for the 2012 Champions League final at the Allianz Stadium.
He did not play when the Blues overcame German giants Bayern Munich on penalties to be crowned champions of Europe.
Nevertheless, he was regarded as a valued member of the squad and was invited to the trophy parade that followed.
Despite mixed emotions about his time at Chelsea due to injury, Hutchinson has not forgotten how the club looked after him.
"They brought me up and gave me values," he says. "I look back at the club fondly and what they did for me. I do bits of work now for Chelsea TV."
Hutchinson has also done work to support the British Heart Foundation and raised awareness about mental health.
How is his mental health these days?
"I'm in a different place," he says. "I do have regrets [because of the injury] but I have also lived a life that has been good.
"There are many players who have gone through a lot worse than me."
