Locked offices and millions in donations: Inside India's little-known political parties
- Published
There was little to suggest that the locked flat in Anand, in the western Indian state of Gujarat, was the headquarters of a political party.
There was no signboard, campaign poster or obvious trace of political activity. But on paper, the Satyawadi Rakshak Party had recently received an extraordinary amount of money.
In the financial year ending in March 2024, official records show the Gujarat-based party received more than 3.3bn rupees (approx $35m; £25m) in donations. A few months later, when India held the world's largest general election, it fielded a single candidate, who lost his deposit.
Its accounts say that 84.8m rupees went towards election campaigning, while more than 3.16bn rupees were listed as spending on "public welfare".
"We have spent the money on charity but have not maintained records," said Swati Ben Patel, the party's president, who lives in the same residential complex as its registered office.
The party is one of more than 2,800 Registered Unrecognised Political Parties, or RUPPs - a vast but little-known tier of Indian politics. These parties are legally registered but have not won enough votes or seats to be recognised at the state or national level.
Some contest elections only sporadically or field a handful of candidates. Yet, like larger parties, they can receive donations and claim tax exemptions. Donors can also reduce their taxable income through eligible contributions.
The rules are intended to support political activity, but tax officials say they can be misused.
A months-long BBC investigation examined six RUPPs that reported some of the largest donations in 2023-24. Together, they received about 17bn rupees, despite fielding just 15 candidates in the 2024 election. None came close to winning.
The gap between the money some parties receive and their limited electoral presence has drawn increasing scrutiny from India's tax authorities.
An internal Income Tax department document reviewed by the BBC shows that officials have been investigating suspected misuse of RUPPs since at least 2022.
It identifies 55.91bn rupees in suspected bogus political donations made by taxpayers seeking tax benefits, as well as 6.65bn rupees in foreign transactions. It also notes possible violations of tax, foreign-funding and election laws.
None of the six parties examined by the BBC has been publicly named in these wider inquiries. The BBC has not established that any of them committed financial wrongdoing.
But in several cases, it found a striking gap between the way the organisations were described in their records and what reporters encountered on the ground.
Some registered offices were closed or appeared inactive. Party officials sometimes said they did not control their organisations' finances or could not explain how large sums had been spent.
The BBC found signs that the political presence of some of these parties was limited. Although their websites sometimes carried photographs of door-to-door canvassing, one candidate, Indradevi Hiralal of the Garib Kalyan Party, said she had not visited her constituency to campaign in 2024. She showed a single poster printed for the election.
There were also signs of scrutiny from the authorities. Three parties said they or their officials had faced action by the Income Tax department. At a fourth, a relative of a party official said the family home had been searched. The other two denied facing such action.
Tax authorities in Bihar, Gujarat and Delhi, as well as the Central Board of Direct Taxes, did not respond to questions about whether any of the six parties had been investigated or subjected to searches.
Of the six parties, Aam Janmat Party reported receiving the most money.
Founded in Patna in 2020, it reported no individual donations above 20,000 rupees - the threshold at which donors must be identified to the Election Commission - during its first two years.
Then its finances changed dramatically.
Aam Janmat Party reported 2.16bn rupees in donations in 2022-23. The following year, the figure nearly tripled to more than 6.2bn rupees - more than twice the roughly 2.8bn rupees received by the Indian National Congress, the country's main opposition party.
Aam Janmat Party officials could not explain the sudden rise.
Aam Janmat Party party fielded just one candidate in the 2024 general election. He received a tiny share of the vote and lost his deposit.
The BBC traced its founding president, Anamika Paswan, to Patna city in Bihar state. Paswan, now a vice-president of the governing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in the state, said she had resigned from Aam Janmat in 2022.
When reporters later sought documents relating to her departure, Paswan was not present. Her husband produced what he said was her resignation letter and another document stating that the party had moved hundreds of miles west to Ahmedabad in Gujarat state with Gaurav Mishra as its president.
But the office at its registered address there was shut.
Its treasurer, Dharmendra Vaishnav, said by telephone that Aam Janmat had "shut operations". He said he knew nothing about its finances and directed questions to Mishra, who did not respond to repeated calls and messages.
The party's listed bank account, however, could still receive money. The BBC transferred a small donation and the payment went through.
The registered office of the Garib Kalyan Party was also closed.
It reported receiving 1.38bn rupees in donations in 2023-24, but fielded just three candidates in the general election.
At the home of its president Neeraj Kumar Kshatriya, his mother said she knew little about the party. But she recalled Income Tax department officials searching the family home, although she did not know why.
Researchers who track political finance say the pattern raises questions about what these parties do with the money they receive.
"These parties are not electorally active, yet they are getting such huge funds and they are spending the money as well," said Shelly Mahajan, a researcher at the Association for Democratic Reforms, an election watchdog.
But tracing such transactions can be difficult. Tax officials told the BBC that money can pass through a web of taxpayers, political parties and intermediaries, obscuring where it came from and where it ultimately went.
The BBC could not establish that any donations to the six parties had been returned in this way.
It did, however, trace two people listed as donors to the New India United Party who said they had claimed tax benefits on their contributions.
One Ahmedabad resident confirmed donating 500,000 rupees. The other said he had donated on a friend's advice. "I did it as a way to save tax, and have declared the same," he said, adding that the authorities had not contacted him.
Three tax officials in Ahmedabad, Delhi and Patna, speaking on condition of anonymity, said chartered accountants and other middlemen can connect taxpayers seeking deductions with parties willing to receive donations.
In some cases, they said, intermediaries can also exercise considerable control over party finances.
Surender Tiwari said that was what happened at his Swatantrata Abhivyakti Party, which reported receiving 2.19bn rupees in donations in 2023-24.
Although he was its president, Tiwari said he did not control the party's money. Its chartered accountant handled the finances and gave him campaign funds, he said.
"The chartered accountant gave me some money for the election campaign," Tiwari said. "He would then show videos of the campaign to clients who wanted to get tax relief through donations."
Tiwari said the party received a notice from the Income Tax department in July and accused its chartered accountant Mayur Singh of keeping him "in the dark".
Singh denied wrongdoing. He said his role was limited to preparing audit reports that parties must submit to the Election Commission, although he acknowledged working for several examined by the BBC.
"Try to understand, it's the same people behind these parties," he said, without elaborating.
Concerns surrounding India's little-known parties extend beyond their finances. The Election Commission has also been trying to remove inactive parties from its official list.
Last year, it delisted more than 800 RUPPs that had not fielded a candidate in six years. But it cannot cancel a party's legal registration, limiting the effect of such action.
The BBC asked the commission whether tax authorities had shared information about suspected financial irregularities involving RUPPs, including the six examined. It did not respond.
As scrutiny grows, the challenge for authorities will be to establish who controls these parties, where their money comes from and how it is ultimately spent.

The day Bengal's political chessboard turned upside down for Mamata
With barely a month to go for the Nandigram bypoll, Bengal's political chessboard shifted dramatically on Friday. In a day of reversals, Mamata Banerjee lost her party name and symbol to an Election Commission freeze, was left without a Nandigram candidate, and saw the Congress candidate she said she would back get arrested.
There is a common sentiment that plays in Kolkata: time moves relatively slower. But that was not to be on a politically charged day in Bengal, when the needle swung rapidly. And at the heart of it was Nandigram.
The symbolism was not lost.
While the pieces were being moved from the Chief Minister’s Secretariat in Howrah, the battlefield lay 150 kilometres away in the far-flung South Bengal town.
Nandigram had once made Mamata, helping topple the powerful Left government. Now, it has unmade her. She is left without a candidate in the upcoming bypolls, and the one she said she would back from the Congress was arrested moments later.
And between then and now stands Suvendu Adhikari.
Her aide-in-chief, who helped Mamata spring up the ladder during the Nandigram uprising nearly two decades ago, is now hastening her descent as her bete noire.
All this happened on a day when her party’s 28-year legacy was at stake. The Election Commission froze the grass with two flowers symbol -- the one Mamata had once hand-drawn — along with the party’s name.
And the key challenger to the Trinamool’s name and symbol is the other faction, which goes by “Bhalo Trinamool” in Bengal, translating to “good guys”. It is led by Ritabrata Banerjee, who would have been barely voting age when Mamata walked out of Congress to form the party she is now wrestling over.
Now, Ritabrata is her key challenger.
Mamata’s camp has been given the football player symbol, while Ritabrata’s camp has been given the envelope.
To sum it up, before untangling the threads of an eventful day: Mamata lost her party name and symbol -- though both remain up for grabs depending on how the EC adjudicates the tug-of-war between her and Ritabrata, alongside a legal battle by the aggrieved party in the Supreme Court.
She also lost her Nandigram candidate, and even the Congress candidate she said she would support.

Congress candidate Milan Pradhan for the by-election for the Nandigram constituency was arrested on Friday (September 18, 2026) by the West Bengal police in an old case. This came an hour after Mamata Banerjee said she would support the Congress candidate after her own candidate withdrew the nomination.
“I am shocked by the Bharatiya Janata Party’s aggressive mentality; they will not let anyone contest the elections. Will no other party exist, and will there be no democracy?“ Congress State president Subhankar Sarkar said after their candidate’s arrest.
Mr. Sarkar also said that their candidate was getting threat calls that he may be picked up by the police and that he was worried about his safety.
Criticising Mr. Pradhan’s arrest, Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge said it was “a brazen attempt at voter chori and chunav chori (voter and election theft)”. “The BJP is so insecure that even in a by-election, it is misusing agencies to target and arrest an Opposition candidate. The Congress will neither be intimidated nor silenced,” he said in a post on X.
Sources in the Congress alleged that WBPCC general secretary Subhasish Bhattacharya had also been arrested.
“Mr. Pradhan is a strong candidate; that is why arresting him in an old case is not a good image for democracy. If the warrant was pending against him for so long, then what were you doing for so long? This is completely politically motivated,” senior Congress leader and spokesperson Suman Roy Choudhuri told The Hindu on Friday (September 18, 2026).
Mr. Pradhan was one of the frontline leaders during the Nandigram protests, according to Congress leaders.
On Friday afternoon (September 18, 2026), Sanchita Pradhan (De), the Mamata All India Trinamool Congress candidate for Nandigram, revoked her nomination after an alleged meeting with Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari.
However, police sources have said that this arrest has no relation to the elections, and the arrest was merely based on an old case against Mr. Pradhan.
Nandigram is a prestige constituency for all parties in elections, because it is Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari’s home bastion, and he had already won from this seat in the Assembly polls, for which he resigned and kept his MLA position in the Bhabanipur seat. Mr. Adhikari won this seat by 9665 votes in the 2026 elections. In the 2021 elections, Ms. Banerjee lost to Mr. Adhikari in this seat by a margin of 1956 votes.

$1.3bn in US health funds left unspent by Trump ‘could lead to 150,000 preventable deaths’
Funding for tuberculosis, malaria, HIV and maternal healthcare has to be released for spending by 30 September
More than $1.3 billion (£975 million) in US funding for tuberculosis, malaria, HIV and maternal healthcare could go unspent within two weeks because it has not yet been released by the Trump administration, potentially resulting in tens of thousands of preventable deaths.
An analyses of US global health spending by international health non-profit Partners in Health found that the money, which had been approved by Congress, is being withheld by the Office of Management and Budget.
The funding authority expires on 30 September, at the end of the US federal financial year.
“The result will be deadly consequences for patients, the incapacitation of history's most successful global health programme, and the fuelling of a flourishing new HIV pandemic,” the organisation said.
The analysis predicts the cost to global health programs will result in an estimated 121,000 deaths from tuberculosis, with $150m of the funding for programmes targeting the disease, 47,600 deaths from malaria and the loss of lifesaving nutrition products for 22.9 million children.
Of the finds at risk, $250m for bilateral malaria programmes, $320m for maternal and child health and $330m for HIV programmes, according to Partners in Health.
The money could be transferred to the State Department or otherwise the period in which it can be used could be extended, said Vincent Lin, an associate director of health policy and advocacy at Partners in Health.
Yet unless the money is actually released to programmes and countries, it would not help people in need.
Last year, hundreds of millions of dollars for nutrition programmes and neglected tropical diseases were held and “it took them a year to even think about how to start programming the funds”, Mr Lim said.
The warning comes as separate analysis by the organisation found that the US has spent $2.3bn less on its flagship HIV programme, the President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR), than it had at the same point two years ago.
PEPFAR has supported HIV treatment and prevention programmes since 2003 and has saved more than 26 million lives, according to figures cited by Partners in Health.
US government data showed that about two million people were removed from PEPFAR-supported treatment programmes following cuts in 2025, while mother-to-child transmission of HIV was increasing.
“The result will be deadly consequences for patients, the incapacitation of history's most successful global health program, and the fueling of a flourishing new HIV pandemic,” said.
The warning comes ahead of the first anniversary of the Trump administration's America First Global Health Strategy, which has reshaped how the US distributes international health aid. The organisation said the reductions were likely to deepen as the strategy is implemented through new agreements with individual countries.
An analysis of 18 bilateral agreements obtained through a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit found planned cuts in US health spending over the next five years in countries including Sierra Leone, Burundi and Malawi, Mr Lin said.
While advocates have long called for reforms to the global health funding system to ensure sustainability and uphold human rights, the America First strategy has made US global health policy more “transactional, exploitative and short-sighted”, advocacy organisation Physicians for Human Rights said to mark the anniversary.
“Data from PHR and other independent groups clearly show that services are weaker than they were a year ago,” said Emily Bass, an expert consultant with PHR.
Dr Alain Casséus, head of infectious diseases at Zanmi Lasante, a Haitian organisation affiliated with Partners in Health, said the consequences of funding cuts would not necessarily arrive as a single dramatic event.
“There will be no major announcement, but there will be signs,” Dr Casséus said.
“Ordering windows will pass quietly, regions will run out before drugs, and diagnosis will lack.”
Patients could lose access to viral-load monitoring and remain on ineffective drug regimens without knowing that their treatment had failed, increasing the risk of drug resistance.
The Independent has contacted the White House for comment.

As European militaries adapt to the use of AI and drones in modern warfare, a NATO-backed startup is helping to deploy AI-driven target detection and selection that can run on small drones for surveillance and attack missions.
The company Scaleout Systems was originally founded by researchers from Uppsala University in Sweden in 2018, and initially focused on training and deploying machine learning models directly on the hardware available in commercial trucks and other vehicles. But once Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the company pivoted toward defense applications.
“With the war in Ukraine and a shifting world, we realized that this technology can be very important to operationalize edge data and sensor data for machine learning to make sure that NATO allies have found that strategic advantage,” Andreas Hellander, cofounder and CEO of Scaleout Systems, told Ars.
Instead of using frontier AI models from OpenAI or Anthropic, Scaleout is harnessing leaner ones, such as machine learning models that can perform computer vision tasks on the hardware of drones or computers used at forward bases. “They need to fit on forward-deployed hardware and edge hardware, which can vary quite a bit from small embedded devices to quite powerful edge workstations,” Hellander said.
Scaleout was selected to join NATO’s Defence Innovator Accelerator for the North Atlantic (DIANA) Challenge Program in 2025. There, it has worked on the Federated Aerial Intelligence for Recon project to adapt machine learning models for the edge computing hardware found in drones, drone pilot tablets, and field command posts.

Asiana Fund, the investment platform of the Dani Family Office, and Taiwan-based VC firm JC Capital have launched the ₹1,000 Cr Asiana-JCC Advanced Manufacturing & Innovation Fund. The fund comprises a primary corpus of ₹600 Cr and a greenshoe option of ₹400 Cr. Sponsors from Asiana Fund and JC Capital will collectively commit more than 20% of the fund corpus. It will primarily invest in Series A and Series B startups operating across advanced manufacturing and robotics, semiconductors and computing, materials and sustainability, and aerospace and defence. The fund plans to build a portfolio of 12 to 15 startups, with a portion of the corpus reserved for follow-on investments. Its initial deal pipeline includes startups working on compound semiconductors, motion-control systems for EVs and robotics, secure silicon, smart grids, robotic vision, and optoelectronics. Beyond providing capital, the fund will seek to facilitate collaboration between Indian startups and Taiwan’s technology ecosystem. It plans to support technology and know-how transfers, connect portfolio startups with global supply chains and strategic partners, and assist them with manufacturing scale-up and international expansion. The partnership combines Asiana Fund’s experience in India’s industrial and technology sectors with JC Capital’s network across Taiwan’s semiconductor and electronics ecosystem. More than 80% of JC Capital’s investors are corporate limited partners across the US, Japan, Taiwan, and Malaysia. The VC firm said this network would help portfolio startups access technology partners, supply chains, and international markets. Founded in 2017, Asiana Fund has deployed more than ₹700 Cr across 11 private equity investments. Its portfolio spans advanced manufacturing, robotics, drones, medtech, and cleantech. The investment platform was founded by Asian Paints co-promoter Jalaj Dani, who is also the chairman of aerospace startup EndureAir and robotics startup Addverb. JC Capital, meanwhile, has invested more than ₹1,000 Cr across 30 startups since its launch in 2019. Its investment portfolio spans semiconductors, artificial intelligence, and clean technology. The fund’s launch comes as the Indian government seeks to expand the country’s domestic semiconductor and electronics manufacturing capabilities through initiatives such as the India Semiconductor Mission and production-linked incentive schemes. Electronics and IT minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said at Semicon India 2026 yesterday that global companies have committed around ₹1 Lakh Cr under the Semicon 2.0 initiative to strengthen India’s electronics and semiconductor value chain. US-based semiconductor equipment maker Applied Materials also committed to investing $5 Bn in India over the next decade to expand its research, engineering, and manufacturing presence.

Kimi Antonelli was 10 when his father Marco first realised the boy sitting on his lap, operating the steering and gears, might have an exceptional talent as a racing driver.
The pair were at the Adria circuit in north-east Italy, Marco with his Lamborghini sports car team, Kimi competing in a karting race.
It was the end of the day and Marco, a former driver himself, asked his son: "Do you want to try the Lamborghini?"
Of course he did.
Marco strapped himself and Kimi into the car, belts extended around both. Dad was in charge of the throttle and brake, his son would control the rest.
"I couldn't see the track because he was in front of me with a helmet on," Marco tells BBC Sport. "I could only see beside me the marker panels before each corner - 100m, 50m.
"We started to drive, step by step, faster, faster, faster. In the end, I pushed like I was alone and I arrived at the braking point at the end of the straight, 320km/h, braked very hard and at the limit.
"The car had a lot of oversteer. Kimi controlled the oversteer perfectly, then I went on the throttle, Kimi finished the oversteer, changed gear, and went.
"I said: 'OK, stop, because it has now become dangerous.' But when I saw the video, 10 years old, on my leg, oversteer, everything perfect, I said: 'Maybe he has something special.'"
Now a 19-year-old Kimi is dominating this year's F1 championship in only his second season.
This is the story of a boy his dad says was "born in a garage".
"Kimi from 15 days old was in the garage and heard the sound of the engine and the smell of the exhaust," says Marco, who worked with his wife Veronica on their racing team business.
It was the Christmas holidays when Kimi was about three, and Marco had brought home a simulator he had bought for his guests to try out at the Bologna Motor Show.
"Each evening, Kimi wanted to drive," Marco remembers.
Just like seven years later in the Lamborghini, Kimi would sit on Marco's leg, the controls divided in the same way.
"I remember one night I started to fall asleep because I had been at work very early and we had a crash because I didn't brake when we arrived at the end of the straight," Marco says.
"And Kimi said: 'Dad, dad, no sleep, no sleep. I have to drive.'"
Marco Antonelli did not originally want his son to become a racing driver, because of his own struggles during his career.
"Sometimes you are fast but not in the right position to become a professional driver," he says.
In the 1990s, Marco Antonelli was on the cusp of becoming a works driver in the DTM touring car series, then a huge hit with audiences across Europe.
He tested for Alfa Romeo, but then the team boss left and the opportunity evaporated. Another chance came up with BMW, alongside Roberto Ravaglia and Steve Soper - stars at the time. Again, the same thing happened.
"I suffered a lot for it," Marco says. "And, of course, I was scared that my son [would] relive the same situation. At the beginning, I was very stressed about the passion my son had for motorsport."
Kimi tried a go-kart for the first time when he was five, and immediately showed an awareness of racing lines, braking points and car control.
The Antonellis were what Marco describes as "a normal family". They could not possibly afford to pay for Kimi to take part in all the categories on the way to Formula 1.
Marco decided he could fund Kimi through karting and a year of the basic single-seater category, Formula 4. After that, he figured he might be able to put him in one of his GT cars and become professional that way.
But Kimi immediately started to impress. Whatever category he got into, he was quick, and won.
By the time Kimi was 11, his name was buzzing around motor racing circles. Mercedes heard about him, and their driver academy scout Gwen Lagrue flew to Italy to check him out.
It was a season in which Antonelli had ended up driving a kart with less power than those of his rivals. Marco had told Kimi this would be good for him - he should think not about the result, but about how to improve, always push hard.
"Gwen was impressed about this condition of power and driving in this category that Kimi did," Marco says. "And maybe they understood that Kimi was a different child."
Now Kimi was a member of the Mercedes driver academy, Marco could stop worrying about money, and start focusing on helping his son achieve his full potential.
Mercedes were not the only big names in F1 who had noticed Antonelli's promise.
"When he was in karting, you could already see he was one of the stand-out talents," says four-time world champion Max Verstappen, the only other teenager to win an F1 race.
At 15, Antonelli was ready to move up to cars, and, as a final preparation, did a couple of races in a karting category with gears. On his debut, with minimal pre-event testing, he took pole position. After that, he went to the world final, and stuck it on pole again.
This was the end of 2021, after which Antonelli moved full-time into cars. Through 2022, he swept the board in various championships in Formula 4, and the same happened in Formula Regional in 2023.
1 of 4
By now, Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff was already thinking that Antonelli would be his next F1 driver, potentially a replacement for Lewis Hamilton. With the seven-time champion approaching 40, Wolff was planning on taking control of that generational transition.
So when it came time to negotiate a new contract with Hamilton in 2023, Wolff played hardball. Hamilton wanted to sign for at least two firm years, Wolff only one. In the end, they compromised on a contract for 2024 with an option for 2025.
Hamilton, unimpressed, decided to look at his options, and signed to join Ferrari in 2025, telling Wolff in late January 2024, before the start of that season.
Wolff immediately phoned Marco Antonelli, to tell him the "very big news".
"'We put Kimi in Formula 1,'" Marco remembers Wolff saying. "'What do you think?'
"I said: 'Oh, [it] is a difficult question you ask me. Of course I'm happy that you think about Kimi but are you sure he's ready?'"
Mercedes were at a management away day. Wolff called his senior engineers together to tell them about Hamilton's decision.
"We were reviewing options and trying to come to a fairly rapid conclusion," says trackside engineering director Andrew Shovlin.
"We were all keen to just go with Kimi, which we knew was a bit of a risk. But it was quite exciting and we thought, based on his career to date, he had a good chance of being very good. It seemed like a good challenge."
Antonelli had not even driven an F1 car when Wolff made the call. Mercedes put together a testing programme for him, 20-odd days in cars a couple of years old at tracks all over the world to prepare him for his F1 debut in 2025.
Shovlin and the engineers were immediately impressed.
"It was how rapidly he would get up to speed," Shovlin says. "What you normally see with drivers is they're just incrementally going a little bit quicker, braking a bit later.
"If you compare with other drivers we've seen in an F1 car for the first time, the best I'd ever seen until then was George [Russell]. You suddenly saw someone who was quite similar.
"With Kimi, he took a couple of runs to work out how the car behaved and then he'd be more or less on the limit.
"The other thing you can see is the fidelity of the car control, how they can sit with it right on the edge of breaking away from them on entry to a corner, but they can just control it in that condition.
"Equally, when you looked at the mistakes he was making, they were often errors of judgement or lack of experience. They weren't run-out-of-talent mistakes."
Antonelli made one of these at the 2024 Italian Grand Prix. Wolff decided to give him his first experience of an F1 weekend in first practice at his home race at Monza.
It was a spectacular debut - for both good and bad reasons.
Antonelli set the fastest time on his first lap. Then he went for another. He was flying, miles quicker than anyone up to that point, but then he crashed heavily at the final corner, Parabolica.
"No-one on earth could have got the car around the corner at the speed he was attempting," Shovlin says. "He clearly got into his head that he would try and do something special and it was an error of judgment."
Wolff took Antonelli aside, told him it was OK, and not to worry about it. But the crash had a significant impact on Antonelli.
Wolff was very clear in public about managing expectations of Antonelli going into his debut season.
"I conditioned myself so strong that I said: 'There's going to be moments of brilliance and moments where you want to tear your hair out'," Wolff says.
There were stand-out moments - Antonelli out-qualified Russell at the second race of the season on the high-speed Jeddah street circuit and stuck it on pole for the sprint in Miami.
But the middle part of the season, through Europe, was a disappointment. A change to the rear suspension design made the car nervous and rocked his confidence. His pace was not impressive, and he made too many mistakes.
"We expected more highlights from him," Shovlin says.
Marco Antonelli explains: "Mercedes needed to have a good result after a period that was not like the Hamilton era. And, of course, needed two cars that always take points.
"Kimi felt this necessity. The crash in Monza was very tough for him to forget. It created on him a big pressure."
Wolff said the "moments of brilliance were there" but then there was "a spell of nine races that was really not good".
"Me, personally, I never doubted," says Wolff. "Other people doubted. In the team and externally."
A year on from his practice debut, Antonelli crashed again in Monza practice.
"This was the point where I said: 'Kimi, you've got to turn this around. This is just not good enough'," says Wolff. "He said: 'I know.'"
Marco Antonelli says he and his son talked a lot during this period and that Kimi "understood that everything can change".
"The period was bad but you can see light at the end of the tunnel," he says. "And step by step he started to take confidence."
Once F1 had left Europe in the autumn of last year, there was a shift.
"Suddenly, we felt like we were making really good progress," says Shovlin.
"There were signs towards the end of the year. I'm not saying any of us thought we'd see what we've seen so far this year, but that we had a decent F1 driver."
Antonelli has been rather more than that this year. He has taken the season by storm, and established a consistent supremacy over Russell.
In the best car in the field, Antonelli has taken six poles and six wins in 11 races and heads into the second half of the season, starting at the Dutch Grand Prix this weekend, with a 50-point lead in the championship, and well on course for his first world title. If it had not been for dodgy reliability, he could be even further ahead.
The extent of this turnaround has shocked almost everyone.
"We were all surprised," Wolff says. "My thoughts were always that he needed to make the experience of knowing all the tracks, the pressure of performing on such a high level under the spotlight of the media, the constant public feedback, whether you're doing well or not, the situations everyone wanted to be close to him.
"There wasn't one single defining factor where I would have said that made it difficult for him, but this year, he knew exactly what to expect. What was really nice to see is that the self-confidence, without feeling any entitlement, has shone."
Marco points to his son's "very strong" mentality.
"In F4 and Freca, he started with not good results, and he was able to remake everything and, at the end, work hard and win the championship," he says.
"We talk about F1. I don't know what the spark is in his brain, but Kimi in the past did the same."
Verstappen says: "For me, there was never any doubt that he would make the jump the year after and already be a lot more consistently competitive.
"It's normal in the progression of a driver. In your rookie season, it can be quite tough, but at the moment, of course, he's doing an amazing job."
Kimi pays tribute to his father, describing him as his "rock", while Wolff also praises the driver's "typical Italian family".
"They are caring, they are loving," Wolff says. "Kimi's character, he's gentle, he has empathy, he has charisma, he has the right amount of intelligence for being a racing driver."

Mercedes have been talking to Antonelli about managing his emotions, which have flared at times this season, such as in the sprint in Canada, when the racing between the two Mercedes drivers came close to boiling over.
Shovlin says: "He just says: 'I'm young, I'm Italian, what do you expect?'"
The remark reveals Antonelli's sense of humour, but also a maturity and self-awareness that might not always be expected in someone so young.
Wolff says: "He has all that. He's actually not a typical emotional Italian. He's so clear [in] what he needs to do in a car. I don't see lots of emotion. I see full focus, full concentration. I see, 'OK, this is a problem, let's analyse it, and move on.'
"You see him in a debrief afterwards. You couldn't really say whether there was a bad or a good session. It's all very balanced and stable."
Antonelli took advice on this when he met tennis legend Roger Federer at Wimbledon this summer.
"We chatted about my races," Antonelli says. "About when he used to play, and about life in general.
"About pressure, he just told me to focus on one race at a time, just focus on what you can control, and also to control the emotions, especially the ones that can make you do mistakes."
Federer's words echoed something Marco has always impressed on his son.
"In our family, we use this concept in normal life as well," he says. "We have to live every day our best day. You work hard every day to arrive at the end of the project you have."
Back in February 2024, Wolff followed up his phone call to Marco with a meeting in Milan.
"Toto said: "Of course it will be difficult, but I think after one year of experience, we can do very well with Kimi in F1," Marco says.
"The project was 2025 experience, 2026 start to achieve results. I think we overachieved."

The Supreme Court reportedly sought a progress report from Infosys co-founder Nandan Nilekani-led task force, which was formed to suggest structural reforms in the National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test (NEET).
The alleged irregularities in the NEET examination led to mass protests by the Congress Janata Party in June-July 2026.
The Centre told the Supreme Court that the panel has held exhaustive consultations and is likely to submit its first interim report by the end of this month, news agency PTI reported.
Solicitor General Tushar Mehta told a bench of Justices PS Narasimha and Alok Aradhe that all the suggestions had been placed before the panel, which held consultations with the members of an earlier committee led by former ISRO chairman K Radhakrishnan.
According to Bar and Bench, the Supreme Court remarked that the panel's recommendations should not remain limited to paper and must translate into some effective changes on the ground.
It told Mehta that the most important thing in the matter is that the government should look into institutionalisation of the entire process to conduct NEET.
"Progress is one matter. What are the suggestions made? Most important is the institutionalisation of it. See, you know what we are a little concerned about. We had the Radhakrishnan Committee. So what we have today is only a committee report. Correct? Full stop. It must progress further. Consideration of the recommendations and it's implementation is the most important part," the Bench said, as per the report.
A Bench of Justices PS Narasimha and Alok Aradhe directed that an affidavit in this regard be filed within two weeks. The bench asked the joint secretary to the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT), who is assisting the Nilekani panel, to file the affidavit before the court on the steps taken so far.
"We direct the Joint Secretary coordinating with the High-Powered Committee, Joint Secretary, DoPT, who is coordinating with the High-Powered Committee, to file an affidavit indicating the progress made by the Committee. Let the affidavit be filed within another two weeks from today. List after Three weeks," the Court directed, as per Bar and Bench.
Justice Narasimha said he and Justice Aradhe would like to visit the newly-upgraded facility of the National Testing Agency (NTA) to examine the system.
"We'll come and see whether the system is actually in place, whether it is working or not working, manpower, all these things," the judge said.
The Supreme Court was said that the NTA now has a separate permanent space near Minto Road. Justice Narasimha said that they would physically visit it and examine whether manpower is in place for a working system, Bar and Bench reported.
Justice Narasimha added that at least half of the staff of NTA should be permanent and not everyone should be on deputation from other departments.
"You must know that permanency of the entire system is key. There should be a permanent setup, permanent staff, permanent verticals. Very less deputation should be there. Only then a permanent structure will come up," the bench told Mehta.
"Also, your relationship with other working institutions, how you are collaborating with them, how much data is... Whether we need statutory backing," the Court was quoted as saying.
The Supreme Court was hearing a batch of petitions filed in light of the question paper leaks connected to the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (NEET) this year.
The petitions before the court include one filed by the Federation of All India Medical Association (FAIMA) through advocate Tanvi Dubey, seeking replacement or restructuring of the NTA.
Among other prayers, the plea has sought the “digital locking” of question papers, transition to a Computer-Based Test (CBT) model and publication of centre-wise results to detect anomalies.
The petitioner also filed an application with suggestions on how the shift to CBT could be carried out.
Another petition, filed by the United Doctors Front through advocates Ritu Reniwal and Charu Mathur, seeks the establishment of a statutory national testing body, with better oversight and direct parliamentary accountability.
A separate plea has also been filed by Rashtriya Janata Dal (RJD) MP Sudhakar Singh, social activist Anubhav Garg, Indian Medical Association national spokesperson Dhruv Chauhan and political leader Harisharan Devgan.
The plea seeks a transition of NEET-UG to a CBT format and the replacement of the NTA with a new independent examination authority, among other prayers.
On August 19, observing that there is a need to institutionalise the reforms in the NTA, the top court directed the Centre to inform it about the steps taken to implement the recommendations of the Radhakrishnan panel and the Nilekani committee.

(With inputs from Bar and Bench)

Welcome to Edition 9.11 of the Rocket Report! The most interesting story of the week, in our view, is a deep dive by Stephen Clark, linked below, into the dwindling fortunes of United Launch Alliance. As recently as a decade ago, the launch company, co-owned by Boeing and Lockheed Martin, could claim dominance over the US industry. But those glory days are fading fast. So what’s next for a company that is tied to an expendable rocket?
As always, we welcome reader submissions, and if you don’t want to miss an issue, please subscribe using the box below (the form will not appear on AMP-enabled versions of the site). Each report will include information on small-, medium-, and heavy-lift rockets as well as a quick look ahead at the next three launches on the calendar.
Avio seeks to cash in on Falcon 9 retreat. Italian launch services provider Avio has seen an influx of customers who were unable to secure launch opportunities with SpaceX, European Spaceflight reports. “I can tell you SpaceX has already gone captive because we have a whole bunch of customers coming to us and saying, ‘Oh my God, can you fly us?’” Avio CEO Giulio Ranzo said during the company’s September 10 earnings call. In recent months, SpaceX told multiple prospective customers that it was no longer accepting new orders for commercial Falcon 9 launches.
Europe’s answer to this, a subsidy? … According to Ranzo, some customers who had been turned away by SpaceX used the International Space Summit in Paris last week to lobby European institutions for financial support that would help offset the higher cost of launching with a European provider. Although prices for Avio’s Vega C rocket are not public, it likely costs about $60 million for a launch on the solid-fueled rocket. In our view, subsidizing launches on expendable launch technology is a poor plan. The continent should increase investment in developers of more competitively priced rockets.
Vega C successfully lofts two satellites. Speaking of Avio, a Vega C rocket launched on Tuesday from French Guiana, successfully carrying the European Space Agency’s FLEX Earth Explorer satellite and the Copernicus Sentinel-3C into low-Earth orbit. It was just the second launch of the Italian-made Vega rocket this year. A new launch adapter called Vespa allowed both satellites to be stacked inside the rocket’s fairing, the European Space Agency said.
Two for the price of one … An evolution of Europe’s Vega family of rockets, Vega-C can launch 2.3 metric tons into low-Earth orbit. “Preparing and launching two satellites together is no easy task,” ESA’s director of Earth observation programs, Simonetta Cheli, said. “My thanks go to the many experts who have contributed throughout both satellites’ development, testing, and preparation for launch, and who have worked tirelessly to ensure that both satellites have reached orbit safely.”
Rocket Report
Keep up with the latest in space exploration and rocket launches.
French company test-fires new rocket engine. French launch startup Sirius Space Services has successfully test-fired a complete prototype of its STAR-1 rocket engine for the first time, European Spaceflight reports. The company announced the milestone on Sunday, stating that it had conducted the first hot-fire tests of the complete STAR-1 engine at Airborne Engineering’s propulsion test facility in southern England.
Playing a starring role … According to the company, the testing included multiple successful ignitions. These tests marked the first time that all of the engine’s critical subsystems had operated together. These included the turbopumps, combustion chamber, injector plate, avionics, and software. The liquid oxygen and methane-fueled STAR-1 is designed to produce 55 kN of thrust. The engine will be used across the company’s planned family of launch vehicles, which will use a common core stage featuring nine STAR-1 engines.
China launches four rockets in two days. China carried out four launches in quick succession, starting Tuesday, using its Jiuquan and Hainan spaceports and a maritime mission from the East China Sea, Space News reports. The rockets were: LandSpace’s Zhuque-2E; Orienspace’s Gravity-1; the Chinese space agency’s Long March 12; and ExPace’s Kuaizhou-11. The launches occurred within 44 hours of one another.
A maturing commercial industry … Notably, three of the four launches were from commercial or quasi-commercial entities distinct from the Chinese government. This highlights the growth of the country’s commercial space industry and suggests that the buildout of constellations in China will no longer depend on the country’s traditional fleet of Long March rockets. The industry, as well, is moving rapidly from rocket test flights to operational missions.
SpaceX hits Falcon 9 milestone. SpaceX launched a trio of satellites for its oldest commercial customer, SES, on a Falcon 9 rocket flying Sunday afternoon from Florida. Notably, this was SpaceX’s 700th Falcon rocket launch to date, split between 687 Falcon 9 rockets and 13 Falcon Heavy rockets, Spaceflight Now reports.
A lot of missions for a single rocket … SpaceX launched the mPOWER-F mission using the Falcon 9 first stage booster with the tail number B1080. This was its 29th flight after launching four missions to the International Space Station, the European Space Agency’s Euclid observatory, SES’ Astra 1P, and 22 batches of Starlink satellites. This was also the 400th orbital launch to take flight from Space Launch Complex-40, of which SpaceX was responsible for launching 345.
Two launch companies spar over Mars mission. NASA finally reached a decision earlier this month on the development of a “Mars Telecommunications Network” spacecraft, selecting Blue Origin to develop, launch, and operate a $700 million spacecraft at Mars, Ars reports. However, the other main competitor for the award, Rocket Lab, was not happy—at all. The company filed a protest of NASA’s decision with the US Government Accountability Office.
A war of words … “The agency’s punitive review of Rocket Lab’s technical volume was inconsistent, making incorrect assertions and conclusions,” Rocket Lab said as part of the protest. In response, Blue Origin said the protest could potentially delay the mission’s goal of launching in 2028. “We remain confident in the strength of our proposal, in NASA’s rigorous selection process, and in Congress’s clear intent to support competition for the Mars Telecommunications Network program,” Blue Origin replied.
SpaceX set for first Starship orbital flight. Pending regulatory approval, SpaceX said this week it intends to launch its 14th Starship mission as early as September 22, Ars reports. The company set a target liftoff time of 7:15 am local in Texas (12:15 UTC), with a 75-minute launch window. (Note on Thursday, new notices to mariners indicated the launch target had slipped to September 28.) This flight is notable, as it will be the first time that SpaceX attempts to launch the experimental vehicle into orbit.
Delivering a long-promised capability … The super heavy lift rocket will be carrying 26 of the larger V3 Starlink satellites into an orbit 275 km above the Earth. SpaceX said the Starship upper stage will seek to complete six orbits around the Earth before completing its mission after about 10 hours. Reaching orbit would mark a significant milestone in the company’s Starship development campaign, which conducted its first test flight on April 20, 2023, and has since made progress in fits and starts.
What does the future hold for United Launch Alliance? Pretty much every rocket company in the United States, save one, has embraced two fundamental tenets: reusability and diversification. The exception? United Launch Alliance, which was founded in 2006 during an era when the US government was the dominant force in the domestic launch market. But 20 years later, with the rise of SpaceX and a host of new startups building medium-lift and large rockets, the time of ULA’s dominance is long past. In a new feature, Ars explores where the company may go from here.
Getting back to flying … The rollout of the company’s new Vulcan rocket has been dogged by problems with the vehicle’s solid rocket boosters. But soon, perhaps by the end of this month, Vulcan could return to flight with a commercial launch of satellites for Amazon. This comes amid worsening finances for the company, co-owned by Boeing and Lockheed, which has been seeking to raise additional funding. A new owner willing to invest in new technology could be the company’s only long-term hope.
Chinese space company reveals Raptor 3-like engine design. The Chinese launch startup Space Pioneer, which has raised nearly $1 billion, showcased a new design for its Tianhuo-21 methane-liquid oxygen engine this week, which was subsequently shared on social media. From outward appearances, the engine looks strikingly similar to SpaceX’s Raptor 3 engine. Its thrust, 2,450 kN at sea level, is also virtually identical to that of the Raptor 3.
Would it be difficult to replicate? … In response to Space Pioneer’s engine design, SpaceX founder Elon Musk said copying Raptor 3 would not be easy. “I would recommend against a new company trying to make Raptor 3,” he said on X. “While it appears simple on the outside (necessary to survive extreme heat without a heat shield), the inside has very complex geometry that can only be manufactured using highly modified 3D metal printing.”
Falcon Heavy nailed Roman telescope’s launch. NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is gliding toward its distant observation post on a pinpoint trajectory so precise that engineers estimate the spacecraft’s fuel load will last twice as long as their initial expectations, Ars reports. The $4.3 billion observatory’s designers originally planned to load enough propellant into Roman’s four fuel tanks for a minimum lifetime of five years, plus a potential five-year mission extension.
That was a conservative estimate … “As a result of exquisite planning by our orbital dynamics team, brilliant execution by the operations team, and a precise launch from SpaceX, Roman has fuel for at least 22 years of potential science operations,” Jamie Dunn, center director at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center, said. The Roman telescope launched August 30 from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket, kicking off a mission to widen our view of the Universe.
Blue Origin studying full-flow staged combustion. Blue Origin and the Rocket and Space Propulsion Division of the Air Force Research Laboratory at Edwards Air Force Base have announced an expanded private-public partnership to develop new rocket propulsion technologies, the company said this week. The new agreement comes as “we work to develop next-generation rocket propulsion technologies,” said Nicholas Robertson, senior vice president of engines at Blue Origin. “Studying these historic and technical artifacts grounds our engineering models in real government research.”
Also working on lunar-lander engine … The Blue Origin news release notes that the Air Force lab has done pioneering work in oxygen-rich and full-flow staged combustion technologies. The company said it would also continue to collaborate on testing and maturing the BE-7 lunar lander rocket engine with the Air Force at the Area 1-42 High Altitude Rocket Test Facility at Edwards.
Next three launches
September 19: Electron | Owl by the Dozen | Māhia Peninsula, New Zealand | 03:15 UTC
September 19: Long March 2D | Unspecified payload | Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center, China | 10:50 UTC
September 20: Falcon 9 | Starlink 15-27 | Vandenberg Space Force Base, Calif. | 01:47 UTC
Eric Berger is the senior space editor at Ars Technica, covering everything from astronomy to private space to NASA policy, and author of two books: Liftoff, about the rise of SpaceX; and Reentry, on the development of the Falcon 9 rocket and Dragon. A certified meteorologist, Eric lives in Houston.

At least 48 people have died and about 100 others are receiving treatment in southern Nigeria after consuming a locally brewed alcoholic concoction suspected to contain methanol, officials said on Thursday.
Banji Ajaka, Ondo state’s commissioner for health, said the cases had been reported in the Odigbo and Irele local government areas. A total of 182 people are believed to have been affected and some are being treated in the hospital, he said.
“I took like two shots and I went out on Friday. On Saturday, I noticed that I could not see,” 32-year-old Sola Adebayo told the local TVC News channel from a hospital bed.
Drinking locally made alcohol is common in Nigeria, Africa’s most populous country, especially in rural areas where it is more affordable and poorly regulated.
“This thing happened rapidly. Once they consume, depending on the quantity, the kidneys will pack up, the eyes will go, the brain will be damaged,” Ajaka told The Associated Press, speaking about the drink.
Ondo state police spokesperson Abayomi Jimoh said in a statement that 15 people were arrested in connection with the incident, including one allegedly “involved in the production of substances suspected to contain methanol and is currently assisting the police with investigations.”
Locals told the AP they suspected a popular herbal drink with high alcohol content, known as “Monkey Tail,” was mixed with methanol, causing the deaths.
A trader who sells the concoction in Odigbo, speaking on condition of anonymity for fear of being arrested, told the AP there are two versions of Monkey Tail: an original, safe version, and another version which is unsafe.
Local media reports said the first death was reported nearly two weeks ago.
Nigeria’s National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control is now enforcing a nationwide ban on alcohol in sachets and small plastic containers, which it said are easily accessible to children and young people.

WASHINGTON — Health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. returned to his roots on Thursday during a keynote address at a conference hosted by the Children’s Health Defense, an anti-vaccine nonprofit he helped start.
The CHD speech served as a victory lap for Kennedy at a key moment for the MAHA movement — just before midterm elections that could determine the viability of his agenda, and serve as a referendum on the GOP’s approach to health care reform. Kennedy, who had previously tried to downplay his anti-vaccine activism, has now made it central to his legacy as health secretary.
His remarks appeared at first to be a recap of Kennedy’s agenda over the past year — flipping the food pyramid, scrutinizing chemical additives, and changing hospital meals. About halfway through, however, after mentioning work his agency is doing on electromagnetic frequency and “chemtrails,” he delivered for his fervently vaccine-distrusting base.
“The question is: Should we be looking at the potential that some of these chronic illnesses are associated with vaccines?” Kennedy said as an image of a Hepatitis B vaccine package insert appeared on screens inside the conference center ballroom.
“ADVERSE REACTIONS,” the insert read, above text describing how researchers collected adverse reaction information from 147 healthy infants and children enrolled in three clinical trials.
“They were monitored for only five days, and there was no placebo,” Kennedy said. “There’s no way any other product would get FDA approval with that few people.”
At the time, the Food and Drug Administration accepted the trials including 147 participants alongside data from thousands of babies vaccinated with an older version of the hepatitis B shot. Trials including thousands of children that were conducted after the hep B vaccine entered the market have provided further evidence of efficacy and low risk.
Universal newborn vaccination led to a 99% drop in chronic hepatitis B infections among children and teens. The Trump administration ended the policy last year.
Kennedy spent over 20 minutes casting doubt on the safety of vaccines at the CHD gathering, saying the public has “no idea” about the risk profile of shots that have been administered tens of millions of time. While saying serious harm from vaccines was probably “very rare,” the secretary at various points suggested – without evidence – that vaccines were underpinning an epidemic of chronic illness in the United States. He used the package insert as proof.
In order to market their product, vaccine makers are required to disclose conditions that people (adults and children) reported after getting vaccinated, but which are not necessarily correlated with vaccination. “It is not possible to reliably estimate their frequency or establish a causal relationship to a vaccine exposure,” the Hep B insert says.
Nevertheless, Kennedy drew a link between chronic disease and the 18 vaccines previously recommended for American children.
“There are 454 adverse events listed in total, and they include almost all of the injuries, like diabetes, death, sudden infant death syndrome, anorexia, allergic reactions, allergies, asthma, autoimmune diseases,” he said. (The Trump administration’s changes to the childhood immunization schedule are the subject of an ongoing lawsuit.)
The Department of Health and Human Services is now conducting research on over 150 of the most serious adverse events that have been reported after vaccination to determine whether they could be linked to certain vaccines, he said. Kennedy also noted a litany of other vaccine-related initiatives happening across agencies, including a task force review of the safety, timing and sequence of childhood vaccinations, and an expansive project involving health data from Medicare and Medicaid, states and private health insurers.
Kennedy blamed the nation’s poor system for reporting adverse events for letting issues fly under the radar. HHS is working to make the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System more user-friendly, and planning to compensate doctors for their time when they submit information about possible vaccine side effects and injuries, he said without offering additional details.
The secretary previously said he wanted to automate the VAERS system in order to boost data collection.
Even if vaccine-related injuries are rare, he said, “In our country, we care about rare illnesses and deaths. We care about every child who dies from measles. They get headlines.” This was the only time the secretary mentioned measles, which has been rapidly spreading in the U.S. and has contributed to at least four deaths in Pennsylvania.
Despite uproar among physicians, biotech companies and others in public health over the Trump administration’s vaccine policy, Kennedy has gotten even the president to embrace his ideology.
On Thursday, he emphasized that he had Trump’s support. “Let me be clear: You have a strong and steadfast friend at the White House,” he told the crowd.
As Kennedy ended his speech, walking offstage to hearty applause, a voice overhead announced the next speaker: Andrew Wakefield, the discredited British physician whose work in the late 1990s helped kickstart the anti-vaccine movement.
Nicholas Florko and Matthew Herper contributed reporting.

Several Hyderabad clinics came under the Telangana Medical Council’s (TGMC) scanner on Sunday, September 13, after people without required medical qualifications or statutory registrations were found practising allopathy, prescribing medicines and treating patients during surprise inspections.
The inspections were carried out by TGMC members Dr. G. Srinivas, Dr. V. Naresh Kumar and Dr. K.U.N. Vishnu. At Shifa Clinic in Golconda, M. Shabbir Hussain with a BUMS qualification, was allegedly providing allopathic treatment to both paediatric and adult patients without required registration.
At Health Care Clinic in Rajendranagar, two persons including Farooq, who stated that he had completed Intermediate, and Gazala, with a BUMS qualification, were found treating patients without the requisite medical qualifications.
At Sai Ganesh First Aid Centre, Ch. Narayana, and at Mother First Aid Centre, Dileep, were also providing medical services without the requisite qualifications. At Sai Clinic, Rajasekhar was allegedly practising medicine in the name of B. V. Ramanath without the required registrations.
The council also flagged the medical credentials and surgical practice of a doctor at Shreya Hospital in Serilingampally. Dr P. Sharath Babu, with an MBBS degree, was presenting himself as an MS Orthopaedic and performing orthopaedic procedures, including joint replacement surgeries. At Bhaskar Clinic, Bhaskar with a BA degree was operating a clinic in the name of Dr. Anita and providing medical services. Further investigation is underway.

Rosenberg: Russia's elections will have few surprises, but for the Kremlin they matter
- Published
The system of power in Russia is often referred to as "managed democracy" (where the Kremlin does the managing).
That means huge powers for the president and few political surprises.
This weekend's election is set to deliver another parliament dominated by the party of power, United Russia, and a house of MPs fiercely loyal to Vladimir Putin.
Critics dismiss the vote as neither free nor fair.
But the Kremlin doesn't care what the critics say.
"We have our own political system, our own political process," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov explained recently.
That means no curveballs for the Kremlin. No surprises. So no story?
Far from it.
For the Kremlin, the election of 450 deputies to the lower house of parliament, the Duma, is important. This is the first parliamentary election here since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The Kremlin will use it to claim that most Russians back the president and the war, as well as to promote the political careers of soldiers back from Ukraine: officials say nearly two hundred war veterans are taking part in the election.
As for the election campaign, that has provided a window on Russian society four-and-a-half years into the war.
I said no surprises. But there have been some.
"Good evening and welcome to tonight's campaign speeches by candidates for Duma Electoral District 158," said the anchor on state TV.
The studio director cut to a wide shot revealing six empty lecterns.
"The candidates haven't turned up," admitted the host. "So, it's goodbye from me."
In another TV debate (where the politicians were present) one crooning candidate sang his pitch:
"The Communist Party, onwards we go!
"We're with the people, don't you know?"
More X Factor than exit poll.
Yet a musical manifesto is strangely appropriate. In the previous Duma, everyone seemed to be singing from the same hymn sheet. At the final session of parliament in July, MPs stood and applauded as the speaker of the house chanted repeatedly:
"Russia, Putin, Victory! Russia, Putin, Victory!"
It was a signal that all MPs in parliament should back President Putin and the war.
"All parties in the Duma, every single one, voted in favour of 170 laws to support the special military operation," Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov told me with obvious pride about the last parliament.
"In that sense there is 100% agreement in the Duma."
I caught up with Zyuganov on the campaign trail outside Moscow at a bread and biscuit factory. As I watched rows of identical-looking loaves speeding along the conveyer I thought about Russia's parliament. It's not that all parties in the Duma are identical: some are more nationalist, others – like Zyuganov's party - more left-wing.
But when it comes to backing the Kremlin's legislative initiatives and supporting the "special military operation" they vote the same way. Such "systemic" parties are vital cogs in Russia's Kremlin-centric political machine.
And if a party doesn't support the war?
One such party - Yabloko - is calling for a ceasefire in Ukraine. Back in July it was the only anti-war party in Russia to be registered for the election. Twelve days later, though, the Supreme Court removed it from the ballot. That was widely interpreted as a sign of Kremlin concern that anti-war messaging could strike a chord with Russian voters.
Despite Yabloko's exclusion from the party list, some of its candidates are still running in individual constituency races. Though in recent weeks growing numbers of Yabloko candidates have been detained by police, prosecuted for various offences and barred from the election.
"The police are carrying out a political order. That's no secret," Yabloko candidate Grigory Grishin tells me.
"This way, the authorities are setting the boundaries within which they believe the elections should take place.
"It is well known that the demand for an end to the bloodshed in this conflict with Ukraine is very popular. In my opinion, most people in Russia now want peace and Yabloko helped people express this. That's why it's been excluded from the party lists, and why individual candidates are being barred."
For now, Grigory remains a candidate. But the police recently came to his flat.
"Three policemen in civilian clothes asked me to accompany them to the station, which I did. The police said I had posted what they claimed was an extremist symbol: the word 'Navalny' and that, by doing so, I had propagandised extremism via my Telegram channel."
Alexei Navalny was Russia's most prominent opposition leader and Kremlin critic who died in prison in 2024. He'd been convicted on several charges, including extremism.
The Russian authorities insist that the Duma elections are transparent and fair. Critics of the vote point to opposition politicians who have been forced into exile or put in prison. Last year one of the leaders of a prominent independent election monitoring group in Russia was jailed for five years. Grigory Melkonyants was convicted on charges of working with an "undesirable organisation". His election monitoring group, Golos, has shut down.
Fifty miles from Moscow, in the town of Dmitrov, I see little sign of an election.
In the town centre there's a memorial to "Heroes of the special military operation": local people killed fighting in Ukraine.
The war is front and centre of people's minds here.
"We feel it," says Olga, whose son-in-law is a soldier in the "special operation". "Because of the people who've gone to fight and the families left behind with sons, husbands, children and grandchildren there. But these elections can't influence what will happen."
"I'd like us to live in a peaceful country, with no war," Polina tells me, "So that you don't have to worry that a drone will fall down in front of you."
Russians have other concerns, too. Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian oil refineries have sparked widespread fuel shortages, while economic pressures are increasing.
"What worries me," says a barber called Ivan, "is that no matter how much you earn it's not enough. Prices are rising faster than wages. I speak to lots of people in my job. I know how hard-up they are."
Expectations are low that this election will change much.
"Western elections and elections in Russia are completely different things," Grishin explains. "Elections in the West are a way of forming a government, which is replaced later if voters aren't satisfied.
"Elections in Russia never bring a change in government. At best, they're a way of influencing it, of sending a signal. But power in Russia never changed because of an election. That's how Russia is."

At 8.37am local time last Wednesday, a huge mass of rock and ice sheared free from a mountain, sliding 1,200 metres to the valley floor in Nepal’s Langtang national park, about 60km north of the country’s capital, Kathmandu.
Horrifying images and videos soon emerged of a torrent of mud, water and debris that swept down the Lhende Khola valley at speeds approaching 150km/h. Flowing down the Lhende Khola, Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers that run between Tibet and Nepal, the flood water swept away homes, roads, bridges and power plants. Along the Trishuli, water levels rose by as much as nine metres in half an hour. As of the time of writing, the death toll of the disaster approached 1,000 people, with more than 4,400 on both sides of the border missing.
As the rescue effort continued – hampered by bad weather, poor access and the threat of further flooding due to two lakes that have formed after the landslide – Nepali prime minister Balendra Shah said the catastrophe was “not an ordinary” event.
Shah said on social media that “the risks we face in the Himalayan region are increasing alongside climate change … It is now time for us to strongly raise with the international community the issue of the disasters we are experiencing as a result of climate change.”
More on the scale of this disaster and what it tells us about our climate crisis, after this week’s headlines.
In focus
What caused last week’s catastrophe was not immediately clear: initial reports suggested the floods could have been caused by an earthquake in the area that triggered a landslide, while early satellite imagery suggested that a glacial collapse was to blame. Subsequent satellite analysis showed that bedrock underneath a glacier collapsed, with the landslide registering as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event.
“It seems that a massive rock face with the glacier on top of it has essentially gone,” says Adrian McCallum, a senior lecturer in geotechnical engineering at the University of the Sunshine Coast in Australia. One seismologist called the landslide “one of the largest in the last decade or two in the world”.
As Nepal’s Shah said in his statement, our environmental crisis cannot be separated from this disaster. The Himalayas – spanning Nepal, India, China, Bhutan and Pakistan – are warming twice as fast as the global average, putting the region at increased risk of avalanches, landslides and floods. The UN said in 2023 that Nepal’s mountains had lost close to one-third of their ice in just over 30 years due to global heating.
While scientists haven’t definitively linked the Lhende Khola landslide to the climate crisis, they have pointed out that rising temperatures mean permanently frozen mountain slopes are at risk of melting and destabilising.
“Increased temperatures result in increased melt, which results in increased water,” McCallum says. “Movement of water into voids within either soil or rock … destabilises what once may have been a more solid rock mass or soil environment.”
With global heating, mountainous areas are also at risk of permafrost degradation, “glacial lake outburst floods” (GLOFs), and increasingly erratic rainfall, raising flood and landslide risk.
Glacial lakes form behind natural dams as a result of glacier melt, and can cause catastrophic outburst floods if their natural dam walls are breached. More than 12,000 deaths have been attributed to such floods globally.
Given the risks to downstream communities in the Himalayas, scientists have pointed to the need for early warning systems, which would require coordinated international monitoring efforts.
“Wherever the glaciers are receding … you have the potential for a GLOF to occur,” McCallum says, such as in the European Alps and the South American Andes. In North America, an outburst flood causes periodic problems in Juneau, the capital of Alaska.
To be clear, there was no GLOF involved in last week’s landslide. But Nepal has more than 2,000 glacial lakes, and 21 of those, according to the UN, are considered potentially dangerous.
As climate academic Bill McGuire wrote for the Guardian this week, global heating will “leave no part of the planet untouched. As the world processes the horror of the events in Nepal and Tibet, it is a lesson that we ignore at our peril.”

Louisiana firefighters responding to a small house blaze found a wildcat native to sub-Saharan Africa illegally enclosed in the back yard, and an animal welfare agency is now seeking to place the creature in an appropriate environment, according to officials.
Firefighters investigating a report of a minor fire at a home in the suburban New Orleans community of Marrero on Tuesday spotted the cat in question – an African serval – behind the residence in a chain-linked enclosure resembling a cramped baseball batting cage, a spokesperson for the local animal protection services said.
A statement from Jefferson protection and animal welfare services (JPaws) said its director, Michelle Brignac, and humane department supervisor, Victoria Clark, joined firefighters at the scene after they were summoned there. Local laws require an exotic animal permit to legally keep a serval as a pet, and the owner of the home at the center of the case did not have such a document, JPaws spokesperson John McCusker told the Guardian on Thursday.
The statement said Brignac and Clark therefore “subdued the hissing serval and wrangled it” into a transport carrier from its 9ft-by-9ft (7.53-sq-meter) cage that McCusker likened to “a dog kennel”. Brignac and Clark then brought the serval to the JPaws facility in the nearby community of Harvey, according to the statement from the agency, which also shared vivid photographs of the wildcat.
Beside their black spots, svelte physiques and striking facial features, servals are known for their ability to leap as high as about 7ft (2 meters) in the air. So McCusker said JPaws gave the serval an entire room to itself while the agency sought an appropriate refuge for the wildcat, which was born in captivity but whose natural habitat is African grasslands.
Servals share some similarities with domesticated cats that make them immensely popular as pets, including their affinities for grooming themselves, purring, yowling and stalking potential prey.
Nonetheless, they are not easily sustained pets, JPaws’ statement maintained. Servals in captivity do not have the physical space and stimulation needed to engage in normal, healthy behaviors, and they endure chronic stress as a result, the agency’s statement said.
They mark their territory, become aggressive as they mature, cannot be fully house-trained and destroy furniture, and they have been known to barge through walls and doors, according to JPaws. Experts also say servals require a diet and specialized care beyond what house cats need, making them a major responsibility.
JPaws’ statement said the agency would explore having the serval held temporarily at New Orleans’ Audubon zoo. A zoo spokesperson, however, said the institution did not plan to take the serval in and understood JPaws was looking into another arrangement, the details of which were not immediately available on Thursday.
The Marrero serval was the latest of several indicators of the wildcats’ growing popularity, a boom driven in part by social media content creators showing them in videos online.
Cases involving servals have also tended to generate widely read news headlines in North America.
That happened in Ohio in 2023, when officials in the Cincinnati area captured an African serval named Amiry that was spotted in a Cincinnati neighborhood tree and later tested positive for cocaine.
In late 2025, a search for an African serval that escaped a Pennsylvania wildlife center culminated in heartbreak after a motorist fatally struck the wildcat, as Philadelphia’s NBC News affiliated reported.
And the news outlet People reported on authorities in the Canadian city of Vancouver returning an African serval to its owners after it escaped and nestled under a neighbor’s porch in June.
The British Columbia province to which Vancouver belongs had just banned keeping exotic cats such as African servals as pets. But, People reported, the owners of such cats were given until the beginning of May 2027 to apply for permits to legally possess them.

Are the doors to German universities closing for China’s STEM researchers?
As Berlin pursues de-risking, hundreds of visa applicants in China are rejected each year, an investigation finds
Chinese AI researcher “Joy” waited more than seven months to hear that his visa application for Germany had been rejected.
The 30-year-old had been offered a postdoctoral position at a German technical university but the rejection letter said there was an Ausweisungsinteresse, or public interest in denying him entry.
