An Islamic State group member was sentenced on Wednesday to 20 years in prison for aiding the terrorist organization that took credit for a suicide bombing that killed 13 US service members and about 160 Afghans at the Kabul airport five years ago during the US military’s chaotic withdrawal from the country.
A federal jury in Virginia had convicted Mohammad Sharifullah in April of providing material support to the IS affiliate known as Islamic State Khorasan Province (ISKP). But jurors could not agree whether he bore some responsibility for the airport bombing on 26 August 2021.
US troops were conducting an evacuation operation at the airport when a suicide bomber detonated an improvised explosive device near an entry point known as Abbey Gate. Sharifullah’s role in the attack was scouting a route to Hamid Karzai international airport, prosecutors said.
Sharifullah, 28, received the maximum sentence for his one-count conviction in an international terrorism case that Donald Trump heralded last year during a speech to a joint session of Congress.
Sharifullah did not testify at his trial and declined to address the court before the US district judge Anthony Trenga imposed the sentence. The judge said the defendant was a “dedicated terrorist” who expressed no remorse for the “unfathomable” grief and suffering that he had caused.
Trenga heard victim impact statements from several parents of US service members. From a podium only a few feet from where Sharifullah sat, they took turns paying tribute to their children’s sacrifices and describing how the attack has shattered their families.
Mark Schmitz of Missouri asked Sharifullah to turn and look at him as he spoke about the life and death of his 20-year-old son, Marine Corps L/Cpl Jared Schmitz.
“They may have taken his life, but they’ll never take his legacy,” Mark Schmitz said. “A bomb killed my son. It did not kill what he stood for.”
Paula Knauss-Selph, whose son, army SSgt Ryan Knauss, was killed in the Abbey Gate bombing, said the family was “forever changed” by the attack.
“No justice will ever be enough to mend my broken heart,” she said.
Sharifullah requested a 17-year prison sentence, while prosecutors sought 20 years. His lawyers said he was never an ISKP leader and had not been convicted of any conduct related to the airport suicide bombing.
“He was brought here because the government believed he participated in the Abbey Gate attack, a theory which it was unable to prove at trial,” defense attorneys wrote.
Prosecutors said in their sentencing memo that “from his teenage years, when he pledged an oath of allegiance to [ISKP], Sharifullah’s carnage was driven by hate. Hate towards Americans.”
Jurors convicted Sharifullah of providing material support to ISKP. They deadlocked on whether any deaths at the airport “resulted from” that conspiracy. Sharifullah could have faced a possible life sentence if the jury had unanimously decided that question.
According to prosecutors, Sharifullah told a journalist that he wanted to “catch and kill the crusaders” from the United States for invading his country after the attacks of September 11. They said Sharifullah was involved in dozens of other attacks, including a March 2024 assault on a Moscow concert hall that killed roughly 140 people.
Defense lawyers argued that prosecutors failed to present any evidence tying Sharifullah to the Kabul bombing besides his own words during hours of FBI questioning. His team said Sharifullah told FBI agents what he thought they wanted to hear, possibly because he was afraid of being tortured in Pakistani custody before he was brought to the US.
A review by US Central Command found that the Abbey Gate bomber was Abdul Rahman al-Logari, an IS member who had been released from an Afghan prison by the Taliban. According to an FBI affidavit, Sharifullah recognized the alleged bomber as an operative he had known while incarcerated.

Dozens of suspected illegal miners die in Nigerian custody
- Published
Thirty-seven people accused of illegal mining in north-central Nigeria have died in custody, local officials said.
Police have set up an investigation into the deaths, which the Nigerian Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) blamed on an apparent disease outbreak.
However, an intelligence report shared with AFP news agency suggested the group died because of overcrowding and poor ventilation inside the detention facility in the Nigerian state of Niger.
State governor Mohammed Umaru Bago called the deaths "sad and tragic" during a press conference on Thursday.
An NSCDC commander has been detained following the deaths, Bago added.
He declared three days of mourning and postponed the start of campaigning for elections scheduled for January.
Officials had arrested the group of young men on Tuesday for suspected illegal mining near Borgu, in the mineral-rich state of Niger. The region is known for small-scale gold mining.
Two days later, 37 people detained as part of the suspected unlawful operation were found dead inside the detention centre run by the NSCDC.
The NSCDC had earlier said the detainees were possibly victims of a diphtheria outbreak, a serious bacterial infection that can be fatal.
But the agency's national headquarters later said the cause had not been established and would require medical and laboratory tests.
"The NSCDC wishes to clarify that reports attributing the deaths to any specific disease remain subject to medical and laboratory confirmation," it added in a statement.
A survivor told the Associated Press news agency that about 65 people had been held in an overcrowded and poorly ventilated cell, suggesting the dead may have suffocated.
Some relatives of the deceased have disputed the official explanation of events, claiming to local media that they were deliberately killed.
One father told Nigerian media that his son had appeared healthy when relatives brought him food the day before his death and called for an independent post-mortem examination.
Another relative, whose 17-year-old brother was among those who died, said the family had visited him during his detention and questioned how a disease could have killed so many detainees without apparently affecting their guards.
Post-mortem examinations are expected to help establish what happened.
Niger's police chief ordered an immediate investigation into "the unfortunate death of suspected illegal miners while in the detention facility of the NSCDC", spokesman Wasiu Abiodun wrote in a statement.
The victim's bodies have since been taken to the general hospital in nearby Minna for examination.

After wearing it day and night for a week, I found that better health tracking, faster charging, and a simpler interface make Apple’s latest smartwatch noticeably easier to live with.
New Health Sensing System increases frequency and breadth of health metrics. New Readiness score. Audio Intelligence. Faster charging. Cleaner watchOS 27 interface. Beautiful bronze finish, and ceramic is back.
TIRED
Still only 24 hours of battery life. Privacy concerns around Siri Recap and Live Rewind.
On the surface, the Apple Watch Series 12 doesn’t appear to be a major upgrade over last year’s release and, in many ways, it isn’t. But after a week of wearing it day and night, I noticed that the Series 12 feels more intuitive, putting fewer steps between me and the information I need from my everyday smartwatch.
Health tracking is more thorough, thanks to a new Health Sensing System and faster S11 chip. The watchOS 27 update, first announced at WWDC in June and finally available to consumers, gives the Apple Watch a cleaner, streamlined interface that positions Siri AI at the center of the user experience. The most notable addition is perhaps Audio Intelligence, a suite of listening tools powered by Apple Intelligence. Plus, in a fun return, the Series 12 also comes in ceramic, a premium finish Apple discontinued in 2020.
Not everyone needs the upgrade, though. If you’re coming from the Series 8 or older, the Series 12 is a generational leap, with a better display, longer battery life, and newer health features, including sleep apnea and hypertension notifications. Owners of the Series 9 or 10 have fewer reasons to swap, but the battery improvements alone (18 hours to 24 hours) may be compelling. If you already have the Series 11, Audio Intelligence probably isn’t going to be enough to justify replacing a watch that’s already capable of most of the same functions.
Polished, Inside and Out
Visually, Apple isn’t fixing what isn’t broken, and I’m not mad about it. The Series 12 looks nearly identical to its predecessors, but Apple highlights it as its thinnest Apple Watch yet. The aluminum and titanium models measure 9.7 millimeters thick, and the ceramic option is 9.85 millimeters thick. I didn’t notice a difference during everyday wear, but the Apple Watch Series remains one of the most comfortable smartwatches I’ve tested. Aside from the new Hermès collection, there aren’t any new band designs this year, but Apple has added new colors to the existing lineup.
Photograph: Boutayna Chokrane
The new finishes are exciting, particularly the return of ceramic. Apple first offered a ceramic option with the Series 2 in 2016, and it was discontinued in 2020. Today, it’s available in pearl white and night blue, both of which give the Series 12 a softer finish that looks more like an accessory. The ceramic feels more like a fashionable move rather than a functional one, but Apple is following a trend seen across brands like Oura.
I’m testing the aluminum model in the new dark bronze finish, which has become my favorite. It complements most of my wardrobe and gives the watch a more cosmopolitan look than some of Apple’s sportier colorways. Aluminum models are also available in the standard light gold, black, and space gray; titanium comes in natural and a new radiant gold. The aluminum models are now coated with Ceramic Shield 2, which Apple says is 60 percent tougher than the previous Ion-X glass. I haven’t had enough time with the watch to meaningfully test that durability claim, but for someone who tends to knock their smartwatch on doors and countertops, it’s an improvement I’ll happily accept.
Battery life remains rated at 24 hours, which is slightly disappointing when competitors can go longer between charges. The saving grace is faster charging. Fifteen minutes of charging now provides up to 12 hours of battery life, and five minutes gets you up to 10 hours of sleep tracking. This has been the most useful upgrade for me. I can set the watch to charge while I’m getting ready for bed and put it back on for sleep tracking.
Photograph: Boutayna Chokrane
The Series 12 ships with watchOS 27, but most of the software changes will also arrive on compatible older Apple Watches. I particularly love the revamped app layout. Instead of having to hunt through a sea of icons or scroll through an exhaustive list, Apple now surfaces five Siri AI-suggested apps, the Siri app, and a shortcut to the full app grid. The apps I need most are immediately available without cluttering the display.
Apple is also making the watch easier to navigate with one hand, adding a single-tap gesture to Apple’s existing double-tap and wrist-flick controls. Tap your index finger and thumb together to select widgets in Smart Stack; double-tap lets you scroll through them. A wrist flick can return you to the watch face, silence timers, or dismiss notifications. These gestures are particularly handy (ha) when you’re multitasking or if you want to use your watch discreetly.
Better at Reading You
The new S11 chip brings the standard round of faster CPU and GPU performance, along with a more efficient Neural Engine. S11 also powers a remodeled pedometer to improve step counts and distance measurements, particularly during indoor walks and runs. Compared to Series 11, I didn’t notice much difference in numbers. I do, though, appreciate the new Steps complication, which puts my real-time step count on the watch face, so I can check my progress without opening the Activity app.
Video: Boutayna Chokrane
The bigger hardware upgrade is Apple’s new Health Sensing System. The Series 12 has 32 electrodes for improved skin contact during ECG readings, compared with two on the Series 11. The photodiodes have been rearranged in a ring configuration for improved optical sensing, and larger green LEDs have been added for more accurate heart rate readings.
The result, and one of the watch’s biggest selling points, is that it takes more frequent readings. The Series 12 measures heart rate every five seconds, even while you’re moving, whereas the Series 11 takes readings every five minutes when you’re relatively stationary. The Series 12 can also measure heart rate variability (HRV) as often as every five minutes, compared with every two hours on the Series 11, and it measures two variants: recovery HRV and overall HRV. For health-conscious people, the higher sampling frequency gives you a more continuous picture of how your body responds to stressors throughout the day instead of a handful of isolated snapshots. You can see those readings in the Heart Rate app or through the new live heart rate complications.
Video: Boutayna Chokrane
Readiness has at last arrived for anyone who has been anticipating a unified recovery score from Apple. The new Readiness app pulls together activity, sleep, and other health data to estimate how prepared you are for the day ahead. It takes seven days of sleep data before the score becomes available, which is standard for wearables to determine a baseline.
I like having the score as a quick shorthand instead of attempting to contextualize the individual metrics myself, but I stay skeptical of any recovery score that simplifies complicated physiological states using a proprietary algorithm. That said, Readiness is useful as a prompt to pay attention to your body, and I’m glad Apple finally has one.
Apple is also planning a redesigned Health app later this year, including a new Longevity tab and metrics such as Health Age, which compares your health data with that of your demographic. I haven’t been able to test those features yet, but I have a feeling my Health Age will either be oddly gratifying or immediately anxiety-inducing.
A Little Too Attentive
Audio Intelligence may be Apple’s most controversial addition. The suite brings four audio-focused features, including accelerated Shazam and Sound Recognition, the latter of which has been available on the iPhone since 2020. The more intriguing additions are Siri Recap and Live Rewind, which push the Apple Watch into murky waters by using its microphone to capture and process audio. I haven’t been able to test either feature yet; both are slated to arrive later this year.
Siri Recap is Apple’s answer to the AI notetaking boom. When enabled, it can transcribe conversations and generate summaries using Apple Intelligence. I can see the appeal for meetings and classes. During a briefing, I saw Siri Recap turn a PTA meeting into a detailed set of notes and reminders that seemed genuinely useful.
Live Rewind is harder to wrap my head around. The feature maintains a rolling buffer of recent audio so you can ask the watch for a transcript of the last 15 seconds of a conversation. Double-press the Digital Crown and, in theory, you can recover something you just missed without asking the other person to repeat themselves.
The privacy concerns are justified, and you can read more about them here. Apple says the audio is processed in a protected memory area called the Secure Enclave. The S11 chip has an isolated buffer for sensor data, and Apple says raw audio isn’t accessible to the operating system, apps, the user, or Apple. The company also says these features don’t create or store audio recordings.
That’s somewhat reassuring, but it doesn’t eliminate the always-listening worries. Live Rewind supposedly plays an audible chime when activated to alert people nearby. Whether a beep is sufficient consent is a personal judgment call. I will test these features myself once they roll out and will report back.
Apple has refined the everyday experience, added health metrics people actually want, and resisted the temptation to bury the watch under a pile of new features. It’s a thoughtful update, and that makes the Series 12 the best Apple Watch yet.

In 1920, Danish physiologist August Krogh was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine “for his discovery of the capillary motor regulating mechanism.”
His work addressed a fundamental question: how does muscle receive enough oxygen when its demand rises sharply during exercise? Krogh showed how changes in the capillary circulation could help meet this increased demand by bringing blood closer to muscle fibres and increasing the surface available for oxygen exchange.
The work had important implications for medicine because understanding how oxygen reaches tissues is central to conditions in which blood supply is impaired, including cardiovascular disease, peripheral vascular disease, diabetes and wounds that fail to heal. The principles of microcirculation and tissue oxygenation that Krogh helped establish are now relevant to understanding tissue injury, wound healing, exercise physiology and the effects of impaired blood flow.
From zoology to physiology
Schack August Steenberg Krogh was born on November 15, 1874, in Grenaa, Denmark. He entered the University of Copenhagen in 1893, initially studying medicine before turning to zoology.
At the university, he joined the laboratory of physiologist Christian Bohr and became interested in respiration and the exchange of gases in living organisms. He obtained his zoology degree in 1899 and continued working in Bohr’s laboratory.
Krogh combined experimental biology with quantitative measurements and developed instruments for studying physiological processes. His research included respiration, gas exchange and water and electrolyte regulation.
In 1916, he became professor of zoophysiology at the University of Copenhagen.
The oxygen supply problem
Krogh focused on how oxygen moves from blood to tissue.
Muscles can increase their oxygen consumption considerably during exercise. Oxygen carried in the blood must diffuse from capillaries through surrounding tissue before reaching individual cells. The distance between a cell and a perfused capillary therefore affects oxygen delivery.
Krogh investigated capillary distribution in muscle and compared resting and active tissues. He observed that more capillaries appeared to contain blood when muscles were active.
In papers published in The Journal of Physiology in 1919, he combined these observations with mathematical calculations of oxygen diffusion. He proposed that bringing additional capillaries into functional use during activity would increase the available exchange surface and shorten the distance oxygen had to travel through tissue.
This work formed the basis of what became known as the Krogh cylinder model, a conceptual model describing oxygen diffusion from a capillary into the surrounding tissue.
The Nobel-winning discovery
Krogh went further than describing differences in capillary perfusion. He proposed a capillary motor regulating mechanism, through which capillary diameter and blood content could change according to the functional needs of tissue.
The Nobel Committee recognised this work in 1920.
In his Nobel lecture, Krogh described how the number of blood-filled capillaries varied with the activity of tissue. He argued that additional capillaries were brought into use during muscular activity, helping increase the area available for oxygen exchange.
The discovery shifted attention towards the microcirculation — the network of small vessels responsible for delivering oxygen and nutrients to tissues and carrying away metabolic products.
What modern physiology says
Some elements of Krogh’s original explanation have since been revised.
Modern studies do not support the simple idea that skeletal-muscle capillaries are routinely switched between completely closed and open states. Nor are capillaries considered the principal site of active blood-flow regulation.
Much of that regulation occurs upstream, particularly in arterioles. Modern microscopy has also shown that many muscle capillaries are already perfused at rest.
Capillary recruitment is therefore understood more precisely as changes in the pattern and extent of capillary perfusion rather than simply the opening of previously closed vessels.
Krogh’s central insight, however, remains important: the organisation of the capillary network and the distance oxygen must travel through tissue are crucial determinants of oxygen delivery.
From capillaries to insulin
Krogh’s career later intersected with another major medical development -- insulin.
In 1922, he and his wife, physician Marie Krogh, travelled to North America. Marie had diabetes and encouraged him to investigate the newly developed insulin treatment.
During the trip, Krogh visited Toronto, where Frederick Banting, Charles Best and their colleagues had developed methods for producing insulin. Krogh subsequently obtained permission to produce insulin using the Toronto method in Scandinavia.
Back in Denmark, he worked with physician Hans Christian Hagedorn and pharmacist August Kongsted. The first Danish patient was treated with insulin in March 1923, and Nordisk Insulinlaboratorium was established that year.
Scientific legacy
Krogh continued studying physiology after receiving the Nobel Prize. His work on respiration, gas exchange and the microcirculation demonstrated how physical principles and quantitative measurements could be used to understand biological processes.
The Krogh cylinder remains a useful conceptual model for studying oxygen diffusion, although modern research has refined the model using more detailed knowledge of blood flow, oxygen gradients and the three-dimensional structure of capillary networks.
Krogh retired from the University of Copenhagen in 1945 but continued his research. He died in Copenhagen on September 13, 1949, aged 74.
More than a century later, oxygen delivery to tissues is understood to involve cardiac output, blood flow, arteriolar regulation, capillary perfusion, blood oxygen content, diffusion and tissue metabolism.
Krogh’s original explanation has evolved, but his decision to study circulation at the microscopic level changed the understanding of how blood supplies individual tissues. His work established the capillary network and oxygen diffusion as central to the study of tissue oxygenation and microcirculation.

“DealShare is today an empty vessel with $90 Mn in cash.” That’s how an investor who is aware of the company’s financial status, describes the startup. Once valued at $1.7 Bn, this is what DealShare has been reduced to, and the company is actively looking for a potential acquirer, with many names reportedly close to acquiring it at a 95%-plus haircut. Truemeds is said to be one such suitor but the proposed acquisition is not a done deal yet, according to another investor aware of the development. Active discussions are ongoing, but Truemeds’ existing investors are not necessarily aligned with the deal. DealShare is also in talks with other potential buyers, the investors added. Captain Fresh is another name that had surfaced in connection with a possible acquisition but Inc42 has learnt that the company is not pursuing the transaction. The talks for an acquisition at a distressed valuation come after years of restructuring and attempts to find a viable business model for DealShare, which once enjoyed unicorn status. But as the company’s current situation shows, a lot of that was down to the timing of DealShare’s fundraising spree when VCs were investing at valuations that seemed unsustainable. Questions sent to DealShare, WestBridge and Truemeds didn’t elicit any response at the time of publishing the story. For investors, that raises an old question related to distressed investments but with renewed urgency: what should be done with the roughly $90 Mn still sitting on DealShare’s balance sheet? The DealShare 2.0 Plan Tanks The first few years of DealShare’s existence were all about proving that its hybrid B2B and B2C model would be able to compete with the startups that were making inroads into B2B supply chain as well as ecommerce marketplaces. DealShare was pitched as the ecommerce and supply chain destination for consumers and small retailers or kiranas in Tier II, Tier III and beyond. By January 2022, it already had major investors on board and turned unicorn after raising $165 Mn from AlphaWave, Tiger Global and others. The startup raised its next round in rather quick time and was all set to enter the private label business towards the end of FY23. However, the business struggled to gain traction or show growth in the next year. Much of the money was spent in acquiring customers on both sides and by August 2023, DealShare exited the B2B vertical to focus only on B2C ecommerce operations. The company’s net loss crossed the ₹500 Cr mark in FY23 against a revenue of ₹1,963.5 Cr, despite raising more than $200 Mn in the previous year. After two years of struggle, where the company saw the departure of founders Vineet Rao, Sankar Bora and Sourjyendu Medda, DealShare was a shadow of the unicorn it once was. Towards the end of 2025, there emerged a new plan and a so-called DealShare 2.0 vision. Investors brought in Kamaldeep Singh, a former Big Bazaar executive, to run the company and build the next phase of DealShare. DealShare’s FY25 numbers also showed the strain. Revenue fell 13.4% YoY to ₹432.4 Cr, while net loss narrowed to ₹87.7 Cr from ₹167.7 Cr a year earlier. The idea behind this new DealShare was to return to the B2C value commerce, but with a different delivery model. While DealShare was never a quick commerce platform, with its reinvention it tried to reduce the delivery time to a two hour delivery. DealShare realised in comparison to 10-minute deliveries, standard fulfilment timelines would give the startup more room to curb delivery costs while continuing to serve customers looking for lower priced groceries and everyday products. As per sources the startup already had 40 dark stores and was doing about 25,000 - 30,000 orders a day. It focused primarily in cities such as Jaipur, Ghaziabad, Lucknow and Kolkata. The two-hour delivery timeline was a conscious choice. The startup did not want to spend heavily trying to match the delivery times of Blinkit and Zepto. “The 10-minute delivery model was not sustainable,” a source familiar with the operations at the time said, arguing that the economics of quick commerce made it difficult to generate profits after delivery and fulfilment costs. While DealShare did touch close to 38,000 orders a day at some point, another source added that gross margins in this business were around 5%-6%, leaving little to no margin for the company after subtracting costs. A separate industry source said DealShare’s online business faced high customer acquisition and fulfilment costs. “The new leadership had an offline retail background and lacked the technology, product and marketing know how needed to build an online-first business, which is why the company was forced to change tack again,” one of the sources said. By April 2026, DealShare had started cutting back its online operations, and turned to a physical store network as its next bet. The person familiar with the startup said the online business began going through changes from April onwards. At the same time, DealShare was expanding its physical store network, moving from around eight stores to 22. Sources said around 8-10 stores were profitable and that the offline business began generating revenue soon after opening. DealShare had plans to open more stores, including in markets such as Lucknow and Ajmer. Another industry source said DealShare had around 15-20 stores in Jaipur and was preparing to open another 15 stores in Lucknow and Kanpur. The stores were doing “decently well”, as per the source who has seen the numbers. The shift to offline, however, did not settle the question of what DealShare should become. The company considered several versions of the business, including an offline-only mode, retaining the online operation and an omnichannel setup where stores would fulfil online orders. “Multiple variations of AOPs (annual operating plan) and things were discussed, and nothing was sort of closed on by the board,” sources said. One person familiar with the discussions said the board, which was led by WestBridge and Alpha Wave was unable to agree on which business model to pursue. “The board was not able to decide on which way we should go forward with the organisation,” the person said. Investors Struggle To Agree On DealShare’s Future The majority institutional stakeholder in DealShare, WestBridge holds roughly 18.4% of the company, whereas Alpha Wave owns around 16.39% stake in the startup. For investors, the problem was not simply choosing between online and offline. It was finding a model that could make the remaining capital work. The startup had already spent years and hundreds of millions of dollars trying to build a growing business. This online vertical was struggling with low gross margins and high customer acquisition and fulfilment costs, while the newer offline business was still being tested. The indecision became harder to sustain with roughly $90 Mn, or around ₹800 - ₹900 Cr, still sitting on DealShare’s balance sheet, according to another investor familiar with the startup. One source said investors had been discussing how to salvage the remaining money for the startup. “The plan is to sell the startup off to someone who can take the money which we have in a bank account to fund their operations,” the person said. Sources told Inc42 that the talks between Truemeds and DealShare were primarily driven by WestBridge, which is a mutual investor in both the startups. That is where DealShare’s strategic uncertainty meets its acquisition talks. The strategy changes have also coincided with a steady churn in the organisation. Having come to steady the ship, new CEO Singh himself is on his way out. The person familiar with the startup said Singh is serving his notice period. CFO Ashish Shah is also close to the exit door. Besides this, several key employees have also left the startup. As per sources, the company has not carried out a blanket layoff, with employees leaving of their own accord. At the same time, DealShare’s online business has come to a complete halt. The startup began cutting back its online operations around April 2026 and eventually stopped fulfilment from its warehouses. The physical stores continue to operate, but the online business is now “next to zero,” according to the source. The app remains available and sources said around 30,000 users open the app every month, although many leave without placing an order. Roughly 22 DealShare stores are currently operational, but plans to add more stores in Lucknow and Kanpur have been put on hold. The result is a business that looks very different from the one investors were trying to build less than a year ago. The two hour delivery model has effectively been shut down, offline expansion has stopped and the management team brought in for DealShare 2.0 is changing again. Truemeds Talks Put The Cash In Focus The acquisition discussions with Truemeds come against this backdrop. Truemeds has emerged as the frontrunner, but the potential transaction is still subject to investor alignment, according to a person aware of the development. DealShare is also speaking with other potential parties. The roughly $90 Mn cash balance is likely to be a key part of any transaction, and sets the floor for the deal. But another source put it more bluntly. “Why will Truemeds buy a grocery business? It’s just an acquisition of DealShare’s cash reserves,” the source said. It seems that DealShare’s leftover VC backing will be the only thing worth buying. The same source questions whether investors in the potential buyer would be comfortable with such a transaction, particularly if the deal involves issuing shares and diluting their holdings. That is also why the Truemeds deal cannot yet be treated as a done transaction. There are many moving pieces here that may result in the deal falling through. DealShare’s investors appear to be looking for a way out after years of backing a business that has struggled to find a model that can deliver any meaningful growth or returns. For a startup that has raised $400 Mn in funding and touched a valuation peak of $1.7 Bn just over four years ago, the turn in fortunes is nothing short of astounding. 73 goals from dropping deep - we ask Kane to break down how he did it
- Published
As Harry Kane's career has progressed, the 33-year-old has taken an increasingly complete role, popping up to collect the ball as deep as his own box.
Many wonder why a talisman tasked with scoring doesn't spend more time closer to goal, but last season the England and Bayern Munich striker scored 73 goals - the highest tally of his career - while playing deeper than he ever has done.
When I mention this paradox, a grin spreads across his face.
"Until you really understand football and understand what we've been talking about, it's so easy to say 'stay high, you're going to score' but it doesn't work like that," Kane says.
I sat down to speak to Kane about the finer details of his game, shedding light on his unique role.
Watching Kane train, his professionalism is palpable. England's record goalscorer is one of the first out on the pitch. The younger players indulge in playful kick-ups as he watches, engaged in conversation with a member of staff.
From a distance, that makes it easy to confuse him with a coach but, given his role on the pitch, it is a fitting mistake.
Kane's style of play reflects who he is as a person, with those who know him saying he is well-rounded and humble on and off the pitch.
The season is in its infancy but Kane isn't basking in the success of the past 12 months. With only five days of pre-season training under his belt, the England captain completed 90 minutes of Bayern's 2-1 win over Borussia Dortmund to lift the German Super Cup.
As demanding as his roaming role is, he has taken the physical demands of it in his stride. Across the past six seasons, STATSports - a sports technology company Kane has invested in - found his distance covered, high-speed running and accelerations were up 8%, 22% and 42% respectively.
And given how the tactical landscape has changed over that time, it is particularly impressive Kane has been able to not only keep up, but stay ahead.
"Over the last five or six years, man-to-man pressure has become bigger," Kane says.
"European football is physical and top teams are trying to win the ball back high, trusting their defenders and midfielders to defend man for man to win their battles."
Given that change, the best teams have recruited physical athletes and brilliant dribblers who can beat their man when the game becomes a series of one-against-ones.
Kane, not known for his dribbling - and by his own admission "not the fastest", has thrived on his own terms.
Against Dortmund, there was a specific moment Kane dropped deep, looking to arrive in space unmarked. Recognising the danger, two players converged on the Englishman.
Kane's dribbling is cerebral. His speed of thought provides him solutions to problems others would attempt to solve with their feet alone.
After getting low and using his strength to shrug centre-back Waldemar Anton off him, Kane rose, slightly adjusting his body to the right. These micro-adjustments are a hallmark of his game and through them he is able to shift an entire team's momentum.
Fooled by this feint, Daniel Svensson and Jobe Bellingham found themselves wrong-footed as Kane snapped the ball back the other way, opening up the entire pitch from within Bayern's half.
1 of 4
Earlier this year, Bayern boss Vincent Kompany shed light on Kane's unique role, explaining it as being 50% coached and 50% Kane deciding what to do.
"I think it's partly instinct, using my football brain and getting the feeling on the pitch," says Kane. "If, for example, I want to drop and see if the centre-back really wants to commit, he might commit into midfield, but is he going to commit if I drop all the way to my box?
"After the first five or 10 minutes you really get an understanding of how the opposition are going to play, which dictates how I play."
There is a shared understanding at Bayern of an approach that allows team-mates to make sense of rotations that, to the naked eye, appear random.
Kane, who is given more freedom than most, is at the centre of it.
"I feel like my position now is as one of two 10s, and you work together," he says. "You can double up on one side to overload, which causes the opposition centre-backs a problem of who to mark.
"If they want to mark both, they've got to go man-to-man and then that leaves space for our wingers or full-backs to run into.
"It's posing all these questions to the opposition but, personally, I love having someone close to me who I can link with."
Kane built his reputation playing as a lone number nine, so it is interesting to hear him identify instead as a number 10 - in a front two.
"When you're the number nine on your own you can get marked by two centre-backs and you struggle to get touches on the ball," he says. "You're relying on everyone else to find you with the ball."
Showing Kane two clips from last season, I ask him to talk through what was going through his head.
"The thing with our formation is, as long as there's someone in each position, it doesn't really matter who it is. Lucho [Luis Diaz] in this clip is playing as one of those 10s.
"I've come off to try and create a bit of space and Lucho's gone through the centre."
Distracted by Kane's dropping-deep movement, one of the opposition midfielders is pulled towards him. This creates space, allowing Joshua Kimmich to punch the ball through to Diaz.
"I think it's Serge [Gnabry] making the run in behind which takes the defenders back, which allows me and Lucho that space in between. Lucho lays it off and whenever I'm in that position, around 20-25 yards out, I'm always looking if I can get my shot off."
It is one of many examples of Kane initially dropping deep before scoring.
"By playing deep when the play develops, I end up coming into a number 10 spot when everyone's dropped," he says. "I can get shots off from the edge of the box, which is a big strength of mine, or I'm running off the back of players where no-one's picking me up - because the midfielder finds it hard to [track]."
1 of 3
The second clip is from Bayern's Champions League tie against Club Brugge.
Usually Kane is marked by an opposition centre-back, but the Belgian club give that responsibility to their holding midfielder - something he recognises and exploits.
Lennart Karl scores without Kane touching the ball, but the striker's involvement is undeniable.
"These are the little runs, again, not everyone sees," Kane explains. "With Jamal Musiala and Lenny, they're so good at receiving the ball and dribbling so there'll be times where I will actually stay higher and let those guys get on the ball a bit deeper, and I'll try and make runs in behind.
"Without changing my game too much, I try and complement the players around me.
"I know Lenny is so good in those pockets and when he gets there, I'm more thinking of running in behind because, one, he can play me in and I can go through on goal, or two, he can dribble with the ball and do exactly what happened here.
"As soon as Lenny gets in that pocket I make the run and not always to get the ball, sometimes it is just to drag the defender away.
"Now he's one-against-one with a centre-back in the middle of the pitch and that's dangerous for any centre-back."
1 of 3
With the Ballon d'Or announcement on the horizon, Kane's name is in the conversation, primarily for the sheer volume of goals he has scored. What is easier to miss in that debate is the rest of his game.
Kane plays for the team in each phase of the game across the entirety of the pitch, while at the same time producing extraordinary individual numbers that match the likes of Cristiano Ronaldo, Lionel Messi and Erling Haaland.
He has described himself as playing in the role of a number 10, nine and six at times.
In a football world of specific and heavily drilled tactical roles, that is quite the achievement.

For the last 52 days, residents of Jyoti Nagar colony in Kolkata’s Cossipore have been surviving without drinking water. Five public taps serving the area had run dry since July 29, following pipeline work carried out by the Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC).
The colony is located on the bank of the Ganges next to the centuries-old Cossipore Guns and Shells factory under ward number 6. Around 5,000 people, mostly from the Muslim community, reside in the area. However, on July 29, the water supply stopped at all five taps serving the area and has not yet resumed.
The residents alleged that the water connection has been cut off deliberately in the name of repairing the pipeline. “We saw the KMC labourers working on the pipeline at the entry area of our colony in mid-July. On July 28, their work was over and they left. The next morning, the water supply was stopped in our area. We approached the KMC and the local MLA. But nothing has happened so far. We are probably facing this because of our religious identity. The people in the neighbouring colonies have proper water connections,” said Nazma Bibi, a resident.
Residents are forced to use water from the Ganges for bathing and washing. But the water is turbid and unhygienic with many children developing skin infections. Many of them have been undergoing treatment.
Eviction plan
Residents have also alleged that this as an attempt to evict them as the land of the colony is currently under dispute with the Syama Prasad Mookerjee Port Authority. According to the officials, the land historically belonged to the port authority. But the residents have been living in the area for a long time.
In February this year, the port authority moved the civil court to reclaim the authority of the land, comprising over 3000 sq mt. The court issued an eviction order in the same month, but the port officials issued the notice to the residents of the colony in June, asking them to vacate the area in the next 15 days.
“Meanwhile, local BJP workers also started intimidating by calling us illegal immigrants from Bangladesh and forcing us to leave the colony as soon as possible,” said another resident, Alamgir Biswas. On August 19, the residents filed a petition at the Calcutta High Court seeking relief from the eviction order. The High Court issued an interim stay till Thursday on the eviction order.
Yet, the water supply connection has not been restored.
Indifferent MLA
BJP MLA from Kashipur-Belgachhia constituency Ritesh Tiwari did not respond to The Hindu’s request for a response to the matter. However, the locals said he did not pay heed to their problems despite several requests.
“A group of women from the colony went to his office to speak to him regarding the issue in August. He said that the ones who didn’t vote for the BJP will not get any facility. Is this how we should be treated?” said Pinki Bibi, who was one of the residents in the group.
Reacting to the development, Trinamool Congress MP Samirul Islam said it is because of the BJP’s divisive politics. It has been nearly two months since their water supply connection was disconnected. “Why? Because those people are from a minority community. The PM always uses the slogan Sabka Saath, Sabka Vikas. Is depriving people of drinking water an example of that? Why is the Bengal government not taking action on this?” the TMC MP said in a post on X.
CPI(M) MP Bikas Ranjan Bhattacharya held a protest rally condemning the government. He said that the government is violating people’s fundamental rights.
Activists from Association for Protection of Civil Rights (APCR) also issued a statement. “Access to clean water is not a privilege or favour extended to any particular community, locality or individual; it is a basic human necessity. It is the responsibility of the authorities to ensure that citizens are not deprived of essential public services and that such issues are addressed promptly, effectively and humanely,” said secretary Umar Awais.

Flock CEO Garrett Langley has said the company made its first license plate cameras in his Atlanta home, permanently scratching his dining table with drill marks. A decade later, where the company assembles its signature—and fiercely debated—product has become more of a mystery.
For years, Flock touted publicly that its devices were produced in the United States. But more recent marketing materials from the company reviewed by WIRED no longer specify where its cameras come from. One US manufacturer that previously identified Flock as a customer quietly removed a mention of the company from its website earlier this year as public backlash against the company’s surveillance technology grew.
The startup has become the subject of a nationwide protest movement that has prompted dozens of local governments to abruptly stop using its cameras. Congress is also considering legislation that would cut federal funding to states that fail to limit use of Flock and other license plate readers. While police have argued the cameras are crucial tools for deterring and solving crime, activists have criticized Flock for enabling officers to track the cars of their exes, share footage with immigration authorities, and follow the movements of pedestrians.
But Flock’s manufacturing supply chain has received scant attention, even though where its hardware is produced could have implications for US national security. WIRED spoke with current and former Flock employees and supply chain analysts, reviewed data from US import records, and watched past marketing videos featuring Langley to piece together the first account of how its hardware pipeline has evolved.
| Got a Tip? | 
|---|
| Do you know more about Flock’s assembly and supply chain? We'd like to hear from you. Using a nonwork phone or computer, contact the reporter securely on Signal at peard33.24. | 
Flock’s cameras largely rely on suppliers around the world that provide non-custom parts, which are also used in products from other companies. “Our value is in the aggregation and the packaging of all of these things … in a nice waterproof, consumer-friendly device,” Langley said in one marketing video from 2021.
Import records collected by ImportGenius show the company has been increasingly bringing “commodity” cameras, radar systems, and other components over from Primax Electronics in Thailand. Primax is based in Taiwan, but has manufacturing facilities in China, Thailand, and elsewhere.
“My understanding is that these are components, but it looks like Primax manufactures whole security camera solutions,” ImportGenius’ analyst Lynn Hughes says. “Quite a few shipments include ‘Radar’ in the product description which might be related to the radar sensor pods they're attaching to their cameras.”
Flock didn’t respond to most of the detailed questions WIRED asked for this story, though it did provide some general information. “All products that Flock builds are National Defense Authorization Act compliant,” Flock spokesperson Paris Lewbel said in an email, referring to a US law that effectively bars government contractors from using parts made by a handful of Chinese tech companies over security concerns.
Cris van Pelt, creator of the anti-Flock advocacy project Have I Been Flocked, says that while where the cameras are made may have relatively minor implications for US communities, the lack of transparency about their origins underscores a broader problem.
“It all speaks to the fact that there is no real oversight, and that tens of thousands of literal and figurative black boxes are being installed on American roads,” van Pelt says. “If any part of the supply chain is compromised, we would never know. That’s a much bigger problem than where the final product is assembled.”
“Aggregation”
The earliest Flock prototypes were made using cameras ripped out of Android phones bought on Alibaba, which were then attached to batteries and soldered onto a solar panel, Langley recalled in one video. The goal was to prove that a useful device could be created from parts collectively costing between $200 to $300. (WIRED reported earlier this week that Flock’s cameras continue to use smartphone-style processors and leave significant data unencrypted.)
As Flock began securing contracts with homeowners associations, it shifted into a corporate office that also doubled as an assembly line. Langley described the setup as fun, but also unprofessional and arduous—pallets of parts shipped in from China had to be dragged a quarter of a mile through the building multiple times a week.
Around 2020, Flock moved its assembly line to a WeWork-style warehouse facility in Atlanta, according to a marketing video produced by the space’s operator. A handful of Flock employees cranked out as many cameras as they could, with engineers assembling the main camera device and less technical staff attaching solar panels and mounts.
Rather than opening up warehouses, Flock stored cameras in self-storage locations across the country for its installation crews to retrieve as needed, according to two former employees. One described the system as “janky,” noting it may have left cameras more vulnerable to tampering than they would have been if kept in more secure locations operated by Flock itself.
In marketing materials from 2019, Flock touted its cameras as “manufactured in the United States.” The following year, it said they were “made in the USA.” In 2021, it got more specific, telling potential customers that assembly was done by “Flock Safety in Atlanta, GA.”
Over the next couple of years, Flock began shifting final assembly to contract facilities in North Carolina and Wisconsin operated by East West Manufacturing and Plexus, according to a person familiar with the matter. It also opened up its own warehouses.
The person says Flock wanted to keep assembly in North America, both to ease security concerns—particularly about potential Chinese surveillance—and to keep factories close enough that it could quickly customize products in response to customer needs.
A Flock marketing brochure from 2023 described its cameras as “designed & manufactured in the U.S.” By 2024, Flock’s manufacturing partners were capable of producing 500 cameras a day, a ten-fold leap from several years prior, one of the people familiar with matter says. Parts still largely came from Asia.
In mid-May, as backlash against the startup swelled, East West removed reference to Flock from a list of case studies on its website, according to archived versions on the Wayback Machine. (A video from East West promoting its work for Flock shared on LinkedIn in late 2021 remains online.)
East West and Plexus didn’t respond to requests for comment.
WIRED was unable to determine where Flock’s cameras are assembled now. A Flock marketing presentation from this year does not mention a location.
In July, the US Occupational Safety and Health Administration cited Flock for allegedly failing to promptly report a June incident in which an employee was hospitalized for a leg amputation, according to records from the workplace regulator. The records indicate the injury happened at a Flock “audio and video equipment manufacturing” site in Houston, Texas. It’s possible that the location is actually the site of a camera, and the injury came during an installation or maintenance procedure. Flock and OSHA did not respond to WIRED’s requests asking for clarification about the nature of the site and what work may occur there.
Flock is contesting a proposed penalty of about $9,500, saying it reported the injury quickly after learning about it.
Even if Flock’s manufacturing supply chain remains in the United States, it may do little to calm bipartisan backlash against the company.
“Domestic manufacturing is no substitute for accountability over how these systems are built, sold, and used,” says Matthew Guariglia, senior policy analyst at the civil liberties advocacy group Electronic Frontier Foundation. "The multi-billion dollar industry churning out mass surveillance technology is not safer or more acceptable based on where it is assembled.”
Flock’s top competitors vary in terms of how much they disclose about their manufacturing. Motorola Solutions has described its license plate cameras as being assembled at its own facility in Richardson, Texas. Axon has said little about where its Outpost cameras are produced, but has noted it assembles other products in Scottsdale, Arizona.
Motorola and Axon didn’t respond to requests for comment.
US-Made Drone
Flock has been more upfront about the manufacturing of its new surveillance drone. Last October, it announced the opening of its own facility in Smyrna, Georgia to assemble drones and solar panels, as well as refurbish various other products. US law now largely restricts foreign-made drones, including the models from China-based DJI that Flock has been deploying. No similar US rules apply to license plate cameras.
It’s unclear how well the Smyrna operation is faring. Flock repeatedly postponed the timeline for launching its first so-called Alpha drone, which finally “hit the field” in May, according to a company executive. This year, Flock told Berkeley, California officials it would swap out DJI drones for the US model “within two years.”
Lewbel, the Flock spokesperson, says it continues to “bring more Alpha drones online.”

Aerospace propulsion startup DheyaTech has raised ₹43 Cr (around $5.1 Mn) in a funding round led by Avaana Capital, with participation from Unimech Aerospace and Manufacturing. The Bengaluru-based startup plans to use the fresh capital to scale production, establish an integrated testing facility for its gas turbine engines, and work with domestic and global OEMs to accelerate commercial deployments. DheyaTech is targeting flight trials of its engines in Q4 2026. The startup said it has already secured orders from Indian and global OEMs, without disclosing their names or the value of the contracts. Founded in 2018 by aerospace engineers Gurushankara KC, Abhinav Alva, and Chetan Kumar, DheyaTech develops indigenous small gas turbine engines for advanced aerial platforms and energy systems. Its engine portfolio spans thrust capacities ranging from 20 kgf to 400 kgf. The startup said the engines are now entering the commercial deployment stage after years of research and development. DheyaTech claims to have built the entire product development pipeline in-house, covering engine design, development, assembly, and testing. It has also developed a proprietary adaptive engine control unit (ECU), which manages and adjusts an engine’s operation. The startup claimed that it is the first Indian private company to pursue independent airworthiness certification for its gas turbine engines under the guidance of the Centre for Military Airworthiness and Certification (CEMILAC), a DRDO laboratory. Beyond propulsion, DheyaTech is expanding into hydrogen-based technologies and distributed power-generation systems. In collaboration with the Indian Institute of Science (IISc) Bengaluru, DheyaTech has also developed a hydrogen-based flexi-fuel combustor for its 60-kW turbogenerator. A turbogenerator combines a gas turbine with an electrical generator to produce power. DheyaTech’s fundraise comes amid growing investor interest in Indian aerospace and spacetech startups developing indigenous hardware and propulsion technologies. In January, aerospace propulsion startup D-Propulse raised ₹25 Cr from IAN Alpha Fund to develop indigenous propulsion systems based on rotating detonation engine technology. Meanwhile, spacetech startup InspeCity raised ₹100 Cr in August in a round co-led by Ashish Kacholia and Speciale Invest. It plans to use the capital to fund four in-orbit missions and advance its satellite-servicing and propulsion technologies. Advanced hardware and technology startups, including aerospace, defence, semiconductor, and robotics ventures, raised $365 Mn across 66 deals in the first half of 2026.

Venezuela closing in on deal to move $4bn gold reserves from Bank of England to New York
Venezuela is nearing a deal to move $4 billion (£2.9 billion) in gold from the Bank of England to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York after a years-long legal tussle, it has been reported.
Led by acting president Delcy Rodriguez, the government and the opposition reached a rare consensus in August - to work together to recover 31 tonnes of precious metal locked away in London’s underground vaults.
Under the terms of the agreement, the Interim President would gain legal control over the bullion, but would not be unable to sell it immediately, the Financial Times reported.
“The gold is going to the US but Delcy won’t have direct access to it,” said an opposition figure reportedly involved in the ongoing negotiations . “It will be supervised and restricted.”
The reserve could be deployed as collateral for government borrowings, including for reconstruction after the twin earthquakes devastated the South American country at the end of June, killing more than 6,000 people.
The World Bank previously estimated that the damage of what has been described as the biggest natural disaster in decades amounts to $19.6 billion (£14.4 billion).
If finalised, the deal would bring an end to a major dispute, which has lasted almost eight years, after Britain refused to recognise Nicolas Maduro as the legitimate president of Venezuela, claiming the 2018 elections were rigged.
In practice, the move blocked the Venezuelan government’s access to the gold.
The bullion has since been the subject of a prolonged legal dispute in UK courts, and has not been released despite Maduro's capture by the US in January.
The UK Foreign Office said the government is not a party in the legal case to determine who should have control of the reserve.
“The matter is being considered through independent legal processes and is not a decision that HMG can direct or influence,” a spokesperson said. “UK Courts and the Bank of England are independent of HMG.
“The UK maintains its longstanding position of support for a democratic transition of power in Venezuela which reflects the will of the Venezuelan people.”
Reports of the deal come as Donald Trump is making plans for a first-ever meeting with Rodriguez, as early as next week, sources familiar with the discussions told Axios.
It is unclear if the deal will be discussed, if the meeting between the two leaders takes place.
“Iran is tough, but Venezuela is without a doubt the president's top success and Delcy is a key to that," a Trump adviser cited by Axios said. “Unless something goes really wrong, the president wants to make time.”
The Independent has contacted the Bank of England for a statement.

Last year, the District Child Welfare Committee in Chennai dealt with a case where a 15-year-old girl from Nepal had married a 28-year-old man working in Chennai, the two having met on Instagram. With the help of friends, they got married in Chennai.
A month into the marriage, the girl was traced after she made a call to her sister in Nepal. The girl’s family lodged a complaint with the police following which India Child Protection, a civil society organisation working in the area of child protection, intervened to rescue the girl.
Social media and online dating are increasingly exposing vulnerable girls to greater risk of child marriage.
“With advancement in digital communication, the modus operandi in child marriage is changing, making more children vulnerable,” says Bhuwan Ribhu, a child rights activist and founder of Just Rights for Children.
Bhuwan Ribhu says trafficking is a borderless crime, and it requires a borderless response. Online methods of enticement or grooming for marriage, sexual abuse and trafficking have become possible irrespective of distance and geography.
In a study taken by NGO Save the Children, they observed that girls in India faced greater online risk of child marriage and trafficking during the pandemic. The agency continues to work with children and teachers to raise awareness about staying safe online.
According to the National Family Health Survey (2019-21), the national average in India for child marriage is 23%. The prevalence rate in India for child marriage has fallen by 10 per cent. The Bal Vivah Mukt Bharat campaign launched by the Central Government in November 2024 promises to make India child marriage-free by 2030 and is seeing various state governments running different initiatives.
A dedicated CMPO needed
Natharsha Malim H, state coordinator - Tamil Nadu, India Child Protection, says while Tamil Nadu has been making steady progress in reporting and stopping child marriages, gaps continue to exist.
Tamil Nadu, he says, does not have Child Marriage Prohibition Officers (CMPOs) that are appointed to prevent marriages, gather evidence, raise awareness and report data. The District Social Welfare Officer (DSWO) is notified as the Child Marriage Prohibition Officer of the concerned district.
“This is an additional role that the DSWO takes up. We have been asking for a dedicated person to be appointed as many other states have done based on a Supreme Court recommendation,” says Malim.
For example, in Karnataka, the Department of Women and Child Welfare has included pre-university (PU) college principals as child marriage prohibition officers, whose responsibility is to prevent any girl child studying in their college from marrying before 18 years.
Dedicated officials tasked with curbing this practice is particularly required in places such as Salem, Dindigul, Namakal and Cuddalore which has reported maximum cases of child marriages, says Malim. Grama panchayats have to be empowered in these districts to curb child marriage
A rule book for intervention
Malim notes that State Governments have to draw up a Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) for elimination of child marriages.
“The Supreme Court came out with a landmark judgement on child marriages in October 2024, but Tamil Nadu is yet to come out with an SOP,” he says.
Panchayats that make an earnest effort to stop child marriage should be rewarded; and the bravery of young girls that resist coercion by family into child marriage should also be acknowledged.
Bhuwan Ribhu cites the example of a study done by India Child Protection in 2025, wherein cases in Assam dropped by 84 percent following a continuous crackdown by law-enforcement authorities.
How to report a child marriage
File a complaint with
* Child Marriage Prohibition Officer
* District Magistrate
* Nearest police station
* District Child Protection Unit
* ASHA Unit of District Legal Services Authority
* Bal Vivah Mukt Bharat portal https://stopchildmarriage.wcd.gov.in
Source: Ministry of Women and Child Development
Although Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006 has been in existence for decades, enforcement leaves a lot to be desired.
“With amendments to the law and judgments by the Supreme Court, we have been able to see much impact on the ground, along with greater awareness,” says Ribhu, adding, “awareness needs to be supplemented with the enforcement of policies, accountability of institutions, and the use of technology for monitoring.”
Residents association in Chennai hails UN declaration
On September 4, 2026, when the United Nations General Assembly declared November 27 as the International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage, a residents group in Anna Nagar celebrated the announcement.
A small number of residents, close to 150, of Kambar Colony in Anna Nagar gathered at the park in the neighbourhood to watch the live proceedings of the United Nations General Assembly on the designation of November 27 as the International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage.
The programme was organised by the ICWO Tamil Nadu and Kambar Colony Welfare Association. The designation is a significant global commitment to strengthening awareness, prevention and action against child, early and forced marriage. This is a victory for children and civil society organisation that have been fighting to end child marriage.
Awareness banners and charts were displayed, and the gathering concluded with an oath-taking ceremony to strengthen the community’s commitment to end child marriage.
ICWO is a partner agency with Just Rights with Children in Chennai, working with educational institutions and communities on rights concerning children.
A.J. Hariharan, founder secretary, ICWO, says reporting is the key to preventing child marriage. He notes: “we work closely with schools and colleges to help eradicate child marriage. All what we ask them is report any cases of child marriage to the helpline number or a teacher.”
ChildLine Helpline 1098 can also be dialled to report a case.

In a three-day strategic dialogue, Belgium and WHO reviewed progress in their longstanding partnership, and agreed to further boost their collaboration on universal health coverage, health-systems strengthening and equitable access to essential vaccines, medicines and health technologies.
The Belgian delegation – headed by H.E. Christophe Payot, Ambassador of Belgium to the United Nations and other international organizations in Geneva – discussed issues of strategic importance, exchanged views on how to smoothly align WHO strategic directions and Belgium's development cooperation priorities in the context of an evolving global health landscape.
The partners exchanged updates on Belgium's support to global health areas brought in the spotlight during the Belgian presidency of Council of the European Union in 2024. WHO was represented by leadership and technical experts from Headquarters and from the Regional Offices for Africa and for Europe.
"After listening to the leaders and experts of WHO we now better understand how they are navigating these challenging times", said Mr Koen Van Acoleyen, Minister Counselor at the Permanent Representation of Belgium to the UN. "We are honoured that we can walk this road together."
Accelerating equitable access to vaccines, medicines and health technologies
The partners reviewed the current status and the most noticeable results achieved by the Access to Medicines programme funded by Belgium. WHO illustrated its work and challenges with an example of country-level implementation in Senegal. It also explained WHO's policies and work on equitable access and local production. Both parties recognized a shared goal for sustainability of the Access to Medicines initiative, as market shaping is key to ensure long-term success.
Health emergencies and pandemic prevention, preparedness and response
Discussions covered WHO's role in strengthening the global architecture for health emergency prevention, preparedness, response and resilience, including the pandemic agreement negotiations and the One Health approach. WHO's crucial field work on health emergency response was demonstrated by presenting the activities in Gaza. The debate also touched upon threats posed by acceleration of biological risks and zoonoses, along with WHO engagement, in particular, risk mitigation.
Universal Health Coverage (UHC)
Elaborating on progress made on UHC-Partnership, the participants reviewed results achieved by WHO with Belgium support in the period 2021-2024, specifically in Belgium's partner countries. They discussed the way forward, exploring the potential for enhanced collaboration at country level, including eventual alignment between WHO country office programmes and Belgium's country level bilateral cooperation. Examples included a summary of the work and challenges at country level from the Democratic Republic of Congo. The visitors listened to a recap of WHO's policies and work on mental health in the context of primary health care.
The partners also reviewed progress in other areas of collaboration on WHO programmes supported by Belgium, such as Neglected Tropical Diseases and Sexual, Reproductive Health and Rights. The review underpinned the importance of an evidence-based approach in these areas.
WHO appreciates Belgium's commitment and engagement, displayed by the participation of representatives of the country's Federal government as well as the Flemish and Walloon governments. "We thank you for your support, honesty, and strong engagement for global health", said Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Director-General, External Relations and Governing Bodies. "Your efforts in supporting our work in Mozambique and Senegal are clear examples of the crucial work we accomplish together".
Looking into the future
The partners discussed ways forward for the Belgium-WHO collaboration framework and multi-year agreement, including progress towards a renewed WHO-Belgium Country Cooperation Strategy.
The enhanced collaboration between Belgium and WHO will support a strong global health agenda under the WHO 14th General Programme of Work (GPW14). There was a shared vision that UHC and health systems strengthening being at the heart of GPW14 ambitions will be taken as essential scope in WHO's ongoing prioritization work.
"We recognize WHO as a trustworthy partner in global health. We felt proud hearing how crucial our support is to the Organization and how it is having a positive impact at country, regional, and global levels", said Mr Dirk Brems, Director of Thematic and Multilateral Cooperation, Directorate-General Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Aid. "It's important we continue these discussions as we tread uncharted territories, and we look forward to working together for strong and sustained multilateralism".

South Africa 'feels like a prison' for women amid spate of femicides
JOHANNESBURG — Elizabeth Moselakgomo, a 38-year-old manager, mother, and keen runner, went out for her usual afternoon jog in her neighborhood near the Johannesburg airport last week and never returned.
When she failed to come home, her 8-year-old daughter called relatives, who contacted the police. Five days later Moselakgomo's half-naked body was found in the area, with her face so badly beaten it was unrecognisable.
Moselakgomo is one of nine women who police say have been found slain, most of them in a period of a few weeks, in the same area of South Africa's biggest city. The majority of them were sexually assaulted.
Even in a country notorious for some of the highest rates of gender-based violence in the world – with over 100 rape cases reported and some 15 women killed daily, according to police statistics -- the latest spate of murders has left South Africans shocked, angry and afraid.
Police haven't ruled out a serial killer and have warned women to be "vigilant" and not to walk or run alone. The approach is drawing backlash from women on social media who said the onus should be on the police to protect them, not for them to have to curtail their movements.
President Cyril Ramaphosa has promised "no stone will be left unturned" in the hunt for the perpetrator or perpetrators. But many South Africans say the government – which declared gender-based violence and femicide a national disaster in 2025 -- has not done enough to keep women and girls safe.
"Women in South Africa continue to be hunted and denied the most basic right to life and security," said Amnesty International's South Africa Director Shenilla Mohamed. "Women are tired of platitudes. We want to know what is going to be done to make women and children feel safe."
'I can't move freely'
There have been protests in Kempton Park, the suburb where many of the killings have been, as well as in Cape Town, with South African women saying enough is enough.
As Moselakgomo was a keen runner, many local running clubs across the country have been holding runs in her honour and in remembrance of all the victims. At one in Johannesburg, men and women of all ages and races came dressed in black and held a minute's silence before they set off.
"Gender-based violence, but particularly femicide, is such a big issue in South Africa. As a woman you can't do anything alone," one of the runners, 26-year-old Shari Maluluke, told NPR.
"You jog, you can get killed, you go to the post office, you can get killed, in your homes you can get killed…It just makes me angry that I can't move freely, my whole country feels like a prison."
All the women NPR spoke to at the event said they did not feel safe in South Africa.
"You send your location, you share your Ubers," said 31-year-old Didi Tsitsi of the precautions women have to take.
Asked why she thought femicide was such a big problem in South Africa, Tsitsi said she thought there were a number of factors.
"Failure of government and policing, I do think there's a deep-rooted societal issue of what men are brought up to be and what they believe it is to be a man," she said.
"And we still haven't really, I think, dealt with all of the legacies of apartheid – this is I think one of the ways it's manifesting."
Some academic research supports this idea, with studies suggesting years of brutal white-minority rule, under which Black men were denied agency and autonomy, has led to a crisis of masculinity and the entrenchment of patriarchal attitudes.

No fire alarms or sprinklers at Pakistan neonatal unit where fire killed 14, report finds
- Published
An official inquiry into a Pakistan hospital fire that killed 14 babies last month has found the neonatal unit lacked fire alarms and sprinklers, while firefighters reported that escape routes were "locked or obstructed".
One firefighter, who asked to remain anonymous, told the BBC he had heard from other rescue workers that entering the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) hospital in Islamabad was "extremely difficult".
"The doors were locked so they had to break through the windows to enter. Even after getting inside, the doors leading towards the ward were locked."
PIMS has not provided a comment on the report and its findings.
The firefighter said he arrived once the blaze had been put out.
It was "difficult for me to even describe what we saw," he said. "The medical equipment above [the babies] had melted and collapsed onto them."
The report from an investigative committee headed by a retired senior civil servant found "systemic and institutional failure" which meant what began as an electrical spark became a "catastrophe".
- At least 14 babies die in Pakistan hospital fire 
  - Published26 August
- Inside hospital after fire kills 14 babies in Pakistan 
  - Published26 August
For many inside the hospital on the morning of 26 August, the first warnings were shouts.
Abdul Ghafoor was in a nearby ward with his mother, who was a patient, when he heard someone warning that a fire had erupted. He went upstairs to see if he could help.
"The entire ward was filled with smoke, we could not see anything," he told the BBC.
CCTV from the corridor outside shows how quickly the fire spread. According to the report, the first indication that something was wrong came at 06:38 when a nurse can be seen running from the ward to get help, returning 20 seconds later with a security guard.
Another nurse, Razia Noreen, is then seen rushing into the ward, emerging seconds later with one of the babies who turned out to be the only one to survive.
Within a minute, the report says, dense smoke had obscured the camera.
Hivsa Walid, her newborn niece and sister-in-law were in the ward next door. Hours later she told the BBC that they had heard a loud commotion and then realised it was a fire when they saw smoke emerging from the unit where the babies were sleeping.
"In that moment, I couldn't understand what was going on. We just focused on getting downstairs and saving ourselves."
On the day of the fire, authorities suggested the fire had started from a spark in the ward's air conditioner.
The report agrees that this was the most probable source of the fire, due to an overheating electrical supply cable - although it remains unclear what exactly the electrical defect was.
The fire then spread quickly, igniting plastics, equipment and bins.
Several babies in the ward were on oxygen support, but the report says that while oxygen may have intensified the fire, there isn't evidence that it created a pathway for it to spread.
The air conditioning units had undergone maintenance, but the report says this is not the same as a safety check. Back in 2018, the hospital's air conditioning units had been approved to be replaced and upgraded, but eight years later this hadn't happened.
The report states that there was no functioning smoke detection, fire alarms or sprinkler system. It found no evidence that the staff in the unit had been trained or had ever rehearsed how to evacuate the ward of newborns, many of whom were premature or "medically fragile". It also found staff had not been trained on how to isolate the oxygen supply in the case of an emergency.
Several people described chaos and confusion in the hospital.
"There should have been fire extinguishers and protocols, but no one was doing anything," Walid said. "Everyone was just running."
Ghafoor said that he was part of a group of seven or eight who tried to find a way to relieve the thick smoke; they managed to break glass panels at the end of the corridor before firefighters arrived.
The emergency services weren't notified about the fire until 06:54, the report says, nearly 20 minutes after it first began. It says the first rescue workers arrived at 07:01.
Like the firefighter who spoke to the BBC, Ghafoor also said rescue staff struggled to get through some of the hospital's doors.
At the time, the hospital's executive director had told BBC News that the door to the newborns' ward was not locked, but guarded, because of previous incidents of baby abductions from government hospitals.
The report says that while "ordinary access restrictions may be legitimate for security purposes… they cannot render designated emergency routes inaccessible when needed."
The report also found that the hospital had received previous warnings about fire risks. A month before, a fire had broken out at its nursing hostel, raising issues with smoke detection, alarms and general fire preparedness.
It says that the hospital and its senior management "bear the principal institutional responsibility for failing to convert known risks, prior warnings and assigned duties into an effective safety system".
Pakistan's prime minister has directed the inquiry's short-term measures to be implemented within the next three months and ordered fire safety audits of public and private offices and buildings.
He has also suspended eight officials and asked for criminal proceedings to be initiated against them.
