Central Board of Film Certification issues new guidelines after nearly 35 years
Issued by Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, the guidelines retain existing provisions on violence, obscenity, sexual violence, communal content, national security
The Central Board of Film Certification (CBFC) has issued new film certification guidelines for the first time in nearly 35 years, retaining most existing provisions while introducing a specific warning for films depicting narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances. The guidelines also reiterate age-based UA markers for parental guidance, which were incorporated into the framework in 2025.
The CBFC had previously issued guidelines in December 1991.
Issued by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting on September 16, the guidelines retain existing provisions on violence, obscenity, sexual violence, communal content, national security, public order and other grounds for certification.
The only technically new substantive provision in the September 16 guidelines relates to narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances. The 1991 guidelines said scenes that tended to encourage, justify or glamorise drug addiction should not be shown. The new guidelines instead specifically cover scenes depicting or involving the consumption, use or trafficking of narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances.
Such scenes are required to carry the warning: “Illicit Narcotics Destroy Health and Guarantees Imprisonment. Say No to Drugs.”
The new guidelines also provide for three UA age markers — UA 7+, UA 13+ and UA 16+ — under which parental guidance is advised for children below the respective age. However, the markers are not new. They were introduced in the Cinematograph (Certification) Rules, 2024, and the Cinematograph Act also defines them. The government subsequently amended the 1991 guidelines in May 2025 to incorporate the three markers into the guidelines themselves.
CBFC chairperson Shashi Shekhar Vempati took to X to specifically highlight the age markers. He wrote, “Film makers need to highlight these markers in promotional material so that these are clearly understood by the audiences before exposing children to a film.”
Speaking to HT, he explained why the markers have been specifically highlighted in the new guidelines despite already being part of the certification rules. “Reinforcing their importance and creating awareness both within the industry and broader society,” he said.
Much of the rest of the 1991 framework has been carried forward. Several of these provisions have drawn renewed discussion and criticism on social media following the publication of the new guidelines. These include the provision that the modus operandi of criminals should not be depicted, as well as restrictions on visuals or words promoting “communal, obscurantist, anti-scientific and anti-national” attitudes.
The guidelines also continue to state that films should not strain friendly relations with foreign States, endanger public order or the security of the State, question India’s sovereignty and integrity, or contain defamatory or contemptuous material.
The guidelines come days after the government reconstituted the CBFC after nine years, appointing an 18-member board. The previous full board reconstitution took place in 2017. The new board includes actors Suniel Shetty, Preity Zinta, Pankaj Tripathi and Prosenjit Chatterjee, filmmaker Priyadarshan, musician Ricky Kej and television actor Rupali Ganguly, among others.
The reconstitution also followed the appointment of Vempati as CBFC chairperson in May this year, after Prasoon Joshi stepped down following his appointment as Prasar Bharati chairperson.

Boks power & All Blacks of old - what did we learn from series?
- Published
South Africa further cemented themselves as the world's best team with a 3-1 victory over New Zealand in the Rugby's Greatest Rivalry series.
After losing the opening Test in Johannesburg, the world champions won three straight games, comfortably claiming the series with a 43-28 win in Baltimore.
The fourth Test, played in the United States, came after three Tests in South Africa where the All Blacks continued to show promising signs under Dave Rennie.
With the Rugby World Cup next year, what did we learn from the series, which replaced this year's Rugby Championship and will be played again in 2029?
Power remains Springboks' trump card
New Zealander Tony Brown's arrival as attack coach in 2024 pointed to South Africa's ambition to dominate in all facets of the game.
The former Highlanders head coach, who will join the All Blacks in 2028, is known for creating a cohesive attacking shape built on sharp ball movement.
But having been outscored in terms of tries over the first two Tests, the Springboks flipped their pack-power trump card - pivotal to their back-to-back World Cup successes - to prevent a repeat of New Zealand's victorious 1996 series win in South Africa.
Nothing illustrated that more than a monster maul that started just inside New Zealand's 22 and ended with Malcolm Marx peeling off to score the decisive try under the posts.
That came after a penalty try from a scrum in the first half. In Baltimore, their power again proved too much.
"South Africa have tried to play expansively a couple of times when we have dominance after hurting teams in the maul or scrum," Schalk Brits, a 2019 World Cup winner, told BBC Sport.
"New Zealand didn't have that dominance in the forwards, but people said they played beautiful rugby. I don't care if it is beautiful or not.
"Beauty is in the eye of the beholder and I love a maul and scrum."
Fly-half Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu, who was injured at the end of May, returned to start all four Tests. He was initially named on the bench for the second match, only for Handre Pollard to withdraw.
Despite improving as the series went on, the 24-year-old lacked his usual flashes of individual brilliance.
It remains to be seen whether South Africa turn back to 32-year-old Pollard, as they did in 2023, on the biggest occasions to close out games.
Rassie Erasmus' experienced back-to-back World Cup winners - Marx (32), Eben Etzebeth (34), Pieter-Steph du Toit (34), Siya Kolisi (35), Damian de Allende (34), Cheslin Kolbe (32) - all remain regular starters.
The world champions have proven they can also play an exciting brand of attacking rugby, but appeasing the masses will not matter if a familiar formula can bring them three straight World Cups.
All Blacks return to what made them great
Scott Robertson's dismissal in January after two years as head coach sunk New Zealand to a new low.
Rennie, not the flashiest appointment, had to hit the ground running, and a stunning Test win over South Africa at Ellis Park was a case of doing just that.
The 33-16 victory injected jeopardy into a series which many had the Springboks winning comfortably, given their home advantage and recent dominance.
Hurricanes half-backs Cam Roigard and Ruben Love, both aged 25, were trusted by Rennie to instil a return to the All Blacks way - the ability to score from transition from anywhere on the field and compound scoreboard pressure.
Four or more tries in each Test in South Africa showed just that, with the third Test all square at half-time.
"Scott Robertson was a good culture coach but maybe not a brilliant technical coach. Dave Rennie is a brilliant technical coach," former England wing Ugo Monye told Rugby Union Weekly.
"After the Nations Championship, you could see the structures and how they want to play. I think the All Blacks' backline is the most skilled in World Rugby."
Love struggled to have the same commanding impact in Tests two and three, with fly-half Richie Mo'unga returning for the Baltimore game, his first Test since the World Cup final.
The 32-year-old Mo'unga, who is back after a stint in Japan, was not at the standard that made him one of the best fly-halves at the 2023 World Cup.
However, getting him back up to speed will be an All Blacks goal over the next 12 months.
Former England scrum-half Danny Care said: "Imagine what New Zealand would do with a platform and some dominance. It is great for the game that they are coming back to be the All Blacks of old, and the next 12 months will be fascinating."
World Cup rivals: France 'can play multiple styles', and be 'careful of Ireland'
South Africa live for must-win games. That is when, according to Brits, the Boks "come alive".
Defeat at Ellis Park cost them their world number one status - which was quickly regained - but also exposed a vulnerability.
South Africa, who lost matches in the pool stages of the past two World Cups, are currently the favourites to win next year's tournament in Australia, bringing a pressure they have not experienced previously.
"We hate being the favourite, we almost have to have our backs against the wall," Brits said.
"We prefer not to have the eyes on us and move under the radar. I think that is the best way for any team."
Back-to-back Six Nations champions France sent a weakened side to Christchurch in July and lost 34-32 to New Zealand.
When matched against the Springboks last November, France were beaten emphatically, 32-17.
Brits believes France are "the most settled" and offer tactical flexibility similar to that of the world champions.
"I feel like South Africa have an advantage as they can play multiple styles, and it feels like most other nations don't have that capability," Brits said.
"The only team that can play multiple styles is France, as they can grind it out with the forwards, play the kicking game and the expansive game as well."
He added that England still need to become what they are "supposed to be" and to keep an eye on Ireland, who are travelling "under the radar" after peaking in previous World Cup cycles prior to the tournament.
"Ireland still have amazing rugby players and coaches – the best coaches out there - and a top-four squad," Brits added. "Be careful of Ireland."

WHO and Netherlands Strategic Dialogue in The Hague, Netherlands 10 April 2024. Credit: Michel Mees Photography
The WHO and the Netherlands convened in The Hague on 10 April 2024, to discuss joint priorities and alignment between the Dutch Global Health Strategy and WHO’s key strategic goals, marking a new milestone in their longstanding partnership.
Rooted in the Netherlands' unwavering commitment to global health, human rights, and universal access to comprehensive health services, the collaboration between the WHO and the Netherlands is instrumental in addressing global health challenges and fostering health and well-being, worldwide and in the country.
Against the backdrop of ongoing conflicts, disasters, and the escalating impact of climate change, and the interconnectedness of the Dutch public health landscape in the Netherlands with global health challenges, this year’s Strategic Dialogue emerged as a critical platform for reflecting on this partnership’s long-term vision.
“In this Strategic Dialogue, throughout all sessions, WHO and the Netherlands showed a commitment to cooperation and to deepening their partnership based on the strong alignment between their respective priorities and objectives”, said Ms Marjolijn Sonnema, Director General for Public Health at the Netherlands’ Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport.
A key outcome of the Strategic Dialogue was the recognition of the alignment between the Dutch Global Health Strategy and the WHO's forthcoming 14th General Programme of Work, paving the way for synergies in areas such as health system strengthening, pandemic preparedness, climate change and health, anti-microbial resistance (AMR) and mental health support.
"At a time when inequity in health and in access to essential health services and financial protection is increasing, disproportionately impacting the poor and most vulnerable, the Netherlands stands as a global health leader and trusted WHO partner. With shared priorities and commitment to sexual and reproductive rights, gender equity, health systems, security, climate resilience, and mental health, we look forward to strengthening our partnership to enhance the health and well-being of all, globally and in the Netherlands", said Dr Bruce Aylward, WHO Assistant Director-General, Universal Health Coverage, Life Course.
WHO acknowledged the Netherlands' global leadership as a flexible donor, with an agreement around the imperative to ensure WHO's financing is more sustainable, through the inaugural WHO Investment Round. This WHO initiative aims to mobilize predictable, sustainable and flexible resources essential for the WHO to respond swiftly and effectively to global health challenges and improve health outcomes, particularly for vulnerable populations.
Addressing contemporary challenges such as geopolitical tensions while seizing opportunities for advancing global health objectives were also on the table during the dialogue. Both parties stressed the importance of sustained collaboration to address pressing health issues comprehensively.
Taking stock of the joint achievements since the previous strategic dialogue in 2022
In 2022, the Strategic Dialogue between the Netherlands and WHO called on both partners to enhance synergies between WHO priorities and the new Dutch Global Health Strategy. Implementing this approach, the Netherlands and WHO:
- Expanded their cooperation to new areas of joint interest, e.g., climate change and health;
- Renewed their longstanding cooperation on Water, Sanitation and Hygiene and Mental Health and Psychosocial Support in health emergencies and humanitarian settings;
- Improved the flexibility and predictability of the Netherlands’ financial support through renewed General Arrangements with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (2022-2025) and the Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport (2024–2028) demonstrating the Netherlands’ commitment to WHO’s sustainable financing;
- Hosted together the 2nd World Local Production Forum in the Netherlands;
- Continued and deepened their technical cooperation through secondments, Junior Professional Officers and the Collaborative Centres.
The outcomes of the 2024 dialogue will inform future collaboration between the Netherlands and the WHO, so that efforts are aligned, and the optimal use of resources is helps achieve improved health outcomes worldwide. The enduring partnership between the Netherlands and the WHO stands as a cornerstone in the global health landscape, reflecting a shared commitment to advancing health and well-being globally.
-----------------
The Netherlands is a key supporter and strategic partner of the WHO.
In 2022- 2023, the Netherlands was one of the top five flexible WHO contributors with nearly US$ 19 million in core voluntary contributions. Overall, the Netherlands contributed more than US$ 106 million to the WHO in 2022 - 2023, of which US$ 93 million, nearly 90%, was voluntary funding.
The Netherlands also supports the WHO's technical expertise through secondments of staff and helps boost young people's careers in public health via the WHO's Junior Professional Officer Programme.
This demonstrates the Netherlands' commitment through its Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport to the WHO’s central role in the global health architecture.
Through this support, the Netherlands contributes to crucial activities in the areas of sexual and reproductive health, water and sanitation, mental health in emergencies, emergency preparedness, tuberculosis, One Health, primary health care, antimicrobial resistance, while facilitating cooperation with top Dutch institutions.

Anthropologists and community leaders from Nagaland, a remote state in north-eastern India bordering Myanmar, have expressed joy and relief that human remains belonging to their ancestors that had been on display in a British museum for nearly a century are finally being returned.
On Monday, the Pitt Rivers Museum in Oxford announced that 39 pieces of human remains – including parts of skulls, a finger and a piece of skin with hair – belonging to the Naga tribes, will be returned to Nagaland after six years of negotiation between the community and the museum.
For the Nagas, the repatriation is not just about “bones and ancestral remains … It is about memory returning to where it belongs,” the community said in a statement.
“We are at peace,” said A Peihwang Wangsa, an Indigenous Konyak man involved in the repatriation negotiations. “Our forefathers are coming back.”
Wangsa, whose ancestors’ remains are among those being returned, added that the homecoming would be a moment of “mourning and celebration”.
NT Thamlong Phom, a Naga community leader from the Phom sub-tribe, said: “I feel joy, I feel blessed.
“Ever since the announcement was made, my entire community has felt happy,” he said. “Our ancestors’ spirit will have a final resting place.”
Thejao Vihienuo, who is also part of the repatriation discussions and went to Oxford in 2025, said he had been “angry and unhappy” to see the remains of his ancestors, which he said had been “taken in a most dubious manner”.
“It was displayed as if it was a trophy, but they silently spoke of the atrocities the British committed on our people,” he said.
The return caused “mixed feelings”, he said, but added: “We owe it to our ancestors to bring their remains back and put them to peaceful rest. And also to our younger generation to decolonise their minds and show that our children are not inferior to any white man.”
The Nagas are a transnational Indigenous group of tribes living in India’s north-east and parts of Myanmar, once associated with headhunting but now predominantly Christian.
The Pitt Rivers Museum, home to one of the world’s largest ethnological collections, has more than 6,500 Naga objects, 898 of which were on display. Most of the collection was “coercively” acquired by the colonial administrators James Philip Mills and John Henry Hutton.
The human remains were displayed at the museum for 80 years. In 2020, they were put into storage during a revamp aimed at addressing the institution’s colonial past and how exhibiting human remains “reinforced racist and stereotypical thinking” of other cultures.
The museum said in a statement: “Thirty-nine Naga ancestors will soon begin their journey home from Oxford to Nagaland.”
In November, a Naga delegation will visit Oxford for a handover ceremony and the remains are expected to arrive in Nagaland before the end of the year. They will be laid to rest in a traditional community ceremony in the state capital, Kohima.
The repatriation negotiations were led by representatives from all of the Naga tribes.
“It has been a journey of redemption,” said Prof Dolly Kikon, a Naga anthropologist. “This shows that we are no longer victims of colonial violence. We embrace our roles as people who find redemption and healing by giving dignity and honour to a very violent past.”
The negotiations started in 2020, when Kikon wrote to the museum after reading “an article in the Guardian that they were doing an ethical review” of the collection. “They replied within 24 hours,” said Kikon.
That was just the beginning of a lengthy process that soon expanded into a wider community-led campaign.
The Forum for Naga Reconciliation, a community peace group, assembled a team known as Recover, Restore and Decolonise, bringing together Naga volunteers from across the region to work on the repatriation effort.
“They travelled to villages and organised meetings to inform people about the remains,” said Arkotong Longkumer, a Naga anthropologist who worked closely with Kikon to lead the initiative, which he described as “open and transparent”.
“It was an intergenerational journey that brought together students, civil society, tribal leaders and the church,” said Longkumer, who teaches at Edinburgh University.
A Naga delegation, including tribal leaders, visited Oxford in 2025 to officially register a claim to the remains.
“I had never known our ancestral human remains had been taken away like that,” said Wangsa. “I felt angry when I saw them.”
Laura Van Broekhoven, director of the Pitt Rivers Museum and a professor of museum studies and ethics at Oxford University, said the museum was completing paperwork to enable the return of the remains.
“We will then start working towards the ceremonial aspects so we can have everything ready,” she said. “In our experience, handover ceremonies can be very emotional.”

The rules, being drafted by the U.S. Treasury Department, are likely to allow U.S. drugmakers to invest in promising new drugs being developed by Chinese companies as long as they are not related to pathogens or biotechnology that could be weaponized.
An analysis of U.S. Food and Drug Administration data found hundreds of post-market studies listed as delayed and, in some cases, the work was delayed by more than a decade or the manufacturer was still developing a plan for the study, KFF Health News confides. Relying on post-approval studies to resolve questions risks exposing patients to products that do more harm than good. Whoever is paying the bills — patients, insurance companies, employers, or government health programs such as Medicare and Medicaid — can end up wasting money and rewarding manufacturers for useless or risky products.

At least 16 killed after vehicle loaded with explosives rams into Pakistan mosque

At least 16 people, including five police officers, have been killed after a vehicle loaded with explosives rammed into a mosque in north-western Pakistan, according to a senior police official in Peshawar.
A gun battle is still ongoing between attackers and security forces at the mosque, near police headquarters, in the Kohat district of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
One of the assailants has reportedly been killed, an officer says, and a rescue operation is under way.
In a statement, Pakistan's President Asif Ali Zardari expressed "his best wishes for the swift recovery of those injured in the explosion."
Khyber Pakhtunkhwa police chief inspector general Zulfikar Hameed described the attack as a "suicide attack", according to Reuters news agency.
There has been no immediate claim of responsibility.
Prime Minister Muhammad Shehbaz Sharif also condemned the blast.
Militancy in Pakistan's border areas has risen sharply in recent months, targeting the military and police.
Islamabad says militants use safe haven in Afghanistan to train and plan attacks in Pakistan. Afghanistan's Taliban government denies the accusation and says militancy is Pakistan's domestic problem.

Europe’s dilemma over AI was rendered in stark terms this week. The head of the continent’s central bank, Christine Lagarde, said Europeans have two options: shun the technology and lose out on growth; or embrace it and become dependent on tools developed by the US and China.
The great debate over AI safety that has erupted in recent days threatens to make the choice moot. If the worst scenarios come to bear – and experts have differing views on this – then the technology will impact the continent regardless.
Europe has largely been absent from the highest levels of that debate, a result of the continent’s longstanding inability to produce a Silicon Valley-scale titan like Apple, Google or newcomer OpenAI. While it is a powerhouse in regulation, much to the White House’s chagrin, its lack of an Anthropic or Nvidia-sized frontrunner in the AI race has diminished its voice in the safety debate.
Ursula von der Leyen, a powerful political figure on the continent as president of the European Commission, the EU’s executive arm, addressed the issue this week by saying she will “invite the main frontier labs for a discussion on how we can support ongoing industry efforts to pace the frontier”.
Her remarks gained nowhere as much traction as Donald Trump and China’s dismissal of a slowdown. Without the support of Washington or Beijing, any sort of pacing is impossible – with our without Europe’s input.
Lagarde’s speech on Monday underlined the continent’s relative weakness. She asserted that Europe must develop its own AI technology and build more datacentres in order to nullify the threat of being cut off by the US or China.
If Europe invests in its own AI tech, said Lagarde, “the threat of being cut off loses its force.” Self-sufficiency would also give Europe a chance to develop its own answer to the AI safety crisis.
Margrethe Vestager, who clashed with the US tech industry as the EU’s former competition commissioner, co-authored a report this week – A Transformative AI Strategy for Europe – that echoed Lagarde’s warning. AI threatens to accelerate a development already affecting Europe, where citizens “are already bearing the economic and social consequences of decisions taken elsewhere”, she says.
Solutions to this, according to the report, include building more datacentres – the central nervous systems of AI – and also to ensure the continent is resilient enough to withstand “AI crises” like a powerful model slipping out of control.
Vestager said that Europe does have a voice in the safety debate through its EU AI Act, the rare piece of AI legislation that sets out requirements for developers of “high-risk” AI systems to report safety incidents and address risks like a cutting-edge model evading control.
But she adds: “Europe must … build its own AI to strengthen the ecosystem, retain talent, and inspire innovation.”
Vestager acknowledges that if there is an existential threat, it requires a global solution; one that does not hand power to the US and China. And that requires a different kind of supranational body.
“As for existential threats to humanity, we must first assess the actual level of threat – then act with urgency. The UN general assembly is an opportunity to address this. It is vital to move beyond the US-China rivalry narrative. There must be space for humanity between the egos of leaders like President Xi and President Trump.”
Frederike Kaltheuner, an adviser to the AI Now Institute, a research body, says that Europe is dependent on US technology in ways that will be hard to undo, from search engines to chips to datacentres. But the narrative that Europe is grievously behind in the race depends on a particular view of artificial intelligence aggressively promoted by American tech bosses.
Because of their doomsday warnings, “we are exclusively talking about AI in a very narrow, specific kind of way – namely, the idea that there is such a thing as the AI frontier, which is getting better and better, and that access to the frontier is the most important thing that Europe needs for its security and economy.”
The reality of the market points at something else, she says: many companies are not adopting so-called “frontier models” – like ChatGPT and Anthropic – because of high costs and fears over what might happen to their data.
If this trend continues, Europe may not be so terribly positioned: the EU AI Act has a number of pragmatic measures which address how consumers might encounter AI on a day-to-day basis, legislating over matters such as labelling AI content, and the use of AI in medicine and hiring.
“Europe has a competitiveness problem, that’s true,” says Itxaso Dominguez de Olazabal, a policy adviser at EDRI, a European digital rights organisation. But US tech boosters are “blaming it on laws and protections, and have promised that deregulation will make European companies more competitive … in a race to the bottom to see if we can catch big tech”.
Nonetheless, the EU AI act is not viewed as model legislation for other countries or a vehicle for a global slowdown. Georgina Kon, a partner at law firm Linklaters, says the act is unlikely to be adopted as a global benchmark for several reasons, including criticisms of the heavy compliance burden, which has led to delays in parts of the act becoming active, and a narrow territorial focus on Europe. Those criticisms have also meant that lawmakers elsewhere have looked to differentiate their approach to AI legislation from the EU’s. 
 “The EU AI Act is not something that everybody else in the world feels constrained by, although many tech companies will of course want to sell to the EU,” she says.
Big tech still has a vast customer base in Europe. Kaltheuner worries that the doomsday narratives will push Europe towards dependency, encouraging it to adopt US AI models across the economy out of ill-defined fears over being left behind.
“There’s a vision of the future where Europe’s economy, its public sector, its education system runs on models and on infrastructure that is controlled by a very small number of companies that happen to be also in the US. This would be a sovereignty problem.”

Back in black: Princess Diana's 'revenge dress' goes on show ahead of Sotheby's auction
A striking black dress worn by Princess Diana on the day her estranged husband admitted adultery is going up for auction at Sotheby’s
Revenge has rarely been so stylish.
A striking black dress worn by the late Princess Diana on the day her estranged husband publicly admitted adultery is going up for auction at Sotheby’s, with a presale estimate of up to $300,000.
First, the “revenge dress,” as it has become known, is going on an international tour, testament to the enduring global fascination with Diana almost 30 years after her death.
The garment, which went on public display Friday at Sotheby’s in London, was worn by Diana on June 29, 1994, the broadcast date of an interview in which the then-Prince Charles acknowledged infidelity.
Diana, who knew the revelation was coming, chose to wear the figure-hugging, off-the-shoulder silk dress by Greek designer Christina Stambolian for a gala at London’s Serpentine Gallery.
Morgane Halimi, Sotheby’s global head of handbags and fashion, said Diana chose the “beautiful and powerful outfit” as a way to seize control of her own story.
“She always used fashion as a way of expression, but this time (it) was a way to communicate her personal expression of herself,” Halimi said. “The way she felt on that day is that, ‘I’m taking back the story and I’m here and I stand for myself.’”
Images of Diana in the dress, accessorized with a sapphire necklace, black pumps and bright red nail polish, shot around the world. The Sun tabloid proclaimed on its front page the next day: “Revenge is chic.”
The following year Diana gave an interview in which she acknowledged her own extramarital affair, and famously said “there were three of us in this marriage,” in reference to Charles’ paramour Camilla Parker-Bowles, now Queen Camilla. Charles and Diana divorced in 1996, a year before Diana was killed in a car crash in Paris at the age of 36.
The dress is being auctioned for the first time since 1997, when Diana sold it and other garments to raise money for AIDS charities. It has a presale estimate of $150,000 to $300,000, but Sotheby’s experts would not be surprised if it far exceeds that price.
A red sweater adorned with sheep that Diana wore to a polo match in 1981 sold in 2023 for $1.1 million, many times its presale estimate and a record for an item owned by the late royal.
“I personally believe that this dress is the most powerful item linked to Diana,” Halimi said.
“The Diana provenance always attracts collectors,” she added. “But the story of this dress and the universal message that it brings will definitely attract also institutions as well as private collectors who are looking for unique pieces and one-of-a kind items.”
In her lifetime, Diana was a style icon and one of the world’s most photographed women. Her star power has not dimmed, and neither has the fascination with the dramatic disintegration of her marriage to the now King Charles III. A new book by Diana’s brother Charles Spencer has seized headlines again and reignited a public feud between the Spencers and the royal family over the treatment of the princess.
The revenge dress is on show in London until Sept. 24 and travels to Hong Kong and Geneva ahead of its sale in New York on Dec. 9.

‘The Best Thing That Happened to Him Was Losing in 2020’
Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan explain how the four years between Donald Trump’s first and second terms changed the presidency.
Few reporters understand as much about Donald Trump’s thinking, motives, and behavior as Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan. Haberman has been covering the president closely for more than a decade at The New York Times; she started with his first campaign in 2015, and her record of scoops quickly brought her into the public eye. Swan was, for many years, her chief professional rival: He worked for Axios, where he landed a controversial 2018 one-on-one interview with Trump. In late 2022, the Times announced that it was hiring Swan, turning the rivals into colleagues.
This past June, they published Regime Change: Inside the Imperial Presidency of Donald Trump. The book, an instant best seller, advances a new understanding of the first year of Trump’s second term, relaying in minute-by-minute detail how, since retaking office, he has pursued his personal goals with few limits on his power. The Atlantic staff writer Tim Alberta sat down with both authors at The Atlantic Festival, where he asked them about the 2028 election and the future of the presidency and the Republican Party.
This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.
Tim Alberta: Maggie, this country has been through a lot, and I’m wondering if you could help us understand how a “regime change” of this sort came to be.
Maggie Haberman: Essentially, we have had a series of national traumas since 9/11: two forever wars, a fiscal crisis, immense populist anger that started rising in 2010. To me, that was the year that set the tone. It was also the year that the proto-Trump, Carl Paladino, was the Republican nominee for governor in New York State. One of the issues that he ran on was the planned mosque to be built near the World Trade Center; it became known incorrectly as the “Ground Zero Mosque,” and it became a clear avatar of a change in this country after the era of George W. Bush. So you get to 2014, when immigration and particularly border crossings were on the rise under President Obama. Suddenly, this became a massive issue within the Republican Party. You had this mix of anger over the wars, anger over the massive accumulated debt under President Bush, then Obamacare, anger about immigration, and a shifting job market. The time was ripe for a candidate who presented himself as a fighter—and who was already known to most of the Republican electorate, not just as a celebrity on The Apprentice but as a cultural figure.
Alberta: 2016, Trump 1.0, is its own story. So much of what this book is about is how the end of that first term, and then his time in exile after losing in 2020, shapes this dramatic, radical, wholesale change to government and to executive power.
Jonathan Swan: When we were reporting for this book, we heard from a couple of people who were close to Trump at a pretty high level that, in their view, the best thing that happened to him was losing in 2020. Which is something they could never say publicly or in his presence, because, of course, he never lost the election and what have you. But it’s indisputably true. Let’s say Trump ekes out that victory in 2020: He comes back in; he is hobbled by COVID. He has the same inflation that every other country around the world has. He still has the rump of a team around him that he really doesn’t like very much, who are, in quite a few instances, pushing back on some of his more extreme desires. He really can’t get his arms around the presidency.
Instead, he loses. People like Stephen Miller spent those four years very productively. It wasn’t just drawing up the plans—you saw that blitz of executive orders at the start of 2025, which was all very well prepared. They also spent a lot of time thinking about Who are the lawyers that we want to fill the government with? And I’m not just talking about the White House counsel’s office; I’m talking about across the government. Agency lawyers, general counsels—they would constantly say, Well, no, what you’re proposing is illegal. But when you have lawyers who are saying, Well, actually, if we turn it this way and then turn it this way and then give it a little bit of a spin, then they can bless what you want. And that’s what’s happening.
I’ll give you the perfect example that describes the difference between term one and term two: In term one, Trump was saying almost yearningly, You know, they don’t have a drug problem in China, because Xi Jinping, he just kills the drug dealers. And they don’t have a drug problem in the Philippines, because Rodrigo Duterte just kills them. Trump was very fond of these extrajudicial killings. In term one, there wasn’t a huge amount of enthusiasm for this idea among the leadership of the Defense Department. Now you have Pete Hegseth, and you have lawyers inside the government that allow a policy where Donald Trump decided, in his mind, that people on fishing boats transporting cocaine in the Caribbean Sea are not drug traffickers who are to be interdicted by the Coast Guard and dealt with in a criminal-justice system. No: They’re enemy combatants in a war. We’re not going to interdict them. We’re not going to arrest them. We’re just going to kill them. And that’s something that has been blessed within the government. They haven’t even bothered to try to legally justify this in a public setting. They just do it, knowing that they have the right lawyers in place.
The other big element making this term unrecognizable from the first term is the immunity decision. Maggie and I talk about this all the time. Trump would say early on, I’m immune; I’m immune. He has said privately that he’s going to pardon anyone who came within 250 feet of the Oval Office.
The point is, he had the time to rebuild, and his team had time to prepare. That’s how you get this second term.
Alberta: Trump can’t stay in power forever. He will soon be a lame duck after these November midterms. I’m wondering how he’s handling that: whether he is going to allow a neat and tidy process to unfold for his successor, and whether or not J. D. Vance, who got a bit crosswise with him over Iran, is going to be tortured over the next several years as the president deliberates over whom he should hand all of this over to.
Swan: We have a scene in the book that I think illustrates what you’re describing. Rupert Murdoch comes to the White House for dinner. This is October of last year, and they’re in the Blue Room of the White House. And at the table are J. D. Vance and Marco Rubio.
Haberman: And, like, 10 other people.
Swan: Halfway through the conversation, Trump says, I really like J.D. I really like Marco. Rupert, what do you think of J.D.? And he starts this beauty pageant, essentially, in front of both of them, with the most powerful proprietor of conservative media—knowing full well that Rupert Murdoch is no fan of J. D. Vance and, in fact, tried to stop him from becoming the vice president. There’s this pause, and Rupert Murdoch says, J.D. has the potential to be great—just withering. Vance says, Oh, gee, thanks, Rupert. It’s a very awkward moment. Trump says, What do you think of Marco? And Rupert doesn’t miss a beat: He says, Marco’s brilliant. This savage moment just foretells what the next two years are going to be like. How is he grappling with being a lame duck? The way he’s grappling with it is by refusing to be a lame duck.
Vance is in a really difficult position because, as you noted, there were several meetings leading up to the Iran war, in the Situation Room and the Oval Office, where Vance was the only one in the room arguing against it. That did not go down well with Trump. And so the notion that this is going to be some smooth glide path to the 2028 nomination is contradicted by every piece of evidence we have about who Donald Trump is and how he behaves.
Alberta: Maggie, that point that Jonathan makes about Trump’s refusal to be a lame duck over the next two years—what does that look like?
Haberman: I don’t want to limit anyone’s imagination here on what it would look like. The question that we get a lot is, Will he try for a third term? I truly don’t believe he will, but I’m absolutely willing to be wrong. I don’t actually think he wants that, and he doesn’t need it. He will be the dominant figure in this party until he is no longer on this Earth, whether he’s in office or not. He has made more money than he ever made in his life during this presidency—at least just liquid, that we know of, assets.
Swan: By orders of magnitude.
Haberman: The crypto money is, I think, $2.2 billion in the first year-ish of the presidency. His children have continued to make money. There were very valid questions about Hunter Biden, but it is so dwarfed by everything that we are seeing now, everything that Hunter Biden was doing.
What the next two years I expect will look like will be the projects Trump really cares about, which are these monuments to himself in Washington—the ballroom. I’m very curious to see what happens with the Kennedy Center; that’s a big open question. This is not going to look like any kind of congressional flip that we’ve seen before in a lame-duck presidency, because to Jonathan’s point, Trump knows that he is immune from federal prosecution. He has talked about pardons very openly. We spoke with a number of people who are counting on their pardons. We’ve never seen a government just not respond to subpoenas in Congress. The only recourse that Congress has if they don’t get cooperation is a contempt-of-Congress vote and a referral to the Department of Justice, where I’m confident Attorney General Todd Blanche is not going to do a lot. This is a government that has done so little in terms of legislating. Everything, for the most part, was by executive action.
Alberta: Your reporting describes a government that is not recognizable at a fundamental level. How do we come back from that?
Haberman: That’s the reason for the title.
Swan: It’s such an interesting question, because on the one hand, there will be a desire by many to restore what was before. On the other hand, Trump has also shown what you can do unilaterally. He’s demonstrated, particularly in the second term, that a lot of the constraints that we take for granted around the presidency are not legal constraints. They’re self-restraint or norms. Just take the ballroom, for example. Yes, in the end, it was green-lighted, right? The court system is not stopping him from building this ballroom. But by the time the court system got up to that point, there was a giant hole in the ground. There were cranes in the sky; there were shovels going through the earth.
The tariffs are another great example: Yes, ultimately, the Supreme Court checked him on his tariffs—months after he started a global trade war, which had all kinds of rippling consequences. This is a legal system that is not built to deal with a president like Donald Trump; he has shown that you can just get away with acting and forcing others to react. That was a deliberate strategy—overwhelm the opposition; overwhelm the legal groups.
So you have two models: One is a figure who comes back and says, Actually, we need to restore checks and balances and the constitutional system. Or you have either a right-wing populist or a left-wing populist saying, You know what? Donald Trump has actually shown us what nirvana could look like if we do it on behalf of our chosen priorities. That’s how you can get potentially even more of an expansion of executive power and the imperial presidency.
Haberman: The one addendum I would make is that I think that for the most part, President Biden did try going back. He really did. He did fairly little by executive action; he had big legislation; he left the Justice Department alone. What I hear from Democrats I speak with is that they want someone who is going to fight in the manner that they have seen Republicans fight. I agree with Jonathan that I don’t think there is another Donald Trump walking around; I think he is sui generis for a lot of reasons. But that doesn’t mean there are not aspects that would be appealing. And certainly, I believe that whoever the next Republican nominee is, they’re going to be in the mold of Donald Trump. I mean, this is Donald Trump’s party until there is another Republican president, not just nominee, or for as long as he is alive. Whatever you see the Democrats form will be a reaction to that.
The only other asterisk is that if ever there was an election cycle that was ripe for a Ross Perot type, it will be 2028. There is so much anger at the system. Part of why Trump is struggling right now in polls is that he broke several campaign promises, and voters can feel that. They can feel $4.50 gas. People want to feel like somebody is actually helping them.

- The claim that an image shows U.S. President Donald Trump kissing White House aide Natalie Harp on a golf course remains under investigation.
- The rumor stems from two versions of the image shared on social media in mid-September 2026. The higher-resolution version had telltale signs of artificial intelligence, such as hands with too many fingers, as well as a watermark confirming it was created or edited using OpenAI's generative AI tools. The lower-resolution image did not have an OpenAI watermark and was too blurry for telltale anomalies to be apparent.
- The White House declined to provide Snopes with legitimate photos of Trump and Harp golfing that could be compared to the images shared online. A spokesperson said the image was "clearly a fake."
- Hany Farid, co-founder of deepfake detection company GetReal, told Snopes the higher-resolution image was AI-generated and was clearly derived from the lower-quality version. While he said the lower-resolution version's quality itself was "a bit of a red flag," he said he considered its authenticity inconclusive.
- Snopes will update this report if additional information surfaces.
In summer 2026, many people scrutinized White House aide Natalie Harp following news reports of what appeared to be an unusually close relationship with U.S. President Donald Trump.
In September, following a Trump visit to Ireland during which he took time to golf at his Trump Organization-owned course, people started sharing multiple versions of an image that appeared to show Trump kissing Harp, whose back is turned toward the camera, while on the golf course.
For example, one X post (archived) shared a low-resolution version of the image. Another popular X post (archived) shared a higher resolution version with crisper colors.
Users also widely posted the image on Threads (archived) and Instagram (archived). Snopes readers emailed us to ask whether the image was real.
Snopes could find no credible evidence or source supporting the authenticity of the image, but we were able to find multiple red flags indicating the higher-resolution version was generated or edited with artificial intelligence tools. The lower-resolution version did not have those same red flags, in part because of its poor quality. Therefore, we've left this claim unrated until more evidence comes to light.
We used Google Lens to run a reverse image search on both versions of the image. The oldest example that turned up was a thumbnail image for a Sept. 14 YouTube video uploaded by political commentator Keith Edwards. We've fact-checked images originating from Edwards' thumbnails twice before. In one of those fact checks, Edwards confirmed he had used an AI tool to generate the image.
Snopes reached out to Edwards by email to confirm the origin of the image of Trump kissing Harp. He responded:
My thumbnail team found the image online. We did not create or alter the underlying image, but we also did not independently verify its original source or that the woman pictured is Natalie Harp. Given that only the back of her head is visible, I don't think her identity can be confirmed from this image alone.
Following this, Snopes used the thumbnail to conduct another reverse image search. While it failed to unearth any older versions of the image, the results (archived) included a wider shot of the subjects than any other we could find. That version, which included the "wtf" text on Edwards' thumbnail, linked to the same Edwards video.
None of the reverse image searches turned up links to credible news sources or even less-credible tabloids sharing the image. Considering the reporting already scrutinizing Trump's relationship with Harp, it's unlikely, if the image were real, that not a single credible news source would report on it. The image also did not appear among photos kept by credible photo repositories, such as Getty Images and The Associated Press.
Although there was no photographer, date or location listed for any version of the image, the timing of its spread suggested it was likely meant to depict something that took place while Trump was visiting his golf course in Ireland on Sept. 13, an activity listed on his calendar as "Executive Time." Photos of that golf course and Google Maps satellite view don't show any trees, in contrast to the image of Trump and Harp kissing.
Snopes reached out to the White House by email to ask if any photos of Trump and/or Harp at the golf course over the weekend exist in order to compare what either was wearing in those images with what they supposedly wore in the image of the kiss. The White House did not send or confirm the requested images, but a White House official said the image shared online was "clearly a fake photo."
While many of those who spread the photo presumed the woman was Harp, there's no way to confirm that considering the subject's face isn't visible.
Some people online claimed the image was actually a 2017 photo of Trump exchanging a cheek-kiss with Norwegian golfer Suzann Pettersen as a greeting. This is false. That kiss was not actually on the golf course, Pettersen was in a different outfit than that of the woman in the recent image and Trump was also dressed differently, as shown in images capturing the moment from 2017.
AI evidence
A tool by OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, detected a watermark in the higher-resolution version image consistent with those generated or edited using the company's AI tools. Moreover, the image depicts Harp holding her golf club with six fingers.
The lower-resolution version of the image was too blurry to clearly identify AI tells such as an excessive number of fingers on either person's hands. While OpenAI's tool didn't identify a watermark within the lower-resolution image shared across X and Threads, the tool did detect OpenAI watermarks on the thumbnail for Edwards' video.
Separately, Snopes tested what the tool would find on a real photo where a small portion had then been edited by AI. OpenAI's tool detected the watermark on such an image, even when the photo was cropped to remove the part that had been edited.
Hany Farid, co-founder of deepfake detection company GetReal and a professor at Drexel University, told Snopes over email that "the high-resolution version was clearly derived from the lower-resolution version and has a SynthID watermark. As for the lower-resolution version, there is not a lot to go on here given the quality and resolution."
"While there are no obvious visual anomalies, the low quality/resolution is a bit of a red flag. In particular, given the apparent narrow depth of focus, this does not appear to photographed with a mobile device and is more likely taken with a DSLR that would afford this type of narrow depth of focus," Farid continued. "Assuming this to be the case, I would expect the image quality to be better. At this point, I'd say the authenticity is inconclusive."

Sachin Pilot with Charanjit Singh Channi and Amrinder Singh Raja Warring during a protest to demand justice for the late Gulzar Singh in Chandigarh on Tuesday.
NEW DELHI: The Congress in Punjab has finally hit the ground running. Sachin Pilot, who replaced Bhupesh Baghel as the party’s state in-charge, successfully navigated the state unit out of months of internal turmoil and ensured the party’s campaign for the 2027 assembly elections could finally take off.With arch-rivals - former chief minister Charanjit Singh Channi and state Congress chief Raja Warring - on board, Pilot led a mega protest demanding the resignation of Punjab finance minister Harpal Cheema, who faces charges of abetment of suicide of a Dalit, Gulzar Singh.The entire state leadership and thousands of party workers marched towards Cheema’s residence. Police used water cannons to stop the protesters’ march. But the point was made. The Congress was finally in action mode.Pilot ensured that Channi and Warring, whose open power tussle has derailed Congress’s Punjab campaign, not only shared the stage but also did a “tense” handshake.Putting up a huge show of unity during the protest, Channi said, "We will fight together." Warring reciprocated. The state Congress chief called Channi and other leaders his 'pagg da lar' (the fold of his turban).
Expressing gratitude to party workers for mobilising in such huge numbers at short notice, Pilot assured each one of them that the Congress will always stand by them. The Congress in-charge assured party workers that he was the representative of the high command and would not leave any stone unturned to restore the dignity and honour of every Congress worker.
But will Pilot’s truce hold?
That’s the big question. The Punjab Congress has seen a no-holds-barred battle between Channi and Warring ever since the high command announced on July 1 that Warring would continue as Punjab Congress chief, ignoring Channi’s claims.The announcement triggered immediate protests from Channi’s supporters. They demanded that Channi should be projected as the party’s CM face in the assembly elections. What followed left the Congress leadership red-faced. From war or words to slogan-shouting at party meetings, the wide split in the state unit was out in the open. The Congress sent Chhattisgarh chief minister Bhupesh Baghel to firefight, but he was also singed in the crossfire. Channi camp leaders accused him of siding with Warring.Pilot, who was then air-dashed to Punjab to set the house in order, has passed his maiden test. But assembly elections in the state are still at least 5 months away. Holding the rival factions together till then will indeed be a daunting challenge for the former Rajasthan deputy chief minister.
Well begun is half done
So, how did Pilot cross the first hurdle smoothly? What did he do differently, which Bhupesh Baghel couldn’t?Former Chhattisgarh chief minister Bhupesh Baghel was sent to Punjab in February this year. The Congress in Punjab then was a deeply divided house. Baghel worked hard on the ground to bridge differences between the state leaders. But on July 1, when the Congress high command announced to continue with Raja Warring as the state Congress president and made Channi the head of the campaign committee, the rebellion in the state unit came out in the open.Channi’s supporters openly opposed the decision. When Baghel reinforced the leadership structure and ruled out any change, the rebels openly protested and even raised slogans against him.Baghel tried to pacify the rebels by announcing that Punjab elections would be fought under the leadership of Rahul Gandhi and no state leader would be projected as CM face. But the rebels had lost his trust and refused to budge.With the rebels refusing to relent and their open infighting embarrassing the party leadership, the Congress high command decided to do a course correction to set its house in order.Baghel was shifted out, Pilot was brought in with a clear message: Congress would contest the 2027 assembly elections under collective leadership, and Rahul Gandhi would be the face of the campaign. This was a half-way compromise. The party leadership relented on Baghel but refused to budge on replacing Warring - at least for now.Warring was handpicked by the Congress high command to lead the Punjab unit after the party’s rout in the 2017 assembly elections - which saw the grand-old-party reduced to 17 assembly seats - its worst-ever performance in the state.
“No CM face” compromise
So, Pilot has crossed the first hurdle. But at what cost? Congress’s decision to fight the Punjab assembly elections under collective leadership, with Rahul Gandhi as the face of the campaign, may have at best delayed the inevitable power tussle.But it creates another challenge for the party. Much of the Congress’s success in the state till now has been driven by a strong local leadership - Captain Amarinder Singh, who is now with the BJP.The AAP has already announced to contest the upcoming assembly elections under the leadership of Bhagwant Singh Mann. Arvind Kejriwal, who is the face of AAP has largely worked from behind the scenes - planning and strategising for the Punjab challenge. For the Akalis, Sukhbir Singh Badal is the undisputed leader and the party’s campaign revolves around him.That leaves us with the BJP and the Congress.
PM Modi vs Rahul
The Congress decision to contest Punjab assembly elections with Rahul Gandhi as the party’s face makes the upcoming electoral contest interesting, and perhaps also challenging for the party.The BJP has already launched an aggressive campaign for Punjab with Prime Minister Narendra Modi leading the party’s campaign. PM Modi has already held two rallies in the poll-bound state and has announced a slew of development projects. As the campaign progresses, we will see the Prime Minister go all out against BJP’s political opponents. The BJP, which is in the process of building the party in the state, also has no visible local leadership. It has acquired quite a few prominent leaders from AAP and Congress, but it is unlikely any of them would be projected as the CM face. BJP’s campaigns in states are mostly centralised, with all top leaders campaigning for the party and PM Modi leading the charge. Punjab should be no exception.And that is what should worry the Congress. The fight to conquer Punjab could well become another PM Modi vs Rahul contest. In several such direct contests in the past, the Congress has struggled. However, Punjab could be different. The BJP, for a greater part of its existence in the state, has played second fiddle to the Akalis.
The BJP has announced a solo contest in 2027 elections.For the Congress, Punjab has been one of the happiest hunting grounds. Despite the haunting memories of Operation Blue Star and the anti-Sikh killings, Punjab has voted for the Congress. Now, it is over to Pilot to take the Congress beyond the winning line.

eGPUs do work, but they come with some notable limitations
Just buy a basic gaming PC instead.
If you've been looking to get more gaming power out of your laptop but don't want to pay for a replacement amid RAMpocalypse pricing, an eGPU could be your best bet. An eGPU is an external graphics processor, usually a desktop graphics card in an enclosure connected to a compatible laptop or gaming handheld through Thunderbolt or USB4. They can be pretty good at taking over rendering, meaning even thinner and weaker machines can run more demanding games with one plugged in, but there are many caveats.
A GPU run as an eGPU will typically operate slower over Thunderbolt than it would inside a desktop. The enclosure to house it costs hundreds of dollars too, and some devices, like Apple Silicon-based Macs, can't use an eGPU for gaming at all. That said, eGPU hardware is in better shape today than it has been in years. Razer revived its eGPU line with a Thunderbolt 5 dock in July 2025, and Framework is building an eGPU kit for its Laptop 16.
How much performance is lost with an eGPU?
A Thunderbolt 4 port carries 40Gbps, and Intel's spec allots PCIe data 32 Gbps of it, an eighth of the bandwidth a desktop PCIe 4.0 x16 slot provides. Most of what the card in an eGPU enclosure does will never cross the Thunderbolt cable. Textures and shaders get loaded into VRAM once and remain there, meaning the cable only gets busy when a game pulls in new assets or sends finished frames back to the display.
Portables review site Notebookcheck tested an RTX 2080 Ti enclosure back in 2021 and found deficits ranging from seven to 32 percent when compared to a desktop. Losses did shrink to single digits at 4K on an external monitor, but rendering to a laptop is slower because finished frames travel back down the same cable. In contrast, PC Gamer tested an RTX 4070 Ti and 4090 over Thunderbolt, OCuLink and desktop PCIe. Its RTX 4070 Ti ran around 25 percent slower over Thunderbolt than OCuLink in many 1440p tests, with lower 1 percent lows and more stuttering.
PC Gamer also claimed that upgrading from the 4070 Ti to the 4090 delivered smaller gains over Thunderbolt and OCuLink compared to desktop. So, the faster the card, the more of its performance the Thunderbolt cable restricts, making a mid-range GPU the more sensible choice for an eGPU enclosure. Thunderbolt 5 provides 80 Gbps of connection bandwidth, while Razer's $350 Core X V2 connects the GPU through PCIe 4.0 x4, nominally 64 Gbps. That gives an x16 graphics card four lanes instead of the 16 available in a suitable desktop slot.
Cost and compatibility
The Core X V2 comes with only the enclosure; no power supply, USB ports or Ethernet. You'll need to add your own ATX PSU, and Razer now sells the missing I/O separately as a Thunderbolt 5 dock starting at $390 for the Mercury version. Throw in the graphics card itself and there's really little point in buying all these components when you could just invest in a budget gaming rig instead. At least in doing so, you'll be avoiding the external connection's bandwidth limit. Thunderbolt 5 laptops are also few and far between outside premium gaming machines and mobile workstations, so connecting the enclosure to a compatible Thunderbolt 4 laptop limits the connection to 40 Gbps regardless.
OCuLink does manage to get around Thunderbolt by running bare PCIe over a cable. That's the route Framework is taking. Its OCuLink Dev Kit exposes an eight-lane PCIe connection on the Laptop 16, rated at up to 128 Gbps. You end up sacrificing some convenience here given that OCuLink doesn't power the host, and there's none of the plug-and-play that makes a Thunderbolt box a one-cable dock.
Apple dropped eGPU support with its move away from Intel silicon back in 2020. No macOS release since has brought it back for graphics acceleration. However, Apple did approve TinyGPU earlier this year, a driver extension from the tinygrad project that runs newer AMD and Nvidia cards over Thunderbolt or USB4. It's for AI workloads only, and its lack of display output means it won't get you anywhere for gaming use cases.

Uh oh, we got a cute alert! It’s Bezzy, your adorable, cuddly, anthropomorphized server-rack and stuffed-animal friend! Give this soft lil’ doll a squeeze, and it shall sing you its telltale song: the piercing, grinding ambient squeals emitted from a real US data center.
The Bezzy doll is a stuffed plushie made in a satirical collaboration between the New York–based creative studio Basura and Big Data, the musical project of producer Alan Wilkis, best known for the song “Dangerous,” a 2013 collaboration with the band Joywave. The joint project, which is coming out the same day as a new Big Data single, is called Adopt a Data Center. The goal is to present people with a “cuddly introduction to life with a real data center.”
Data Centers are very un-vogue right now. Built out by all the big AI companies to power their increasingly power-hungry AI tools, data centers have spread across thousands of acres of land in the US. They have been heavily criticized for their energy consumption and expansion of gas power. They have also proven to be audibly annoying, stirring up complaints about noise pollution from those nearby.
The Adopt a Data Center stunt aims to make people think differently about how services produced by data centers fit into their lives. That manifests as a plush stuffie that looks like a server rack in a data center, albeit with long arms and legs and googly eyes. It’s cute in the way Don’t Hug Me I’m Scared is cute. Squeeze Bezzy’s torso and the sound bursts out. It’s a screeching few seconds of a recording taken by a neighbor of a data center in Virginia. The tag on the Bezzy plushie reads, “Hug me for ear-piercing forever hum.”
“We picked this recording as it was the clearest and most suitably irritating,” wrote Rajeev Basu, the founder of Basura, in an email to WIRED. In an interview with the person who recorded the audio, Basu says they described the sound as “like a car alarm going off nonstop. It's high-pitched, and it's all you can focus on.”
Basura has worked on other projects like making luxury wear for dogs and a partnership with Yerba Madre that made dirt shoes designed to break apart during a walk to spread wildflower seeds.
Along with Bezzy, the data centers project includes a collection of stickers that say things like “Every data center deserves a forever home” and “Open your heart. And your power grid.” Basu says the project is the result of dozens of interviews with people who live near data centers in the US. The website itself reads, “Adopt a data center: All they ask for is everything.”
Wilkis, whose band Big Data has “It’s giving Black Mirror, but make it music” in its Spotify description, says that the one upside of the data center debate is that the backlash is genuinely bipartisan.
“AI is a proxy for decades of widening wealth inequality in America, and data centers are its physical embodiment,” Wilkis wrote to WIRED. “With roughly 40 percent of the stock market's value riding on a handful of tech companies, the US economy is already a bet on AI's success.”
Sadly, only 20 Bezzy dolls are available for $99 from the Adopt a Data Center website and the Big Data storefront. Basura designed the toys, which are handmade in the US. But the physical toy isn’t the real point. The satire is meant to hook people into looking at the facts for themselves. When you click “adopt now” on the website, you’re taken to a statement with links to research and stories about how data centers fit into the world.
“It’s not about whether AI data centers should exist,” Basu says. “It’s about who gets to decide where they go, what resources they consume, and whether the communities living beside them actually benefit.”

Bilateral merchandise trade between India and Nepal fell from a peak of about $11.02 billion in FY22 to $8.92 billion in FY23 and $7.87 billion in FY24—a cumulative decline of roughly 28.5%. It has since recovered to $9.39 billion in FY26, according to commerce ministry data published by the Embassy of India in Kathmandu. India's exports to Nepal were $7.45 billion, while Nepal's exports to India stood at $1.94 billion. India is Nepal's largest trading partner, accounting for about 62.3% of Nepal's total external trade, according to the same official data. Nepal was India's 12th-largest export destination in FY26. India and Nepal are planning to strengthen customs cooperation through pre-arrival exchange of information, electronic verification of certificates of origin, and greater customs automation and digitalization. When a man with a terminal illness wrote to his local MP Andrew Hastie, telling him he planned on ending his own life with voluntary assisted dying, Microsoft Copilot suggested Hastie reply with “congratulations!”, “great to hear from you” or “that is wonderful news!”.
Hastie shared the episode at a parliamentary inquiry on Friday to underline the shortcomings of the American-run software as he called for AI run by Australians.
The hearing offered the some of the most detailed explanations of the Albanese government’s desire to bring Anthropic and OpenAI to Australia, in the face of calls to slow them down or shut them out.
The defence establishment told the inquiry that cutting the companies out could be catastrophic.
Abigail Bradshaw, the director general of the Australian Signals Directorate, said her agents needed advanced AI every day to fend off “highly capable malicious cyber actors”.
“If a digital adversary has access to newer, more capable models than we do, they may be able to identify and exploit vulnerabilities in systems and networks before we can identify them,” Bradshaw said.
But Australia’s top cyber-intelligence agency is “entirely reliant” on US-housed processing and would “dramatically” lose capability if cut off in a conflict, Bradshaw said.
The defence department’s chief AI officer, Chris Crozier, said the government was already trying to keep its tech needs local, contracting Google to build a series of interlinked datacentres spread across the country and disconnected from the US.
“Somebody can’t wake up and have a bad day and decide they’re going to turn it off,” Crozier said.
“We do not want to be using AI tool sets that are located offshore … we want the compute, we want the application, we want the data, we want the decision making, all based in Australia.”
Bringing big tech into the country would make the job much easier, he said, and not just by allowing the army to protect and maintain its datacentres.
The Office of AI, set up in the prime minister’s department, said bringing firms under Australian law would make it easier for local law enforcement to combat threats on the platforms.
Tight conditions on access could also materially improve Australia’s chances of using and defending itself with the best AI tools in the world, the inquiry heard.
“We will get more assured access, earlier access, more detailed technical access, and better integration with technical experts at the frontier,” Bradshaw said.
These would be assured by strict requirements on any top developers looking to train models in Australia, such as demanding government oversight and early access to advanced models, she suggested.
The government is already planning to set the rules for companies that come here. It is consulting on standards that would force AI companies to report issues and breaches and potentially reserve some computational power for local research.
Large datacentres will have to engage with communities, build away from schools and homes, and underwrite new renewables in most states.
Another pillar of the standards – copyright law – is yet to be settled, with AI developers refusing to train models here without law reform.
A proposal to give the companies access to everything Australians create online by default sparked a wave of backlash from creatives, who say the companies could pay for local licensing deals to access Australian content.
But Jenna Priestly, the assistant secretary at the attorney general’s department, on Friday confirmed looser copyright laws would also affect AI access to foreign-made content distributed in Australia.
She said the companies wanted to train models on “maybe billions” of pieces of information and claimed it was practically “impossible” to make deals with every rights holder.
“As Australia’s copyright framework protects not only copyright material that’s Australian in origin, but worldwide, I think it is a fairly large number that [companies] would need to go and strike deals with,” Priestly said.
The Greens senator David Shoebridge, who is among those fighting calls for copyright reform and demanding a pause on AI development, on Friday said Labor had refused him a seat on the inquiry committee.
Labor ministers have spent the week meeting with OpenAI’s vice-president, and Anthropic’s special envoy Jeff Bleich, who this week suggested Australia had just months to bring in effective regulation.
The attorney general’s department told Friday’s hearing the shape and timing of any copyright reform was yet to be decided. But the prime minister’s department said Anthony Albanese wanted draft laws on the broader AI standards by the end of 2026.
Australia’s chance for influence on and special access to the models could be at risk by a delay, Bradshaw said.
“Decisions around training are a matter of urgency,” she said. “I think it is inevitable that those providers will look at other places to locate.”

The overlooked factor making everything more expensive
The cost of diesel quietly raises the price of goods across the economy. You’re likely paying for it already.
Diesel hit a record $6.40 per gallon this morning, up 73 percent from a year ago. “Not really my problem,” you might be thinking. “I don’t drive a semi or excavator.”
But you know who does drive semis and excavators and all the other machines that rely on diesel fuel? The people who farm your food, ferry your online orders, and repave the streets in your neighborhood. All that means the price of diesel trickles down into virtually every segment of the economy. (We’ll get into that a bit more shortly.)
Like gas prices, diesel has been rising since the US war with Iran began more than six months ago. But this particular surge was also driven by two incidents in particular: an attack on Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline, which has made it costlier and more time-consuming to get oil out, and a Ukrainian drone campaign against Russian oil infrastructure, which has forced major refineries to scale back production.
In the aftermath of those attacks, President Donald Trump implored Ukraine to stop targeting refineries. His administration has also relaxed some labor rules for fuel-truck drivers in the hopes of getting more gas and diesel moving.
There’s reportedly also talk of invoking the Defense Production Act to scale up America’s refining capacity, or even restricting diesel exports to help drop domestic prices. Not on the solution list, notably: winding down the war in Iran, which kickstarted this whole thing.
Go a little deeper
The cost of diesel quietly raises the price of many other goods and services. This is difficult to quantify, but researchers at Brown University estimate that the extra cost paid for diesel between the start of the Iran War and the time I’m drafting this newsletter works out to roughly $374 per US household.
Part of that cost springs from the fact that so many commercial, agricultural, and industrial machines run on diesel fuel. At the risk of sounding like one of my toddler’s “things that go” books, the list includes semis, tractors, excavators, freight trains, buses, cargo ships, and garbage trucks — to say nothing of other machines, like heavy industrial equipment and backup generators.
But part of the cost also springs from the fact that demand for diesel fuel is, compared to other goods, pretty inelastic. When the price of regular gas goes up, consumers can cut back on road trips, opt for public transit, or even contemplate an EV purchase.
Diesel-dependent industries frequently lack those options, however. As one fuel industry analyst put it in a recent column for the trade publication Oil & Gas 360, a farmer halfway through the harvest — as many are right now — can’t just stop running a combine or tractor because diesel gets pricey.
In other words, it’s difficult for businesses to avoid or offset the higher cost of fuel. And that makes it more likely that they’ll pass on the cost to consumers, even if they’re able to absorb it for a little while.
Where will you likely see those added costs first? Your grocery bill, for one. Look for price increases on highly perishable products that travel long distances, like milk, meat, fruits, and vegetables.
One link for later
➨ Gossip more ethically. Talking about other people is interesting, common, and — often! — quite fun. But it’s neither very kind, nor particularly moral, to reduce your acquaintances to conversational trading cards. So when you gossip, consider whether your story affords its subject “the concern and respect” you’d expect yourself. If not, try a safer conversational topic: stories about your own experiences.
Before you go…
- Did you know…that “money dysmorphia” is a real (and common!) cognitive bias? It describes the irrational feeling that money is tight, when you’re actually — on paper — doing just fine.

Satellite image reveals major damage that shut crucial Saudi oil pipeline
- Published
Satellite imagery shows a key oil pipeline in Saudi Arabia has been badly damaged after a strike last week, which experts have told BBC Verify could take more than a month to repair and force oil prices even higher.
The image shows the most significant damage is at a pumping station along the East-West Pipeline, which Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on to export crude oil via the Red Sea rather than through the Strait of Hormuz, where ships have been attacked by Iran and the US during their six-month war.
The Saudi government has accused Iranian-backed militias in Iraq of the pipeline strike, which followed days of renewed missile and drone attacks on south-western Saudi Arabia by Yemen's Houthi group - which is also backed by Iran. Saudi Arabia has retaliated by carrying out strikes on Houthi-controlled areas of western Yemen.
New satellite images also show damage to Saudi Arabia's King Khalid Air Base after a Houthi strike last week.
The Saudi government said on Tuesday it would respond "firmly" to attacks by the Houthis.
While the Houthis have been fighting a long-running civil war against Saudi-backed Yemeni pro-government forces, the group has stepped up its campaign in recent weeks.
It seized control of significant new territory across Yemen's south-western coast last week, including areas overlooking the crucial Bab al-Mandab waterway, strengthening its ability to enforce its declared blockade of Saudi shipping.
The price of a barrel of oil has surged since Saudi Arabia said on Friday it was closing the pipeline as a precaution. Brent crude was trading as high as $108 (£80) a barrel on Tuesday, down slightly from $109.80 on Monday.
Experts from trade intelligence firm Kpler said the pipeline's closure could reduce oil supplies by as much as 3.6 million barrels per day - or about 3.6% of global demand.
"Based on new information we've received, damage to the pipeline could take four to six weeks to resolve, given spare-parts availability and impaired supply chains," said Homayoun Falakshahi, Kpler's head of crude oil analysis.
Anne-Sophie Corbeau, from the Center on Global Energy Policy at Columbia University, said pipelines are "like sitting ducks" and recent strikes are a "very important signal" indicating workarounds being used to avoid the Strait of Hormuz "may not be super useful because they can be destroyed".
The Houthis have targeted other Saudi oil infrastructure with drones and missiles which has led to some operations being suspended.
There have also been attacks on military bases. New satellite images captured on Monday show damage to Saudi Arabia's King Khalid Air Base near Khamis Mushait which the Houthis said they had targeted with ballistic missiles and drones last week after it was used to carry out air strikes on Yemen.
At least three aircraft hangars or shelters appear to have been damaged at the Royal Saudi Air Force facility where US-made F-15 fighter jets are based.
The Saudi-led anti-Houthi military coalition of Arab states said on Tuesday that a Houthi missile and drone attack had injured 13 people in attacks on what the coalition said were "civilian objects".
The Houthis said Saudi Arabia had carried out with more than 50 strikes in western Yemen over the previous 24 hours.
The UN Refugee Agency has said that more than 100,000 people have been internally displaced by the renewed conflict.
