A shopkeeper’s alleged murder in West Bengal’s Titagarh on September 11 has triggered a controversy after Barrackpore BJP MLA Koustav Bagchi attempted to give it a communal spin by describing the victim as a ‘Sanatani’ murdered by ‘jihadis’.
In a 33-secong-long video that has now gone viral for over a week, the MLA’s claim was challenged on camera by the victim’s son, who interrupted Bagchi to say that there was nothing communal or political about his father’s murder.
The victim, Ramji Shaw, used to run a small corner shop from a portion of his home in the GC road area of Ward 18 of Barrackpore Municipality. He was allegedly killed after he refused to sell cigarettes on credit.
According to the locals, on September 11 afternoon, Shaw was trying to protect his son, who was allegedly being assaulted by three young men who were demanding to buy cigarettes from the shop without paying money on spot. As Shaw declined to sell cigarettes on credit, the men allegedly began attacking him and his son.
In the physical altercation, Shaw was pushed and heckled and lost consciousness. His family members rushed him to Barrackpore B N Bose sub-divisional hospital, where he succumbed to his injuries. According to locals, the three accused have been identified as Banti Ghosh, Sk. Sahil and Md. Nasir. Shaw’s wife had told Bengali news channel ABP Ananda that the accused had assaulted their son in the past.
Deceased’s Son Corrects MLA
As news of the alleged murder spread in the locality, Bagchi visited the deceased’s family the same day. Speaking to news channels while at Shaw’s home, he attempted to present the murder as communally motivated, specifically targeting the identity of the two accused who belong to the Muslim community.
In the viral clip, Bagchi can be heard saying (translated from Bengali), “This incident is not just related to an altercation over payment. Three Jihadis have killed a Sanatani. They wouldn’t have killed someone from their own religion.” However, even before Bagchi could finish his sentence, the deceased’s son corrected him, (translated from Bengali), “Sir, there is nothing related to religion in this case. The accused had come to my shop, looking to buy things on credit. When my father objected, they beat him up.”
The BJP MLA, seeming baffled by the interruption, responded: “I am speaking! Why are you not letting me speak!”. A few moments later, a person in purple shirt can be seen escorting the son to another room. While leaving the scene, the son stated, “This is not a matter of party politics.”
‘Politicians Inciting Locals for Electoral Gains’
Alt News visited the locality to independently verify the claims surrounding the murder and Bagchi’s allegation of a communal motive. While the bereaved wife and son both declined to speak, Shaw’s daughter Rikita confirmed to Alt News that it was indeed her brother who was seen correcting Bagchi in the viral video.
Sheikh Afroz (Ripon), who is Shaw’s immediate neighbour, said that the people in the area lived in communal harmony, as Hindus and Muslims co-existed there for generations. He added that politicians were, in fact, attempting to incite hostility between the communities. He also confirmed that Shaw’s son was seen in the video. “After the tragic incident, locals started to protest against the ‘gundagardi’ culture, and police officers had to come and pacify the situation. As the area is predominantly occupied by Muslims, most of the protesters were also Muslim. Does this not prove that this was not a communal incident?” asked Afroz.
A few metres from Shaw’s house, Md Mansoor, who runs a mobile repairing shop, said that Shaw’s shop used to have ‘ittar’ (perfume) and ‘surma’ (kohl) which were not found anywhere else in the area. “Every Eid, people from the Muslim community thronged to his shop to buy these products. Given that this was the reality which we saw every day, we don’t understand where this communal angle is coming from,” he said.
According to Mansoor, the accused youths were “known troublemakers”. “It is unfair to malign the name of an entire area and community for the wrongdoings of a select few. One of the accused is a Hindu, but the MLA still went on to claim that Shaw was murdered by Jihadis. Most of the shops in the neighbourhood, which is a predominantly Muslim area, were all shut in protest of Shaw’s murder for a few days after, only because there is no feeling of communal tension in this area,” Mansoor added.
No Communal Motive: Police
Alt News spoke to Titagrah officer-in-charge (OC) Atanu Chakraborty. The police station is located 1 km away from the crime scene. The officer confirmed that three people had been arrested in connection with the case. He said police did not find any communal motive behind the incident. The accused had pushed and beaten Shaw, following which Shaw suffered a stroke and died, he added.
“The accused are Sk Sahil, Md Nasir and Banti Ghosh. We have primarily booked them under sections pertaining to murder and further investigation is on. We couldn’t find any communal angle behind the crime,” he said, adding, the accused have been involved in public nuisance in the area in the past.
The police account, therefore, refutes Bagchi’s claims of a communal motive behind the alleged murder.
My Comments Twisted, Victim’s Son Apologised later, Claims MLA
Speaking to Alt News, Bagchi alleged, “There is no confusion. Some people are trying to do mischief with my quote. If I wanted, I could have done a lot of things over this issue, but I restrained myself considering the situation of the family. The area where this family lives are surrounded by Muslims — 90 out of 100 people living here are Muslims. The Hindu’s are constantly under a lot of pressure. So, whatever they said that day is due to fear.”
“I have a video of Ramji Shaw’s son. He had made a video and had sent it to me, clarifying their position. He also called me and apologised. Since my comments are being twisted, now I feel I have to publish the video that I have. I told his son that I can understand his emotions, his pain and fear. In the video, he also said that Hindus in that area are very few in number compared to the Muslims. However, they haven’t yet realised that the TMC government is gone and they [Hindus] are safe. I told him to be fearless,” Bagchi claimed, adding, “There definitely is a communal angle to this incident. The Muslims have kept the Hindus in that are terrorised.”
When asked about the one Hindu accused and how he could confidently claim that Shaw was murdered by ‘jihadis’, Bagchi said, “Banti Ghosh is a rowdy element and he mixes with them [the other two accused]. However, the main culprits are the two Muslims men. They have continued this for long, and you won’t find them attacking any Muslim.”
Alt News’ interactions with the locals and an observation of how they live, however, contradict Bagchi’s ‘fear of Muslims’ narrative. Shaw’s house is 550 metres from the Titagarh railway station. About 200 metres from the station, beside G C Road, stands a Muslim shrine (mazar), and next to it, a Ganesh Puja pandal has been erected. The two structures are separated only by a food stall.
A search on Google Maps of the area brought up an image from two years ago, in which a Durga Puja pandal was erected right next to the same Muslim shrine.
Further down the road, opposite to Mansoor’s shop, is Hasanjan Sporting Club, and a Hindu temple stands right next to it.
Pointing towards the narrow path beside the club, Mansoor said, “Ten families live there. Six are Muslim and four are Hindu.”

Pay No Attention to the Russian Oligarch at My Wedding Weekend
He’s just a dear friend we know nothing about!
Welcome to our wedding weekend! It’s going to be a beautiful occasion, followed by an intimate gathering of family, dear friends, and one Russian oligarch nobody knows who will be handed the bill afterward. The bride will wear white, the groom will wear white, and the Russian oligarch nobody knows will wear camouflage in case someone tries to take a picture of him and ProPublica finds out. We will try to pass him off as a tropical plant, or suggest that he was doing close-up magic. In a sense, he was. That whole celebration was magic!
To be clear, there is no ethical concern involving the Russian oligarch (part of Vladimir Putin’s recent delegation to China) sponsoring this lavish event. This was not actually a wedding after-party; it was a fun weekend that had been planned long in advance of the wedding, which our guests also happened to attend right after we got married. Totally different!
To those who say, “I still don’t know if a friend of Putin should be paying for this,” we say, “Who can truly say who is friends with another person?” This man paid hundreds of thousands of dollars for our three-day post-wedding celebration, but Eric Trump says he has “absolutely no clue who this person is,” nor has he ever heard his name. Probably Putin feels the same way.
A dear friend? A total stranger? Doesn’t matter. What’s most important is: money. The Supreme Court says money is speech, and we’ve taken that to heart. Money is just how people speak to us. Fifty dollars means “Hello.” Five hundred thousand dollars means “I want to hang out with Donald Trump Jr. in an unmarked Georgetown basement.” Footing most of the bill for a three-day island extravaganza is just “Congratulations to the happy couple!”
To those worried that the president might owe special favors to people present for his offspring’s wedding day, relax! This is not like The Godfather. In The Godfather, his daughter was getting married. Totally different. The president doesn’t have to grant any favors you ask on his son’s wedding day. In fact, it’s bad luck to ask for favors at a son’s wedding! Let alone his second one.
Also, the attorney general, Todd Blanche, says there’s nothing sketchy here to investigate. Everyone knows that it is only corruption when it comes from the Biden family. Anyways, having an oligarch of unclear provenance at your most intimate celebrations (sorry, the after-party for your most intimate celebrations) is a very normal thing, we think. These are the little details that make every wedding: the bridesmaids, getting their hair and makeup done; the best man, rushing to finish his toast; and the oligarch, handing over fistfuls of unmarked bills to all of the entertainers.
Every American can relate to this! Remember Ross’s wedding on Friends, when Monica and Chandler couldn’t find Ross’s oligarch, and everybody thought the wedding couldn’t go forward? Remember the morning of your own wedding, when you were scrambling to make sure you had something borrowed, something blue, and somebody’s oligarch paying for you? (The oligarch has nothing to do with something borrowed, because that implies we’ll be paying him back somehow; this is just a gift from the kindness of his heart.)
You may be wondering what to bring us! No gifts, please. Unless you are the Russian oligarch. Then we also accept $TRUMP coin.

In a significant relief for cinema exhibitors, the Karnataka High Court has quashed notices that had made the collection and remittance of a 2% cess on cinema tickets mandatory. The order, delivered on September 10, 2026, came in response to a writ petition filed by the Multiplex Association of India (MAI), PVR INOX, and other stakeholders in the exhibition sector.
Karnataka High Court quashes 2% cess on movie tickets; big relief for multiplexes and moviegoers
The petitioners had challenged the notices on the grounds that they lacked legal backing. The Court agreed, noting that the Karnataka Cine and Cultural Workers (Welfare) Act, 2024, under which the cess was to be levied, had not yet been formally notified. In the absence of this notification, the Court held that the notices directing exhibitors to collect and remit the levy were issued without jurisdiction, and accordingly quashed them.
The ruling comes alongside a related development on the administrative front, with the State Government having already withdrawn its office order dated August 29, 2026, which had pertained to the same cess.
The case stemmed from concerns raised by MAI over the proposed additional levy on movie tickets. The association had argued that an added cess would push up the cost of cinema-going for audiences, potentially discouraging footfalls at a time when the exhibition sector is already navigating a challenging business environment. MAI further contended that such a levy would work against the broader push towards simplifying the indirect tax structure for the entertainment sector.
With the High Court's order now in place, questions remain around what lies ahead for welfare mechanisms intended to support cultural workers in the state, and whether alternative frameworks will be explored to address that objective without directly burdening ticket prices.
MAI has indicated that it is open to facilitating discussions with its representatives on the matter, including the broader implications of the ruling for exhibitors and consumers, industry concerns around taxation and affordability, potential alternative mechanisms for worker welfare initiatives, and the road ahead for Karnataka's cinema exhibition sector.

Nearly two decades ago, a group of researchers at the Idaho National Laboratory ran a secret experiment, known as the Aurora Generator Test, on a massive emerald green diesel generator. Using 30 lines of code, they hacked into the generator’s virtual backroom, corrupting safeguards and flipping switches that left it out of sync with the rest of the power grid.
We’re worrying about the wrong AI apocalypse
America’s infrastructure was already hackable. Then came AI.
Before an audience of electrical utility executives and energy department officials watching from a nearby room, the 27-ton generator jolted violently, sputtering out a dark smoke as its rubber innards rapidly tore themselves apart.
“The implication was that with just a few lines of code, you can create conditions that were physically going to be very damaging to the machines we rely on,” lead researcher Michael Assante later told the journalist Andy Greenberg for his book Sandworm: A New Era of Cyberwar and the Hunt for the Kremlin’s Most Dangerous Hackers. “I had a very real pit in my stomach. It was like a glimpse of the future.”
That future seems to have creeped much closer this week, with leading AI developers and executives casually admitting that they believe their creation is, to paraphrase one winking X post, as likely to end humanity as the New York Jets are to make the playoffs this season. Now, exactly how AI would pull off killing everyone is far murkier territory. But as Assante sensed all those years ago, AI may not need to be all-powerful to leap from its virtual cage and into the critical infrastructure that powers our hospitals, flushes our toilets, and pumps water to our faucets. It just needs to fall into the wrong hands.
Almost any AI doomsday scenario you can think of begins with a swarm of shadowy bots slithering through cyberspace, poking their noses behind the scenes of power plants, toaster ovens, traffic lights, or even, in an utterly extreme case, our nuclear weapons arsenal. If destroying the Aurora generator, at the very least, required a human hacker to write the code, AI has since completely torn down the barrier to entry for wreaking havoc, as the Hugging Face incident demonstrated earlier this year.
But AI need not go rogue to threaten the power grid or mess with your tap water. A new age of AI-powered, but human-directed hacking is already upon us, experts say. With some of the nation’s most sensitive infrastructure startlingly vulnerable to attack, the most likely AI apocalypse could in fact start with the water tower or generator idling in your backyard. In a worst-case scenario, this could lead to a cascade of scary failures in the systems we rely on to live comfortably modern lives, from running our AC in blazingly hot summers to geolocating our ships and planes.
“Before, you needed to have highly skilled technical expertise,” to pull off some version of a real-life Aurora Generator Test, said Alvaro Cardenas, a computer science professor at UC Santa Cruz. “And now, you just have to have a general idea of what’s possible.”
AI is making an old threat much worse
Not long after the Idaho National Laboratory hacked that poor generator into combustion, the federal government mandated that electrical utilities engage in basic cybersecurity hygiene.
And yet much of America’s critical infrastructure — like gas pipelines, water desalination plants, or cargo terminals — remains woefully unprepared for even conventional cyber attacks, much less the coming onslaught of AI.
That’s in part because cyberattacks like the one simulated in the Aurora Generator Test have long been — and still are, to some extent — exceedingly rare, unappealing to most criminal hackers because they’re optimized for disruption rather than financial gain. But in the process of making it extremely easy for anyone to code, AI has also made it extremely easy for almost anyone to vibe hack their way into your online bank account, or, in theory, a local reservoir or the power grid. AI agents can also vastly widen the scope on easy targets because, as Andy Bochman, an expert in infrastructure resilience at West Yost, put it — “they don’t sleep; they don’t get tired; and they don’t get sick.”
In the past, even those who did want to launch large-scale attacks on infrastructure probably weren’t savvy enough to do so. And while other nations such as China, Iran, and Russia have indeed already breached many of our infrastructure systems (as we have theirs), they haven’t opted to make much of a ruckus once inside.
“Geopolitics is eroding the idea that those with capability lack the intent, and AI is eroding the other part of it, that those with the intent lack the capability.”
— Jason Healey, Columbia University cybersecurity scholar
But that norm is now changing, said Jason Healey, a cybersecurity scholar at Columbia University. “Geopolitics is eroding the idea that those with capability lack the intent, and AI is eroding the other part of it, that those with the intent lack the capability,” he told me. So, on the one hand, a nation like Russia might be much more inclined to actually disrupt our power grid now than it used to be. And, on the other hand, a nihilistic lone wolf or terrorist group could use AI to do much more damage than they ever could before.
Just last month, we saw a glimpse of what this could look like when dozens of water and wastewater systems in small towns across the nation were attacked by a group of hackers most likely associated with Iran, leading to temporary water stoppages and flooding. These attacks have not been definitively linked to AI, but the National Security Agency warned soon afterward that hackers have been actively using AI to target US infrastructure like it. A few weeks later, President Donald Trump declared a national emergency over foreign interference in the power grid, which referenced the growing threat of cybersecurity.
Preparing for the worst
Most of the nation’s water systems are extremely local and absurdly exposed to such attacks, so much so that “it’s almost like having a welcome mat” for a would-be hacker, said Bochman, mostly because these utilities are too small and underfunded to do much to stop them. “You have a million other problems to take care of, like aging infrastructure — your stuff’s falling apart because it’s been in the ground for 100 years,” he said. Addressing that deferred maintenance often feels far more urgent than doing “something more on cybersecurity.”
Whether it’s a rogue cluster of agents or a hostile nation-state trying to mess with our electricity, we should prepare our most important infrastructure for the worst. In Bochman’s view, that may mean rejecting the pressure to digitize everything in the first place and moving toward something that resembles the days when “people manned things like substations, communicated by a landline telephone, and read gauges, the analog things,” he said. “The screen is the thing that is infinitely manipulatable.”
Healey, who advised the Biden administration heavily on cybersecurity and infrastructure, believes that the nation desperately needs a coordinated response, between the federal government and AI companies, but also between the US and other countries like China, where similarly powerful models are being developed. And utility systems need to assume they will be a target and improve their cybersecurity practices accordingly, Healey says, ideally with funding from the federal government or, perhaps more appropriately, AI companies.
Nobody knows precisely how vulnerable America’s infrastructure is to AI right now, in part because policymakers — and perhaps more disturbingly, AI’s creators themselves — seem woefully unsure of how to stop the technology from acting badly (or obeying bad orders) in the first place. For now at least, the solution might be, as Bochman suggests, to pull as many of our critical systems offline as possible, the better to hide it from AI and those who would misuse it.
“When bad things start to happen, no one will know what to do or why because they’re black boxes; the people that make them don’t know what’s going on inside,” Bochman said. “And the poor utility people who ultimately own the risk when someone gets hurt from a system” won’t understand what went wrong either, “and they’ll wish to God they’d never taken it on board.”

My dream was to be a doctor, now it could come to zero
- Published
Nooria, which is not her real name, still remembers one of the moments that made her want to be a doctor.
It was back home in a village in Afghanistan, where she was born. A 13-year-old boy there became sick and died because of appendicitis.
"He was completely healthy, but the road was blocked and he died on the way. There are multiple incidents just like this."
"That and the potential I saw in myself, I thought I can be a doctor for them, I can help."
She fears that dream could now be over and that she could be sent back to Afghanistan. That would be the end of any chance at a career for Nooria who, as a woman, is barred from studying or working by Afghanistan's Taliban government.
Earlier this month, Pakistan's Medical and Dental Council - the medical education regulator - issued a letter to all medical and dental colleges across the country saying that students from Afghanistan studying in their colleges must return to their home country. Failure to follow the directive, it said, would be "viewed seriously" and may lead to regulatory action. A temporary stay order from the Lahore High Court stopped students in Punjab, such as Nooria, from being deported immediately until the next hearing, scheduled for Friday. There is no certainty that the stay will continue.
Since 2023, hundreds of thousands of Afghans have been deported from Pakistan and over two million have left according to the UN. These numbers increased as the relationship between Pakistan and Afghanistan dramatically deteriorated in the last year. Pakistan has accused Afghanistan's Taliban government of harbouring militant groups, which it denies.
The announcement from the medical council was met with a strong reaction. Amnesty International called the decision "patently discriminatory and arbitrary" and said that "Pakistan has obligations under international human rights law to uphold the right to education without discrimination on the basis of national origin." Several of Pakistan's former envoys to Afghanistan also urged the council to reconsider; one called it "shocking" and "a question of humanity, compassion and Pakistan's own moral responsibility".
The council told the BBC that they can give no further comment while the court case continues, but their lawyer has told the BBC that none of the Afghan students were registered with PMDC. The students say that this is the responsibility of their colleges, not them; a notification issued by the PMDC earlier this year, external directs colleges to ensure that students are registered.
The medical and dental students the BBC has spoken to say they do not see how the relationship between the two countries should affect their ability to study.
For Nooria, this stings even more because she says it took a lot for her to get here. She first began studying at Kabul University, but as the Taliban forces approached the city, she left. She was offered what she thought at the time was a lifeline: the opportunity to study medicine in Pakistan on a scholarship. Now a final year student at a medical university in Lahore, she says she has given everything to the course.
"I was studying, day and night. I couldn't sleep because there was so much pressure and knowledge that I had accumulated in my mind. I got used to it a bit, but I have compromised a lot. My relationships, talking to my family, spending time with my friends. I think I haven't lived for these years, I have only studied for my dream."
So when she heard about the letter, Nooria was in shock. She's still nervous about the repercussions of speaking out, which is why she asked we don't reveal her name.
"We knocked on every door, our teachers, organisations, anyone we thought could help us. We are under so much pressure that we have completely forgotten about our studies, we don't know what will happen to us."
Final year students like Nooria have their last exams in just a few months. Said Mubin, another final year student in Punjab, is in the same position.
"I was in complete despair, my mind was blank. It was like a panic situation because they were giving us very short time to evacuate the (accommodation), the college," he says.
Other students have also brought cases across the country, but different directives have been issued, adding to the confusion. Some students told the BBC that they have finished their exams but not completed the practical training - known as a 'House Job' - to complete their medical education.
Without completing their degrees, both Mubin, Nooria and many other medical and dental students the BBC spoke to, fear that none of their credits will be recognised by another institution.
"It means you have to start from zero, from your first year," Mubin says.
Both Nooria and Mubin have valid student visas, seen by the BBC. The PMDC did not provide the BBC with the number of students they believe are affected, but Anayatullah Momand, a spokesperson for the Afghan medical students, has said that they estimate it's approximately 1,000 medical and dental students, 65% of whom have visa holders. Some are still waiting for a visa, but Momand said that 15% have had their visas cancelled or have not yet applied for one.
While the medical council's letter makes no distinction between students with the right documents, Pakistan's Ministry for Foreign Affair's spokesman did. "Our policy is that those Afghan students who are in Pakistan on a valid visa and registered for a valid course will continue and complete his or her education," said Sajjad Haider Khan during a recorded press conference at the ministry.
Similar comments were made the previous week, but the students say they have not seen any change to their situation.
With the outcome of her studies still uncertain, Nooria has been trying not to think about what returning to Afghanistan could mean.
"My family counted on me. These five years I have sacrificed everything that would be zero, multiplied by zero. And then I would become a poor and helpless Afghan female, facing this destiny. I cannot imagine this."

The Centre has told the Delhi High Court that an adult can nominate a partner, including one in a non-heterosexual relationship, to make medical decisions if they become incapacitated, potentially opening the way for same-sex partners to act for each other despite existing rules not clearly recognising such arrangements.
The submission comes in a case filed by Arshiya Takkar, who has been in a relationship with her partner since 2015 and married her in New Zealand in 2023. Her plea highlighted that in the event of a medical emergency, she could be left without any legal mechanism to make critical decisions for her partner, despite the couple having lived together in Delhi since 2018.
Responding to her plea, the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and the National Medical Commission said that allowing a competent adult to nominate a partner, including one in a same-sex relationship, to take medical decisions in the event of incapacity was “substantially capable of being accommodated within the existing legal and ethical framework”.
“Permitting a competent adult to nominate his/her partner, including a partner in a non-heterosexual/same-sex relationship, to take medical decisions on his/her behalf in the event of incapacity would constitute a logical and tailored extension of the same principle,” the affidavit said. It added that such a nomination could be subject to appropriate safeguards and the applicable law.
The Centre said decisions concerning an adult patient who is unable to make or communicate a decision must be considered in light of the nature of the treatment, the circumstances requiring the decision, the patient’s own wishes, and the legal framework governing such representation.
It further submitted that where a competent adult has nominated or otherwise authorised their partner to act on their behalf in the event of incapacity, “there appears to be no medical or ethical rationale for excluding such person merely on account of the sex, gender or sexual orientation of the partners or because their union does not fall within the conventional understanding of marriage...”.
The Centre also said it recognised and respected the constitutional guarantees of dignity, privacy, autonomy, equality and individual choice available to all persons, including members of the LGBTQIA+ community.
The petition is likely to come up for hearing on Thursday (September 17, 2026).
Ms. Takkar, in her petition filed last year through advocates Manjira Dasgupta and Bhargav Ravindran Thali, highlighted the lack of a clear legal framework or common law recognising “partners in a union”, making it difficult to provide consent during medical treatment or emergencies.
The plea stated that the existing regulation, Clause 7.16 of the Indian Medical Council (Professional Conduct, Etiquette, and Ethics) Regulations, 2002, mandates consent for medical procedures or treatment from a “husband or wife, parent or guardian in the case of a minor, or the patient himself”.
“This lack of explicit recognition of partners in a union renders the petitioner effectively powerless to make critical medical decisions for her partner, or vice versa, a right readily available to heterosexual partners under the current regulations,” it stated.
The petition contended that despite the Supreme Court directive for a high-powered committee to address entitlements of LGBTQIA+ couples, including their recognition as “family” for medical decision-making, the authorities have failed to take expeditious measures.
“This inaction leaves the petitioner and other same-sex couples vulnerable and unable to exercise the fundamental right to care for each other in medical emergencies,” the plea said.

‘Moving towards Atmanirbhar Bharat’: Rajnath Singh hails handover of aircraft, helicopters by HAL to IAF and PHL
Speaking at the event, Defence Minister Rajnath Singh said, "Today, we are witnessing three important achievements together.
Asserting that India is rapidly moving towards self-reliance through indigenous defence manufacturing, Defence Minister Rajnath Singh said on Friday that the country is witnessing a major milestone in its aerospace capabilities and technological self-confidence.
Singh was addressing a ceremony marking the handover of indigenously manufactured aircraft and helicopters by Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) to the Indian Air Force (IAF) and Pawan Hans Limited (PHL).
Speaking at the event, Defence Minister Rajnath Singh said, "Today, we are witnessing three important achievements together. First, the indigenously designed and developed Dhruv-Next Generation Civil helicopter is being handed over after being granted Type Certification by the DGCA. Second, the final batch of the LCA Final Operational Clearance, that is, FOC Trainer, is being handed over to the Indian Air Force. And third, today we are handing over the first aircraft of the HTT-40 Basic Trainer series production to the Indian Air Force. On this occasion, I congratulate all of you."
Emphasising that the event was not just a routine handover, Singh added, "Today's day is not merely a formal handing-over ceremony. It is an important milestone in the direction of our progress towards India's indigenous aerospace capability, technological self-confidence and self-reliance."
Recalling the past reliance on foreign nations, the Defence Minister noted, "If I talk about nearly a decade ago, projects in the defence sector were being carried out at a very slow pace. We used to be dependent on imports for most things, whether in the sense of technology or in the sense of products... After that, under the leadership of our Prime Minister, we began working with the core mantra of self-reliance."
Highlighting the need for a unified aerospace sector, Singh stated, "The development of a strong aerospace industry should not be limited to merely fulfilling defence requirements. We need to develop such an ecosystem that can effectively address the requirements of both civil and military aviation sectors... Therefore, we need to build such an integrated aerospace ecosystem that is self-reliant in every sector."
Praising indigenous military advancements, he said, "The second important milestone of today is the handing over of the last batch of LCA FOC Trainer to the Indian Air Force. If Dhruv-NG is an example of our indigenous civil aerospace capability, then LCA FOC Trainer is a symbol of India's indigenous military aerospace capability and the maturity of the fighter aircraft ecosystem."
Defence Minister Rajnath Singh challenged the nation's scientific and engineering community to pioneer cutting-edge technologies and position India as a global leader in aerospace.
He said, "Today I want to challenge our young scientists, engineers, designers, test pilots and technicians: 'To create technologies that do not exist today.' You have to develop such capabilities which will give India a leading position in the global aerospace technology landscape in the coming decade."
Highlighting the importance of synergy between different sectors, Singh emphasised moving past traditional divisions, stating, "Now is the time that we do not see public versus private as a competition, but rather see the public and private sectors as complementary to each other."
Later, the Minister also stressed the importance of indigenous production in modern warfare, stating, "Developing such things indigenously is the need of the hour for India. Because today the nature of warfare is rapidly changing. In the future, air operations will be information-intensive and technology-driven."
Commending HAL's contribution, the Defence Minister said, "Hindustan Aeronautics Limited has indigenously constructed the HTT-40, and its first aircraft for series production has also been handed over to the IAF today... And most importantly, our dependence on foreign countries in this matter will now come to an end. And in the case of the HTT-40, another good thing is that, on the strength of its features, this aircraft also holds possibilities for export."
The handover included two LCA FOC Trainer aircraft to the IAF, completing Twin Seater deliveries under the Final Operational Clearance contract; four Dhruv NG helicopters to PHL; and HTT-40 Basic Trainer aircraft to the IAF, marking the start of deliveries under the 70-aircraft contract.

Rare two-headed turtle is found on Cape Cod
The last rare two-headed turtle hatchling in Cape Cod was found in 2021
Double trouble! A rare two-headed baby turtle has been discovered on Cape Cod.
The diamondback terrapin, weighing 5.2-gram, was found Thursday at a protected nesting site in Wellfleet and brought to the Cape Wildlife Center by the Mass Audubon Wellfleet Bay Wildlife Sanctuary.
The center shared three photos of the hatchling from different angles on Facebook, showing its two distinct heads — a rare developmental anomaly known as bicephaly.
“While we’ve encountered this unusual condition before, every case gives us another opportunity to learn more about these fascinating animals’ anatomy and physiology,” Cape Wildlife Center wrote in the post. “Our veterinary team will be closely monitoring the little terrapin as we learn more about how their two heads and bodies work together.”
Bicephaly occurs when conjoined twins fail to fully separate during development, according to National Geographic. The rare condition is most common in turtles and snakes but can occur in other animals, too.
The turtle is only the second case of bicephaly the Cape Wildlife Center has seen in the past five years. In 2021, a two-headed “McNugget-size” turtle with six legs made the internet do a double take.
Many two-headed animals die young because of physical difficulties, including competing for food or attacking each other, although reptiles tend to survive longer, according to National Geographic.
“For now, our team is monitoring this little one’s (two’s?) appetite, growth, and behavior closely,” Cape Wildlife Center wrote in its Facebook post.
Diamondback terrapins are considered a threatened species in Massachusetts, making the finding even more exciting, New England Wildlife Center CEO Zak Mertz told CBS News.
“We're looking forward to learning everything we can about these two young turtles,” Mertz said. "What I've heard from the vet team is that they are behaving normally, and both sides are looking very good.”
The wildlife center’s veterinary team has handled a variety of unusual animal cases in recent years. Last year, the team treated a screech owl that somehow ended up inside a Barnstable resident’s bathroom, CBS News reports.
In 2022, the center cared for a coyote pup after a family mistakenly thought they had found a lost puppy. A year before to that, veterinarians performed foot surgery on a goose while its mate remained nearby, watching the procedure.

Montreal mayor mulls legal action against Quebec after baby found at encampment
Baby is safe with a family member, police say
Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada is threatening to take legal action against Quebec after a baby was found living with their mother in an encampment on Notre-Dame Street.
The baby, who is just over a year old, was found last Friday in a tent with their mother, according to the Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM). Police officers recovered the child, who was then placed into the care of Quebec youth services (DPJ), while their mother was taken into the care of social services.
According to police, the baby's life, health and safety are not at risk, and they are currently in the care of a family member.
After saying on Thursday that the case is a sign that the province is not doing enough to address the homelessness crisis in Montreal, Martinez Ferrada doubled down on her criticism in an interview with Radio-Canada on Friday.
"I believe there are concrete actions the Quebec government can and must take," Martinez Ferrada said in French, adding that a lack of provincial funding is limiting her administration's ability to address homelessness in Montreal.
"If I have to go to court to secure that support, it is an option I am seriously considering right now," she said.
The people living in encampments along Notre-Dame Street are on land owned by Quebec, and Superior Court judges have on several occasions blocked the city's efforts to dismantle tents there.
Mathieu Morin, director of the community organization Carrefour Familial Hochelaga, says it is still extremely rare to find kids on the street, but a baby living in an encampment shows how severe the housing crisis has become.
"We are past saying this is a crisis," Morin told Radio-Canada.
Politicians respond
Quebec premier and Coalition Avenir Québec Leader Christine Fréchette said the case is heartbreaking, and that it must not happen again.
She said all levels of government need to work together to combat homelessness in Montreal and across the province, adding that she plans to meet with Martinez Ferrada in the coming days.
Quebec Liberal Party Leader Charles Milliard echoed Fréchette's sentiment, saying that elected officials at all levels shoulder responsibility for the homelessness crisis. He also said that officials should focus more on addressing the root causes of the crisis.
Ruba Ghazal, meanwhile, expressed anger at the situation. The Québec Solidaire co-spokesperson said she was shocked at the news, while arguing that more investment and political will is needed to solve homelessness in the province.
Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon also expressed outrage at the situation, saying that it was embarassing for Quebec. He argued for better social safety nets for vulnerable people in the province.
When asked about the situation, Éric Duhaime was more blunt. The Conservative Party of Quebec leader said he was sympathetic to people living in encampments, but he argued that encampments should be dismantled as soon as possible.
All five party leaders have agreed to participate in a forum on homelessness in 2027.

For years, researchers have known that, among people diagnosed with lung cancer, the prevalence of nonsmokers has been increasing. But they have been trying to determine what factors — whether genetic, environmental, or something else — might put these “never-smokers” at heightened risk.
Now, researchers have identified a very rare genetic variant that is associated with 25-fold higher odds of lung cancer, they reported in the journal Science on Thursday. In the U.S., the variant is far more common among people in Southern Appalachia than in other regions.
Experts said that the variant likely only plays a role in a small portion of never-smoker lung cancer cases. But the research provides further evidence that these types of tumors can be tied to distinct risk factors, which may in turn require thinking differently about screening programs and treatment strategies. More broadly, the new study highlights the types of narrow but crucial discoveries that can be made by turning to large datasets replete with health information from millions of people. In this case, the investigators relied on genetic data from 23andMe.

Justice delayed: Acknowledging women pioneers in science
The debate in the scientific world has often been about glory. Who deserves the glory for a discovery, for an invention, for defining a procedure, a drug, a vaccine? Does credit ever attach to the patients who were experimented upon, the participants of a clinical trial, people who gave of their time and body in order that science may advance, in order that people who come after them do not suffer. Codes of ethics are mutable, they keep changing, and the grant of credit in science also operates on this arc. This story is a page from such an omission, a blunder. Nearly 150 years later, some form of reparation was attempted.
For the world, for the longest time, perhaps even till today, J. Marion Sims was the ‘Father of Modern Gynaecology.’ Sims reportedly earned the title for his ‘groundbreaking surgical innovations, notably the development of a cure for vesicovaginal fistula.” For his achievements, Sims not only received the soubriquet, but also statues and memorials and hospitals and wards named after him. The number of girls on whom he perfected his techniques were not even a footnote in the glorious history he covered himself with.
Among them was Anarcha Westcott, a teenage mother, a patient who developed a terrible vesicovaginal fistula, tears or holes that develop between the bladder and vagina, sustained after three days of labour. The tears made it impossible to control her bowel or bladder and the condition caused her immense pain and suffering. That is how she came under the ‘care’ of Sims, if care could be used to describe what he went on to do.
Anarcha was a young African American woman wrested down in slavery. Sims reportedly believed that African American women do not feel pain, so he experimented on her repeatedly (we know of two others -- Betsey, and Lucy), operating without anaesthesia (though it was available). Sims himself records that he had performed nearly 30 procedures on her, consent was a casualty of the times, before he perfected his technique using silver to suture the fistula, that prevented infection.Before this, a vesicovaginal fistula was considered untreatable, and women would continue to suffer the rest of their life.
Anarcha did not disappear after this though. J. C. Hallman, in his 2023 book Say Anarcha- A Young Woman, a Devious Surgeon, and the Harrowing Birth of Modern Women’s Health, did extensive research to uncover that far from disappearing after the Sims experiments, she went on to serve in Sims hospital, as a midwife, nurse, and ‘doctor woman’ to her own people, women who were also slaves. Many decades after Anarcha died, a groundswell of support arose for her from women who objected to the way she was quietly erased from history, and instead calling for her to be celebrated as the “mother of gynaecology.”
Say Anarcha excavates history, deconstructing the biographical smoke screen of a surgeon who has falsely been enshrined as a medical pioneer and bringing forth a heroic Black woman to her rightful place at the center of the creation story of modern women’s health care. She was more than a medical ‘specimen’, she worked at Sims’ slave hospital near Montgomery, Alabama. She trained and served as a surgical nurse and went on to help other women, also being experimented upon at the hospital.
More recently, efforts have been made to honour her contribution to gynaecology. The American college of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists have dedicated two days – February 28 and March 1—to Anarcha, Lucy and Betsey. Recognition also saw expression in art: At Harvard’s Hutchins Center exhibition in 2023, a prominent exhibit was artist Jules Arthur’s paintings of Anarcha, Luch and Betsey through her work titled “Call and Response: A Narrative of Reverence to Our Foremothers in Gynaecology“.
Artist Michelle Browder created a 15-foot public monument honouring them as “the mothers of gynaecology“ in downtown Montgomery. Tangentially, it was also seen as a victory that Sims’ statue was removed from Central Park in April 2018 and relocated. Hallman’s book was preceded by a documentary Remembering Anarcha.
Unfortunately, Anarcha’s story is not merely a historical wrong. It serves to remind health practitioners and policy makers that several inequities still govern access and affordability of high quality care; that for women, it could be tougher than it might be for men. For that, we will have to keep saying her name, so it will be a reminder. Say her name, say Anarcha.

Beijing, Taipei need peace deal before reunification, Taiwanese scholar says
An agreement ending hostilities could allow the two sides to discuss the future on an equal footing, Chang Ya-chung
A formal peace deal between Beijing and Taipei should be signed to build trust before discussions on post-reunification political arrangements, a prominent Taiwanese political scientist has argued at a security conference in Beijing.
Chang Ya-chung, who heads the Taiwan-based Sun Yat-sen School advocacy group, said the “one country, two systems” formula, which has been applied to Hong Kong and Macau, had so far failed to resonate in Taiwanese society.
“If reunification means that one side, with greater power, puts forward a proposal and the relatively weaker side simply decides whether to accept it, it is only natural for people in Taiwan to have concerns,” Chang said on the sidelines of the Xiangshan Forum, Beijing’s leading security platform.

"I expect him to be on the pitch and it's my duty to get him on the pitch," said the England boss. "That was totally on me. He didn't put a foot wrong during the World Cup.
"He was class in behaviour on the training pitch. There was big competition; we played Reece (James) in central midfield also. Elliot Anderson is amazing for us; Declan Rice is a very unique player.
"We trusted them more than we trusted Kobbie. It was difficult for him. It was on me."
The competition for places in England's midfield remains fierce. But clearly Mainoo is a part of Tuchel's plans and there are no hard feelings. The nature of the camp, spanning three weeks and including four fixtures, should allow him chances to prove his worth.
Nick Wright
Trent's shock selection
It should not be a shock to see an Englishman playing for Real Madrid selected in the England squad but Trent Alexander-Arnold's selection is exactly that.
This marks a massive shift from Tuchel, who previously said Alexander-Arnold was not the profile of right-back he wanted in his side and repeatedly declined to select the former Liverpool star - even when Tino Livramento suffered a pre-World Cup injury and Tuchel had the opportunity to call up a replacement.
Questions over why Tuchel overlooked the technical 27-year-old reoccurred when the England boss questioned the natural ability of Three Lions players to be able to retain the ball and control games under pressure.

Alexander-Arnold had not been in an England squad since the summer of 2025 so what has changed?
"He was never non-selectable," said Tuchel when asked about Alexander-Arnold. "Now is his chance to show, come to camp, be the best version of himself. He comes as a right-back for us."
His performances for Real Madrid this season did not shift the needle alone.
He has one assist from five appearances and his deployment in midfield for the Champions League win over Inter Milan was a reminder of the continuing conundrum managers are having in getting the most out of Alexander-Arnold's potential.
Real boss Jose Mourinho used Alexander-Arnold in central midfield due to injuries and applauded his application - but also noted how he had lost possession and noted the physical challenge of the role.
Last season, Alexander-Arnold was battling with Dani Carvajal for the right-back spot at Real Madrid. This season it is summer signing Denzel Dumfries challenging him for the place.
The brilliant on-the-ball ability remains but defensive concerns continue. How Tuchel uses Alexander-Arnold - and what this change of stance means longer term - will be an intriguing narrative through the international break.
Peter Smith
If England cannot control games, why not 'embrace the chaos'?
Tuchel was critical of England's 'DNA' after the loss to Argentina, suggesting the players were unable to control high-pressure matches with possession in the way a team like Spain can.
The return of technical players Palmer and Alexander-Arnold to his squad seemed to be an admission he had left some of the best English players at looking after the ball out of the group. But in his press conference on Friday Tuchel hinted that perhaps it is better for England to go the other way - and "embrace the chaos".
"The more I reflect on it [the Argentina loss], it's more buying into our strengths and playing more like in the second half against Croatia, or first half against France," said Tuchel. "We get a lot of value out of it [this style]. This is what the Premier League reflects.
"Football is about adapting to situations, and football without any control is sometimes hard to digest for a coach. If you look at the 6-4 against France, people talk about it like it's one of their nicest experiences ever to watch a football match.
"Maybe I have to compromise in my wish for control - maybe we need more chaos, to embrace the chaos. Maybe it brings out the best.
"We will adjust our style but always to put the strengths of the players on the first priority."
Peter Smith
Gibbs-White crowded out in No 10 battle
Morgan Gibbs-White can feel justifiably aggrieved by his omission. The 26-year-old was outstanding last season for Nottingham Forest, racking up 15 Premier League goals and registering four assists. He has continued in the same vein this term.
Gibbs-White continues to face intense competition for places in the No 10 position. Palmer has been recalled to a squad which already features Bellingham, Rogers and Eberechi Eze. Tuchel says the numbers do not add up.
"He was close but it's always the same," he said. "It makes no sense to choose three, four or five No 10s. It just doesn't help anyone. We can see the form that Morgan is in. He ended the season strongly and was the key player for Forest to not be relegated."
Gibbs-White might wonder why Eze was preferred. The Arsenal man has not started a Premier League game this season and produced roughly half as many Premier League goal involvements as Gibbs-White last term. But all Gibbs-White can do is keep pushing, and be ready if the recalled Palmer does not deliver.
"It's one thing to be chosen, like Cole, and get your ticket back to the squad, but it's another thing to perform for England," added Tuchel. "Cole, especially, needs to step up when he comes and show these kinds of numbers and performances to get his place, keep his shirt and justify the nomination."
Nick Wright
Foden's England future in doubt?
Gibbs-White is not the only No 10 to have been crowded out. Phil Foden is also on the outside looking in having been overlooked for Tuchel's World Cup squad too.
The Manchester City star was included in Tuchel's squads in March of this year and November of 2025, but this omission comes after an encouraging start to the season was interrupted by his red card in last weekend's Manchester derby.
Foden now faces an almighty battle, in an area of the pitch in which England are well stocked, to win Tuchel over and earn a place back in his plans. His latest omission, as Tuchel returns to other technicians such as Alexander-Arnold, will feel painful.
Nick Wright
Is Tuchel embracing England's next generation?
The England manager has pivoted from the experienced squad he selected for the World Cup and made a marked effort to give chances to a plethora of young talent in his latest camp.
Veteran England presences like Jordan Henderson, Ivan Toney and Ollie Watkins have been omitted, leaving room for the inclusion of Myles Lewis-Skelly, Alex Scott and Rio Ngumoha - all of whom are under the age of 23, with the latter having turned 18 less than a month ago.
Ngumoha's inclusion is without doubt the most eye-catching.
The teenage sensation travelled with England's squad to Florida for their pre-tournament training camp and has appeared in five of Liverpool's six games to start the season, impressing enough to be called up even without recording a goal contribution thus far this campaign.
Perhaps easier choices were that of Lewis-Skelly and Scott in the midfield. The former has excelled for unbeaten league leaders Arsenal, recording two assists from deep-lying midfield and keeping £75m summer signing Bruno Guimaraes out of the champions' starting line-up.
Scott has continued to build on an impressive 2025/26 campaign in which he represented arguably the key component in a Bournemouth side that qualified for European football for the first time. Those performances - alongside earning him his place - meant he was linked to high-profile suitors like Chelsea and Manchester United throughout the summer.
"We had three players in prep camp with us [before the World Cup], Alex Scott, Rio Ngumoha and Josh [King], all three of them were fantastic members of the squad," Tuchel said.
"Not only because they were nice and reliable and excellent characters, but they showed the quality, courage and curiosity on the pitch, which was very nice to see."
Whether Tuchel ushers in new tactics remains to be seen - but his first England squad since the World Cup has shown a willingness to at least include new players.

Trump to sign Russia sanctions bill today that threatens 100% tariffs on India: Report
The legislation will give Trump the authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries that continue to buy Russian oil and gas, which includes India.
US President Donald Trump is expected to sign the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 on Friday, news agency ANI reported citing a White House official.
Notably, the proposed law would allow the US president to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries that continue purchasing Russian oil and gas, including India.
The legislation cleared the House of Representatives with a 262-159 vote after receiving approval from the Senate last month.
It also includes measures against vessels associated with Russia's "shadow fleet". According to the US, these ships have helped Russia continue energy exports despite Western sanctions.
Under the bill, countries importing less than 15 per cent of Russia's natural gas exports could qualify for an exemption if they have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.
For India, the bill creates a legal framework that could enable Washington to levy tariffs of up to 100 per cent on Indian goods if New Delhi continues purchasing Russian energy.
However, the legislation does not automatically introduce a 100 per cent tariff on Indian imports. Instead, it grants the executive branch the power to impose such duties under specific legal conditions, provided the bill becomes law and Trump chooses to implement them.
India and China remain major buyers of Russian crude oil. Their ongoing energy trade with Moscow has therefore become a key part of discussions surrounding the legislation.
India on Russia sanctions bill
India warned on Thursday that the proposed legislation could affect its relationship with the US as well as global energy markets.
In a statement, India's external affairs ministry said the government was determined “to take all necessary measures to protect its trade and economic interests” and would coordinate with trade and industry organisations to address the possible impact.
The ministry said India had discussed the legislation “at high levels in recent months with various US interlocutors”. It added that New Delhi had “very clearly articulated” the potential consequences — “for not just the bilateral relationship but also the international energy market.”
Reaffirming its position, the ministry said India's energy purchases are based on national interest. “India remains firmly committed to ensuring energy security for its 1.4 billion people,” it said, adding that the country would continue buying energy through “diversified sourcing and on the basis of evolving market dynamics.”
Russia sanctions bill
The US Senate passed the legislation in an 86-11 vote on August 7. However, its passage through the House was delayed by disagreements over tariff provisions and their potential impact on American trade policy.
The package also includes Trump's proposal to extend existing sanctions on Iran by five years. This provision played a significant role in obtaining his support for the bill.
Trump backed the inclusion of Iran in the proposed Russia sanctions legislation in July. He wrote on Truth Social, "Republicans should add Iran to the Russian Sanctions Bill. That's what Lindsey wanted to do, and it was going to happen. Important!!!"

Could trees developed with gene-editing technology protect Florida's citrus industry?
Could genetically modified trees protect Florida's citrus industry?
Citrus growers in Florida are planting new trees that have been modified using gene-editing technology to ward against the lethal citrus greening disease.
Growers have tried everything from tents to sprays to protect citrus trees from the bacterial infection, which has killed off many of Florida's citrus trees and led to a massive decline in the amount of citrus the state produces. Now growers are waiting to see if the genetic modifications, which the Environmental Protection Agency approved earlier this year, will keep the trees alive.
Citrus greening arrived in Florida in 2005. The disease is spread by a tiny winged insect called an Asian citrus psyllid. It attacks the trees' immune system, so they can't fight the infection. Once infected, a tree produces bitter, discolored fruit and usually dies a few years later. There's no cure.
Ron English's family ran a citrus business in Valrico, Fla., for generations until greening wiped it out, forcing them to close in 2015.
"We had some of the best looking groves around, and all the time and effort that we had spent, you just see it diminish right before you," English said.
In the late 1990s, before citrus greening arrived in Florida, growers were shipping out around 300 million boxes of fruit each season, said Matt Joyner, CEO of Florida Citrus Mutual, a trade association that represents citrus growers. By comparison, they shipped a little more than 15 million boxes during this year's season, which ended in June, he said.
Soilcea, a Tampa-based company, used CRISPR gene-editing technology to design a rootstock that resists greening. Known as CarriCea T1, it keeps a tree's immune system working, allowing growers to rely less on insecticides.
Focusing on the rootstock to fight the bacteria is key, said Soilcea CEO Yianni Lagos. He explained that although the first sign that a tree is infected is yellowing leaves, "before you even have symptoms, half the root system is already dead."
Lagos is now waiting to see what happens when the rootstock is grafted onto trees and planted.
In a SoilCea test field, the results so far are promising. Trees with the CarriCea T1 rootstock are taller and greener.
English cares for the dozens of trees in the test field that have the modified rootstock. They were planted last summer next to trees without it.
"That's the CarriCea rootstock — see how big the leaves have filled out," English said, pointing to a tree with the modification.
The smaller tree next to it does not have the CarriCea T1 rootstock. It's smaller with yellower leaves.
"See the discoloration, that's the disease already working through the tree," he said.
The real test for the CarriCea T1 tree will be the fruit, which takes years to show up — not only how it grows, but also how it tastes.
"The data suggests it's gonna work, but until you have a 10-year-old tree, you don't know how the tree is going to perform," Lagos said.

Napster is back. The name that struck fear into the hearts of music executives in the early dotcom era may be coming to a classroom near you.
In Dubai, United Arab Emirates, it has signed a strategic partnership with Gems Education to build AI agents and digital personas for education. In doing so, the once-notorious music-sharing company is bringing its technology into the classroom and testing how AI can augment the work of both teachers and students.
Today’s Napster, of course, bears no resemblance to its original incarnation as a peer-to-peer music-file-sharing service. Launched in 1999 by Shawn Fanning and Sean Parker, the platform revolutionized how people downloaded music, forcing the entire entertainment industry to rethink how content was distributed, sold, and controlled.
Napster eventually became the subject of a string of legal battles over copyright infringement and, following a series of adverse court rulings, had to shut down its original service in 2001.
Following its shuttering, the company went through various iterations, most recently as a music-streaming platform, until it was purchased by the Florida-based tech company Infinite Reality in 2025 for $207 million and pivoted to become an artificial intelligence platform. In January this year, it abruptly shut down its music-streaming service.
The company is now establishing a regional hub in Dubai, with Samuel Huber, formerly the founder and CEO of UK-based technology company Landvault—itself acquired by Infinite Reality in 2024—taking the helm as Napster’s CEO for the Middle East and Africa.
“The name has always been about giving power to the users,” says Huber. “Twenty-five years ago, it was about music and how music should be owned by people, not the gatekeepers. And now this is the same fight, the same ethos, but it’s about data and intelligence.”
Huber says that means challenging the power of the big AI companies. “The AI model companies have a lot of power; they’re building incredible models, and we want Napster to be an alternative to that.”
Napster’s work for Gems will develop proof-of-concept projects and showcases, including digitalising instructors, gamified learning, AI-assisted content creation, and classroom simulations.
The first phase will be anchored at the Gems School of Research and Innovation, where the Gems Global Education AI Hub and Gems Intelligence 360 platform will provide a real-world environment for educators, students, and partners to codesign, test, and evaluate AI agents and digital personas.
Napster will provide dedicated design, development, and product management resources based on Napster Learn, its AI-powered learning system. Digital twins of teachers, for example, will provide around-the-clock support.
Trained on a teacher’s material, courses, and papers, these digital twins will live online, becoming a “copy of yourself that you can then use to scale your time.” Students will be able to talk to them outside class, ask questions, refine concepts, and learn at their own pace, while teachers receive insights into the questions students are asking and where they may need additional support.
“We’re creating a better experience using voice, using video, to create a better way to interact with AI to make it more natural, so AI becomes more like coworkers rather than a machine or tool that you prompt, and we apply this technology in different verticals.”
According to Huber, AI agents and digital personas extend what teachers can do without replacing the human relationship at the heart of education. He also says student data will remain within the country and, where required, can be hosted on a company’s own servers. He also says Napster does not use user data to train its AI models.
While reassuring, much of this may well scare teachers fearful of losing their jobs. Although AI has caused considerable upheaval across multiple industries, Huber argues that its use in education should be about augmentation rather than replacement.
“I think it’s absolutely critical for educators, for professors, and for students to learn how to use AI in the right way. Because you’re right, there are two paths. We could let AI replace us. But if you’re using it in a smart way, you’re bringing insights, and then you use AI to augment yourself, just like you use word processors to type faster; then AI becomes a tool that augments you, not replaces you. I think students have that choice as well.”
The question is whether students and teachers actually want this and whether AI avatars can deliver meaningful educational benefits rather than simply offering a more sophisticated chatbot. In response, Huber says Gems will help Napster understand what students actually want from the technology.
“We’re not at the point yet where AI can fully replace humans, and therefore we want to leverage that technology overlaid on top of humans to get the most of it. What we’re building here is not about replacing the course, the lesson, the primary interaction between teachers and students that still happens in the real world.
“I think every student and every professor would want to support their students better,” he adds. "They would want to do one-on-one discussions with 200 students if they could, but there’s just no time. You can’t scale yourself this way.”
Napster’s move into the region is, in large part, driven by the UAE’s ambitious plans for AI. In May, the UAE Cabinet approved a federal framework for implementing agentic AI across ministries and government entities, supporting a plan to transition 50 percent of government services and operations to agentic AI models within two years. Napster wants to be part of that push.
Its partnership with Kameha Ventures, a Dubai-based venture platform led by Sheikh Ahmed Bin Mana Bin Khalifa Saeed Al Maktoum, is intended to help it tap into that market, bridging the gap between global AI capability and local deployment. Kameha will provide regional market development and institutional support, with localization of Napster’s offering a key priority.
“Localising the offering here is probably more important than in any other part of the world. Here, there’s a lot of cultural nuances that really matter, and even in digital products.”
Napster is also investing in local AI infrastructure. It has partnered with G42 in the UAE to host its data and run AI models locally, says Huber. In Saudi Arabia, it has collaborated with Lenovo and data center operator Detasad to run its infrastructure in-country, part of what Napster’s regional CEO describes as a broader push towards AI and data sovereignty.
Napster also plans to grow its roughly 20-strong regional team to about 500 by 2030.
“I’m here because there is a vision for AI in this country, which I find incredibly motivating and exciting as an entrepreneur, and we want to be one of the companies that help make that vision a reality. So we’re investing a lot in the country to make that happen.”

Why US plan to sell F-35 warplanes to Saudi Arabia is controversial
- Published
President Donald Trump's administration says it has approved the sale of nearly 50 F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia in a policy shift for the US that has raised concerns from some members of Congress.
Saudi Arabia has sought for years to buy the world's most advanced warplane, equipped with stealth technology that allows it to evade enemy detection.
Washington had resisted, partly because it supplies F-35s to its ally Israel, which is guaranteed under US law to receive top-of-the-range American weapons compared with those its regional neighbours can access.
Congress has 30 days to scrutinise or attempt to block the $24bn (£17.8bn) sale to Riyadh, which is the largest customer for US weapons.
Representative Raja Krishnamoorthi of Illinois, a Democrat, opposed the sale on Thursday.
He warned "it could put the crown jewels of American military technology within reach of the Chinese Communist Party".
Other Democratic lawmakers and some American defence officials have raised similar concerns about giving F-35s to Saudi Arabia.
They said Riyadh might share the sensitive technology with China under a security partnership between the two countries.
The state department said in announcing the deal on Thursday that it would support US "foreign policy and national security objectives".
It said the deal would improve "the security of a major non-Nato ally that is a force for political stability and economic progress in the Gulf region".
"The proposed sale of this equipment and support will not alter the military balance in the region," the state department added.
Trump has a close relationship with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who visited the White House last November.
The two also met in May last year in Riyadh, where a $142bn arms sale was sealed – described by the White House as the "largest defence sales agreement in history".
The latest proposed sale announced to Saudi Arabia would include 48 F-35s, which are built by the arms company Lockheed Martin.
This would place the country on a level with Israel, which currently has a fleet of 50 jets.
However, Israel's ministry of foreign affairs announced in May, external that it would procure another F-35 squadron.
This deal would double the size of Israel's F-35 fleet to 100, according to the Jerusalem Post, external.
Just one of Lockheed Martin's F-35A jets costs about $82.5m.
Congress has previously questioned arms deals with Riyadh after the murder of Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi in 2018.
Former US President Joe Biden's administration considered supplying F-35s to Saudi Arabia if Riyadh would normalise its relations with Israel, but that diplomatic effort faltered.
The proposed sale comes as the Saudis are engaged in fighting with the Houthis, an Iran-backed armed group that controls much of western Yemen.
The Houthis have recently seized control of swathes of Yemen's Red Sea coast from Saudi-backed pro-government forces.
The Saudi crown prince has personally pressed Trump to take military action against the Houthis, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News, the BBC's US media partner.
But Trump has so far declined to involve the US military directly, the sources said.

The Union Health Ministry has proposed making CCTV surveillance mandatory at licensed premises selling prescription drugs, as part of proposed amendments to the Drugs Rules, 1945.
The draft notification, G.S.R. 791(E), issued on September 8, proposes inserting a new provision in Rule 65 requiring the supply of drugs on the prescription of a registered medical practitioner, other than through wholesale dealing, to take place under a CCTV surveillance system installed and maintained at the licensed premises. The recordings would have to be preserved for at least three months.
The proposal follows deliberations by the Drugs Consultative Committee (DCC) and subsequent consideration by the Drugs Technical Advisory Board (DTAB). The DCC had earlier recommended that CCTV cameras be made mandatory at medical stores and that they be positioned so that drug sales could be verified.
The move is aimed at strengthening oversight of the sale of prescription medicines and providing a mechanism to verify transactions in cases of suspected unauthorised sale. Under the existing Drugs Rules, medicines covered by Schedules H, H1 and X cannot be sold at retail without a prescription from a registered medical practitioner, with additional record-keeping requirements for certain drugs.
The draft, however, is not yet a final rule. The Ministry has invited objections and suggestions from affected persons and other stakeholders for 30 days from the date the Gazette was made available. The proposed rules will be considered after the expiry of this period.
The Ministry has said submissions may be sent to the Under Secretary (Drugs), Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, U-6, Work Hall-C Wing, First Floor, Kartavya Bhawan-1, New Delhi, or emailed to drugsdiv-mohfw@gov.in.
“The draft does not merely propose CCTV for Schedule H, H1 and X medicines by name. Its wording is broader — it covers any drug supplied on a registered medical practitioner’s prescription, except wholesale transactions,” said a senior health official.

Reading for pleasure is linked to better mental health, greater empathy and a lower risk of dementia, Cambridge University scientists said on Tuesday.
As part of a National Year of Reading tie-up with the Queen's Reading Room, a charity founded by Queen Camilla to highlight the benefits of reading for pleasure at any age, the scientists argue that it doesn't matter what or how we read.
In a review published in 'Psychological Medicine', Professor Barbara Sahakian and Christelle Langley said reading for enjoyment can bring huge benefits and reading with others, whether it's as part of a book club or a parent reading with their children, can bring even greater rewards.
"Reading is a great way to support our brain health, develop important cognitive skills and boost our wellbeing. It's something we ought to be encouraging from an early age, given the increasing evidence of its benefits, particularly to children, but really, it's never too late to start, and it can bring benefits throughout our lives and into old age,” said Sahakian.
Some of the strongest evidence of the benefits of reading for pleasure comes from a study by Sahakian, Langley and colleagues of more than 10,000 young people, which found that children who began reading for pleasure in life showed benefits including: better attention, memory, and executive functioning, greater academic achievement, fewer mental health problems, and healthier lifestyles, including more sleep and less screen time. Langley said: "Given how beneficial reading for pleasure is at a young age, we should be doing everything we can to introduce children and young people to reading.
"The important thing is to find something they really enjoy – it might be a TV programme or a game – and use this as a way in. Reading comics and graphic novels could also be a helpful introduction as they might be seen as less intimidating, maybe less boring, than novels.”
In ‘Reading and associations with brain health, cognition, well-being, and mental health’ published this week, the experts draw on subjective surveys and objective studies using longitudinal, neuroimaging, and behavioural methods to highlight converging findings that link reading engagement with improved brain and mental health, better cognitive performance, and reduced risk of cognitive decline.
"Shared reading groups and book clubs appear to provide additional benefits through social interaction. They can help people feel less isolated and more connected to others, which has been shown to reduce the risk of dementia,” said Sahakian.
“While these clubs can be fun and beneficial at any age, they're perfect for older people who may be not so mobile – they might not be able to go out as an exercise group or a cycling group, but a reading group is something most people can enjoy,” she added.
