“India will need hundreds of semiconductor companies to build a globally competitive chip ecosystem, as the country looks to move beyond setting up fabs and develop capabilities across the wider value chain”, Sandeep Kumar, CEO, L&T Semiconductor Technologies (LTSCT), reportedly said during at the Semicon India 2026 today. As per a report by PTI, Kumar highlighted how it is difficult for a single company to address the breadth of the global semiconductor market. Thus, he believes that the ecosystem’s growth lies in the emergence of multiple Indian chip companies rather than monopolisation of a select few companies. India has developed capabilities in digital and compute technologies, analogue and mixed-signal design, and radio frequency technologies. However, it still has gaps in system architecture, high-power semiconductors, memory, optics and manufacturing. He said system architecture, which is understanding customer requirements and designing products around market needs, is a bigger gap than chip architecture, partly because Indian engineers have historically had less direct exposure to global end customers. During the event, L&T unveiled 40 semiconductor products at the conference, including its first silicon carbide (SiC) product platform and a fully designed-in-India BLDC motor controller. The company's 1,200V SiC MOSFET platform is designed for applications including EV fast chargers, microgrids, solid-state transformers and traction inverters. Its BLDC motor controller is aimed at energy-efficient ceiling fans and is designed to serve multiple models while reducing bill-of-materials costs. LTSCT's portfolio also includes a vision camera SoC with on-device AI acceleration, a secure identity platform for applications such as e-passports and payment cards, and connectivity modules for smart metering, automotive and digital payments. SEMICON India Shifts Focus To Ecosystem Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurated the fifth edition of Semicon India in Delhi on Thursday (September 17). The first day saw Applied Materials commit $5 Bn through 2035, while the government announced around ₹1 Lakh Cr in investment commitments under Semicon 2.0. As part of the next steps, MeitY Secretary S Krishnan said India now has semiconductor production at six locations and that Semicon 2.0 will focus on closing gaps in advanced packaging, industry-linked R&D and manufacturing talent. Meanwhile, foreign secretary Vikram Misri said India does not need to replicate the entire global semiconductor supply chain domestically, but should focus on building sovereign capabilities in strategically important areas such as chip design and packaging, while partnering with trusted global players for other parts of the value chain. Separately, the government has introduced tighter conditions for companies receiving incentives under Semicon 2.0, barring them from selling or mortgaging supported projects until they achieve full commercial production and requiring them to maintain operations for at least three years thereafter; promoters must also retain at least 51% equity and voting rights during the support period. Meanwhile, global semiconductor giant Micron said it expects its Sanand facility to process hundreds of millions of chips in 2027, up from tens of millions this year. The plant is already in commercial production, processing DRAM and NAND wafers shipped from Micron's global manufacturing network and sending finished products to customers worldwide. On the domestic front, Tata Electronics said its Dholera fab and Assam packaging facility’s operational timelines are on schedule. During the event yesterday, the company also entered a strategic partnership with Netherland-based Nexperia under which Nexperia’s MOSFETs will be manufactured at Tata’s upcoming Dholera fab, while its discrete chips will be assembled and tested at Tata’s Jagiroad facility. The partnership comes as the Dutch chipmaker seeks to diversify its manufacturing footprint amid an ongoing rift with Chinese parent Wingtech. Its partnership with Tata Electronics will now give it a manufacturing foothold in India, spanning wafer fabrication in Dholera and assembly and testing in Assam.

F-16 fighter jet crashes in Michigan and bursts into flames with residents told to evacuate
A witness described seeing a big plume of black smoke and said ‘explosions kept happening’
An F-16 fighter jet has crashed in rural Michigan, sparking an evacuation order for anyone within one mile of the crash site.
The pilot of the fighter jet ejected before the crash and was rushed to the hospital, according to Sgt. Derek Gutierrez, a public affairs specialist with the 149th Fighter Wing. Citing military protocol, Gutierrez declined to provide further details about the pilot’s injuries or identity.
The Grand Traverse County Emergency Management warned anyone within a mile of the crash site to evacuate.
“Evacuate away from the intersection of Co Rd 633 and Jefferson Pl. Follow instructions from emergency personnel. More information to follow,” officials wrote.
The aircraft, from Texas, was taking part in training drills based out of Alpena, Michigan's National Guard Base, according to the military.
Witnesses reported a loud impact and photos on social media platforms showed a tall column of dark smoke rising from the crash site.
Wendy Sobeck said that she and her spouse heard a "very loud crash" down the street from their home.
"We thought there was a car accident outside our house. We saw big billowing black smoke. We couldn’t tell what it was, so my husband got into his pickup truck and saw what happened," Sobeck said. "You could see the plane debris in the field. Explosions kept happening."

Srinagar, Sept 18: Lieutenant Governor Manoj Sinha on Friday handed over appointment letters to newly selected candidates of the Jammu and Kashmir Police (Gazetted) Services at Lok Bhavan, Srinagar, saying the appointment is not merely a government job but a call to serve and protect the people of Jammu and Kashmir.
Addressing the newly selected officers, the Lieutenant Governor said the appointment letters carried the “burden of the faith of the whole of Jammu and Kashmir” and represented a commitment towards the security, dignity and future of the people.
“I do not consider it just an appointment letter, but I see it as an invitation to service. This invitation is a call to accept the responsibility of the security of Jammu and Kashmir. It is also a promise that their security, their honour and their future will be in a position of honesty and duty,” he said, as per the news agency—Kashmir News Observer (KNO).
Sinha congratulated the selected candidates and their families, saying they had successfully cleared a rigorous selection process that tested their intelligence, patience, character, discipline and ability to withstand adverse situations.
“You have faced tough competition among the talented youth of your generation. You have gone through such a difficult process, which has not only tested your intelligence, but also your patience, character, discipline and strength to withstand adverse situations,” he said.
He told the officers that receiving the appointment letter was “not the end of your journey” but the beginning of a new one, in which their responsibility would shift from personal achievement to protecting others, serving the people and upholding the rule of law.
“You are about to embark on a new journey. Now you have to enter that struggle, whose purpose is not to achieve success for yourself, but to fulfil the responsibility of protecting others, to serve the people and to protect the rule of law in Jammu and Kashmir,” Sinha said.
‘PSC selection process strengthened faith in merit’
The Lieutenant Governor also congratulated the Jammu and Kashmir Public Service Commission (JKPSC), saying the commission had, in recent years, strengthened the principles of impartiality, transparency and merit in its selection process.
“At a time when doubts are being expressed on institutions many times, I understand that the protection of Jammu and Kashmir Public Service Commission’s impartiality and trust is like a holy lamp,” he said.
Recalling the earlier system of government recruitment, Sinha said merit-based employment had now become an established practice in Jammu and Kashmir.
“I do not need to tell you what used to happen here. How did you get a job? A complete book can be written on it. The people sitting here know more about that book than I do,” he said.
“But employment with qualifications has been prepared in such a heritage of Jammu and Kashmir, where a government job can only be obtained with your qualifications, hard work and talent,” he added.
Recalling the 2022 Jammu and Kashmir Employment Festival, Sinha said people had begun to believe that children from ordinary and economically weaker families could also aspire to become government officers.
“I remember that in 2022, the Jammu and Kashmir Employment Festival was celebrated with the qualification of a government job. At that time, for the first time, people said that the son of a vegetable vendor can also be a KAS officer,” he said.
“This time has come to Jammu and Kashmir. Even a father can see his son becoming a government officer. Perhaps after a long time, this arrangement was established,” he added.
Sinha said recruitment should be based on merit rather than recommendations and again congratulated the JKPSC for what he described as an impartial and trustworthy selection process.
“In Jammu and Kashmir, a job will not be obtained with a recommendation, but with the qualifications and qualities of a young man,” he said.
‘Uniform is a symbol of service, not power’
The Lieutenant Governor told the selected officers that their responsibilities after completing training would extend beyond a conventional career.
“The responsibility you will take after this training is not just a career, but a mission,” he said, adding that their training at the Sher-i-Kashmir Police Academy (SKPA), Udhampur, would give them an understanding of that mission.
He said discipline, hard work, rigorous training and leadership would become integral parts of their professional lives.
Sinha said the badge on a police uniform should not be seen as a symbol of power over the people, but as a symbol of service and responsibility.
“The badge on your uniform is not a symbol of power on the people of Jammu and Kashmir, but a symbol of the service and responsibility of the people,” he said.
Changing terrorism, radicalisation pose new challenges
The Lieutenant Governor said the security environment in Jammu and Kashmir was changing rapidly, with terrorism increasingly extending beyond traditional methods.
“Today’s Jammu and Kashmir is facing such challenges that the police officers of a decade ago may not have been able to imagine,” he said.
“The form of terrorism is changing and the war is not only being fought with traditional weapons. The virtual world has faced many challenges. Radicalisation is also leaving a strong and deep impact,” Sinha said.
He said methods of terror financing had also evolved, with cryptocurrencies, money laundering and other emerging mechanisms posing new challenges.
“The means of financing for terrorism have also changed. Instead of the traditional methods, cryptocurrencies, money laundering and these new methods have emerged,” he said.
Sinha said the newly inducted officers would therefore have an important role not only in maintaining security in Jammu and Kashmir but also in the broader national security framework.
‘Police will stand as wall between terrorists and citizens’
After completing their training, the officers would have to act as a protective shield between terrorist forces and ordinary citizens, he said.
“When you wear a khaki uniform, you will become a strong wall between the terrorist forces, terrorist organisations and ordinary citizens. You will protect the dreams of every citizen. This is not a small responsibility,” Sinha said.
He said ensuring the security of every citizen was among the biggest responsibilities entrusted to officials in a democracy and expressed hope that the officers would help instil confidence among people to live without fear.
Sinha also asked the officers to learn from the experience and sacrifices of their seniors in the Jammu and Kashmir Police.
“The Jammu and Kashmir Police Force is considered to be a symbol of duty, dedication, love and sacrifice. This is the only force in the country that has faced every challenge related to security with full determination and courage,” he said.
He said the sacrifices and determination of police personnel over the past decades had contributed to establishing peace and urged the new officers to draw lessons from their leadership and experience.
‘Duty not limited to fighting terrorism’
Sinha stressed that the officers’ responsibilities would not be limited to countering terrorism but would also include enforcing the law, protecting citizens’ rights and maintaining social harmony.
“Always keep in mind that your responsibility is not limited to fighting terrorism. You have to keep the law in place. You have to establish the rule of law. You have to establish social harmony. And you have to play a very important role in protecting the rights of every citizen,” he said.
He said the true test of democracy lay in protecting its weakest citizens and called upon the officers to combine authority with compassion.
“The real condition of democracy is that it ensures the protection of its weakest citizen and its prosperity. After training, you will have power and you will have to add the values of compassion to that power so that there is human compassion in all your actions,” he said.
Sinha reminded the officers of the long-standing principle of the J&K Police: “Do not touch the innocent and do not leave the culprit.”
He urged them to take pride in the uniform while ensuring that their conduct remained rooted in honesty, courage and humility.
‘Choose truth and duty, whatever the situation’
The Lieutenant Governor asked the newly selected officers to commit themselves to upholding truth and duty, regardless of the circumstances.
“No matter how difficult the situation is, you will always choose truthfulness and duty on the basis of priority. Always remember that the uniform is respected only because of the honesty, courage and determination of the officers who wear the uniform,” he said.
“Only the uniform is not respected. So move forward with honesty, courage and humility,” he added.
Sinha said the appointment also represented the hopes and aspirations of the people of Jammu and Kashmir and called upon the officers to use their authority for justice.
He also expressed gratitude to the parents and relatives of the newly selected officers, saying they had supported their children through the difficult journey and shared their dreams.
“All of you have prepared your children for the service of Jammu and Kashmir. You have supported them in their struggle. You have lived their dreams as your own dreams,” he said.
“India and Jammu and Kashmir will always be grateful to you for this contribution,” Sinha added.—(KNO)

New Delhi, Sep 18: India on Friday strongly rejected Islamabad's allegations regarding a collision between a Pakistani vessel and an Indian Navy warship in the Arabian Sea, asserting instead that "dangerous" manoeuvres by the ship from the neighbouring country caused the incident.
The incident had happened on Tuesday night after the Pakistani vessel closed in on the frontline Indian Navy warship that was on a routine surveillance mission in the north Arabian Sea, according to the Indian side.
India summoned Pakistani charge d'affaires Saad Warraich on Wednesday and lodged a diplomatic protest.
The Pakistan foreign ministry subsequently summoned Indian charge d'affaires Satyanjal Pandey and alleged that "aggressive" manoeuvres by the Indian warship triggered the collision.
At a media briefing, External Affairs Ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said on Friday that Pakistani vessel carried out a "dangerous" manoeuvre in violation of a 1991 agreement requiring naval ships to maintain a distance of three nautical miles.
Jaiswal identified the Indian warship as INS Kolkata, a stealth guided missile destroyer.
"We have seen Pakistan's response to the protest we had lodged. It is the usual prevarication that we expected. We reject the allegations and insinuations contained therein," he said.
"Let me reiterate the facts of the matter. INS Kolkata was on a routine deployment in the western Arabian sea when Pakistani Naval ship Hunain conducted itself in an unacceptable and unprofessional manner at sea that resulted in a collision," he said.
Jaiswal said the "dangerous overtaking manoeuvre by PNS Hunain was in gross violation of Article 10 of the agreement between India and Pakistan on advance notice on military exercises, manoeuvres and troops movements of April 1991, which specifies that naval units at sea are not to be within three nautical miles of each other.
The spokesperson said the Pakistani ship also "infringed the international regulations for preventing collisions at sea". "The Pakistan side has once again been advised about the need for all military units to observe due care and respect the provisions of the relevant agreements between the two sides in order to prevent any repeat of such incidents," he said.
Jaiswal said the incident did not cause "any major damage" to INS Kolkata and she remains at sea.
The Pakistani foreign ministry had alleged that the incident happened following a "highly provocative and unacceptable action" by the Indian vessel in the Pakistan's Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ).

Jammu, Sep 18: To meet the anticipated festival rush and facilitate passenger movement, the Northern Railway's Jammu division will operate three special trains connecting Shri Mata Vaishno Devi Katra, Jammu Tawi, Varanasi and New Delhi from next month.
Terming the decision a "big gift" to rail passengers, a railway spokesperson said the operation of the three reserved trains will help clear the extra rush and waiting list during Dussehra, Diwali and Chhath Puja.
“The Railway has decided to operate three pairs of reserved festival special trains via Jammu Division. The operation of these trains will not only make it easier for passengers to secure confirmed tickets but will also ensure a more comfortable and safe journey,” the spokesman said.
He said the first train, 04604/04603 Katra-Varanasi-Katra Special, will make nine trips in each direction.
The train departing from Katra will run every Sunday from October 4 to November 29, at 6:15 PM, while the train departing from Varanasi will run every Tuesday from October 6 to December 1 at 4:30 AM, the spokesman said.
He further said that the train will halt at Jammu Tawi, Pathankot Cantt, Jalandhar Cantt, Ludhiana, Ambala Cantt, Saharanpur, Moradabad, Bareilly, Alamnagar, Rae Bareli and Pratapgarh, among other stations.
The spokesman said the second train, 04610/04609 Jammu Tawi-Varanasi-Jammu Tawi Special, will also make nine trips in each direction.
Train 04610 will run every Thursday from October 1 to November 26, while 04609 will operate every Friday from October 2 to November 27, providing additional connectivity to passengers from Pathankot, Jalandhar, Ambala, Saharanpur, Moradabad, Shahjahanpur, Lucknow and Sultanpur.
The third train, 04081/04082 New Delhi-Shri Mata Vaishno Devi Katra Festival Special, will make four trips in each direction to meet the Dussehra rush.
Train 04081 will operate on October 8, 9, 10 and 11, while 04082 will run on October 9, 10, 11 and 12, providing direct connectivity between New Delhi and Katra.
The spokesman said these trains will directly connect two of the most important religious places in North India, besides providing direct and fast connectivity to commuters from Delhi, Haryana and Punjab.
He said running of these trains would reduce pressure on regular trains and will provide relief to passengers from the rush for tickets during festivals.

Jagtar Singh Johal granted bail nine years after being detained in India
- Published
A Scottish Sikh activist who has been locked up in India for almost nine years without conviction has been granted bail.
Jagtar Singh Johal, from Dumbarton, was arrested and detained in 2017 in connection with alleged terror offences.
The Indian authorities have accused him of having a role in a series of targeted killings of religious and political figures.
His family said they were still waiting for the details of what will happen next but are "relieved" by the Indian court's decision.
Court documents show Johal was granted bail at Delhi High Court.
As part of his bail conditions, he has to surrender his passport and is barred from speaking to the media about the case.
He must pay a personal bond of 500,000 rupees (£3,907) and is only allowed to access one phone.
The 39-year-old was acquitted last year in a case in which he was accused of financially supporting terror group the Khalistan Liberation Force (KLF), which has carried out attacks in the Punjab region.
But he still faces federal charges lodged by the Indian authorities.
Johal's imprisonment was recognised by a UN panel as arbitrary detention in 2022 and he has claimed to have been tortured.
Indian authorities have previously denied the torture claim and have repeatedly maintained due process is being followed.
He was arrested in the Punjab region just weeks after his wedding in the country.
His supporters say he was targeted for blogging about alleged human rights abuses against the Sikh community in India and was coerced into signing a false confession to participation in the killings.
His brother Gurpreet Singh Johal has lobbied successive governments calling for his brother's release.
"It is a really important milestone for Jagtar's campaign," Gurpreet told the BBC's Radio Scotland Breakfast programme.
"It has been a long haul and an expensive rollercoaster but the community and the public have kept me going to campaign to bring Jagtar home.
"This will be a huge relief for him."
He added that while it is a major step and the family are relieved Jagtar can be at liberty, more work will be required to bring his brother back to Dumbarton.
"It is a momentous moment for the family, his wife has been crying since this morning," Gurpreet added.
"Everyone was joyful, my kids went to school saying they cannot wait to see their uncle coming home.
"It is just a first step, but it is a step in the right direction."
Gupreet previously urged the UK government to provide "diplomatic representation" to bring his activist brother home.
He described his last meeting, with then-Foreign secretary Yvette Cooper in December, as "disappointing".
At the time, a spokesperson for the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office said concerns about Johal's "prolonged detention" were raised with the Indian government at every appropriate opportunity.
Johal was previously denied bail in 2024.
Johal's family have insisted that no concrete evidence has been presented against him.
They say the case was built on the testimony of unreliable witnesses, some of whom have given statements against him only for them to be later recanted in court.
'Flawed proceedings'
First Minister John Swinney said it was a "significant and positive development".
"I hope to see Mr Johal released from custody as soon as the necessary procedures are completed and continue to underline the importance of a fair, transparent and timely judicial process," he added.
Johal is represented in the UK by the legal charities Redress and Reprieve, which have welcomed the judgement.
Reprieve's deputy executive director Dan Dolan said the news was welcome but Johal still faces the death penalty for "trumped up charges".
He said: "We must now watch closely to ensure this order is actually implemented and not obstructed in any way.
"The conditions attached are likely to be onerous."
Redress senior legal advisor Chris Esdaile said granting bail "can't undo the intolerable suffering caused by nine years of arbitrary detention".
He added: "The need for accountability for the allegations of torture and the deeply flawed proceedings against Jagtar remains urgent."

- The claim that six images circulating online showed Iranian damage to U.S. military bases in the Middle East is still under investigation.
- According to CBS News, the outlet that first shared the images, they came from active service members who shared them on condition of anonymity "because of rigid media restrictions within the military."
- Snopes does not rely on anonymous sources. We could not independently verify the authenticity of the photographs because we could not speak to the people who took them and verify their metadata (information about where and when a photo is taken). As such, we leave claims about the authenticity of the images unrated.
- At least one of the images showed another angle of damage to a sentry aircraft that other outlets previously verified. Others corroborated reports of damage at U.S. bases.
- Snopes will update this report if, or when, additional information surfaces. We contacted the CBS journalist who published the pictures to ask how he verified their authenticity and CENTCOM for further comment and await replies to our queries.
In September 2026, a series of images circulated online that social media users claimed (archived) showed Iranian damage to U.S. military bases in the Middle East.
For example, one X user shared a video consisting of six photographs that appeared to show a damaged aircraft, vehicle and structures, and wrote:
BREAKING: Troops leaked photos of their wrecked bases to CBS, saying they're "standing there with our eyes closed getting punched in the face"
Active service members sent the images anonymously.
The images also circulated on Facebook (archived), Instagram (archived), Threads (archived), Bluesky (archived) and Reddit (archived).
The images came from an exclusive CBS News report that said its reporter Jonah Kaplan had received the photos from "active service members on condition of anonymity because of rigid media restrictions within the military."
It wasn't possible for Snopes to independently verify the authenticity of the images. We don't rely on anonymous sources. Therefore, in order to independently verify them, we would need to speak to the people who took the images and verify their metadata (information about where and when a photo was taken). This did not appear possible given the sources told CBS News they didn't want their names published alongside the images. Therefore, we leave claims about the authenticity of the images unrated.
We contacted Kaplan to ask how he verified the authenticity of the photos. We also contacted U.S. Central Command, which directs U.S. security operations across the Middle East, to ask about the authenticity of the images. We await replies to our queries.
What we know about images
The CBS News report included six photos. The first claimed to show a damaged plane at the Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia. The image resembled photos verified by the BBC in March 2026 after Reuters and The Wall Street Journal reported that Iranian strikes damaged an E-3 sentry aircraft and injured 12 troops at the base.
Snopes could not verify the exact location of the plane at the base, though CBS News' image did show a sign reading "35L S2." 35L is the name of one of the runways at the Prince Sultan Air Base, suggesting the damaged plane was parked on or near that runway when Iranian strikes hit. The image showed what appeared to be a drain or tunnel under the runway. Google Earth imagery showed identical structures along the 35L runway.
A report about Operation Epic Fury (the U.S. government's name for the war in Iran) that the lead inspector general submitted to Congress in September 2026 found one E-3 aircraft had been "damaged on the ground in Saudi Arabia by Iranian strikes" during the conflict (Table 5).
The next two images in the CBS News article claimed to show damage to a large tent structure and several trailers at Camp Buehring in Kuwait. According to the Institute for the Study of War, a public policy research organization that analyzes military and foreign affairs, Iran has claimed to have struck Camp Buehring at least five times since the start of the war.
One of the images, which showed a burned-out vehicle, also showed a mural that included a hand grasping three lightning bolts. This was the same imagery used by the 136th Expeditionary Signal Battalion. That battalion has previously been deployed to Camp Buehring. The unit was deployed to Central Command's area of operation, which includes the Middle East, around April 2026.
Another image appeared to show damage to the Unaccompanied Officers Quarters at Camp Arifjan, Kuwait. The ISW reported that Iranian forces had struck Camp Arifjan at the start of March 2026. CNN reported on March 3 that six U.S. service members had been killed in strikes on the Port of Shuaiba, which is around 18 miles north of Camp Arifjan, suggesting the Iranian military had targeted the area.
The sixth image claimed to show damage to a large tent structure at Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia. Snopes could not independently confirm the location or date of that image.
Foreign base damage difficult to confirm
Verifying damage to U.S. bases or equipment overseas is difficult because U.S. authorities generally do not publicly confirm such strikes so as not give away equipment locations or military capabilities. For example, in April 2026, the Pentagon declined to comment on reported damage to U.S. bases in Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Jordan, Kuwait, Iraq and Saudi Arabia for operational security reasons.
The September 2026 report to Congress about Operation Epic Fury included damage estimates only for diplomatic facilities such as embassies and consulates (Page 19), not military bases.
U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth said (at 32:57) on March 3, 2026, that the six people killed near Camp Arifjan in early March 2026 died because a "squirter" passed through U.S. air defenses and hit a "tactical operation center."
Hegseth said such incidents happened "every once in a while."
Speaking to CBS News about the September 2026 images, a service member reportedly refuted that characterization of the alleged damage caused to U.S. bases in the Middle East, instead saying, "We're not defending these bases. We're just watching them get destroyed."
For further reading, Snopes has investigated a number of claims related to the war in Iran.

Geneva 17 October 2024 – This afternoon, His Excellency Mr Jérôme Bonnafont, Permanent Representative of France to the United Nations in Geneva, and WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus met in the WHO headquarters for the signing of seven contribution agreements.
The contribution totalling €24 million comes through the Ministry of Europe & Foreign Affairs. It fits in the France–WHO Framework Agreement for 2020 to 2025, which provides both a strategic framework for engagement, aligned with WHO priorities, while providing legal, administrative and financial instruments for operationalizing collaboration.
This latest contribution includes a generous €4.5 million in fully flexible voluntary funds for the Core Voluntary Contributions Account (CVCA).
Additionally, France will support key areas of WHO’s work, addressing some of the most pressing health challenges, including non-communicable diseases (NCDs), urban health labs, One Health, funding for the WHO Contingency Fund for Emergencies (CFE), and several emergencies, such as the WHO response in Gaza, response to cholera outbreaks and mental health support in Ukraine.
France will also continue to support the WHO emergencies centre in Lyon which is playing a crucial role in preparedness and response to epidemics.
Ambassador Jérôme Bonnafont underscored the importance of this collaboration: “France remains deeply committed to supporting the World Health Organization in its efforts to tackle critical global health challenges. These agreements reflect our shared priorities of promoting health equity, responding to emergencies, and strengthening healthcare systems worldwide.”
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of WHO, expressed his gratitude, stating, “We are immensely grateful to the French Government for its steadfast support to WHO, continued partnership and leadership in global health. This contribution will enable us to address key health threats, from non-communicable diseases to emergency response, helping to save lives and protect the most vulnerable populations.”
France is a strong supporter of a fully and flexibly financed WHO, providing leadership and support to the increase of assessed contributions to the Organization. France is also one of the co-hosts to WHO’s first Investment Round towards the mobilization of predictable and flexible resources for WHO’s core work on the Fourteenth General Programme of Work (2025–2028), approved by the World Health Assembly in 2024.
This signing ceremony marks another milestone in the strong and longstanding partnership between WHO and France, reinforcing their joint commitment to a healthier, safer world.

Alibaba open-sources medical AI model that can detect cancer and nearly 150 conditions
Tested on nearly 40,000 real-world exams, the model outperformed most radiologists, according to a new study published in Science
Alibaba Group Holding’s research arm, Damo Academy, has open-sourced an artificial intelligence model capable of identifying nearly 150 abdominal conditions – including cancers – by reading computed tomography (CT) scans, marking the latest step in the firm’s growing medical AI efforts.
The vision-language model, called Damo Radar, was designed to analyse contrast-enhanced CT scans covering 18 abdominal organs and identify a broad range of diseases and other abnormalities, such as malignant tumours, the institute said on Friday.
The model was trained using CT scans paired with clinical reports. In nearly 40,000 real-world examinations, it achieved an average area under the curve (AUC) of 0.913 across 146 clinical findings. An AUC of 1.0 represents perfect diagnostic accuracy.
The research team said the training method could eventually be extended to other types of medical imaging, calling the model “the world’s first expert-level generalist medical imaging model”.

Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger (D) ordered the state government to take steps that could empower local communities to have a larger say in data center development and slow down approvals in a state that is already home to the data center capital of the world.
Virginia governor creates an AI task force and moves to restrain data centers
Gov. Abigail Spanberger (D) signed an executive order addressing data canters and AI risks.
Executive Order 22 bans executive branch officials from signing non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) for data center projects, requires expedited noise regulations, and a review of backup-generation operations used by data centers, among other requirements. The order also establishes an AI task force responsible for evaluating how the state government can address risks to Virginians like workforce displacement and data privacy issues, and determining how existing law can be applied to AI harms.
The order represents the latest signal that states are taking data center and AI policy into their own hands as Congress and President Donald Trump have been slow or resistant to sweeping changes. Also on Friday, California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) issued an executive order convening experts to tackle AI safety issues, and earlier, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) and Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R) have both taken executive action to rein in rapid data center development.
In addition to Virginia’s new executive order, Spanberger unveiled a new “Data Center Accountability Framework” for the state, which lays out additional priorities. These include eliminating “by-right approval,” like the kind that existed in Loudoun County for many years allowing developers to build on certain land without additional approvals, removing some state subsidies, establishing environmental guardrails, and safeguarding residents against increased energy prices that are associated with data centers.
A press release for the actions includes many statements from environmental groups praising Spanberger’s approach, but others reportedly wish she’d gone even further. Piedmont Environment Council (PEC), for example, is a nonprofit that has advocated for a moratorium on new development to deal with existing concerns, and PEC president Chris Miller said in a statement that “It largely addresses standards on new data centers and does not deal with what’s already built and in the pipeline, along with the ongoing impacts piling up in communities now.”

Gurugram-based test-prep major Aakash Educational Services Ltd (AESL) managed to narrow its net loss for the financial year FY26 by 15.5% to ₹186.5 Cr from ₹220.8 Cr loss incurred in the previous fiscal. The improvement in the bottom line came despite flat top line performance in the fiscal. Operating revenue rose marginally by 0.4% to ₹2,040.5 Cr in FY26 from ₹2,032.1 Cr in the previous year. While coaching revenue — the core business — inched up 0.3% YoY to ₹1,956.2 Cr, franchisee revenue grew 4% to ₹84.4 Cr. The real swing factor came with revenue registered from non-operating income, with other income more than doubled to ₹113.7 Cr. This was driven largely by a ₹76.1 Cr write-back of provisions or liabilities alongside a ₹19.7 Cr gain from remeasurement of lease liabilities. Including other income, total income rose 3.3% to ₹2,154.3 Cr in the year under review from ₹2,085.1 Cr in FY25. Aakash is one of India's largest test-prep brands for engineering and medical entrance exams and has been operating under the ownership of BYJU’S parent Think & Learn since its 2021 acquisition — a deal that has since been entangled in the broader financial and legal troubles at the BYJU’S group. As of September, Byju Raveendran proposed relinquishing his claimed beneficial interest in 17.89 Mn shares of Aakash Educational Services to settle Qatar Holding’s arbitration claim of more than $235 Mn against him. The latest proposal further places Aakash at the centre of overlapping disputes over ownership, creditor recoveries, and the future of BYJU’S, which once commanded a valuation of $22 Bn. Creditors have been separately exploring a broader settlement centred around Aakash as it remains the most valuable surviving asset within the collapsing edtech. Global TLB lenders, represented by GLAS Trust, are said to be in advanced talks to acquire a 30% stake in Aakash Educational Services, valuing the coaching chain at around $2 Bn. Zooming Into Aakash's FY26 Expenses Total expenses were largely flat, up almost 1% to ₹2,397.8 Cr in FY26 from ₹2,378 Cr in the previous year. As a result, loss before exceptional items and tax narrowed nearly 17% YoY to ₹243.5 Cr from ₹292.9 Cr. However, a ₹23.3 Cr exceptional charge widened this to a pre-tax loss of ₹266.8 Cr — still 8.9% narrower than FY25's ₹292.9 Cr. A deferred tax credit gain of ₹80.3 Cr brought the final loss after tax down to ₹186.5 Cr. Here is a more closer look at where AESL spent the most in the reported year: Employee Benefits Expense: Aakash’s single largest expense declined 2.4% to ₹1,299.6 Cr in the fiscal under review from ₹1,331.5 Cr in FY25. Depreciation And Amortisation Expense: Spending under this head declined 4.4% to ₹234.8 Cr in FY26 from ₹245.6 Cr a year ago. Advertisement And Publicity: The company’s promotional expenses fell 6.9% to ₹145.7 Cr in the year under review from ₹156.5 Cr in FY25.

Hyrox athlete apologises for continuing race after soiling herself
- Published
An Australian athlete who faced criticism for continuing to compete in a Hyrox event after soiling herself has apologised and said she will retroactively withdraw from the race.
Joanna Wietrzyk offered her "sincere apology" for the incident during the indoor fitness competition in Beijing on Saturday, saying she should have "made a different choice" and exited the event.
Footage of Wietrzyk competing after soiling herself raised concerns about hygiene, leading Hyrox co-founder Moritz Fürste to apologise for the handling of the situation.
In a statement shared on Thursday, Wietrzyk said: "I know my actions had an impact beyond myself, and I am genuinely sorry to everyone who was affected."

After the backlash, Wietrzyk, who won the race in Beijing, said she would forfeit her win.
Wietrzyk said in a social media post: "I want to offer my sincere apology to the people of China, my fellow competitors, the spectators and the HYROX organizers for what happened during the race in Beijing."
She wrote in a social media post, external that she was "completely fit and healthy" at the start of the race, and had "no reason" to expect any illness.
"Looking back, I regret the decision to not have stepped off the track. I recognize that I should have made a different choice. I take responsibility for my decision to continue and am deeply sorry for the discomfort and disruption it caused," Wietrzyk continued.
Hyrox insisted it had "clear biocontaminant and medical procedures in place".
It said "an unforeseen situation arose" during which protocols became blurred, "creating ambiguity in how they were applied and understood".
In a statement posted on Instagram, Fürste committed to "improving event processes" to "prevent situations like this from happening again".
After Wietrzyk's identity was shared online, Hyrox said anyone sending abuse or threats to the athlete would be banned from any future events.
It said on Monday: "There is no place in our community for threats of violence or encouragement to harm an athlete."
In each Hyrox race, participants alternate between running a kilometre and doing fitness exercises, including a sled push, burpee jumps, indoor rowing, and lunges while carrying a sandbag.
The competition has exploded in popularity since it was founded in 2017 in Hamburg, Germany, and is now held across the world. The sport debuted in mainland China in late 2024.
Some have questioned why those officiating the competition in Beijing last weekend did not intervene when the athlete soiled herself, given that Hyrox penalises acts including "spitting, nostril clearing, littering, and water abuse".

In late summer 2026, social media posts claimed that new laws had gone into effect requiring all car drivers and passengers below a certain height to use a booster seat, regardless of their age.
The details changed from post to post (archived), and varied from state to state, but the most common version of the rumor suggested the law applies to anyone under 5 feet, 2 inches in height.
(Facebook)
Snopes readers contacted us looking for more information about the variety of claims.
In short, all the similar rumors are false. No such laws have been passed or are set to come into effect anywhere in the United States.
Searches on DuckDuckGo, Google and Yahoo uncovered no news reports or evidence about the supposed changes. Reputable local news media outlets would have covered such a story if any of them were true.
It was not possible to definitively determine the origin of the claims. They appeared to be part of a series of AI-generated images promoting new, fictitious state laws. AI-generated fake laws have become a relatively common "template" of rumor that circulates on social media. Snopes has debunked several examples over the past year.
However, the posts spreading the booster seat claim include a second type of image — also AI-generated — of an adult woman sitting in a car seat. Investigating those alleged photos revealed numerous signs they were AI-generated.
For example, one image (shown below) includes a strange white artifact in the center of the harness-style buckle 
(Facebook user Kelsey Biggs)
In addition, Facebook, the platform where most examples of the claim were posted, had labeled the above image and several others as AI-generated content. Running the images through other generative AI detection tools supported this. (Let us note: these tools are fallible, and we recommend using them only as supporting evidence).
Investigating the laws around child-safe car seats and booster seats in each U.S. state and territory led to several sites that contain lists of all car seat, booster seat and seatbelt laws, as of this writing. The laws all specifically mention children, and many designate their requirements based on a combination of age, height and weight. When limitations based on height and weight are included, they tend to be set at for children under 80 pounds and shorter than 4 feet, 9 inches, several inches below the limits suggested by the fictitious laws. None of the authentic laws mention adults under 5 feet, 2 inches being mandated to ride or drive in booster seats.

Swimmer killed in shark attack off Australian west coast
- Published
A swimmer has been killed in a shark attack at a beach in Perth, on the west coast of Australia, police have said.
Emergency crews were called to a "shark-related incident" at Sorrento Beach at around 10.15 local time on Friday.
Police said an extensive search of the area was carried out by authorities in helicopters and on boats but did not say whether a body had been found.
One witness described seeing a man being pulled under the water by a shark, just 50 metres off the shore, while another said they saw a "pool of blood" in the water, according to local media.
One witness told local outlet WAtoday that she saw the man being "mauled" as the shark "tossed him around like a fish".
"I'm a nurse, so I mean I obviously see a lot of gruesome stuff, but to see somebody being mauled to death in the water in front of me is pretty hard to clock," she told WAtoday.
"I only live just down the road, and I swim every day. I mean, there's no way I'm going to be getting in that water again."
Another witness said she was walking along the beach with a friend when the attack happened.
"I looked out to the ocean and I could see a pool of blood," Jacqui Rapaic told national broadcaster ABC.
She said she believed two people had been swimming, but only one had made it back to shore.
Members of the public had reported seeing a 2.5-metre-long shark at around the same time.
The beach remains closed to the public and authorities have asked the public to avoid the area.
There have been multiple fatal shark attacks in Australia over the past year, including on a 12-year-old boy in Sydney in January.

The Union Health Ministry has asked States and Union Territories to ensure that stem cell therapy is offered as standard clinical care only for disease conditions and indications approved by the Ministry, with its use for Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) restricted to duly approved clinical trials.
In an advisory issued on September 16, the Ministry reiterated the existing regulatory framework governing stem cell research and therapy. The advisory was issued to States and Union Territories that have adopted the Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Act, 2010, following a January 30, 2026, judgment of the Supreme Court in Yash Charitable Trust & Ors. v. Union of India & Ors.
For ASD, the Ministry said therapeutic use of any type of stem cell must remain confined to duly approved clinical trials in accordance with the National Guidelines for Stem Cell Research, 2017, issued by the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) and the Department of Biotechnology.
Stem cell interventions that have not been approved for routine clinical use, including those offered for autism, should not be provided as routine, standard or commercial clinical services, the advisory said.
The move comes against the backdrop of the continuing use of stem-cell interventions for autism despite the lack of established evidence supporting them as a standard treatment. An ICMR review has said that available evidence does not support stem cell therapy over behavioural and supportive therapies for ASD and recommended that such therapy be restricted to approved clinical trials.
The Ministry has asked States and Union Territories to disseminate the Supreme Court’s directions to State and district regulatory authorities as well as government and private clinical establishments involved in stem cell research, treatment, promotion or administration.
The advisory also draws attention to the consequences of non-compliance. The Supreme Court, in its January judgment, said violations of the statutory framework could attract consequences including professional misconduct under Regulation 7.22 of the erstwhile Indian Medical Council Regulations, 2002, as well as action under Sections 32 and 40 of the Clinical Establishments Act, including cancellation of registration and penalties.
The National Medical Commission (NMC), in an advisory issued on September 5, has separately reiterated that stem cell therapy may be offered as standard clinical care only for approved indications. It said unauthorised administration, prescription, promotion or advertisement of stem cell therapy beyond approved indications would constitute professional misconduct.
The NMC has asked State Medical Councils to examine allegations of violations and, where professional misconduct by a registered medical practitioner is established after due process, take disciplinary action under the applicable provisions.

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Republic of Korea have a long-standing partnership spanning over 75 years. As a result of their fruitful collaboration, there has been significant progress in health and development all around the world. The Republic of Korea has gone from being a donor-recipient country to a donor-country and is now a leader in global health and playing a critical role on the world stage.
Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Director-General for External Relations and Governance (WHO) and Dr Hye-Jin Kim, Deputy Minister for Planning and Coordination (Ministry of Health and Welfare, Republic of Korea), together with counterparts from WHO and the Government of the Republic of Korea. © WHO
To further strengthen this partnership and our commitment to working jointly to address global health challenges, WHO and the Republic of Korea convened their second Strategic Dialogue in Seoul from 28 to 29 August 2024. Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Directory-General for External Relations and Governance, led the WHO delegation and was accompanied by an in-person team and colleagues participating virtually from the three levels of the Organization (headquarters, regional, and country offices).
Dr Hye-Jin Kim, Deputy Minister for Planning and Coordination, Ministry of Health, led the Republic of Korea delegation and was joined by senior officials including Dr Young-Mee Jee, Commissioner, Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency, as well as senior counterparts from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and the Ministry of Food and Drug Safety.
In addition, in line with WHO's work to enhance collaboration with parliamentarians, the WHO delegation also met with various Members of the National Assembly that are championing the global health agenda.
The recently concluded two-day meeting resulted in an alignment of priorities and paved the way for enhanced collaboration between WHO and the Government of Korea.

On the morning of June 9th, Laura Lin was working from her home in Lanesville, a rural southern Indiana town about 15 miles from the Kentucky border. She was on a Zoom call, unaware that the heavy rain outside was beginning to flood her yard.
Flash floods can strike without warning — this new technology could change that
Satellite data combined with machine learning gives meteorologists new tools to predict deadly floods sooner.
Flash floods can strike without warning — this new technology could change that
Satellite data combined with machine learning gives meteorologists new tools to predict deadly floods sooner.
“I look over to where the barn is over there, and I see pieces of my wood floating, and I was like, ‘What?’ And I immediately was like, ‘I have to go.’ Close my laptop, and I get my kids up, and I’m like, ‘Something’s wrong,’” Lin recalls.
Lin and her family got out safely and sheltered at a neighbor’s house, but Lanesville got over 8 inches of rain within just a few hours that day, way over the threshold for what is considered “heavy” rainfall. The water was gone a few hours later.
Floods are the second-deadliest type of weather event in the United States and the deadliest globally. Just 6 inches of fast-flowing water can knock an adult off their feet, 12 inches can lift a car, and 2 feet can move larger vehicles like trucks and SUVs. A warming climate means more instances of extreme rainfall in the US, creating more opportunities for floods to occur. The deadly flash flooding in Nepal in August caused by a glacier collapse shows the power of water to devastate communities worldwide.
Fortunately, new tools are being developed to counter this threat. A new software called the Transient Artifact and Continuous Learning System (TACLS) uses satellites and machine learning to try to spot areas that could flood sooner and help the National Weather Service (NWS) make better decisions when it comes to issuing flash flood alerts.
“We didn’t get the ‘get on your roof’ warnings until I was already at that person’s house,” Lin says. “All the people in town were already flooded when they started sending out alerts, being like, ‘Get on your roof. We’re dispatching boats.’ So it was way too late.”
TACLS has the potential to help change that.
“It will help you save lives,” says Ivory Small, science and operations officer at the NWS San Diego Weather Forecast Office. Without TACLS, Small says, a storm moving into your area “could kill some folks.” With TACLS, “you can put out the warning and save some folks.”
Follow the water
Weather forecast offices are responsible for issuing severe weather alerts, including flash flood warnings. There are 122 of them throughout the US and its territories, says Jayme Laber, senior service hydrologist for the NWS Weather Forecast Office in Oxnard, California, which oversees the LA area. Small and Laber worked closely on the TACLS project with a broader team of scientists and researchers, and they hope this new project will streamline weather alerts. To understand TACLS, it’s important to first understand how the NWS issues flood alerts.
Currently, the people working in weather forecast offices use a variety of tools to monitor flood conditions. They rely on rain and stream gauges to tell them how much water is in a certain place at any given time, Laber says. They track developing storms using satellites and weather radars. The staff monitors rainfall, but their computers also alert them when it rains more than what is considered safe for a specific area. “Based on the type of soils we have, the steepness of slopes, we have developed flash flood guidance so that we know that if we get this amount of rain in this amount of time in that area, it could result in flash flooding,” Laber says.
“It will help you save lives.”
— Ivory Small
All of that, plus the years of expertise inside those buildings, determines whether or not someone presses a button to issue a flood alert for their area, Laber says.
A watch is the least serious alert. It means that there’s a chance a flash flood could happen. The watch might be issued anywhere from 12 to 48 hours in advance, Laber explains. He says local emergency teams should start working on “flood protection measures” when the flood watch is issued, so there’s enough time to prepare before people are stuck and forced to find higher ground. Response teams might review evacuation plans, set up sandbags and road barriers, and identify the highest risk areas ahead of a potential flood.
An advisory is the next level up. It might be flooding, “but it’s more nuisance-level. It’s not going to threaten life or property,” Laber says. A warning is the most serious alert. “That’s a life-and-death possibility of being swept off your feet [or] being run over by a car floating down the stream,” Small says.
The NWS differentiates a regular flood from a flash flood based on time, says Small. If an area floods in under six hours, it’s a flash flood.
The NWS has a lot of different ways to determine whether or not it needs to issue a flash flood warning, but its tech has limitations, says Yehuda Bock, TACLS project lead and research geodesist at the Scripps Institution of Oceanography at the University of California, San Diego. The satellites the NWS uses are more detailed over oceans than land, he says. And tracking rainfall as it’s happening doesn’t give you enough lead time, “because once there’s precipitation, you’re already in the event itself,” he explains.
Deserts and other less populated areas typically have fewer rain gauges, Laber says. “We have a fairly dense network [of rain gauges], but it doesn’t cover every inch of the Earth.”
Up in the air
TACLS uses satellites and machine learning to identify places on a map — for now, just in California — that risk transitioning from rain to dangerous flash floods. But soon, the technology will be available to every NWS office. Scientists from UCSD, the NWS, and NASA worked together to create TACLS. NASA’s Earth Science Technology Office funded the project through its Advanced Information Systems Technology program.
TACLS relies on the Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS), which is primarily used to predict earthquakes, says Bock. But the GNSS network, which consists of satellites and ground sensors, also happens to provide data that can help forecasters decide if they need to issue a flash flood warning. The more water vapor, or moisture, there is in the atmosphere, the longer the delay in communication between the GNSS satellites and the sensors on the ground.
The amount of moisture, or “precipitable water,” in the atmosphere tells the NWS what is actually happening in the skies leading up to a storm, Laber says.
TACLS uses satellites and machine learning to identify places that risk transitioning from rain to dangerous flash floods.
Before TACLS, Laber and his colleagues had to rely on the forecast, which wasn’t always accurate. TACLS provides real-time data about the precipitable water in the atmosphere to compare to the forecast. This helps them determine whether the storm is actually moving at the speed predicted by the weather models. “It helps us to make better decisions in our warning decision process,” Laber says.
Even with the GNSS moisture data, forecasters still need something to analyze all of it. Bhavik Chandna, a UCSD graduate student, spent about a year developing the machine learning side of TACLS using what’s called long short-term memory architecture. According to Chandna, this specific machine learning system works especially well for things like developing storms and other weather patterns that change over time.
Years of atmospheric measurements from the GNSS network, as well as data about atmospheric rivers, precipitation, and flash flood warnings, were used to train the machine learning model to understand moisture changes in the atmosphere “as a storm develops,” Chandna explains. At the same time, the machine learning system was trained to determine if the conditions are right to issue a flash flood warning.
“Machine learning sucks at some things and excels at some things,” says Joel Johnson, associate professor in the department of earth and planetary sciences at the University of Texas at Austin. Johnson, who was not involved in the TACLS project, knows firsthand the challenges of working with these types of tools. “In general, it’s very easy to have artifacts in your data, false positives. A sensor goes funky, and things like that,” Johnson says. Still, he says TACLS seems “well suited” to the task of predicting flash floods.
False positives do happen, Chandna says. “A real weather system usually affects an area, not just one isolated GNSS station. If one station shows a strong signal but its neighbors do not, that detection can be suppressed. If several nearby stations see the same pattern, we have much more confidence that it represents a real atmospheric signal,” he adds.
Chandna says TACLS is not intended to replace the forecasters who issue weather alerts. It’s just another piece of information that can assist in their decision-making, he says.
Finding a better way
TACLS software is already being used in the LA and San Diego weather forecast offices where flash flooding is a common occurrence, says Laber. “In the West, we deal with a lot more flash flooding, where it happens a lot quicker,” he explains. Today, TACLS shows them a graph with various points telling them what is going on in real time.
A newer version of TACLS with improved graphics is currently being loaded onto the NWS system and is nearly done, Laber says. It will be available to all of the NWS offices in the second half of October, he adds. This iteration has a map with detailed graphics showing how much it’s raining and whether an extreme weather event is occurring.
According to Laber, having more tools — like this latest update to TACLS — will further improve their decision-making when it comes to issuing flash flood alerts, and, in turn, maybe speed up alert times so people know there’s a problem sooner.
Laber says TACLS will likely be used the most in the Western US because the majority of the GNSS sensors are located in places known for earthquake activity. But Chandna thinks TACLS could work well elsewhere too. As long as there are some GNSS sensors and available local weather data, “we could use the same ideology that we have in our system around different parts of the world,” he says.
Small is thinking beyond TACLS. He believes ongoing research is crucial to improving how the NWS issues flash flood warnings. “We learn what’s going on a little more every time we do a storm because they’re all different,” he says. “It’s imperative that you do the research after, especially big events, and see what caused it to do what it did, and why, if it was different than what we already knew, did this occur.”
Lin’s concern is Lanesville and her home. “It would have been helpful to know [water was coming] before I was locked in. I couldn’t go anywhere,” Lin says. “If I got an alert that was like, ‘You need to get out now if you’re in lower-lying ground, this is coming.’ Yeah, that would have [been helpful]. But it came in so fast.”

Jammu, Sep 18: A birthday celebration in Jammu turned tragic after a young man was allegedly stabbed to death following a dispute that reportedly began when cake was smeared on the birthday boy’s face, police said on Friday.
According to police, the incident took place on September 17 near Lower Roop Nagar, where a group of friends had gathered for a birthday celebration.
Police said Police Post GMC Jammu informed Police Station Janipur that a man identified as Pawan Nair alias Sameer had been brought to Government Medical College (GMC) Jammu in an injured condition. He was accompanied by his friends John Sotra, Gaurav Singh and Sugandh Bhatti.
Doctors at GMC Jammu examined the injured man and declared him brought dead, police said.
Following the information, a team from Police Station Janipur immediately reached the hospital and began inquiries into the circumstances surrounding the death.
Preliminary investigation revealed that Neeraj alias Anshu was celebrating his birthday near Lower Roop Nagar in the presence of his friends, including Pawan Nair alias Sameer. Neeraj’s brother Rishu was also reportedly present at the spot.
Police said a confrontation broke out during the cake-cutting ceremony after Pawan allegedly smeared cake on Neeraj’s face. The act reportedly led to a heated exchange between the two.
As their friends attempted to intervene and calm the situation, Neeraj allegedly took out a khokhri that he was carrying and attacked Pawan, causing a serious injury to his neck.
The injured man was rushed to GMC Jammu by his friends. However, despite being taken to the hospital, he was declared dead by the attending doctors.
Following the incident, Police Station Janipur registered a case under Section 103(1) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) and launched a detailed investigation.
Police said that acting swiftly, they apprehended Neeraj alias Anshu and his brother Rishu, who are currently in police custody at Police Station Janipur in connection with the case.
The police have also initiated proceedings to recover the alleged weapon used in the crime. The body of the deceased has been shifted to the mortuary for post-mortem examination.
Further investigation is underway to establish the complete sequence of events and determine the role of all persons involved.
Jammu Police said that strict and time-bound action will be taken in accordance with law. (KNC)

New Delhi, December 1975. It was love at first sight when a Swedish hippy called Lotta von Schedvin sat down to be sketched by an Indian street artist, Pradyumna Kumar Mahanandia, known to everyone as PK. In the 10 minutes it took PK to complete her portrait, everything clicked into place for the pair. They were swept headlong in a whirlwind romance, and PK took Lotta to his village in the east of India to meet his family. But soon after, the time came for Lotta to pack up her VW campervan and head back home with her friends.
Heart-stricken PK promised to follow, but a plane ticket to Sweden was an impossible dream. Determined not to lose the love of his life, PK bought a secondhand Raleigh bike, and with $80 sewn into the waistband of his trousers, set off to cycle 6,000 miles to Lotta. He knew the sun set in the west, so that was the direction he took. His plan was to follow the hippy trail, cycling through India, Pakistan, Afghanistan, Iran and Turkey, crossing Europe, finally arriving in Sweden.
Actually, he was heading to Switzerland until a fellow backpacker pointed out that Switzerland and Sweden were two different countries. In a new Netflix documentary, The Cycle of Love, PK jokes that his strength was his fuzzy grasp of European geography. Watching the film, you wonder if his superpower might have been his smile – warm and joyous, it lights the room. Either way, he made it to Sweden. The journey took 123 days, and ended up involving a flight or two, and a couple of trains. In May 1977, PK knocked on Lotta’s door in Borås, Sweden. They have been together ever since.
Documentary-maker Orlando von Einsiedel first heard about the story when he gave a talk in Sweden. “At the end, two young people came up and handed me a book,” he says. “They said: ‘This is about our parents’ story. We know your work. Would you be interested in this as a film?’” The book was The Amazing Story of the Man Who Cycled from India to Europe for Love by Swedish journalist Per J Andersson.
The two young people were PK and Lotta’s grownup kids Emilie and Karl. Von Einsiedel politely took the book but didn’t think too much about it. “Normally in my experience, when somebody approaches you and says ‘I’ve got a brilliant story’, it doesn’t work out.”
A couple of months later, Von Einsiedel picked up the book as a holiday read, opening it on the flight out of London. “The moment I started I thought, ‘Oh my God, you idiot Orlando! This is extraordinary.’” It wasn’t just the against-all-odds, 6,000-mile cycle ride, PK’s story was a tale of fate and destiny. When he was born, the astrologer in his village made four predictions about his future wife: she would be a Taurus, born outside India, musical and own a jungle. So naturally the first question he asked Lotta was: “Are you a Taurus?” Her answer was yes. She was also a gifted musician, and – most bonkers of all – her family owned land with a forest in Sweden.
“When you tell people the story, it’s almost too good to be true,” says Von Einsiedel, cheerful and chatty on a video call from New York. The previous night he attended the US premiere of The Cycle of Love with PK and Lotta, who have been happily married for nearly 50 years. The pair have been getting the celebrity treatment wherever they go. “Everybody in the cinema stands up for them, people are weeping when they come on stage.” What do the couple make of the film? He grins. “I know they like it, because whenever they go to a festival, they watch every single screening from beginning to end.” How many times have they seen it? “A lot.”
The film tells their story with enormous warmth. It includes a dramatisation of the epic ride, with PK played by the British-based Indian actor Chirag Lobo, and Mina Dale as Lotta. Everybody else is non-professional, explains Von Einsiedel. “Our producers would go out and street-cast people on the morning of filming.”
What about the script, I ask? There are gorgeous, heartwarming scenes as PK shares his story with people he meets on the road, who in return tell him about their life and loves. How were those scenes scripted? “No script. Everything is improvised. When PK interacts with everyday people he meets along the way, those are just normal conversations about love and hopes and dreams.”
Wasn’t that a bit risky – getting a plane to India with two actors, no script and trusting that deep and meaningful conversations would materialise from conversations with ordinary people? “Massively risky, except I tested if it might work in Lewisham town centre,” Von Einsiedel says, grinning. “I have a friend who’s an actor. We went to Lewisham with a bike.” Armed with a notepad, his friend told people that he was cycling from London to Cape Town for love. “He pretended to draw portraits. What was extraordinary is the first person he sat down to draw turned around and said: ‘I love your story. I’ll buy you a plane ticket immediately.’”
It’s the kindness of strangers that makes the documentary so uplifting. When PK cycles out of Kabul, he stops to help an Austrian backpacker, Linea, who crashed her car, knocking out most of her teeth. He stays with her for several days at hospital, even though it means his visa expiring and further delay. Later, when he arrives in Istanbul and checks his post, there is a train ticket to Vienna – a thank you from Linea for his kindness.
What struck Von Einsiedel when he met the real-life PK was that his story about love went beyond boy-meets-girl. “For me, it’s not just about romantic love. It’s about self-love and love for all the people that we share this planet with.” PK was born into a dalit family, the marginalised group in India formerly known as “untouchables”. At school, he was made to sit outside during lessons and not allowed to play with the other children. Even after he won a scholarship to study fine art in Delhi, he experienced periods of homelessness and isolation.
“From the moment I started talking to PK it became clear what a difficult and traumatic childhood he’d had,” Von Einsiedel says. “He spoke so movingly about being on the journey and how it was the first time that strangers would touch him and hug him. That it was key to him starting to believe in himself and love himself. He said: ‘How can you love anybody if you can’t love yourself?’ I get emotional just saying that.”
PK explained how he felt accepted on the journey, hanging out with hippies and locals in the villages and towns he passed through. People with very little offered him hospitality, a meal or a roof for the night. In the documentary, this warm feeling of togetherness thuds to the ground when PK arrives in Europe, grilled by hostile and overtly racist German border officers. “That was his first experience,” says Von Einsiedel. “He travelled through all these countries, Afghanistan and Iran, and everybody treated him with respect. Then as soon as he got to Europe he immediately experienced racism.”
Von Einsiedel grew up in south London. At university he studied social anthropology and in his 20s was a professional snowboarder. “I learned the craft of film-making making snowboard films,” he says. “When I knew how to do that, I segued into making films about social issues I believed in.” He started working with Al Jazeera, travelling to conflict zones.
In 2015, he was nominated for an Oscar for his first full-length documentary, Virunga, about the battle to save a national park in eastern Congo, home to some of the world’s last mountain gorillas. His documentary short, White Helmets, following Syrian volunteers rescuing civilians, won an Oscar. Next he made Evelyn, an incredibly moving film in which Von Einsiedel turned the camera on his own family. His brother Evelyn took his own life aged 22 over a decade earlier. In the film, Von Einsiedel and his two surviving siblings hiked the routes their brother loved to walk with friends and family. “I was very emotionally closed for a long time after my brother died,” he says. “I used to think being emotionally open was a sign of weakness. I was terrified of my own emotions. I see the opposite now. I think being emotionally open is a sign of strength.”
When it comes to picking a subject for a new documentary, he says he is attracted to people who inspire him. “I’m drawn to stories that show the better side of human beings. That’s a thread that runs through the work I like to make.” The Cycle of Love is by far the sunniest film he has made to date. What’s that all about, I ask? “I wanted to make an optimistic film that’s about joy and human connection. The world is difficult. Love is one of those things that all of us can agree on. This story just felt so important to tell.”
