After years of visiting Europe from Los Angeles, I took the plunge and relocated to Barcelona in 2020.
I've spent the past six years really making Spain feel like home, but when I first moved, there were definitely a few experiences and cultural norms that took some getting used to.
Here's what surprised me the most when I moved from the US to Spain.
I knew Barcelona was in Spain, but the region of Catalonia has its own language and culture.
Barcelona is the capital of Catalonia, a northeastern region of Spain. When I first moved, I assumed Spanish would be the go-to language, but I was quite mistaken.
When you walk into stores and restaurants, the menus and signs are usually in Catalan. And although everyone speaks Spanish, it's still good to know a few Catalan words and phrases to be polite and respect the culture.
A few of my favorites are "adéu" ("goodbye"), "si us plau" ("please"), "molt bé" ("very well"), and "merci" ("thank you").
There are a few unique holiday traditions I had to learn when I moved.
There's no Valentine's Day here, but in late April, they have Sant Jordi — a celebration of love during which women are supposed to give a man a book in exchange for a rose.
Many people also celebrate La Mona on the Monday after Easter. Traditionally, godparents give their godchildren an egg-shaped cake for the whole family to enjoy.
My all-time favorite Catalonia traditions come at Christmas.
For the whole month of December, children leave food and water out for Caga Tió, which translates to pooping log. Then they hit the log with a stick on Christmas Eve, and Caga Tió "poops out" presents.
People take this tradition very seriously; the streets of Barcelona are decorated with this pooping log, and just about every store has one in its window.
In the same vein, caganers are another fascinating Christmas tradition in Catalonia. The little pooping figurine is placed in nativity scenes to represent fertilization and hope for the new year.
Now, there are caganer shops all over Barcelona year-round for tourists. Nearly every celebrity has been transformed into a caganer, from Freddy Mercury to SpongeBob SquarePants to Joe Biden.
Tapas are genuinely a way of life here.
Tapas, small, shareable plates, are prevalent in restaurants across Barcelona.
I love this way of dining because you get a little taste of everything. I typically order between three and six tapas to share with a friend or two.
Some of the most popular tapas include croquetas, which are kind of like a breaded meatball; patatas bravas, cubed potatoes served with mayo and a tomato sauce; pimientos del pardón, small fried green peppers; and tortilla espanñola, a Spanish omelet prepared with egg and potato.
I've found it surprisingly easy to have a balanced lifestyle here.
Barcelona is known for its nightlife, from great cocktail bars to decadent nightclubs that stay open until the wee hours of the morning. However, it also offers more relaxed activities than I imagined.
Because of the great, warm weather nearly year-round, there are countless outdoor fitness and yoga classes in the parks and on the beaches. I've also seen plenty of volleyball and paddleboarding.
I can always balance out a wild night of drinking and dancing with a long stroll on the beach and an afternoon yoga class.
Sandwiches for breakfast are the norm.
A typical Spanish breakfast is a bocadillo, a sandwich served on baguette-style bread.
The bread is first rubbed with fresh tomatoes, referred to as "pan con tomate," to get the perfect amount of flavor and texture. Then it's traditionally filled with ham, but sometimes there's also cheese or a potato omelet inside.
The affordable dish is usually served alongside a coffee in the morning.
I didn't know about calçots or that there was a traditional way to eat them until I got here.
Calçots season typically runs from late winter into early spring, and it's quite the experience.
Eating calçots and experiencing the tradition behind them was a first for me. They're part of the onion family, similar to scallions, and they're grilled and served with a romesco sauce made from puréed tomato, garlic, and almonds.
Traditionally, you're given a bib and gloves to dive into the onion dish. The bib is simply to keep you from making a mess of yourself, and the gloves allow you to remove the outer layer of the onion before indulging.
Then you dip your calçot in the sauce, tilt your head back, and eat it in one big gulp.
Here, dinner is served way later than I'm used to.
In the US, I ate dinner around 7 p.m. every night — maybe 8 or 8:30 p.m. if I was working late.
But in Spain, I had to get used to a whole new dining schedule. Dinner is typically served around 9 or 10 p.m.
People really take their time to eat and socialize with whoever they're dining with, so by the time you've finished dessert, it could easily be midnight.
There are mountains and beaches surrounding the city, and you could visit both in a single day.
The Collserola mountains cradle Barcelona from the west, and it only takes about 30 minutes to reach the foothills by public transportation.
From there, you can hike up to the famous Tibidabo amusement park or simply stroll through the trails.
After working up a sweat, you can easily cruise down to the sea and go for an afternoon swim.
Many weekend trips are easily accessible and breathtaking.
Costa Brava, accessible primarily by car or bus, is a short ride from Barcelona.
The coast runs between Spain and France, and it's simply magical. I can't help but be hypnotized by the clear turquoise waters and sandy beaches.
In the summer, the beaches are lined with xiringuito, pop-up restaurants that serve tapas and sangria.
The coastline is also jam-packed with history. In the town of Tossa de Mar, you have to crawl through an old castle door to get to one of the beaches, and near Cadaqués, you can visit the house where Salvador Dali lived.
The afternoon siesta is a real thing, and you have to plan accordingly.
"Siestas," Spanish for naps, are truly a way of life here. If you're trying to run errands in Spain, be prepared to plan around afternoon and weekend closures.
Although larger retailers like Zara, H&M, and big supermarkets stay open during regular working hours, the smaller mom-and-pop shops usually close from about 2 to 4 p.m. every day.
This is the time for employees to go home and rest, have lunch, or simply take a nap. And just about everything, including the big shops, is closed on Sundays.
Gaudí architecture is everywhere, and it's beautiful.
Barcelona is full of history and beautiful architecture. Antoni Gaudí was a Catalan architect whose incredible and intricate designs can be seen all around the city.
I genuinely find myself walking in amazement on a daily basis — I can't believe I get to take in these incredible sights on my morning commute.
The Sagrada Familia church is arguably his most famous work. Although Gaudí died in 1926, the project was completed in 2026.

Soon after the news of Hindutva fanatic Swatantra Bhardwaj getting interim bail for three weeks went out, a 1.16-minute video of him got viral, in which he is with another person who boasts about Bhardwaj’s release and compares him with a lion on the hunt. Bhardwaj then threatens those who had attacked his supporters while he was in detention. He says (in Hindi), “You are like insects.. why did you target my brothers? if they wanted they could have beaten you up.. but for some reason, they followed the law… I will not do anything to you.. tell your father Chandrashekhar Azad (Bhim Army chief whom Bhardwaj compares to Ravana), that this Brahmin lion (referring to himself) will avenge the attack. It is an open challenge…”
Bhardwaj faces criminal charges under Sections 115(2), 126(2) and 3(5) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, along with provisions of the POCSO Act and SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act and an attempt-to-murder charge for an alleged assault on the father of Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) activist Nishu Azaad. On September 7, he had been sent to 14-day judicial remand.
An X user named Gen-Z of India shared the said video on September 17 and wrote (in Hindi), “As soon as Swatantra Bharadwaj stepped out, he started up again, even though the court had imposed the condition that he would not make any grandstanding statements in the media, but listen to what he is saying.” The post has received close to 1 million views. (Archive)
भारतीय न्याय व्यवस्था एक बार फिर से फ़ैल हो गयी है…
स्वतंत्र भारद्वाज बाहर आते ही फ़िर से शुरू हो गया है, जबकि कोर्ट ने शर्त रखी है कि मीडिया में कोई बयानबाज़ी नहीं करेगा लेकिन यह तो क्या कह रहा है वह सुनिए। pic.twitter.com/pBPNKeQtRs
— Gen-Z of India (@GenZ_of_India_) September 17, 2026
This post was reshared by several influential and verified handles, including Trinamool Congress MP Mahua Moitra, journalist Vir Sanghvi, CJP leader Ratna Singh and others, making it go viral. Others like film writer Darab Farooqi and verified X user @tanmoyofc shared the video as well.
Media outlets Prabhat Khabar and The Mooknayak published reports on the video presenting it as recorded after Bhardwaj’s release on bail in the assault case.
Fact Check
First of all, we found that India Today posted a video on September 17 stating that Bhardwaj came out of Tihar Jail around 9.45 pm on that day (September 17). The caption of India Today’s Instagram post said, “Although he was granted bail two days ago, he was released around 9:45 pm after the remaining procedures were completed. He immediately ran towards a taxi and left without speaking to the media.”
View this post on Instagram
Several other media outlets reported that Bhardwaj walked out of jail late at night on Thursday, September 17, and rushed into a car avoiding media persons.
Next, a reverse image search with some key frames from the viral video led us to a Facebook post and a YouTube video from September 7. This makes it clear that the video was not recorded after Bhardwaj’s release on September 17. Check the screenshots in the gallery below:
By scraping our database of active Right-wing vigilantes, we then identified the other individual in the video as Vaibhaw Kumar alias Vaibhaw Pandey. While going through his Instagram timeline, we found the now-viral video uploaded on June 26.
According to another video posted by Vaibhaw, Bhardwaj was detained on June 22 for threatening CJP leaders at Jantar Mantar.
To sum up, the viral video of Hindutva fanatic and attempt-to-murder accused Swatantra Bhardwaj threatening Chandrashekhar Azad was not recorded after his release on interim bail on September 17. It was shared on social media by another Hindutva vigilante on June 26.

Hyrox athlete apologises and forfeits victory after defecating during race
Joanna Wietrzyk said she is ‘deeply sorry for the discomfort and disruption’ that her defecation caused during a Hyrox event in Beijing
An Australian Hyrox athlete who went viral after soiling herself during a race in Beijing - before going on to win - has apologised and forfeited her victory.
Joanna Wietrzyk defecated during the global indoor race event in Beijing, and initially responded to her win with a post on Instagram stating “Go hard or go home they say… a win is a win.”
However, after the fallout from the now-notorious incident continued, she has now announced she will “retroactively withdraw” from the race and forfeit the points she won during the event.
“I want to offer my sincere apology to the people of China, my fellow competitors, the spectators and the Hyrox organisers for what happened during the race in Beijing,” she wrote.
“I felt completely fit and healthy at the start of the race, with no reason to expect any illness. Looking back, I regret the decision to not have stepped off the track. I recognise that I should have made a different choice. I take responsibility for my decision to continue and am deeply sorry for the discomfort and disruption it caused,” she added.
The 22-year-old holds the Hyrox women’s solo world record, and on Saturday completed the Beijing race in 1 hour, 1 minute and 23 seconds.
Hyrox is a gruelling indoor fitness event that combines running with functional exercises like sled pushes, rowing, burpee broad jumps, and wall balls. Unlike a traditional marathon or obstacle race, every Hyrox event uses the same format and distances, allowing competitors around the world to compare their times directly.
Facing backlash over the incident, Hyrox co-founder Moritz Fürste apologised to “everyone directly or indirectly affected”.
“Hyrox made a mistake by not reacting immediately during the race. In the end it is my job to foresee these potential incidents and I did not,” he said in a statement posted on Instagram.
Fürste said that Hyrox had also begun “ improving event processes, plus making rulebook changes immediately”.
“As of this moment, there are new rules and procedures in place to prevent situations like this from happening again. We learn and try to get better everyday.”
The revised rules will allow a race director to withdraw an athlete on medical grounds if their “blood, vomit, urine, or faeces poses a welfare or contamination risk to the racer or to other racers”.
Wietrzyk added in her statement: “I know my actions had an impact beyond myself, and I am genuinely sorry to everyone who was affected. I am learning from this experience and will carry those lessons with me, including remembering that there is more to life than racing and knowing when it is right to step away.
“On reflection, I have decided to retroactively withdraw from the race and forfeit the points I earned.”

An AI tool is set to start advising air traffic controllers on managing air traffic in the congested airspace above the Washington, DC, area. The expected launch would be the first step toward a planned nationwide rollout covering the 29 million square miles of US national airspace overseen by the Federal Aviation Administration.
The FAA describes the SMART system as using AI models to predict air traffic flows and identify potential conflicts based on operational factors like airline schedules, weather, airport capacity, and airspace conditions. US government and industry officials told The Wall Street Journal that SMART could debut for the three major airports in the Washington, DC, area as soon as Monday, September 21.
The decision to launch SMART in limited scope before going nationwide is the “right call,” said Philip Mann, principal consultant at Vector Strategic Consulting LLC, where he advises on aviation safety and AI governance. Mann previously worked at the FAA in multiple roles for 17 years.
“SMART’s risk was never any single prediction—it is a national-scale system with AI components carrying more unknowns than anything the FAA has fielded,” Mann wrote in an email to Ars. “Every cut in scope shrinks the unknowns.”
The AI-driven forecasts and recommendations are meant to give the FAA, airlines, and aircraft operators the same shared view of operational conditions so that they can agree on the most efficient routes and departure times. The goals of SMART include reducing aircraft fuel burn, improving on-time performance for flights, and speeding up recovery from weather and air traffic congestion events.
However, the airline industry was reportedly confused for weeks about the agency’s plans to deploy the AI tool, according to Politico. Anonymous airline officials told Politico that their concerns only eased after the FAA said the SMART AI tool would not change any procedures for air traffic controllers or airlines, and would instead produce “alternative route information” that is made available through existing FAA systems.

Warren Buffett's road to investing glory
Billionaire and philanthropist Warren Buffett is stepping down as chairman of Berkshire Hathaway.
Warren Buffett, Berkshire Hathaway's former CEO and legendary investor, is stepping down as its chairman, marking the end of his executive duties at the firm he helped build into one of the world's largest conglomerates.
Buffett, 96, will become chairman emeritus, an honorary title that typically does not include decision-making responsibilities. He will remain a member of the board and offer his judgment and perspective, Berkshire said.
Here's a timeline of major milestones under Buffett's leadership:
1965: Buffett took over Berkshire, a struggling New England textile company, after winning a dispute with prior management, marking the origins of the famed conglomerate. The textile business shuttered in 1985 after two decades of effort to turn it around proved unsuccessful.
1967: Berkshire acquired National Indemnity, setting in motion a theme that would eventually become the financial engine of the company. The strategic acquisition gave Berkshire a growing pool of capital from insurance premiums that could be used to deploy into investments.
1988-1989: Berkshire began buying into Coca-Cola in 1988, an investment that remains one of its largest holdings to date. By 1989, he was investing heavily in Gillette, illustrating his preference for owning simple businesses that were easy to understand.
1991: Buffett personally stepped in as interim chairman of Salomon Brothers after a trading scandal pushed it to the brink of collapse, putting Berkshire's US$700 million investment at risk. He spent months repairing relations with regulators, which ultimately helped keep the investment bank alive.
1996-2000: Between 1996 and 1998, Berkshire started expanding aggressively into insurance, taking full ownership of GEICO and buying out General Re, cementing the sector as a foundational investment theme in its portfolio. Buffett entered utilities in 1999 after taking control of MidAmerican Energy, which was later renamed Berkshire Hathaway Energy.
2006: Buffett pledged to donate nearly all of his Berkshire stock to philanthropic foundations. Since then, he has donated over half of his shares, including more than US$47 billion to the Gates Foundation and over $17 billion to four family charities.
2008-2011: Berkshire injected US$5 billion into Goldman Sachs at the peak of the global financial crisis in September 2008. In 2011, it invested another US$5 billion in Bank of America when the bank was dealing with the fallout from its disastrous acquisition of Countrywide Financial during the crisis. Berkshire later made an US$11.5 billion profit on that investment in 2017, not including dividend payouts. It also made a monumental acquisition of the railroad Burlington Northern Santa Fe for US$26.4 billion in 2010.
2016: Berkshire began accumulating Apple, initially taking a stake worth roughly US$1 billion. What began as a relatively small position eventually became Berkshire's largest holding at the end of 2025.
2022: After years of relatively subdued dealmaking, Berkshire deployed tens of billions of dollars into large stock purchases of companies including Chevron, HP Inc and Occidental Petroleum.
2024: Berkshire's market value topped US$1 trillion, becoming the first non-tech US company to reach the milestone.
Jan 1, 2026: Buffett handed over the reins to Greg Abel after stepping down as CEO, culminating a storied tenure in which the firm returned over 6,100,000 per cent since 1965.

Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay is set to launch a scheme providing one-gram gold rings to newborns on September 28, the state government said on Friday.
The government has procured 1.28 lakh gold rings for the first phase of the programme. The rings will be distributed to babies born at government-run hospitals across the state. Each ring will carry a distinct serial number and be packed in tamper-proof packaging, according to an official government statement.
The Thaimaaman Thanga Mothiram Thittam (Maternal Uncle Gold Ring Scheme), is a key pre-poll promise of the ruling TVK. Gold rings will be provided at the time of discharge of beneficiaries from the hospitals.
The scheme will cover all districts except Chengalpattu and Tiruppur. These two districts include the Maduranthakam and Dharapuram Assembly constituencies, respectively, where bypolls are scheduled for October 6.
Eligibility criteria
Under the eligibility criteria, the mothers of newborns must be permanent residents of Tamil Nadu to receive the benefit.
They must also be registered under the Pregnancy and Infant Cohort Monitoring and Evaluation (PICME) system and possess a Reproductive and Child Health (RCH) identification card.
The identity card is issued following registration.
A look at arrangements to distribute gold rings by TN govt
For the scheme, the state government invited tenders to procure 4.41 lakh 22-carat gold rings carrying 916 hallmark certification. The rings are planned to be distributed to beneficiaries in four phases. The first phase covers 1.28 lakh rings from the total procurement planned under the scheme.
Appropriate arrangements have been made to distribute gold rings in 107 centres to children born in government hospitals between June 22 -- the CM's birthday-- and the scheme's launch date, at a rate of 100 children per day.
The government said that the scheme not only increases public trust in government healthcare services but also promotes safe delivery practices in hospitals.
A Government Order on the implementation of the scheme was notified on June 23, 2026.
The announcement on launch date follows a review meeting chaired by the chief minister at the Secretariat in which Health Minister KG Arunraj, Chief Secretary M Saikumar, DGP Mahesh Kumar Aggarwal and several other top officials took part.
The Tamil Nadu government estimates that around 7.80 lakh children are born in the state every year. Data from the National Family Health Survey-6 (NFHS-6) shows that 99.9% of these births take place in healthcare facilities.
Of the total deliveries, around 4.20 lakh, or 53%, are conducted at government hospitals. About 90% of these deliveries take place at Comprehensive Emergency Obstetric and Neonatal Care (CEmONC) Centres.
Why was the launch postponed?
The one-gram gold ring programme was initially planned for launch on September 15, coinciding with the birth anniversary of Dravidian leader CN Annadurai. However, the launch was postponed as Vijay travelled to the UK as part of efforts to attract investments to Tamil Nadu.

Yatsushiro, Kumamoto Pref. – A section on the Kyushu Shinkansen bullet train line that had been halted due to the impact of a major earthquake in Kumamoto Prefecture in late July returned to service on Friday.
All sections on the high-speed train line linking Hakata Station in Fukuoka Prefecture and Kagoshima-Chuo Station in Kagoshima Prefecture are now back to operations 52 days after the July 28 temblor, which measured up to 7, the highest level, on Japan’s seismic intensity scale.
Restarted on Friday was the section between Kumamoto and Shin-Minamata stations, both in Kumamoto Prefecture.
Kyushu Railway, or JR Kyushu, the operator of the line, said that trains will travel at a reduced speed of 70 kph on a section of about 10 kilometers near Shin-Yatsushiro Station, located between Kumamoto and Shin-Minamata stations, for the time being to ensure safe operations. The section sustained heavy damage from the earthquake.
Therefore, the number of the trains linking Kagoshima-Chuo and the Sanyo Shinkansen line will be reduced by 10% from the normal level. As the travel time between Kumamoto and Kagoshima-Chuo stations will be about eight minutes longer, the departure time at Kagoshima-Chuo will be moved up by up to nine minutes.
At Shin-Yatsushiro Station on Friday, passengers formed a long line from slightly after 6 a.m., waiting for the day’s first trains.
A 53-year-old male corporate worker from the city of Yatsushiro who commutes to the city of Minamata said: “The reopening (of the section between Kumamoto and Shin-Minamata stations) was earlier than I had expected. I’d like to express gratitude to those who worked hard for the restoration.”
One 17-year-old local student is using the line as an alternative route for commuting to the city of Kumamoto, where his high school is, because a train line he regularly uses is still being halted due to the impact of the quake.
He said that he now leaves his home 30 minutes later than usual. “I’m grateful because I don’t have to wake up early,” he added.
The Kyushu Shinkansen line was halted on all sections after the earthquake.
Services between Hakata and Kumamoto stations were resumed July 31, three days after the quake. The section between Shin-Minamata and Kagoshima-Chuo was reopened Aug. 7 while the number of trains in operation was reduced.
Operations between Kumamoto and Shin-Minamata stations had remained suspended, however, due to damage, including rail distorti.

Ukraine lashes out at Russian elections ‘held at gunpoint’ in occupied territory
Russians are going to the polls for the first time since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022
Ukrainians in territories occupied by Russia are being “held at gunpoint” and forced to vote in parliamentary elections that “bear no resemblance to democracy,” the Ukrainian foreign ministry has warned.
For the next three days, 111 million people will head to the polls for Russia’s first parliamentary election since the since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 - and one that includes the regions of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson, as well as the annexed Crimean Peninsula.
“This is a farce orchestrated by the occupying state; it bears no resemblance to democratic elections and establishes no legal grounds for extending Russian jurisdiction to any part of Ukraine's territory,” a statement from the ministry said.
“No ‘vote’ organised by Russia at gunpoint alters the internationally recognised status of these territories. Temporary occupation confers no sovereign rights upon the occupying state.”
Ukraine refuses to recognise either the holding of the “illegal elections” or their “null and void results,” the ministry added.
With virtually no opposition, Vladimir Putin’s United Russia party is expected to cement its grip on parliament it has held for 23 years - result that will be held up by the Kremlin as evidence of widespread support for his war policies.
“Your choice and resolve will once again demonstrate that millions of people stand behind our fighters, that we are a united people, bound by shared values, historical memory, and love for the Motherland," the Putin told the nation before the vote.
An advert on state TV urging people to vote showed Russian military commanders down the ages before cutting to troops holding up the national flag after winning a battle in Ukraine with the slogan: "Their voice is the voice of victory. Your vote is the strength of Russia!"
The State Duma election, which will vote in the lower house of the Russian parliament, is happening against the backdrop of Ukrainian drone strikes on refineries and warehouses far from the frontline, a war economy that is hitting its limits and fears of a mass mobilisation as soon as the polls are closed.
As Putin himself was shown casting his vote from his office, France accused Russia of launching hybrid attacks in recent weeks.
President Emmanuel Macron told reporters after meeting in Paris with political party leaders to discuss the impact of both the Ukraine and Iran wars: “The threat - particularly the Russian hybrid threat - facing Europeans and France has intensified.”
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez later added on X that all relevant services would be mobilised to fend off interference from Moscow.
“The goal is clear: to mobilise all state services and local stakeholders so as to be ready to face these new threats,” he said.
France becomes the latest Nato member to accuse Russia of such attacks, only days after Germany pointed the finger at the Kremlin for the attempted drone strike at Leipzig Airport in August.
Citing unnamed intelligence agencies, Poland also sounded the alarm that Russia is plotting hybrid strikes with drones or missiles against Nato countries supporting Ukraine.
Prime minister Donald Tusk told Parliament: “These potential strikes would be quote-unquote 'accidental' in nature, intended to paralyse or at least weaken the resolve of Nato states to invoke the relevant Nato provisions in the event of aggression against a member country.”
Poland said it had deployed fighter jets in response to a Russian attack in western Ukraine, near to the Polish border, this week.
Airports in Rzeszow and Lublin were temporarily closed, and residents of two eastern regions of Poland received air raid warnings. Local media reported that sirens had sounded and that pupils in some schools had sought shelter.

The EU plans to ban chatbots from simulating emotions or interpersonal relationships in interactions with anyone under the age of 18 as the bloc tries to stop children from developing emotional dependencies on the technology.
The rules will be part of the EU Kids Act, proposed on Thursday, which includes similar restrictions on minors’ access to social media and video-sharing platforms. Children under 13 will be banned from accessing chatbots without their guardians’ supervision, and digital platforms will have to build child-safety protections into their products or face fines of up to six percent of total worldwide turnover, according to a draft of the legislation seen by WIRED.
Chatbots operating in the EU will also not be allowed to retain memory of interactions between separate conversations under the new rules, since the Commission worries this could lead to systems accumulating sensitive data of minors over time and potentially reinforcing harmful interaction patterns.
Providers of online social networking sites, video-sharing platforms, and games should not automatically activate or encourage the use of AI chatbots on their services, the proposed law will also stipulate. That includes not pinning AI companions and general conversational chatbots at the top of a minor’s contacts list, it says—as had been done by Snapchat.
The proposal is limited to AI companions and general conversational chatbots seen by the Commission to pose serious risks to minors health, safety, and well-being. Simeon de Brouwer, a policy adviser at the Brussels-based advocacy group European Digital Rights, welcomes the chatbot measures, but tells WIRED it doesn’t make sense to restrict them to young people only. “Don’t we all deserve to be protected from AIs designed to be addictive, from AIs which create emotional dependencies, or from AI features which are activated and pushed by default onto users?” The EU says its Digital Fairness Act, due to be unveiled later this year, is expected to propose clamp downs on addictive design more widely.
In documents seen by WIRED the European Commission says it is worried that dependency on chatbots may negatively impact a child’s development and its relationships with other humans. It’s also concerned by chatbots giving minors dangerous advice, including on their mental health and personal development, which it said can shape and encourage risky behaviour.
“Platforms have been playing fast and loose with children’s mental health,” President Ursula von der Leyen said in a press conference on Thursday. Around half of Europeans aged 11 to 25 have discussed intimate or personal matters with AI chatbots, according to an Ipsos BVA survey across France, Germany, Sweden and Ireland. Australia and the UK are both attempting to restrict minors’ access to chatbots through their social media bans.
It also highlighted the harms of deepfakes generated by chatbots, which von der Leyen nodded at in Wednesday’s State of the Union speech: “We do not have to accept that girls have their photos used for AI-generated sexualised images … Europe has the power to act.” While the EU AI Act has required synthetic content to be labeled as AI-generated since August, the rules currently only apply to deepfakes generated for commercial use.
The Commission also blames digital distraction for a decline in basic skills in young people. Children who say they use AI chatbots for schoolwork get lower test scores than those who don’t, according to research spanning 91 countries by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. Concerns about cognitive impacts and deskilling “expose the absence of children’s rights from the design of GenAI’s tools,” researchers from independent network EU Kids Online wrote in a report.

Former Chief Justice of the High Court of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh, Justice Ali Mohammed Magrey, on Friday described teachers as the “quiet architects” of a child’s character and called for greater investment in their dignity, professional development and well-being.
Addressing the Dronacharya Awards for Teachers 2026, organised by BMS Academy for Professional Courses under the aegis of the BMS Educational Trust at BMS College of Engineering in Bengaluru, Justice Magrey said teachers do much more than impart academic knowledge.
“A teacher does not merely transfer information from a textbook to a notebook,” he said, highlighting the role of teachers in encouraging students, building confidence and shaping their character.
Justice Magrey said education in its true sense goes beyond marks and examinations, encompassing curiosity, integrity, resilience and empathy.
“It is the teacher who instils the discipline to keep trying after failure, the courage to ask an honest question, and the values that will guide a child's conduct long after the syllabus is forgotten,” he said.
Reflecting on his experience as a judge, Justice Magrey said that long before law, family and society leave their imprint on an individual, teachers play a crucial role in shaping a child's character.
He said that behind the success of doctors, engineers, scientists and judges, there is often a teacher who believed in them before they believed in themselves.
Describing teachers as “nation-builders”, Justice Magrey said India’s aspirations for growth, knowledge and innovation are closely linked to the collective efforts of teachers working in classrooms across the country.
He also commended the BMS Educational Trust and BMS Academy for Professional Courses for instituting the awards and bringing attention to the contribution of teachers and principals.
As part of the event, 100 teachers and principals from State, CBSE and ICSE schools were felicitated.
Justice Magrey said the contribution of teachers could not be fully measured by awards, adding that their real impact is reflected in the lives and confidence of their students.
He urged parents, administrators, policymakers and civil society members to view the occasion as a reminder of their collective responsibility towards teachers.
“A society that wishes to prosper must invest in its teachers: in their dignity, their continuous learning, their working conditions and their well-being,” he said.
Justice Magrey also traced the educational legacy of the BMS Educational Trust, recalling its origins in 1946 and the establishment of B.M.S. College of Engineering by Late Sri B. M. Sreenivasaiah.
He said the legacy was subsequently expanded by his son, Late Sri B. S. Narayan, into institutions covering law, science, commerce, architecture and management.
Concluding his address, Justice Magrey said the “true Dronacharya award” would continue to be given silently in classrooms through the lives of students whose teachers helped them understand difficult concepts, overcome challenges and dream bigger.
He congratulated the award organisers and paid tribute to the teachers and principals honoured at the ceremony.

AI-assisted air traffic control is coming to some of the nation’s busiest skies
The software will initially serve only as a real-time decision tool during unexpected disruptions, though it is eventually designed to predict traffic flows and map routes days ahead
Federal officials plan to launch an artificial intelligence-powered system in the Washington, D.C., area as early as Monday, the first step in a broader push to modernize U.S. air traffic management.
The software — known as Smart, or Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories — is designed to analyze flight schedules, weather forecasts, airport runway capacity and operational limits to predict traffic flows and spot potential bottlenecks ahead of time.
Developed by Air Space Intelligence under an $875 million, 12-year government contract awarded earlier this year, the tool is intended to function as a central intelligence center for the nation’s airspace once fully operational, as reported by The Wall Street Journal. The primary goal is to help the Federal Aviation Administration and major carriers navigate schedule disruptions, cutting down on delays and cancellations.
Though industry insiders previously anticipated a broader initial release after months of planning, government officials told the publication that the rollout was always meant to begin on a limited scale.
In its current phase, Smart will serve as a decision-support tool during operational disruptions. Future iterations are expected to handle complex tasks, such as managing flight arrival intervals and mapping out routes days in advance.
As part of the launch, federal authorities plan to open a centralized office for the program at the Transportation Department’s headquarters on Monday.
The initiative comes amid a broader push by the Trump administration to modernize the country’s aging aviation infrastructure through multi-billion-dollar technology investments and expanded controller hiring to address persistent staffing shortages.
However, the transition presents coordination challenges. The FAA has been holding talks with commercial carriers regarding schedule alignment, though industry representatives have raised concerns over how the automated system will operate amid intense market competition for peak flight slots.
During Senate testimony earlier this year, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford addressed the need for structural change in airspace management.
“The way we manage traffic today is chaotic, and we can do better,” Bedford said. “We need to manage that at the FAA, rather than rely on commercial airlines to simply schedule however they want.”
Despite operational questions, industry advocates have welcomed the technology. Airlines for America, a trade association representing major domestic carriers, told The Wall Street Journal that the software offered significant potential to boost safety, expand airspace capacity and enhance overall efficiency.
The organization described the project as “one of the most exciting and bold initiatives taken on by the FAA in decades.”

While the Tokyo Deaflympics in 2025 helped boost public awareness of the sporting event, issues regarding public perception have remained almost a year on.
The Yamaha Motor Foundation for Sports conducted a survey before and after the Deaflympics, an international sporting event for deaf athletes, on the public’s recognition of it. A total of 2,060 responded to the part of the survey conducted before the event, and 1,400 responded to the part conducted after.
According to the survey, 24.3% of respondents age 20 and over said they knew of the Tokyo Deaflympics, before the competition was held last November. The recognition rate rose to 55.4% in 2026.
The rate of recognition among Tokyo residents after the event stood at 72.4%, jumping from 33.3% before the tournament.
“As the tournament approached, I felt there was an increase in people who knew about the event,” said Rina Komokata, who won gold in the women’s tennis doubles and bronze in the singles event at the Tokyo Deaflympics, at a recent seminar in Tokyo for media organizations hosted by the foundation.
“There was a surprisingly large crowd of spectators,” she said, adding that the survey results “made sense.”
While the event was significant for making progress toward an inclusive society, the survey also highlighted issues remaining after the Tokyo Deaflympics.
The proportion of respondents who felt the bias against those with hearing loss had gone, and that such people were a familiar presence in their daily lives, fell to 40.8% from 45.7% before the tournament.
The survey also showed a decline in the proportions of those who wanted to learn sign language and those who thought they could play sports with other people regardless of whether they had hearing difficulties.
Tokyo’s hosting of the Deaflympics “was a positive thing in terms of boosting public interest,” University of Tsukuba professor Mayumi Saito said.
“On the other hand, (the event) has not been enough to bring changes to (public) attitude,” she said, citing as a reason a lack of competitiveness in the Deaflympics.
There may have been a gap between people’s high expectations for deaf sports and what they saw during the Deaflympics, Saito added.
Meanwhile, Komokata highlighted a need for steady work to help develop deaf sports and enhance understanding for people with hearing loss.
One of the four Grand Slam tennis tournaments, the Australian Open, has an event for deaf athletes.
“Creating opportunities where those with disabilities could shine helps garner public interest,” Komokata said. “I hope that we’ll see more of such chances.”

Key executives running Berkshire Hathaway's US$1 trillion empire
Warren Buffett has stepped down as Berkshire Hathaway’s chairman, handing leadership of the company to Greg Abel as CEO and his son Howard Buffett as chairman.
Warren Buffett stepped down as chairman of Berkshire Hathaway on Friday (Sep 18), handing the top role to his son Howard and completing a historic leadership handover that started with Greg Abel's appointment as CEO earlier this year.
Investors will likely be keen on how the new leadership steers the US$1 trillion-plus conglomerate. Here is a look at its major pillars:
Greg Abel, CEO
Buffett announced Abel's promotion at Berkshire's annual meeting, in May 2025. Many Berkshire managers describe the 64-year-old as knowledgeable and compassionate, with a capacity to listen.
Abel, known for his hands-on style, came into the Berkshire fold with its acquisition of MidAmerican Energy in 2000. He turned the unit, since renamed as Berkshire Hathaway Energy, into one of the largest power providers in central and western United States.
After helming that business as its CEO for a decade, Abel was appointed vice chairman in 2018 to oversee Berkshire's non-insurance businesses - railroad; chemical, energy and industrial companies; and businesses such as Fruit of the Loom and See's Candies.
He is believed to be a billionaire, selling his 1 per cent stake in Berkshire Hathaway Energy to Berkshire for US$870 million in 2022.
Howard Buffett, Chairman
The eldest son of Warren Buffett has served on Berkshire's board since 1993, gaining deep familiarity with its operations. Now 71, he has held directorships at major companies, including Coca-Cola Co, Archer-Daniels-Midland and ConAgra Foods.
Beyond Berkshire, Howard is a farmer, a former sheriff and leader at a foundation that works towards food security and conflict-mitigation.
Ajit Jain, Vice Chairman
Jain, who Warren Buffett has credited with generating tens of billions of dollars of shareholder value, has long been seen as a potential CEO. But Buffett said he did not want the job.
India-born Jain, whom his boss called a "unique" talent, has day-to-day oversight of Berkshire's insurance businesses. He has been key in expanding the reinsurance business, with a specialty in pricing high-risk policies such as those covering natural catastrophes.
The eventual retirement of Jain - he joined the Omaha, Nebraska-based company in 1986 - has been closely watched, particularly in the wake of Buffett's departure. Some media reports earlier this year threw up the name of Gen Re Chairman Charlie Shamieh as a potential successor. He has led the Berkshire-owned reinsurer since 2018.
Adam Johnson, President, Consumer Products
Johnson leads NetJets, the world’s largest private jet operator, and also has day-to-day oversight of Berkshire's consumer products, services and retail businesses.
He joined the company in 1996 and became the CEO of NetJets in 2015, leading it through a period of sustained growth. During his tenure, the business expanded its global fleet, maintained its lead in the fractional aircraft ownership market and invested in sustainability.
Ted Weschler
The investment manager oversees a significant and growing portion of Berkshire's massive public equity portfolio. Weschler, along with another key investment manager Todd Combs, were once expected to take over the portfolio, having helped Buffett invest in stocks, but the former CEO had in recent years said Abel could handle it.
Combs left Berkshire in December 2025 for JPMorgan Chase, in a major management shakeup before Abel took over as CEO.

Herpetologists first discovered in 1933 that rattlesnakes are immune to their own venom. Native to the Americas, rattlesnakes are pit vipers, a family of vipers with a heat-sensing pit organ between each nostril and eye.
Venom resistance in snakes comes in two forms: either the targets in their bodies have evolved such that the venom doesn’t attack them, like in cobras, or they possess specific molecules in their bloodstream that serve as “toxin sponges”, like in vipers, Sean B. Carroll, chair of biology at the University of Maryland, U.S., said.
In 1972, Japanese researchers discovered the first example of a so-called toxin sponge — a serum protein dubbed Fetuin-A — from Okinawa habu (Protobothrops flavoviridis), a pit viper endemic to the Ryukyu Islands. Fetuin-A could inhibit metalloproteinases, a class of venom toxins that could cause haemorrhage, damage tissue, and disrupt the coagulation system.
Metalloproteinases are the most abundant toxin family in rattlesnake venoms, and researchers have studied metalloproteinase inhibitors such as Fetuin-A in great detail. However, only recently did they discover that Fetuin-A belongs to a larger family of FETUA proteins.
In a 2022 paper, Dr. Carroll and his team identified four FETUA proteins from the western diamondback rattlesnake (Crotalus atrox).
Curiously, understanding the principles of venom resistance from C. atrox led the researchers to leverage these antitoxins, which had evolved over millions of years, for human benefit.
In a new study in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the team at Maryland has shown that specific combinations of C. atrox FETUA proteins can fully neutralise rattlesnake venom lethality in mice, with roughly 10-times the potency of commercial antivenom.
‘String of surprises’
On discovering metalloproteinase-inhibiting FETUA-2, 3, 4, and 5 proteins from C. atrox, the research team studied their antivenom potency. By injecting various protein combinations preincubated with C. atrox venom into experimental mice, they found that some combinations successfully blocked haemorrhaging, while some even staved off death.
“Rattlesnake venoms have 10-15 different kinds of toxins,” Dr. Carroll said. “So it was entirely unexpected that just blocking metalloproteinases would block the lethality of the venom.”
The test results that followed were a “string of surprises”. Encouraged by the success of FETUA proteins against C. atrox venom, the team tried them against the eastern diamondback rattlesnake (Crotalus adamanteus), which proved successful. Then they tested them against two Asian snakes: the Malayan pit viper (Calloselasma rhodostoma) and the Chinese moccasin (Deinagkistrodon acutus). The proteins could protect against those as well.
The team then moved to candidates outside of pit vipers. Of the two true vipers they tested against, the proteins protected significantly against the Sochurek’s saw-scaled viper (Echis carinatus sochureki) — but none against the puff adder (Bitis arietans).
“Our surprises ran out, you could say,” Dr. Carroll said.
According to him, an antivenom needs potency and broad reactivity. And not only could these proteins recognise and neutralise the venom of a spectrum of distant species, when tested against CroFab, a commercial antivenom obtained from animals immunised with four pit viper venoms, including C. atrox, the proteins proved tenfold more potent.
The findings are a “real advance” for antivenom development, according to Kartik Sunagar, an associate professor at the Indian Institute of Science, Bengaluru; he was not involved in the study. “The paper shows convincingly that a combination of naturally evolved FETUA proteins can fully neutralise rattlesnake venom lethality by inhibiting metalloproteinases alone.”
However, Dr. Sunagar also pointed out that the study did not exactly measure clinical capacity.
“Every efficacy experiment premixed venom and inhibitor before injection,” he said. “So the study measures neutralising capacity, not treatment of an animal already envenomed, which is the clinically relevant scenario.”
Next-generation antivenom
According to Dr. Carroll, unlike lab-made compounds, FETUA proteins have been tested in nature.
“Rattlesnakes have evolved these proteins for 50 million years, with remarkable specificity and potency to inhibit their own venom, which gives me the sense that it is worth exploring,” he said.
Manufacturability and purity are added advantages, he added: “We can make recombinant FETUA proteins in the lab in unlimited quantities — whereas traditional antivenom requires animals to be immunised, and then the obtained antibodies have to be purified.”
Dr. Sunagar also shared the view that the recombinant and defined nature of FETUA proteins will help sidestep the low purity of animal-derived products.
While the study showed that these proteins can protect experimental mice from venom lethality, toxins other than metalloproteinases will have physiological effects on humans, Dr Carroll said: “What we don’t know is what else we will have to use in conjunction with these proteins to make an antivenom” for humans.
“FETUAs do nothing for the neurotoxins that dominate many medically important venoms,” Dr. Sunagar said. “The honest reading is that these proteins form the metalloproteinase-neutralising component of a next-generation antivenom, but it is not yet a standalone therapy.”
Dr. Carroll also said his team has found a new component that could aid human antivenom development, but did not elaborate on ongoing research.
Implications for India
In countries like India, which host both vipers and elapids such as cobras, FETUA proteins alone cannot provide a complete antivenom solution, Dr. Carroll said.
Although the study revealed partial protection against saw-scaled vipers (Echis carinatus sp.), one of India’s ‘Big Four’ and a major cause of death and disability, partial cross-reactivity need not translate into clinical protection, Dr. Sunagar added.
But India’s bigger takeaway is the strategy: “The logical path for India is to identify and test FETUAs from our own vipers rather than relying on rattlesnake versions, and to pair them with agents covering the neurotoxic elapids the FETUAs cannot touch,” according to Dr. Sunagar.
Nikhil Sreekandan is an independent journalist.

Mamata's TMC faction gets football player symbol and new party name; Ritabrata camp gets envelope
The ECI on Thursday prohibited both factions from using the party name and its reserved "Flowers and Grass" symbol in the October 6 bypolls.
The Election Commission has allotted separate names and election symbols to the two rival Trinamool Congress factions led by TMC founder and former West Bengal chief minister Mamata Banerjee and present leader of the opposition (LoP) in the Bengal assembly, Ritabrata Banerjee.
The Ritabrata Banerjee-led faction has been allotted the name ‘Democratic Trinamool Congress’ and the ‘envelope’ as its election symbol.
Meanwhile, the Mamata Banerjee-led faction has been allotted the name ‘Mamata All India Trinamool Congress’ and the ‘football player’ as its election symbol.
Election Commission's order for TMC factions
The ECI on Thursday prohibited both factions from using the party name and its reserved "Flowers and Grass" symbol in the October 6 bypolls to West Bengal’s Nandigram and Rejinagar assembly constituencies, as well as Assam’s Nagaon parliamentary seat.
The poll body said the temporary arrangement was intended to keep "both the rival groups on even keel and to protect their rights and interests" until it issues its final ruling.
The rival factions had previously filed separate Form-B nomination documents, each claiming the TMC name, for the by-elections in West Bengal and Assam.
How did the dispute begin?
The conflict began after rebel leader Ritabrata Banerjee questioned the validity of the Mamata Banerjee-led National Working Committee.
He claimed that the term ended on February 11, 2025, making all decisions and appointments made after that date invalid.
The faction led by Mamata Banerjee dismissed the argument, saying the opposing group was referring to older constitutional provisions and had failed to account for subsequent amendments submitted to the commission.
Rahul Gandhi slams BJP, EC
Leader of the Opposition (LoP) in the Lok Sabha and Congress MP Rahul Gandhi criticised the ECI's decision, alleging that the BJP and the poll panel were collaborating to undermine opposition parties. He described the development as "party theft" and linked it to what he called India's continuing democratic decline.
Gandhi alleged that the BJP and the ECI had used a similar approach in disputes concerning the Shiv Sena, the Nationalist Congress Party (NCP) and, most recently, the Trinamool Congress.
"First Shiv Sena, then NCP, and now Trinamool Congress. Every time, the same pattern—BJP and the Election Commission join forces to split a party. Then its election symbol is snatched away. When an entire party can be stolen, it's hardly surprising that the votes of millions of Indians can be stolen too. Vote theft. Government theft. Now party theft—these have become symbols of our democratic decline," he said in a post on X.
The Congress leader also alleged that the ECI was neglecting its constitutional duty to safeguard voters and was assisting the BJP in reversing election outcomes.

- A massive batch of GTA 5 source-code files from Rockstar’s 2023 breach is going public, revealing new details about the cancelled Liberty City expansion.
- The files reveal a new layout for GTA 5’s cancelled Liberty City expansion, which could potentially return as GTA 6 DLC.
- The leak also reveals a full outline and dedicated shoreline audio zones, suggesting Rockstar made significant progress on the expansion.
Rockstar Games could make the GTA 6 map much bigger than currently expected by adding Liberty City alongside the State of Leonida. A massive batch of GTA 5 source-code files from Rockstar’s 2023 breach, reportedly totaling around 200 GB, has now surfaced publicly, revealing new details about the cancelled Liberty City expansion and fueling speculation that it could be a part of the GTA 6 map.
According to X user TJGM, who received the information from Ook, a developer and member of the World Travel modding team behind the Liberty City Preservation Project, the leaked files include an expanded layout of GTA 5’s planned Liberty City expansion, reconstructed using shoreline data.
The user claimed Rockstar likely pushed the Liberty City DLC to GTA 6. The leaked layout also looks expanded from GTA 4’s Liberty City, which already felt huge for its time. The leaked files also reveal new areas of Liberty City, suggesting Rockstar made decent progress on the expansion.
Thanks to GTA Online and its unwavering support, the company eventually cancelled development on the expansion. However, with recent reports suggesting GTA 6 online launch in 2027, Rockstar could easily implement the expansion to make its biggest game ever even bigger.
Take-Two has also confirmed GTA Online support after GTA 6 launches on November 19, 2026, leaving room for a major Liberty City DLC. Rockstar could still scrap the project and focus on Leonida. But its reported progress implies it may not be off the table just yet.
For now, Rockstar is focusing on making Leonida the biggest GTA map ever. The GTA 6 map is said to be 2x bigger than GTA 5 and 3x bigger than Red Dead Redemption 2, so even without a Liberty City DLC, it’s still incredibly massive.
If they did make a Liberty City DLC, support for the game would go beyond what Rockstar originally did with GTA 5’s campaign. That said, what do you think about a GTA 6 Liberty City DLC? Tell us in the comments section below.

NEW DELHI: India’s karate team is heading to the Asiad without a dedicated coach while five equestrian riders in Tokyo are scrambling to get accreditation for their personal coaches. Some are even considering a two-hour train journey to Nagoya to sort out the issue in person, TOI has learnt.
For the karate contingent, reigning Asian champion Alisha Choudhary’s repeated pleas to sports authorities and Indian Olympic Association (IOA) officials for accreditation for her coach, Vikas Panchal, have gone unheard. The two-member team also includes Chetan Bhatt (men’s kumite 84kg), with Adikessava Peroumal Sinouvassane the designated ‘team leader’.
When the sports ministry’s sanction clearing coaches was issued on September 2, no coach was named for karate. Alisha has since sent multiple emails and reminders, underlining that Panchal has trained her for 11 years and guided her to every major international achievement, including her historic gold at the 2026 Asian Karate Championship. He is certified by the World Karate Federation and Asian Karate Federation and has accompanied her to international camps and competitions.
Interestingly, during a bout, only a coach can occupy the coaching corner and seek a video review by throwing the challenge block onto the mat. The team leader cannot perform those duties, leaving India’s karate athletes without vital technical and tactical support.
The equestrian camp, meanwhile, is caught in its own accreditation scramble. All five foreign coaches are awaiting accreditation and, without it, cannot enter the competition or training venue. The riders are coordinating by phone with IOA contingent staff based in Aichi and Nagoya, a logistical headache made worse by the distance between the two locations.
Some riders are now contemplating a roughly two-hour train journey from Tokyo to Nagoya simply to meet IOA officials and get their coaches’ accreditations sorted, potentially losing an entire day of crucial training.
It is learnt the five coaches were approved late by the IOA and sports authorities, despite the rider-horse combinations and coaches’ names having been shared with the IOA in May. The riders had also been following up on travel approvals.
None of these five coaches are govt funded. Their entire Games expenses will be borne by the riders themselves. Yet, they are still struggling for the accreditation needed to do the job. The accreditation troubles come on top of the equestrian contingent scrambling for hay, bedding and fodder for their horses, with the IOA-appointed ad-hoc committee citing a “shortage of govt funds”.

Is Russia proving better at protecting friends than fighting enemies in West Africa?
- Published
When mutinous soldiers seized a strategic military base in Niger's capital last Saturday, the country's ruling junta turned to a foreign partner it has increasingly relied on since coming to power: Russia.
Following a night of intense fighting in Niamey, Russia's Africa Corps helped Nigerien loyalist forces to regain control of Air Base 101 at Diori Hamani International Airport.
Africa Corps, unlike its predecessor the Wagner Group, is directly under the control of the defence ministry in Moscow. It provides combat support and military training and is thought to have some 200 to 300 men in Niger.
Russia's ambassador to Niger, Viktor Voropaev, publicly acknowledged the weekend intervention, saying his country's forces had helped "repress a mutiny".
"This is seen as a symbolic victory," according to Beverly Ochieng, senior analyst at Control Risks. "[One] that will continue to put them at the centre of not just the counter-insurgency campaign, but even in the protection and prolongation of military rule."
The attempted coup offers perhaps the clearest evidence yet that Africa Corps' role in three Sahel countries extends beyond its stated mission of helping governments fight jihadist insurgencies.
Russia is increasingly demonstrating that it can provide something perhaps even more valuable to the military rulers of Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso: protection for the governments themselves.
"It was not sufficient to bring stability," said Ochieng, "but it's enough to allow these military governments to have a political lifeline."
The thwarted mutiny also highlights something the ruling junta may not want to admit - just how dependent on Moscow it has become for security.
In January, Africa Corps personnel also played an important role in repelling an attack at the same airport.
"We saw videos of the jihadists walking around the airport basically completely unimpeded," said Jacob Boswall, a security analyst who tracks jihadist activity for the BBC's media monitoring service.
"Probably there is some substance to the claim that Africa Corps was able to restore power in that case [in January]. And I think, again, in this case as well, that intervention was very significant."
One of the Nigerien military's central justifications for the July 2023 coup, which saw Gen Abdourahamane Tiani seize power, was the deteriorating security situation and alleged failure of Niger's civilian authorities, under elected President Mohamed Bazoum, to tackle it.
They also blamed Western partners at the time for their inability to contain jihadist violence.
Yet, three years later, that insurgency remains unresolved.
Militants linked to al-Qaeda and Islamic State have continued to launch attacks, including in the Tillabéri and Dosso regions. Some, inflicting heavy casualties on security forces.
Ochieng described this latest mutiny as evidence of longstanding grievances within Niger's own military, compounded by the pressure the soldiers have been facing.
"Counter-insurgency forces do not feel adequately supported by the military government," she said. "There have been challenges in providing equipment and replenishments."
Niger's government is facing threats on two fronts: extremist militant groups attacking the state, and grievances within its armed forces responsible for fighting them. Africa Corps may have helped contain the latter this past weekend, but it has yet to resolve the former.
Unlike Wagner mercenaries, whose status in a private military company allowed Moscow some deniability, Africa Corps is more clearly an instrument of the Russian state.
"The whole point of Africa Corps is that it brings the power back under the control of the Russian Ministry of Defence," said Boswall.
Officially, its forces are deployed to help Sahel governments combat Islamist militant groups.
But dissidents contemplating moves against military governments elsewhere in the Sahel region may now have to factor Russian forces into their calculations.
Despite the struggle to contain the jihadists, no-one anticipates Africa Corps leaving the Sahel any time soon. Keeping those governments in power protects Russia's investment.
"Wagner - and now Africa Corps - have always had a very transactional interest in Africa," Boswall said.
"If they can get mineral resources in exchange for providing protection and defence, then they will. We see that in Mali with gold… and then in Niger, it really is uranium [that] seems to be the main resource that Africa Corps is protecting."
Analysts say Russia also benefits from having friendly governments that could support it in international forums.
"Having that kind of international group of supportive countries, Russia sees as giving Russia credibility - diplomatic credibility," Boswall explained.
Like Mali and Burkina Faso, Tiani's government has built much of its legitimacy using the language of sovereignty, pan-Africanism and liberation from former colonial powers.
All three governments ordered French troops to leave. They also formed the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) and subsequently withdrew from the West African regional bloc Ecowas, presenting the new alliance as an assertion of regional independence.
Some analysts regard this as at odds with its growing reliance on Africa Corps.
"The military governments argue that they have selected Russia on their own terms," said Ochieng.
"Russia is seen as a partner that respects that sovereignty, unlike their previous partnerships with France or even the EU and, to some extent, with the US."
An army captain on Niger state television accused foreign powers, including France and Chad, of being behind last weekend's unrest, while Russia's foreign ministry described the mutineers as "extremists seemingly incited by European former colonial powers".
France has repeatedly rejected accusations that it is attempting to destabilise Niger. Chad's government did not respond to a BBC request for comment.
"[Niger is] underplaying the role that Africa Corps has in these countries, and they're overplaying the resource-nationalism narrative - the idea that the government is in control and fighting back against the jihadists," explained Boswall.
"There is a huge media war going on in the Sahel to control the narrative around that."
Russia's war with Ukraine is another important factor shaping its strategy in the Sahel.
The conflict continues to consume Russian personnel and military equipment, limiting how far Moscow can expand its operations in Africa.
"It's quite a tightrope for Russia because ultimately its priority will always be Ukraine," Ochieng said.
"It will maintain at least enough numbers to allow it to reassure the military governments in the Sahel that it continues to be a reliable partner. They'll continue to deploy just enough weapons and supplies and logistics… to continue supporting Africa Corps."
But there are limits to what that support can achieve. "Russia cannot afford a sustained counter-offensive anywhere in the Sahel," Ochieng said.
This may help explain why protecting allied governments appears to have become such an important part of Russia's regional strategy.
Defending a capital or helping loyalist forces defeat a mutiny requires fewer resources than recapturing and securing vast areas affected by an insurgency.
"These are quite limited interventions, but with an outsized impact," Boswall said.
"I think at that level they'll be able to sustain that over the foreseeable future, even with the war in Ukraine."
Russia may have helped Tiani survive this latest security challenge, but it has not removed the conditions that could produce the next mutiny.

A team of three independent security researchers at Hacktron says it took less than 72 hours for them to hack into OpenAI employee accounts using Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.8 and 5, the Wall Street Journal reports. They were able to access OpenAI’s GitHub repository, called “Monorepo,” which reportedly contains “OpenAI’s algorithmic secrets,” according to the Wall Street Journal’s sources.
Security researchers used Claude to help them hack into OpenAI
A three-person team of researchers used a corrupted image file and forum software to hack into OpenAI.
They stopped short of accessing internal code in Monorepo themselves, but sent a pull request from an employee’s Codex account to prove they gained access. They were able to get in through Discourse, the third-party service that hosts OpenAI’s community forums, by exploiting an issue with the system it uses to process HEIF images. According to Hacktron, Claude Opus 5 launched in the evening on July 24th, and by 10AM the next day they had used it to achieve RCE on Discourse Cloud and accessed OpenAI’s instance.
Their HEIF Heist project took “only one or two days” to adapt to different companies, including OpenAI, Slack, Meta, GitHub Ent, Rails, Next.js, ImageMagick and others, using less than $3,000 in tokens, and to their knowledge, was only detected by one target, Shopify. The vulnerabilities Hacktron reported to Discourse and OpenAI have since been fixed, and Hacktron says OpenAI paid it $6,500 for finding the bug, but as Hacktron CTO Mohan Pedhapati said to the WSJ, “I don’t think we are as strong as Chinese threat actors… We’re just three guys with Claude and Codex subscriptions.”

For three decades, May Lee had built her professional life around Hewlett-Packard (HP). She joined the technology company as an intern in 1987 and had expected to eventually retire from it, according to a report by Business Insider. Instead, a layoff at 59 forced her to rethink what came next. After struggling to find another job in the technology sector, Lee took a path far removed from her previous corporate career. In 2025, she travelled to Antarctica to work as a supply technician at McMurdo Station. Lee shared her experience in an as-told-to essay for Business Insider, describing how an unexpected career break eventually led her to a completely different working environment. Lee had not planned to leave HP. She said she had deliberately chosen to build a long-term career at one company rather than continually move between employers. “As a graduate, I wanted to sign on for life with a good company that I knew I could be loyal to and would be as loyal as a company could be. I didn’t want to climb the corporate ladder or jump from company to company. If I hadn't been downsized last February, I would never have left,” she explained. There had been indications that the company was undergoing changes, including a hiring freeze and a temporary reduction in working hours. But the eventual layoff was still difficult for Lee after spending most of her working life at HP. “I felt a combination of disappointment and sadness. This was the company I’ve devoted my entire career to and had hoped to retire from,” she added. Following the layoff, Lee initially tried to continue along the same career path. She applied to technology companies and reached out to people in her professional network. But despite her experience and referrals, she could not secure an offer. About a month into her job search, a friend suggested she look beyond finding another high-paying technology role and instead consider work she actually enjoyed. That suggestion mattered because Lee was in a different financial position than someone who needed to replace a salary immediately. She had already paid off her house and had savings. That gave her room to consider an unconventional option: Antarctica. Lee had already travelled to Antarctica twice as a tourist and had developed an interest in the continent. After her friend's suggestion, she began looking into whether there were opportunities to work at research stations. She eventually came across Amentum, a contractor that provides services to the United States Antarctic Progra, and applied for a supply technician position. The selection process included an application, background checks and physical examinations. Lee was ultimately selected. The move represented a significant financial trade-off. The position paid considerably less than her technology-sector roles had, but her financial circumstances meant she could make the change without worrying about a mortgage. “The only downside was the extremely low pay. However, my dad raised me to understand the importance of saving and not spending money you don't have. So, I had the luxury of having financial groundwork in place and did not have to worry about paying a mortgage or affording bills,” Lee explained. Lee travelled to Antarctica in 2025, stopping in Auckland and Christchurch before boarding a Boeing C-17 Globemaster III military transport aircraft to the continent. At McMurdo Station, her work is centred on an IT and communications warehouse. Her responsibilities include handling supplies, operating a forklift, moving cargo and checking deliveries against station records. The job was a stark departure from spending decades in the technology industry. Yet Lee finds aspects of her new workplace refreshing. “This was refreshing because it meant nobody was on their phones. Everybody sits and talks with each other at meal times,” she said. Life at McMurdo Station is not limited to work. Lee participates in art shows, line dancing, marathons and bingo. She also volunteers as a DJ and hosts a weekly 1980s-themed music show. The social environment has become an important part of her experience. Within a week of arriving, Lee realized she wanted to stay. Lee says her move to Antarctica has given her a different perspective on what a career can look like after spending decades in a corporate environment. Lee said her experience in Antarctica has changed how she views her life and career. “I don’t think I could ever approach my life in any other way, now that I’ve been there. The community is so supportive of each other. I’ve never seen that kind of camaraderie and inclusivity anywhere else....My life is not what I thought it would be when I first started my career, but I’ve learned that when something happens, I just kind of roll with it. You can always reinvent yourself.” Anjali Thakur is a Senior Assistant Editor with Mint, reporting on trending news, entertainment and health, with a focus on stories driving digital conversations. Her work involves spotting early signals across news cycles and social media, sharpening stories for SEO and Google Discover, and mentoring young editors in digital-first newsroom practices. She is known for turning fast-moving developments—whether news-driven or culture-led—into clear, tightly edited journalism without compromising editorial rigour.

Before joining Mint, she was Deputy News Editor at NDTV.com, where she led the Trending section and covered viral news, breaking developments and human-interest stories. In September 2026, people shared an image purportedly showing U.S. President Donald Trump leaving a brown stain on a chair during his trip to Ireland that month.
One X post (archived) featuring the alleged photo had amassed roughly 4 million views as of this writing.
(@StillADog via X)
Trump visited the country on the weekend of Sept. 12-13, during which he met with Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin. The U.S. president sparked controversy following that meeting after calling for Irish unification, an act that would merge the United Kingdom's Northern Ireland with the Republic of Ireland. Trump also met with Ireland President Catherine Connolly and attended the Irish Open at his golf course in Doonbeg.
Several Snopes readers asked if the image of Trump leaving the stain — which also spread on Bluesky, Facebook, Threads, TikTok and YouTube — is authentic.
One Threads user claimed artificial intelligence was not used to create the alleged photo, though it was not clear whether or not this was said sincerely.
(@becca_reptile_and_human_momma via Threads)
Some users commenting under the posts seemed genuinely unsure whether the image was real, while other remarks of bewilderment were possibly written in jest.
In sum, the image is fake and originated from an AI-generated video. That AI-generated clip originated from a prompt seemingly using an authentic photo that did not display a stain.
Creator Tom Adelsbach first posted the content as a fake video on Facebook, Instagram and X on Sept. 12, as confirmed by a reverse image search. His posts' captions read, "BREAKING: Donald Trump causes an international incident during his meeting with Ireland President Catherine Connolly."
Snopes emailed Adelsbach to ask for the exact text prompt he submitted to the AI tool to create the fake video. We also emailed the White House to request comment and will update this article if we receive additional details.
Adelsbach's 22-second, AI-generated video features a fake depiction of Trump sitting next to Connolly. The U.S. president appears to sigh, stand up and shake Connolly's hand. The sound of photographers taking pictures can also be heard. As the inauthentic clip continues, Trump exits left, revealing the brown stain on his chair. The stain then grows in size and drips on the floor, leaving Connolly's AI depiction audibly reacting in horror.
Adelsbach previously labeled similar content with disclaimers about comedy, parody and satire. His posts featuring the fake chair stain do not show the same disclaimer. However, Meta's "AI content" label does appear on Facebook and Instagram.
The original photo
Another reverse image search revealed that the Northern Irish Belfast Telegraph newspaper published an authentic photo that Adelsbach appeared to use when creating the AI-generated video. The newspaper credited the picture of Trump and Connolly to photographer Tony Maxwell. The caption says the pair were seated inside Áras an Uachtaráin, the Irish president's residence. The full caption reads, "President Catherine Connolly and President Donald Trump at Aras an Uachtarain (Tony Maxwell/Maxwells/PA)."
President Connolly's social media accounts also feature a similar photo of her sitting next to Trump.
For background, here is why we alert readers to rumors created by sources calling their output humorous or satirical.

The average price of rice in Japan fell below ¥3,000 for the first time since early September 2024, the agriculture ministry said Friday.
Across around 1,000 supermarkets, a 5-kilogram bag of rice cost ¥2,971 in the week leading up to Sunday, down ¥32 from a week before and the fifth straight week that prices have dropped.
Rice prices had been rising since the summer of 2024, when a supply shortage triggered what became known as the Reiwa-era rice crisis. In January, the average price of rice was ¥4,416.
But supply-demand conditions have recently eased, reflecting the government’s release of rice from its stockpiles as well as increased production.
Lower rice prices benefit households. But with prices expected to fall further, farmers are concerned that they may fail to cover production costs.
Agriculture minister Kazuo Yana has voiced concern over the issue.
“The situation is becoming extremely difficult and simply unacceptable for farmers trying to stay in business,” Yana said at a news conference on Friday.
The average price of brand rice, which accounts for 85% of total sales volume, fell ¥35 to ¥2,988, while that of relatively cheap blended rice fell ¥34 to ¥2,866.
Rice harvested in 2025 and sold to wholesalers in August fell in price month on month for the first time in two months. The average price for 60 kg of unmilled rice stood at ¥31,556, down ¥930 from the previous month. The figure is the average of transaction prices between wholesalers and rice buyers dealing with farmers.
Rice prices in both retail and business-to-business transactions have been on a downward trend.
