To encourage residents of the merged areas to obtain water and sewerage connections, Chennai Metrowater has outlined the procedures and charges involved in receiving them. Applications, along with the required documents, must be submitted online, according to the water agency.
Metrowater has been executing projects to expand its water supply and sewer network in the merged areas. Areas provided with piped water supply infrastructure include Idayanchavadi, Porur, Madhavaram, Kottivakkam, Madipakkam, Sholinganallur and Neelankarai. Similarly, areas such as Nerkundram, Manapakkam, and Uthandi have been provided with sewer network, a press release said.
Officials said several residents had raised queries regarding the procedures to obtain connections in localities where the water supply and sewer networks had been completed. On average, the water agency receives about 2,000 applications for house service connections.
The online process (on https://wsc.chennaimetrowater.in/#/nc/login) has been simplified to enable residents to apply and remit charges, and the connections would be provided within 15 days of verification.
According to a press release, residents can apply online with documents such as the property tax assessment order and the infrastructure development charges receipt.
Connection charges
Water and sewer connection charges of ₹5,000 each will be collected from individual houses measuring between 46.47 sq.m. and 100 sq.m., and ₹7,500 each from residential buildings measuring up to 200 sq.m.
Similarly, ₹7,500 will be collected for new connections to commercial and partly commercial establishments and for the renewal of old connections.
The water agency would collect infrastructure development charges of ₹319 per sq.m. from two-storey residential buildings, multi-storey buildings with more than six units, and commercial buildings measuring more than 300 sq.m., the release said.
G. Sathish, a resident of Semmencheri, said several residents in the southern suburbs had been waiting for piped water supply and sewer network for many years.
“The online process has made applying for connections easier and helps avoid visits to Metrowater offices. The facility to pay connection and road cut charges in 10 instalments will encourage more residents to apply for new connections. Residents in various areas are waiting for sewer infrastructure and comprehensive works will help create sustainable civic infrastructure,” he said.

China’s porcelain city carries centuries-old heritage to a new generation
China’s Jingdezhen porcelain sites were inscribed on UNESCO’s World Heritage List in 2026
JINGDEZHEN, China -- Chinese porcelain artist Chen Qing has a vivid memory of her grandfather. It was the only time he wrote down the formula for her family’s distinctive red pigment.
He asked her mother to memorize it and burned the paper minutes later. The secret has since been passed down orally from one generation to the next.
“My mother did not reveal the formula to me until I was over 30,” Chen said.
Her family has practiced the craft since around 1860 in Jingdezhen, known as China’s “Porcelain Capital.” It is located in Jiangxi province, about 1,180 kilometers (735 miles) southeast of Beijing.
Jingdezhen’s pottery-making history spans more than 2,000 years. It began during the Han Dynasty and its porcelain sites were inscribed on UNESCO’s World Heritage List in 2026.
Jingdezhen’s craftsmen have kept alive techniques once used to produce porcelain for the imperial court. That knowledge later spread to private artisans.
Chen’s ancestors adopted some of those traditions after the fall of the Qing Dynasty in 1912.
“The craft is very difficult for an outsider to master,” Chen said. “A family might spend nearly a century developing a single technique.”
Two tables in her studio are covered with brushes, unfinished pieces and pigments. She works in silence, a lamp lighting her strokes.
Chen’s fingers never touch the porcelain’s surface. She steadies her hand against its outer edge, holding the brush firmly as she paints delicate, precise strokes.
Painting a porcelain teacup can take days to complete. A single particle of dust or sweat could ruin the piece and require her to start from scratch.
Landscapes are the most difficult scenes to paint because their boundaries are not clear. A mountain summit might be emerald green, gradually shifting to brown and other warmer colors farther down the slope.
“Mastering a craft is a lifelong process,” Chen said. “Few people are willing to spend more than 10 years learning such a painstaking craft.”
Artists like Chen work alongside archaeological sites and museums to preserve China’s porcelain heritage.
Jingdezhen’s Imperial Kiln Institute researches and restores ceramics excavated from an adjacent complex, where pieces for emperors were crafted in kilns whose remains are still visible today.
The institute is incorporating new technologies into its work, including artificial intelligence, to help match and reconstruct ancient porcelain fragments.
“By the establishment of our ceramic gene bank, we can collect all kinds of information,” said the institute’s president, Weng Yanjun. “We hope that we can retrieve ancient technology with modern science.”
That research can also shed light on the culture and beliefs that surrounded porcelain-making centuries ago.
Among the tiles made at Jingdezhen’s imperial kilns were those used in the Bao’en Pagoda.
It was part of a Buddhist temple complex that was destroyed during a 19th-century rebellion in the city of Nanjing. Its exterior walls were covered with porcelain tiles, each bearing an image of the Buddha.
Traces of other religious traditions can also be found in porcelain studied by the institute, Weng said.
“Islam, Buddhism, Taoism and, later on, European Catholic Christianity harmoniously blend into the porcelain decorations,” he added.
Within Jingdezhen’s imperial kiln complex stands a shrine commemorating Tong Bin, the protective spirit of ceramics.
Known as the “Immortal Master of Wind and Fire” or “Kiln God,” Tong was revered during the Qing dynasty for sacrificing himself in protest against the abuse of kiln workers, according to local tradition.
The shrine remains open today, with a statue honoring Tong inside alongside figures representing other traditional roles in porcelain-making.
“In ancient times, the technology was not as advanced as it is today, so, in many cases, people had to rely on their beliefs — their gods — to help bring good luck and better results,” Weng said.
Some Jingdezhen craftsmen say they hold no particular beliefs associated with porcelain-making. Others display figures of Budai — or the laughing Buddha — in their workshops as symbols of good fortune and prosperity.
For artisans like master Sun Lixin, however, the work retains a spiritual dimension. He is a fourth-generation practitioner who learned the trade from his father at age 13.
“Some traditional rituals have faded considerably,” Sun said. “Yet in the hearts of craftspeople, that reverence remains.”
Every time he paints or fires a piece, Sun is mindful of the hundreds of millions of years of geological history the white clay has undergone before reaching his hands.
He does not visit Jingdezhen’s shrine, but has a practice of his own. Sun instinctively bows to the Kiln God before a firing, wishing for it to be successful and for fine porcelain to emerge.
“If we do not care for it, paint it with devotion and treasure it, how could we possibly do it justice?” Sun said.
While Jingdezhen’s pottery-making continues to be passed down within families, universities and residency programs host new generations of Chinese and international practitioners.
Paola Masi is an Italian ceramic artist in a residency program through October.
She said Song dynasty porcelain shaped her early training. So coming to Jingdezhen feels like going back to the roots of her own path as an artist.
Chinese artist Huang Qi graduated from Jingdezhen Ceramic University in 2015 and left the city to work elsewhere. She eventually decided to come back and is also now an artist-in-residence.
“Jingdezhen is where my dream began,” Huang said. “More and more people are coming and the city is attracting growing attention.”
Encountering fellow craftspeople has allowed her to learn new techniques, while Jingdezhen’s inscription on UNESCO’s World Heritage List makes her optimistic about the future.
“It gives us confidence,” Huang said. “Things will continue to get better.”

When Gloria Steinem’s plane touched down in Bombay in 1957, she could not have known that her stay in India would become what she later called a “pivotal, life-dividing event [that] made me who I am”.
She was 22, with a degree in government from Smith college and was travelling on a Chester Bowles fellowship.
India was “not only a place I’d always wanted to go, but (also) an escape from a very kind and tempting man to whom I was engaged and knew I shouldn’t marry,” Steinem later wrote. The prospect of marrying Blair Chotzinoff, a pilot from a well-connected New York family, depressed her “enormously because marriage meant the end of life to me”.
Funds were short, so she wangled a free airline ticket in exchange for an article “that I still feel guilty to this day because I never wrote”.
While in London waiting for her Indian visa, she discovered she was pregnant and obtained an illegal abortion – an experience that underpinned her conviction that, without control over reproduction, women could not control their own lives.
Steinem, who died this week at the age of 92, arrived in Delhi with romantic expectations of “ageless beauty and jewelled elephants”. They were quickly displaced. Driving from the airport, she had what she called her “first glimpse of Asian poverty”, seeing people sleeping on pavements and doorsteps.
She lived at Miranda House, one of Delhi University’s leading women’s colleges, immersing herself in student life.
“At night in our rooms we have long sessions and are asked everything: the Christians’ conception of God, the intricacies of western lingerie, the dating system, how much milk the American cow gives,” Steinem wrote.
Steinem’s Indian years have been extensively documented by Rashida Shafiq of Southern Methodist University, who drew on her fellowship reports and other archival material for a recently published PhD thesis.
She adopted the sari as everyday dress, writing: “Saris make one stand straighter and walk more slowly and worry less about time and efficiency.”
India was not entirely unfamiliar territory. Her mother and paternal grandmother had been Theosophists, part of a spiritual movement that drew heavily on Hindu and Buddhist ideas such as karma and reincarnation, and at college Steinem had written a paper on the Communist party of India.
When her fellowship money ran out, she supported herself by writing for Indian newspapers, doing advertising work and taking occasional modelling jobs – including posing in saris.
Wider travel in the country brought some of her most important encounters.
She met Rajkumari Amrit Kaur, the former princess and follower of Mahatma Gandhi who became independent India’s first health minister, and spent two hours with Indira Gandhi, whom she described as “shy to uncertainty, gentle and a little whimsical”.
At a Radical Humanist study camp in Mussoorie, followers of the former communist MN Roy debated democracy, individual freedom and political organisation. Steinem later said she learned there that “radical” need not mean violent or extremist, but could mean “going to the root,” and that “the means we choose dictate the ends we achieve”.
But some of her most lasting political education happened on the road.
On a journey from Calcutta to Kerala, Steinem travelled third class in a railway carriage reserved for women, which she later described as “a dormitory on wheels”.
Women settled in with children and food, nursing babies, sharing tiffins and talking. They wanted to know everything about her and conversations ranged across marriage, childbirth, contraception and family life. “Had I been isolated in a car, this talking circle could never have happened,” Steinem wrote later.
Years before American feminist “consciousness-raising” groups brought women together to discover that supposedly private problems were widely shared, Steinem had watched women in India exchange intimate experiences among themselves.
But the experience she regarded as most important came after caste violence erupted in what was then Madras state in 1957.
Steinem joined workers associated with the movement of Vinoba Bhave, a leading disciple of Gandhi, who were walking from village to village trying to counter rumours, discourage revenge and bring people together to talk.
She travelled with little more than “a cup, a comb and the sari I wore”.
In settlements scarred by violence, meetings were held beneath trees and in village courtyards.
“I listened as villagers narrated burnings, murders, thefts and rapes, with fear and trauma needing no translation,” she wrote.
The lesson was to listen before offering solutions. “Ask the people what they want, don’t tell them what they need,” was how Steinem later described it.
She remembered “the ancient and modern magic of groups in which anyone may speak in turn, everyone must listen and consensus is more important than time”.
“If you want to know how people live, you have to go where they live; if you want people to listen to you, you have to listen to them,” she later said. “I believe I learned that in India.”
Steinem returned to the United States in 1958, more than a decade before she became one of the leading figures in the women’s movement.
“I couldn’t integrate into the rest of my life these two very, very crucial years,” she recalled. “It was only after the women’s movement started that links began to be forged.”
She repeatedly connected her later organising methods with India. “The first organising I did was in India, though I didn’t realise it then,” she said.
Her years travelling across America as a feminist activist, she later wrote, were “just a western version of walking in villages”.
And when Ms. magazine, which Steinem co-founded, produced its spring 1972 preview issue, its cover featured an American housewife depicted as the many-armed Hindu goddess Kali, pregnant with her hands clutching a frying pan, duster, telephone, iron and other symbols of the domestic demands placed on women.
Steinem said the image “had come out of my Indian past”.

The latest GTA 6 content leak rabbit hole has taken fans straight back to GTA 5, revealing the unseen dialog from the game’s original Option A ending. Trevor Philips was apparently supposed to meet an even more horrifying fate.
The newly surfaced material comes from the enormous 192 GB batch of scrapped GTA 5 source code files that suggested GTA 6 may get Liberty City DLC. Recently, the enormous batch of files has been circulating publicly, and data miners continue to dig through the years-old development material.
Among these, X user TJGM received a leak from HeySlickThatsMe that showed an unseen dialogue connected to the ending where Franklin targets Trevor over Michael.
Instead of Trevor crashing into an oil tanker, the leaked dialogue suggests that Rockstar originally considered having him slam into a truck filled with liquid nitrogen. The result would have been brutally fitting for Trevor, as he would freeze before shattering to pieces.
But Trevor isn’t the only familiar face making a surprise appearance in the latest discoveries. TJGM also revealed cut dialogue involving Brucie from GTA 4, who was apparently planned to appear in GTA 5’s single-player campaign and have missions with Franklin.
The GTA 5 and GTA 6 content leak goes far beyond these alternate possibilities. The whole archive reportedly contains cut GTA 5 content, early dialogue, vehicles, mission information, Agent Trevor, DLC assets, and possibly early GTA 6 files.
Fans should remember that most of the material originates from Rockstar’s 2022 security breach and was not newly created. The archive also reportedly contains evidence of a planned Liberty City expansion for GTA 5 alongside some low-quality GTA 6 map assets that resemble the areas shown in the game’s trailers.
These discoveries underline just how many ideas, characters, and storylines Rockstar explored before settling on GTA 5’s final form.

A man has died after being bitten by a shark off Sorrento beach in Perth’s north.
Emergency services were called to the popular beach at about 10.30am on Friday after reports of a shark-related incident.
Western Australia police said a man had been bitten by a shark while swimming along the coast. He died as a result of his injuries, police said.
Emergency services, including water and air personnel, conducted an extensive search of the area. The swimmer’s body had not been found.
The Alkimos Surf Life Saving Club said Sorrento beach would remain closed until 12pm on Saturday. Locals were urged to stay out of the water until the beach was declared safe for swimming.
The City of Wanneroo closed all other beaches along its coastline until 12pm on Saturday.
The local state MP, Liam Staltari, extended his condolences to the man’s family, friends and loved ones.
“Like all locals and people from across WA, I’m deeply saddened by the tragic death of a man following today’s shark attack at Sorrento beach,” he said.
“Our entire community is thinking of you at this incredibly difficult time.”
A witness, Darrel Haythornthwaite, told 7News that he could not believe the incident had occurred, “especially in a place like this”. He said the man’s friend, who was swimming with him, made it back to shore but was inconsolable.
“He felt bad because he didn’t go back to save his mate and I said, ‘Nah you couldn’t have done that’,” he told the outlet. “There’s nothing that anyone could have done.”
Another witness, Ingrid Mitchell, told 9News she swam at the beach every day and did not expect sharks to attack outside of dawn and dusk.
“There was other swimmers in there … just near the seaweed, and there was one poor girl there who was sun-baking, and she saw the whole lot as well,” she said.
A third witness, Jacqui Rapaic, told the ABC she was walking along the beach with a friend when the incident occurred.
“My friend said, ‘Jac, I think there’s been a shark attack’ and I looked out to the ocean and I could see a pool of blood,” she said.
“I hugged onto my friend … [we] felt rather traumatised at that point. It happened so quickly.”
The fatality followed a shark attack on Monday at the remote Glenfield beach, north of Geraldton on WA’s mid-west coast, which left a surfer with serious injuries.
He was taken to the nearby Geraldton health campus and was in a stable condition.

Can an AI chatbot save lives by answering texts about pregnancy?
It started with an accident.
A network of clinics for pregnant women in Kenya set up an automated text messaging service to send out appointment reminders. But when the moms received the texts, they started to write back.
Some asked if it's safe to eat avocados during pregnancy (you can!). Others asked if certain symptoms they were experiencing, like swelling or headaches, are normal during pregnancy.
"At the time I joined I think we were getting less than 100 questions a day," recalls Jay Patel, director of technology for Jacaranda Health. "Now it's 15,000."
At first, Jacaranda hired nurses to answer questions one by one. But over the years since 2020, developers have created a program that uses artificial intelligence to understand patient's questions, prioritize them and flag when a user may need immediate medical care. It's called PROMPTS — and is used by patients visiting public clinics in 24 Kenyan counties.
For women without a smartphone, cell reception, or easy access to the internet, a text to PROMPTS may be the fastest way to get a question answered. Other times, it's a reliable way to determine if a long trip to a hospital is necessary.
"If a mom in a rural part of Kenya starts bleeding at 2 a.m., she can't just Google it," Patel says. "But this service runs completely over SMS. It's completely free to the user, and it's accessible to anyone who has a basic phone."
About 7% of messages are flagged by the system as potentially urgent. These are routed directly to a nurse.
"It bypasses all AI functionality and gets straight to the help desk, into a special queue," Patel says. "They can pick it up immediately, look at the mom's question history and call her."
That kind of quick response is critical in Kenya, where about 6,000 women die each year from childbirth or pregnancy-related causes. That's 16 women a day. Almost a third of those deaths are believed to be related to delays in seeking care.
Lisa Mushega, a policy expert for HENNET, a Kenyan coalition of health care providers, says PROMPTS helps prevent these delays by giving women a direct line to a health professional. (Jacaranda Health is a member of the coalition).
"It's a referral," Mushega says. "[PROMPTS] is data driven and can improve the quality of care — informed by the voices of mothers themselves."
Mushega says she has met women who used PROMPTS to correctly identify signs of pre-eclampsia, a life-threatening condition that can start with swollen legs. Another new mother used the system when her newborn seemed sick, and she wasn't sure how to calm him.
"She was told to go to the nearest health facility, because her baby was actually having jaundice," Mushega says. "It really comes in handy."
At a time when the use of artificial intelligence is drawing existential concerns and calls for regulation, a program like PROMPTS demonstrates its potential value, says Smisha Agarwal, director of global digital health at Johns Hopkins University.
The AI Edge
Historically, most public health messaging is one-sided: Public service advertisements, billboards or automated messages written by health authorities and disseminated to the public.
"That conversation is really bounded by what a health system decides a mother should know," Agarwal says. Artificial intelligence sets a different course: "What the LLM really changes is the direction of conversation. Because now we can center it on what the mother actually wants to know, and in a private space on her own phone. There is a fundamental change in power."
In Kenya, PROMPTS understands messages in English, Swahili and Sheng — a popular dialect in Nairobi that is a mix of the two languages. Jacaranda has also expanded to parts of Ghana, Nigeria and Tanzania, building versions for speakers of Twi and Hausa.
"There's local context," Patel says. "If there's a question about nutrition in Kenya, and you give the same answer from a question about nutrition in Nigeria, you're going to get laughed out of the room."
Jacaranda Health is also using PROMPTS to help doctors identify areas of need, based on anonymous feedback from some of the estimated 700,000 users each year.
"Lots of mothers are reporting that they're getting blood pressure checks, but very few report getting breast exams," says spokesperson Laura Down. "It gives mums more agency in the health system — as well as a better understanding of their pregnancy history."
In other cases, Down says the questions mothers are asking can help doctors understand what's happening in their own community.
"So for example, we're starting to see correlations between a spike in extreme heat and a spike in mothers reporting issues like headaches or swelling or dehydration," Down says.
Any potential drawbacks?
But there are limits. These interventions work best in places that already have functional healthcare systems, Agarwal says. There's very little margin for error when human medical needs are processed by a machine. The way the system is trained to do a rapid handoff to a human nurse in an emergency becomes a key factor.
"The first thing I want to know is, what happens when the system gets a message wrong?" says Javaid Iqbal Sofi, a researcher focusing on AI policy and governance at Virginian Tech University. "Suppose a woman describes something urgent, but the system treats it as routine. Would someone catch that? How quickly?"
Patient privacy issues and missed opportunities for care are common concerns, as AI platforms are adopted in medical contexts worldwide. Last month, the use of platforms developed by Palantir to automate staff schedules in hospitals in the United States drew protests by a national nursing union. The use of AI by insurance companies to process and deny medical claims — even without a human reviewing them — has led to outrage and calls for regulation.
In contrast, PROMPTS operates as a limited-use program, trained on a relatively narrow set of issues and concerns. Its developers say the human element of the system is the most important part. A team of 18 nurses are employed to monitor, audit, and respond to PROMPTS questions around the clock.
"Humans are responsible for ensuring the quality of messages going out, and we audit the quality of the answers," says Javan Waita, Jacaranda Health's director of programs in Kenya.
Maintaining a significant human component of the program improves accuracy but raises the cost. Right now, it costs about $2 per user to maintain PROMPTS, which is absorbed by the nonprofit. That gets a mom through pregnancy, and stays with her for a year after birth.
Waita says this is an important backstop, especially when mothers might not have an alternative.
"The sooner a mother is able to access care, the sooner doctors will be able to understand the problem," Waita says. "If PROMPTS isn't there, it means more complications for mothers, more complications for newborns."

'This is our company': Nigerians show off oil wealth after share-buying frenzy
- Published
Every Nigerian is now an oil magnate.
At least that is what the social media memes would have you believe as investor fever hits the country.
Nigerians have been eager to have a piece of the energy business that was built up by the country's – and continent's – richest man: Aliko Dangote.
More than four billion shares in his giant oil refinery – representing just over 3% of the company - went on the market on Monday in Africa's biggest-ever sale of its kind.
The minimum purchase was 10 shares for about $4 (£3) and despite this only representing a miniscule portion of the firm, many are now celebrating and joking about their new-found (part-)owner status.
One popular social media video has a Nigerian narrating how he stopped a speeding Dangote company lorry driver, telling him not to be reckless with company property.
Other memes show investors trying to phone up Dangote to discuss business matters.
And the term "Yangote" – a pun in the Hausa language essentially meaning "we all have a share now" - has been trending on social media.
On the first day of the Initial Public Offering (IPO), investment apps crashed as they could not handle the high demand.
Bamboo, which runs one of the most popular investor tools here, later apologised, saying: "We know we let you down."
Public affairs analyst Jamil Ubah said he had rarely seen Nigerians as excited about something as this. He argued that it fed the dream that it could lead to greater riches for a population that is often battling to make ends meet.
"I think the hope for the common man is that his money will grow into something big, and don't forget this is coming at a time when many are struggling as the economy is not doing great," he told the BBC.
Dangote wanted this to be "the people's IPO" with drivers, cooks, cleaners and servants having the chance to be part of something big.
And they took him at his word.
Twenty-five-year-old clothes seller Idris Lawal Musa made his first-ever stock exchange purchase and told the BBC he was happy after investing 21,000 naira ($16; £12) in 40 shares.
"It is no longer Dangote but 'Yangote', the company belongs to us now," he said while laughing.
But he may make a quick sale.
"I am a trader by profession and when I see that the shares have increased in price I will sell," he noted.
The popularity also reflects a growing investment culture among younger Nigerians who have embraced mobile trading platforms, cryptocurrencies and digital savings products.
But fear of missing out may have also pushed some to get into the investment business.
In the build-up to the IPO, social media platforms were awash with financial conversations. People shared subscription guides, debated valuation metrics and encouraged friends and family to participate.
But amid the frenzy, experts have warned that there are risks – shares can go down in value, as well as up, meaning people could lose some, or all, of their investment.
Financial analyst Shuaib Uwais said prospective investors should avoid thinking of the IPO as a guaranteed route to wealth.
He urged people to consider a number of factors that could impact the refinery's future performance, including disruptions to crude oil supply, operational challenges, regulatory changes and fluctuations in demand for refined petroleum products.
"If for any reason the company experiences difficulty in sourcing its raw materials, there could be challenges," he told the BBC.
Nevertheless, the IPO has given people the chance to be part of this home-grown success story.
Dangote's sprawling refinery on the outskirts of Lagos, which began operating two years ago and now processes around 700,000 barrels of crude a day, has transformed the fortunes of Nigeria's oil sector.
Until recently, Africa's largest crude oil producer had no refining capacity and had to import the finished product. Now the Dangote refinery is feeding much of the domestic demand.
But for Dangote, the share offer is about raising cash to fund the growth of the business, something that the country's mini-magnates may now be able to get behind.

Between surviving an illness and returning to regular life, lies a journey of a thousand small victories. Physiotherapy helps people take those victories, one step at a time.
There is a moment after a heart attack or stroke that very few people talk about. It is not the moment the ambulance arrives. It is not the moment the doctors say the patient is out of danger. It is the moment when the hospital doors close behind you, you return home, and everyone expects life to slowly return to normal.
But what does ‘normal’ mean?
For someone who has had a stroke, it may mean learning to walk again, using an arm that suddenly feels unfamiliar, finding their balance, or simply getting out of bed without someone holding their hand. For someone who has survived a heart attack, it may mean taking that first walk outside without constantly wondering whether their heart can handle it.
And sometimes, the hardest part is not the physical limitation. It is the fear. “What if it happens again?” That question can stay with a person long after they have left the hospital. This is where physiotherapy becomes much more than a set of exercises.
What rehabilitation entails
We often imagine rehabilitation as someone working hard in a gym, lifting weights or walking on a treadmill. The reality can be much quieter.
For a stroke survivor, the first goal may simply be to sit upright without support. Then to stand. Then to take a few steps. For the family watching, it may seem like very little. For the person doing it, it may feel like climbing a mountain.
A physiotherapist is there for these moments. Not just to count repetitions or measure strength, but to help someone understand that progress does not always have to be dramatic. Sometimes, progress is one extra step. Sometimes, it is standing for ten seconds longer. Sometimes, it is being able to walk to the bathroom without asking for help. And sometimes, it is simply finding the confidence to try.
What patients go through
Imagine being someone who used to walk to work, play with their children, exercise regularly or climb four flights of stairs without giving it a second thought. Then you have a heart attack. Suddenly, your heartbeat becomes something you constantly notice. You begin questioning every sensation. Is this normal? Am I too tired? Is my heart rate too high? Should I stop?
That fear can lead people to become overly cautious and inactive. Cardiac rehabilitation can help break that cycle. With appropriate medical assessment and supervision, patients can gradually return to physical activity, improve their exercise capacity and learn how to manage their cardiovascular health with greater confidence. The physiotherapist’s role is not simply to say, “Push harder.” It is to say: “Let us understand what your body can safely do today—and build from there.”
Not only for the elderly
A stroke or heart attack is often imagined as something that happens late in life, after the age of 60 or so. But when it happens to a younger person, the shock can be enormous. Someone in their 30s or 40s may suddenly find themselves worrying about things they never expected to question. Will I be able to go back to work? Can I take care of my children? Can I travel? Can I exercise again? Can I return to the sport I love?
They may look perfectly healthy from the outside. But inside, they may be dealing with fatigue, weakness, uncertainty and fear about what comes next. That is why rehabilitation cannot simply be based on a person’s age or diagnosis. A younger patient may need to return to a physically demanding job. A sportsperson may want to return to competition. A parent may simply want enough energy to play with their children. Rehabilitation has to fit the life that person wants to return to.
The patient is not a diagnosis. This may be one of the most important things a physiotherapist learns. A medical report might say stroke. It might say heart attack. It might list numbers, test results and medications. But none of those words explain who the patient is. They do not tell you that the patient loves taking their morning walk. They do not tell you that someone has a child waiting at home. They do not tell you that being able to climb the stairs independently means more to that person than almost anything else. Good rehabilitation starts with a simple question: “What do you want to get back to?” The answer may be different for every person. And that answer becomes an important part of the treatment.
Preventive goals
Physiotherapy is also about preventing the next story. Rehabilitation should not only begin after a crisis. Physiotherapists also have an important role in helping people become more physically active, develop healthier movement habits and reduce preventable health risks. Physical activity is an important part of cardiovascular health, but exercise is not a prescription that can simply be copied from one person to another.
The right type, intensity and amount of activity depend on the individual. For someone recovering from a cardiac event, exercise may require appropriate medical guidance and monitoring of symptoms, heart rate, blood pressure and exercise tolerance. For someone recovering from a stroke, rehabilitation may involve improving balance, strength, coordination, walking and everyday functional activities.
The goal is not to push everyone to do more. The goal is to help each person do what is right for them—safely and consistently. The greatest thing a physiotherapist restores is not movement. It is the part of someone’s life they thought was gone forever.
We often say that physiotherapists help people move. But perhaps that does not quite capture the whole story. Physiotherapists help people return to the things that make life feel like life.
(Shanthi Dass is a sports physiotherapist and managing director of Synergy The Clinic, Chennai. synergytheclinic@gmail.com)

Interestingly, Nani said he had never discussed his admiration for Raghav with The Paradise director Srikanth Odela. During the narration of the film, however, Odela described the antagonist to Nani as “the villain in Kill — perfect casting.” The description immediately caught Nani’s attention, given his familiarity with Raghav’s work.
At the same time, Nani had some questions about how Raghav’s performance would translate into Telugu. The actor wondered whether working in a language that was not Raghav’s own might affect the spontaneity and small nuances that can emerge naturally during a performance.
Those concerns changed once filming began. Nani revealed that Raghav went beyond simply learning and delivering his Telugu dialogues and remained closely involved with the nuances of each scene. “From day one, when I met him and we started shooting, he did so much with it. He did even more than he had done in Hindi,” Nani shared.
The Paradise marks Raghav Juyal’s Telugu debut and brings him into a new language and film industry. The project is directed by Srikanth Odela and stars Nani in the lead role.
The film is slated to release on September 24, 2026. With Raghav taking on the antagonist, Nani’s comments offer a glimpse into the actor’s approach to his first Telugu-language role and the expectations surrounding his performance.

In August 2026, Trump expanded a U.S. beef import quota by roughly 660 million pounds. The European Union did also adopt restrictions on Brazilian beef in summer 2026.
The quota expansion of roughly 660 million pounds was not specifically for Brazilian or JBS beef, according to a presidential proclamation. It was not possible to rule out the prospect that, despite not being mentioned in the proclamation, JBS or Brazilian beef could be the main or sole beneficiaries of the expansion. It is also imprecise to say the imported beef would be tariff-free.
The Wall Street Journal reported that JBS controlling shareholder Joesley Batista asked Trump to lower tariffs on Brazilian beef. It was not possible for Snopes to independently verify this report.
The suggestion appeared to be that the imported products would come from Brazil despite the European restrictions on Brazilian beef, and that JBS would benefit from the reduced tariffs.
One Instagram post (archived) featuring the rumor describes JBS as the "primary beef supplier" for McDonald's, Burger King, Sysco, Walmart's Great Value brand and Kroger private-label products. Its caption reads, in part:
The owner of JBS met privately with Trump in the Oval Office, and discussed lowering the import tax on Brazilian beef.
The next day, Trump opened the border to 660 million pounds of tariff-free imported beef. JBS is the world's largest meat processing company. Their headquarters are in Brazil.
The EU banned Brazilian beef after Brazil couldn't prove their cattle met antibiotic safety rules. China rejected beef from Argentina after it was lab tested to contain a drug linked to cancer.
Versions of the rumor also spread on TikTok, Facebook and Threads, and readers contacted us to ask whether the elements of the claim were true.
In short, the claim contains a mixture of accurate, false and unconfirmed information.
In August 2026, Trump did expand a U.S. beef import quota by roughly 660 million pounds, and the European Union did adopt restrictions on Brazilian beef. However, that expansion was not specifically for Brazilian or JBS beef, according to a proclamation Trump signed in August 2026, and it is imprecise to say the imported beef would be tariff-free. The Wall Street Journal also reported that Batista, JBS' controlling shareholder, asked Trump to lower tariffs on Brazilian beef, but it was not possible for Snopes to independently verify that report.
Trump expanded beef imports in August 2026
On Aug. 26, 2026, Trump signed a proclamation temporarily increasing the amount of lean beef trimmings that could enter the U.S. under an existing tariff-rate quota by 300,000 metric tons. That increase equals roughly 660 million pounds.
Describing the imports as "tariff-free," however, is imprecise. Under a tariff-rate quota, a set amount of a product can enter at a lower tariff, while imports above that amount face a higher tariff. The White House said Trump's measure increased the amount of beef eligible for the lower tariff rate rather than eliminating duties for beef altogether.
Moreover, the proclamation did not explicitly say the beef would come from Brazil. It allocated the additional quota to "other countries or areas" and directed U.S. Customs and Border Protection to ensure that "all eligible countries have full access" on a first-come, first-served basis. JBS is also not mentioned in the proclamation.
However, i
Did JBS co-owner meet Trump?
Batista and his brother, Wesley Batista, are JBS' "ultimate controlling shareholders," according to the company's filings with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. As of March 18, 2026, the brothers held about 86% of the company's voting power.
Citing anonymous sources, The Wall Street Journal reported (
However, the policy was not implemented immediately. Trump formally expanded the quota on Aug. 26, and the first tranche opened on Sept. 1.
Reuters later reported the Journal's account but said it could not independently verify it. Snopes also was unable to independently verify the report, given it was based on anonymous sources.
We contacted JBS via email to confirm whether Batista met with Trump and, if so, what was discussed. We will update this story if we receive a response.
Snopes also reached out to the White House with similar questions and to ask how much beef would come from JBS or Brazil. Replying via email, a spokesperson said the tariff-rate quota expansion was not the result of a single conversation (emphasis ours):
President Trump's action to address a short-term supply crunch in the beef market was the result of a long policy planning and coordination process involving domestic stakeholders; this action was not done as the result of any one conversation. At the same time, the Trump Administration continues to work with American farmers and ranchers to grow America's cattle herd, which is currently at a multi-decade low.
JBS has ties to some named companies
JBS does have documented relationships with several companies named in the social media posts, but it was not possible to confirm that it is the primary beef supplier for all of them, as of September 2026.
For instance, a 2017 JBS report (Page 87) says its Seara division supplied 75% of McDonald's hamburger requirements in Brazil at the time and listed McDonald's and Burger King among its global customers. A 2020 JBS sustainability report (Page 76) also says Friboi, a JBS beef brand, received Burger King's Best Supplier Award that year.
There is also evidence of relationships with Sysco and Kroger. Sysco 
But those sources do not show that, as of September 2026, JBS was the primary beef supplier for all the companies listed in the social media posts. McDonald's, for example, 
Walmart also disputed the post's description of JBS as a supplier of its ground beef. Annie Walker, director of Walmart U.S. communications for food and U.S. manufacturing, said via email, "We do not source ground beef from JBS."
Snopes contacted JBS, McDonald's, Burger King, Sysco and Kroger to clarify their current supplier relationships. We will update this article if we receive responses.
EU did restrict Brazilian beef
The posts were also broadly correct that the EU restricted Brazilian beef. On June 4, 2026, the European Commission adopted a regulation changing the list of countries authorized to send certain animal products to the EU under rules concerning the use of antimicrobial medicines. The changes took effect Sept. 3, 2026.
The regulation says Brazil was previously authorized for bovine products, among other categories, but that the commission did not receive information guaranteeing Brazil had implemented the measures needed to comply with the antimicrobial requirements by Sept. 3. Brazil's authorization for bovine products was therefore removed.
Importantly, the regulation does not say Brazilian beef tested positive for unsafe antibiotic residues. Rather, it says Brazil did not provide enough information to show it met the EU requirements laid out above, which a European Commission spokesperson confirmed via email. The spokesperson said Brazilian exports could resume once the country meets those requirements.
Brazil's government also said the restrictions concerned new rules governing the use of antimicrobial medicines, adding that Brazilian authorities are continuing engagement with European officials.
Snopes contacted Brazil's Ministry of Agriculture for additional context on the restrictions and will update this story if we receive a response.
China case unrelated to Brazil
Chinese authorities did suspend (Page 1921) the export authorization of one Argentine beef plant, ArreBeef, after detecting the antibiotic chloramphenicol in a shipment in March 2026, as Snopes previously reported. 
As we previously reported, that incident was separate from Trump's August import plan. The president's Aug. 26 proclamation does not assign the additional 300,000 metric tons to Argentina, Brazil or any other individual country.

Identity and access management startup OTPless has elevated cofounders Satyam Nathani and Tanmay Sagar as CEO and COO, respectively, as incumbent CEO Bhavik Koladiya steps away. Koladiya told Inc42 that he plans to retire but did not comment further on his future plans. Under the new leadership structure, Nathani will lead the startup’s strategy and expansion, while Sagar will oversee its operations and execution. OTPless said the appointments come as it looks to expand its offerings across authentication, identity, and payments. In a LinkedIn post announcing the leadership transition, Koladiya described his entrepreneurial journey as “exhilarating and exhausting”. He also expressed confidence in Nathani and Sagar leading OTPless through its next phase of growth. Before joining OTPless, Koladiya cofounded fintech unicorn BharatPe and later founded VC firm Finix Partners. OTPless was founded in 2021 by Nathani and Sagar, with Koladiya taking charge as CEO in January 2023. Nathani and Sagar were founding members of BharatPe. The Bengaluru-based startup helps consumer internet enterprises offer authentication services through its SDKs and APIs. Its offerings include silent network authentication, WhatsApp authentication, device intelligence, and passkeys. These offerings are aimed at reducing dependence on OTPs, PINs, and passwords while enabling enterprises to identify users, prevent fraud, and improve conversion during sign-ups and transactions. OTPless claims to authenticate more than 300 Mn mobile users and serve enterprises including Meesho, Navi, PhysicsWallah, ShareChat, Shiprocket, ixigo, and Zepto. It said it has reached ₹36 Cr in annualised revenue, representing a 2.5X increase over the previous year. The startup also claimed to have been profitable for the past two quarters. OTPless has raised over $6 Mn to date from Venture Highway, White Venture, FJ Labs, SIDBI , Piper Serica, among others. It last raised $3.5 Mn in a pre-Series A funding round led by SIDBI in May 2024. At the time, OTPless said it would use the capital to expand globally and extend its product suite beyond authentication into authorisation.

A United Nations (UN) fact-finding mission on Iran said it had reasonable grounds to believe the United States was behind two military strikes on a school and sports facility in Iran in February, news agency Reuters said in a report.
These instances constituted war crimes, the report said on 17 September. The report also found that Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity during their deadly crackdown on anti-government protests.
The findings in a new report by the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran examined US conduct during the Iran war that began in February and the Iranian government's response to nationwide unrest that began in late December. The findings will be submitted to the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva.
The Reuters said that Pentagon declined to comment on a report conducted by an outside organization. "Our investigation remains ongoing, and we have nothing to announce at the moment," Pentagon said in a statement, according to the agency report.
White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly was quoted in the Reuters report that the UN Human Rights Council had "accomplished nothing for human rights," adding that Iran was the only party in the current conflict that had committed war crimes.
The Iranian permanent mission in Geneva did not respond to Reuters requests for comment.
US officials have previously said military operations are conducted in accordance with the law of armed conflict, while Iran has consistently rejected allegations of systematic rights violations.
UN Fact-Finding missions are investigative, not judicial bodies, and therefore do not initiate any criminal cases. Their findings, however, can be used in criminal investigations by national courts or international tribunals such as the International Criminal Court.
The UN experts said they found reasonable grounds to believe US forces were responsible for an attack on the Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School in the city of Minab, where more than 150 people were killed, including around 120 schoolchildren, according to Iranian officials.
The attack occurred on February 28, 2026, when a missile strike hit the School in Minab, Hormozgan province, southern Iran, during the US-Iran war. Evidence and satellite analyses quoted later by international media indicated the school was struck near a neighboring Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) compound, though the school itself was clearly identifiable and separated by a wall.
The attack constituted an indiscriminate attack causing civilian deaths and damage to civilian infrastructure, amounting to a war crime under international law, the mission concluded as per Reuters report.
According to the report, the US failure to update information in relation to the school, which was adjacent to an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps naval complex, in its targeting databases and to confirm the building was a military objective amounted to more than mere negligence.
"Rather, the US directed the strikes at the building of the school while being aware of a substantial risk of striking a civilian object and acting recklessly as regards the possibility that this would happen."
In June US President Donald Trump said that "nobody" purposefully attacked a girls' school in Iran in February, citing an investigation into the incident. The Pentagon has since elevated the probe but it has not published any preliminary findings.
UN experts said the school was a clearly identifiable civilian object and found no evidence that it was being used for military purposes.
The experts reached a similar conclusion over a strike on a sports centre in Lamerd. The report said the attack damaged nearby residential buildings and a school and killed and injured 22 civilians. It concluded that the strike was indiscriminate and therefore constituted a war crime.
U.S. Central Command said in a statement in March that U.S. forces did not launch any strikes into the city of Lamerd on that day.
The UN mission probe found that the Iranian authorities carried out a widespread and systematic attack against civilians during protests that erupted in late December last year, involving unlawful killings, torture, arbitrary detention, enforced disappearances and severe restrictions on freedom of expression.
Rights groups say bystanders were among those killed during the biggest crackdown since Shi'ite Muslim clerics took power in the 1979 revolution. Tehran blamed "terrorists and rioters" backed by exiled opponents and foreign foes the US and Israel.
The probe said it could not independently verify the death toll, but that it believed the number of dead and injured was likely far higher than official figures which say 3,038 people were killed, and 25,000 people injured.
The government's response to the protests — including violence and killings, cutting off the internet and use of the death penalty — marked a significant escalation from previous patterns of suppressing dissent, the report said.
(With Reuters inputs)

A Swedish teenager known as Chai has been sentenced to more than 10 years in jail for attempted murder, rape and aggravated assault – crimes committed via the internet, including against a teenage girl in Australia.
The district court found that Chai, 18, was active in online networks notorious for their sadistic extortion of young and vulnerable people, coercing them to create sexually explicit material or engage in acts of violence – and for the youth of those involved.
The teenager was between 15 and 17 when the offences were committed.
Chai was convicted of two counts of attempted murder against a young person in Germany, and multiple sexual and violent offences against the Australian teenager, among other offences.
Jenny Östling, a senior public prosecutor at Sweden’s national unit against international and organised crime, said the court had clearly understood the phenomenon of “nihilistic violent extremism” and the Com – an umbrella term for a loosely connected online network that engages in cybercrime, extortion and violence.
“I’m really glad that they realise how serious this is and what it is,” she said.
She noted that the sentence was among the longest possible in Sweden for someone of Chai’s age. The court also found that it was possible for someone to be convicted of violent offences even where they were committed remotely via the internet.
“That is a very important tool for us when we proceed [with] these kinds of cases,” Östling said.
The crimes committed by those involved with sadistic extortion networks, such as one globally known as “764”, often cross borders, with cases in the US, the UK, Germany and Australia, and alleged victims in multiple jurisdictions.
Material is often created and traded among participants to build status and control, lawyers and researchers told the Guardian as part of its investigation into these groups, as well as a means of accessing closed servers and chatrooms.
“These are young people recruiting other young people,” Bjørn Ihler, the founder of the security firm Revontulet, said at the time. “It is a youth phenomenon.”
Chai’s conviction is one of several cases that have resulted in significant terms of imprisonment for young men found to be involved in this ecosystem, including an American, Kyle Spitze, 27, who was sentenced in August to 77 years in prison – the longest federal sentence yet imposed on someone the US government has labelled a “nihilistic violent extremist”.
During the trial, Chai underwent a forensic psychiatric examination that found he was not suffering a serious mental disorder when the offences occurred.
His lawyer, Emily Tovedal, told the Guardian: “The defence’s view is that the court has made an error of judgment regarding a large proportion of the charges.”
  Authorities internationally have increasingly raised the alarm about sadistic online exploitation of young people, detailing potential warning signs including self-harm and isolation.
“Sadly, I’m confident that … they will probably grow,” Östling said of these networks. “And we will also be aware of more of them, because now we know what to look for.”

A post (here & here) is being shared on social media claiming that a pregnant woman gave birth on the road in Unnao, Uttar Pradesh, after a government hospital refused her admission due to her inability to cover the medical expenses. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Visuals of a woman giving birth on the roadside in Unnao, Uttar Pradesh, after a government hospital denied her admission.
Fact: The visuals are from Rajbiraj, Nepal, where a woman gave birth on the street outside a government Hospital in September 2026 after being denied care over unpaid preliminary test fees. However, a similar incident took place in Uttar Pradesh in April 2026, when a woman delivered her baby on the roadside outside a government hospital in Shamli district after staff allegedly demanded a bribe and refused her admission. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A reverse image search of viral visuals directed us to Nepali news reports (here, here & here) covering the same incident. The event reportedly occurred in the town of Rajbiraj, Nepal. According to these reports, on 10 September 2026, Babita Kumari Paswan, a 30-year-old woman, delivered her baby on the pavement outside the state-owned Gajendra Narayan Singh Hospital in Rajbiraj, Nepal, after her family couldn’t get the money required for preliminary tests.
After a video of the incident went viral, six hospital staff were reportedly suspended pending an investigation. A Google Street View of the hospital’s location matching the area seen in the viral video can be viewed here. However, it is worth noting that in April 2026, a similar incident (here & here) did occur in Uttar Pradesh, where a 30-year-old woman gave birth to a baby boy on the roadside outside the Shamli District Combined Hospital after staff allegedly refused her admission and demanded money. Hospital authorities formed a committee to investigate the matter.
To sum it up, the viral video depicting a woman delivering an infant on the street is from Nepal, not from Uttar Pradesh.

U.S. health regulators will review the scientific evidence on testosterone use in menopausal women on Thursday, including its benefits, risks, dosing and role in female health, as well as perspectives from doctors and patients.
The public meeting, which the U.S. Food and Drug Administration said could help guide future research and drug development, comes as a growing number of women are turning to testosterone to manage menopause symptoms.
There is no FDA-approved testosterone therapy for women, despite years of off-label use to treat low sexual desire, known as hypoactive sexual desire disorder, or HSDD.
Last year, the FDA removed the boxed warning about increased cardiovascular risk from testosterone products for men after reviewing post-marketing studies, though the products still carry warnings about increased blood pressure.
Physicians who prescribe testosterone to women typically rely on low doses of products approved for men, often dividing existing products such as AbbVie's AndroGel and Keenova Therapeutics' Testim, or on compounded formulations.
The lack of a female-specific product creates practical challenges for clinicians, said Diana Tordoff, an instructor in obstetrics and gynecology at Stanford, noting that an approved product could provide standardised dosing, labeling and safety-monitoring guidance and potentially improve insurance coverage.
Still, some experts say key questions remain unresolved. More long-term safety data are needed, said Stephanie Faubion, director of Mayo Clinic's Center for Women's Health.
The United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa have approved or licensed testosterone products specifically for women.
The FDA's request for public comments ahead of the meeting attracted hundreds of submissions, many from women describing improved libido, energy and quality of life while using testosterone.
Evidence and safety gaps
Interest in testosterone among menopausal women has grown alongside claims on social media that it can improve energy, muscle mass, bone health and cognition, though specialists say the evidence is strongest for HSDD.
"We do not have any evidence in women that it will improve muscle mass or bone density or mood or well-being or really any other metric," Faubion said.
Karen Adams, director of Stanford Medicine's Program in Menopause and Healthy Aging, said testosterone has been reviewed by the FDA four times for use in women but has never been approved because of a lack of long-term safety data and concerns about cardiovascular and breast cancer risks.
The FDA has approved non-testosterone options like Sprout Pharmaceuticals' Addyi and Cosette Pharmaceuticals' Vyleesi for certain patients with HSDD.
Testosterone is generally not recommended for women with a history of breast cancer because it can be converted to estrogen in the body that can drive some cancers.
Excessive testosterone exposure can cause acne and increased hair growth, physicians said, while rarer effects such as voice deepening and hair loss may be irreversible.
Studies show that testosterone therapy is generally considered safe for men with medically diagnosed low levels of the hormone when prescribed and monitored by a doctor.
Tordoff and Adams are leading Stanford's MIX-T pilot study examining how low-dose testosterone affects vaginal health and the vaginal microbiome in postmenopausal women. Results are expected within the next two years.
