Below, we look back at the celebrities we lost in 2026, listed in alphabetical order.
Scott Adams, 68
Scott Adams worked at a telephone company in the 1980s. The experience inspired his beloved comic strip, "Dilbert."
By the end of the decade, the character and his satirical office humor began appearing in comic strips.
At its peak, "Dilbert" was syndicated in over 2,000 newspapers. A cartoon series debuted in 1999, running for two seasons.
Adams gained notoriety when he began writing blog posts praising Donald Trump during his 2016 presidential run. In 2023, "Dilbert" was pulled from newspapers across the US following racist comments made by Adams.
Adams died on January 13 from metastatic prostate cancer.
Brad Arnold, 47
The lead singer of 3 Doors Down, Brad Arnold launched the group into fame with the 2000 rock anthem "Kryptonite," which peaked at No. 3 on the Billboard Hot 100 that year.
The success led to other hits like "Loser," "Here Without You," and "When I'm Gone." Arnold's vocal range and lyrics focused on love and love lost, which fueled the group to stardom.
Arnold died on February 7 from a type of kidney cancer.
Afrika Bambaataa, 68
A hip-hop pioneer during the 1970s and 1980s, Lance Taylor, known professionally as Afrika Bambaataa, first gained attention as a DJ in the Bronx.
He signed with Tommy Boy Records in 1981 and released landmark songs like "Jazzy Sensation" and "Planet Rock." He would go on to influence the likes of Queen Latifah and A Tribe Called Quest throughout his career.
Bambaataa founded the hip-hop awareness group, Universal Zulu Nation, in the 1970s to steer kids away from gang life. Bambaataa stepped down as the head of the organization in 2016 after accusations of sexual abuse.
Bambaataa denied all claims.
He died on April 9 due to prostate cancer.
Rob Bass, 59
One of the icons responsible for bringing hip-hop to the mainstram, Rob Bass crafted the iconic track "It Takes Two" alongside DJ E-Z Rock.
The track, released in 1988, reached No. 3 on the Billboard Hot Dance/Club Songs chart and later went certified platinum. In 1989, it was voted the greatest single of all time by Spin magazine.
Bass died on May 22 following cancer.
Nicholas Brendon, 54
Nicholas Brendon was a television actor, best known for playing Xander Harris in all seven seasons of "Buffy the Vampire Slayer."
He also starred in "Criminal Minds" and "Kitchen Confidential."
Brendon died in his sleep on March 20 due to natural causes, according to his family's statement.
In 2023, Brendon suffered a heart attack and was diagnosed with a congenital heart defect. He also had cauda equina syndrome, which led to several spinal surgeries.
"While it's no secret that Nicholas had struggles in the past, he was on medications and treatment to manage his diagnosis, and he was optimistic about the future at the time of his passing," the statement to The Hollywood Reporter read. "Our family asks for privacy during this time as we grieve his loss and celebrate the life of a man who lived with intensity, imagination, and heart."
Peabo Bryson, 75
Two-time Grammy winner Peabo Bryson is best known for his classic love ballads.
Bryson began releasing music in the late 1970s, but one of his first major hits was opposite Roberta Flack on the 1983 duet, "Tonight, I Celebrate My Love." He continued hit-making a year later with the smash "If Ever You're in My Arms Again," and in 1991, he topped the R&B charts with "Can You Stop the Rain."
Bryson found global stardom with his renditions of two Disney classics. In 1991, he released the pop version of "Beauty and the Beast," alongside Céline Dion, and a year later, he duetted with Regina Belle on "A Whole New World" from the 1992 release of "Aladdin."
Bryson died on June 2. No cause was given.
James Burrows, 85
An 11-time Emmy winner and co-creator of "Cheers," director James Burrows helped shape modern TV comedy through his work on iconic sitcoms including "Will & Grace," "Friends," and "Frasier."
Known for his comedic timing and elaborate blocking, Burrows got his start directing episodes of "The Mary Tyler Moore Show." Throughout his career, he directed episodes of "Frasier" (winning an Emmy for the pilot episode), "Will & Grace," "Friends," and "The Big Bang Theory." He directed over 50 pilot episodes.
Burrows died on June 19. No cause was given.
Kyle Busch, 41
Two-time NASCAR Cup Series champion Busch was considered one of the greatest racers of all time.
Busch was hospitalized on May 21, before two upcoming races. Hours later, he was pronounced dead.
Busch died from severe pneumonia that progressed into sepsis.
Robert Carradine, 71
Robert Carradine was best known for his roles as Lizzie McGuire's dad and as the iconic geek Lewis Skolnick in the 1980s franchise "Revenge of the Nerds."
As a member of Hollywood's famed Carradine family, Robert was destined for an onscreen career.
He received one of his first screen credits starring in his brother David Carradine's popular 1970s TV series "Kung Fu" and went on to land roles in everything from Samuel Fuller's World War II classic "The Big Red One" to the "Lizzie McGuire" series.
Carradine's family shared statements with Deadline that emphasized being open about his struggles with mental illness.
"We are bereft at the loss of this beautiful soul and want to acknowledge Bobby's valiant struggle against his nearly two-decade battle with Bipolar Disorder," Carradine's family said. "We hope his journey can shine a light and encourage addressing the stigma that attaches to mental illness."
Carradine died by suicide on February 23.
If you or someone you know is experiencing depression or has had thoughts of harming themself or taking their own life, get help. In the US, call or text 988 to reach the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. Help is also available through the Crisis Text Line — just text "HOME" to 741741. The International Association for Suicide Prevention offers resources for those outside the US.
Bud Cort, 77
Most famous for his role as Harold in the 1971 cult-classic "Harold and Maude," Bud Cort became the epitome of 1970s counterculture thanks to his baby-faced looks, wit, and sophisticated persona.
The dark comedy starred Cort as Harold, a man in his 20s who is obsessed with suicide until he meets 79-year-old eccentric Maude (Ruth Gordon).
Before that, Cort scored bit parts in Robert Altman's "M*A*S*H*" (1970) and "Brewster McCloud" (1970).
After "Harold and Maude," Cort worked steadily for the rest of his life, occasionally showing up in hit movies like Michael Mann's "Heat" (1995) and Wes Anderson's "The Life Aquatic with Steve Zissou" (2004).
Cort died on February 11 following a long illness.
Tim Curry, 80
Curry is best known for playing Dr. Frank-N-Furter in the cult-classic musical "The Rocky Horror Picture Show," after originating the role in the original stage production.
Over six decades, Curry carved out a niche playing outlandish villains like Rooster Hannigan in the 1982 film "Annie" and Pennywise in the 1990 miniseries "It." Other notable roles include Wadsworth the Butler in "Clue" (1985) and Mr. Hector in "Home Alone 2: Escape from New York."
Curry suffered a major stroke in 2012, which required brain surgery. He said in 2025 that he was "still recovering."
Curry died at his Los Angeles home on August 26. No cause was given.
Eric Dane, 53
Long before becoming one of TV's most recognizable heartthrobs, Eric Dane was building his career with guest roles on series like "Saved by the Bell" and "Married… with Children."
He later gained wider attention with appearances on "Charmed" before landing his breakout role as Dr. Mark "McSteamy" Sloan on "Grey's Anatomy." He most recently starred in HBO's "Euphoria," where he played Cal Jacobs, the father of Jacob Elordi's character, Nate Jacobs.
Dane has two children with his wife, Rebecca Gayheart. In April 2025, the actor said that he was diagnosed with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS.
Dane died on February 19 at age 53, his publicist confirmed in a statement to Business Insider.
"He spent his final days surrounded by dear friends, his devoted wife, and his two beautiful daughters, Billie and Georgia, who were the center of his world," his publicist said.
Clive Davis, 94
A legend in the music world, Davis was responsible for elevating pop music to unthinkable heights by discovering talents like Aretha Franklin, Barry Manilow, Bruce Springsteen, Billy Joel, Whitney Houston, and Alicia Keys, to name a few.
Over his 50-year career, along with being an executive behind millions of album sales, he also won five Grammys, including two for Album of the Year ("The Bodyguard" soundtrack and "Supernatural" by Santana).
Davis died on June 22. No cause was given.
Robert Duvall, 95
Robert Duvall starred in a plethora of timeless classics, including "The Godfather," "The Godfather Part II," "Apocalypse Now," "THX 1138," "The Natural," "Days of Thunder," and "The Apostle."
Duvall will be best remembered for starring in three of director Francis Ford Coppola's iconic films: playing Tom Hagen in the first two "Godfather" movies and Lieutenant Colonel Bill Kilgore in "Apocalypse Now," in which he delivers one of the most memorable lines in movie history: "I love the smell of napalm in the morning."
Duvall was lauded for his acting talent, from not saying a word while playing Boo Radley in his first big screen role in the 1962 classic "To Kill a Mockingbird" to his portrayal of a country singer dealing with alcoholism in 1983's "Tender Mercies," which earned him an Oscar.
He died on his ranch in Virginia on February 15. No cause was given.
Brenda Fricker, 81
This Irish actress was a fixture on the stage and screen for six decades. But she's most known for showing up in the "Home Alone" sequel.
As The Pigeon Lady in 1992's "Home Alone 2: Lost in New York," Fricker has become a fixture for families during the holiday season for decades (and in 2020 became the subject of a popular meme).
But Fricker's acting talents go beyond playing a spooky wanderer of Central Park.
In 1990, she became the first Irish actress to win an Academy Award, as she was given the best supporting actress Oscar that year for her performance in "My Left Foot."
Fricker died on July 16; no cause was given.
Mark Fuhrman, 74
Fuhrman cemented his place in popular culture as one of the lead LAPD detectives on the 1995 murder case of O.J. Simpson's ex-wife, Nicole Brown Simpson, and her friend Ronald Goldman.
Fuhrman found the famed bloody glove on the Simpson estate, and during the trial, he gained infamy when Simpson's defense team used his past racist language to discredit him as a witness.
Fuhrman retired from the LAPD after the Simpson trial and moved to Idaho, where he wrote true crime books.
Fuhrman died on May 12 of throat cancer.
Valentino Garavani, 93
For over six decades, one name has been synonymous with women's high fashion: Valentino.
The Italian designer launched his fashion business in Rome in 1960 and never looked back. Soon, every star wanted to be seen in his creations. They've been worn by icons like Elizabeth Taylor, Joan Collins, Jackie Kennedy, Princess Diana, Sharon Stone, and more.
Though Garavani retired from designing in 2008, his label is still a red carpet staple, as is his famous shade of bright red dubbed "Valentino Red."
Garavani died on January 19. No cause was given.
Donald Gibb, 71
No one defined a bully for a generation more than Gibb's hulking fraternity character Orge in the "Revenge of the Nerds" movies of the 1980s.
Since the original raunchy comedy was released in 1984, Gibb's intimidating size and loud yells of "NERDS!" have become as memorable as the pocket protectors worn by the movie's geeks.
Gibb went on to star opposite Jean-Claude Van Damme in his classic 1988 action movie "Bloodsport." He also landed guest star roles through his career on shows like "Quantum Leap," Magnum P.I.," "MacGyver," "Night Court," and "Cheers."
Gibb died on May 12 following health complications.
Glen Hansard, 56
Irish singer-songwriter Hansard was the frontman of the rock band The Frames and one-half of the band The Swell Season. But he was perhaps best known for writing and starring in the hit 2007 indie film "Once," in which he and his Swell Season bandmate Markéta Irglová play two struggling musicians who fall in love. The duo won an Oscar for best original song for the film's standout track, "Falling Slowly."
Hansard also embarked on a solo career; his 2015 album, "Didn't He Ramble," was nominated for a Grammy for best folk album.
Hansard died on July 29 in a motorcycle crash in Dublin.
Anthony Head, 72
Rising up through the UK stage scene in the 1980s, Head found fame when he was cast as Rupert Giles, who became a father figure to Sarah Michelle Gellar's Buffy Summers in all seven seasons of "Buffy the Vampire Slayer."
Most recently, he played the bitter former owner of AFC Richmond on "Ted Lasso."
Head's death was announced by his family on June 5. They stated the cause was "complications due to pneumonia."
David Hockney, 88
British painter David Hockney was renowned for his striking portraits and figurative pop art. Many of his best-known paintings, including 1966's "The Splash" and 1972's "Portrait of an Artist (Pool with Two Figures)," were inspired by the bright colors and sun-dappled pools of Los Angeles.
Hockney moved to Los Angeles in the late '60s, and his work became synonymous with the warmth and leisure of Southern California. He was also one of the few popular artists at the time to depict openly gay scenes, and Hockney was outspoken about anti-gay censorship.
Throughout his career, Hockney split time between California, England, and France. He died at his home in London on June 12 at age 88, his publicist confirmed to The New York Times. No cause of death was given.
Jesse Jackson, 84
The Rev. Jesse Jackson was a leader of the Civil Rights Movement, a minister, and an activist icon who twice ran for president.
Born on October 8, 1941, in Greenville, South Carolina, Jackson experienced Jim Crow segregation on public buses and at school firsthand. It would shape the rest of his life.
His fight for civil rights began in the 1960s, when he helped organize protests and demonstrations across the US and worked closely alongside civil rights icon Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.
His decadeslong career as a leading civil rights activist included support for modern national movements, such as the push for voting rights, the fight against racism, and a higher minimum wage.
Jackson ran for president twice, both times as a democrat. He placed third for the party's nomination in 1984 and second in 1988. This marked the most successful presidential runs of any Black candidate prior to Barack Obama.
Jackson announced in 2017 that he'd been diagnosed with Parkinson's disease. In November 2025, Jackson was treated in a Chicago hospital after complications from progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), a rare neurodegenerative condition.
Jackson died on February 17.
Yayoi Kusama, 97
Kusama was a famed Japanese pop artist who often used polka-dot motifs in her work, initially rising to prominence in Japan in the 1950s.
In 1959, Kusama presented her first solo exhibition in New York: a collection of abstract paintings that an ARTnews review praised as "strong, advanced in concept and realized."
Kusama later branched into sculptures, performances, and immersive installations. She continued to expand her influence and relevance into the social media era, when her mirrored "Infinity Room" installations became Instagram-friendly attractions that inspired many copycats.
Kusama died on August 14 in Tokyo. She was 97.
Bob Mackie, 87
As one of Hollywood's most renowned costume designers, Bob Mackie's eye set the style for decades.
Known as the Sultan of Sequins, the Rajah of Rhinestones, or the Guru of Glitter, a signature of Mackie's work was its use of sparkle, which made everyone from Cher to Elton John to Dolly Parton to Sabrina Carpenter shine on stage.
He also was the costume designer on "The Carol Burnett Show" for all eleven seasons through the 1970s. He won nine Emmys, a Tony Award, and was nominated for three Academy Awards for his work.
Mackie died on September 14; no cause was given.
Patrick Muldoon, 57
In the 1990s, you couldn't escape the piercing eyes of Patrick Muldoon.
He played Austin Reed on "Days of Our Lives" for most of the decade, and when he wasn't on the soap, he was over on "Melrose Place" playing the villain role of Richard Hart.
If being on two iconic shows wasn't enough, he also showed up on "Saved by the Bell" and had a role in the cult classic movie "Starship Troopers."
Muldoon died on April 19 after a heart attack.
Sam Neill, 78
With a career spanning more than five decades and including countless memorable performances in movies and television, Sam Neill was one of the most versatile actors of his generation,
The New Zealand actor starred opposite Nicole Kidman in the 1989 thriller "Dead Calm," played the loyal first officer opposite Sean Connery in 1990's "The Hunt for Red October," played the lead in John Carpenter's 1994 horror "In the Mouth of Madness," and most recently starred in the hit series "Peaky Blinders."
But Neill will be best known for playing the brave and all-dinosaur-knowing Dr. Alan Grant in the "Jurassic Park" franchise.
Neill died on July 13; no cause was given. Neill was battling a rare and aggressive form of blood cancer, but was cancer-free at the time of his death, according to a post on his Instagram account announcing his passing.
Tom Noonan, 74
Standing at a towering 6' 5", Tom Noonan was born to play the bad guy. And he did just that, starring as the villain in movies like "Manhunter," "RoboCop 2," and "Last Action Hero."
But this actor had more to show off. He showcased his comedy chops as Rodney Dangerfield's degenerate gambling friend in the 1983 comedy "Easy Money," and set up the heist for Robert De Niro in Michael Mann's 1995 classic "Heat."
His knack for storytelling also translated behind the camera. Noonan wrote, directed, and starred in the drama "What Happened Was," which won the grand prize at the 1994 Sundance Film Festival.
Noonan died on February 14; no cause was given.
Chuck Norris, 86
Few action stars have Chuck Norris' credentials.
Before he ever stepped in front of a camera, he was a martial arts champion and a black belt in Karate, judo, Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu, Taekwondo, and Tang Soo Do.
His talents would become known the world over in 1972, when he faced off against Bruce Lee in "The Way of the Dragon."
Through the 1980s, Norris became one of the biggest action stars in the world thanks to movies like "A Force of One," "The Octagon," and the "Delta Force" and "Missing in Action" franchises.
In the 1990s, he took over the small screen, playing the lead in the "Walker, Texas Ranger" TV show, which aired in over 100 countries during its run from 1993 to 2001.
Norris was hospitalized on March 19 in Hawaii and died the following day, according to his family. No cause was given.
Catherine O'Hara, 71
O'Hara, who was best known for her roles in "Beetlejuice" and "Home Alone," got her start in the Canadian comedy scene, appearing in the now-legendary cast of "SCTV."
It would mark the beginning of a fruitful partnership with fellow actor Eugene Levy, who became her frequent costar and collaborator in memorable appearances in Christopher Guest films like "A Mighty Wind" and "Best in Show" and television series like "Schitt's Creek," which earned her an Emmy Award for outstanding lead actress in 2020.
O'Hara's representation confirmed her death to Business Insider on January 30. Los Angeles County Department of Public Health confirmed in a death certificate viewed by People that O'Hara died of a pulmonary embolism, with rectal cancer listed as an underlying cause.
Hayden Panettiere, 36
Panettiere began acting as a child, landing one of her earliest major roles as Sarah Roberts on the ABC soap opera "One Life to Live," on which she appeared from 1994 to 1997.
As her career progressed, she became best known for portraying Claire Bennet on "Heroes" and Juliette Barnes on "Nashville."
Over the years, Panettiere had spoken openly about her struggles with alcoholism and postpartum depression. She detailed those experiences in her memoir, "This Is Me: A Reckoning," which was released in May.
Her representative confirmed to Business Insider on August 17 that Panettiere had died at 36 but did not disclose a cause of death.
Dolly Parton, 80
Parton released her debut album, "Hello, I'm Dolly," in 1967 and went on to pen country hits like "I Will Always Love You" and "Jolene," both of which were released as singles in 1974.
In addition to her music, Parton was beloved for her flamboyant style and her philanthropy. She founded the Dollywood Foundation in 1988, a charitable organization focused on education and community initiatives in her home state of Tennessee. She continued to fund scholarship programs and donate to hospitals, public health initiatives, and disaster relief programs throughout her life.
Parton is known as the best-selling female country music artist of all time. She was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 1999, the Songwriters Hall of Fame in 2001, and the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2022.
Parton's 49th and final solo studio album, "Rockstar," was released in 2023. The tracklist included both original material and covers of classic rock songs, featuring an array of guests like Paul McCartney, Ringo Starr, Sting, Joan Jett, and Parton's goddaughter, Miley Cyrus.
News broke on August 25 that Parton died following unspecified health issues. She was 80.
Vincent Pastore, 80
This character actor found fame appearing in a string of mob movies in the 1990s, like "Goodfellas," "Carlito's Way," and "Men of Respect." But Pastore truly became a star when he was cast in the hit HBO series "The Sopranos."
As Salvatore "Big Pussy" Bonpensiero, Pastore was part of the main cast for the first two seasons of the show, playing Tony Soprano's mob enforcer-turned-FBI informant. Bonpensiero's shocking death was one of the most famous in the show's history and proved that no one was safe from getting whacked.
Pastore died on August 1. No cause was given.
Valerie Perrine, 82
Perrine found herself cast alongside the biggest stars of the 1970s.
She played the love interest opposite Jeff Bridges in 1973's "The Last American Hero" and Robert Redford in 1979's "The Electric Horseman." She earned an Oscar nomination for starring alongside Dustin Hoffman in 1974's "Lenny."
For most, she'll be remembered best for sharing the screen with Gene Hackman as the secretary to his evil Lex Luthor in 1978's "Superman." She also starred in the sequel. As Ms. Teschmacher, her loyalty to Luthor is questioned when she rescues Superman (Christopher Reeve) after he's chained with Kryptonite.
Perrine died in her home in Beverly Hills on March 23. She was diagnosed with Parkinson's disease in 2015.
Sonny Rollins, 95
One of the most influential jazz musicians in history, Rollins recorded more than 60 albums over his seven-decade career.
His live album, "A Night at the Village Vanguard," is considered one of the greatest jazz albums ever made.
Rollins died on May 25; no cause was given.
Neil Sedaka, 86
Sedaka is responsible for some of the biggest pop songs of the 1960s and 1970s.
The Brooklyn native wrote over 500 songs, including classic hits like "Laughter in the Rain," "Breaking Up Is Hard to Do," "Bad Blood" and the Captain & Tennille song, "Love Will Keep Us Together."
Sedaka died on February 27; no cause was given.
Gene Shalit, 100
Before there was Rotten Tomatoes or even Siskel & Ebert, movie lovers got their recommendations from Gene Shalit.
The iconic movie critic could be seen sporting his signature look of glasses, bushy hair, and big mustache as a staple on the "Today" show from 1973 to 2010. If he wasn't interviewing the biggest movie stars, he was reviewing movies with incredible puns ("'Ishtar' is Ish-terrible.")
His larger-than-life presence left a mark on pop culture: he was parodied as a Muppet and on countless episodes of "SCTV" and "Saturday Night Live."
Shalit died on June 12; no cause was given.
Duncan Sheik, 56
Sheik found success in the late 1990s with his hit song "Barely Breathing." He later pivoted from alt-rock to a career on Broadway, composing the music for the Tony-winning musical "Spring Awakening." His other stage credits include "American Psycho" (2013) and "The Secret Life of Bees" (2019).
Sheik died on September 17 after a cardiac arrest.
Kiki Shepard, 74
In her 15-year tenure as a co-host on "Showtime at the Apollo," Kiki Shepard was considered royalty at Harlem's famed Apollo Theater.
Known in the building as "Apollo Queen of Fashion" thanks to her dazzling outfits, Shepherd was a fixture on the show from 1987 to 2002.
Throughout her career, Shepard also appeared on TV shows like "Baywatch," "A Different World," "NYPD Blue," and "Grey's Anatomy."
Shepard died on March 16 after suffering a heart attack.
Gloria Steinem, 92
An icon in the women's liberation movement of the 1970s, Steinem dedicated most of her life to fighting sexism.
Starting her career as a journalist, she became a columnist for the newly founded New York Magazine in 1968. She cofounded Ms. magazine in 1971, which focused on women's issues. She also helped launch the Women's Action Alliance, which focused on tackling sexism.
Steinem was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2013.
Steinem died on September 2, according to a post on her social media. No cause was given.
Béla Tarr, 70
Hungarian filmmaker Béla Tarr became a legend in the arthouse world for his unflinching work featuring several-minute-long takes.
With movies like "Family Nest" (1979) and "The Turin Horse" (2011), Tarr showcased his slow cinema style while focusing on marginalized characters living bleak lives. Tarr pushed the envelope with his style when he made "Sátántangó" in 1994, which had a run time of 450 minutes.
His work influenced several arthouse filmmakers, including Jim Jarmusch and Gus Van Sant's "Death Trilogy" ("Gerry," "Elephant," and "Last Days").
Tarr died on January 6 following a battle with a "long and serious illness."
James Tolkan, 94
You might not recognize the name, but if you're a movie fan, you know the face.
Tolkan's tough-guy persona made a mark on movie history in films like "Top Gun" and the "Back to the Future" franchise.
In "Top Gun," he played Commander Tom "Stinger" Jardian, who famously gives Tom Cruise's character a tongue lashing, saying, "Your ego is writing checks your body can't cash."
In "Back to the Future" and its sequels, he played Principal Strickland, who had zero tolerance for "slackers."
Other credits include "Serpico," "WarGames," "Masters of the Universe," and "Dick Tracy."
Tolkan died on March 26; no cause was given.
Ted Turner, 87
Ted Turner changed the television landscape thanks to his maverick maneuvers to harness the 24-hour news cycle.
After taking over his father's advertising company in the 1960s at the age of 24, Turner embarked on a path to change the media landscape by buying up radio and TV stations around the South. He even bought sports teams including the Atlanta Braves MLB team and the Atlanta Hawks NBA team.
All of that programming would eventually become part of TBS, a "super station" that showed old movies, reruns, and Braves and Hawks games.
Turner then set his sights on the news. He founded CNN, the first 24-hour news channel, in June of 1980.
Over the decades, Turner gained celebrity status, particularly after marrying with Jane Fonda, a union that lasted from 1991 to 2001. In 1991, he was named Time's "Man of the Year." He sold his networks to Time Warner for $7.5 billion in 1996.
Turner died on May 6; no cause was given.
Bonnie Tyler, 75
Welsh singer Bonnie Tyler became one of the biggest artists of the 1980s thanks to her legendary power ballads.
Tyler was behind hits like "Total Eclipse of the Heart" and "Holding Out for a Hero," which was also featured on the 1984 "Footloose" soundtrack. Both songs were chart-toppers that have since become two of the best-selling singles of all time.
Over her career, Tyler was nominated for three Grammys and was appointed a Member of the Order of the British Empire (MBE) by Queen Elizabeth II in 2022.
Tyler died on July 8 in Portugal, where she was being treated for an illness, according to a statement posted on her social media.
James Van Der Beek, 48
Van Der Beek was beloved all over the world for his role as the titular teen Dawson Leery on the WB series "Dawson's Creek."
The series, which ran from 1998 to 2002, turned Van Der Beek into a star and a teen heartthrob. While "Dawson's Creek" was still airing, he'd cement his stardom playing the lead role of high school quarterback "Mox" Moxon in the 1999 coming-of-age drama "Varsity Blues."
Van Der Beek found steady work the rest of his career in movies like "Texas Rangers" and "The Rules of Attraction, and memorably played a fictional version of himself on the TV series "Don't Trust the B---- in Apartment 23," and performed on "Dancing with the Stars" in 2019.
Van Der Beek learned he had stage 3 colon cancer in 2023, and publicly announced his diagnosis in late 2024.
Van Der Beek previously told Business Insider that the news came as a shock, given the subtleness of his symptoms and his efforts to stay as healthy as possible.
"I was doing everything," he said. "I was doing sauna, cold plunge, weightlifting, Pilates. I would dance and also do football training."
Van Der Beek died on Feb. 11.
Bob Weir, 78
Weir was one of the founding members of the Grateful Dead.
The singer-songwriter wrote and/or sang on songs like "Sugar Magnolia," "Playing in the Band," "Truckin,'" "I Need a Miracle," and "The Other One."
After the Grateful Dead disbanded in 1995, Weir went on to form several other bands, including Kingfish, Bobby and the Midnites, RatDog, The Other Ones, and, alongside John Mayer, Dead & Company.
In the summer of 2025, Weir was diagnosed with cancer.
Weir died on January 10.
Victor Willis, 74
Willis was the lead singer of the iconic disco band the Village People.
Along with being the lead vocalist and dressing as the police officer (and sometimes naval officer), Willis was also the cowriter on many of the band's hits, including "In the Navy," "Macho Man," and the song that will keep the Village People in pop culture lore until the end of time, "Y.M.C.A."
Willis left the band to embark on a solo career in 1979, then re-formed the Village People in 2017.
Willis died on June 30 following a "short but aggressive illness," according to the Village People Facebook page.
Frederick Wiseman, 96
For over five decades, Wiseman's brand of non-fiction storytelling put a spotlight on everyday people.
From high schoolers to hospital workers to Air Force cadets training for nuclear war, Wiseman's close to 50-film catalogue is an unvarnished reflection of America over the last half century.
Wiseman died on Februay 16, no cause was given.

RFK Jr switches gears from anti-vaxx promotion to amplify 5G conspiracy theory
The conspiracy theory, which got its start in the pandemic, has long been debunked
The Robert F. Kennedy Jr -led Health and Human Services Department, which has been working to limit vaccines, is now targeting 5G networks with a callout for the public’s comments on potential health effects related to the debunked theory.
A statement, posted by HHS this week, asked that Americans share information related to potential exposure to electromagnetic fields and wireless radiation associated with cellphones and a long list of other smart devices including Wi-Fi, smart meters, wireless infrastructure, wearable technologies, wireless medical devices and autonomous vehicles.
HHS said the comments will help to identify gaps in research and strengthen rules designed to protect Americans’ health.
5G, the most advanced cellular network which connects devices to the internet, was launched nationwide in December 2019. Three months later, Covid-19 cases exploded across the country, and a conspiracy theory began making the rounds online that 5G was spreading the virus. In 2018 - before 5G was released - people had alleged it was tied to cancer cases.
RFK Jr., a prominent voice for other debunked claims on the role of vaccines in autism and chemtrails, has previously said he is concerned about the impacts of 5G.
“Generally speaking, electromagnetic radiation is a major health concern,” Kennedy told USA TODAY in January, when asked for his thoughts about 5G towers. “I’m very concerned about it.”
He also claimed in the same interview there are “literally over 10,000 studies” that document a number of ill effects from electromagnetic radiation, including cancer, tumor growth and opening the blood-brain barrier.
But the link has been widely disproven. A 2024 review of 63 peer-reviewed, academic studies which examined potential links between cellphones and cancer found no justification for health concerns, according to the World Health Organization.
The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, which falls under the HHS umbrella of agencies, also states it does “not have the science to link health problems to cell phone use.”
“The MAHA [Make America Healthy Again] Strategy directed HHS to examine electromagnetic radiation and health research, and this RFI delivers on that commitment,” HHS Press Secretary Grace Davis Jamison department told The Independent on Friday.
The callout came as Kennedy spoke to anti-vaccine group Children’s Health Defense - a group he founded, which has sought to combat the installation of cell towers - telling the organization they have “a friend in the White House.”

Gender disparity in organ transplantation is a global problem affecting each step of the transplantation process, from organ donation, recipient listing, waiting times and access, to post-transplant outcomes. This inequality is most visibly expressed in the overrepresentation of women as living donors, while men continue to be the majority of transplant recipients.
What the data reveals
India’s case is a particularly striking example of this gender imbalance. Women constitute the majority of living organ donors, but men get the majority of transplants. As per recent data from the National Organ and Tissue Transplant Organization (NOTTO), between 2019 and 2023, 63.8% of living organ donors were women and 69.8% of transplant recipients were men.
This is not a new divide. In 2019 and 2020, roughly two-thirds of living donors were women, but only about a quarter of recipients were women. A 2025 analysis found that women accounted for 36,038 of the 56,509 living donations over the five-year period studied, also highlighting the scale of the imbalance. Of these, however, only 17,041 were transplanted into women, as against 39,447 transplanted into men.
This gendered pattern raises a fundamental question: why are women expected to give and men positioned to receive in disproportionate numbers? The answer goes far beyond biology.
Behind the donations
Women’s decisions to donate organs are shaped by a complicated interaction between sociocultural expectations, economic conditions and family structures. In many Indian homes, women, particularly wives and mothers, are still expected to put the needs of their families before their own. The expectation can be particularly sharp in the case of a life-saving transplant for a close family member.
Studies have noted the role of women in familial organ donation. Mothers are, on average, 73% of all parental donations, and wives are 91% of donations between married couples. These figures are suggestive of a long-standing social tendency to assign the bulk of care work to women, and perhaps even to the final act of bodily sacrifice.
Psychological and experiential reasons may also play a role in women’s higher willingness to donate. Past experiences with the health care system, such as pregnancy and delivery, may increase familiarity with medical settings and trust in health care providers. But these explanations have to be discussed in the light of the strong influence of social conditioning. What seems like a personal choice can sometimes be influenced by expectations, emotional duties or an unspoken belief that a woman should make sacrifices for her family.
Patriarchal attitudes can also be a disincentive for men to become donors. Men are generally considered the primary breadwinner and economic provider for their families. Thus, the prospect of a man needing major surgery, a long recovery period or a temporary loss of income might be seen as an unacceptable financial risk. Such pressure can transfer the burden of donation to women.
This dynamic is particularly problematic when financial dependency is a factor. The costs of evaluation, surgery, recovery and the potential loss of household income may make male donation seem less feasible. In such cases, women may be subtly, and in more troubling cases, explicitly encouraged to donate, because they are seen as more expendable in the family’s economic structure. Thus, the line between voluntary altruism and coercion can become perilously blurred.
It is, therefore, the duty of healthcare providers to fully discuss these issues at every stage of the process, explain the ramifications of a donation and t ensure that they are indeed personal choices of women, and not influenced by other factors.
What needs to change
This has implications for more than just transplant statistics. Essentially, it’s a question of equity, autonomy and justice in healthcare. An organ donation system cannot be truly equitable when it is based on social and familial pressures about who is supposed to donate, and on socioeconomic or structural barriers about who gets the transplant.
Interventions are required at several levels to address this gap. Awareness must be the starting point, but awareness is not enough. Transplant services and community-based initiatives should be extended to rural, underserved and marginalised regions and not be confined to major urban centres. In particular, women should have equal access to information, evaluation and transplantation services.
Equally important is strengthening psychosocial assessment of potential living donors. Pre-transplant evaluation should not only include medical suitability and financial considerations, but also explore the wider social environment in which the donation decision is being made. Healthcare professionals should be trained to recognise warning signs of coercion, domestic abuse, threats, violence, manipulation and financial dependence. Donors must be provided with real opportunities to make informed and voluntary decisions, including the opportunity to withdraw without fear of repercussions.
Better and more comprehensive data collection is also needed in India. Good, disaggregated data on donors and recipients – disaggregated by gender, age, socioeconomic status, geography, relationship to recipient and other relevant factors, would enable policymakers to better identify disparities and design evidence-based interventions. Grassroots research is important because national averages can hide significant inequalities at the regional and community level.
The challenge is to move beyond the financial transaction of organ donation, and to acknowledge the quieter pressures that can exist within families. Sometimes coercion doesn’t take the form of an explicit threat. It could be the expectations of a wife, the responsibilities of a mother or the assumption that a woman should sacrifice herself for the family’s survival.
The bigger message is hard to miss: gender inequality does not stop at the hospital door. It can influence who gives, who gets, who waits and ultimately who gets a chance to live.
(Dr Shivakumar S. Patil is consultant, renal transplant surgery, Manipal Hospital, Hebbal. shivakumar.patil@manipalhospitals.com)

Pawar cites El Niño-induced deficient rain in Maharashtra, says declare drought
Former Union minister Sharad Pawar sought at least ₹50,000 per hectare for farmers and ₹25,000 for every farm labour family
Former Union minister Sharad Pawar on Friday cited deficient rainfall and asked the Maharashtra government to declare a drought due to the El Niño effect, which is primarily associated with a weak monsoon and below-normal rain in India. He sought a comprehensive relief package for farmers and the rural population.
In a letter to chief minister Devendra Fadnavis, Pawar sought at least ₹50,000 per hectare for farmers and ₹25,000 for every farm labour family. He called for an immediate farm loan waiver and fresh crop loans. Pawar argued that the government should not wait for formal drought assessment criteria when parts of the state are facing severe conditions.
A crop damage assessment is scheduled to begin on October 5 as per the National Disaster Response Force guidelines.
Pawar said inadequate rainfall had damaged soybean, cotton, bajra, maize, tur, moong and urad crops in 31 of the 36 districts. He added that pest and disease attacks had also increased. Pawar warned the situation could further aggravate problems related to drinking water and fodder.
Pawar sought direct financial assistance to protect the rural economy. He asked the government to address a growing debt burden on farmers. “The loan waiver scheme should be implemented immediately, and crop loans should be made available without delay.”
He sought an increase in the incentive for farmers who regularly repay their loans from ₹50,000 to ₹1 lakh. He called for including farmers who took crop loans in 2025-26 and defaulted in the loan-waiver scheme.
Pawar demanded retrospective implementation of the ₹1 premium scheme and restoration of farmer-friendly triggers that had earlier been excluded from the crop insurance. He sought immediate disbursal of the ₹17,000 per hectare assistance announced for crop losses caused by unseasonal rains last year.
“Special schemes should be implemented through the Employment Guarantee Scheme in drought-like areas, including agriculture and water-conservation works,” Pawar said. He added that tanker arrangements should also be made to protect orchards.
Pawar demanded immediate surveys of villages facing drinking-water shortages. He said fodder camps should be opened based on demand. Pawar said drinking water and veterinary services should be ensured for livestock.
Pawar cited the uneven rainfall deficit and data to underline the severity of the situation. He said Marathwada recorded a 69% rain shortfall from June to August. Pawar added the deficit was 61% in Vidarbha and 33% in Konkan. Parts of western and northern Maharashtra reported rainfall deficits of up to 28%.
Pawar referred to data showing the rainfall shortfall coincided with a contraction in the area under sowing in some regions. In Vidarbha, the area sown by the end of August fell from 50.04 lakh hectares last year to around 47.5 lakh hectares this year. In Marathwada, the sown area dropped from 48.21 lakh hectares to 46.19 lakh hectares over the same period.
Pawar cited World Meteorological Organisation data to flag the possibility of the El Niño phenomenon exerting a greater impact in the coming years, saying its effects could become more pronounced from 2027.
A presentation made before the state Cabinet on Tuesday said 20 of 36 districts recorded a rainfall deficit of at least 20% during the monsoon. Many areas did not get any rain for over 30 consecutive days, damaging Kharif crops and worsening the water crisis.
The presentation said Maharashtra received 632.5 mm of rainfall during the monsoon against its average monsoon rainfall of 866.4 mm, a deficit of 27%. Twenty districts recorded a rainfall deficit of upwards of 20%. Affected areas included six of eight districts in the drought-prone Marathwada region, and four out of five districts in the Amaravati division, a farmer suicide-prone area.
Pawar flagged the possibility of worsening power-supply problems. He sought a special drive to complete repairs of faulty transformers and prevent prolonged load-shedding.

The Eiffel Tower has reopened after a one-day strike was called in response to the landmark’s management ordering female staff to keep out of sight at the request of a visiting religious group.
City Hall, which operates the Paris landmark, has apologised for breaching France’s republican principle of equality and ordered a full inquiry.
Workers at the tower walked out on Monday, closing the landmark to visitors, after female colleagues were sidelined and replaced during a visit organised by a Hindu religious group at the weekend.
In a statement, staff said they objected to “professional instructions that led to female employees being sidelined, replaced and made invisible because of their sex” during the visit.
“Some were asked to leave their posts and wait in separate rooms. In some posts, women were replaced by men. All female employees were instructed not to pass through or enter certain areas while the [Hindu] delegation was present,” they said in a statement.
Employees said they were shocked to find themselves in a situation that was “deeply contrary to the values of equality and nondiscrimination”.
“The Eiffel Tower is the symbol of France. We believe it must also be exemplary in the values it promotes and the way it treats staff,” the statement said.
The Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) spiritual movement, whose members made the request in advance of a visit on Saturday, apologised.
“To our knowledge, nobody was refused access to the Eiffel Tower at any moment. Nevertheless, We offer our sincere apologies to anyone who may have been hurt or offended by this situation,” it wrote in a statement.
BAPS is close to India’s ruling Hindu nationalist party, Bharatiya Janata, and was in France to consecrate its first major temple in the country on Sunday.
The public-owned Eiffel Tower operating company (SETE) acknowledged that BAPS had requested that “interactions with women” be limited, and said it should not have accepted these conditions. “They are not in keeping with SETE’s values or the principles of equality between women and men and the neutrality that must guide the organisation of visits to the monument,” it said.
Emmanuel Grégoire, the mayor of Paris, has promised an investigation to “get to the bottom of this as soon as possible”.
He said moving female staff out of sight was unacceptable.
“These are not my values nor those the Eiffel Tower must represent,” he wrote on X.
Ariel Weil, mayor of the Paris Centre district and president of SETE, said he was unaware of the “shocking and unacceptable” conditions afforded the visiting group.
“I confirm again the Eiffel Tower’s commitment to republican values and gender equality,” he said.

Scammers have been inserting fake songs onto real artist's pages on Spotify and other platforms
A distribution loophole lets them collect royalties.
Bad actors have been uploading fake songs onto real artist's pages on Spotify and other platforms, according to a report by 404 Media. The scheme is fairly simple. They use generative AI to whip up slop songs and then take advantage of a distribution loophole to insert them directly onto a pre-existing artist's catalog.
The loophole even gives them access to proceeds generated from the tracks, as the money does not go to the original artist. The payout is also likely to be much higher than with typical AI slop, as the fake track is co-opting an artist's name and profile page.
it is shockingly easy to post AI generated music under the name of real artists on Spotify. It took us five minutes to do. You can do it to small bands, dead artists, even Taylor Swift. This is a giant loophole in digital music distribution that's widely abused www.404media.co/spotify-ai-m...
— Emanuel Maiberg (@emanuelmaiberg.bsky.social) 2026-09-17T13:39:28.579Z
Here's how it works, which was confirmed by 404 Media as they tested the process with the Brooklyn band Lathe of Heaven. The scammer makes a slop song via something like Suno or Udio. Next, they use generative AI to whip up an album cover. Finally, they sign up for a digital music distribution service, like DistroKid (the service 4040 Media used in its test). Once the song is uploaded, they just lie and say they are a real band and the platform does the rest.
Before too long, the song shows up on Spotify, Tidal, Apple Music, Amazon Music and other streaming services as an actual new track from the real artist. All it takes is a willingness to make stuff up and the ability to check a few boxes on a website. Neither the distribution service or the streaming platform catches the error, so the song is allowed to garner wages for the scammer and ruin the reputation of the artist.
As always, smaller artists are more vulnerable to these scams. That's because famous musicians often have teams of people checking for this type of thing. It's also become an issue for dead artists, which is pretty gross. Spotify confirmed to 404 Media that "profiles that aren't actively managed can be especially vulnerable."
"Being able to enjoy the process of creating something and putting it out into the world knowing it is distinctly a product of our own hands is essentially one of the last driving forces behind making music," Lathe of Heaven's vocalist told 404 Media. "The fact that someone could ruin our reputation by dropping this cringe garbage under our name is insanely disheartening and speaks volumes about distribution and streaming services that allow this to happen."
The musical group Odette Child began keeping track of the problem back in July and have since found more than 300 AI-generated songs pretending to be from major acts like Taylor Swift, random celebrities, dead jazz musicians and just about everything in between. The loophole existed before AI slop began taking over music-streaming platforms, but now it's a matter of scale. It's one thing to create a dummy song on your own and upload it pretending to be someone else. It's another thing to use generative AI to quickly "create" and upload hundreds in a day.
Spotify is working on a tool that lets musicians review releases before they go live and become associated with their profiles, but it's still in a limited beta. This feature was first announced all the way back in March. Statistics vary, but it's been estimated that around 50,000 AI-generated songs get uploaded to Spotify every single day.
"We can just see very clearly that they are not interested in the best possible solution to this problem," Odette Child said. "We need some sort of infrastructure that can protect us from this as consumers, listeners and especially as artists."
Spotify has said that "protecting artists' identities is a top priority for us, and we continue to invest heavily in detection and prevention." It also said that it's "working directly with distributors to stop bad submissions at the source," which could mean that this loophole eventually gets closed.
Amazon Music issued some corporate speak and said it's "committed to continuously improving our enforcement through advanced detection technologies and refined monitoring systems, and we're in regular dialogue with partners and rights holders to ensure we're protecting artists' and songwriters' interests as the landscape evolves."
It's not as if these platforms have been sitting idly by. They have been taking steps to address the issue, but these steps don't seem to be working. Spotify has a new verification badge that confirms a song is not AI-generated. It has also introduced a spam filter that looks for "mass uploads, duplicates, SEO hacks, artificially short track abuse and other forms of slop"

Yemen has long been described as the graveyard of Saudi ambition. And this month Riyadh learnt its latest lesson.
For more than a decade, the kingdom has spent billions of dollars, deployed advanced weapons and invested enormous political capital in trying to contain the Houthi movement on its southern border. What began as a northern Yemeni insurgency has developed into a formidable military force capable of launching missiles and drones across the region and threatening one of the world's most important shipping routes.
The latest setback came this month, when Houthi forces captured the Red Sea port of Mocha and then advanced towards the strategic island of Perim, also known as Mayyun, at the mouth of the Bab el-Mandeb strait.
Mocha was not the whole story. It was the door to a much bigger one.
The Houthi advance has brought the group closer to one of the world's most important maritime chokepoints at a time when 
Saudi Arabia
 is already dealing with disruption around the Strait of Hormuz and attacks on its energy infrastructure. For Riyadh, a war that once looked like a campaign to defeat a relatively weak neighbour has become a problem involving shipping, oil, national security and regional influence.
A decade of war has transformed the Houthis from a local insurgency into a force capable of threatening Saudi Arabia, Israel and international shipping
The question is no longer simply why Saudi Arabia has struggled to defeat the Houthis. It is why its enormous military and financial advantages have failed to produce a lasting political and military victory.
What is happening now
The latest escalation comes amid a wider Middle East conflict, with the US and Israel fighting Iran. What we know about the Houthi attack:
- Mocha falls: Houthi forces captured the Red Sea port of Mocha in September, expanding their control along Yemen's western coast.
- Perim comes next: The Houthis then moved onto Perim, an island sitting inside the Bab el-Mandeb strait, bringing them closer to a vital global shipping route.
- Saudi oil routes face pressure: With the Strait of Hormuz disrupted by the wider regional conflict, Saudi Arabia has relied more heavily on its East-West Pipeline to move crude to the Red Sea. The pipeline was subsequently hit by a drone strike linked to Iran-aligned forces elsewhere in the region.
- The war reaches Saudi Arabia: Houthi missiles and drones have continued to target Saudi territory and energy infrastructure, including the Jazan area. Saudi authorities also reported intercepting a drone approaching the southern sector of Mecca, an incident the Houthis denied was a deliberate attempt to target the holy city.
- Riyadh has not returned to ground war: Saudi Arabia has responded with air strikes and defensive operations but has so far avoided a major ground intervention.
The war that never really ended
The roots of the current crisis go back much further than 2015.
The Houthis, formally known as Ansar Allah, emerged from a Zaydi revivalist movement in northern Yemen during the 1990s. Zaydism is a branch of Shia Islam with deep roots in Yemen, particularly in the country's north.
The movement grew partly in opposition to the spread of Saudi-backed Salafi religious influence in Yemen. During the 2000s, the Houthis fought several wars against the Yemeni government and developed a growing military organisation.
In 2014, the movement captured Sanaa and forced President Abd Rabbu Mansour Hadi's government out of the capital. The Houthis then expanded southwards.
The biggest weakness in the anti-Houthi camp has often been political rather than military: the forces opposing the Houthis have rarely shared the same vision for Yemen.
Saudi Arabia saw the rise of the movement as a direct security threat. A hostile force with links to Iran was now controlling large parts of the country next door.
In March 2015, Saudi Arabia assembled a coalition and launched Operation Decisive Storm. The objective was to restore the internationally recognised government and push the Houthis back.
The campaign began with overwhelming Saudi and coalition air power. But the expected quick victory never came.
Saudi aircraft could destroy weapons depots, command centres and military positions. What they could not do was create a stable political order on the ground. Yemeni forces fighting the Houthis were divided, while the Houthis adapted to the campaign and became increasingly experienced.
The war dragged on for years.
A UN-brokered truce in 2022 brought a major reduction in fighting. It did not produce a final political settlement. Instead, the conflict entered a period of uneasy calm.
For Saudi Arabia, the truce froze a conflict in which the kingdom had failed to restore the Yemeni government to power across the country.
Why Saudi Arabia could not turn military power into victory
Saudi Arabia has some of the most advanced military equipment in the region. It operates sophisticated US-made fighter aircraft, precision-guided weapons and missile defence systems.
Yet the Yemen war exposed a basic problem with military power.
An insurgency cannot normally be defeated through air strikes alone.
Saudi Arabia has the weapons. The harder problem has been turning that firepower into victory
Air power can destroy targets. It cannot hold a town after the bombs stop falling. It cannot build a functioning government, persuade local communities to support an unpopular administration or settle rival political claims.
That problem became particularly severe in Yemen because Saudi Arabia did not have a single, unified Yemeni partner capable of taking territory and holding it.
Instead, the anti-Houthi camp has been deeply divided.
The internationally recognised government has struggled with internal disputes. The Southern Transitional Council, backed by the United Arab Emirates, wants greater autonomy and has long pushed for southern independence. Other forces, including the National Resistance Forces and Islah-linked groups, have their own interests and networks.
Saudi Arabia and the UAE have also backed different actors at different points in the war.
That rivalry matters because defeating the Houthis requires more than driving them away from a particular battlefield. Someone has to take control afterwards.
If the forces fighting the Houthis disagree about what Yemen should look like, military victories become difficult to turn into lasting political gains.
The Houthis have benefited from precisely this weakness.
They have had years to develop military experience while their opponents have spent much of the same period fighting among themselves.
That is one reason the latest loss of territory is significant. The problem is not simply that the Houthis are advancing. It is that there is no obvious unified force capable of reversing those gains and then governing the territory.
How a rebel movement built a modern arsenal
The Houthis Saudi Arabia first fought in 2015 were a very different force from the one now threatening the Red Sea.
When the movement seized Sanaa in 2014, it inherited large quantities of weapons from Yemen's collapsing military, including Soviet-era missiles and other ageing systems. The Houthis had fighters, experience and a huge stock of weapons, but they were still primarily a local insurgency.
A decade of war changed that.
The Houthis received training and technical assistance from Iran and Hezbollah, while adapting their tactics through years of fighting. A 2025 UN report found evidence of both domestic weapons production and Iranian technical assistance, while Reuters reported this week that the group now has an estimated 350,000 fighters.
The Houthis' growing self-reliance has made them harder to contain, allowing Tehran to provide critical technology while the group develops much of the rest of its war machine locally
Iran remains crucial, particularly for sophisticated missile technology and key components. But the Houthis have become increasingly capable of assembling and producing weapons inside Yemen. According to The New York Times, larger components such as missile chassis are now manufactured in Houthi-controlled territory, while parts can be sourced through complex international smuggling networks.
That has made the group harder to cripple through sanctions, blockades or attacks on individual weapons shipments. Components can be moved separately through commercial supply chains and assembled later.
The result is an arsenal that bears little resemblance to the force Saudi Arabia encountered at the start of the war. Houthi ballistic missiles have reached Israel, more than 1,000 miles away, while anti-ship missiles and naval drones have allowed the group to threaten commercial vessels in the Red Sea. Drones have also become an increasingly important part of its battlefield operations inside Yemen.
The Houthis are also experimenting with newer technologies. 
The New York Times
 reported that an Anthropic investigation identified a group in northern Yemen using AI tools in an effort to develop guided weapons. Anthropic said there was no evidence that an operational weapon had ultimately been produced, but the episode showed the group's willingness to use new technology to expand its capabilities.
Iranian support helped transform the Houthis' arsenal, but the movement has increasingly learned to adapt, assemble and produce weapons inside Yemen
There is another source of strength: the battlefield itself. Years of fighting have given the Houthis experience in missile warfare, drones, infiltration, mining and attacks on shipping. The 2022 ceasefire then gave them time to regroup, recruit and expand their military infrastructure.
Their recent advance has added another advantage. As Saudi-backed forces retreated from the Red Sea coast, they abandoned or lost American- and Saudi-supplied vehicles, weapons and other equipment. Reuters reported that the Houthis captured some of this hardware during their advance.
The transformation is therefore not simply about getting more weapons from Iran. It is about learning how to make, modify, smuggle, deploy and replace them.
That is what makes the Houthis such a difficult opponent for Saudi Arabia. Riyadh is no longer fighting a lightly armed mountain insurgency. It is confronting a battle-hardened military organisation with domestic production networks, a large pool of fighters, long-range strike capabilities and a decade of experience adapting to a far richer enemy
The Saudi-UAE rivalry has made the problem worse
One of the most damaging weaknesses in the anti-Houthi camp has been the rivalry between Saudi Arabia and the UAE.
Both countries entered the Yemen war on the same side, but their interests in Yemen have never been identical.
Saudi Arabia has generally wanted a Yemeni government capable of maintaining the country's territorial unity and preventing a hostile force from controlling the north.
The UAE has built strong relationships with southern forces, including the Southern Transitional Council, which supports southern independence.
Those competing interests have repeatedly produced tensions within the anti-Houthi camp.
Saudi Arabia has also sought to strengthen its own preferred Yemeni partners, including Islah-linked forces, while trying to limit the influence of groups backed by Abu Dhabi.
The result has been a complicated network of alliances in which forces that share an enemy do not necessarily share the same political objective.
For the Houthis, that fragmentation is an advantage.
A united opponent could concentrate its military strength against Houthi positions. A divided one has to constantly balance the Houthi threat against disputes among its own members.
This is perhaps the clearest explanation for why Saudi military superiority has produced such limited results.
The kingdom has powerful weapons. It has not had a powerful, unified political partner in Yemen.
A problem for MBS and Vision 2030
For Mohammed bin Salman, the timing could hardly be more difficult.
The central promise of Vision 2030 is that Saudi Arabia can move beyond its dependence on oil and become a major hub for tourism, technology, investment and infrastructure.
That requires stability.
Saudi Arabia has spent years trying to present itself as a country moving beyond the conflicts that have defined much of the Middle East. It has hosted international sporting events, expanded tourism, attracted investment and positioned itself as a major economic power.
The Yemen war complicates that image.
The immediate economic threat is also clear. Any prolonged disruption to oil production or export routes can affect government revenue and complicate the enormous spending required by Vision 2030.
Yemen's old lesson
The deeper lesson from the Yemen war is not that military power does not matter. It is that military power has limits when there is no political structure capable of turning battlefield gains into lasting control.
Saudi Arabia can destroy Houthi weapons. It can intercept missiles. It can launch devastating air strikes.
What it has struggled to do is create a unified Yemeni force capable of defeating the Houthis, hold the territory afterwards and build a political settlement that the country's competing factions will accept.
The Houthis, meanwhile, have used years of war to become stronger, more experienced and more deeply embedded in Yemen's political and military landscape.
That leaves Riyadh facing a conflict it once expected to settle quickly but has instead helped transform into a regional security problem.
The kingdom's wealth has bought it some of the world's most advanced weapons. It has not bought it an easy victory.
In Yemen, geography, local politics and military adaptation have repeatedly proved more powerful than the size of a defence budget.
And once again, Yemen is living up to its reputation as the place where Saudi ambitions go to die.

The US state department said on Wednesday that it had again denied entry visas to Palestinian officials ahead next week’s United Nations general assembly gathering in New York.
The state department said in a statement that the Palestinian Authority (PA) and the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO) had “failed to live up to their commitments”, accusing the groups of “taking actions to internationalize the Israeli-Palestinian Conflict including through the International Criminal Court (ICC) and International Court of Justice (ICJ)” and of “glorifying terrorism” among other allegations.
“As a consequence of their failure to reform, contrary to their commitments to the United States, and their ongoing activities that undermine the prospects for peace, the United States will extend sanctions that deny visas to PLO members and PA officials,” the department said.
The move marks the second year in a row that the Trump administration has barred the Palestinian delegation from traveling to New York to attend the UN general assembly in person.
The foreign ministry of the Palestinian Authority denied the allegations made against it by the state department in a statement on Thursday, describing the visa sanctions as an “unjustified measure” that “contradicts the efforts being made to restore trust, develop Palestinian-US relations, and prepare the necessary political climate for implementing the two-state solution and achieving peace and stability in the region”.
Among the Palestinian officials barred from entering the US is Mahmoud Abbas, the longtime president of the Palestinian Authority, according to reports. The UN general assembly is set to vote on a draft resolution on Thursday to allow Abbas to address the gathering remotely, according to two officials familiar with the planned vote, according to the New York Times. Last year, Abbas addressed the gathering by video conference.
This year’s UN general assembly general debate begins on 22 September.

Who Made America Poorer and Dirtier?
The people in charge are really hoping you’ll blame someone else.
At last week’s GOP midterm convention in Dallas, Vice President Vance painted a bleak picture of American life before the second Trump administration:
“Two years ago, we have to remember, our nation, ladies and gentlemen, was tired. We were tired of seeing our factories close. We were tired of our neighbors dying of drug overdoses. We were tired of not being able to afford anything. We were tired of seeing the cartels and the criminals given free rein over our great country,” Vance said. “And we were tired of being called racist for noticing that our country was becoming dirtier and poorer and less safe and less prosperous.”
Who is responsible for this terrible state of affairs? The opposition party and immigrants, apparently. Vance went on to say, “The Democrat legacy of the last few years was that they bankrupted our country and left us poor. They left our country weaker. They left our border wide open and our communities less safe.”
But this account represents a preposterous inversion. Almost every problem Vance lists, the Trump administration has made worse.
The administration’s environmental policies have made American water and air dirtier. Its health-care, tariff, and tax policies have worsened inflation and increased the financial burden on most American households, even as incomes have grown. And its public-health policies have led to outbreaks of contagious disease.
The Environmental Protection Agency under President Trump has revoked regulations on air pollution—including those on particulate matter that can cause heart and lung disease—after being intensely lobbied by the fossil-fuel industry. It has repealed limits on “forever chemicals” in drinking water, which are linked to cancer and other health problems. The Trump Justice Department scrapped a settlement compelling Alabama to provide adequate sanitation systems to residents living with raw sewage, describing it as “DEI.” After the residents of Jackson, Mississippi, learned they had been drinking lead-tainted tap water, a Trump-appointed federal judge ruled that Americans don’t have a constitutional right to clean drinking water.
Although Trump won the 2024 election largely because of Biden-era inflation, he has done everything in his power to make inflation worse. Trump’s arguably illegal and certainly ill-advised war in Iran has led to the closure of strategic shipping waterways, which has provoked a rise in energy prices, which has in turn raised the prices of other goods. Trump’s tariffs worsened inflation by raising the price of imports, and wages seem to be falling behind inflation. To make matters worse, health-care costs are rising rapidly, in part because of the Trump administration’s repeal of Affordable Care Act subsidies in its One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
Crime is down. But that’s not because of the Trump administration’s mass-deportation program, whose brutal and indiscriminate tactics have weakened the economy rather than strengthened it. The reality is that immigrants are far less likely than native-born Americans to commit crimes, and crime has been falling steadily since the pandemic-induced spike in 2020 and 2021. Absent significant changes to the space-time continuum, Trump cannot claim credit for a decline in crime that began before Trump even took office, especially with an FBI director who devotes bureau resources to respond to people mocking him on X.
Vance called out two women, one of whom was born in Somalia, who defrauded Medicaid of $46 million. Vladimir Putin has arrived in India’s capital of Delhi ahead of an 11-member Brics summit set to be dominated by wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, as well as economic challenges.
The Russian president and his Iranian counterpart, Masoud Pezeshkian, were due to hold talks with India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, while Chinese leader Xi Jinping was also expected to attend the two-day meeting.
Putin arrived at Palam air force Station in Delhi, where he was greeted by India’s minister of state for external affairs, Kirti Vardhan Singh, according to footage broadcast by Russia’s Ria Novosti news agency.
The summit will mark Xi’s first visit to India since 2019 and is seen as the biggest step yet in a cautious thaw between the rival neighbours, six years after a deadly military clash along their disputed Himalayan border.
Ties between the nuclear-armed Asian giants have been warming again recently, with flights, visas and high-level contacts gradually being restored.
However, deep mistrust remains, with their contested frontier, a widening trade deficit and strategic rivalry still complicating ties.
On Friday posters of a beaming Modi lined streets in Delhi, along with heavy deployments of security forces across the capital and widespread traffic restrictions in central districts. Delhi police have urged people to be patient and cooperative.
Brics was created in 2009 as a forum for major emerging economies seeking greater influence in institutions dominated by western powers.
It has since expanded and now includes Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, three countries with sharply differing positions on the war launched by the US and Israel in February.
“The Gulf conflict is going to be the central fault line this time during the Brics summit,” said Harsh V Pant of India’s Observer Research Foundation. “What was seen until last year as an achievement – the expansion of Brics – today looks like a big constraint on Brics”.
It will be Pezeshkian’s first visit to India as Iranian president, and will put the Middle East conflict firmly on the agenda.
“The war in Iran will provide a stern test of the [expanded] group’s cohesion,” said Shilan Shah of Capital Economics, noting the failure of the Brics foreign ministers to agree on a joint statement when they met in Delhi in May.
India maintains cordial relations with Iran and Israel, but is also careful to strike a delicate balance in its ties with Washington.
India has navigated the energy crisis caused by the Iran war in part by turning to Russia, one of its most important strategic partners and its most controversial fuel supplier in recent years as the war against Ukraine drags on.
Putin last visited India in December 2025 but he also met Modi in Bishkek, the capital of Kyrgyzstan, this month.
India’s foreign minister, Subrahmanyam Jaishankar, visited Kyiv this month, when the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said he was “grateful to India for its commitment to ending this unjust war”.

Only Celtic fans will be inside Parkhead at the order of the authorities amid a ticket allocation spat between the two Glasgow giants.
