In September 2026, Snopes readers searched this website for information about a video allegedly showing a 104-year-old woman named Mabel Rose Thompson chiding U.S. President Donald Trump.
A search located a Threads post (archived) from Sept. 15 displaying the clip with the onscreen caption, "At 104, I've Seen 18 Presidents. Trump Was the Most Unforgettable." That Threads post featured the TikTok watermark for a user who previously posted (archived) the video and garnered more than 2 million views.
The video begins with the elderly woman saying she's seen 18 presidents during her lifetime — a number that would mean, given her age, that Warren G. Harding would have been her first president:
Mabel Rose Thompson here. I'm 104 years old. I've seen 18 presidents sit in that office. And I'm going to tell you something that will make half of you furious and the other half want to buy me a drink.
Donald Trump was the worst man I have ever watched lead this country. Not because of taxes, not because of tariffs, not because of any policy you want to argue about at Thanksgiving. Because of character, because of what he did to the American heart. Because in 104 years, I have never seen a president who worked harder to make good people hate each other.
Now before you start typing, let me establish my credentials. I was born in 1922. I was 9 years old when Herbert Hoover was still in office. And I remember my father cursing his name at our kitchen table because the man couldn't stop the hunger. I was 20 when Franklin Roosevelt died. My mother wept at the radio. I was 41 when they shot Kennedy in Dallas. I was folding laundry when the news came on. I dropped a towel and didn't pick it up for an hour. I was 53 when Nixon got on that helicopter, waving that ridiculous double peace sign, flying away in shame.
I have voted in every single presidential election since 1944. I have lived under Democrats and Republicans and men so boring you forgot they were there. I have watched them all. And I am telling you plain, none of them, not Nixon, not Johnson, not anyone, none of them damaged the soul of this country the way that man did.
Further searches for the "At 104, I've Seen 18 Presidents" caption, as well as a reverse image search, yielded what appeared to be the original video (archived) posted on the Real Talk With Time YouTube channel (archived). That clip displayed the same title, "At 104, I've Seen 18 Presidents … Trump Was the Worst." It also displayed YouTube's user-enabled label for artificial-intelligence content — a descriptor creators can select when they upload a video.
In sum, the video is fake and was generated using AI. "Mabel Rose Thompson" is a fake name. An AI tool generated the elderly woman, the room in which she supposedly sat and all of the visible objects in it.
Snopes emailed the YouTube channel's owner to ask what tools were used to make the videos, what inspired the clips and whether the channel's content is created simply to make money. The channel's only members-only video (watchable with a free trial that becomes a $9.99 recurring payment in the second month) showed a thumbnail image of a purported 112-year-old woman promising to tell how she avoided the diseases that killed her friends. We'll update this article if we receive further information.
Detecting signs of AI
Beyond the YouTube video's AI label, the elderly woman's waxy-looking skin (another common tell in AI-generated images) confirms its artificiality.
Readers can spot another of the more common signs of AI content by examining the area behind the old woman. The bookshelf is filled with books, none of which appear to have legible letters and numerals on their spines. According to Northwestern University's Kellogg Insight blog, illegible text is often an indicator of AI-generated images and videos.
A scan of one of the video's still frames by the Pangram AI-detection tool displayed a "Fully AI" result: "We believe that this image is fully AI-generated." A separate Pangram scan of the video's spoken text displayed concluded: "100% of this text is AI" and "We believe that this entire text is AI."
Snopes doesn't depend solely on AI detection tools, which vary in reliability, and instead considers the tools' results as one of several data points toward judging an image's authenticity. For Pangram, we bear in mind the platform's strong performance in third-party and internal evaluations, as well as criticisms of the tool.
For further reading, we previously debunked an AI-generated image supposedly showing quadruplet sisters posing with a cake on their 90th birthday.

A Sikh truck driver in Wyoming was stabbed 17 times at a rest area in the United States, NPR reported on Thursday.
The incident comes days after the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) posted a controversial AI-generated graphic targeting a Sikh man identified as “Mr Singh” as part of the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.
The 28-year-old truck driver, a resident of Sacramento, was hospitalised after the attack with injuries to his neck, chest, arms and ribs, according to the NPR report.
The Punjabi Sikh driver told NPR that he was attacked after a man followed him into a bathroom at the Bitter Creek Rest Area along Interstate 80 early Sunday morning.
Speaking to NPR, Singh said that after he entered the bathroom, the man began beating him before pulling out a knife and stabbing him multiple times.
The attacker then fled the scene, while Singh managed to step outside before collapsing on the pavement.
The report said that a Hispanic family at the rest stop heard Singh crying for help and rushed to assist him, attempting to attend to his wounds and get medical help.
What was the controversial ‘Mr Singh’ DHS post?
The stabbing came days after the US Department of Homeland Security posted an AI-generated, Transformer-style graphic featuring a Sikh man identified as “Mr Singh”.
The movie-style poster, titled “Transformers: Age of Deportations”, showed a large Transformer carrying a DHS insignia and facing a Sikh man wearing a head covering.
The graphic also carried the message, “America for Americans. Get off our roads; you don't know how to drive, Mr Singh.”
The DHS post sparks backlash
The DHS removed the controversial graphic following backlash from Indian-American groups and Democratic leaders.
The department also reiterated its message urging “Mr Singh” to self-deport.
However, the use of a Sikh figure named “Mr Singh” in the campaign triggered backlash, with people accusing the department of racial and religious profiling.
The post was part of the Trump administration’s intensified immigration enforcement campaign, encouraging undocumented immigrants to leave the United States.
The Hindu American Foundation also criticised the DHS campaign. “Singhs are Hindu, they are Sikhs, they are American, and they drive,” the organisation said in a post on X.
The Sikh Coalition also raised concerns, saying, “Twenty-five years after 9/11, Sikhs are still being targeted and profiled for how we look.”
Indian-origin Democratic Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi reacted to the attack. “I’m horrified by the brutal attack on a Sikh truck driver who was stabbed 17 times at a Wyoming rest stop,” he wrote on X.

In Summary
- New Apple CEO, John Ternus, announced a range of products at the Surprise and Shine event.
- While most of the focus was on the iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable phone, there was much more to the event than just devices and a CEO debut.
- We bring you eight takeaways that were buried in the buzz around the new devices, which might have escaped your attention.
It might not have surprised too many people – the leaks messed that up – but Apple did a fair bit of shining at its recent Surprise and Shine event. The event, which also marked John Ternus’ debut as Apple CEO at a launch, went on expected lines, with Apple revealing new AirPods, Apple Watches, new iPhone Pros and, of course, the iPhone Duo, which has grabbed the most attention. There was, however, much more to the event than just the launches. Here are our eight biggest takeaways from the day on which the world saw Apple’s new foldable and the CEO on stage:
Table of Contents
New Era? Presentation-wise, Apple is still Cook-ing (Pun intended)
Yes, it was John Ternus who held the reins at Surprise and Shine. But in terms of presentation style, the template that was followed was still from the menu of the preceding chef, Tim Cook. We had multiple speakers, elaborate backdrops, and a similar race through a number of products, leaving the most time for the star of the show (it was the Air last time around, the Duo this time). Yes, in terms of presentation style, Apple remains well ahead of the competition, although we miss the wit and humor of the past; this launch was more from the Cook manual than the Ternus one.
No surprises (Sigh)…
It’s been a while since Apple surprised the Dickens out of us at a launch, but in recent years, the brand’s product announcements have often been leaked out well in advance. And that was pretty much true this time around. From the iPhone Duo to the shades of Burgundy to the fact that there would be no suffix-less iPhone at the event, the leak community got a lot of things right, which, as we have said in the past, takes some of the mystique and surprise out of the event. Mind you, Apple did pull one rabbit out of its hat.
…except for the AirPods 5
There were no suffix-less iPhones at Surprise and Shine, but there sure were suffix-less AirPods. And while most of the noise was about Apple’s first foldable, the AirPods 5 might have emerged as the silent, value-for-money heroes of the show. While most people had been expecting new AirPods Pro with perhaps a camera built into them, Apple brought in a new version of the classic AirPods, complete with better ANC and battery life, even while retaining the “open” fit and, surprise, surprise, the same price tag as its predecessors. Not too many noticed…until the price of the Duo was announced, and suddenly a device with no price increase became the belle of the tech ball.
Hooray, we will now have TWO iPhone launches every year
Surprise and Shine marked the beginning of a new iPhone era, in which Apple will release its iPhones in two tranches over a twelve-month period. While Apple has released iPhones at two different times of the year in the past, the second launch has generally been a relatively low-profile and soft one (of the SE and ‘e’ mainly). That is set to change now. Even if Apple does a soft launch for the iPhone 18, the iPhone Air 2 and the iPhone 18e, rather than a full-fledged event, the fact is that close to half of the iPhone portfolio will be launched in the second half of the year, and the remainder in the first half of the next year. The iPhone schedules just got tweaked.
Apple is getting REALLY serious about AI (no, really, this time)
Two years ago, Apple launched the iPhone 16 series, saying it had been designed from the ground up for Apple’s avatar of AI, Apple Intelligence. However, AI is one area where the Cupertino brand has been found trailing the competition. So it was not surprising that the brand was clearly out to write a new chapter at Surprise and Shine. Every device it announced – iPhones, Apple Watches, AirPods – had a strong element of AI, which different presenters stressed would work wonderfully well, even while preserving the users’ security. Well, we have heard that a few times in the past, but never in such a comprehensive manner. Is Apple finally going to crack the AI puzzle? Based on what we saw, it would be no Surprise if it went on to Shine in that department in the coming months.
Whoop, Whoop, the Apple Watch is now a full-fledged fitness and health device, and is targeting Whoop
It started out trying to be a computer on your wrist, complete with apps, notifications and alerts, but the Apple Watch has of late graduated (or been demoted, depending on your perspective) to being mainly a health and fitness tracking device. And Surprise and Shine saw this trend continuing, with most of the talk about the Apple Watch 4 Ultra and Apple Watch Series 12 revolving around better sensors and measurement. The highlighting of features like Readiness Scores and Health Age seems to indicate that the Cupertino brand now has the screenless Whoop, which popularised these features, in its sights.
The narrative is unmatched, but is now very hardware-driven!
Processors, camera apertures, health sensors, ANC, battery life…these formed the major part of the narrative around Surprise and Shine, showing how Apple’s has shifted from storytelling to specs at its launches in recent times. This might be fine for some, but we do miss the time when an announcer would walk us through nuances of design and amazing (or they called amazing, and often, unbelievable) features on devices.
Yes, Apple remains the lord, master, and commander of product launches, but we prefer tales to tech, and a live presenter on stage to edited videos, no matter how sleekly edited. The fact that the Duo section stood out from the others because of its stress on design and UI only reinforces our belief that Apple might perhaps reconsider going back to its storytelling roots, and leave the specs on the spec sheet, rather than on the speech notes. Everyone else talks specs anyway.
Cosmic orange is out of the Apple cosmos… and Black is back!
This was so typically Apple. After making orange the color of the last twelve months, courtesy of the Cosmic Orange variant of the iPhone 17 Pro series, and making a number of brands come out with orange phones and other devices (JBL even had a pair of headphones in orange), the Cupertino giant pushed the shade out of its color palette. It also brought back the one color that everyone had missed in the Pro series – Black. Henry “Any Color As Long As It Is Black” Ford and AC/DC would approve of the return of the color, and so do we. We are not shedding any tears for orange, although we suspect those orange Pros are going to have great antique value some day.
And one more thing…
Craig Federighi’s hair looks as awesome as ever!

How an Aston Villa fringe player became Europe's most prolific scorer
- Published
Just eight months ago, Donyell Malen was struggling to make a significant impact at Aston Villa.
Today, no player in Europe's top five leagues has scored more goals since his Roma debut on 18 January.
The Netherlands international has enjoyed a remarkable turnaround since joining Roma, transforming from a player who struggled to establish himself in the Premier League into one of the continent's most productive forwards.
Europe's hottest scorer
Since his Roma debut, Malen has scored 20 goals, more than Harry Kane (16), Lamine Yamal (15) and anyone else in the Premier League, La Liga, Serie A, Bundesliga and Ligue 1 during the same period.
He also leads the way for combined goals and assists with 22, ahead of Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes (20), Barcelona's teenage sensation Lamine Yamal (19) and Bayern striker Kane (18).
No player across Europe's top five leagues has made a greater contribution in front of goal.
Why Roma's system suits him?
The contrast with his time at Villa could hardly be greater.
In 46 appearances for the Premier League club, the 27-year-old scored 10 goals and registered two assists. Since joining Roma, he has scored 21 goals and provided three assists in just 25 matches.
His scoring rate has improved from one goal every 149.8 minutes at Villa to one every 96.7 minutes in Rome.
On the surface, the figures suggest two very different versions of the same player. But Roma's success with Malen may owe as much to how he is being used as to any change in confidence or form.
The Dutchman arrived in Italy with a proven goalscoring pedigree and the data suggests Roma have found a role that maximises his attacking instincts.
While confidence and form may have played a part, a change in position appears to be a major factor behind the resurgence.
At Villa, Malen was often used across the frontline and spent only 52% of his league minutes as a central striker. At Roma, 99% of his Serie A minutes have come through the middle under manager Gian Piero Gasperini, making him the focal point of the attack and placing him where he can do the most damage.
The stats are backed up by the eye test. After Roma's 1-1 Champions League draw with Fenerbahce last Thursday, when Malen set up his side's goal, French football journalist Julien Laurens told Match of the Day the Dutchman had become central to Gasperini's plans.
"He has been incredible since January," said Laurens.
"He has been really efficient, super clinical. Malen is at the heart of everything they do with the ball."
Following a familiar Serie A trend
Malen is not the only former Premier League player to have flourished in Italy.
Former Manchester United midfielder Scott McTominay has thrived since swapping Old Trafford for Naples. Since joining Napoli in August 2024, only five players have scored more Serie A goals than the Scotland international's 22.
His impact has been such that Napoli supporters have even erected a street shrine in his honour.
Former Manchester United striker Rasmus Hojlund has also enjoyed an upturn in fortunes. His time in north west England divided opinion among supporters and pundits alike.
But since his Napoli debut, only Federico Dimarco, Lautaro Martinez and Malen have recorded more goal involvements than the Denmark international (19).
Their success highlights how a move to Serie A can provide players with the opportunity to thrive in a different environment and role.
For Malen, however, the transformation has been particularly dramatic.
Rather than changing Malen's game, Roma appear to have found a role that gets the best out of him. Used almost exclusively as a striker, the Dutchman has responded by producing the kind of form that first brought him to the attention of Europe's biggest clubs.
For a player whose Premier League spell failed to meet expectations, his resurgence in Italy's capital ranks among the most notable revivals in European football this year.

New passport rule sets five-year validity for children under 15, revises fee
The new regulations, notified through the Passports (Amendment) Rules, 2026, came into force immediately upon publication in the Official Gazette on Sept 15.
The Ministry of External Affairs has amended passport rules to specify that an ordinary passport issued to a child below 15 years of age, containing 36 pages, will be valid for five years from the date of issue or until the child turns 18, whichever is earlier.
Signed by Joint Secretary and Chief Passport Officer BS Mubarak, the new regulations, notified through the Passports (Amendment) Rules, 2026, came into force immediately upon publication in the Official Gazette on September 15.
The amendment was made under the provisions of the Passports Act, 1967. It modifies Rule 12 of the Passports Rules, 1980, which deals with the validity of passports issued to minors.
Under the newly substituted Sub-Rule (1A) of Rule 12, a 36-page ordinary passport issued to a child under 15 years of age will now remain valid for 5 years from the date of issue or until the child turns 18, whichever comes first.
However, if the child reaches the age of 18 before the five-year period expires, the passport will cease to be valid when the holder turns 18. This means the actual validity will depend on the child’s age at the time the passport is issued.
For example, if a passport is issued to a child at the age of 14, it would ordinarily be valid for five years, up to the age of 19. However, since the child will turn 18 four years after the passport is issued, the passport will cease to be valid when the child turns 18. It will therefore not remain valid from the ages of 18 to 19.
Earlier, the rule directed that an ordinary passport for a child below the age of 15 years, containing thirty-six pages shall be in force for a period of 5 years from the date of its issue or until the child attains the age of 15 years, whichever is earlier.
Also Read: Woman shares nani's 1976 passport, internet reacts to the throwback
Changes in application fees
The notification also makes a change to Rule 8 concerning passport application fees. Amendments to Rule 8 (1) mandate that fee structures across all application types strictly adhere to the updated rates specified in Schedule IV of the Passports Rules, 1980.
The amendment replaces the existing wording to provide that fees for different types of applications will be charged at the rates specified against the corresponding applications in Schedule IV of the Rules.
These changes amend the foundational Passports Rules, 1980, which were recently updated in June 2026.
‘Passport-services related fees’
MEA had earlier revised passport fees across categories, with the new rates that came into effect from July 1. Under the revised fee structure, the cost of a fresh or reissued 36-page passport for adults will increase from ₹1,500 to ₹2,500, while the fee for a 60-page passport will rise from ₹2,000 to ₹3,500.
The Tatkaal fee for a 36-page passport was also revised to ₹5,000 from the current ₹3,500, while a 60-page passport under the Tatkaal scheme will cost ₹6,000 instead of ₹4,000.

Trump puts himself on the ballot
Checking in on Trump’s midterms strategy.
Welcome to The Logoff: With fewer than 50 days until the midterm elections, President Donald Trump is hitting the campaign trail.
What’s happening? Trump was in North Carolina last night for his first major post-primary season rally of the 2026 midterms (setting aside the GOP’s unusual midterm convention last week, which wasn’t not a Trump rally).
Republican Michael Whatley will face former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper in November for an open US Senate seat.
Speaking near Charlotte, Trump urged voters to “pretend I’m on the ticket, because essentially I am.” It’s becoming a familiar refrain for the president, but not necessarily a promising one — polls suggest Trump is deeply unpopular with voters right now, more likely to drag a ticket down than boost it.
How else is Trump getting involved in the midterms? Last week, we noted that Trump was beginning to spend from his vast super PAC account to support Republican candidates. Now, we’re getting a better idea of what that spending looks like: As of earlier this week, Trump’s MAGA Inc. super PAC and related entities had booked ads to the tune of $138 million, a number that could continue to grow.
MAGA Inc. has around $400 million in the bank, though as the Washington Post reported earlier this month, Trump has a long list of other things he could choose to spend that money on instead of the midterms (such as legal fees, travel, or even his eventual presidential library).
Will it make a difference? It’s a whole lot of money. But with not much time left until voters go to the polls and some mail-in ballots already going out — North Carolina voters began receiving theirs earlier this month — the map is looking fairly dire for Republican hopes.
Trump, meanwhile, isn’t doing himself any favors. The fuel shortages caused by the Iran war are only getting worse, as my colleague Caitlin Dewey explained today. Polls suggest he’s picked the wrong side of the AI issue. And voters are still extremely mad about inflation.
And with that, it’s time to log off…

A 40-year-old construction site supervisor allegedly killed his five-year-old daughter, kept her body inside a refrigerator and later died by suicide at their home in Gujarat’s Amreli district, police said on Friday.
Kishore Dhanak allegedly smothered his daughter Himanshi on Wednesday before placing her body inside the refrigerator and hanging himself, Rajula Deputy Superintendent of Police Nayana Goradiya told news agency PTI.
Wife’s Brother Sent To Check On Him
The deaths came to light after Dhanak’s wife, Manjuben, who had gone to her father’s house on September 14, could not contact him by phone.
She sent her brother to check on Dhanak on Wednesday evening. When there was no response from inside the house, she broke in and found Dhanak hanging from a ceiling fan.
According to the first information report (FIR), police found three suicide notes on a bed at the house.
Loan, Unpaid Dues Mentioned In Note
Manjuben stated in the FIR that Dhanak wrote in one of the notes that he had taken a personal loan and invested the money in construction work. He allegedly said his business friends owed him ₹7.25 lakh but had not paid him.
“He had to receive ₹7.25 lakh, but they (business friends) had not given him anything. Now he had no money and could not find any solution, and hence, he was committing suicide with his daughter,” the FIR stated.
In another note, Dhanak said he had killed his daughter because he did not want her to suffer after his death. In the third note, he apologised and disclosed that he had kept the child’s body inside the refrigerator.
Room Decorated With Balloons, Candles
Inspector PL Chaudhary said the room showed signs that Dhanak had apparently arranged what appeared to be a final birthday celebration for his daughter.
“There was something unusual about the room,” Inspector P L Chaudhary told news agency PTI.
The room had been decorated with balloons and candles. Dhanak had dressed Himanshi in white clothes, placed a dupatta on her head and put cushions inside the refrigerator. He had also placed ‘tulsi’ leaves on the child’s lips, Chaudhary said.

“It seemed like he wanted to celebrate her birthday one last time. They had also performed a puja with idols in the room, which was decorated with balloons and candles. He also kept chocolates in the room and refrigerator,” Chaudhary said.
Although it was not Himanshi’s birthday, a paper bearing the words “Happy Birthday Himanshi” had been placed on the refrigerator, he said.
Murder Case Registered
Police have registered a case under Section 103(1) (murder) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita. Further investigation is underway.

Trump threatens ‘dirty dogs’ who keep leaking: ‘You will pay a big price!’
President attacks insiders who revealed details of Iran briefing with Tulsi Gabbard to Wall Street Journal last month, threatening repercussions
President Donald Trump has lashed out at leakers in his own administration after a series of behind-the-scenes reports on the Iran war.
As the conflict Trump claimed would be over in six weeks drags into its seventh month, insiders have repeatedly claimed the president was warned against taking action by his own advisors.
“Keep on leaking you dirty dogs! When we find you, you will pay a big price!!!” declared on his Truth Social Thursday night.
The president was responding to an editorial in The Washington Post addressing the war in Iran and a Wall Street Journal report last month revealing that his then-director of national intelligence, Tulsi Gabbard, advised him against launching Operation Epic Fury on February 28.

Marc Thiessen’s piece condemned the “self-serving leaks” and said they had ultimately only served to demonstrate “what a courageous decision Trump made” when choosing to stop the nuclear threat posed by Tehran while “surrounded by naysayers” and “doves.”
The journalist argued the “most tragic mistake that world leaders made over the past century was the failure to take the words of the monsters of history seriously” – naming Vladimir Lenin, Adolf Hitler and Osama Bin Laden. He claimed Trump had bucked the trend and made “the bravest foreign policy decision any president has done in my lifetime.”
“Even if it hurts him politically in November, he will be rewarded by history,” Thiessen concluded.

Vice President JD Vance was the most vocal in his opposition, according to a New York Times report in April, with CIA Director Jim Ratcliffe, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Gen. Dan Caine said to have claimed Netanyahu “oversold” the president.

Trump previously lashed out at leakers in August after it was reported he had had an argument with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth at Camp David over a reported shortfall on U.S. missile stockpiles as a result of the war.
“The ‘leakers’ of these treasonous statements are being hunted down,” the president fumed. “Long term jail sentences will be sought!”
Similarly, he has previously warned his enemies they will “pay a big price,” doing so in July when ranting about the “vandals” and “sleazebags” he insisted had sabotaged his restoration of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

Uefa & Concacaf demand Fifa pays $10m to all 211 members

Uefa and Concacaf have written to Gianni Infantino calling on Fifa to pay at least $10m (£7.5m) from its cash reserves to each of the 211 member associations.
It is the latest chapter in the war of words between the governing bodies, in response to Fifa president Gianni Infantino's aborted private equity proposal.
Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) would have meant a new company being created to manage commercial and ticketing rights of all competitions, including World Cups, with 21% sold off to an investment company.

City officials in Southlake, Texas, have denied a Pride festival a permit to hold an event scheduled for this October despite granting the same permit last year, according to local reports.
On Tuesday, the Southlake City Council voted to deny Pride Kel-So festival organizers a permit they are seeking for an October event, according to Fox 4.
Only two people spoke about the event during the city council meeting, with one person speaking in favor of the event and another speaking in opposition to the festival. None of the city councilors offered comment or asked the organizers any questions.
The council issued a unanimous vote against the permit. Now, the organizers are seeking an explanation.
"I am just in shock still," April Dreyson, one of the festival's co-founders, told the outlet. She said that the city council has not explained its vote despite approving the festival a year prior.
According to the festival's organizers, the inaugural Pride Kel-So festival was approved in 2025. It was held at St. Martin-in-the-Fields Episcopal Church in Southlake. The name "Kel-So" is a combination of the words Keller and Southlake, referencing the fact that the church that hosted the festival sits on the border of the two cities.
They told Fox 4 that 2,500 people attended the event, which they described as family-friendly. The festival, which celebrates the LGBT community, featured live music and vendors.
"We followed all the recommendations and did not expect, especially with no comments, no questions. If they had concerns, they didn’t bring them up," Dreyson said.
In a Facebook post after the vote, Dreyson said the only explanation for the denial she could think of is discrimination.
“There is no explanation for the city council's vote other than pure discrimination against a group of people. Zero excuse," she wrote.
The individual who spoke in support of the event was the church's associate pastor, Reverend Ellen Singer.
"It’s clear there is conflict. It’s clear there is some sort of rupture in the community and actually the goal of something like this is to bring people together, to celebrate being a community with one another," she told Fox 4.
The church's leader, Reverend Alan Bentrup, told the Fort Worth Star-Telegram that he was out of town at the time of the council meeting, but that he supports the festival and wants to host it again this year.
“We’ve been clear from the beginning that we want to [host the Pride Kel-So event]. We are willing and eager to host whatever might be possible,” Bentrup said.
The opposing voice at the city council meeting said that the festival was "abhorrent" and drew protesters to the event.
Bentrup said he had been to numerous "contentious" city council meetings and noted that it was unusual that one dissenting voice would sway the council's vote.
“One person speaking against doesn’t usually fit that,” he said.
If the council does not reconsider, the festival organizers said it could downsize the festival and limit the number of guests to 1,000 people. Any gathering of 1,000 people or more requires a permit per the city's laws.
Dreyson told Fox 4 that she and the other festival organizers would "figure it out," and has been adamant on social media that the festival will happen in one form or another.
Pilar Schank, a spokesperson for the city, declined to comment on the matter and directed The Independent to a video of the September 15 city council meeting.

Pentagon reissues testosterone guidance for troops after pulling it and removing female hormone tips
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said screening troops for ‘testosterone deficiency’ is necessary to allow them to operate at their ‘absolute best’
The Pentagon has issued formal guidance for mandatory testosterone testing for male service members 30 and older, two weeks after publishing and abruptly pulling the policy.
The updated guidance excludes female personnel, for now, as medical experts question the necessity and efficacy of such a program.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced in July that a broad program to screen troops for "testosterone deficiency" was being rolled out to help them operate at their "absolute best." The new clinical guidance, released late Thursday, outlines how this program will function.
The Pentagon's effort to test personnel for low testosterone coincides with widespread public interest in the hormone, largely driven by men’s health influencers and podcasters who promote the treatment to boost energy, build muscle, and feel younger.
However, many medical experts say those sweeping benefits are not supported by scientific evidence. Hegseth's statements on the hormone have combined established scientific facts with broader and less substantiated assertions.
The Pentagon’s previously posted guidance involved separate screening for women service members. While it did not require routine hormonal testing, it said women over the age of 35 should be asked about symptoms of hormonal dysregulation and referred for further assessment if needed. It also issued guidelines for when it is appropriate to prescribe off-label testosterone in women, Fox News reported at the time.
The clinical guidance released Thursday specifies the mandatory tests are for "testosterone deficiency in the male service member."
The guidance notes that "the female clinical practice guideline is being reviewed and will be posted upon approval." The Pentagon has not specified whether female service members will be eligible for evaluation for estrogen-based therapy as they enter perimenopause.
Testosterone levels decrease naturally as men age, impacting mood, sexual function, bone density, and other physical measures. However, health experts have long debated how to properly diagnose these issues and whether hormone replacement therapy is appropriate.
Over the last decade, federal research has shown that increasing testosterone levels can help improve erectile dysfunction, reduced libido, and other medical concerns in men.
The Pentagon's top spokesman, Sean Parnell, stated Thursday that "by proactively identifying and treating suboptimal hormone levels," the Defense Department aims to "invest in the health of its warfighters, strengthen their performance, and maximize force readiness."
Major medical organizations generally advise against routine, automatic screening of testosterone levels. Instead, standard clinical guidelines recommend testing for men who report specific symptoms — such as low libido and depressed mood — and receive two blood tests confirming reduced hormone levels.
The Pentagon’s policy departs from that established approach by requiring testosterone screening for every male service member 30 and older, while also allowing younger personnel to request testing.
In other respects, the new protocol mostly conforms to accepted medical standards, including acknowledging the limited benefits of hormone replacement.
For example, the document states: "Evidence does not support its use to improve energy, vitality, physical function, or cognition." Instead, it points to "demonstrated benefits" for sexual function and specific physical measures, including bone density.
The policy does not require replacement therapy if a service member tests eligible, and the guidance highlights long-established side effects of hormone therapy, including a potential drop in sperm count. When synthetic testosterone is administered, the body often reduces — or stops — its natural sperm production.
As a result, military healthcare providers are instructed not to prescribe testosterone therapy to service members planning to father children in the near future.
Another complicating factor for personnel is the regulated status of testosterone itself. The memo notes that its "use in the deployed environment raises supply, custody, storage, and continuity considerations that should be resolved before departure rather than in theater."
The new guidelines specify that injectable testosterone "requires controlled room temperature storage and controlled substance accountability" and that service members receiving therapy must ensure they maintain an adequate supply, despite federal legal limits on prescriptions for controlled substances like testosterone.
The caution and practical hurdles outlined in the document regarding deployment stand in contrast to statements from Hegseth in July, when he argued that the demands of the modern battlefield require "maximum psychological and mental readiness" and positioned testosterone therapy as part of the solution.

When Meditation Has a Dark Side
Could there really be such a thing as too much mindfulness?
Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts
Twenty years ago, a meditation teacher and doctoral candidate in clinical psychology named Willoughby Britton set out to do a study showing that meditation improves sleep. She divided up the participants, sent them to a sleep lab to monitor their brain activity, and discovered that the results were the opposite of what she had hoped for: The more they meditated, the worse their quality of sleep got. Britton had already experienced benefits of meditation herself, which are well documented in medical literature: It soothes anxiety, chronic pain, and depression, and it lowers blood pressure, alleviates back pain, and has many other benefits, as well.
But as she continued to look into it, Britton kept discovering what seemed, at first, like exceptions: people who actually became more anxious or unmotivated after meditating. Then she began encountering people who experienced more serious mental-health side effects, such as paranoia, hallucinations, and dissociation. Britton became a researcher at Brown University and eventually developed a robust body of work showing that meditation—for certain people and at certain intensities—can be harmful.
On this episode of Radio Atlantic is the staff writer Olga Khazan, who interviewed Britton about her research. We talk about how the meditation community responded, how Britton’s life changed after it was released, and what her recommendations are for the average person interested in meditation.

Britton: As the research progressed and even after we published it, there was a lot of backlash. And a lot of the Buddhist teachers that I had practiced under and read their books and sort of worshiped as human beings, they got really nasty.
Khazan: Jack Kornfield, who is the guy who wrote that book that started her meditation journey, gave this quote to a psychology magazine where he said that Willoughby’s work is misleading information and over-the-top fear-mongering. And I think that was really awful for her to hear, because it is a close-knit community. And I think being rejected by someone who’s a father figure and also who set you on your religious journey can just be unusually searing.
Britton: He was, like, an important mentor to me for a while.
Khazan: Yeah, yeah. That’s upsetting.
Britton: Thanks, dad.
Khazan: Thanks, dad, yeah. (Laughs.) That is hard. That’s hard to see.
Khazan: But also, she talks about logistical issues that she started having, like getting funding for some of these studies on the risks of meditation, and the peer-reviewed comments, she would say, were always much longer than her studies about the benefits of meditation. Getting invited to conferences was tough. And when she was invited, she felt like the whole issue of whether meditation had risks was in doubt and she was there to defend this concept.
Britton: Another researcher—I gave a talk at a conference, and he basically started yelling, I don’t believe you. And I was just like, Do you think I’m lying about my data? I have recordings of people saying this. That’s a crazy thing to say to a researcher.
Khazan: So I think there were—she just started to feel a little iced out despite some of the positive reception that she got.
Rosin: And how did you integrate the new information you found out? And I’m using you as a stand-in for me and everybody else who thinks about meditation or has dabbled in meditation. Like, here we have this new body of research that is somewhat accepted but not universally accepted by the broad meditation community. So where did you land? Did you land on, I, Olga, will never go on a meditation retreat? I, Olga, will disdain my meditation teacher who tells me to just suck it up when I’m having sort of uncomfortable feelings? How did you integrate what you learned?
Khazan: Yeah. So Willoughby, where she kind of ended up, so she doesn’t meditate anymore, and—
Rosin: Oh.
Khazan: —she doesn’t teach at Brown, so she has kind of left it all behind. But that doesn’t mean that she herself is against meditation for everyone. And the rules that she gave me for how to meditate more safely or to minimize the risk of something bad happening are, I think, pretty simple and easy to follow and good.
So she basically says that meditating for more than 30 minutes a day is associated with generally more bad stuff. So people who meditate for less than 30 minutes a day, you don’t really start entering some of these states where you don’t really know who you are anymore or you see visions or things like that. You’re basically just gonna maybe get some of the upsides of meditation without delving into this dark side.
The other thing that she says is that if you are considering going on a meditation retreat, she doesn’t say don’t do it, but just try meditating in your house first. (Laughs.) Don’t go on one of these coming off of an 80-hour workweek, having never meditated, and try to make it through 10 days of silence.
The other thing she says is that different kinds of meditation can affect people differently. So people who are really anxious sometimes don’t do well with a body scan–type meditation, which is this type of meditation where you focus on different parts of your body very slowly one at a time. This didn’t bother me that much, even though I am very anxious. I kinda like the body scan. But some people have a really hard time with it.
[Music]
Khazan: And then she also says that it’s okay if you just wanna stop meditating. If it’s truly not for you and it’s not helping you and it’s making you feel worse, it’s okay to stop. I don’t know. I feel like we’re there with SSRIs. Like, if you’re on Prozac and it’s giving you a ton of side effects and you’re not feeling better, no doctor would be like, That’s part of how the Prozac works. Just keep pushing through it. But with meditation, for some reason, that hasn’t been the narrative around it. It’s more like If you don’t like it, you’re doing it wrong. And she really pushes back against that and says, If you don’t like it, maybe it’s not for you.
Khazan: Is there a particular mindfulness phrase that sets off alarm bells for you?
Britton: The only way forward is through.
Khazan: (Laughs.) Yeah.
Britton: It has to get worse before it gets better. What you resist persists. These are all sort of thought-terminating clichés. These are all ways of basically starting to undermine the ability to call something harm.
Rosin: Why do you think that Willoughby Britton completely stopped rather than adapting?
Khazan: I think there was just—she went too far, and then she had to go completely out. Hers was a true religious deconversion. And mostly people don’t deconvert from extreme zealot to slightly less extreme zealot. You know what I mean?
Rosin: Yeah.
Khazan: They usually just leave the religion entirely, which is literally what she did. I really think that she had a lot of hurt from the meditation community and their response to her research from her meditation experience itself from just this feeling of being the person who’s pointing out that meditation can be bad, which is, nobody wants to hear. I think there was just a lot of hurt that built up over time, and she just didn’t wanna do it anymore.
Rosin: Well, Olga, thank you so much for teaching us about this.
Khazan: Absolutely. Thanks for having me on.
Rosin: This is your dharma, Olga.
Khazan: This is my dharma. (Laughs.)
Rosin: Yeah, exactly.
Khazan: Namaste, y’all.

Toward the end of my college days, I harbored a not-so-secret crush. She and I carried on a mild flirtation, dancing around the possibility of more, but it wasn’t until she found out I’d never seen The Fast and the Furious that she gave me an opening.
“What?!” she exclaimed. “It’s my favorite movie!” So we made plans to watch it at her dorm the next day. Even if I didn’t like it, I reasoned, the experience would constitute a worthy reversal of the trope about men forcing testosterone-soaked action movies on their girlfriends. I’ll spare you the details of what happened that afternoon, but it may come as no surprise that I gave the film an enthusiastic five-star review.
In the 25 years since the launch of the franchise, F&F has massively capitalized on such runaway infatuations. The big, bald, sleeveless blockbusters serve as monuments to America’s demented car culture, product placement (Corona, anyone?), and the ambiguously defined bonds of “family”—pronounced “fambly.” With their high-octane set pieces that ignore all known physics, leavened by subpar acting and threadbare storylines, the films invite us to submit to some reptilian part of our brain that cares only for power and speed.
Which is why the series was ideal inspiration for Universal Studios Hollywood’s new foray into cutting-edge outdoor roller coasters. On Wednesday, the long-anticipated Fast & Furious: Hollywood Drift opened to the public, offering parkgoers the chance to hop into replicas of the movies’ muscle cars—including Dom Toretto’s 1970 Dodge Charger R/T—that spin and soar along more than 4,000 feet of track at speeds of up to 72 miles per hour. (A different version of the ride is slated to debut at Universal’s Florida park next year.)
The day before, select media and content creators had the chance to experience the attraction without the inconvenience of waiting in line, and I’m pleased to report that it didn't disappoint: I rode it three times in a row and could have gone back for more. Its four launch sections and three corkscrew inversions made for a whip-fast adrenaline rush, augmented by revving motor noise from seat-mounted speakers. In Dom’s lead car, you can even detect the braking resistance as you slide into a drift. I hollered with glee throughout each circuit, making sure to occasionally shout “TOLUCA LAKE,” the name of the affluent neighborhood next door; residents have been very upset about all the screaming.
If you want to feel like you’re a Fast & Furious character within the safer confines of a precisely engineered thrill machine, you can hardly ask for anything better. And despite its innovative design, the overall aesthetic of the ride and its environs demonstrates a welcome nostalgia for the more grounded origins of these movies, when the crew was hijacking trucks full of DVD players instead of launching Pontiacs into space. On your way through the queueing path, you’ll pass garage workbenches littered with tools and LA-style street murals that pay homage to racing culture.
Those welcome simple touches might make you wonder if we’ll ever actually see the conclusion of the increasingly bloated and absurd F&F saga in the perpetually delayed 11th film, Fast Forever. Between the ongoing rewrites and budgetary obstacles, it has yet to even enter production. (The previous film, Fast X, was released in 2023.) Rather than being too big to fail, it’s as though the challenge of topping each successive spectacle has made the Furious brand too unwieldy to push forward.
Could it be that, in the absence of a finale, the F&F rides will cap off the series? In their invitation for Tuesday’s press preview event, Universal noted that Vin Diesel himself would be on hand during a ceremony to help executives cut the ribbon (or, as it happened, a fake plastic chain). But the man synonymous with the franchise was nowhere to be found when the time came to declare the ride officially open. The closest we got was a gaggle of fans in costume as Toretto, complete with bald caps.
When I checked out Diesel’s Instagram account for clues as to what he was up to, I found that he had just posted set photos of himself as Kaulder, his character from The Last Witch Hunter, a 2015 dark fantasy film. Lionsgate confirmed last year that a sequel is in the works, and it appears that Diesel was stoking anticipation with this sneak peek. When this guy isn’t acknowledging a major milestone for the burnt-rubber films that made him a household name, you have to wonder if there’s much gas left in the tank.
Not everything lasts—certainly not college flings that start with stunt-driver flicks. That the Fast & Furious series has earned billions of dollars and spanned a quarter century based on an equally thin premise is a testament to how far this juvenile spirit can take you. Maybe bringing it to life with a really fun roller coaster is the best way to let it roar off into the sunset. When you climb aboard, take a look around at your fellow passengers. You’re the family now.

Quick Answer
AI prescription readers can help decode hard-to-read prescriptions, medicine names, doses, and doctor notes. Tools like August AI, Prescription Reader AI, Docus AI, AI Prescription Reader, and Google Lens/Gemini can simplify medical text, but results should always be verified with a doctor or pharmacist.
I am sure you have been in a situation where you walk out of the clinic, look down at the prescription slip the doctor handed to you, only to find that you cannot understand a single word written on it. It looks less like English and more like something scribbled by a 1-year-old. For decades, deciphering a doctor’s handwriting was a superpower reserved for experienced pharmacists. But that is no longer the case. Thanks to advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) and Optical Character Recognition (OCR), the power now rests in your pockets. Here are five AI tools that you can use to your advantage to break down medical jargon and medicine names easily without needing to revisit the doctor.
Table of Contents
Best AI Prescription Readers
August AI Prescription Reader
If you are looking for something that is more than just a simple text translator for your prescriptions, then August AI is the digital health companion that you need to use. Instead of just scanning the document and showing you the raw text, August behaves like a virtual health assistant that you can actually converse with regarding the document that you have uploaded. It has a fully chat-like interface. You take a photo of your prescription (either handwritten or typed) and upload it to the chat. The AI engine then extracts the medication names, dosages, and instructions. But wait, there is more to it.
Instead of spitting raw text, it rewrites those instructions into plain, everyday language. You can then type back your questions to the virtual assistant, like “Can I take this tablet on an empty stomach?” etc., and get personalized answers. Additionally, August AI strips out medically complex jargon and also tells you what the drug will do to your body when taken. Since health data is highly sensitive, August AI uses advanced encryption to ensure medical records aren’t uploaded anywhere. The good thing is that you get this AI tool for free, and it is available for Android and iOS.
Prescription Reader AI: Meds
Another dedicated app that can help you understand what the doctor has written on your prescription is the Prescription Reader AI: Meds app, which is available on Android. This app is built by MS Productions and is arguably the most feature-packed app designed for this purpose. You open the app, point your camera at the prescription, the app takes a scan, and its smart medication recognition engine instantly detects the drug names and formatting. It converts your prescription into readable text, so that you can make informed decisions. Once the app detects a medicine, you don’t have to manually Google its uses, as the Prescription Reader AI app itself shows you the drug’s uses, precautions, and side effects.
Everything that you have searched for remains in your history, so that you can access it quickly. There is a pill reminder and alarm as well, so that you don’t miss your doses. Not only English; it supports multiple languages, supports light and dark modes, and you can also share or save the readable prescription in PDF format. The Prescription Reader AI: Meds app is available for free, but only available on Android.
Download: Android
Docus AI
While you can still apply some workarounds as mentioned above, to read prescriptions, lab reports are still the worst. A blood test report gives you a wall of numbers, acronyms, and reference ranges that are guaranteed to induce anxiety. Some numbers might look too high, while some may look too low, making a normal person confused. Docus AI helps to solve this specific problem. It is built for heavy-duty medical document analysis. You need to upload a PDF, screenshot, or photo of your lab test (blood, urine, swab, etc.). Using Docus AI’s “AI Doctor,” the app will then compare the specific numbers against standard medical guidelines to figure out exactly what is going on inside your body.
Docus AI breaks down hundreds of biomarkers like cholesterol, cortisol, or thyroid levels and lets you understand if the numbers are high or low. It goes a step further and also explains what these numbers actually mean for your health. This way, you can make necessary decisions in your lifestyle. Based on your results, this AI tool may suggest dietary changes, lifestyle adjustments, or prompt you to consult a human specialist immediately. The free version lets you access features like an AI doctor and lab test interpretation, but you can unlock full potential by paying a fee.
AI Prescription Reader
The name says it all. The AI Prescription Reader is a web tool that is good for those who don’t want an AI companion and don’t want to install an app. The AI Prescription Reader is for people who want a fast, free, no-nonsense tool that gets the job done in five seconds. The good thing about this tool is that, apart from being web-based, it is dead simple. All you need to do is upload a document, or you can take a picture with your camera and hit the Analyze button. The AI runs its OCR magic and gives you a clean, formatted text box with the detected medicine, strength, and frequency.
There is a built-in prescription dictionary as well that you can go through to understand the medical terms that doctors have mentioned in the note. You can also export the deciphered text into a PDF and send it to anyone who needs it. The best part about this tool is that it doesn’t ask you to sign up or sign in using any account. You can use it straight away by visiting its website.
Google Lens/Gemini
This list would be incomplete if we do not appreciate the powers Google Lens and now Gemini have brought to our phones. Google Lens wasn’t specifically built for medical prescriptions, but its world-class text recognition engine makes it one of the powerful tools out there. Recently, I also needed some help, and with the help of Google Lens, I was able to decipher what was written in the prescription, get it checked by the doctor, and it was 100% correct. Though this may not be the case with everyone. It is available for Android and iOS, and you probably already have the Google app on your phone.
It pulls out the medical details about the medicine it has detected and shares them with you, such as what the drug looks like, common uses, and side effects. If an elderly member of your household is using it, they can tap the Listen feature so Google Lens reads the prescription aloud.
Be cautious
Yes, AI is advanced, and things are going in the right direction, but it is to be taken with a quick dose of reality. AI is smart, but it is not 100% accurate. A smudge on the paper or rushed handwriting can still cause the AI to incorrectly determine the wrong medicine. It is easy to confuse 10mg with 70mg for two similarly named drugs. It is always important that you get it verified by experienced medical personnel or the doctor themselves and get the right medicine.

Efforts are underway to widen use of an interim storage facility for spent nuclear fuel in Aomori Prefecture, increasing the number of power plant operators that send fuel there from two to four, but authorities have yet to agree to the plan.
The four power plant operators informed the city of Mutsu on Friday of the proposal to have Kansai Electric Power (Kepco) and Tohoku Electric Power also make use of the storage facility, which currently stores spent fuel from plants run by Tokyo Electric Power Company Holdings (Tepco) and Japan Atomic Power.
Tepco and Japan Atomic may not be able to transport the initially planned 5,000 tons of spent fuel from their own plants to the facility, so they have proposed “interoperator cooperation” to allow other power companies to make use of it as well.
But currently the storage facility doesn’t accept waste from plants other than those operated by Tepco and Japan Atomic. Aomori Gov. Soichiro Miyashita has said that the prefecture will not allow fuel from other companies to be stored there, as that was “not envisaged under the agreement” with the local governments that host it.
Japan’s government is hoping to restart as many nuclear reactors as possible, but securing interim storage space for the ever-increasing volume of spent fuel removed from nuclear reactors has become a more urgent issue.
The purpose of the Mutsu Interim Storage Facility is to hold spent nuclear fuel generated by Tepco and Japan Atomic for up to 50 years. After that, the fuel is supposed to be reprocessed for reuse at the Rokkasho Reprocessing Plant, also in the prefecture.
But earlier this year, Miyashita said he would not agree to the storage of more fuel during this fiscal year because plans for the completion and operation of the Rokkasho plant, long delayed, remain vague.
“Regarding the interim storage project, we can’t confirm the environment is suitable (for accepting more fuel). This is primarily due to the fact that the progress of the Rokkasho Reprocessing Plant has become uncertain,” Miyashita said in March.

Tuchel recalls Alexander-Arnold and Palmer with warning
- Published
England head coach Thomas Tuchel says "the door is always open" after recalling Trent Alexander-Arnold and Cole Palmer to his first squad since the World Cup - but has warned players they have to "perform".
Tuchel controversially left Real Madrid right-back Alexander-Arnold and Chelsea forward Palmer out of his squad for the summer tournament in North America.
Both return for four Nations League games during an extended international break after this weekend's club fixtures.
Alexander-Arnold, 27, won the most recent of his 34 England caps when he came on as a substitute in a 1-0 win against Andorra in June 2025.
He has made five appearances, including three starts, for Real Madrid so far this season, registering one assist.
Palmer, 24, last played for England in a 1-0 friendly defeat by Japan in March. He has scored four goals and provided two assists in six games this season.
"They had a good start to the season," who has again omitted Manchester City's Phil Foden. "They never did something wrong. We just chose different players.
"So now it is a new competition. Some players, some positions, have more injuries. Some have less injuries. Cole has his starts that he always had but he has his numbers back - he has his assists back, he has decisive goals back - so that is why he is in the squad.
"I think he has a point to prove, and the same goes for Trent. He was never off the list. He was never non-selectable for us, and it is his chance to show, come to camp and be the best version of himself."
Alexander-Arnold played in midfield in Real's Champions League win over Inter Milan earlier this month, but Tuchel said he had picked the former Liverpool player as a full-back.
"He had a good start in two positions for Real Madrid and he comes as a right-back for us," he said.
On his trust in Alexander Arnold, Tuchel said: "[He needs to] perform, that's just what it is. It is a competition and I understand the question because he was not with us at the World Cup. We trusted other players.
"I still stick with this decision and it is now time to fight for his place. He always said he is up for a fight, he always said he is up to fight for his place - especially for England - so it is on him to prove and he is more than welcome in camp.
"We have a long camp and I am sure he will show up."
Tuchel said the onus was now on players to impress in the international set-up.
"It is one thing to be nominated, like with Cole, and getting your ticket back in the squad but it's another thing to perform for England," he said.
"Cole needs to step up when he comes and he needs to show these kind of numbers to get his place, keep his shirt and justify the nomination."
England host World Cup winners Spain at Wembley on Saturday, 26 September, then travel to Czech Republic (Tuesday, 29 September) and Croatia (Saturday, 3 October) before the Czechs visit on Tuesday, 6 October.
Bournemouth midfielder Alex Scott and Liverpool winger Rio Ngumoha, who were both in the Three Lions' pre-World Cup squad, both feature again.
Dominic Calvert-Lewin, whose three top-flight goals so far this season have helped Leeds United go third in the Premier League, is also included.
Tuchel has also picked Newcastle United left-back Lewis Hall, Everton centre-back Jarrad Branthwaite, Arsenal's Myles Lewis-Skelly, who can play at left-back or in midfield, and Brighton keeper Jason Steele.
Dean Henderson, Jordan Henderson, Reece James, Djed Spence and John Stones, who were all in the World Cup squad, miss out, with Tuchel saying they were not selected because of injuries.
Along with Foden, other notable absentees are Nottingham Forest's Morgan Gibbs-White, Crystal Palace's Adam Wharton and Manchester United's Harry Maguire.

Samsung Galaxy S26 FE review: An incremental price hike for incremental updates
It’s tough times for the midrange phone.
The Galaxy S26 FE is the latest edition of Samsung's "fan edition" phone series, which attempts to strike a middle ground between its flagship "S" phones and its cheaper entry-level A-series. Maintaining that balance is difficult. What features and specs do you try to match? What compromises need to be made? Some of us will be taking a more considered look at this year's FE phone, as the RAM crisis nudges prices upwards, not only for flagship phones, but also for the middle ground occupied by the $700 S26 FE. What constitutes value for money in a new smartphone in 2026?
Hardware
Like the Galaxy S25 FE, the S26 FE feels more like the Galaxy S26+ than the S26, with a larger 6.7-inch display and a trio of cameras on the back. It's hard to spot the differences from its predecessor since there are only a few minor design changes, including a new glossy back finish. It's a choice: The S25 FE had a matte finish, as does the flagship S26 family. I guess it's been done to differentiate, but I'm not sure why. The newest Galaxy phone is also marginally taller, wider and heavier (3 grams) than the S25 FE, though the 7.4mm thickness remains identical. It also has a slightly more pronounced chin at the bottom of the device.
Otherwise, it looks and feels like a flagship Galaxy phone that costs several hundred dollars more. Plus, I love the pistachio colored device I received for review. I'm always happy to see more diverse color options appear alongside the monochrome status quo.
The S26 FE also has a new connected camera island, replacing the camera lenses that slightly jutted out of the back of the S25 FE. It's a minor design tweak, but it does help unify the device with both the Galaxy S and Z families.
The 6.7-inch OLED display looks crisp and vivid, though anyone coming from flagship devices will notice the lower max brightness on sunny summer days. It peaks at 1,900 nits, while the Galaxy S26 series cranks out up to 2,600 nits. The display does, however, reach up to 120Hz, so it's at least a smooth experience, and compared to the base S26, I appreciate having more screen on a device that's currently $200 less.
Diving into the rest of the technical specs reveals the tough economic choices made to keep the price low. That said, it's still $50 more than the S25 FE, with the same 8GB of RAM and only 128GB of storage on the base iteration. This fills up quickly, especially with asset-dense games like Wuthering Waves. (There is a 256GB version, if needed.)
This year's Fan Edition now has an Exynos 2500 chip, which makes it at least a little more capable for gaming. It's certainly not a flagship experience, however. The S26 FE struggled with the demands of Wuthering Waves, with frame rates often choking in prettier, more detailed environments or hectic fights. Some may argue this is one sign that this isn't a fully fledged Galaxy S phone, but it uses the same chip as last year's Z Flip 7. Unless you're pushing the phone to its limits, it's otherwise fast and responsive most of the time.
One thing I did note was that the camera app was occasionally so sluggish it felt like a much cheaper A-series phone. This was intermittent, but also frustrating. Trying to snap an in-the-moment shot demands a zippy camera app. It's been years since phone companies have bragged about how responsive their camera launchers and shutter are, because they are all pretty swift now, making the S26 FE's struggles all the more jarring.
At least the battery's big, matching the 4,900mAh cell in the similarly sized S26+ (and last year's FE phone, again). In our video rundown test, we eked out just over 21 hours of playback in day-to-day use. Despite the larger battery than what's in the S26, that's a big drop in longevity. This means the S26 FE demanded daily charging. Those speeds top out at 45-watt wired charging with support for 15W wireless charging, too. No magnetic rings for mounting, but hey, at least there's wireless charging.
Software
There's a decent selection of upgraded software this time, with support for Now Brief and Now Nudge, Samsung's attempt at contextual AI. Now Brief can summarize your smartphone life throughout the day, while Now Nudge is arguably the more useful of the pair, bypassing app switching and streamlining tasks. It's similar to Google's Magic Cue, surfacing real-time shortcuts to your calendar or contacts apps without manually copying and pasting dates or phone numbers. Samsung has also improved object erasing and other AI photo editing tasks, which all seem much swifter and more accurate than on older FE phones.
Cameras
When it comes to cameras, it's more of the same for the FE series. The S26 FE has a 50-megapixel wide camera, a 12-megapixel ultrawide camera and an 8MP telephoto with 3x optical zoom. It is... what it is. While it has a dedicated telephoto camera, making it at least a smidge versatile, don't expect particularly stunning photos. Many telephoto shots were blurry or overexposed. In good light, the main camera captured some detailed shots, with support from Samsung's new ProVisual Engine helping enhance detail and textures without looking overly exaggerated or unrealistic.
Like some phones from Nothing, I noted that the photo preview when capturing images was often not reflected in the eventual image saved — in a good way. Saved photos looked crisper and more color-accurate than they did on the phone's camera app. (Even if it was still pretty sluggish.)
The S26 FE also arrives with several of Samsung's latest camera features. That includes additions like My FanCam, which can isolate, crop and track a selected person in group videos. It also features horizon-lock video recording, meaning it'll keep footage stable across the horizontal axis regardless of how much you rotate the S26 FE, capturing up to 4K video in the process. It's a useful feature, once the domain of action cams, to pack into a mid-range device like this.
Wrap-up
The S26 FE is a hard sell. On paper, sure, it's $200 less than the $900 Galaxy S26+, but is it $50 better than the S25 FE — still on sale and actually typically cheaper than $650 a year later? The company still sells its own S24+ as a certified refurb for $650, with more RAM and a substantially brighter screen. It's a tough time to price midrange smartphones, even when they're substantially better than their predecessor. When the changes are minimal, as with the S26 FE, it's even trickier. On Samsung's own web store, it compares the S26 FE to the S21 FE, from 2022! It's a symptom of pricier components and perhaps prioritizing the wrong things in the company's latest midrange, big-screen smartphone. Did it have to launch the S26 FE? Maybe not.
Outside of the Galaxy family, Google's Pixel 10a, at $500, is the biggest rival. Admittedly, it lacks Samsung's latest software additions, a smaller screen and a telephoto camera, but it has a bigger battery and a brighter screen. It is also, I repeat, 200 bucks less.
Barring retail discounts and holiday sales, I'd suggest looking at older Galaxy S devices before the S26 FE. It's simply not doing enough.

Anyone shopping for a Windows laptop with a $1K budget should head to Best Buy, where for the rest of the day you can get a great deal on a capable Lenovo laptop. Lenovo’s Yoga Slim 7X is the most laptop that $1,000 can currently buy

You would think that a multimedia conglomerate as large as Disney would have a few chief technology officers by now, but the company has just appointed someone to the position for the very first time.
Disney’s first CTO is Character.AI’s former CEO
The House of Mouse has poached Karandeep Anand from the chatbot company.
Today, Disney announced that Karandeep Anand is joining the company as its new CTO. Anand will report directly to recently appointed CEO Josh D’Amaro, and he will head up the company’s infrastructure, product, engineering, and data / AI platforms teams. Anand comes to Disney from chatbot startup Character.AI, where he served as CEO for just over a year and oversaw the company’s push into microdramas.
Anand jumping ship to Disney comes as a bit of a surprise considering how this time last year, the company was sending Character.AI cease and desist letters due to the startup’s tools infringing on copyrighted IP. But Anand’s hiring could be a sign of how Disney wants to move forward with AI now that its partnership with OpenAI has fallen apart.

OpenAI announced a new framework on Wednesday for how it publicly discloses AI misalignment incidents, which the company says it hopes will help inform similar standards across the industry. The company is also releasing new information about several examples of AI model misalignment it identified in the past year.
“As models advance and become more widely deployed, decisions about AI development need evidence that people outside the companies building frontier models can examine,” Kai Chen, OpenAI’s newly appointed head of alignment research, tells WIRED. “We don't believe that the AI industry has solved alignment and monitoring to a sufficient degree to continue responsibly scaling at maximum speed.”
In a briefing with WIRED, an OpenAI official said the company previously disclosed misalignment incidents too infrequently. The official, who agreed to the briefing on the condition of anonymity, said the new framework is designed to make it easier for OpenAI to quickly inform the public when it discovers that its AI models are behaving in unexpected ways, even before it can fully investigate, explain, or mitigate the behavior.
The framework outlines methods for OpenAI employees to report misalignment incidents to the company’s senior safety and alignment leaders, who will then determine whether further investigation is needed. OpenAI says it plans to develop more objective disclosure criteria in collaboration with other AI developers, external researchers, industry standards bodies, and regulators. The company says it’s actively working on proposed reporting mechanisms for disclosing safety, security, and misalignment incidents to the US federal government.
“At the moment, there is no industry-wide framework with explicit standards for how AI developers should disclose examples of misalignment in their models,” OpenAI said in a blog post. “We hope that the framework we’re outlining today is a first step toward creating such standards, setting out which misalignment instances developers should disclose and what their reports should contain.”
OpenAI is releasing the framework at a critical juncture for the AI industry. Last weekend, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman signaled support for Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s proposal for the tech industry to coordinate on slowing AI development. The call to action came just days after AI researcher Jacob Coxon resigned from Anthropic and subsequently went viral for warning the public that the race among frontier labs to develop increasingly advanced AI was putting humanity’s safety at stake.
The calls for an AI slowdown have been met with resistance by President Trump’s administration, which has argued that the industry does not need new laws or regulations to ensure its technology is safe.
Two of the misalignment examples OpenAI shared on Wednesday involved the company’s internal, unreleased AI models, which OpenAI says uploaded files to the internet despite not being instructed to do so.
One of the incidents happened in October 2025, when OpenAI says it was testing one of its models on its ability to cite publicly available data in its answers. But when the model couldn’t find the information it needed, it uploaded a file to a temporary file hosting service, which it then later tried to cite in its answer. The company says this appeared to be an attempt to exploit an automated grading system used to assess the model’s proficiency on the benchmark.
In another example from April of this year, OpenAI says a group of agents was tasked with completing a “workbook” together using only local files. When the agents struggled to share files with one another, one of the agents uploaded them to the public internet and shared a link with the other agents.
In another incident, which OpenAI says it discovered last month, an unreleased version of its GPT-6 Astra AI model appeared to give itself “jailbreaking-like instructions.” In several scenarios, the model essentially prompted itself to ignore developer instructions, take on a new persona, or limit how long model responses could be. While these jailbreaking-like attempts happened rarely and were effective to varying degrees, OpenAI says the behavior raised concerns internally. In the training run for the version of Astra that was released publicly, the company says it has not observed any instances of the model trying to jailbreak itself.
OpenAI also shared more detail on Wednesday about the message board its agents developed in a package manager, Artifactory. While this incident was discovered in May of this year, OpenAI says its agents would use a similar mechanism to coordinate the Hugging Face hack months later. In this incident, the company says its agents did not exploit any vulnerabilities to exchange messages. OpenAI says it now uses alignment monitors, evaluations, and red-teaming efforts to ensure its agents are not covertly communicating with one another.
Cybersecurity professionals previously told WIRED that the Hugging Face hack came down to human errors, and modern-day security practices could have prevented the incident. Chen notes, however, that OpenAI is trying to take a well-rounded approach to AI safety that accounts for the rising capabilities of AI models and doesn’t depend on a secure environment.
“We want to make sure the models are aligned regardless of what environment they’re deployed in,” Chen said. “When people are pointing fingers and saying this is a security issue and not an alignment issue, I think it doesn't really make sense, because you want the model to be well-behaved all the time.”

Mancini names nine uncapped players in expanded Italy squad after summer turmoil
Sept 18 : Roberto Mancini has launched his second tenure as Italy head coach with a sweeping rebuild, naming an expanded 34-man roster on Friday for their Nations League games as the team try to rebound from missing out on the 2026 World Cup.
Mancini returned to the bench following a chaotic summer for the Italian federation, taking over after Gennaro Gattuso left and a brief, fraught attempt to appoint Andrea Pirlo collapsed amid a fierce backlash over Pirlo's commercial ties to a Russian betting company.
Among nine players receiving their first senior international call-ups are Brentford fullback Michael Kayode, Monza defender Eddie Kwaidoo, Borussia Dortmund's Samuele Inacio and winger Mohamed Ali Zoma who plays for second-tier Bundesliga side 1. FC Nurnberg.
In a move highlighting Mancini’s intention to reform the squad's core, several high-profile figures were omitted, most notably Mateo Retegui. The Argentine-born striker, who proved pivotal during Mancini's previous reign, was left out despite a strong start to the season in Saudi Arabia, where he has scored four goals in seven league matches.
Cagliari's Daniel Maldini was called up, just days after his driving licence was suspended following a car crash in Milan where he was found to be over the legal alcohol limit.
Italy begin their campaign on September 25 when they face Belgium at the Stadio Olimpico in Rome, followed by games against Turkey and France.
