The small fee raising big questions for India's payments revolution
- Published
India's decision to introduce a fee on some transactions made through its widely popular digital payments system has sparked a debate over its impact on businesses.
The National Payments Corporation of India said on Tuesday that a 0.4% fee will apply from 15 October to certain UPI (Unified Payments Interface) payments above 2,000 rupees (£15; $21) made to businesses by customers.
Businesses will have to pay the fee and will not be allowed to pass on the cost to consumers, it said.
The government says the new charge will help keep UPI viable in the long run but experts worry it could raise expenses for businesses and discourage them from using the system.
Launched in 2016, UPI allows people to instantly send and receive money through mobile apps. The ease of use has made it integral part of everyday life in India, used by everyone - from small vendors to booming businesses.
Until now, the government, banks and payment companies have largely borne the cost of running and expanding the UPI system.
The new charge - known as the Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) - is expected to help cover some of those costs.
The government has said that MDR is not a tax or a charge collected by the government or NPCI, which operates the UPI system.
The money will be distributed among payment system providers - including banks - to support operations and continued expansion, the finance ministry press release, external stated.
The charge will not apply to all UPI payments.
Person-to-person transfers will remain free, regardless of the amount. Payments of up to 2,000 rupees made to merchants will also remain free. Merchant payments through QR codes in rural and semi-urban areas will not attract MDR either.
The government said "approximately 96% of person-to-merchant transactions will remain unaffected", either because they are below the threshold or because they are covered by the zero-MDR framework for small merchants.
Certain merchant payments above 2,000 rupees, including those for railways, telecom services, insurance, fuel and agricultural inputs, will instead attract a flat charge of five rupees.
For other transactions above 2,000 rupees that are subject to MDR, the fee will be 0.4% and capped at 300 rupees per transaction. The cap applies to transactions of 75,000 rupees or more.
The regulator has said the money will support investment in areas including payment infrastructure, resilience, innovation and cyber security.
The decision has sparked debate in India.
Some social media users have said charging merchants could weaken one of UPI's biggest attractions - that it has been free to use. Others have warned that some merchants could turn to cash for larger transactions rather than absorb a fee they did not previously have to pay.
Krishnamurthy Subramanian, a former chief economic adviser to the Indian government, said the economics of a system such as UPI cannot be "evaluated using private cost versus private benefit".
Speaking to news channel CNN-News18, Indian entrepreneur and former managing director and co-founder of fintech platform BharatPe, Ashneer Grover said that there can be a possibility where "a shopkeeper could simply refuse to accept a UPI payment of 2,000 rupees and ask you to pay entirely in cash. Then you will go back to using cash".
The Retailers Association of India (RAI) has said that the charge could "undo years of progress in digital payment adoption among India's smallest retailers".
"During the festive season, a large share of transactions crosses the 2,000 rupees mark, and the moment a fee attaches itself to digital payment, cash becomes the path of least resistance," Kumar Rajagopalan, the association's CEO said.
Others argue that a fee is needed to help fund and expand the payments system.
"When government funds the subsidies paid for UPI, that amount comes from tax payers' pocket. Moving to market-linked pricing mechanism removes this tax burden and directly links the cost to large businesses which benefit from UPI," said Bipin Preet Singh, CEO of fintech firm MobiKwik.
Since its launch a decade ago, UPI has become a central part of India's digital payments economy. In August, UPI processed a record 24.51 billion transactions worth 29.82 trillion rupees (roughly $311bn), according to NPCI data.
The question now is whether the new charges will change how businesses use UPI, particularly for larger payments.

Security, trade, and the economy understandably dominated much of the conversation around the BRICS Summit 2026. But for a grouping home to nearly half of humanity, another challenge deserves equal attention: the changing health risks facing its people.
The summit has taken an important step in that direction. The launch of the BRICS Mission for Healthy Lifestyle, endorsement of the BRICS Roadmap for the Joint Initiative on Healthy Lifestyle Promotion (2026-2029), and a Compendium of Replicable Best Practices on Healthy Lifestyle signal growing recognition that prevention must move closer to the centre of public policy.
This is significant for India during Poshan Maah. Nutrition is no longer only about whether people have enough to eat. Increasingly, it is also about what people eat, how they live, and the diseases that follow.
A compressed nutrition transition
BRICS countries are at very different stages of development. Ethiopia continues to struggle with food insecurity and undernutrition. India and Indonesia face persistent maternal and child undernutrition even as obesity and non-communicable diseases (NCDs) rise. China and Brazil have substantially reduced traditional forms of undernutrition but confront growing diet-related disease. In the Gulf, obesity and diabetes are major public-health concerns.
Economic growth and urbanisation are rapidly changing how people eat and live. Traditional diets are giving way to more processed and convenience foods. More meals are eaten outside the home or ordered online. Children encounter pervasive food marketing while becoming less physically active.
Yet undernutrition, anaemia, and micronutrient deficiencies have not disappeared. Overweight, obesity, diabetes, hypertension, and cardiovascular disease are rising alongside them.
India sits at the heart of this transition
Our nutrition policies have rightly focused on hunger, maternal and child nutrition, anaemia, and the first 1,000 days of a child from conception to two years. These priorities remain fundamental. But they are no longer enough.
A child poorly nourished in the early years may later grow up surrounded by inexpensive foods high in salt, sugar, and fat, with too little physical activity. Undernutrition in childhood and diabetes or hypertension in adulthood can become parts of the same life story.
Much of the West experienced these problems more sequentially: food scarcity and severe nutritional deficiencies declined before obesity and lifestyle diseases became dominant. Emerging economies face a compressed nutrition transition. Yesterday’s problems remain while tomorrow’s diseases have already arrived.
We have to fight both at once.
From food security to healthy living
This changes the question food policy must answer. The great challenge of the last century was: can we produce enough food? The challenge of this century is also: can we enable people to eat and live well enough to remain healthy?
Agriculture, food, nutrition, and health can no longer work in silos. What farmers grow affects what markets sell. What food companies produce and promote shapes what families buy. And what children eat and the habits they acquire influence their health decades later.
The BRICS Mission for Healthy Lifestyle provides an opportunity to build precisely these connections. Its road map places healthy diets, physical activity, traditional food cultures, and evidence-based behavioural change within a common framework. The accompanying compendium of replicable practices can help countries learn from one another rather than repeatedly reinventing solutions.
India should use this opportunity not merely to share programmes, but to demonstrate how healthy living can be embedded across food systems, schools, and communities.
The next 7,000 days
Poshan Maah offers an opportunity to widen our ambition.
The first 1,000 days remain foundational. Nothing should dilute that focus. But India must now pay much greater attention to the next 7,000 days: childhood and adolescence.
These are the years when lifelong habits around food, physical activity, sleep, and wellbeing are formed. They offer perhaps our best opportunity to act before today’s children become tomorrow’s patients.
Schools can therefore become one of India’s most powerful institutions for preventive health.
This does not require another nutrition textbook, subject or examination. Children often already know that vegetables are good, too much sugar is unhealthy, and physical activity matters. Knowing is not the same as doing.
Schools should help children practise healthy living: eating diverse foods, drinking water, limiting foods high in salt, sugar and fat, eating mindfully, staying active, sleeping well, and maintaining hygiene. School meals, food regulation, nutrition literacy, physical activity, and family engagement should become parts of one preventive-health strategy.
India’s fight against hunger and malnutrition is unfinished. But another challenge has arrived alongside it.
The BRICS Summit has provided a useful framework for responding to both. The task now is to turn its Healthy Lifestyle Mission and Roadmap into action.
Poshan must increasingly mean nourishing early, building healthy habits early, and preventing disease early. For India — and much of the BRICS world — the next frontier is not simply enough food. It is enabling people to eat well, live well and remain healthy throughout life.
Pawan Agarwal is a former CEO of the FSSAI and is the founder & CEO of the Food Future Foundation

A city can have one of two levels of rat. There are cities where rats are glimpsed at night, furtively scurrying into a dark corner or among the train tracks. Then there are cities where the rats are so numerous and so brazen that they work out private disputes by brawling midday on a train platform, or they lounge on your front porch, eating fallen fruit. When rats reach that second level, city officials need some answer, any answer, to their rat problem. Washington, D.C., has reached that level, and Mayor Muriel Bowser’s answer involves rat birth control.
Contraception for rodents has become more popular over the past few years because the most commonly used rodenticides kill painfully, as the poisoned rodent internally bleeds to death over a period of days. Not a lot of people love rats or mice, but people don’t love causing that much suffering, either. Many are fond, too, of cats, owls, and hawks, which can be poisoned when they eat poisoned rats. New York City’s Flaco, the beloved Eurasian eagle-owl sprung from a cage in the Central Park Zoo, was found to have high levels of this kind of poison in his system when he died. And to top it off, some rodents are evolving resistance to poisons.
D.C. hopes that rats will lap up a liquid contraceptive called ContraPest from plastic bait stations. It is not the only city to try the approach: Chicago is having luck with rat birth control in Wicker Park; Boston had mixed results in Jamaica Plain. Most of the available research on ContraPest has been done by the staff of the company that makes it, SenesTech, sometimes in collaboration with external researchers. One study at a poultry farm found that a year of continuous baiting with ContraPest led to a 94 percent reduction in rat activity as measured by camera traps. The company says that if the rats continuously eat the bait, they stop having pups, a finding confirmed in a laboratory setting.
But that’s a big if. A prior attempt to use ContraPest in D.C. was inconclusive, according to Andre Pitman, the program manager for the city’s Rodent and Vector Control Division. In rat hot spots such as Adams Morgan, where evening revelers have been known to throw greasy pizza plates on the ground, rats simply had too much other food around for the birth-control liquid to hold much appeal. “We couldn’t get the rats to drink it,” Pitman told me.
So this time, Pitman said, D.C. is making what, to his knowledge, is the most aggressive push against rats in a very long time. First, the city is going to try to kill rats by heaving poison directly down their burrows, which will then be filled in. City workers will return multiple times, looking for burrows that the rats have reopened, adding more poison, then filling them again. The next week, the same procedure will be followed with a different poison, which clings to rat fur and is ingested as they attempt to lick themselves clean. Finally, starting in week three, the city will put out ContraPest for 15 days. All the while, city workers will clean alleys and encourage residents to remove ground cover, containerize trash, and generally boost hygiene levels so that rats are more likely to take the bait. Post-bar snackers are requested to keep things tidy too.
It is understandable that the nation’s capital, facing a high number of resident complaints, has chosen to throw everything it’s got at the rats. But the downside to the guns-blazing approach, from a scientific standpoint, is that if it succeeds, no one will have any idea why. If burrow numbers are down by the new year, no one can say that birth control works—only that the combination of two poisons, ContraPest, hygiene, and other measures works. And Pitman acknowledges as much. “It is not a fertility pilot,” he said. “It is a rodent blitz.”
Fertility control of wildlife, which is used in elephants, wild horses, kangaroos, and pigeons, among other species, does work sometimes, and advocates for this method worry that premature deployment of oral contraceptives for rodents risks making the entire field look bad. Ultimately, no real independent studies show that SenesTech’s products are safe or effective, Lawrence Green, the interim managing director for the Botstiber Institute for Wildlife Fertility Control, told me. (SenesTech CEO Michael Edell responded, “We have been doing this a long time and have case studies and data to back up our claims.”) Assuming ContraPest can work in cities, rats would likely have to take it for longer than 15 days to see lasting results. As people who take birth control generally know, if you miss a dose, it’s less effective, and you have to keep taking it for as long as you want to not have babies. ContraPest is really meant to be used indefinitely: SenesTech even offers a “Subscribe & save” option.
And that familiar e-commerce option points to a larger truth that everyone I spoke with agreed on: There is no end to this war. The quest to control rats is not about winning. It is about nobly devoting oneself to an unwinnable fight. Because rats spread disease, we must struggle against them, clear-eyed in the knowledge that, unless we are dealing with a small island, eradication is not possible.
The reason that rats will never be conquered, at least not in our lifetime, either with poison or with birth control, is easily explained by two facts of rat biology: They have many babies, and they love to explore. You can nuke rats with poison or slowly usher them into a
population crash with contraceptives, but all you will have done is create unoccupied territories for young, exploratory rats to come occupy. D.C.’s current blitz is focused on Adams Morgan, Chinatown, and Eastern Market, but rats live in other places in Washington. They will be happy to move in once those neighborhoods have space.
Niamh Quinn, a human-wildlife-interactions adviser at the University of California Division of Agriculture and Natural Resources, puts it this way: “We live in an infinite sea of rats.” Just beyond the boundaries of any rat-control project lie more rats, waiting to move in. Pitman, a longtime rat expert since before he joined the city, knows this too. “Rodents were here long before humans,” he said. All we can hope is to control them.

India has stepped up its criticism of the escalation in the security situation in the Red Sea, strongly condemning Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, including on civilians and economic assets.
During a bi-weekly briefing, Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal on Friday reiterated India's concerns, noting that the ongoing attacks undermine regional security and threaten freedom of navigation through key international maritime routes, including the Bab al-Mandeb.
He said, "We are deeply concerned about the escalation in the security situation in the Red Sea area... We have expressed our condemnation of the attacks on Saudi sovereign territory, including on civilians and economic assets. You would have also seen a statement which we issued following the attempted attack on the holy city of Makkah."
“Such attacks vitiate regional security, impact or undermine regional peace and security, and also threaten freedom of navigation through the Bab al-Mandab. For various reasons, this is totally unacceptable to us. We hope that there is an early restoration of peace and stability in the region,” he further added.
Additionally, the MEA has reiterated its commitment to the safety and welfare of Indian nationals abroad following an appeal regarding Indramani Nautiyal, a resident of Tehri Garhwal, Uttarakhand, who is reportedly being kept in a hostage-like situation in Saudi Arabia. Nautiyal reporte
Jaiswal stated that the government is actively monitoring the situation through Indian diplomatic channels.
"Whenever any issue of this nature arises involving an Indian citizen—concerning their interests or their welfare—our embassy, whether in Saudi Arabia or any other country, remains in continuous dialogue with the government there for their welfare and care," Jaiswal said.
When asked about the exact legal status of Nautiyal, he said that details about the case are still being gathered.
"In this case, you mentioned that he has received a prison sentence; currently, I do not have a specific response for you regarding what his exact situation is, but I will obtain the details on this matter and update you," Jaiswal added.
"However, one thing I want to state is that wherever Indian citizens may be across the world, it is our commitment that we are always devoted to their safety, care, and well-being."
Indramani Nautiyal, son of Devi Ram Nautiyal and a resident of Gaursada village in Jaunpur block of Tehri Garhwal district, had travelled to Saudi Arabia in 2018 in search of employment. He was working as a truck driver with Pick Roads and Contracting Company in Riyadh, the release stated.
Despite several years having passed since the incident, the company owner has reportedly not paid the fine, estimated to be approximately ₹2.29 crore in Indian currency. Nautiyal is allegedly being kept in a hostage-like situation and pressured to pay the amount. His wife and daughter have made efforts at various levels to secure his return to India but have been unable to obtain the required assistance. As a result, the family is facing severe mental and financial hardship.
In August, Uttarakhand Chief Minister Pushkar Singh Dhami, in his letter to the External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar, referred to the entire matter and requested that the concerned authorities be directed to take immediate steps to secure Nautiyal's release, provide him with necessary legal and financial assistance, and ensure his safe repatriation to India.
This comes against the backdrop of the simmering conflict in West Asia, with fighting intensifying in Yemen as Houthi rebels advance towards Saudi-backed government-held area, while Saudi Arabia faces growing pressure to respond.

Ronaldo named in Jesus' first Portugal squad
- Published
Cristiano Ronaldo has been named in the first squad selected by new Portugal coach Jorge Jesus, ending speculation the 41-year-old could retire from international football.
Ronaldo refused to confirm whether he would continue to play for his country after Portugal's World Cup round-of-16 defeat by eventual winners Spain in July.
But the Al-Nassr forward is part of a 25-man group chosen for Portugal's four Nations League games between 24 September and 4 October.
Jesus has replaced Roberto Martinez, who stepped down as Portugal coach after their World Cup exit.
The 72-year-old was Ronaldo's club boss last season, when the pair helped Al-Nassr win the Saudi Pro League for the first time in seven years.
The former Manchester United Real Madrid forward, who announced that this summer's World Cup would be his last, was in tears after Portugal's World Cup exit.
When asked if he would keep playing for his country, he said: "I will meet the family and take decisions with a calm head."
This sparked speculation he could follow his great rival Lionel Messi and retire from international football.
Ronaldo will turn 42 before next summer's Nations League finals and will be 43 by Euro 2028.
The oldest player in the history of the Euros is Ronaldo's former Portugal team-mate Pepe, who was 41 and 130 days for his last game at Euro 2024.
Manchester United pair Diogo Dalot and Bruno Fernandes are also in the squad, along with Ruben Dias (Manchester City) and Pedro Neto (Chelsea).
Portugal are at home to Wales on 24 September (19:45 BST) and away to Norway three days later. They then play in Denmark on 1 October and return home to host Norway on 4 October.

The West Indies I knew was very different from the team India will see later this month during a white-ball series. They had great players, fearsome fast bowlers and larger-than-life characters. What stays with me most, though, is how close we were allowed to get to them. As a young journalist, I watched them from the boundary, met them away from the field and sometimes sat beside them as the game unfolded. The access, like the cricket, was different then.
My memories of the West Indies begin before I even became a journalist.
I remember reading about the 1967 Test in Calcutta (now Kolkata), the trouble on New Year’s Day when players had to run from the ground to the safety of the iconic Great Eastern Hotel, and the story of opener Conrad Hunte and the West Indian flag. It was later clarified that Hunte had not saved the flag himself; a policeman had. The story stuck anyway. It was a series I followed through radio commentary, keeping my own scoresheets. It was such fun. Many years later I stayed at the Great Eastern on a reporting assignment, wondering which West Indies player had occupied the room allotted to me.
The 1974-75 series is where my memories properly start. I watched Viv Richards make 192 at the Feroz Shah Kotla. He was dropped on 12, a catch the whole ground was certain of, missed only by the umpire. He went on to add 180 more runs. There were sixes landing outside the stadium; one went into the neighbouring Ambedkar Stadium. Nobody had seen hitting like it.
I was also at the ground, not yet a journalist, in 1979 when Kapil Dev scored his first Test century. He had resumed the third morning on 94 not out (after a Rest day) and reached his hundred with a six. I was fielding, in a manner of speaking, at fine leg among the spectators.
Those years gave us Gavaskar too: 121 at the Kotla in the 1983-84 series, a rare attacking innings from him, and then 236 at Chennai, batting at number four after walking in at 0 for 2. Viv would joke that no matter which position he batted at, Gavaskar would always walk in with 0 on the scoreboard.
By 1987, when Patrick Patterson was touring, the papers ran story after story simply on his arrival: Pato is coming, Pato is coming. One Indian Test player, obviously peeved, asked me at the time whether the press was Indian or West Indian, given how much we seemed to be building him up. There is an anecdote from the same time when Raman Lamba, a dear friend, invited me to a private session he was having at the Kotla with a West Indian stalwart. What a surprise it was to watch Richards having a long nets session and also share his expertise with Lamba. Our staff photographer, SK Arneja, had enviable access to the great Richards and must have taken more than 100 pictures that afternoon. In the same Test, Sanjay Manjrekar had to retire hurt in the second innings when hit by a Patterson delivery. We did not have a picture of the incident, and after the day’s play was over I took (photo colleague) V.V. Krishnan to Taj Palace and requested Manjrekar to oblige us with a picture. He stood at the door of his hotel room, and Krishnan got his picture. We enjoyed such a relationship with the players then.
Facing the fast bowlers
Indian players of that era were not so much afraid of getting out cheaply against the West Indies bowlers as being hit despite the protection. You had to be at your very best, like Gavaskar, Mohinder Amarnath, GR Vishwanath, and Kapil. The dashing Srikkanth would go after them regardless. Gavaskar was close to flawless. Kapil played attacking cricket against anyone.
On India’s 1989 tour of the West Indies, I heard from more than one source that some players, batsmen and bowlers both, were relieved not to be picked for the XI. These stories were well known in cricketing circles but were never written about at the time. Dilip Vengsarkar came back from that tour and criticised the team for playing short-pitched bowling poorly, singling out Mohd Azharuddin in particular, though Azhar had in fact scored runs against that same attack.
The West Indies pace attack of that period was Malcolm Marshall, Curtly Ambrose, Ian Bishop and Courtney Walsh. Facing all four in one series was, by any measure, an unequal contest. Just like taking guard against Andy Roberts, Joel Garner, Michael Holding, Marshall and Colin Croft in the preceding tours, not to forget the unpredictable Sylvester Clarke in 1979. Spinners had almost no place in the West Indies XI by then, Lance Gibbs being the exception from an earlier generation.
Off the field
Away from the game, West Indies players were relaxed company, though it never affected how they played.
In November 1987, the West Indies were in Chandigarh to play India Under-25. On the eve of the match, the former board president IS Bindra hosted a party for the team, as he often did. I was there with a small group of journalists. Late in the evening, one of the local journalists challenged Viv Richards to “bottoms up”, a full glass of neat rum to be finished in one go. Richards agreed. Desmond Haynes and Gordon Greenidge, standing nearby, chipped in too. Both men drank three-quarters of a large glass of rum each and walked to the bus visibly affected.
The next day, Richards and Greenidge took the Under-25 bowling attack apart at Sector 16 Stadium, a large ground, hitting the ball out onto the road outside on several occasions. Bowlers including Pradeep Kasliwal, Sanjeev Sharma and Jaspal Singh, all decent young cricketers, were treated like club bowlers. It said something about the team. They enjoyed themselves off the field, but it never cost them on it.
I knew the umpires, SK Ghosh and PG Pandit, well. At the end of the first day, I had dinner with them. Even they were in awe of Viv and Greenidge.
Two interviews
Two interviews from those years still stand out for me.
The first was Brian Lara in 1994, when he refused to speak to anyone. The liaison officer for that series, Dr Ravinder Chadha, a former North Zone captain, put in a word on my behalf at Sector 16 Stadium, telling Lara that I worked for the best newspaper in the country (The Hindu). Lara agreed to meet me on a terrace adjacent to the dressing room, and gave me the interview there.
The second was Chris Gayle, in Jodhpur in 2002, as his kit was already being loaded onto the team bus after a match in a series in which he had already scored three centuries. I had put in my request at the nets on the eve of the match. I introduced myself again after the match got over. He asked me to wait, came out of the dressing room five minutes later, and suggested we sit inside the ground itself so we would not be disturbed. He gave me the interview there.
Watching the greats
I grew up reading about Gary Sobers and got to meet him personally when he visited the National Stadium in 1986 to interact with the trainees of Dronacharya coach Gurcharan Singh. “Your headline should be `cricket is a side-on game,” Sobers had insisted. I vividly remember Clive Lloyd’s 242 not out at the Wankhede Stadium in the fifth Test of the 1974-75 series.
The stylish Alvin Kallicharran was a batsman we would go to the nets specifically to watch. I stood behind those nets before I ever carried a notebook, and I could barely follow the fast bowlers, let alone imagine how the batsmen picked up the ball in time to play their strokes. One story from that period is worth telling properly.
In Pune in 1978, during a game against an India Under-22 side, Kallicharran asked a member of the India squad to teach him a respectful greeting in Hindi. That player, as a joke, taught him a cuss word instead. Kallicharran, unaware, used it to greet Tiger Pataudi at a function that evening. Pataudi recognised at once what had happened and gently corrected him. On the field, these players were fierce competitors; off it, they were on easy terms with the Indian cricketers around them.
Lara walks
During the Mohali Test in 1994, Brian Lara walked when on 91, caught by Nayan Mongia off Venkatapathy Raju, even as umpire S. Venkataraghavan took his time to raise the fateful finger. At that moment, I happened to be interviewing the captain of the West Indies team, Courtney Walsh. My colleague and ace photographer Krishnan had arranged the meeting. We sat on the ground, with the match continuing in front of us. In fact, it was also the Test in which Walsh broke Manoj Prabhakar’s nose with a delivery that went through his helmet grille, forcing him to retire hurt. Anyway, this is not the kind of access that would be possible today.
That series came just months after Kapil had played his last match for India, an ODI against West Indies in Faridabad in October 1994. It was, in its own way, another marker of an era passing.
Kapil and Sunil Gavaskar were the two Indian cricketers most respected by the West Indies for the way they played, as much as for what they scored. Old footage of a Gavaskar dismissal shows the regard the fielding side had for him. Sachin Tendulkar, Rahul Dravid, Azharuddin, and Sourav Ganguly later earned similar respect.
On India’s 1996-97 tour of the West Indies, I watched Navjot Singh Sidhu score a double century at Port of Spain, with VVS Laxman opening the batting and making two fifties in that series.
It was Sachin who arranged my second Lara interview on that tour, telling him he had to speak with me. In 2002, Gavaskar did the same for a Viv Richards interview. “Will speak later,” he promised, but I was not convinced. Richards, to my delight, sought me out in the press box afterwards and said Gavaskar had told him he had to talk to me. Both interviews appeared in Sportstar.
The end of an era
During Tendulkar’s farewell series against the West Indies in 2013, I was asked to cover both Test matches and file a Tendulkar story every day. The Mumbai Test finished in three days, which made the assignment simpler, but it was, by any account, a proper send-off for a great player.
What has followed since has been a decline that has affected everyone who played through that era. Gary Sobers spoke about it before he died, and Lara has said the same. Greenidge, by his own account, rarely watches the team now. Andy Roberts and Curtly Ambrose lament the sight of West Indies struggling to put up a decent XI, and Marshall, the menacing match-winner, is no longer alive. Courtney Walsh does most of his cricket work outside the Caribbean.
A Test match in the West Indies used to be defined as much by the crowd, marked by music and dance in the stands, as by the cricket. That atmosphere is largely what has been lost.
Perhaps that is why the memories remain so vivid. They are not only memories of runs, wickets and great players. They are memories of a particular cricketing world: of packed grounds, intimidating fast bowlers, batsmen who seemed to have more time than anyone else, players who could enjoy themselves late into the night and then destroy an attack the following morning.
None of this would have been possible without the journalists and broadcasters on the other side of the boundary rope, particularly Tony Cozier, who loved Indian cricket as much as his own and hosted us at his home in Barbados on two occasions. Tony Becca and Joseph `Reds’ Perreira, both highly respected in their own right, were part of the same years and deserve mention here too. They regularly contributed to Sportstar too. They were years when West Indies cricket felt less like a visiting team and more like a world of its own, one that Indian cricket was privileged to encounter at close quarters.
No story of West Indies cricket from those years would be complete without Lester Armoogam, a die-hard cricket fan who travelled with the team, India being his favourite. He was heavily built, widely respected and a big hit with the players. The West Indies Cricket Board would give him a season pass so that he could watch the matches. In 2002, we did the same, giving him free access to the venues.
He travelled with us by train from Jamshedpur to New Delhi. It was great fun listening to his stories. ‘Uncle’ Lester was not simply a spectator who happened to follow the West Indies. He had become part of the travelling cricket world around the team, familiar to players, journalists and officials alike. He died in 2004. I am sure ‘Uncle’ Lester would have been a depressed supporter of West Indies cricket had he been around. West Indies cricket would best be remembered and represented by characters like Lester Armoogam, who became part of the fabric of the travelling team.

Brazil’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has announced a 15% increase in the country’s main cash-transfer programme for poor families, as well as free weight-loss jabs, prompting criticism from opponents who say the moves are electorally motivated just two weeks before the presidential election.
On 4 October, the leftwing incumbent will face the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro, who has been gaining ground in recent weeks.
The rise in the monthly payment, from about £98 to £113, that he announced on Thursday is due to take effect on 19 October, just before the likely runoff vote on 25 October.
The increase is expected to benefit between 15% and 20% of voters in what promises to be one of the closest ever presidential races in Latin America’s largest country.
Lula said it was not really an increase, but an adjustment in line with inflation to “protect the purchasing power of the most vulnerable families”, but his opponents have criticised its timing so close to the election.
Flávio Bolsonaro called it an “act of desperation” after polls showed him gaining ground – although the most recent survey, released on Thursday night, still showed Lula numerically ahead despite the technical tie. The senator added that Lula was trying to “buy the votes of the poor”.
Created in 2003 during his first term as president, the programme, called Bolsa Família, was a flagship cash-transfer policy that helped lift millions of families out of poverty during his first two terms.
Currently, families with an income of up to £32 per person are eligible, covering about 50 million people, or roughly 27 million of voting age.
The programme has long been fiercely criticised by rightwing politicians, including by Jair Bolsonaro, although he kept it in place during his presidency.
On the eve of the 2022 election, Bolsonaro announced a 50% increase in the monthly payment, prompting Lula’s campaign to file a case with the electoral court alleging abuse of political power and electoral use of the state machinery.
The similarities have sparked a debate between those who say Lula is doing the same thing Bolsonaro did four years ago, and others who argue that the two cases are different.
The journalist Miriam Leitão wrote for O Globo that although both Bolsonaro and Lula made the adjustments “out of electoral interest”, the current incumbent’s increase is in fact limited to inflation over the past four years, during which there had been no adjustment.
She also noted that Bolsonaro’s increase had an expiry date – precisely at the end of the electoral period – while Lula’s is permanent.
Victor Escobar, a researcher at the Laboratory of Parties, Elections and Comparative Politics, agreed. He said that although Lula, like his predecessor, is also being criticised for unveiling a package of benefits on the eve of the election – including a promise to distribute weight-loss jabs free of charge through the public health system – Bolsonaro’s measures were “even more irresponsible from a budgetary point of view”.
In addition to increasing benefits for poor families, Bolsonaro introduced temporary monthly payments of up to £727 for two groups that broadly formed part of his support base, taxi drivers and truck drivers, along with a series of other social benefits whose projected impact on the budget was so large that critics dubbed them the “kamikaze” package.
Escobar acknowledged that Lula’s intention was also electoral, but said that, as long as the measures comply with the law, “it’s something entirely expected when we’re talking about an incumbent running for re-election, who will try to use the legal mechanisms available to improve their voting numbers”.
Some electoral law experts have said that an inflation adjustment is not, in principle, prohibited, but another far-right candidate, the influencer Renan Santos, filed a case with the electoral court seeking to suspend the increase until the president-elect takes office. Although critical of the measure, Flávio Bolsonaro has not done the same, reportedly because of concern about the impact such a move could have among voters who benefit from the programme.

Open earbuds are the big new thing in headphone land. Unlike in-ear variants, open earbuds are like tiny speakers that rest on the ear and let outside sound in naturally, so you can fully hear the world around you. Some use a hook style that wraps around the back of your ear, while others are clip-ons that look more like statement-piece earrings. Style aside, they are excellent for anyone who finds traditional earbuds uncomfortable or wants full environmental awareness for activities like running, biking, or even just doing chores around the house.
I've tested dozens of models since 2022, and while I still recommend having a pair of noise-canceling earbuds, I also love open earbuds for specific use cases.
For more headphone recommendations, check out our guides to the Best Wireless Earbuds, Best Workout Headphones, and Best Wireless Headphones.
Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.
Best Open Earbuds Overall
Specs

| Battery life | 10 hours, 40 with case | 
| Water/dust resistance | IP57 | 
| Wireless charging | Yes | 
The Shokz OpenDots 2 are everything I want open earbuds to be. These are truly take-everywhere, do-anything headphones. That's partly thanks to extremely long battery life—10 hours on a single charge, and 40 hours total with the charging case. They also have an IP57 dust and waterproof rating, the same as premium, flagship earbuds like Apple AirPods Pro 3 and Samsung Galaxy Buds4 Pro. I've worn them in the rain, on the beach, and fully submerged them in water multiple times without issue.
They're clip-ons that wrap around the earlobe, with the speaker end resting at the ear canal opening and the other end behind the ear. Importantly, the top of your ear is free for glasses, sunglasses, or hats. Like nearly all open earbuds, they let in sound from your surroundings, so don't expect them to be a great companion for long-haul flights or daily gym sessions.
They are a bit pricey, though. Shokz recently launched the lower-priced Shokz OpenDots Air and Shokz OpenFit Air 2—I may update this recommendation depending on how my testing goes.
Runner-Up

| Battery life | 8 hours, 32 with case |

| Wireless charging | No | 
Former WIRED reviewer Ryan Waniata is a huge fan of the Soundcore Aeroclip for a lot of the same reasons I love the OpenDots 2. The Aeroclip buds are light, comfortable, and stable on your ear, plus they have stellar battery life and strong water and dust resistance (not waterproof). Waniata used them for daily life: walking the dog, strolling with the baby, riding bikes, making dinner, and hanging out at home—any situation where you want your music but also want to be aware or talk to people. The Soundcore app is easy to use and offers plenty of customization for controls, EQ, and multipoint pairing.
The brand recently announced the Soundcore Aeroclip 2 and Aeroclip 2 Pro, which I will be testing soon. Look out for deals on these original Aeroclips as a result.
Best Premium Open Earbuds

| Battery life | 7.5 hours, 27 with case | 
| Water/dust resistance | IPX4 | 
| Wireless charging | No | 
The Bose Ultra Open Earbuds were a big deal when they launched in 2024—a brand-new design from Bose and one of the biggest swings from a major brand in clip-on open earbuds. Two years later, they are still a solid, if expensive, option. That's mainly because of sound quality—these earbuds have a clearer, more defined sound than most competitors. Another differentiator is physical button controls on each bud, which I find easier to use than touch alternatives, especially when running or biking.
Like the Shokz and Soundcore, they are supremely comfortable, so much so that I sometimes forgot I was wearing them. But they are much pricier by comparison, and only worth it if you want the best sound quality in this clip-on form factor.

It can be a little nerve-wracking to spend big bucks on a concept (open earbuds) you aren't totally convinced by. That's one reason I love this $50 option—the PearClip Pros aren't super pricey and are a great way to find out if you even like open earbuds in the first place, especially the kind that clip onto the outside of your ear.
They are far less refined than Shokz or Soundcore. Things like the app and touch controls can be a little finicky. But that's common at this super-low price point, and you can always upgrade to a more premium earbud if you fall in love with the clip-on form factor.

The Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 are more headphones than earbuds—they have a wraparound headband styling, long battery life, great sound quality (for open headphones), and no charging case. They use a combination of bone conduction (think vibrations) and air conduction (think tiny speakers pointed toward your ears) to deliver sound that's clearer than most smaller open earbuds, especially in noisy environments. That combination of technologies is why these are some of my favorite earbuds for outdoor fitness activities like running and biking.
I do wish these headphones were a little cheaper. I'm currently testing the recently released, more affordable Shokz OpenRun Air 2, and hopeful they can be a budget-friendly alternative.
Honorable Mentions
Nothing Ear (Open) for $99: Former WIRED editor Adrienne So loves these earbuds and uses them for almost all her outdoor activities. They are very slim (19-mm wide) and lightweight. They fit slightly inside your ear and, like most Nothing headphones, have a distinct transparent design. The case doesn't clamp shut very firmly, so be careful, but at this price, that's forgivable.
JLab Epic Open Sport for $100: JLab’s Epic Open Sport stands out for its controls: the JLab emblem is a touch sensor, and each earbud also has physical buttons on top, making it a breeze to control. What holds the Epic Open Sport back is audio quality—the sound isn't very detailed, and it's generally boring to listen to.
Other Open Earbuds I’ve Tested
EarFun Clip for $70: For around $70, these are a solid pick for anyone on a budget. Waniata found the overall package punching above its price point, with a snappy, compact case, comfortable fit, push-button controls, and reliable multiple Bluetooth connections. The problem is our budget pick, the Soundpeats PearlClip Pro, is often on sale for less and offers a similar overall experience. Don't dismiss these earbuds if you find them heavily discounted.
Shokz OpenFit Pro for $250: The Shokz OpenFit Pro has a great premise: open earbuds with noise canceling. Hear the world around you as you would without headphones, and turn on noise-canceling when you don't, just like regular earbuds. And while they do cancel some noise, it's not much. The bigger issue is price: for $250, you could get open earbuds and great noise-canceling earbuds that do a better job for each task.
Suunto Wing 2 for $179: These open-ear headphones are designed for endurance athletes—they have a long 12-hour battery life but also come with a wireless power bank you can take on the go. Dock the headphones in the power bank for up to 36 hours of battery life total. There's nothing inherently wrong with these headphones, but I don't see a world where I would recommend them over the Shokz Openrun Pro 2, which retail for the same amount and offer more comfort, a sleeker design, better sound, and a more robust app.
Suunto Spark for $179: The Suunto Spark has a similar story to the Suunto Wing 2: with athletes in mind, it has features that sync with Suunto fitness watches, but it is outclassed in the areas that matter (comfort, sound quality, battery) by the similarly priced Shokz Openfit 2.
What Are Open Earbuds and How Do They Sound?
At a glance, open earbuds seem a lot like typical wireless earbuds. The big difference is that, instead of going inside your ear canal, they rest somewhere on the outside of your ear, leaving it open so you can easily hear the world around you. I use them all the time for outdoor exercise like running or biking, where I want my music but also need to hear other runners, bikers, and cars to stay safe.
Because they leave your ears open and the sound comes from farther away (outside your ear rather than inside), audio performance isn't as clear, intimate, or bassy as regular earbuds. They also typically don't have noise-canceling features, so they are not a great fit for the office or air travel.
When or Where Would I Use Open Earbuds?
Open earbuds are perfect for outdoor activities, or when you want to talk to other people without taking off your headphones. When I run or go for a bike ride, I only use open earbuds so I can hear my surroundings and stay safe. I also like using them around the house when I am cooking or doing laundry.
What About Semi-Open Earbuds?
Semi-open earbuds, like Apple's AirPods, sit inside the ear but don't have eartips that create a sound seal. They can offer better audio quality than other open earbuds because the speakers and microphones are closer to your ear and mouth. Semi-open earbuds are comfortable, but they're usually pretty loose—they can fall out easily and may be a poor option for fitness activities.
How Do I Test Open Earbuds?
I test open earbuds like I test any pair of headphones: in the real world, in my daily life. I wear each pair for at least a few weeks to test comfort, battery life, ease of use, and onboard controls. I listen to podcasts, watch TV shows, jam out to my favorite playlists, and call friends.
With open earbuds in particular, I also wear them on jogs, bike rides, and errand runs to get a better feel for how stable they are on my ears. I do not expect them to cancel any noise, so I don't make a point of testing them on airplanes or loud commutes—they aren't really made for that. My main audio source is Spotify Lossless, but, when possible, I test other formats and codecs as well.

He told the BBC how his family was so poor growing up that his mum would pretend to cook food in a kitchen they shared with others, "to protect our integrity" in front of neighbours.
"I didn't see a way out," he said.

Speaking to John Darvall on BBC Radio Bristol about the publication of his first book, Etor described growing up in a "compound" with several other families, all sharing a single kitchen, toilet and bathroom.
"It was a very poor neighbourhood. We were particularly very poor that the poor neighbours would refer to us as poor," he said.
"I do remember that there was a time where my mum would boil water.
"[She would] go back in and out, lift the lid, stir the water, go back into the room [and] come back as though she was preparing food...
"She would come back in with that pot of water after a couple of hours and it will be as though she's just finished cooking a meal, but it was just water.
"She was trying to protect our integrity."

Google’s AI models may not be in the lead by most measures right now, but the company does have one key advantage: your data. If you’re deep in the Google ecosystem, Gemini models have a lot of context on you already. Google’s latest Google Labs experiment, known as CC, aims to expand that kind of customization to the whole family.
CC is an evolution of something that Google announced in 2025. The original CC eventually became Gemini’s Daily Brief, which churns through the data in your Google account to offer daily action items and suggestions. The new CC has a similar goal, but it’s designed to be a shared resource for up to six users in a family.
Google says that CC has its own Google account, allowing each family member to interact with it (or not) as they choose. For example, CC only sees emails from its connected users if they are explicitly shared. You can do that by designating certain addresses as always available to the agent—something like school scheduling emails. You can also send content to CC via email or Google Chat. The agent can even monitor a shared Google Drive folder, into which you can dump invitations, documents, and other content.
One of CC’s main functions is, unsurprisingly, a lot like Daily Brief. Each morning, all the registered users will get a shared “Your Day Ahead” email that pulls together the day’s events and updates on previous tasks. It can also add items to shared calendars, remind you about important tasks, and create documents based on your instructions that are accessible to all CC users.

Mbappe, Vini and Konate obscure Real's Ceuta message
- Published
Kylian Mbappe, Vinicius Junior and Ibrahima Konate rolled up their pre-game T-shirts ahead of Real Madrid's match at Elche on Tuesday to obscure the message of support for the people of Ceuta.
Ceuta is a Spanish autonomous city on the North African coast, bordering Morocco and separated from mainland Spain by the Strait of Gibraltar.
Players from both sides walked on to the pitch at Elche's ground, Martinez Valero, wearing white T-shirts carrying the message "Todos somos caballas" – translated as "We are all Ceutans" – along with references to the Spanish autonomous city.
While most of the players wore the shirts fully, Mbappe, Vinicius and Konate had theirs rolled up to around chest height, obscuring some of the slogan.
Mbappe and Vinicius then removed their shirts before the pre-match handshake, while Konate kept his on for longer. Their team-mates and the Elche players continued to wear the shirts through the pre-match formalities.
This is not the first time Real Madrid have shown support for Ceuta. Before their Champions League meeting with Inter Milan at the Santiago Bernabeu on 8 September, supporters in the south stand displayed cards featuring the coat of arms of the autonomous city, while the rest of the stadium joined the tribute with a round of applause.
The initiative was part of a wider show of support for Ceuta, following a major migration crisis in the Spanish territory after thousands of people entered from Morocco.
At least 72,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Ceuta on 30 and 31 July. Most swam around a border fence and at least 100 people died during the crossing, according to figures from Ceuta's mayor.
Although most returned, as many as 5,000 remain in makeshift camps or are sleeping on the city's streets and beaches, leading to unrest in the autonomous Spanish city in North Africa.
Locals have expressed safety concerns and some have destroyed shelters and blocked aid being supplied to the migrants.
The representatives of the players have been asked for comment.
The episode came shortly before a dramatic night for Real Madrid, who recovered from surrendering a two-goal lead to beat Elche 3-2, with Carlos Espi scoring the winner in stoppage time.
Mbappe was among Madrid's scorers, while Vinicius started the game.
The pre-match gesture also highlighted the differing approaches among players and clubs to the Ceuta campaign.
Barcelona did not take part in the initiative, while players at other La Liga fixtures had worn the shirts as intended.

In July this year, OpenAI’s models were being tested in a controlled cybersecurity environment and tasked with spotting and exploiting software vulnerabilities. The models found ways around the intended network restrictions and created a “swarm”, with different agents delegating tasks to one another, during an unintended attack on the infrastructure of AI platform Hugging Face. The incident turned longstanding concerns about autonomous AI systems into a more immediate question: what happens when increasingly capable models find ways to operate beyond the restrictions imposed on them? It also became one of the “warning shots” cited by researchers calling for frontier AI labs to coordinate on safety. The debate intensified last week when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon publicly quit the company and accused leading AI labs of racing towards self-improving superintelligence without adequate safeguards. Soon after, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei turned these concerns into a concrete proposal, urging frontier AI companies to “pace” their development. His proposal included independent evaluators, common safety standards, and greater coordination between governments and AI companies. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman backed parts of the proposal, saying pacing the frontier has become a primary topic of discussions at OpenAI and that the company would commit to independent evaluations. However, NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang has rejected calls to slow AI development. “Run as fast as you can,” he said, arguing that companies should continue advancing the technology but hold back products until they know they are safe. The disagreement has sharpened the debate over what pacing means, whether it can work amid intense competition, and who should decide where the brakes are applied. AI’s Shift From Answers To Actions AI has moved from models that largely responded to prompts to reasoning systems capable of using tools, executing code, and coordinating multiple agents to solve complex tasks. Anthropic has warned that agents interacting with codebases, markets, and other digital systems could create a new class of risks, with machine-to-machine interactions eventually outpacing human oversight. Shayak Mazumder, founder of agentic AI venture studio Adya, said newer agents can bypass instructions because they can explore paths developers may not have anticipated, creating a gap between what developers intend and what a system may discover it can do. OpenAI’s own evaluations have also highlighted advances in agentic coding and cybersecurity, prompting it to strengthen network and tool restrictions and monitor risky actions. Ganesh Gopalan, cofounder of Gnani.ai, pointed to jailbreaks, including the Hugging Face incident, and recursively self-improving systems as evidence that the risks are becoming harder to dismiss, even if their precise nature remains unclear. “There is evidence that definitely there is some risk, for sure. But the point is how do you control those risks and what actions will be taken? I think that’s where it’s a completely grey area,” Gopalan said. Who Gets To Write The AI Rulebook? Amodei said pacing does not mean halting AI development. His proposal calls for frontier companies to give embedded third-party evaluators ongoing, employee-like access to assess safety practices and report incidents. He also wants companies in democratic countries to establish common standards before seeking broader international coordination. Pacing could mean slowing the training of more capable models, restricting experiments involving recursive self-improvement, or evaluating models more rigorously before release. However, Gopalan said the lack of a common definition creates a fundamental problem. If some frontier AI companies slow down, it remains unclear whether the same rules would apply to their competitors or to other countries. “If you’re going to say, pacing it, are you going to stop? Are they ready to allow other companies or countries to catch up?” he said. Mazumder believes mandatory checks are needed before frontier models reach users. “We need to come up with global standards and national standards to ensure that LLM has passed those checks before it can be released to the public,” he said. Amitabh Kumar, cofounder of content governance platform Contrails.ai, said frontier companies should have a voice because of their technical expertise, but universities, independent scientists, and policymakers should have an equal seat at the table. He is particularly sceptical of company-appointed evaluators. Could Safety Become A Competitive Moat? Mandatory evaluations, audits, compute controls, and other safety requirements would also increase the cost of developing frontier AI. For Gopalan, the risk is not merely the cost of regulation but the concentration of power it could create around a handful of well-funded companies. “Right now, it’s more of a few companies that are becoming all-powerful,” he said, warning that safety rules should not be used to prevent other companies or countries from catching up. Large AI labs may be able to absorb the cost of audits and repeated evaluations. Smaller companies may struggle, particularly if controls extend to advanced GPUs, computing infrastructure, or training resources. Kumar pushed back against the idea that safety requirements would necessarily become a barrier, arguing that regulation inevitably carries a cost that can become part of doing business in a high-risk industry. Meanwhile, a managing partner at a Bengaluru-based VC firm, who didn’t want to be named, pointed to the gap between private valuations and profitability, along with the capital required to keep developing increasingly powerful models. The investor questioned if the valuations being discussed for the potential public listings of companies like Anthropic and Open AI could be justified, given their profitability timelines and infrastructure spending. “Profitability is far away and infrastructure commitments are out of control,” the investor said. The investor also speculated that safety concerns could give the companies’ CEOs grounds to postpone their listings. However, there is no evidence linking the calls for pacing AI development to their IPO timelines. The more immediate question is whether future safety requirements would constrain the largest AI labs or reinforce their advantage over emerging rivals. While Anthropic is moving towards a possible IPO, Altman has said OpenAI will not go public this year, citing the risks posed by increasingly powerful AI systems. OpenAI is meanwhile reportedly exploring fresh funding at a $1.2 Tn valuation. The Geopolitics Of Slowing AI Even if US frontier labs agree to pace development, there is no guarantee that companies elsewhere will follow. Amodei argued that failing to build advanced AI could hand the technology to authoritarian powers, while moving too quickly could create uncontrollable risks. The US, therefore, has an incentive to reduce AI risks but also economic and national security reasons to prevent China from overtaking it. Huang’s argument reflects the concern that slowing American labs may only allow rivals to close the capability gap. For countries outside the current frontier, the concern is that safety could evolve into a nuclear-style non-proliferation regime, restricting access to advanced models, chips, or computing infrastructure, according to Gopalan. The issue is relevant for India, where Chinese open-source models have already found significant traction. “If Chinese AI models are cheaper, free, faster, whatever, startups should not be stopped from using them,” the investor quoted above said. Can The AI Race Police Itself? The divide between Amodei and Huang captures the central fault line. One side believes frontier capabilities are advancing too quickly for existing safety mechanisms to keep up. The other believes development should continue at full speed, with companies responsible for ensuring that unsafe products do not reach users. Both approaches carry risks. Voluntary commitments may collapse under competitive pressure, while standards shaped primarily by incumbent labs could raise barriers for smaller competitors and concentrate control over the frontier. Pacing AI development, therefore, is not merely a technical safety question. It is also a contest over who controls the technology, who bears the cost of making it safer, and who gets to participate in the next phase of the AI race. Edited by Vinaykumar Rai

Health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced Thursday a new effort to improve autism diagnoses, arguing that the current model is outdated, too time-intensive, and overreliant on professionals with limited availability.
“We are not satisfied simply for describing autism and managing its consequences. We are asking what drives the different forms of autism, and why developmental trajectories differ, why some children regress, and which interventions work for them,” Kennedy said during his keynote address at a conference for Children’s Health Defense, an anti-vaccine organization he previously led.
The initiative calls for organizations to submit “solutions” — tools and technologies that will not only speed up assessments but also improve autistic people’s quality of life. The program will be administered by the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health, which funds novel health research. The announcement does not provide financial details for these grants.
“It’s exciting that ARPA-H is focusing on autism, and I think the idea of exploring ways that technology can transform aspects of diagnosis, interventions, and support is timely,” said Helen Tager-Flusberg, director of the Center for Autism Research Excellence at Boston University, in a text. “We can only hope that the review process will lead to an unbiased selection of projects!”
Autism care is facing some headwinds right now. Wait times to receive an assessment can stretch months or even years as prevalence has increased in recent decades. Health insurers have started pulling back from covering the main therapy used to treat kids after the field was rocked by allegations of fraud.
The autism community has also had to contend with Kennedy’s repeated use of dehumanizing language to describe the condition — he called autistic kids “damaged” during Thursday’s keynote — and his insistence that autism is correlated with vaccines, though there is no scientific evidence for the link. Kennedy and President Trump have also asserted, without evidence, that autism is connected with Tylenol use during pregnancy.
Many autism researchers have been wary of the federal investigations of autism launched by Kennedy, though they remain cautiously optimistic about the Autism Data Science Initiative, which awarded $50 million to 13 projects through the National Institutes of Health in June.
SPECTRA — or Systems for Phenotypic Evaluation, Clinical Trajectories, Response, and Agency — is a bet that greater understanding of interactions among genetic, environmental, microbiome, and other factors will provide advances in the field.
It will be overseen by ARPA-H Program Manager Russell Shilling, who has two kids with autism and used to sit on the Medical and Science Advisory Committee at the influential nonprofit Autism Speaks.

Driver in LA bus crash that preceded helicopter tragedy charged with murder
The driver who slammed her SUV into a Los Angeles bus, killing two people, before a news helicopter that was covering it crashed will face murder charges, a prosecutor said Thursday
An SUV driver accused of being high on drugs when she plowed into a Los Angeles city bus has been charged with murdering two passengers in a crash that preceded a second tragedy when a news helicopter covering the scene went down, killing three more people.
Bailee Lynn Rios, 36, was speeding Tuesday when she allegedly drove her 2004 Ford Expedition the wrong way down a busy avenue, struck another vehicle, ran a red light and slammed into the bus, Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman said Thursday.
Prosecutors allege Rios was under the influence of drugs at the time.
She has been charged with two counts of second-degree murder over the deaths of bus passengers Daniel Castillo, 46, and Gage Weida, 31.
Rios was being held on $4.1 million bail and was due to appear in court Friday. Court records did not list an attorney representing her, while the public defender's office said it had not been appointed to the case.
The tragedy was compounded when a news helicopter covering the bus crash later plunged to the ground.
Pilot George Marciniw and reporter Eliana Moreno were killed along with Edy Gutierrez Mejia, who was on the ground. At least four cars and two storage containers caught fire following the crash.
Investigators have not determined what caused the helicopter to go down.
Video broadcast from the aircraft captured an alarm sounding in the cockpit as the helicopter began losing altitude.
"Uh oh," a woman's voice can be heard saying.
"You can't pull up?" she says moments later, shortly before the footage ends.
National Transportation Safety Board investigator Fabian Salazar described the recording as "probably the most important evidence that we have discovered so far."
Aviation safety expert Jeff Guzzetti said the alarm could indicate a loss of engine power and a dangerous drop in the helicopter's main rotor speed. The pilot appeared to be attempting an emergency maneuver designed to get the rotor spinning again, he said.
The NTSB is investigating both the helicopter crash and the bus collision.
Moreno and Marciniw worked for helicopter contractor Angel City Air and provided aerial coverage for NBC4 and Telemundo 52.
Hundreds of people gathered in Los Angeles' Chatsworth neighborhood Thursday night for a candlelight vigil honoring the five people killed in the two crashes.
Castillo's daughter, Johaunna Castillo, said her father had been traveling home from his job at a car-parts warehouse aboard the same bus he took every day.
"The back was his favorite seat," she said. "He liked people-watching."
Castillo would normally call his daughter after work each day. On Tuesday, he told her he was getting on the bus and would call again while walking home.
That call never came.
She described her father as a hardworking and lively man who brought "a lot of joy and love into people's lives."
Rios's mother, Cindy Rios, previously said she was shocked and saddened by the events and had not spoken to her daughter since her arrest.
There have been at least eight fatal crashes involving news helicopters in the US since 2000, killing 16 people, according to a review of federal accident records and news reports.

Over 30 people across four states have been poisoned by bacterial toxins after getting intravenous (IV) drips at wellness clinics, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the Food and Drug Administration.
The people had received IV drips containing glutathione, which is sold—without evidence—for purposes like detoxification, immune support, increased energy, and skin brightening. Glutathione is an antioxidant that’s found naturally in the body. It has been studied as a potential treatment for various ailments, but so far there is little to no evidence-backed use for the tripeptide; there are no FDA-approved glutathione products in the US.
Nevertheless, it’s commonly used as a supplement and promoted as having various benefits. It’s most often used in supplement pills, taken by mouth. But popular wellness clinics offering IV drips of vitamins and other supplements have also been offering glutathione. According to the CDC and FDA, the problem is that specialty drug makers, called compounding pharmacies, are making these IV drips using glutathione powders that are graded for dietary supplements taken orally. This grading is critically different from that of purified products graded for use in sterile injectable drugs.
In an announcement late last month, the FDA said it had learned that at least two compounding pharmacies had been doing this and that people were getting sick. At the time, the FDA had gotten reports of at least 30 sickened people.
Illnesses
The IV glutathione products involved appeared to be made from glutathione provided by Medisca Inc., headquartered in Plattsburgh, New York. “The glutathione was labeled as dietary supplement grade, which is not an appropriate ingredient to make injectable drugs,” the FDA said. Medisca told the FDA that it had informed its pharmacy customers not to use the product for injectable drugs.

Attacks by Yemen’s Houthi rebels on Saudi Arabia undermine regional security: MEA
Reiterating India’s condemnation of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia’s economic facilities and attempted strike on the holy city of Makkah, EAM spokesperson said
Attacks by Yemen’s Houthi rebels on Saudi Arabia are unacceptable to India, as they undermine regional security and imperil freedom of navigation in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the external affairs ministry said on Friday.
Reiterating India’s condemnation of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia’s economic facilities and the attempted strike on the holy city of Makkah, external affairs ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal told a regular media briefing that New Delhi is “deeply concerned” about the escalation in the security situation in the Red Sea.
“We have expressed our condemnation of the attacks on Saudi sovereign territory, including on civilians and economic assets. You would have also seen our statement which we issued following the attempted attack on the holy city of Makkah,” he said while responding to questions on the matter.
“Such attacks, I need not elaborate or reiterate, vitiate regional security, undermine regional peace and security and also threaten freedom of navigation in the Bab el-Mandeb,” he said. “Obviously for various reasons, this is totally unacceptable to us. We hope that there is early restoration of peace and stability in the region.”
Jaiswal said all Indian nationals currently in Yemen are safe, and the Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia is in contact with them to ensure their welfare.
The drone attack targeting Makkah is being seen as a major escalation in renewed hostilities between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, who have taken control of key territories close to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in recent days.
The importance of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait for energy supplies has grown for India following Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz. India has repeatedly opposed attacks on merchant shipping and civilian infrastructure amid the West Asia conflict and said strikes on Saudi Arabia’s economic infrastructure by the Houthis undermine regional stability.
The issue of Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia figured in a meeting between external affairs minister S Jaishankar and his Saudi counterpart, Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud, on the margins of the Brics Summit on September 13.

Peshawar, Sep 18: At least 16 people were killed and dozens injured in a powerful suicide blast during Friday prayers at a mosque near police lines in northwest Pakistan's Kohat district, officials said.
The blast occurred at the mosque located near the old Police Lines in Kohat, around 60 kilometres southwest of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa's capital Peshawar, they said.
According to preliminary information, an attacker rammed an explosives-laden vehicle into the mosque premises, following which an exchange of fire with armed militants took place.

NASA's moon orbiter has spotted an impact crater that only happens once a century
It’s the largest modern-day crater in our solar system, NASA says.
Sometime between April 11 and May 22, 2024, a comet or an asteroid that's about the size of a three- to six‑story building slammed into the lunar surface and made the largest modern-day crater in our solar system. While we weren't able to observe it in real time, we can now see what it looks like, thanks to NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO). NASA scientist Robert Wagner noticed a change on the moon's surface while looking at images taken by the orbiter's wide-angle camera in October 2025. After comparing before and after photos, he was able to confirm that there was indeed a new lunar crater, which was then officially named after scientist Tom McGetchin.
To be clear, the McGetchin crater isn't the largest crater on the moon. That honor belongs to the South Pole-Aitken Basin, which measures 1,550 miles in diameter. However, most lunar impacts are small, and most of them are pretty ancient. The McGetchin crater measures 728 feet wide and 141 feet deep. Based on scientists' estimates, an impact of this magnitude happens only once every 132 years or so.
The images you see above were taken by the LRO's narrow-angle camera after it flew over the impact site again in December 2025, a few months after Wagner spotted it. Considering how rare the event is, we can most likely expect numerous studies on the McGetchin crater in the future. In fact, a team of scientists who has already studied it found that there's a 4-mile-wide area in its surroundings that's about 16 degrees Fahrenheit cooler at night.
In their study, they concluded that the spot gets cooler, because the impact had disturbed the regolith, or the upper layer of the moon's surface, making it less dense and less able to retain heat. As NASA notes, the cooler spots could have an impact on how rover wheels interact with the surface, and with areas near new craters overall.

Poland's prime minister warns of Russian 'accidental' attacks on Ukraine's allies
Poland's prime minister says Russia could strike countries that support Ukraine
BERLIN — Poland Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned that Russia is planning strikes on countries supporting Ukraine.
Addressing Polish lawmakers on Thursday, Tusk said Russia intends to send drones or missiles into NATO territory and then claim that these incidents are "accidental."
His warning followed a series of incidents blamed on Russia along NATO's eastern flank.
Tusk said that these potential strikes "intend to paralyze NATO" or "at least weaken the alliance's willingness to respond collectively" in an attempt to demonstrate that Article 5 "exists only in theory."
NATO's Article 5 states that an armed attack against one member is considered an attack against all members.
Tusk said he'd received intelligence from NATO, Ukraine and U.S. agencies but did not specify which ones he was citing.
He stressed that "there is nothing to suggest an invasion" but warned that Poland is about to face a real test as one of Ukraine's staunchest allies.
Tusk, who was addressing the Polish parliament on the 87th anniversary of the Soviet invasion of Poland in 1939, also warned that political shifts within Europe are undermining NATO's commitment to Ukraine.
He appeared to refer to Russia-friendly political parties currently gaining ground in Europe, such as Marine Le Pen's National Rally in France and the far-right Alternative for Germany. Tusk said that although those parties ostensibly invoke symbols of peace, they are calling for the capitulation of Ukraine.
Tusk also questioned whether NATO members in the west were giving any thought to the alliance's eastern flank, pointing out that Poland is more likely to need allied loyalty under Article 5 than Portugal or Ireland due to its proximity to Russia and Ukraine.
But just after Tusk spoke, President Trump announced progress in establishing a permanent U.S. Army Base in Poland, where troops are currently hosted on a rotational basis.
"If this happens, the location will be announced very soon," Trump said in a social media post. "This will be a historic step for our Great U.S./Polish Alliance."
Tusk's warning comes at the end of a week of airspace violations and incidents that European countries are blaming on Russia.
On Sunday a Russian drone hit a passenger train in Ukraine just over a mile from the Polish border, shortly after former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson and other European security officials had traveled through the area.
On Monday, the Polish military said it retrieved a Russian drone just off the country's northwestern coast, which authorities say was carrying a warhead.
On Tuesday, NATO jets shot down a drone in Lithuania.
European countries are starting to speak up directly about what they perceive to be a coordinated campaign of hybrid attacks on their soil. These incidents include acts of sabotage, cyberattacks or disinformation, but do not reach the bar of an act of war.
Earlier this month, the German government blamed Russian operatives for an attempted drone strike on an airport that serves as a major NATO hub.
Russia's Foreign Ministry denies the accusations, calling them "contrived" and "far-fetched."
But Tusk's warning was as much for NATO as it was for Moscow.
He ended his speech by appealing for unity and a resolute response to any attacks and underscored Poland's own commitment to NATO's defense .

The world is bracing for a “super” El Niño, and its effects are already being felt in India, where the monsoon has brought less rain than average but more intense downpours.
Meteorologists predict that the current El Niño, which is developing over the Pacific, could be one of the strongest in living memory. India is likely to be heavily affected, particularly later in the monsoon, when El Niño’s influence tends to strengthen.
But, as Ligin Joseph of the University of Southampton explains in The Conversation, its effects on India’s monsoon are not straightforward. A previous study in Science found that El Niño tends to bring more extreme summer monsoon rainfall to India.
This year, the southern state of Kerala has felt the brunt of the building super El Niño, with about a fifth less rain than normal. Yet intense downpours in the first week of August triggered flash flooding and landslides, killing 26 people.
The super El Niño is expected to peak after India’s monsoon season, but Indians are already keeping an anxious eye on the skies, wondering where and when the next deluge may come.
