Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian visited New Delhi on 11 September 2026 to attend the 18th BRICS Summit. During his visit, he met Prime Minister Narendra Modi and participated in several engagements on the sidelines of the summit. On 11 September 2026, Iran’s Ambassador to India, Dr Mohammad Fathali, hosted an event in New Delhi where Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian met religious leaders, intellectuals and other dignitaries, including Jain monk Acharya Lokesh Muni and Jagadguru Swami Satishacharya Maharaj.
In this context, a video of Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian bowing down is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows him touching the feet of Jagadguru Ramanandacharya Swami Satishacharya to seek his blessings. Several news outlets, including Times Now Navbharat and ABP News, also reported that Pezeshkian touched the feet of Swami Satishacharya during the event. Let’s verify the claim made in the post in this article.
Claim: The video shows Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian touching Swami Satishacharya’s feet for blessings.
Fact: The video does not show Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian touching Swami Satishacharya’s feet to seek his blessings. Pezeshkian bent down to pick up something that had fallen to the ground, while Satishacharya also bent down at the same time. The Iranian Embassy and people present at the event confirmed that the video does not show Pezeshkian seeking blessings from Satishacharya. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
To verify the claim, we conducted a Google search using relevant keywords and found reports published by News18 Hindi and Moneycontrol, citing sources from the Iranian Embassy, which reported that Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian bent down to pick up a piece of paper. According to News18 Hindi, the Iranian Ambassador and diplomats organised a special reception and interaction programme at The Oberoi Hotel in New Delhi, attended by Jagadguru Satishacharya Maharaj, along with several prominent Indian interfaith leaders, intellectuals and businesspeople. During the event, Pezeshkian bent down to pick up a letter that had fallen to the floor, rather than touching anyone’s feet. Moneycontrol also reported, citing Iranian Embassy sources, that the letter had been handed to Pezeshkian by another leader and accidentally fell from his hand, prompting him to bend down and pick it up.
We then conducted a reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video, which led us to social media posts by INN News (archived) and Ismat TV (archived). An INN News post featuring Sahil Naqvi, who was present at the event, addressed the viral video, claiming that Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian had bowed to touch the feet of a Hindu priest in India. According to the post, Pezeshkian had bent down to pick up a pen that had fallen to the floor, while the priest also bent down at the same time, creating the impression that the President was touching his feet. The post described the viral portrayal as misleading and said the footage was being presented out of context.
Ismat TV shared a video from another angle, showing both Pezeshkian and Swami Satishacharya bending down to pick up the pen. According to the account, Pezeshkian first attempted to pick it up, followed by Satishacharya. The post said that the incident was a gesture of respect and courtesy and did not show Pezeshkian bowing to anyone.
We then contacted Ismat TV and spoke to Hussain Mehdi, a photographer employed by the organisation. Speaking to Factly, he said that the channel’s staff were present at the event and that the claim that Pezeshkian touched Satishacharya’s feet is false. He also shared another video shot from a different angle, showing both Pezeshkian and Satishacharya bending down to pick up a paper.
We found a Facebook post by Acharya Lokesh Muni, who shared pictures of himself at the event standing next to Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian. In the post, he said that he had invited Pezeshkian to host a first-of-its-kind peace summit in Iran, which the Iranian President accepted. He added that religious leaders and peace-loving groups from around the world would gather to promote peace through dialogue and discussion.
We contacted him, and speaking to Factly, he stated that the claim that the Iranian President touched the feet of a Hindu religious leader is false. He said that while he was showing Pezeshkian his magazine, Aahwaan, which is published by the World Peace Centre, an organisation he founded, the magazine fell from his hands. According to him, the video shows the Iranian President bending down to pick up the magazine for him as a courtesy, which was later circulated widely on the internet with a misleading claim.
We also contacted Maulana Taqi Haider Naqvi through the Iran Culture House, New Delhi, via WhatsApp. Naqvi, who was present at the event, also rebutted the claim that Pezeshkian touched Satishacharya’s feet. He also forwarded an Iranian Embassy statement regarding the matter, which reads, “The President bent down to pick up a letter that one of the leaders had given him and that had fallen to the ground.”
To sum up, this viral video shows Iranian President Pezeshkian bending down to pick up something, not to touch a Hindu religious leader’s feet.

As the tech sector sounds alarms about AI’s potential to destroy humanity, entertainment labor groups are urging the public to stay focused on what’s already happening. The Verge reached out to Disney, Netflix, Amazon, Lionsgate, and other studios who have started using AI, as well film startups focused on bringing generative AI into the mainstream to ask for their reaction to the recent warnings surrounding the technology. None have responded to our request for comment. The Screen Actors Guild – American Federation of Television and Radio Artists (SAG-AFTRA) and Writers Guild of America East (WGAE) did, however.
What Hollywood thinks about existential AI warnings
The studios have been silent, but Hollywood’s biggest labor unions aren’t buying the AI apocalypse narrative.
What Hollywood thinks about existential AI warnings
The studios have been silent, but Hollywood’s biggest labor unions aren’t buying the AI apocalypse narrative.
The AI tools used in entertainment production differ from the AI systems that have sparked a recent round of whistleblowing and apocalyptic declarations. They do not seem to be as existentially dangerous as the AI systems that drove former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon to quit his job and prompted Anthropic alignment lead Evan Hubinger to insist that the technology could “kill all humans” at some point “within the next decade.”
But despite the differences between entertainment-focused AI and the models developed by Anthropic and OpenAI, AI models that generate digital facsimiles of actors and attempt to replicate traditional filmmaking tools pose a threat to some human jobs. Similar to the way that the Hollywood unions advocated for protections and increased oversight around AI’s use during the 2023 strikes, Coxon’s Anthropic exit has inspired a wave of AI researchers to speak out in favor of stronger safety protocols. The heads of major AI companies including Anthropic, OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and X have also called for an industry-wide slowdown on the technology’s development. While president Donald Trump has dismissed these concerns as overreactions, some other US politicians have felt pressured to take legislative action. Hollywood unions’ fight for strict rules around gen AI’s use did not stop the entertainment industry from embracing AI, but they have given Hollywood’s laborers a way to fight back in instances when they feel that AI tools are being used to harm them.
When I recently spoke with the Screen Actors Guild – American Federation of Television and Radio Artists’ (SAG-AFTRA) chief negotiator Duncan Crabtree Ireland, he told me that the union recognized early on how AI could impact its members’ livelihoods. Most people might not have been familiar with the idea of studios completely replacing human actors with digital replicas, but SAG-AFTRA understood that it had an opportunity to shape public opinion about AI in Hollywood by “speaking out about it at the earliest possible point we could.”
“We bargained for and achieved enforceable, meaningful guardrails around how this technology can be implemented by the major employers in our industry,” Crabtree-Ireland explained. “That doesn’t include companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google directly, but it does encompass all of the companies who have built up businesses around the creation of professional level entertainment content in the United States.”
Though Crabtree-Ireland believes we “should be concerned about the broader societal and social implications of AI,” he also thinks that some of the warnings about the technology being an extinction-level threat could potentially be hyperbole and overblown. Doomerism has become one of the more common ways that AI companies generate buzz around their products, but the fact that Coxon left Anthropic to sound the alarm has given Crabtree-Ireland pause. Hearing the message from “the CEOs of these companies or the billionaires who’ve made their billions off of doing the exact thing that they’re now warning us might not be good,” has left him unsure “what to trust or what to believe.” But he acknowledged that Coxon was able to achieve “traction with the public.”
“The recklessness of the tech oligarchs pushing AI on our society has been matched only by their rampant dishonesty.”
Getting people to believe that SAG-AFTRA’s fears about AI should be taken seriously was one of the union’s major goals when its members voted to strike. The key to doing that, Crabtree-Ireland told me, was leading the strike with a focused message that clearly laid out to the public what was at stake and steps that could be taken to prevent worst case scenarios. If not for that, Crabtree-Ireland thinks that the Alliance of Motion Picture and Television Producers (AMPTP) might not have agreed to some of the union’s demands like requiring that studios gain permission and compensate actors for the use of their AI-generated replicas. “If that principle hadn’t been established, I think the economic incentive to use replication and to replace human performances would have been much stronger” and “would have resulted in a much greater and faster adoption of digital replication.” Had the protections not been codified, Crabtree-Ireland is confident that entertainment workers would be in a much more dire position now.
Writers Guild of America East (WGAE) executive director Sam Wheeler was much more pointed in his condemnation of the “tech oligarchs pushing AI on our society” whose recklessness “has been matched only by their rampant dishonesty.” But while Wheeler finds it hard to take AI companies’ warnings at face value, he noted that the WGAE “has long warned that unregulated artificial intelligence poses an existential threat to workers, to our democracy, and to the world.”
“Guild members have bargained meaningful AI protections into their contracts; in 2023 WGA members spent 148 days on strike before the film and television studios agreed to real safeguards for film and television writers,” Wheeler said. “But collective bargaining is not a replacement for government regulation, and we are grateful to states like New York that continue to enact meaningful regulations in the absence of federal action.”
Wheeler listed the disempowerment of workers, the degradation of the internet, the spread of disinformation, and increasing energy costs as some of the tangible societal harms AI has exacerbated. He urged policymakers not to be distracted by AI companies’ claims of ushering in an apocalypse because the real issue at hand is people behaving irresponsibly.
“These harms are the result of decisions made by human beings,” Wheeler insisted. “The WGAE believes that addressing those concrete harms and holding AI companies and their executives liable for the destruction their products cause is the surest way to safeguard against any worst-case scenarios.”

St Leger win has removed Osborne's fear of failure
- Published
St Leger-winning jockey Saffie Osborne says the "fear of failure" has left her after she became the first woman to win a British Classic.
The 24-year-old said that despite wanting to achieve "so much more", her victory at Doncaster on Saturday means she will always be able to look back and think her career was "worth it".
Osborne said the sport can be "very lonely" - she estimates she drives 65,000 miles a year, often alone - and she has suffered some serious falls, breaking numerous bones.
But she told BBC Sport that winning one of British Flat racing's five Classics had been a dream since she was five. She has now fulfilled it.
While racing is a sport where men and women compete against one another, opportunities have not been equal.
Only six female jockeys have had rides in British Classics in 250 years, totalling 12 rides, according to the National Horseracing Museum.
They are Gay Kelleway (The Oaks, 1986; The Oaks, 1987), Alex Greaves (The Derby, 1996; 1,000 Guineas, 1996), Hayley Turner (The Derby, 2012) Josephine Gordon (1,000 Guineas, 2017), Hollie Doyle (The Oaks, 2021; St Leger, 2021; The Oaks, 2022) and Saffie Osborne (2,000 Guineas, 2024; 1,000 Guineas, 2026; St Leger, 2026).
"It has been a male-dominated sport for an extremely long time, and I suppose it's becoming less and less of a conversation, which is quite nice," she said.
"When people talk about the firsts of what women have done, I think to have my own one is quite special.
"I think it's also quite poignant because there's so few left of first things for women to do in this sport."
On Saturday's groundbreaking win, she added: "That sort of fear of failure has sort of disappeared. However much more I want to achieve, and I want to achieve so much more, it's kind of like I can always look back on my career and know that it was all worth it.
"I got to achieve what I always dreamed of achieving."
Osborne's ride on Highwayman in the St Leger was her first for trainer Joseph O'Brien, and only came about because of an injury to regular jockey Dylan Browne McMonagle.
She acknowledged that the success of a jockey is dependent on "being chosen", but is adamant that her gender isn't a factor in the opportunities she gets.
"I don't feel like in my position now that I'm ever looked at any differently because I'm a woman," she said.
"Any jockey, when you're starting out, it takes years to gain respect and be looked at as a person that people would want to use. And I don't think my gender at this point would have had anything to do with it.
"Hopefully Saturday will open more doors. But when it comes to me as a female jockey, I don't think I'm viewed any differently within the industry."
Osborne also said she is treated as "one of the lads" in the weighing room, and has never experienced sexism and misogyny unlike other female jockeys, including Bryony Frost.
Jockey Robbie Dunne was banned from racing for 18 months, with three months suspended, for bullying fellow rider Frost in 2021, which was later cut to 10 months on appeal.
Having ridden 60 winners since the start of May, Osborne is currently sitting eighth in the Flat Jockeys Championship, and is open about dreaming of being champion jockey in the future.
She would be the first female jockey to achieve that.
"You wouldn't be a jockey if you didn't want to be champion jockey one day. I think this is the first year that maybe I truly believe that I could one day," she said.
"It's been a phenomenal year that's been topped off by Saturday. But I'm very lucky. I have a very good agent [Tony Hind] and agents are so important in this sport. He's got an amazing book of jockeys, the likes of Ryan Moore, William Buick, Billy Loughnane. And I'm very lucky to be on his team.
"He makes champion jockeys, he's had a lot of them. And yeah, I would love to be the next one on the list."

Why Democrats Might Choose to Impeach Cabinet Members
The power to impeach secretaries and other executive-branch officers is not well known, but it’s an effective accountability measure.
This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.
If Democrats win control of the House in November, they will face a dilemma: Should they attempt a record third impeachment of Donald Trump?
The president and his allies have warned that this would be a Democratic majority’s first move. “I’m going to be impeached. They’re going to impeach me,” Trump said last month at a rally in South Carolina. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has been noncommittal. “We haven’t ruled anything in, and we haven’t ruled anything out in terms of impeachment,” the would-be speaker told ABC’s This Week on Sunday. But Representative Jamie Raskin, the lead manager of Trump’s second impeachment, seemed more open. Earlier this month, on Meet the Press, he said that Trump had “undoubtedly” committed impeachable offenses. “We understand it’s not a panacea. It is a tool in the toolbox,” he said. “We will not hesitate to use it if we need to use it.”
Realistically, House Democrats may have a hard time resisting impeachment. Their voters are in a punchy mood. A new CBS News / YouGov poll found that opposition to Trump is the top motivation for Democratic voters in the midterms, and the political consultant Sarah Longwell recently wrote in The Atlantic that the most important priority for Democratic voters is not left-versus-right ideology but a willingness to fight Trump tooth and nail. Jeffries has already faced criticism for being too passive a leader, as well as for meeting with Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, and he may struggle to ignore a groundswell of support for impeachment.
As a constitutional matter, the case for impeaching the president is solid. Trump has usurped congressional powers, started an unauthorized war or two, defied courts, and used his position for outrageous personal and family enrichment. In 2019, my colleague Yoni Appelbaum made the intellectual case for impeachment as a useful democratic process.
The political case for impeaching Trump is shakier. Regardless of the results in November, Democrats are unlikely to get enough votes in the Senate to convict and remove him, meaning that a third impeachment would hit the same dead end as the first two. An impeachment can still be effective as a way of damaging a president, but Trump is already deeply unpopular and will never face voters again, so the upside is limited, and an impeachment might give him a way to rally his remaining base around him—which would only strengthen his power and resolve.
But what if House Democrats impeached Trump’s Cabinet members instead? The power to impeach secretaries and other executive-branch officers is explicit in the Constitution but perhaps not well known, because it’s been used only twice in history. One reason such proceedings are rare is that a president usually fires a Cabinet member or forces them to resign before they can be impeached, but Trump has shown serious reluctance to fire aides because of public pressure. The congressional scholar Norm Ornstein has argued that if Trump won’t rein them in, Democrats should. On Tuesday, outgoing Representative Thomas Massie, a Republican, brought new attention to the possibility by moving to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth. GOP leadership promptly shut down all voting until after the election.
In 1876, Secretary of War William Belknap was impeached for corruption, but he resigned the same day and the Senate subsequently acquitted him; a number of senators doubted they had jurisdiction post-resignation. (This historical example resurfaced during Trump’s second impeachment trial, which occurred after he’d left office.) In 2024, House Republicans impeached Secretary of Homeland Security Alejandro Mayorkas on vague grounds, but the Senate voted to dismiss the charges as unconstitutional without a trial.
A Democratic House could plausibly launch impeachment inquiries into several administration officials, many of which would dovetail with investigations that representatives say they already have planned. In some cases, Democratic representatives have already filed articles of impeachment against Cabinet members, including Hegseth, Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr., and Secretary of Education Linda McMahon, but those have gone nowhere in the GOP-led chamber. A new Democratic majority could change that.
The conduct of a few particular individuals makes them likely targets for impeachment efforts. Kennedy has done serious damage to American public health, undermining vaccinations and weakening the CDC. At least one Republican senator has accused him of lying about vaccination rules during his confirmation hearings, when he also falsely characterized a trip he took to Samoa. Hegseth has waged an unauthorized war against Iran, for which he seems to have no realistic game plan; mishandled classified information; possibly violated the Hatch Act by appearing at a fundraiser for a political candidate; and left the armed forces bereft of leadership by firing a slew of qualified generals and admirals.
Attorney General Todd Blanche has been instrumental in turning the Justice Department into a partisan tool for persecuting Trump’s political adversaries, and a federal judge rebuked him for his role in Trump’s attempt to set up a $1.8 billion slush fund for political allies. Multiple sources shared with my colleague Sarah Fitzpatrick serious worries about FBI Director Kash Patel’s leadership, including claims of emotional volatility, heavy drinking, and absence from the job. (Patel denied the allegations and sued Fitzpatrick and The Atlantic for defamation, demanding $250 million.) Russell Vought, the director of the Office of Management and Budget, has led a concerted effort to take congressional powers for the White House.
As a policy matter, impeachment of some of these officers could be more effective than ordinary investigations would be in halting the egregious actions taken by their offices and departments. It might also have a couple political benefits over impeaching Trump. First, such an effort could escape the Trump vortex: By moving the focus to officials who don’t command the same personal loyalty as Trump, impeachment might allow more emphasis on actual administration actions and policy, instead of on presidential personality. Second, conviction might still be a remote possibility, but GOP senators who are fed up with the White House might be more willing to vote to convict officers than they would be to risk taking on Trump himself.
The real question is whether controversial Cabinet secretaries will stick around to see whether Democrats try to target them. A midterm election, especially one that goes poorly for the president’s party, is typically a moment for some secretaries to exit. But Hegseth seems entrenched, continuing to push out rivals; Blanche just won confirmation; and Kennedy and Vought are ideologues pursuing treasured agendas. If neither they nor Trump are willing to change course, then a Congress that has done little for the past two years will have a chance to do something novel: act.

The Dead Silence of AI Therapy
By Steven Barrie-Anthony
Therapy can involve a lot of words, but it’s often the pauses that matter most. If you transcribed a session, the pauses would look like nothing: beats of silence, extra breaths, slowing down. But these can represent the crux of the practice: entry points into feeling. My job as a psychoanalyst is to listen as much to silence as to words, to be present with the patient while they’re quiet—to stay with them as they allow their feelings to emerge.
I was trained across diverse theories and techniques, but in my clinical work I have found that the cornerstone of the process is feeling. The patient’s emotional experience is the destination and the terrain. But I also feel; I am moved. And the work I do with my patients relies on our relationship and our capacity for mutual feeling. In many ways, the history of my field from Freud on has been a growing acknowledgement of the reality of this relationship—moving from the therapist as sealed off and standing apart, toward approaches that view the real human relationship between patient and therapist as the territory where healing happens.

A US federal court in Los Angeles sentenced a former Syrian government official who ran one of the country’s most infamous prisons to 60 years in prison on Thursday – the most significant punishment handed to an official of ousted president Bashar al-Assad’s regime by a foreign court and to a defendant present in person.
Samir Ousman al-Sheikh was the head of the Adra prison, on the outskirts of Damascus, between 2005 and 2008, when he oversaw an underground “punishment wing”, known as “Wing 13”, in which prisoners and regime opponents were interrogated and tortured as he watched through surveillance cameras. A federal jury convicted al-Sheikh last March of having tortured prisoners and then lying about it in US immigration forms.
“The conduct was heinous, unimaginably cruel and almost unspeakably violent and brutal,” said Hernan D Vera, a US district judge, before delivering the sentence.
Al-Sheikh’s legal team and the justice department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Following al-Sheikh’s conviction, Bill Essayli, first assistant US attorney, had said in a statement that the case showed the US “is not a refuge for criminals – especially criminals who engage in the brutality of the kind this defendant inflicted on his victims”.
Al-Sheikh, 73, who also served as governor of Syria’s Deir Ez-Zour province in 2011, at a time of violent regime crackdowns against protesters, moved to the United States in 2020, obtained a green card and applied for US citizenship. He was arrested in July 2024 at Los Angeles international airport on immigration fraud charges and prosecutors later added four-torture related charges.
He is the first al-Assad regime official to go to trial in the US and the highest ranking regime official to be tried anywhere in the world in person. Al-Assad was ousted by a lightning rebel offensive in December 2024 which toppled the regime in just 11 days.
Since then, Syria’s new government has held a number of in absentia trials for former regime officials in connection to crimes committed during the country’s years-long civil war, which killed about half a million people and displaced half the country’s prewar population of 23 million. In August, a court sentenced al-Assad and his brother Maher to death for crimes against humanity and war crimes, but the two men have been in Moscow since the regime’s collapse.
Other factions in Syria’s civil war have also been accused of abuse of detainees, including insurgent groups and the US-backed, Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces.
During al-Sheikh’s nine-day trial, several victims and witnesses testified. They described guards folding prisoners into car tires, restraining and beating them. Some they said, were cuffed by their wrists to pipes on the ceiling, beaten with cables, and left suspended for extended periods of time.
Others testified that they were placed on a device known as a “magic carpet,” which consisted of two large wooden panels with hinges in the middle onto which guards strapped prisoners, forcing the panels together to cause excruciating pain. One victim recalled al-Sheikh himself stomping on the device. Another testified he was subjected to the “magic carpet” as punishment for writing a letter of support to a political prisoner and also forced to wear a red jumpsuit assigned to prisoners designated for execution, leading him to believe he was going to die.
“[Al-Sheikh] chose to serve the ruthless, repressive Assad regime in Syria throughout his professional life, including for four years as the warden of Syria’s largest prison,” prosecutors wrote in a sentencing memo. “[He] knew that what he was doing was wrong. Nonetheless he ordered and participated in the torture of his victims because he had the power to do so and because he thought he would never be held accountable.”
Several victims and witnesses also submitted written and video testimonies to the court ahead of the sentencing, in which they spoke of being haunted and traumatized by their experiences two decades later.
“I still hear the screams of others begging for mercy,” said one of the men, Nidal Shikhani.
“Even though 20 years have passed, I still live in the prison of my memory,” said another, Sultan Abdul Malek. “I suffer from sudden panic attacks and constant anxiety.”
His brother, Khaled Abdul Malek, who was taken to “Wing 13” twice during his four years at Adra prison, spoke of the physical and psychological scars he was left with, including chronic back pain and mobility problems.
“My son Battal asks if he could ride my back and with a heart wrung with pain, I am forced to tell him I [am] no longer strong enough to carry him,” he said.
Several witnesses also submitted testimony on al-Sheikh’s behalf, speaking about his age and frailty as they asked the court for leniency. More than 50 people sent letters of support to the court, describing him as “a person of integrity, compassion, and generosity to his family and community”, his attorneys wrote.
Prosecutors had asked the court for a minimum sentence of 80 years; al-Sheikh’s attorneys had called for a five-year sentence, citing his poor health and noting that he was willing to be deported to Syria.
“Whatever moral weight this case carries in the broader arc of history – however much the world, or the victims, or the public might wish the sentence to ‘send a message’ – that desire cannot be the foundation of a just sentence,” the defense team wrote in a memo to the court.
“This case sends a message both to the new government of Syria and to other victims that justice is possible,” said Ela Matthews, an attorney at the Center for Justice and Accountability, which represented several victims. “The transitional justice process that is happening in Syria needs to continue to evolve and bring individuals like this to account, but in the US this sends a message that the rule of law is still functioning and that these types of cases are possible.”

Alice Augusta Ball lived a very short life. In 24 years, she had remarkable achievements, and was predictably forgotten for a while, until the world was shaken up to her brilliance. Her work on distilling chaulmoogra oil for use as effective treatment for leprosy brought hope to a number of patients globally.
An African American woman born into middle class in the late 1800s, Alice Ball benefitted from an early exposure to chemical processes as her family was involved in photography. She went on to shine in science at school, and could hope to move on to university, a rare opportunity for a woman and a person of her race at that time. She lived up to her potential and at the University of Washington, racked up her skills in chemistry and pharmacy. She finished two degrees – a bachelor’s in pharmaceutical chemistry and a bachelor’s in pharmacy – thus arming herself for a career –short lived, but so sparkling, people are still talking about her, though subsequent innovations have transformed care for leprosy.
With a full scholarship, another rarity for the times, Alice moved to the College of Hawai‘i, and became the first woman and the first African American to earn a master’s degree in chemistry. We mention it because it is an achievement, but also because it was an achievement that attracted the kind of attention a career flourishes on. It is said that Harry T. Hollmann, a public health officer, thought her thesis research on extracting active compounds from the kava (awa) root might have implications for his passion – finding cures for leprosy.
Leprosy or Hansen’s disease is caused by Mycobacterium leprae, and was discovered by Norwegian physician Gerhard Armauer Hansen in the 1870s. While it is prevalent in people living in tropical regions, leprosy which affects the nervous system, also has the moniker of being the world’s oldest disease. Evidence of leprosy has been found in skeletons from back in 2000 BCE. Those affected develop visible skin lesions and extremities including fingers and toes malformed and misshapen fingers. Sometimes amputations were also performed on limbs that could not be salvaged. As a result of the disfiguration, the stigma surrounding the disease was so high, those with leprosy had to be sequestered in camps and asylums outside the community.
Alice did accept Hollman’s invitation and what she managed to achieve was to revolutionise the field of leprosy care in the very near future. Described as the Ball Method, Alice devised a method that would “convert the oil’s fatty acids into water-soluble ethyl esters that could be injected into patients. Until then Chaulmoogra oil was promising as treatment for leprosy, but it was thick, not soluble in water, besides difficult to inject and swallow. Soon the world adopted the Ball Method and the landmark contribution changed life for the better for people who were battling leprosy across the world, without hope until then. Alice was in her early 20s at the time of this achievement.
Records of the time say, since the new formulation dispersed in the bloodstream instead of pooling under the skin, patients for the first time celebrated as earlier, there was none of the severe local reactions and oozing oil that the injections caused. Used on patients at Kalihi Hospital in Hawai‘i, researchers managed to show that patients administered the new formulation, became ‘bacteriologically negative, their lesions resolved, and many were discharged from isolation to rejoin their families, without fear of infecting them.’ This injectable preparation remained the best available treatment worldwide until sulfone antibiotics, Dapsone, in combination with other drugs, replaced it in the 1940s, facilitating a future unimaginable until then, for those who were diagnosed with leprosy and condemned to social isolation.
However, Alice’s contribution never made it to the headlines thanks to a set of factors – her gender, age and race were primary. She died young, it is speculated that it could be a result of a laboratory accident, a senior male colleague, her department head Arthur L. Dean appropriated and published her work without sharing any credit, in fact, promoting it as the ‘Dean method’, accounts of that period list.
It went unchallenged until decades later, when researcher Harry Hollmann revisited the archives and credited Ball. Finally, the historical records were righted, and Alice Ball’s name was affixed to the method she had painstakingly developed. By 24, despite the disdvantaged circumstances she worked in, Alice Ball had changed the world, it is a matter of speculation how much she would have achieved had she lived longer, but a safe bet to say she would have left a deeper impact. For the punch she packed in her short life, and the revolution she managed in that life, it’s time we say her name, say “Alice Augusta Ball.”

'I've turned the page' - Camara on Chelsea deal collapse
- Published
Monaco midfielder Lamine Camara says he has "turned the page" and is focusing on the Ligue 1 season after his £47.1m move to Chelsea collapsed.
The 22-year-old had completed a medical but the deal fell through shortly before the transfer window closed.
Two bids had already been rejected, but Monaco lowered their asking price in a turbulent end to the window when it looked likely that Folarin Balogun's move to Everton was in doubt.
When Balogun's transfer appeared to be back on track, Monaco appeared to change their decision to sell Camara, but in the end both players stayed with the Ligue 1 side.
"There was a possibility I could leave," Camara said, speaking before Monaco's game against Strasbourg on Saturday.
"It didn't go through at the last minute and that's part of football. I've turned the page and am focusing on the season."
Sources in France had stated Monaco needed to make a major sale this summer and preferred to sell Balogun. A source at the Ligue 1 club had previously indicated it would take a "substantial fee" to secure Camara's departure.
Monaco have won their first three Ligue 1 fixtures of the season and sat second to Rennes in the table, with a game in hand, heading into the weekend.
"I can help the team a lot," Senegal international Camara said.
"Football moves fast. Maybe other opportunities will come along. But for now, I'm staying focused on the season with Monaco."

Social Security has emerged as a major concern for voters in several closely contested US Senate races, with a large majority saying they would be more likely to back candidates who offer a plan to prevent future benefit cuts, according to a new survey from the nonpartisan Peter G. Peterson Foundation.
The survey covered 2,500 registered voters across five states — Georgia, Michigan, North Carolina, Ohio and Texas — where Senate races are being closely watched. It found that voters broadly want lawmakers to address Social Security's long-term finances rather than avoid the issue.
Here is what the survey found and why Social Security is becoming an important issue in the 2026 Senate races.
Social Security provides retirement, disability and survivor benefits to millions of Americans. But its finances face a long-term imbalance between incoming revenues and scheduled benefits.
According to the 2026 Social Security Trustees Report, the programme's primary retirement trust fund is projected to be depleted in 2032.
If Congress does not change the law before then, Social Security would not simply stop paying benefits. Instead, payments would be limited to the revenue available to the programme. The Peterson Foundation's survey describes this as an immediate 22% reduction in benefits for beneficiaries.
The projected shortfall has made Social Security a politically significant issue because senators elected in 2026 could still be in office when the trust fund reaches the projected depletion date.
The survey found that 81% of voters said they would be more likely to support a candidate who has a plan to prevent automatic Social Security benefit cuts.
The findings suggest that, among the voters surveyed, simply promising to leave the programme unchanged was less popular than offering a plan to address its projected financing problem.
Yes, according to the survey.
77% said lawmakers who promise not to touch Social Security are making the problem worse and agreed that delaying action makes the problem harder to fix.
85% said it is more important than ever for lawmakers to fix Social Security.
88% said current lawmakers should talk more about the programme's financial problems.
91% said they support Social Security reforms.
The Peterson Foundation said majorities across party lines supported potential reforms.
The survey focused on Georgia, Michigan, North Carolina, Ohio and Texas, all of which have competitive Senate races, according to the foundation.
The Senate plays a central role in determining whether legislation addressing Social Security can pass Congress. As a result, the positions taken by candidates in these races could become relevant to the debate over the programme's future.
The online survey was conducted jointly by Global Strategy Group, a Democratic polling firm, and North Star Opinion Research, a Republican polling firm.
The poll included 2,500 registered voters:
Georgia — 500 voters
Michigan — 500 voters
North Carolina — 500 voters
Ohio — 500 voters
Texas — 500 voters
The survey was conducted from August 20 to August 27, 2026, and has a reported margin of error of ±4.4 percentage points.

Who Will Foot The UPI MDR Bill? UPI transformed digital payments by making them virtually free. From October 15, this equation will change as high-value transactions will begin attracting MDR. While the new regime opens a new revenue pool for fintechs, it could reshape user behaviour. So, who will now bear the cost? UPI Ends Free Ride: The new framework imposes a 0.4% MDR on P2M UPI payments above ₹2,000, capped at ₹300 for transactions of ₹75,000 and more. Merchants receiving up to ₹1 Lakh a month via QR codes remain exempt, but sellers crossing the threshold repeatedly will enter the MDR category. This could expose small businesses to payment acceptance costs, particularly during the festive season when higher-value transactions are the norm. The Merchant-Side Test: For many sellers, the financial effect will depend on ticket size and transaction mix. A business selling low-value goods may see little immediate impact, while retailers and D2C brands could face a meaningful recurring cost. More importantly, merchants will now have to weigh MDR alongside gateway fees, logistics and marketplace commissions when calculating margins. The Convenience Question: While the government has prohibited merchants from passing on the costs to consumers, the order does not guarantee that the cost will disappear. Businesses, under margin pressure, may absorb MDR through broad price increases rather than displaying a separate payment fee at checkout. On top of this, many fear that higher-value buyers could move back to cash if UPI loses its frictionless appeal. Sustainability Vs Scale: Nevertheless, fintech startups see MDR as essential for funding technology upgrades and wider payment infrastructure without relying on subsidies. The revenue could also make UPI more viable for smaller payment players competing against dominant apps. But the success of the policy will rest on maintaining a delicate balance between protecting small merchants and ensuring costs are not pushed onto consumers. So, can UPI finally become financially viable without losing the low-cost advantage that made it indispensable? Oracle employees caught in the company's latest round of layoffs now know exactly what they'll leave behind and what they'll take with them.
An internal FAQ document viewed by Business Insider lays out more details for staff impacted, including severance capped at 26 weeks, canceled stock awards, lost bonuses, and deadlines for exercising vested options.
Oracle started notifying affected staff on Monday. Business Insider reported last month that the company had drawn up plans for double-digit percentage layoffs on some teams to reduce payroll as it racks up billions in debt to fund AI infrastructure.
Employees were offered four weeks' base salary plus one week per year of employment, according to documents viewed by Business Insider. The full FAQ document includes the maximum severance payout and what happens to employee bonuses, commissions, and stock options.
The details offer a window into the employee impact of Oracle's latest cost-cutting push. The company has shed tens of thousands of workers while borrowing heavily and spending tens of billions of dollars to build data centers and other infrastructure needed to support its AI ambitions. For employees leaving in the latest cuts, the financial impact extends beyond losing a paycheck: unvested stock disappears, future corporate bonuses are forfeited, and participation in employee stock programs ends.
Oracle executives didn't directly address the layoffs in an employee town hall this week, but Chief Financial Officer Hilary Maxson told staff the company needs to be "thoughtful" about where it spends tims and money.
"I don't mean doing more with less, which is a phrase that I really, really don't like," Maxson said. "It means simplifying processes that don't help customers and making clear choices on where we're going to use our resources where they have the greatest impact."
This latest round of layoffs follows cuts earlier this year. The company's workforce declined by 21,000, or 13%, in the 2026 fiscal year that ended May 31, according to a recent filing.
Oracle's severance package is comparatively less generous than those offered by other Big Tech companies over the past year.
Salesforce's standard policy offers up to 30 weeks of severance pay, with a minimum of 9 or 13 weeks based on role, plus an additional 3 weeks of service per year.
Microsoft offered employees in its latest round of layoffs this summer up to 39 weeks' base pay, with a minimum of 60 days and one or two additional weeks per six months of service, depending on seniority.
Severance
- Employees receive four weeks of base pay for their first year of service, plus one additional week of base pay for each additional year worked. Six months or more in the last year of employment will count as a full year.
- Total severance is capped at 26 weeks of base salary, paid out about three weeks after employees sign a severance agreement and return company property.
- Employees rehired within six months may have to repay a portion of their severance.
Employee Stock Purchase Plan
- Participation ends on the employee's termination date.
- Contributions made during the current offering period are generally refunded without interest in the employee's final paycheck.
- Employees who leave during specific purchase windows (Sept. 16—30 or March 16—31) will have their contributions used to purchase stock instead of receiving a refund.
Stock options
- All unvested stock options are canceled when employment ends.
- Employees generally have up to three months after termination to exercise vested options, subject to the original expiration date.
- Some options granted through acquired companies may have a shorter, one-month exercise window.
Restricted Stock Units
- All unvested RSUs are canceled upon termination.
- Previously vested RSUs remain the employee's property and stay in their Fidelity brokerage account.
Vacation and sick pay
- Accrued vacation is prorated through the employee's termination date and paid out according to company policy.
- Unused paid sick leave is not paid out at separation unless required by applicable law.
Bonuses
- Employees on sales or consulting bonus plans may receive any bonus earned under the terms of their compensation plan.
- Employees on corporate bonus plans are not eligible for future corporate bonus payouts after termination.
Commissions
- Employees stop earning commissions on their last day of employment.
- Commissions already earned but not yet paid remain payable under the terms of the applicable compensation plan.

Zara Larsson criticises White House for using her song in deportation video
- Published
Swedish pop star Zara Larsson has condemned the White House for using one of her most recognisable songs in a social media reel.
The clip used Larsson's Midnight Sun in a video appearing to show immigration enforcement raids. The song has since been removed from the post, but the video is still visible on the White House's TikTok feed.
The video is captioned "never ending deportations", riffing on Larsson's lyrics "never-ending midnight sun".
In a three-minute reaction video posted on social media, Larsson described the clip as "dehumanising", joining a growing list of singers, including Sabrina Carpenter and Ariana Grande, who have told the Trump administration to not use their music.
The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.
The reel splices together multiple videos of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents, as well as other US law enforcement personnel, handcuffing men and putting them into vehicles.
Larsson reposted part of the original clip, which then cuts to a selfie video of her using her fingers to hold an 'L' shape against her forehead.
In the reaction video that has already clocked up more than 4.2 million views on TikTok, she tells her followers the White House video is "so dehumanising".
Larsson continues: "These people in this video – they're real people."
"The vast majority of these people who are undocumented are regular people with jobs and they're just trying to have a better future".
"It's so crazy how everything is so memefied and so 'ha-ha-ha'," she says, accusing the White House of using her song to sow "division", despite the lyrics reflecting a connection between people and nature, according to Larsson.
Earlier this year, Larsson condemned a video of President Donald Trump dancing at various events overlayed with her hit Lush Life.
White House social media accounts have been forced to remove various songs from their feed following interventions from artists.
Taylor Swift's seasonal track August disappeared from a reel shared by the Trump administration in August, while one of Olivia Rodrigo's songs vanished from a video after the singer condemned its use for what she called "hateful propaganda".
Sabrina Carpenter and Ariana Grande have also warned the Trump administration in separate incidents to not use their music in social media content after the White House posted videos featuring their songs.

North Korea said U.S.-led military drills in the region only strengthen its resolve to expand its nuclear arsenal and “help” to boost its defense capabilities, warning of a more forceful response as tensions rise despite U.S. President Donald Trump’s efforts to revive diplomacy with Pyongyang.
“It is inevitable that outsiders’ greater threat to our national security makes our physical power grow stronger ceaselessly in a corresponding manner,” said Kim Yo Jong, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un’s sister, in an early-morning statement carried by North Korean state media Friday.
Kim accused the U.S. of driving tensions on the Korean Peninsula through a series of multinational exercises, including Pacific Vanguard, a naval drill involving South Korea and Japan that concluded last week. She described the exercises as U.S.-led “war rehearsals” and said there would be no change in Pyongyang’s push to strengthen its nuclear deterrent.
“Our will to defend our sovereignty will be expressed in clearer action and there will be never ever change in the course of intensifying the nuclear war deterrence,” she added.
Her warning follows the five-day Freedom Edge exercise conducted by the U.S., South Korea and Japan in international waters south and east of South Korea’s Jeju Island. The drills involved maritime and air assets and training across areas including missile defense and cyber and medical operations, according to the U.S. and South Korean militaries. Seoul has described the annual exercise as defensive and aimed at countering North Korea’s nuclear and missile threats.
A day after Freedom Edge wrapped up, North Korea fired multiple short-range ballistic missiles toward its east coast, prompting South Korea’s National Security Office to convene an emergency security situation review meeting. The missiles flew about 250 kilometers, according to the South Korean military.
In recent months, North Korea has stepped up its efforts to modernize its navy, which has traditionally relied largely on smaller vessels designed for coastal defense. This month, Kim commissioned a second 5,000-ton-class destroyer, part of a push to develop a more capable naval force that North Korea says will eventually carry nuclear weapons.
The escalating rhetoric comes as Trump seeks to revive personal diplomacy with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un that defined the U.S. president’s first term. Last month, Trump abruptly scaled back joint drills scheduled with South Korea, citing his “very good relationship” with the North Korean leader. Kim has yet to embrace his overtures.

A British woman kidnapped in Malawi last week has been rescued by police after a shootout in which four of her alleged abductors were killed.
Nusrat Osman was abducted outside her home in the southern city of Blantyre on 11 September at about 12.30pm. Police had offered a reward of 30m Malawi kwacha (£12,950) for information leading to her rescue and the arrest of the perpetrators.
Malawian police announced Osman’s rescue late on Thursday in a statement. “There was an exchange of fire between police and kidnappers, who were armed with [an] AK47 rifle and a Girsan Regard MC pistol. In the process, the criminals got shot and were taken to hospital where they succumbed to their injuries.” it read.
A police officer, deputy inspector general Mlowoka Noel Kayira, was also shot during the operation. “He is currently receiving medical attention at the hospital and is in a stable condition,” police said.
Osman, a 47-year-old auditor and mother of two, was safe and “not too shaken” after her ordeal, her brother Shobi Jiwa told the Sun, expressing his gratitude to Malawi’s police.
Jiwa reserved special thanks for Kayira. “He is the hero of our family. He’s the hero of the country,” he said. “He’s the hero of the world, actually, for putting his life at risk and taking a bullet into himself for my sister.”
Kidnappings are rare in Malawi, which has experienced a rise in pickpocketing and house burglaries by often armed men in recent years amid unstable, crisis-ridden economic conditions.
The landlocked southern African country is one of the world’s poorest nations, with a population of about 22 million and an average annual income of just $672, according to the World Bank.
In 2024, a country report by the US state department’s diplomatic security service said: “Kidnappings are not a widespread concern in Malawi, and there have been no recent high-profile incidents involving westerners.
“Historically, expatriates have not been significant targets for kidnappings in the country. When kidnappings do occur, they often involve members of the Asian business community rather than foreign travellers or residents.”
Osman, who is originally from Leicester, worked for a local audit firm and had lived in Malawi with her husband and children for several years. Before her rescue, her family said they had not had any news of her, including any contact from the kidnappers demanding a ransom.
Her husband, Nazil Osman, told the local news outlet Nyasa Times: “I don’t know where she is or how she is. My wife is an auditor, and I have no issues with anyone.”
Her brother told the Sun on Tuesday: “My sister has been missing for five days with no trace or call,” adding that the family could not think of a motive for her kidnapping.
Police did not say whether information received in response to the offered reward had led to Osman’s rescue, adding that investigations were ongoing and more details would be shared “in due course”.

Pocket FM is betting heavily on AI to improve its content economics and lift its EBITDA margin to 15%-20% from around 5% currently, cofounder Prateek Dixit told Inc42. Dixit did not disclose a timeline for achieving the margin target. However, he said AI already powers about 90% of Pocket FM’s production, while its post-production process is entirely AI-driven. Overall, AI is involved in 80%-90% of the startup’s creative processes. The audio series platform is using AI to reduce production costs, accelerate content creation, and scale its IP across languages, geographies, and entertainment formats. The margin expansion target comes shortly after Pocket FM claimed to have crossed $500 Mn in annual recurring revenue (ARR). Founded in 2018 by Dixit, Rohan Nayak, and Nishanth KS, Pocket FM offers audio content across multiple languages and genres. Backed by Lightspeed, StepStone Group, Tencent, and Times Internet, the startup has raised $196 Mn to date. It was last valued at $750 Mn during its $103 Mn Series D funding round in 2024. The startup claims its entertainment ecosystem comprises more than 7.7 Lakh titles, 5.5 Lakh creators, and 5.5 Bn hours of playtime and engagement data. It also has more than 1.4 Mn hours of text and voice content. Inside Pocket FM’s AI Content Engine As part of its broader AI push, Pocket FM has launched Sherpa, a fiction-writing platform designed to help creators build long-form stories spanning anywhere from 10 to 1,000 episodes. The platform is currently free for all writers, and Pocket FM does not expect it to become a revenue generator in the near term. “Closed-source frontier models can write one or two episodes reasonably well, but they struggle with long-form planning across 100 or 200 episodes and with creating strong IP. That was the thought process behind launching Sherpa,” Dixit said. Unlike a single generative AI model, Sherpa uses multiple specialised agents across ideation, research, story planning, prose generation, feedback, and narrative memory. The platform is intended to maintain consistency across characters, relationships, conflicts, and storylines extending over hundreds of episodes. Dixit said Sherpa’s planning and prose models use Pocket FM’s proprietary data, while its assistant layer can draw on frontier models such as OpenAI’s GPT and Anthropic’s Claude. “We have around 2.5 Mn hours of content on the platform, which is massive and gives us proprietary engagement data. We have used this data to train a model for writing great prose,” Dixit said. Taking Pocket FM’s IP Beyond Audio The startup is now looking to expand into new geographies while taking its existing IP into additional entertainment formats, Dixit said. It plans to enter Japan and South Korea over the next six to eight months. It is also exploring markets such as the Netherlands, Belgium, Turkey, and the Scandinavian countries. Beyond audio, Pocket FM is evaluating interactive storytelling and gaming opportunities, although Dixit said no specific launches have been finalised. Pocket Saga is currently the startup’s key video bet. Through the platform, Pocket FM is adapting its existing IP into long-form, AI-generated anime content. Dixit said Pocket Saga titles could run for 50 to 100 hours, comprising two-to-three-minute episodes, with individual shows potentially spanning 1,000 to 2,000 episodes. The strategy follows Pocket FM’s decision to shut down Pocket TV, its short-form video drama product. Dixit said Pocket TV suffered from weak user retention and operated in a segment where AI had increasingly commoditised short-form video production. The cofounder declined to comment on Pocket FM’s IPO and fundraising plans. Recent media reports suggest that Pocket FM is looking to raise $100 Mn to $120 Mn at a valuation of about $2 Bn. However, Inc42 could not independently verify this.

Gas prices are dropping. You can thank the 'winter blend' for that
Gas prices fell 8 cents overnight and could dip by a few more still: expert
Drivers rejoice: gas prices in Canada are dropping, thanks to a yearly switch.
Gas prices ticked up earlier this week, reaching a national average of 194.5 cents per litre yesterday according to affordableenergy.ca, but dropped by about eight cents overnight to 186.9 cents per litre as of Friday.
The cost of gas usually goes up in the summer and comes down in the fall because of a mid-September switchover from summer-blend gasoline to a winter blend, says Dan McTeague, the president of Canadians for Affordable Energy.
The different mix of fuel is used to prevent fuel-line freezing and make engines run better in the cold.
McTeague forecasts the cost of gas could drop by another few cents over the weekend before settling.
"But that's probably as good as it's going to get unless someone … can wave a magic wand and get a lot more oil, diesel, jet fuel and gasoline into global markets," McTeague told CBC News Network.
Fighting in the Middle East has all but shuttered the Strait of Hormuz and compromised the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, disrupting the flow of oil to the rest of the world. Fewer barrels flowing from the region has sent the price of oil way up: the price of a barrel of Brent crude oil soared past the $100-per-barrel U.S. benchmark last week and is now hovering around $104 US.
But diesel, on the other hand, is soaring. The average cost for a litre of diesel across Canada sat at $2.751 as of Thursday, according to Natural Resources Canada, though certain cities like Calgary hovered lower, at $2.513. Vancouver topped the three-dollar mark, with a litre of diesel costing drivers $3.055.
That's bad news even for those who don't drive, according to experts. Trucks that deliver consumer items to stores — including your groceries — as well as tractors that harvest food all tend to run on diesel.
It could mean consumers see higher sticker prices, because companies will have no choice but to pass on the higher cost of fuel to consumers, said Tej Dulat, director of government and public affairs with the Canada Truck Operators Association.
"You're going to see that impact coming on the grocery prices," Dulat told CBC News last week.

Delhi HC grants bail to UK national Jagtar Singh Johal in 7 NIA cases after 8 years in custody
A Division Bench of Justice Navin Chawla and Justice Ravinder Dudeja set aside the trial court orders refusing bail and directed Johal’s release.
The Delhi high court on Friday ordered the release of UK national Jagtar Singh Johal on bail in seven cases being investigated by the National Investigation Agency (NIA), noting that he had remained in custody for more than eight years and that the trials were unlikely to conclude in the near future.
A Division Bench of Justice Navin Chawla and Justice Ravinder Dudeja set aside the trial court orders refusing bail and directed Johal’s release subject to stringent conditions, including surrender of his passport, restrictions on communication and social media activity, fortnightly reporting to the Investigating Officer and a bar on contacting or influencing witnesses, according to an ANI report.

Bail conditions imposed by Delhi HC
Johal has been directed to execute a personal bond of ₹5 lakh with two sureties of the same amount. He must surrender his passport, if any, or file an affidavit stating that he does not hold one.
The court directed him to use only one mobile phone and/or one landline number during the trial, which must remain switched on.
He must also furnish his residential address, contact number and email address to the Investigating Officer and trial court, and cannot change his residence or contact details without seven days’ prior written intimation, said the report.

A video is going viral on social media (here, here, and here) claiming that Prime Minister Narendra Modi said he would eliminate poverty from the country in one stroke. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows Prime Minister Narendra Modi saying that he will eradicate poverty from the country at once.
Fact: The viral video is presented out of context to make it appear that Prime Minister Narendra Modi said he would eradicate poverty from India in a single stroke. In the original video, PM Modi was referring to Congress leader Rahul Gandhi’s earlier statement about eradicating poverty and questioning the claim, rather than making the claim himself. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to an extended version of the same video uploaded on Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s official YouTube channel on 14 April 2024, titled “PM Modi addresses a public meeting in Hoshangabad, Madhya Pradesh”. According to the video description, PM Modi addressed a public meeting in Hoshangabad ahead of the 2024 Lok Sabha elections and paid tribute to Dr Babasaheb Ambedkar on his birth anniversary. At the 28:05 timestamp, PM Modi can be heard referring to a statement by Congress leader Rahul Gandhi, saying that Gandhi had claimed he would eradicate poverty from the country in a single stroke.
PM Modi said, “Modi’s guarantee begins where expectations from others end. That is why a desperate Congress is making announcements that even its own leaders fail to comprehend. The Congress ‘Prince’ made a declaration that would make you laugh too: he claimed he would eradicate poverty from the country in a single stroke. The entire nation is astonished to hear this. People ask where this ‘royal magician’ has been hiding all these years. Fifty years ago, his grandmother had announced the eradication of poverty. Before 2014, they ran the government via remote control for a decade. And now, they claim to have found a magic mantra that can do the job in one stroke. Where did they get this ‘one-stroke’ mantra? Tell me, isn’t this a mockery of the poor? Isn’t this an insult to the poor? You tell me, can poverty really be eliminated in a single stroke? What are they saying? Who would trust them? It is because they make such claims that they become a laughingstock across the country; the nation does not take them seriously.”
We also found that the Bharatiya Janata Party’s (BJP) official YouTube channel uploaded the same video on the same day, featuring a longer version of the viral clip.
The full transcript of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s speech at the Hoshangabad rally was also available on his official website. The transcript confirms that PM Modi was referring to Rahul Gandhi’s claim about eradicating poverty in a single stroke, rather than making the claim himself, as the viral video suggests.
A few days before PM Modi’s rally, Rahul Gandhi said at a rally in Anupgarh, Rajasthan, “The Congress government will give one lakh rupees annually to one woman in every family. One lakh rupees, or 8,500 rupees every month, will be deposited into your bank account every year, and in one fell swoop, we will eradicate poverty from India.”
To sum up, PM Modi did not say he would eradicate poverty in one stroke; he was referring to Rahul Gandhi’s earlier statement.

Police begin operation to move migrants from Ceuta beaches
- Published
Police have begun moving hundreds of migrants in Ceuta to a new tented site in the port area of the Spanish territory in north Africa.
Officers struggled to contain crowds of people jostling to secure a place at the site after weeks of living on the beaches. Shots could be heard, with reports that police fired into the air.
Several hundred migrants have now reached the camp, which has a capacity for 1,700 people.
Most of the 72,000 migrants who breached the border from Morocco in July have returned, but it is believed that more than 13,000 remain in the enclave.
The operation began at about 07:00 local time (05:00 GMT) on Friday, with more than 3,000 migrants being transferred, according to the Spanish government-owned news agency Efe.
During the process, some migrants broke through the cordon along the designated 2km (1.2 mile) route to the port. Video shows young men running in the darkness as police tried to maintain control.
More than 170 police officers have been deployed, including drone technicians, Efe reported. It added that the situation was later "brought under control quickly", and the operation was able to continue.
The operation is part of the government's attempt to concentrate the migrants in facilities where they can be identified and cared for while their administrative status is individually determined.
The chaotic scenes will do little to dampen opposition criticism in Spain of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, who has faced strong criticism over his handling of the crisis.
Since the migrant influx, residents of the 18.5 sq km (7.2 sq miles) territory have expressed safety concerns. Some have destroyed shelters and blocked aid being supplied to the migrants.
Ceuta's Mayor Juan Jesus Vivas told lawmakers in the European Parliament earlier this month that the migrants had turned Ceuta into a "pressure cooker".
"The city is completely different than it was before this event, Ceutans have lost their joy and their lifestyles have been completely shaken up," the conservative mayor said.
The opposition also accused Sánchez of knowing about the influx of migrants in advance. Sánchez has insisted that it was impossible to predict, but according to government documents, its intelligence services had warned of social media calls for a mass migrant crossing into Ceuta the day before the events happened.
Ester Muñoz of the conservative People's Party said the government was "directly responsible for the invasion of Ceuta and for those who died".
The incident has also created diplomatic headaches for Sánchez.
The prime minister is at odds with Italy, with the two countries earlier this week extending temporary border controls imposed on each other. He is also trying to maintain his bilateral relationship with Morocco.
The influx of migrants in late July came after Spain's Supreme Court ruled that migrants stopped at sea while trying to reach Ceuta cannot be summarily returned to Morocco.
After the ruling, some social media accounts spread misinformation and offered to help migrants cross the Spanish border for hundreds of pounds.
Thousands of people then flooded across the border fence and swam around the ocean barriers. At least 100 people died during the crossing, according to local authorities.
