Throughout the Trump era, Democrats have wrung their hands about how they can win over working-class voters.
These Democrats won over working-class voters. Here’s their advice for candidates.
A new report explains which topics they emphasize — and which they don’t.
Why not ask the Democrats who’ve actually done it?
That’s what Robin Johnson — a political consultant based in rural Illinois, and a part-time political science professor at Monmouth College — set out to do after Donald Trump first won the presidency, asking Democratic state legislators who won tough districts how they pulled it off.
But after Trump’s shocking second win in 2024 revived concern about Democrats’ working-class woes, the time seemed ripe to ask legislators about how they’ve managed to cope with the challenges of a new decade.
So, working with the center-left Progressive Policy Institute and co-authors Stuart Malec and Jolie Libert, Johnson interviewed 28 state legislators who won in heavily working-class areas in the seven main presidential battleground states.
They include Nevada state Assemblymember Max Carter, a retired union electrician; Michigan state Rep. Tullio Liberati, a construction small business owner; Arizona state Rep. Lorena Austin, a self-described “five-time college dropout” with sleeve tattoos; and Wisconsin state Rep. Karen DeSanto, a nonprofit executive and former professional circus clown.
The report, which Vox reviewed exclusively ahead of its publication, comes amid a factional debate within the party between rising left-wing and socialist candidates who have argued for more far-reaching policy proposals, and more moderate Democrats who have pushed for concessions to working-class cultural sensibilities. In the report, the authors said that lawmakers they focused on “could hardly be more different from the left-wing populists who’ve captivated the national media this summer.”
Generally, the legislators in the report focused on pocketbook issues, though in different ways — some embraced populist causes, while others positioned themselves as business-friendly. And they broadly agreed that cultural issues were Democrats’ biggest challenge in reaching the working class.
“It’s really interesting how common the themes and the challenges are from rural Georgia, right down to the border of Arizona, to Las Vegas, northern North Carolina, and then up in the ‘Blue Wall’ states,” Johnson told me.
I spoke to Johnson last week about his findings, and about what these state legislators’ experience has to tell us about the debate over the Democratic Party’s future. Our conversation, which has been condensed and edited, is below.
What’s changed in 10 years of interviewing legislators facing tough races
Walk me through where the idea for this project came from.
I’ve been working on this for 10 years. It started at a conversation at a little diner in Maquoketa, Iowa — a little “choke and puke,” as we call those places. I was with a former state senator from Iowa named Jeff Danielson, and it was right after Trump won. Most of the focus was on what happened at the congressional or presidential level, and we thought, why not take a look at state legislators competing in these tough districts?
I approached my friend and my congresswoman, Cheri Bustos, who I’ve known really well and helped on her campaigns, and said, would you be interested in working with us and sponsoring it? She said, absolutely, because her district, the 17th in Illinois, is rural working-class. And she was able to win these voters.
We talked to probably 75 current and former legislators for that first report. We did another one in 2021, focused on members of Congress and state legislators who win Trump districts. Then we did a third one last year, on Democrats in working-class districts in the heartland. Then she retired from Congress and I went to a PPI conference this past February, and PPI agreed to partner on this with a different focus, slightly — on the seven battleground states, on districts that are really close and have more working-class voters than the national average.
So, having done this several times before, what’s new in the latest version? What are people saying now that they weren’t, necessarily, in previous rounds of this?
In the past, when we focused on the Midwest, it was mostly all white, mostly men, some women. Now, we went to North Carolina and Georgia, and there were African American legislators, men and women. And we went to the West, and there were Latinos.
But what was interesting to me was: Nobody brought up their identity in these interviews. I had to bring it up to one woman from Nevada, mentioning, “Well, you’re Native American.” “Yeah, but I don’t really talk about that much,” was the response.
That was one big takeaway: Nobody talked about identity. Their focus was totally on their constituents, their working-class constituents.
What were some of the common themes you saw in the responses?
There’s no secret sauce. They’re deeply rooted in their communities, they know the people that live there, they know the language, they work hard.
But they focus on economic issues. If somebody asks them about cultural issues, they’ll respond, but they try to get back to economic issues, because that’s what they’re hearing about from voters, mostly.
These folks are from a variety of backgrounds. Some are true working-class, they don’t have college degrees. One guy near Detroit runs a construction company, didn’t get a degree. Another woman we focused on from Arizona had tattoos all over and took 14 years to get her BA. Some are the traditional route — attorneys, some small business people.
But it’s a lot of different backgrounds, and we want to contrast that with the consultants who tried to make the perfect Frankenstein candidate out of [former Maine Senate candidate Graham] Platner. These people are out there — you don’t need to create it. They’re out there.
Cultural issues
On how politics has changed over the years, there’s a particularly vivid quote in the report from state Assemblymember Elaine Marzola from Nevada.
She tells you: “My campaign’s biggest adjustment in 2024 was shifting away from leading with social and cultural issues and instead focusing more directly on affordability and economic concerns.” And she adds, “While I remain progressive on many social issues, voters across backgrounds increasingly want leaders focused on affordability, education, and public safety rather than endless culture war debates.”
How widespread was that sentiment?
It’s very widespread. Their focus is on the issues that matter, that they’re picking up from their constituents. A lot of times they reported that some of the people in their campaigns told them they should talk more about abortion or other social issues — mainly abortion — and they refused to do it.
A lot of them talked about a major problem in the party being these litmus tests that groups have, that you can vote with them on nine out of 10 issues, but on the tenth issue, if you’re not with them, you’re an enemy.
If you’re going to have a true big-tent party, you’ve got to have some room for disagreements on some of these issues that reflect the local voters that people have in their districts. Several in Georgia told me pointedly that their leadership understood and would give them passes on votes that they knew they couldn’t be with them on. But in other cases, I heard a lot of pointed comments about these groups demanding 100 percent allegiance, that it’s all or nothing.
In a lot of districts down South, I heard from a couple gentlemen; it’s the Bible Belt. People go to church regularly. African Americans, the older generations of African Americans, are more middle-of-the-road, if not conservative on some of these cultural issues. So there’s got to be room for people to vote their districts on some of these cultural issues.
But on the economic issues, they’re there. They’re unified with the rest of the party.
Economic issues
Well, it’s interesting on economic issues, because there’s unity on focusing on affordability and pocketbook issues in some form. But you also describe how some people take a more populist approach, and others have a more business-friendly approach. Is there tension there?
We asked people, how would they describe themselves? And most of them describe themselves as moderate. But the range of issues you have at the state level may differ some compared to the federal issues. A true populist approach at the state level may not have the same meaning as a populist at the federal level.
In fact, some of the folks with business backgrounds were pretty aggressive in some of their policy ideas. I think [Assemblymember] Joe Dalia from Nevada is one, he actually combined with [Rep.] Ro Khanna on a policy idea, the congressman from Silicon Valley who’s definitely a progressive. Dalia’s background is in business entrepreneurship.
Is all politics local?
The dynamics are a little different in state legislative races, even tough competitive ones, because there’s just so much less national money, national interest, group interest, virality, all of the dynamics that are so important to national politics. These are truly local races. So do you think these lessons can apply to national politics?
These state legislators are easy to overlook. They’re close enough to the people that they’re in, they can knock doors more than like a member of Congress. You can’t really knock doors in a congressional race — you can do some and have volunteers do it, but these people are out doing it individually.
But they still get hit on national issues. Some of them didn’t do much TV — Georgia’s got smaller districts — but they’re on TV in Wisconsin. And they’ve got to raise money and then have the party help them out. They’re used to getting hit on national issues because the Republicans try to tie them to some of the more far-left ideas.
They also feel that the deep roots they have in the community help overcome that because they’re better known, they’re battle-tested in that regard. A lot of times, especially with social media, you think you’re going to come up with some neat little line to put on social media that’s going to carry you to a victory, or some pithy slogan or whatever. It’s really not. For these folks anyway, it just comes down to doing the hard work.
But this is the bench that the Democrats need. You want to pick some people down the road that have proven ability to win these tough districts — here they are.

Rescuers dig 4 bodies from a Nepal hydropower tunnel as families demand answers
Rescuers in Nepal have recovered four bodies from a hydropower plant tunnel three weeks after a devastating flash flood
KATHMANDU, Nepal -- Rescuers in Nepal have recovered four bodies from the tunnel of a hydropower plant as search operations continued for those still missing three weeks after the devastating flash flood last month that killed hundreds and left thousands missing.
Families of the thousands missing, meanwhile, are seeking answers from authorities on their whereabouts.
Nepal's army said that four bodies were recovered Wednesday from the Chilime Hydropower plant, which was situated on the Trishuli River that flooded on Aug. 26.
Nepal's disaster management agency said five more bodies were located in a different location and equipment was being sent to recover them.
The number of bodies that have been recovered since the flooding has reached 1,403 while 6,150 people are still missing, according to Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority.
Families of the missing have been pressuring the government to speed up the rescue and recovery process from the tunnels.
They have held rallies and many have called on the government to declare the missing as dead because they want to receive death certificates, which would allow them to move forward with legal proceedings and religious rites and give them some emotional closure.
At the Tribhuvan University Teaching hospital in Kathmandu, the lobby walls have been pasted with photos of hundreds of missing people. Relatives go there seeking news of their loved ones.
Usha Khatri's husband Indra Bahadur was working as a cook with a group of pilgrims when the flood hit the Nepal-China border. Since then she has been searching for him in many of the towns where the river flows and where bodies have been recovered.
“The government has not done much for us. They have not met us or given any information or any assurances. I am by myself searching for my husband,” Khatri said.
There were 13 hydropower plants that were damaged by the flooding and many workers were either swept or trapped by the raging water or debris.
Finding the workers who were trapped has been a priority for the government and rescuers. But access to the tunnels has been hampered by thick mud, debris and damaged infrastructure, making it difficult for rescue teams to reach the areas.
Two Nepali workers were found alive by rescuers on Sept. 4, days after the flooding. A day later a Chinese worker was pulled out alive from a separate area.
The government estimates the country's reconstruction costs at around $4.78 billion.

Combining healthy dietary practices with regular physical activity is the most effective non-drug strategy for achieving sustained weight loss and improving key metabolic health indicators among adults with overweight or obesity, according to a major review by the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition (NIN) here.
The findings, published in the international journal Obesity Pillars, are based on an umbrella review that analysed evidence from 112 systematic reviews and meta-analyses covering 2,332 randomised controlled trials and more than 5.07 lakh participant observations across over 50 countries.
The review, led by ICMR-NIN scientists Mahesh Kumar Mummadi and Samarasimha Reddy, compared the impact of dietary interventions, physical activity, lifestyle changes and combined approaches on weight management and cardiometabolic health.
Researchers found that all major non-pharmacological interventions produced statistically significant, though generally modest, reductions in body weight and Body Mass Index (BMI). However, the combination of diet and physical activity delivered the most sustained results, with participants losing an average of 3.68 kg beyond 12 months compared with control groups.
Low-calorie diets were found to be the most effective for short-term weight loss, resulting in an average reduction of 2.64 kg within the first three months. Physical activity alone led to smaller reductions in body weight, but its benefits increased over longer follow-up periods.
Lifestyle interventions such as behavioural counselling, goal-setting, self-monitoring and health education also showed positive outcomes, with their effectiveness improving over time. Beyond weight loss, the study highlighted significant improvements in metabolic health. The combination of diet and physical activity produced the greatest benefits in blood sugar control, reducing fasting blood glucose levels and insulin resistance after 12 months.
Physical activity emerged as the most effective strategy for lowering blood pressure, reducing systolic blood pressure by about 6.1 mmHg between six and 12 months. Intermittent fasting showed the largest short-term reduction in diastolic blood pressure and supported weight loss for up to a year, although these benefits were not sustained beyond 12 months.
ICMR-NIN director Bharati Kulkarni said the findings underscore the importance of an integrated approach to tackling obesity. “Healthy dietary practices, regular physical activity and behavioural support each have a role, but their combination can provide broader and more sustained benefits. This is particularly relevant for India, where scalable and sustainable approaches are needed to address the growing burden of overweight, obesity and related non-communicable diseases,” she said.
Mr.Mummadi noted that although the review drew evidence from more than 50 countries, most studies originated from high-income and upper-middle-income nations. India and other lower-middle-income countries remained under-represented, highlighting the need for more locally relevant research, said a press release on Saturday.

When we think about the stakes in healthcare, we tend to think of them in terms of life and death, being sick or being healthy. The conversation is about your physical well-being and maybe your mental health — and it pretty much stops there.
How bad healthcare can derail a woman’s entire life
Exclusive: Melinda French Gates on the ways the US health system fails American women — and how to turn it around.
But health affects so much more than your body’s biology or even just you personally, as a new survey from Gallup and Pivotal, a philanthropic group founded by Melinda French Gates, shows. That’s especially true for women, who frequently report negative experiences with the health system and ongoing struggles to get their concerns taken seriously; poor health affects the trajectory of their careers and their ability to be engaged with their families, friends, and wider community.
It starts at the doctor’s office or hospital: 51 percent of women say they have had a negative healthcare experience in the past five years, versus 39 percent of men. About 1 in 3 said that a doctor did not take them seriously when they said they were feeling pain or other symptoms, versus 21 percent of men, and 33 percent said that they either were misdiagnosed or did not receive a diagnosis. The cost of paying for care is another deterrent: 32 percent of women said they have skipped or delayed care in the past year because of the cost, compared to 25 percent of men.
“To see that half of women in the United States who sought care in the last five years came out feeling like they hadn’t gotten the help or care they needed, that’s frankly staggering,” French Gates told me in an email. “It says a lot about how little we’ve invested in women’s health and how much we expect them to just push through pain or accept uncertainty.”
And the effects of those experiences, the failure to receive proper treatment, ripples out into the rest of the women’s lives. More than half of US women, 54 percent, said they had experienced at least one health-related impact on their family life or relationships; 42 percent said their health had led to a negative effect on their career or work. It also affects their community: 32 percent said their health had affected their ability to participate in civic life.
The toll is not only physical but mental: 48 percent of women said they’d dealt with a mental health condition like depression or anxiety. And socioeconomic disparities abound. Black and Hispanic women are more likely to report being in poor or fair health. Women who have lower incomes are more likely to face career struggles because of their health than those who make more.
I had the opportunity to interview French Gates, who has made women’s health a priority in her work, over email about the survey; its findings on community engagement, menopause, caregiving, and more; and what could be done to address the problems that it reveals. Our exchange is below, lightly edited for clarity and length.
Which of these survey findings surprised you most and why?
The number of women [54 percent] who said they experienced a mental health challenge during or after pregnancy should stop us all in our tracks. And the fact that less than one in three women who sought care found it helpful is really concerning. It’s why I feel so strongly about integrating women’s mental and physical healthcare, especially during pregnancy and postpartum. Mental and physical health are so linked together.
Too much of the burden is placed on women to get answers. All of us deserve so much better.
Other findings from the Gallup/Pivotal survey:
- 28 percent of women said menopause had affected how much effort they could give at work, while 22 percent said it had led to them being less involved in their community
- 56 percent of women say they have to do their own research in order to make an informed decision about their contraception
- 64 percent of women reported finding misleading or inaccurate information about contraception on social media when doing their own research
- 37 percent of women who have been through menopause said they first learned about menopause when they started to experience symptoms themselves
Nearly one-third of women said in the survey that health problems limited their ability to be involved in their community. What does that look like in practice, and what do communities lose when women can’t fully participate?
Women are so often the backbones of their communities, whether they’re rallying their neighbors around a cause, leading the PTA, or serving in elected office. Without having women — and their ideas and voices — in those roles, we’re missing half of the conversation. Issues that affect women and families are less likely to get on the agenda. They’re less likely to be solved.
When a woman has a health challenge, and she has to spend so much of her time and resources chasing down answers, that makes it harder for her to show up in those spaces. We saw that in the survey: 30 percent of women said their health limited their ability to be involved in their communities. And when women couldn’t get the care they needed, that percentage doubled.
Women’s health is often talked about as a personal issue, but this data is helping us prove that it’s also an economic issue, a family issue, a community issue — it affects all of society.
Caregiving and family responsibilities prevent many women from getting medical care, in particular Hispanic and Black women. That seems to create a vicious cycle: Women are often so busy being the caregivers in their families that they neglect their own health. Eventually, they are the ones who will need care. What do you think can be done to break that pattern? Is there a philanthropic solution? What public policy changes could be made?
Women are often taught to put themselves last and minimize their own needs. They don’t always have time to care for themselves because they’re so busy caring for others. And they might not be able to afford childcare or home health support for their aging parents. Our survey showed one in six women delayed healthcare because of their responsibilities caring for their family members. For Black women it’s one in five, and Hispanic women one in four. Too many women are facing an uphill road to even just get to a doctor’s office.
It’s possible to make it easier for people to balance healthcare and family responsibilities — but it’s going to take action from many angles. That’s exactly why I invest in both women’s health and in caregiving, and I’d encourage more philanthropists to do the same. Businesses can also support employees with good paid leave policies and reliable but flexible schedules.
But for women everywhere to benefit, we need government leaders to prioritize increasing access to affordable childcare, home health supports, and paid family medical leave. These are policies that have the support of large majorities of Americans because these are issues that affect everyone. So there’s a real opportunity here to offer meaningful help to families.
I am struck by our collective failure on menopause: Women report that they aren’t aware of menopause symptoms until they experience them on their own, that they struggle to get their doctor to take menopause symptoms seriously, and that their menopause experience has held them back in their career. What are some short-term and long-term steps we can take to address those problems?
If more than a third of women only learn about menopause symptoms when they go through them, the system is clearly not working. Women need to learn about menopause from their doctors before they experience it. But doctors aren’t getting the education and training they need on menopause while they are in school. One doctor told me she got just one lecture on menopause across all her years in medical school. One said it was mentioned one time. They are seeking out better training but it can be hard to find. That’s why Pivotal is partnering with the Menopause Society to expand physician training on menopause so doctors, nurses, and other health care providers can access the information they’re looking for to better help their patients.
Because menopause isn’t just about being uncomfortable; it can also bring anxiety, heart palpitations, insomnia — significant symptoms that can really hold women back. More than a quarter of women who’ve experienced menopause or perimenopause said it made it harder to live up to their full potential at work. One in 10 had to take leave or leave their jobs entirely. That just shouldn’t be. Women shouldn’t have to step back right at the moment when they could be stepping into leadership roles.
The most immediate steps can come from policymakers, especially at the state level. They can include menopause care in insurance and Medicaid coverage and offer workplace protections to women in menopause the way they do for pregnancy, so women can get the care they need without losing their jobs. I’m also focused on longer-term solutions, like expanding training for healthcare providers and investing in research to accelerate treatment options.
Women are at the forefront of a lot of wellness trends these days and yet, as the survey reveals, women also report encountering a ton of health misinformation on social media. Why do you think women are so often the targets of this kind of content? What can be done to point women toward and build their trust in sound medical information?
One in three women said she left an appointment without a diagnosis, with her pain being dismissed, or with no answers or next steps. You can understand why those women would start looking for information online. And because women’s health has been underfunded and under-researched, there just isn’t as much reliable information out there as there should be, which leaves a lot of room for people to come in with misinformation. Investing in credible scientific research to fill that vacuum will give both women and their doctors more information going into their appointments.
In terms of your own organization’s work, which investments are you making that you think can make progress on the underlying problems revealed in this survey?
We need to address the right now and we need to address the longer term. Right now, women need better care at critical moments in their lives.
One way we’re investing in that at Pivotal is by making it easier for women to get the mental health care they need during and after pregnancy. So we are investing in integrated models that put mental and physical healthcare under one roof. I visited a health clinic in Alabama earlier this year where they identify issues like depression and anxiety right at the outset and then help the mom all the way through her pregnancy care, all in the same place. That model is something we strongly believe in.
Better care for menopause will require better training, which we are thinking about in both the immediate and long term. I mentioned that we’re making more menopause training available to doctors who are currently practicing. That is something I’m really excited about because I’ve heard from physicians who really want to better support their patients and are looking for better information so they can do that. And longer-term, menopause needs to be a much bigger part of the curriculum at medical schools moving forward.
Another longer-term focus of ours is trying to make up for decades of lost time in research. We are funding medical research focused on how diseases specifically impact women, in partnership with an innovative organization called Wellcome Leap. They are working to accelerate progress in women’s health on everything from autoimmune diseases to cardiovascular disease in years, not decades, which is how long health breakthroughs usually take. That’s the kind of urgency women need and deserve.

- Social media users alleged in September 2026 that U.S. truckers planned to strike over high fuel costs beginning on Oct. 1, leading to food and supply chain shortages.
- There was no evidence to support this unfounded rumor.
- Searches indicated the claim largely spread because of a video one social media user originally posted on Sept. 15. Other users then reposted his clip without first looking for credible evidence.
- A spokesperson for the Owner-Operator Independent Drivers Association said they had no knowledge of an upcoming strike. We also emailed the International Brotherhood of Teamsters and the man from the video, and will update this article if we receive more information.
In mid-September 2026, social media users alleged U.S. truckers had announced a plan to strike beginning on Oct. 1 to protest record-high diesel fuel costs of more than $6 a gallon. The posts claimed the stoppage of transportation would lead to nationwide food and supply chain shortages.
There was no evidence to support this unfounded rumor. Queries of DuckDuckGo, Google and other search engines found no news media outlets or other authoritative sources reporting about truckers planning to strike. Reddit's r/Truckers subreddit, a forum with hundreds of thousands of weekly visitors, featured a post with commenters saying they had heard nothing of a strike.
We emailed the Owner-Operator Independent Drivers Association to ask about this rumor. The organization's website says it has over 150,000 members in the U.S. and Canada operating more than 240,000 trucks and truck fleets. A spokesperson responded, "Our awareness is consistent with yours in that it seems to be social media chatter at this point in time."
We also emailed the International Brotherhood of Teamsters to ask about the rumor. The labor union has a freight division it says is made up of tens of thousands of Teamsters. We will update this article if we receive a response.
Where the unfounded rumor spread
Searches of social media websites indicated a video, first posted on Facebook (archived) and Instagram (archived) on Sept. 15, was potentially the most-popular content promoting the rumor. Users have since reposted the same video across platforms, including Facebook (archived), Instagram (archived) and X (archived). Others also generally shared the rumor of a trucker strike.
In the video, which ends with a request for users to buy paid subscriptions, a man tells viewers about the purported strike and subsequent food shortages:
In the trucking world, they put out a deal to strike until the fuel prices drop. Shut down Oct. 1. Park it. Stand together. Make their voices heard. Truckers are done.
You know what that means if they do that? Food shortages. Food's not getting to grocery stores. Nothing's getting anywhere.
What have I been telling you? Make sure you've got enough f***ing food for a month to three months, even six months. S***'s gonna hit the fan. S*** is hitting the fan, currently. And with this deal, this is huge.
A lot of people don't understand if trucks aren't moving, you're not getting anything. Grocery stores aren't getting a f***ing thing. Nobody's getting a thing. Just FYI.
That should probably freak you out a little bit because that happened basically during COVID. Remember when you couldn't find anything in the f***ing stores. This'll be a lot worse, if it comes to fruition. Just FYI. 
Please like, share, follow. Share my s***. Subscribe for a buck. 
We messaged the man in the video on Facebook and Instagram to ask for evidence, and will update this story if we receive more information.
A TikTok user's video (archived) also promoted the rumor with the caption "50,000 Truckers Threaten Strike: What It Means For America." In the video, the user claims, without evidence, that 50,000 truckers "are reportedly said to" no longer drive as of Oct. 1.
The unfounded rumor potentially originated out of a previous strike claim (archived) appearing to pertain to the dates of Oct. 1-10, 2025.
For further reading, we previously reported the truth of a story regarding truckers banding together to save someone from jumping off an overpass.

Why dealing with defeat is key for Lampard at Coventry
- Published
Managing a newly-promoted team in the Premier League is very demanding, as Frank Lampard is finding out at Coventry.
It's the highest level, not just for the technical ability of the players that your team faces but also the sheer physicality that these players possess, and it feels like the gap to the Championship is getting greater every season.
From my experience in the same situation, you have to be really smart in the way you approach each game and recognise the importance of preparation for each specific opponent, because your team has to be organised in possession, and definitely out of possession.
Teams in the Premier League counter-attack with greater efficiency so being solid behind your own attacking play is absolutely vital.
But the real advice I would give to managers in Frank's shoes is to manage yourself, and your own time, as well as your players.
By that I mean you have to try to stay fresh and positive, because invariably you are going to go on bad runs of defeats like Coventry are on, which can drag your mood down.
Find a way of getting everyone back on track
I can tell you now that, whoever you are playing, if you get beaten - and especially beaten heavily like Coventry were by Brighton on Sunday - then it resonates with you. It's the same for every manager.
For Frank, whether it is losing at home to Hull or Brighton, or against Arsenal and Manchester City, then it will hurt.
But it is how he deals with those defeats that will decide what happens next.
Being the leader of a group of young men, you cannot look washed out and empty on a Monday morning after a heavy loss.
Yes, inside you will be hurting and your pride will be taking a bashing but everyone at the club will be waiting for your reaction, and will act accordingly.
Walking into the training ground in a dark mood and with your head around your backside just does not work, irrespective of what you are feeling inside.
I've been in that situation many times myself as a manager and what you have to do is puff your chest out and find a way of getting everyone back on track and working even harder with a set focus on the next game.
That's what all good leaders do. It is draining at times, but that is why managing your time and prioritising the issues that you can resolve is so important.
When I took Stoke up to the Premier League in 2008, I was learning on my feet.
We did not make a great start and I had to roll my sleeves up and get on with what I'd got in my squad, and really focus on getting results.
But away from that I was always forward thinking and I was quick at recognising what was needed to improve our chances of staying up.
When the window opened again in January, we were already in discussions with Tottenham for Matty Etherington, to supply us with crosses and chances from the wing.
We needed more goals too, so I took James Beattie from Sheffield United. They were a Championship side but that didn't matter because he had a record of scoring goals in the top flight.
We have heard so much about recruiting the right players in the right positions, and it is true today as it was in my day. Both lads played a significant role in keeping us up.
Coventry haven't scored a goal yet, and people might look in from the outside and feel the forward areas are an issue for them because the usual thinking is that the centre-forward has to lead the scoring charts, or a wide player or the number 10.
But the emphasis is on everyone to chip in and I would also reinforce one of the points I made in this column last season, about the importance of defending properly too.
On average, clean sheets earn you more points than scoring a goal, which is something I always stressed to my players. Nailing down the importance of both ends of the pitch is the narrative, whatever kind of run of results you are on, because games are won and lost there.
Why I was confident Stoke would stay up
Coventry have made a poor start but what has happened in their first four games does not have to become the story of their whole season.
With Stoke, we got a win in our first home game - against Aston Villa - but that was our only victory in our first seven league matches after getting promoted.
The thing I remember most from that time is that Hull had come up with us and, after seven games, they had won at Newcastle, Arsenal and Tottenham and were in the top five in the table, while we were third or fourth from bottom.
I went out for dinner with my chairman, Peter Coates, and he said how Hull had made a wonderful start. I replied by telling him I bet you now that we finish above Hull... and we did.
The reason I thought that was because of the mindset of the team, and the fans.
I was confident my players were not going to go weak at the knees, and the togetherness we needed was already there in the squad, while the support was just off the scales, which helped us enormously at home.
Every defeat was taken on the chin, and accepted, but the lads were always ready to go, again and again.
Survival is success for every promoted team
It was Steve Coppell who said to me how you have to deal with the fact you are going to lose a lot of games - or at least not win a lot of them - when you take a team up into the Premier League.
It is a very unusual situation, to go from being in the Championship and winning regularly week after week, to dealing with defeat after defeat.
Steve told me to get ready for going on runs where we would not win for five or six games on the bounce, but then if we could win two or three games in the same period after that, we would fly up the table.
But getting your head around that is hard, and it is the same for the players who were part of that promotion - especially if you were dominant like Coventry were last season.
They were expected to challenge at the top of the Championship, but in my opinion over-achieved by finishing clear at the top.
It was different for Hull, who achieved a promotion under Sergej Jakirovic that no-one outside that club believed was possible.
They have started the season on fire, just like the Tigers did in 2008 when Phil Brown was in charge, and now they have to try to sustain it.
They are third at the moment but if they are 17th come the end of May, which is where they finished under Brownie, then that will be a successful season.
I will be taking a closer look at Hull's progress in this column in the weeks to come, as well as the other promoted team, Ipswich.
Gary O'Neil has a really tough gig at Portman Road but it is one he will relish. I gave Gary his senior debut with Portsmouth in the Championship in 1999 and he's a smart lad who was always football mad.
Ipswich are a great club and I hope both are successful this season. Gary has experience of the Premier League with Bournemouth and Wolves, and he is going to need it.
New season, nine new managers - which appointments make sense?
Including O'Neil, there are nine new managers starting with clubs in the Premier League. It's a bigger number than usual and I wanted to quickly run through all of them.
Enzo Maresca at Manchester City seemed like common sense to me, even before they started the season with four league wins out of four, because he has worked with Pep and the club before.
City had a large turnover of players with their ins and outs over the summer, but I'd expect them to be in the mix for all the trophies again this season.
Another place where lots of changes have taken place is Stamford Bridge. Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso has experience of playing in England and will understand that no game in the Premier League is a shoe-in - as Saturday's draw with Hull showed us again.
Andoni Iraola did an amazing job at Bournemouth but he will need all of his managerial ability and acumen to succeed at Liverpool.
At Liverpool, teams will drop deep and rely on counter-attacking situations. At Bournemouth that did not happen very often.
So, Andoni has to prepare his coaching philosophy to overcome teams who will definitely play deeper and be much more defensive-minded against Liverpool than they were against Bournemouth.
In my opinion, given time he will a great success but as he prepares to take his new team back to face his old one at Vitality Stadium on Sunday, we are already seeing that Liverpool will need more changes to develop into the title-winning side that their fantastic supporters demand.
At Nottingham Forest, Oliver Glasner did a wonderful job at Palace and I am sure we will see more of the same at the City Ground.
At the moment I know less about Marco Rose, Matthias Jaissle, and Pierre Sage, at Bournemouth, Newcastle and Crystal Palace.
Unlike the other managers I have mentioned, they have no experience of the Premier League but they are all joining established top-flight sides which is a huge help.
Finally, there is Alvaro Arbeloa at Fulham. He had a fantastic playing record at Real Madrid and Liverpool and coached in the Real Madrid academy and their B team before taking charge of the first team for the second half of last season.
While he has not had much experience in the dugout, he has worked with many top managers and players.
Fulham will be a real test for him, as we've seen from the way they have started the season, so again they are a club I will be keeping a close eye on - but there are plenty of those!

I was 8 years old, sitting at dinner with my grandparents, watching Gong Gong’s face turn bright red after a few sips of yellow wine. He loved making me laugh, and though he enjoyed his drinks, I think he liked my reaction even more.
Over a decade later, I would recognize the same alcohol flush reaction at parties and happy hours in some of my East Asian friends, and in myself. A few of these friends took histamine blockers like Pepcid AC before going out, hoping to hide the anticipated redness. Once, I watched someone keep drinking through the flush to prove they had a higher tolerance than what their body was communicating.
Most of us knew the reaction by its colloquial name: “Asian glow.” The phrase makes the phenomenon sound harmless, even playful.
It was not until I started medical school and attended an Asian American and Pacific Islander Heritage Month event that I understood the science behind the reaction. After taking an ethanol patch test that turned positive, I learned that flushing is a common marker of reduced activity in mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase 2, or ALDH2, an enzyme involved in breaking down alcohol. This inherited deficiency affects an estimated one-third of people of East Asian descent and is exceedingly rare in other ethnicities. (Its associated redness may be mistaken for rosacea, which some studies suggest that drinking can raise the risk of developing, but rosacea is a separate condition involving chronic inflammation that affects all skin tones and types.)
There is no safe or healthy level of alcohol consumption for any given person. However, people with ALDH2 deficiency face both immediate discomfort and long-term cell damage and susceptibility to developing cancers of the upper digestive tract. Every clinician with East Asian patients should dedicate time to explaining the biological consequence behind what has long been dismissed as an aesthetic quirk.
When ALDH2 activity is reduced, acetaldehyde, a toxic intermediate in alcohol metabolism, accumulates in the body, dilating blood vessels, promoting histamine release, and causing facial redness, nausea, and rapid heartbeat. Acetaldehyde is also a DNA-damaging mutagen with implications in cell death pathways.
Not every person with deficiency presents the same way. People heterozygous for the most common ALDH2 reduced-function mutation, or ALDH2*2, have one active copy of the gene inherited from one parent and one variant copy inherited from the other. Their symptoms are not severe enough to discourage continued drinking, so they often keep going, even though their alcohol consumption is associated with a greater risk of cardiovascular disease, brain disorders, pancreatitis, and malignancies, particularly esophageal cancer. Homozygotes, who inherit two inactive copies of the gene, are less likely to develop cancer because they get such severe reactions to drinking that they avoid alcohol.
Although many East Asians recognize that they flush after drinking, they might not understand the associated risks. Health care providers should identify patients who experience alcohol flushing and counsel them on what it means for their health. Simple questionnaires about past flushing reactions, and in some settings ethanol patch testing like the one I took in medical school, have been shown to reveal ALDH2 deficiency with relatively high sensitivity and specificity. These tools can be incorporated into routine social history taking, alongside questions about alcohol use and family history.
For some groups of people, alcohol may hold special social and cultural meaning. For them, education should be widespread and, importantly, tailored and considerate.
Teenagers and young adults like me, for example, navigate significant peer pressure around drinking. My East Asian college friends deserved to know that taking antihistamines to hide flushing might reduce visible redness, but it would not lower acetaldehyde levels in their blood. They deserved to know that masking their body’s warning signals can make it easier to drink more than they otherwise would.
Recently, Nectar, a canned hard seltzer and cocktail brand, launched an AAPI Heritage Month campaign urging people to reframe the alcohol flush reaction as an “Asian Glow Up.” Though the intention may have been to turn a source of embarrassment into a viral beauty moment, the company’s failure to include a disclaimer mentioning the health indications pushes a narrative that encourages more drinking within an already vulnerable, under-informed population. An Instagram caption for the promo said: “Sharing drinks with friends before so you can share your glow with everyone after.”
Of course, young people, the target audience for ads like these, deserve to receive information about the reality behind “Asian glow” not as a reprimand, but as knowledge that preserves their agency and could help them make more informed choices.
On my medical school campus, many of the events promoting alcohol intolerance awareness are small focus groups led by my own peers, where attendees are more willing to trust and ask questions. A 2010 randomized study found that personalized ALDH2 genetic feedback reduced 30-day drinking frequency and quantity among Asian American young adults with one inactive ALDH2 allele; future studies may want to consider seeing what the results are if such feedback were given by peers.
A similar principle applies to counseling older adults and immigrant families. Telling an entire subset of the population simply to stop drinking risks being dismissive of the worlds that patients hail from. Alcohol serves as a social lubricant in certain East Asian cultures. To ignore that reality may deepen mistrust and gaps in culturally responsive care for Asians.
Providers can bridge this gap by partnering with trusted community centers and leaning on hospital advisory boards to host events that reinforce clinical counseling within familiar spaces. This year, I plan to host a service event inviting a Stanford physician to speak on ALDH2 deficiency after service one day at a nearby Chinese Baptist church.
When immigrant families like mine moved to the United States, they had to decide what to carry with them and what to leave behind. Some things were obvious: loved ones, places, languages. Others were quieter: recipes, rituals, and everyday habits, including drinks poured at mealtime, for guests, or before making a business deal. I grew up at the crossroads of their world and my American one, where blame or exclusion rarely led anywhere useful.
When I first learned about ALDH2 deficiency, I itched to call family and friends back home, some of whom do not have access to health insurance or a regular primary care provider, to tell them about it. But I had to approach it carefully: I’m not a doctor yet.
My father ended up having an ethanol patch test performed at a free clinic visit, while I was on FaceTime with him. Since hearing about ALDH2 deficiency, he has been drinking significantly less. He probably would not have responded as well to an order for him to abstain completely from alcohol or a lecture about acetaldehyde-induced DNA adducts and cross-linking in white blood cells.
My mother, too, may not need to know every molecular pathway by which acetaldehyde-induced oxidative stress impacts bone formation. But she deserves to know, in language that is accessible to her, that ALDH2 deficiency increases the risk of osteoporosis that she may already be more vulnerable to as a post-menopausal East Asian woman.
In my family, roles reverse as I grow older. Gong Gong, now 91, is the one I try to make laugh. Medicine, I am learning, is not only what I know. It is how gently and truthfully I offer what I know to the people I love, and to the strangers who one day trust me with their care.
Brian Zhang is a second-year M.D. student at the Stanford University School of Medicine, where he currently serves as student body president.

Lindsay Clancy holdout juror says he had no doubt she deliberately killed her children
- Published
The lone holdout juror in the trial of Lindsay Clancy has said he "didn't have any doubts" that she was criminally responsible for killing her three children.
"Based on all the physical evidence, key witnesses and what the prosecution presents, I thought it was enough proof that she knew exactly what she was doing and planned it," Michael Desronvil said in a statement to CBS News, the BBC's US partner.
The judge declared a mistrial on 4 September after the jury failed to reach a unanimous verdict following nearly 40 hours of deliberating.
Clancy admitted to the killings but her lawyers argued she had been suffering from postpartum psychosis. Prosecutors said the killings were calculated.
Warning: This article contains distressing details
The 36-year-old was charged with three counts of first-degree murder after strangling Cora, five, Dawson, three, and Callan, eight months, at the family's Massachusetts home before jumping out of the second-floor window.
To find Clancy guilty, jurors had to be unanimously convinced beyond reasonable doubt that she intentionally killed her children and that she did not do so as a result of postpartum psychosis, a rare and serious condition.
The jury - nine women and three men - considered a range of options including not guilty by reason of insanity, manslaughter and first-degree murder.
Several jurors have said following the mistrial being declared that the panel was ultimately divided 11-1 in favour of finding Clancy not criminally responsible.
Desronvil said he believed the evidence presented in court showed she had planned the killings.
"I didn't have any doubts," he said in a statement to CBS on Thursday.
"As I tried to explain different possible theories during deliberation, I kept getting cut off as if I had doubts based on the evidence presented."
- What happens next after Lindsay Clancy's murder case ends in a mistrial? 
  - Published5 September
Paula Devlin, one of the other jurors, told CBS Mornings that the panel had spent several days trying to convince Desronvil to change his mind.
"We all worked together to convince ourselves once we got to that point where it was 10 to 2," she said.
The jury foreperson, a retired fifth-grade teacher, described not being able to reach a verdict as "awful" and an "emotional rollercoaster".
She told NBC that Desronvil had "admitted he had reasonable doubt", but as she started filling out the verdict sheets, he apparently said: "But I'm still not going to say that she's not guilty by reason of insanity."
Another juror told local CBS station WBZ-TV that most of the jurors had been "very firm in their stance" from the start and "the stand-alone juror was not the only one that was unwilling to see things from the other side".
But they added that because Desronvil would not "follow" his reasonable doubt nor offer logical reasoning for his position, they felt Clancy had not received a fair trial.
The identities of all 11 jurors have not been officially disclosed but in the US, once a case is over, any juror can choose to speak publicly about a case and their deliberations.
Patrick Clancy, the children's father and Lindsay Clancy's ex-husband, is due to speak publicly about the case in an interview with the CBS programme 60 Minutes on Sunday.
In it, he is expected to discuss his grief, his memories of his children and the conspiracy theories that have flooded social media since the trial began.
He said he still speaks to his children "all the time", describing it as "a way I stay connected to them".
During the trial, Clancy's defence team had attempted to use her being put on more than a dozen medications in the lead-up to the killings, as well as seeking help from a suicide hotline and an emergency room, as evidence of her psychosis.
Postpartum psychosis can involve hallucinations and delusions, and her lawyers argued that she was unable to understand the nature of her actions or distinguish right from wrong.
A forensic psychiatrist who testified for the defence said Clancy experienced a "command hallucination" and a "delusion of influence" when she killed her children.
However, her psychiatrist testified for the prosecution that Clancy did not show signs of psychosis during their sessions, while another psychiatrist noted that the condition was not currently recognised by the American Psychiatric Association.
Under Massachusetts law, prosecutors had to prove beyond any reasonable doubt that Clancy was criminally responsible for the jury to find her guilty. The defence did not have to prove her mental illness or lack of criminal responsibility.
The mistrial leaves the case unresolved. Prosecutors have not said whether they will seek a retrial.
Clancy's lawyer, Kevin Reddington, has said he hopes to reach an agreement with prosecutors to avoid a second trial.
He told ABC's Good Morning America that he was upset that the lone juror would not acquit Clancy.
He said the holdout "would not apply the law of reasonable doubt" as instructed by the judge, adding: "That's not right. And that's why I was upset."
The next court hearing is scheduled for 29 September at Plymouth Superior Court in Massachusetts.

College Is Coming Apart
Successive, overlapping crises reveal that American higher education makes no sense.
Sign up for Ordinary Extraordinary, Ian Bogost’s newsletter on making everyday life vivid.
Artificial intelligence arrived on campus as a crisis but has since become banal. Students can now do basically all their schoolwork automatically with AI—answering scientific problem sets, writing computer code, and drafting essays. Professors like me have no idea whether we are really teaching or just LARPing for students who are also pretending to occupy their role. Worse, some of us are offloading the drudgery of writing recommendation letters, grant proposals, and even scientific papers to AI.
But at the same time that AI fouled up the student-teacher relationship, the technology benefited other corners of campus. Researchers quickly discovered that AI is enormously useful for knowledge production, especially in the natural and applied sciences: in protein-structure prediction, materials design, and drug discovery, for example. Pressured, in part, by donors, boards, employers, and parents, college administrators have announced AI initiatives, invested in AI infrastructure, and established AI degree programs.
These two forces—students using AI to their detriment and colleges using it to their benefit—might seem to be in conflict. Students are supposed to do everything longhand to preserve the sanctity of learning, but they are also urged to meet the new professional demands created by AI. Faculty and administrators are policing the classroom for AI, largely in vain, while also using AI liberally in their own work. Campuses are defending themselves against AI as an interloper while concurrently retooling themselves for the AI future. Colleges are racing toward and away from AI simultaneously. It feels like artificial intelligence is wresting higher education apart.
That’s what I thought at first too. But I’ve come to the conclusion that something bigger, stranger, and more damaging has been taking place for a long time. AI has combined with two other recent campus crises—the coronavirus pandemic and the research-funding cuts of the second Trump administration—to amplify a deeper truth: American college is incompatible with itself. Americans speak of “college” as if it is one coherent thing. That’s wrong. Higher education is a bundle of unrelated things held together by custom, history, and accident. The college bundle was always a tenuous one. It has little reason to remain together, even as the institutions inside it are too entrenched to separate.
College in America makes two promises. On the one hand, college is a credentialing service: It awards a degree that affirms knowledge and sends a graduate into a career. On the other hand, college is a coming-of-age service. It forms identity through social exploration and intellectual development. It is the American ideal for how a young person figures out who they are. Partying, drinking, Greek life, sports, and other forms of college life always risked undermining the educational project—and vice versa. But the two categories coexisted well enough.
Now two things that got packaged together as “college” have begun to unbundle and disperse. The coming-of-age experience—friendships, independence, experimentation—has become less obviously dependent on the campus surrounding it, partly because college’s monopoly on exposure to a wider world weakened. Globalization and the internet bring much of that world to students long before they arrive on campus. Other aspects of college life have been moving off campus too. College football has gone national, abandoning regional affinities and local rivalries. Greek rush has become an outsourced industry. Campuses are hospital systems, major local employers, and real-estate-investment operations as much as, or more than, they are schools.
Optimizing college for professional preparation also began to pull the two purposes apart, and eroded the unrepeatable social experience that college is supposed to provide. The economy demanded more of students outside the classroom—internships, networking, publications, volunteering. In a brutal job-search environment, where entry-level gigs seem to demand nepotism, luck, and 10 rounds of interviews, today’s undergraduates may feel that their older professors do not fully understand the gap between the delivery of the credential and the career it promises.
Then COVID-19 revealed that the credentialing process could continue if campus life was reduced or even eliminated entirely. Considerable controversy and confusion accompanied this moment; some students tried to sue expensive universities on the grounds that a closed campus was not worth the full-freight price. But in the end, credentialing proved entirely possible with a compromised or absent version of campus life.
Now AI has separated the two purposes of college almost entirely. Writing an essay previously required doing something resembling the assigned academic work. Because AI makes it possible to complete coursework without much or any intellectual labor, AI has disconnected the output from the process (if students choose the shortcut). Suffering through a term paper no longer inherently affords opportunities to take a break to get a late-night coffee with your fellow students, to commiserate with hallmates over a difficult professor, or to reach an unexpected realization while drunk at a house party. Social and academic progress are no longer woven together. No particular quantity of shared time or deliberation is required to carry out one inside the other.
A combination of factors (among them shifting values, educational entrepreneurship, regulatory arbitrage, and the speed of technological change) has altered the meaning of a diploma. Yet schools have had no trouble continuing to award degrees to the students who spent their whole undergraduate careers on campuses that tout the same traditional look on quads and inside libraries, but that AI has hopelessly mangled beneath the surface.
Immediately after taking office, the second Trump administration embarked on a series of attacks against higher education. The attacks were politically motivated, but they were effective because they hit campuses where it hurt. Since World War II, the American research-university sector has become defined as an enormous, distributed, scientific-research industry. The Trump attacks undermined this project by disrupting the tens of billions of dollars of federal funding that pays for that research (which includes graduate education).
At the same moment that AI was widening the conflict between credentialing and coming of age, the Trump cuts exposed a different structural incompatibility, between education and research. The fact that big universities were driven by research was not a secret, but it was also not well understood by the American public, including parents and students. If you find out that a friend or neighbor is a university professor, you’d probably ask them, “What do you teach?” And if they squirm when asked, that’s because many faculty often do not see teaching as their primary job. Yes, a professor is expected to teach undergraduates and produce research, because a university’s mission entails education and scholarship. But national universities do not value or reward those activities equally.
Research brings grants, prestige, graduate students, rankings, and career advancement. At research universities, undergraduate teaching is seen, if not described, as a necessary act to keep the tuition dollars flowing and to maintain the appearance of undergraduate education as predominant—the thing that people think of first when they imagine what college is for.
University administrators often argue that the research and teaching missions bolster each other: A star researcher, the story goes, can bring the latest knowledge to the classroom. Basically every college tour on an American campus will include a schtick about how undergraduates can participate in faculty research. Universities have a strong incentive to make research and teaching appear to align. But in truth, those purposes sit more in tension than in unity.
A revealing term helps explain how tenuous this relationship really is. A researcher who gets a big grant can use part of those funds for a “teaching buyout,” paying their way out of the classroom. Success at one of the university’s missions literally purchases relief from the other. (There is no research buyout.)
Campuses such as mine, Washington University in St. Louis, take in $1 billion or more of research funding every year. That money pays for the work done in labs, but also for equipment, buildings, and staff. It forms the foundation for the metrics (grants won, and “research expenditures,” or money spent from those grants) that campuses use to compete against one another for faculty, graduate students, philanthropic gifts, and other forms of prestige. Threaten the flow of research money and you don’t merely endanger the labs; you destabilize the financial and organizational structure of the whole sector.
Every major college and university touts the liberal arts as the core of an undergraduate education, but the humanities in particular—fields of arts and letters such as literature and languages, which generally do not receive much, if any, federal research funding—enjoy mostly vestigial value that does not match the underlying economics of higher education very well. Universities are different from colleges in this regard. Small liberal-arts colleges focus almost exclusively on undergraduate education and are earnestly committed to the arts and letters. That’s one reason they are particularly well positioned to weather the Trump attacks. But these schools serve much smaller populations, and they are still tied to the broader American university system, from which they draw faculty and to which they send students on to grad school. And even at these schools, the humanities are particularly vulnerable to AI, because the intellectual labor that the technology can now eliminate—wrestling with the meaning of texts, figuring out how to express complex ideas—is the fundamental point of that type of education.
The AI crisis on campus, mated to the COVID-19 and federal-funding crises that flanked it, dismantled the pretense that everything happening on campus shared any kind of common project. AI might substantially improve scientific research while destroying the humanities. And AI might troublingly reduce the effort a student must exert to complete a degree while allowing a scientist to carry out experiments with reduced labor, uncontroversially.
Undergraduate education, credentialing, scientific research, professionalization, and coming of age still occupy the same campuses. But they are clearly no longer parts of the same enterprise. They have not been so for many years—probably many decades. Looking back at my own career, I can see clearly that every single term of it has taken place in the shadow of this family of mismatches. Teaching and research sometimes align, but not always. Becoming educated has little to do with becoming an adult, apart from taking place on the same campus. I used to understand a university as akin to a city—expansive, diverse, and necessarily host to multiple purposes. But now I wonder if even that generous account is a fantasy. I wonder if one organization can support all of these conflicting projects well—and if it ever did.
Now that these incompatibilities are harder to ignore, will the American collegiate project reinvent itself in a way that would resolve them? Perhaps, but also: I doubt it. Universities are purpose-built to resist change of almost any kind. College leaders have repeatedly adopted a “wait and see” or “keep our heads down” approach, treating disruption as mere interruption: The pandemic ended, AI will settle down, federal funding will resume, and all of this, whatever it is, will blow over. These are far more tolerable conclusions to reach than, say, the idea that credentialing has no business sharing a venue with coming of age, or that undergraduate education is at odds with the mission of a research institution.
Each recent crisis gave college an alibi. AI was an alien technology that corrupted an otherwise functional educational institution. The Trump funding cuts were an aberrant political attack on a healthy research enterprise. COVID-19 was an emergency that forced campuses to suspend campus life and education alike in the interest of public health. But surviving any one of these crises, let alone all of them together, changes nothing about the underlying circumstances that they exacerbated. The incompatible purposes of college carry on.
I see no reason to believe that the structural inconsistencies that have come to define higher education will resolve. The degree will become ever more a goal and less a process of self-discovery. The research and teaching missions will further retract from each other. College is at war with itself as much as it is with the public, or the government, or the private sector, or the technology industry.
As a degree or a ritual, college will continue to have value, and you or your kids may want to attend one for a credential or a coming-of-age experience (or both). The old names will persist, and the campus buildings will still stand. The coursework will continue whether humans or machines complete it (or assign it). The leaves will fall onto the quad in the autumn, and the caps will fly into the air in the spring. The appearance of college can endure, even as its spirit—a community organized for the education and formation of young people—comes undone.

A survivor from a prison cell in Nigeria where 37 suspected illegal goldminers died while in the custody of a paramilitary group this week has recounted his panic and struggle for breath, as police on Friday fired teargas at people protesting against the deaths.
Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) – a paramilitary group that works with police – initially blamed the deaths in Minna, the state capital of the mineral-rich state of Niger, on a disease outbreak.
However, an intelligence report seen by Agence France-Presse said preliminary information suggested that overcrowding and inadequate ventilation were responsible.
Dauda Shehu, a survivor from the cell, told journalists at a hospital on Friday: “We were jam-packed in the cell, no ventilation for us to breathe well. All of a sudden we realised that we could not breathe and we were all scampering for where to get fresh air, we even appealed to them several times, banged the cell door, but they refused to answer us.”
A video shared online showed the bodies of dozens of young men clad only in shorts, most of whom appeared to be teenagers, sprawled on the ground out in the open. Volunteers wearing gloves can be seen standing over the dead, while veiled women try to identify the bodies of their relatives. Voices shouting curses on those responsible can be heard in the background.
Protests over the deaths broke out on Thursday evening in Minna. On Friday dozens of young people, including miners and their relatives, gathered near the NSCDC’s office in the city. Police cordoned off the area and attempted to disperse the protesters by firing teargas.
A Reuters witness saw security forces fire live rounds as protesters – some armed with sticks, machetes and traditional hunting rifles – called for justice. Some protesters tried to set fire to government buildings in the Tunga neighbourhood. “We are not thieves – we are simply seeking a way to make a living by mining,” Yusuf Auwal, a miner who joined the protesters, told Reuters. At least one body lay on the streets. Soldiers and police officers patrolled Minna to try to restore order.
The NSCDC said the detainees had been held in raids on suspected illegal mines on 15 and 16 September in the Wushishi-Lukoto area west of Minna. Nigeria’s interior minister, Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo, ordered the immediate suspension of Niger state’s NSCDC commandant, Suberu Siyaka Aniviye, pending the outcome of a full investigation.
Niger state, which is Nigeria’s largest and more than twice the size of Belgium, is rich in minerals and attracts thousands of artisanal miners, most lured by gold.
Police and the NSCDC did not initially provide a precise number of deaths but the state governor, Mohammed Umaru Bago, later confirmed 37 people had died.
“It’s so sad, it’s so tragic,” he said, adding an inquiry into the deaths had already started work. He declared three days of mourning and postponed the start of campaigning for elections due in January. The men were buried on Thursday, according to Islamic tradition, without any forensic investigations.
The scramble for gold reserves dug up in illegal mines in Niger state is fuelling violence by criminal gangs, according to officials and experts. The gangs tax the miners and demand a cut from the extracted ore as a levy to allow them access to the pits.
