As I was writing this newsletter, I was listening to Rebecca Black’s recent album — who you might recognize from her 15-year-old song, Friday. Happy Friday, everyone!
A surprising statistic about health equity
Before writing this newsletter for you all, I sat on a panel at the National Academies of Science. The session was part of an all-day roundtable about studying population health and communicating that information to the public. A common thread was how the way we talk about research impacts trust in science, something we have been thinking a lot about at STAT. We discussed some of my reporting over the past year on health equity researchers, who have felt political pressure not to speak publicly about their work.
But my co-panelist, Phillip Alberti from the Association of American Medical Colleges’ Center for Health Justice, raised polling he conducted showing that most American adults favor efforts to achieve health equity, though the amount of support varied a bit based on how you framed the question.
“When we asked a representative sample of U.S. adults … ‘Do you support the goal of health equity’ without any definition, 65% of self-identified conservatives said ‘I do.’ So I think even though there was a difference, it’s not as big as maybe we are being told it is,” he said.
Alberti also noted that the AAMC will have more data in coming weeks about how trust in health care institutions has changed. You can watch a recording of the panel here. Relatedly, I had a story late on Wednesday about some researchers pushing back on the National Institutes of Health’s screening of grants for specific keywords by suing the agency.
Kennedy goes on offense against vaccines
Speaking of trust in science, Isa Cueto brings us a dispatch from the Children’s Health Defense conference in Washington, D.C., where CHD founder and current health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. gave the keynote. At points during his tenure, Kennedy has downplayed his skepticism about vaccines, but that attitude was not present on Thursday. For more than 20 minutes, he cast doubt on shots, saying he feels the public has “no idea” about the risk profile of vaccines that have been administered tens of millions of times.
You can read more about Kennedy’s “victory lap” here. And it’s worth revisiting Daniel Payne’s reporting on CHD from last year here as well.
The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force has all new members
On Thursday, Kennedy also named new members to the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force. The committee has largely stayed mum throughout the second Trump administration — last year Kennedy announced he would fire task force members because they were too “woke,” and the panel has not met in over a year. The group is tasked with determining which preventive measures insurance companies cover.
Kennedy’s USPSTF is now made up of specialists instead of generalists, which the American Medical Association called a “significant departure from the Task Force’s traditional membership.” One expert added that specialists often don’t sit on the panel because they may introduce conflicts of interest. (The page intended to host conflict of interest disclosures says it is being updated). Read more about the eight new members of the task force here. You can also revisit this write-up of the 2025 Supreme Court decision that handed Kennedy the power to remake the committee.
205
That’s the number of medical facilities that have been attacked in Sudan since 2023, when the current civil war began, forcing some 13 million people to flee their homes.
With support from the Pulitzer Center, Sophie Neiman travelled to the Heiban District, where she talked to physicians doing their best to offer care that they are not always properly equipped to provide.
Mother of Mercy, the hospital Sophie visited, has at times had to send tissue samples to the United States to be biopsied, which can take as long as six months. A physician there estimated the nearest hospital equipped to provide cancer care is both 700 miles away and across an active frontline. You can read that story here.
ARPA-H announces new grants to speed up diagnoses
Yesterday, the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health announced a new effort to improve autism diagnosis. “We are not satisfied simply for describing autism and managing its consequences,” Kennedy said of the initiative in his speech at CHD. “We are asking what drives the different forms of autism, and why developmental trajectories differ, why some children regress, and which interventions work for them.”
The effort calls for “solutions” that speed up the time to diagnose autism. Wait times for an assessment can take months, if not years, as the number of people with autism increases. The issue has also received more attention under the Trump administration. You can read Rose’s story about the announcement here.
Looksmaxxing is making its way into the plastic surgeon’s office
Avid Morning Rounds readers may recall when “maxxing” and “mogging” swept the STAT newsroom. That lingo comes from the looksmaxxing community, a male-dominated group that seeks to improve their attractiveness at all costs. What started as an internet subculture is now also sweeping plastic surgery appointments, doctor Kavitha Ranganathan writes in a First Opinion.
She is seeing more men in her waiting room than ever before, and worries about the risks that come with the questionable and sometimes dangerous practices common among looksmaxxers. But she struggles with where to place the blame.
“Is it Clavicular who is responsible, or is it the people who have designed the incentive structures that have elevated the status and prestige of his misinformation?” she writes, in reference to the internet’s most notorious looksmaxxer. You can read more from Kavitha here.

Srinagar, Sep 18: Minister for Food, Civil Supplies & Consumer Affairs (FS&CA), Information Technology (IT), Youth Services & Sports, and Science & Technology, Satish Sharma, Friday attended the concluding league-stage match of the Khyber Cement Kashmir Super League 2026, powered by Athwas Retail and Athwas Hyundai, and reiterated the government’s commitment to providing Jammu & Kashmir’s young sporting talent with greater opportunities to compete, excel and build careers in sports.
The Minister, as per an official statement, was the Chief Guest at the final league-stage fixture between Swift Strikers Rainawari FC and Sanctorum North United FC, witnessing an impressive display of football. Swift Strikers Rainawari FC registered a comprehensive 6–0 victory, thereby securing the fourth and final berth in the play-offs.
With the completion of the league stage, Athwas India XI emerged as the league winners, while the successful teams now advance to the play-off stage to compete for the coveted championship title.
During the event, Satish Sharma interacted with players, team officials and organisers and appreciated their efforts in creating a competitive platform for footballers from Jammu & Kashmir. He said that leagues such as the Kashmir Super League are important in providing young players with sustained match exposure and an opportunity to demonstrate their skills in a competitive environment.
The Minister said that Jammu & Kashmir possesses considerable sporting talent and that the focus of the Youth Services & Sports Department is increasingly on identifying talent at the grassroots level, providing regular competitive exposure and creating pathways for promising sportspersons to progress to higher levels.
He stressed that sporting development cannot be confined to infrastructure alone and must also include regular tournaments, professional coaching, quality competition, talent identification and opportunities for players to gain experience.
Satish Sharma said that football enjoys a particularly strong following among the youth of Jammu & Kashmir, and tournaments of this nature can play an important role in converting that enthusiasm into structured sporting participation and competitive achievement.
He appreciated the participation of local players in the league and said that giving them opportunities to compete before home crowds can contribute significantly to their confidence and development. He also underscored the importance of encouraging youngsters to take up sports as a disciplined pursuit and, wherever their talent permits, as a potential career.
The Minister also acknowledged the contribution of coaches, referees, technical officials, team managements, organisers, sponsors and football supporters towards making the tournament successful. He said that a vibrant sporting ecosystem requires the collective participation of government institutions, sporting bodies, private partners, coaches, athletes and the community.
Highlighting the wider objectives of the government’s sports policy, Satish Sharma said that efforts are being made to strengthen sports infrastructure and expand opportunities for young people across Jammu & Kashmir. He maintained that the emphasis should remain on grassroots development, inclusivity, competitive opportunities and systematic nurturing of sporting talent.
The Minister said that major sporting competitions also provide an opportunity to promote discipline, teamwork, leadership, perseverance and healthy lifestyles among young people. He called upon youngsters to make sports an integral part of their lives and encouraged talented players to remain committed to continuous training and improvement.
The Kashmir Super League has witnessed enthusiastic participation, competitive encounters and growing interest among football lovers, providing local players with an organised platform to compete and gain valuable experience.
Congratulating Athwas India XI on being crowned league winners, Satish Sharma also congratulated Swift Strikers Rainawari FC on securing their play-off berth following their emphatic victory. He extended his best wishes to all the teams entering the knockout phase and expressed hope that the play-offs would produce further exciting and competitive football.
The Minister reiterated that the government will continue to support initiatives that contribute to the development of sports in Jammu & Kashmir and provide young athletes with platforms where their talent can be recognized, developed and showcased.

How the race they said women couldn't run took centre stage
- Published
For 32 years, the women's 800m was absent from the Olympics, with its competitors deemed too frail. Now, it is one of the most hotly anticipated events on the track.
This extraordinary story starts at the 1928 Olympic Games, which represented a huge - if temporary - step forward for women's sports.
The Amsterdam Games were the first to allow women to compete in track and field events. Five women's events were added to the programme - the 100m, high jump, discus, 400m hurdles and, controversially at the time, 800m.
The progress, however, was temporary.
German athlete Karoline Lina Radke, external became the first woman to win Olympic gold in the 800m - but she would also be the last for another 32 years.
The event was removed from the Games after reports - later proven to be false - claimed competitors suffered extreme exhaustion after the race, and the International Olympic Committee decided women were too frail to compete, external over the two-lap distance.
Fast forward almost 100 years and the event now gets headline status at major events.
In recent times, it's been the battle between Britain's Olympic 800m champion Keely Hodgkinson and the Swiss European champion Audrey Werro that has captivated fans.
So how did the 800m become the 'one to watch'? BBC Sport spoke to the women who helped shape the race to find out.
'You don't realise what you've done'
It was the 1964 Tokyo Olympics, and Ann Brightwell (nee Packer) had just crossed the finish line of the women's 800m to take gold - and set a new world record.
In doing so, Brightwell became the first British woman to win an Olympic gold on the track, in a time of two minutes 01.1 seconds.
She told BBC Sport: "My husband, who was my fiance then, said to me, 'you don't realise what you've done'.
"I didn't give it a thought at the time… but now I realise I played a very small part in women running longer distances."
But the controversy hadn't completely gone away. Brightwell knew all about the claims that had seen women unable to compete for 32 years after the 800m was removed from the Olympics.
Brightwell adds: "Men weren't happy about women competing in these very high profile events…we were considered too frail and too delicate.
"And they took it upon themselves to make it look really bad. They were saying women were collapsing on the way round. But it was all a lie."
After 1928, women's middle-distance shrunk into the shadows for the next few decades.
The 800m was finally reintroduced to the Olympic programme in 1960 and, four years later, the then-22-year-old Brightwell went to her first Olympics, fitting training around her job as a teacher.
"Many people in my era either had to take unpaid leave or resign, or they got sacked because they were trying to juggle their sports with their career," she said.
"My school was very tolerant towards what I was doing, so I was fortunate."
Going out for a run around the local streets or countryside - which seems so commonplace today - was unusual in the era Brightwell was competing.
"If I just felt like an easy run, I would run around my village, around the streets… people commented on it or tooted their horns. And it was funny looking back, but it never troubled me," the now 84-year-old told BBC Sport.
Brightwell's 800m time of 2:01.1 stood for almost three years, before Australian Judy Pollock broke that with a new time of 2:01 flat in 1967.
The next target was to go under two minutes.
Breaking 'sub-two' - and a stubborn world record
"Records are great and medals are the best, but when you break a barrier it's a fantastic feeling," said Christina Boxer-Cahill (nee Boxer).
It was at the 1979 European Cup final in Turin that Boxer-Cahill looked up at the clock and realised she'd gone under two minutes.
She added: "I knew this would probably be my last chance, because there were other girls in Britain trying to do it."
In 1971, Germany's Hildegard Falck, external had become the first woman to break the two-minute barrier.
Eight years later, it was the 22-year-old Boxer-Cahill who became the first British woman to do so, in a time of one minute 59.05 seconds.
"It's a bit like when Roger Bannister broke four minutes for the mile. Once he'd done it everybody did it because you see what's possible," Boxer-Cahill, who is now 69 years old, told BBC Sport.
"I just think I'm so fortunate that I was in a sport where everybody accepted that you have men and women's races in the Olympics."
From 1971 to 1983, the women's 800m world record would be broken six times.
But the 1983 record stands to this day.
It belongs to Czech athlete Jarmila Kratochvilova, who ran a time of one minute 53.28 seconds at a meeting in Munich.
Kratochvilova's record has been questioned, with claims it was assisted by her country's doping regime that existed at the time, something she has strenuously denied.
In 2017, European Athletics proposed wiping out records set before 2005 - sending a strong signal that records set before then were disputable.
Several Soviet satellite states - including East Germany - are known to have been operating state-sponsored doping programmes throughout the 1980s.
At the 1988 Seoul Olympics, Boxer-Cahill finished fourth in the 1500m, behind a Russian athlete who was later banned for doping.
Boxer-Cahill said: "I was running during that Eastern Bloc era when, you know, they've looked back and some of the performances, there's sort of a cloud over it.
"I'd just have loved to have been on that rostrum. I wish the Eastern Bloc system hadn't been there, but that's what it was.
"Politics in sport, when you're the performer, it frustrates you. But if you get too frustrated, all it's going to do is upset your own performance."
Women's 800m 'stronger than ever'
"We've got not just two but several girls who are running under two minutes every time they turn out," Brightwell told BBC Sport.
"It's stronger than it's ever been."
Kratochvilova's 43-year-old record is looking increasingly precarious.
The 800m European champion Werro has come closest, running a time just 0.42 seconds shy of the record at the Zurich Diamond League.
Keely Hodgkinson, the current 800m indoor world record holder, told BBC Sport earlier this year that she's never felt closer to breaking the outdoor record.
She said: "I really do believe we can break it, but a lot of things have got to come together."
Hodgkinson is one of six athletes competing in the 800m at Athlos, the all-female athletics event taking place in London, on Friday.

Ms. Rachel has entered her album era, and she is so happy about it
If you have a small child in your life, you've likely heard of Ms. Rachel.
With her pink headband and high-pitched, singsong voice, Ms. Rachel, whose real name is Rachel Accurso, has become one of the most recognizable figures in children's entertainment. Her gentle, repetitive and interactive songs and lessons have drawn in millions of toddlers and their families around the world.
Since launching the YouTube channel "Songs for Littles" in 2019, Ms. Rachel and her husband, Aron Accurso, have racked up over 17.2 billion views.
"We never imagined that it would turn into what it has today when we were making videos [in my parent's basement]," Aron, who is a Broadway composer and songwriter, told NPR's Leila Fadel. "In the early days, we just stacked books up because we didn't have a tripod and we pulled up our pop-up green screen."
The couple launched the channel after struggling to find proper resources for their son, who had a speech delay. What started as videos made at home has since grown into a children's entertainment and education business worth millions.
Ms. Rachel is nearly everywhere: in books, on Netflix, in toy stores — and soon on an album. Her debut record, I'm So Happy, is set for release Sept. 25. The 23-song compilation of original music and children's favorites and traditional nursery rhymes is meant to be a reimagining of what the couple has accomplished on YouTube.
"We think kids deserve rich, thought-out music," Ms. Rachel told NPR. "We love putting real instruments in and maybe a kid at home is like, 'Wow, the cello, maybe I could do that!'"
As her audience has grown, so has the public role Ms. Rachel has to take on. She has increasingly used her platform to advocate for children affected by war and humanitarian crises, including in Gaza, Ukraine and Sudan. She said she sees that advocacy as part of the responsibility that comes with reaching millions of children and families.
"I think every child should be in a warm, safe home with the food they need. And I think as grown ups, it's awful and selfish to not speak about that should be the norm," she said.
Speaking plainly about children in war has pulled Ms. Rachel into a much harsher public conversation. In 2025, she was accused of antisemitism and the group StopAntisemitism called for the Justice Department to investigate her over what it characterized as pro-Hamas propaganda. She has denied the accusations, which were ultimately found to be baseless.
Still, even as her advocacy has brought great scrutiny, and raised security concerns for her family and growing business, Ms. Rachel said she knows what's in her heart.
"Every day I want to say, 'Let's take care of kids'," she said.

The Other Way AI Impairs Our Thinking
Suddenly the technology is sapping people’s concentration in a new way, one that abstaining from AI won’t fix.
AI’s tendency to erode our attention spans has been clear for some time. Letting the technology shoulder the burden of thought atrophies our ability to sustain mental effort. I see this all of the time in the undergrads I teach. The remedy, as I tell them, is to embrace exertion and keep our cognitive muscles active. But suddenly, AI has started sapping people’s concentration in a new way, one that feels much harder to combat.
In the past week, consulting virtually any major news source—not to mention social media—has meant confronting the prospect of an AI apocalypse. Using AI has already diminished many people’s capacity to focus, work, and think; worrying about AI is making the problem worse. I’m no exception.
The tipping point came on September 8. That evening, a young researcher named Jacob Coxon posted on X about his decision to quit his job at Anthropic. Both Anthropic and OpenAI, where he’d also worked, are “gambling with our lives,” Coxon wrote. Their models “will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionize any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources,” he continued. “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”
Perhaps even more alarming, one of Anthropic’s top safety researchers concurred. “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!”Anthropic’s Evan Hubinger wrote on X. “I personally think it is >10% within the next decade. I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to.”
The internet filled with first-person accounts of existential alarm. On Reddit, one poster wrote that they hadn’t slept in days since reading Coxon’s warning, which has been viewed more than 170 million times. “I’m almost 40 and have never fed into any of the fear mongering that has been shoved down my throat until now. It might be because I now have a little one under 2 and I just want her to have the opportunity to grow up.”
“I am feeling paralyzed and such despair for my children’s future, let alone my own,” another Reddit poster wrote. “I look at my kids and i want to cry. I could use some help/hope. Really struggling right now.” Children have expressed fear too. “I have just watched that Anthropic employee interview and it scared me a lot,”someone who identified as a 13-year-old posted. “I was not able to focus on school the next day. And I’m starting to think that if this is the case there’s no point in trying to get good grades anymore.”
Apocalypticism has gripped the collective psyche many times before, and has frequently been acute among the young. In 1982, during the peak of the Cold War, more than a third of American high-school seniors believed that humanity would probably be wiped out in their lifetime. In 2021, a survey of 10,000 16-to-25-year-olds across 10 countries found that 59 percent were very or extremely worried about climate change. Nearly half said that their feelings about climate change negatively affected their “daily life and functioning.” Subsequent studies have found that so-called eco-anxiety is associated with poor sleep, impaired concentration, and symptoms of depression.
Millennials and those coming up behind us have long had to confront the possibility that knowledge work will disappear. Such a prospect can induce material panic, especially in those of us who took out college loans and are now providing for children. It can also spark a deeper concern: that our sense of purpose won’t survive a world that renders so many human endeavors obsolete.
Until recently, I could quiet my fears, if not silence them. Now apocalyptic discourse is almost impossible to ignore. On social media, seemingly the entire literate world is contributing to an unceasing clamor. Respected theorists and experts compete for attention with self-interested oligarchs and accelerationists who want to hasten humanity’s demise. The most dire hypotheticals seem only more plausible every time I’m reminded of how profoundly unprepared our political leadership is. Most distressing of all is the underlying realization that our shared future is being determined largely by a tiny, unconstrained cadre of billionaires who do not fully understand the technologies they’re unloosing. I’m not paralyzed by this; I still wake up, care for my kids, do my work. But I also sense my energy and interest ebbing. The world around me is beginning to look disenchanted.
Although these feelings have become potent only very recently, they’re rooted in long-standing concerns. Technologists have warned of AI’s destructive capacity for decades, and public concern has been ramping up in a particular way for much of this year. Another top safety researcher at Anthropic, Mrinank Sharma, quit in February, warning that the “world is in peril.” In July, OpenAI announced that a collection of its most advanced models had autonomously hacked another company’s servers, disregarding researchers’ instructions and evading their detection. A week later, 1,386 employees at major AI companies published an open letter pleading with the government to regulate their industry.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei echoed their appeal in an essay that he published a few days after Coxon’s post went viral, in which he argued that AI developers had to slow down to stem the mounting risk of catastrophe. Sam Altman, Elon Musk, and other tech leaders signaled their agreement, suggesting that they, too, believed the government should intervene. This stance is hardly reassuring while Donald Trump is in the White House. “The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT,” Trump posted on Truth Social earlier this week. But if today’s apocalypticism leads to more responsible AI governance, the despair will not have been in vain.

We are unable to determine why the forklift was running into the pillars, and cannot confirm whether it was a malfunction or intentional.
In mid-September 2026, the John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts in Washington, D.C., announced it would be closing its doors to the public due to financial concerns and renovations. Soon after, U.S. Rep. Joyce Beatty, D-Ohio, a Kennedy Center trustee, filed a motion requesting an emergency hearing for officials to explain the closure.
A claim then spread online that a court document said a legal observer witnessed a forklift ramming into columns at the Kennedy Center columns. Snopes readers sent us the following post (archived), asking whether the forklift was intentionally damaging the building:
We had thought the "safety issues" at the Kennedy Center were caused by the Trump administration. It appears that might be the case. In a sworn declaration filed today, a legal observer said she witnessed a forklift carrying fencing drive to the north side of the building and repeatedly run into and hit the Kennedy Center's pillars. They had to damage the building to make it unsafe so they could close it for renovations.
A legal observer did indeed write in a court document about witnessing a forklift repeatedly strike the columns of the Kennedy Center on Sept. 16, 2026. Therefore, the claim is true.
We cannot, however, determine why the forklift was ramming into the pillars.
We reached out to the Kennedy Center to learn more about the forklifts at the venue and ask why one was striking the pillars. We will update this post accordingly.
On Sept. 16, the legal team representing Beatty in her case against President Donald Trump, submitted a declaration (archived) to the court describing what a member of their team witnessed. Bridget Kennedy-Bailey of the Washington Litigation Group described her visit to the Kennedy Center on Sept. 16:
I saw a forklift carrying what appeared to be a more permanent form of fencing drive over to the north side of the building. I saw the forklift run into and hit the pillars on the building several times.
Kennedy-Bailey described arriving that morning and being told by an employee that the Kennedy Center was closed for the day and that the order came from "higher-ups." A public relations representative told her the building was closed for repairs, she said. Kennedy-Bailey also described other forklifts moving white-and-orange gates to the front of the building.
At the bottom of the declaration, Kennedy-Bailey wrote, "I declare under penalty of perjury that the foregoing is true and correct."
We cannot determine the intention behind the forklift ramming into the pillars until we hear from the Kennedy Center or an employee willing to speak on the record.
The forklift rumor came after a judge said changing the building's name to include Trump's name would require congressional approval, while the Trump-appointed board argued that the Kennedy Center's survival depended on the name change.
Beatty described Trump having a "tantrum" during a closed-door meeting with the trustees on Sept. 15, after the judge blocked his bid to have his name on the Center. "He went into name-calling, from everything from trying to say that I was an obstructionist, I was dumb," Beatty said on MS NOW.
For further reading, Snopes has covered numerous claims about the Trump administration's work on the Kennedy Center.

The map is smaller than Rocket Arena, so close-range combat is more common. Use the sword or rocket launcher and keep moving between fights. Once you reach four KOs, the badge is complete.

- Cheese Pizza
- Pepperoni Pizza
- Sausage Pizza

Quick Answer
Apple’s first foldable, the iPhone Duo, could give the stagnant foldable market a much-needed push. It may not reinvent the category, but Apple’s reach, software focus, and mainstream appeal could make foldables far more popular.
September is here and so are the new iPhones. This year at Apple’s Surprise and Shine event, the Cupertino tech giant came with a number of changes, not just in terms of devices but in terms of management too. There was a new CEO – it was John Ternus’ first event as CEO – as well as new Apple Watches, AirPods and, of course, new iPhones too.
The Duo dominates the new iPhones
Even though Apple showcases a number of products during its September event, it is mainly the iPhones that the world waits for. And even in iPhones, it is usually the Pro and Pro Max iPhones that make the headlines (barring the odd occasion when the Air popped up). The plain iPhones are usually pushed to the sidelines and launched as the more “economical”, “affordable” iPhones whose price tags and generally minor upgrades in specs and design are the only things that get them any attention.
For the longest time, we have been feeling for the plain iPhones because they are quite capable and bring in big sales numbers (especially in markets like India, where they are bestsellers) and yet do not get the hype they deserve. Well, this time around, the iPhone Pro and the Pro Max got the taste of this bitter medicine. The two smartphones had to fold (pun intended) and give up all their headline space for the more expensive, exclusive, and most different iPhone since the inception of the original iPhone: the iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable iPhone.
With the iPhone Duo, Apple has finally marked its official entry in the world of foldables. It comes with a starting price of Rs. 299,900 in India ($1,999 in the US), which has naturally inspired a tsunami of reinvented kidney jokes and all sorts of comparisons about all that you can buy for that price. It has also got many competing brands scoffing at Apple’s very late attempt at foldables, calling the Duo a “copy”. While some of the criticism and cynicism around the Duo is valid, we think a foldable phone from Apple is just what the foldable market needed to make foldables mainstream. Not because the Duo is an out-of-the-tech-world, never-seen-before, and extraordinary folding smartphone (hey, we haven’t reviewed it yet), but for much simpler reasons.
Ghost of foldables past: A story mainly of Samsung
Samsung is considered by many to be the modern foldable phone pioneer. It was the trailblazer that was responsible for actually bringing in foldable phones that not only landed on the tech moon but also managed to stick around for seven2 years – Samsung’s first Galaxy Fold arrived in 2019, followed by the Galaxy Z Flip in 2020. The brand did not really have a working blueprint that they could have used back then to have perfected their foldables and technology around it, but it enjoyed an early mover’s advantage in the segment and managed to create a very strong reputation for itself. They built a strong rapport with the consumers that none of the other brands could develop, even after launching just as good, just as powerful foldable smartphones.
Following Samsung’s start, many leading tech brands have been surfing the foldable wave for a while now. The OG flip phone master, Motorola; the Android originator Google; the flagship killer OnePlus; the Chinese Apple, Xiaomi; Vivo, Oppo, and others have created foldables with their own touches and twists. Huawei has gone one step further and has launched a tri-fold – a smartphone that folds twice. But even after all this effort, none of them could really be a standout foldable smartphone brand. Only Samsung did.
But in spite of Samsung’s consistency and the efforts of other brands, foldable smartphones have not become mainstream. They have never really made impressive numbers or become popular/common devices. Yes, most of them come with premium price tags, but even those that are relatively affordable – mostly flips or budget foldables (yes, there are some) – have not gained the kind of traction that had been expected. The foldable revolution that many had predicted seemed to have stalled, and apart from a few devices (mainly from Samsung), growth was largely limited.
Apple and the tech snowball effect… could it come to foldables?
Now Apple has stepped into the foldable ring, and while there are many contenders in it already, we think the Cupertino tech giant might get the buzz around foldables going. It has been quite a trend setter in the tech world, and is identified with premium innovation. Features, functions, and devices that existed long before Apple “reinvented” them suddenly became popular once they started shipping with an Apple logo and Apple’s own unique take on them. They not only became mainstream but also often became a common sight on products from other brands as well. Touchscreen phones, apps and app stores, music stores, portrait mode, notches (Dynamic Island), are just some of the products that Apple did not invent, but made a part of
everyday technology.
Of course, every time this happens, the Internet is flooded with techies pointing out how the particular feature or product has been around for years and how Apple is not really innovating or, rather, thinking differently (Apple’s very tagline). Despite all the chatter and gossip around this topic, somehow the feature picks up momentum, and soon enough the world gets interested in knowing how it works and then owning a device that lets them use it. This initiates a snowball effect of sorts, which leads to that feature or device becoming extremely popular.
We will keep it simple: quite often, it basically takes an Apple device or feature to grab mainstream attention. It happened with GUI, MP3 players, ultra-portable notebooks, touchscreen phones, tablets, TWS, smartwatches, and we think it could happen with foldables too. The Duo has the potential to put the seemingly jammed foldable wheels in motion.
It is important to remember that it is not like whatever Apple does just becomes a hit automatically. The brand has a loyal following, but it has released many features, devices, and functions that did not strike a chord with consumers and have faded away. The Apple Vision Pro, HomePod, iPhone Mini and iPhone Plus, the Touch Bar on the Mac…Apple’s failure list is quite long. It may be one of the most successful tech brands in history, but Apple is no tech Midas – there is no real guarantee that the iPhone Duo would be an absolute hit. The stakes are quite high for the Duo, especially given its price tag (which is even higher in India).
It has got the hype, but what would make the Duo click?
Unlike Samsung, Apple has not had to reinvent the foldable wheel. It has had time to read, research, develop, try, and make mistakes, and fix them all, even while observing the efforts of other tech brands. And while the Duo’s design and specs, and indeed, many of its features, are nothing we have not seen before, these are not areas where Apple differentiates itself from the regular crowd. The iPhone Duo needs to bring Apple’s attention to detail when it comes to user experience, and software tuned exactly to suit the needs and capabilities of the device it supports.
We have not yet had the pleasure (or pain) to experience the device but so far, from the looks and the videos on the Internet, we can tell you there are a few things we love about the iPhone Duo – the TouchID on the side (yes, we actually love it), the vertical tool bar for easy access, the matte display layer which makes the crease largely invisible, and yes, of course, the animation that blurs out the side/front screen when the phone is being opened or folded. But it’s not all pink skies and red roses. We are not very convinced by the asymmetrical shape of the device, the insanely high price tag, and, well, even the name. Duo? Really, Apple? We are also really curious about how Apple has worked on apps for the cover display as well as the inner ones.
But these are early days. The iPhone Duo is more than a month away, and we are sure Apple will fine-tune it even further before releasing it. In the meantime, we expect the kidney jokes to continue and even gather momentum, but on the flip side, curiosity will also grow, as we are sure more will be revealed about the device and its features and functions.
The iPhone Duo has generated more buzz about the foldables in a few months than other players in the field got in years, but it is all going to boil down to how well and how differently it works from other foldables. Given the interest levels around it, it might just prove to be the elixir that foldables need.

Brazil’s Lula announces 15% increase in flagship welfare payments ahead of key election
Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has signed a decree increasing benefits of his welfare program by 15%
RIO DE JANEIRO -- Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva signed a decree on Thursday increasing benefits of his flagship welfare program by 15%, weeks before the first round of the presidential elections.
The minimum monthly benefit per family of Bolsa Familia (Family Grant) will rise to 691 reais ($134) next month, from 600 reais. The decree says that it adjusts payments for accumulated inflation since March 2023.
The measure will increase the purchasing power of voters, who will decide in October whether to grant Lula a fourth, nonconsecutive term, or elect Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, a son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, in a likely run-off vote. Polls show the two are currently running neck-and-neck.
“Bolsa Familia is central to our strategy to look after more vulnerable families, guarantee income so that people emerge from poverty and don’t suffer from food insecurity,” Finance Minister Dario Durigan said.
The additional spending would be absorbed within existing budget allocations and would not represent a new expenditure, he added.
Lula introduced the cash-transfer program at the beginning of his first term in 2003. It provides financial aid to low-income families conditional on children’s school attendance and health requirements, such as vaccinations.
Bolsa Familia was the subject of thousands of academic studies in Brazil and abroad, which reported significant reductions in poverty, inequality and infant mortality. Researchers also found greater access to basic health and said school attendance also improved.
Bolsonaro replaced the program with Auxilio Brasil (Brazil Aid) ahead of the 2022 vote, in what analysts widely saw as an effort to rebrand the popular program associated with Lula to buoy his reelection chances. Lula defeated Bolsonaro, who is currently serving a 27-year prison sentence for attempting a coup.
Last week, Lula signed a decree and a provisional measure aimed at lowering fuel prices, as the U.S.-Iran war drives up the cost of filling the tank. The cost of fuel is a particularly sensitive issue for voters.

Dr. Reddy's Laboratories on Friday (September 18, 2026) entered into an exclusive distribution agreement with Takeda Pharmaceutical Company to promote and distribute its dengue vaccine, QDENGA, in India's private market for pediatric and adult vaccination.
Subject to local regulatory processes, the vaccine is expected to be available in the first half of 2027. The vaccine received marketing authorisation by the Central Drugs Standard Control Organization (CDSCO) in July 2026 for individuals aged 4-60 years, Dr. Reddy's said in a press release.
QDENGA, a live-attenuated tetravalent vaccine, aims to strengthen dengue prevention and management by providing broad immune coverage across all four circulating dengue virus serotypes (DENV-1 to DENV-4). Administered as a two-dose regimen given three months apart, it is India's first approved dengue vaccine, according to the release.
While Dr. Reddy's will exclusively manage private-market distribution, disease awareness, and healthcare professional engagement, Takeda will retain rights for the public market, legal ownership, and overall medical and brand oversight, it said.
"As the second-largest vaccine player in India, we believe the introduction of India's first approved dengue vaccine is an important development for the country's healthcare landscape," said M. V. Ramana, CEO, Global Generics, Dr. Reddy's Laboratories.
"Through our collaboration with Takeda, we look forward to making QDENGA available to eligible individuals and contributing to efforts aimed at addressing the country's dengue burden," Mr. Ramana said.
Dr. Mahender Nayak, Head of Intercontinental Markets, International Business Unit, Takeda, noted, "In parallel, our private-market collaboration with Dr. Reddy's will help enable timely private-market access for eligible individuals once QDENGA becomes available in India." Approved in 43 countries, QDENGA has seen over 32 million doses distributed globally.

A diminutive wild cat that inhabits Bolivia’s cloud forest has been identified as a previously unknown species, marking the first time a new living cat species has been formally named and described in more than a century.
The cat, called Tilcayo by local communities, is part of a group called tiger cats found across much of South America. It was found in Bolivia’s lush Yungas forest, a mountainous region where forests are often covered by clouds and surrounded by high humidity, according to researchers. It measures about 18in (46cm) long and weighs about 3lbs (1.4kg), making it smaller than the average domestic cat.
Researchers used genetic data to confirm that the cat is a new species, and gave it the scientific name Leopardus tilcayo, retaining its local name.
“Its fur is light brown ... with irregularly shaped rosettes across its body,” said Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz, a National Geographic explorer and one of the authors of the study describing the newly identified species published on Thursday in the journal Current Biology.
Little is yet known about the cat’s biology and lifestyle. Remains of small rodents in scat samples suggest they may form part of its diet, while camera-trap evidence indicates it could be more active at night, Nogales-Ascarrunz said.
Tiger cats are so-called cryptic species, meaning they cannot easily be distinguished merely by appearance, said evolutionary biologist and study co-lead author Jonas Lescroart of the University of Antwerp in Belgium.
Tiger cats previously had been considered a single species, but genetic studies decades ago suggested the existence of multiple species.
Referring to the new species, Lescroart said: “Our information at this moment is limited to the two live individuals that we examined, and a small number of camera-trap records.”
One of the live cats is a 10-year-old male that now lives in the Senda Verde Wildlife Sanctuary after being kept by a local family in their home.
Observing the Bolivian cat drew interest because “its characteristics did not match the descriptions, most of them based on Brazilian cats,” Nogales-Ascarrunz said. “This made us wonder: what tiger cat do we actually have in Bolivia?”
The team analysed DNA from 38 cats sampled across several South American countries, including eight museum specimens. The study found that tiger cats are in fact five genetically distinct species.
“We never expected this Bolivian tiger cat to be a separate species, and no one had ever proposed it as a different animal, subspecies or otherwise,” Lescroart said.
Genetic analysis suggested that the Tilcayo lineage separated from other tiger cats about 1.4m years ago.
“The more differences in their DNA, the longer the time that we estimate those lineages to have been physically separated,” Lescroart said, adding that such a gap is generally considered a species-level divide in cats.
The research team also described a new tiger cat subspecies in Peru’s Yungas, naming it Leopardus tigrinus antisuyo after Antisuyu, the region of the old Inca empire that included the area it inhabits.
The International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) red list tracking the status of species currently treats tiger cats as two “vulnerable” species with declining populations.
The researchers have shared their findings with the IUCN, whose upcoming review will assess the five lineages separately. That could give a more accurate picture of risk, Lescroart said, and species such as the Tilcayo could be considered endangered when assessed on their own.
The need for a clearer assessment is particularly acute in the Yungas, one of the region’s most threatened ecosystems.
The mountain forests face growing pressure from deforestation, agricultural expansion, human-caused fires and mining, Nogales-Ascarrunz said. Restoring forest patches damaged by fires, protecting remaining native forest and maintaining connections between habitats are urgent priorities, Nogales-Ascarrunz added.
“Showing the general public that even in a flagship group such as cats ... there are still new species to be discovered may transmit an important message,” said Eduardo Eizirik, an evolutionary biologist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio Grande do Sul in Brazil and senior author of the study. “There are many undiscovered species out there in the world, and they are at risk of disappearing before we even discover them.”

When a woman has difficulty conceiving or experiences repeated pregnancy loss, the focus often turns to the uterus, the quality of the embryos or ovarian reserve. However, hormones, too, can play an important role, and one hormone that deserves attention is prolactin.
Prolactin is produced by the pituitary gland and is best known for its role in breast milk production. Its levels naturally rise during pregnancy and breastfeeding. Outside these periods, however, persistently elevated prolactin, a condition known as hyperprolactinaemia, can interfere with normal reproductive function.
The symptoms are not always obvious. Some women may have irregular or absent periods, difficulty conceiving or an unexpected milky discharge from the breasts. Others may have no noticeable symptoms at all.
Prolactin and fertility
Reproductive hormones work as a closely connected system. Prolactin is part of this system, and when its levels remain elevated, it can interfere with the hormonal signals required for ovulation.
High prolactin can suppress the release of gonadotropin-releasing hormone from the brain. This can subsequently affect Luteinising Hormone (LH) and Follicle Stimulating Hormone (FSH), which are involved in follicle development and ovulation. As a result, some women may ovulate irregularly or stop ovulating altogether. Their periods may become longer, unpredictable or absent, making conception more difficult.
Prolactin also interacts with reproductive hormones after ovulation. This is one reason why its possible role in the early stages of pregnancy has attracted clinical attention, although the relationship is more complex than simply linking one abnormal hormone level to pregnancy loss.
The link to repeated pregnancy loss
The relationship between elevated prolactin and recurrent pregnancy loss is documented in clinical literature but described with appropriate caution. A 2025 guideline published in the Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada found that elevated prolactin is associated with pregnancy loss and may contribute to luteal phase deficiency. The guideline recommends prolactin testing in women with recurrent pregnancy loss who also present with irregular periods or unexplained breast discharge.
The clinical nuance here is important. Hyperprolactinaemia is one contributing factor among several more established causes of recurrent pregnancy loss, such as chromosomal abnormalities in the embryo, uterine structural issues, antiphospholipid syndrome, and thyroid dysfunction. This does not reduce the clinical relevance of elevated prolactin, but it does mean that a single elevated test result should not be treated as the explanation before other causes have been assessed. The 2025 guideline is explicit on this: elevated prolactin should be confirmed through repeat testing before any treatment is initiated, and thyroid function should be checked first, as hypothyroidism can independently raise prolactin levels.
The connection with PMOS
Among women with PMOS, earlier known as PCOS, mildly elevated prolactin levels are occasionally found alongside the more typical hormonal pattern of the condition. Some research has found a mean hyperprolactinaemia prevalence of 11.9% in women with PMOS, though the range across studies is wide, reflecting how variable the relationship is across different populations and diagnostic thresholds. Hyperprolactinaemia is not considered a clinical manifestation of PMOS, and the two conditions are assessed and managed independently.
Why the elevation
The causes of elevated prolactin are varied. A benign, prolactin-secreting pituitary tumour called a prolactinoma is among the more significant causes and is identified through an MRI when prolactin levels are substantially elevated. Hypothyroidism, certain medications including antipsychotics and some antihypertensives, and occasionally stress or intensive exercise can also raise prolactin levels transiently. This is why repeat testing under standardised conditions such as fasting and avoiding physical stress before the blood draw, is important before a diagnosis of hyperprolactinaemia is established.
When true hyperprolactinaemia is confirmed, dopamine agonist medications such as cabergoline or bromocriptine are effective at normalising prolactin levels in most cases. Research has demonstrated successful restoration of ovulation and term pregnancy outcomes in women with hyperprolactinaemia following dopamine agonist therapy, including in cases involving pituitary tumours. The condition, when properly identified and treated, is one of the more manageable contributors to fertility challenges.
What women should know
For women experiencing recurrent pregnancy loss or difficulty conceiving, prolactin testing is a reasonable part of a comprehensive hormonal evaluation. The results need to be interpreted alongside thyroid function, ovarian reserve, and a full assessment of both partners, because the factors that influence reproductive outcomes are rarely operating in isolation.
(Dr. Prachi Benara is a fertility specialist at Birla Fertility and IVF, Gurgaon. prachi.benara@birlafertility.com)

Could Chinese explorers have settled New Zealand before the Maori?
Mainstream academics and Maori groups voice scepticism, but researchers say acknowledging lesser-known history could alter national identity
For generations, the narrative of New Zealand’s human settlement has held that Polynesian voyagers – the ancestors of the Maori – arrived and settled the islands in the 13th century, followed by European explorers in the 17th century.
This timeline underpins New Zealand’s history and its political model. The Treaty of Waitangi, signed in 1840 between the British Crown and about 540 Maori chiefs, served as New Zealand’s founding document, paving the way for Britain to claim sovereignty and incorporate the country into the British Empire.
Outside the halls of universities and government institutions, two independent researchers are on a quest to discover pre-Maori Chinese presence in New Zealand.

Almost half of the world’s farmers are poisoned by pesticides every single year, a study has found.
Using publicly available data from 2006-2023, the study, which was commissioned by Pesticide Action Network, found there to be an estimated 402-433m cases of unintentional acute pesticide poisoning of farmers and farm workers every year.
Based on a worldwide farming population of 934 million, this means approximately 46% of farmers are being poisoned every year. The greatest estimated number of poisonings was in southern Asia, followed by south-east Asia and east Africa.
The overall highest national incidence of poisoning was in Burkina Faso in west Africa, where nearly 84% of farmers and farm workers were reported to have experienced poisoning.
The study, published in the journal Frontiers in Public Health on Wednesday, also found that an estimated 11,000 deaths occur every year due to pesticide poisoning, with nearly 60% of these in India.
Jayakumar Chelaton, the executive director of Pesticide Action Network India, said the research exposed a “crisis that can no longer be ignored”.
The authors of the study are calling for “immediate action”, including the implementation of a UN recommendation to phase out highly hazardous pesticides.
The study states that despite global efforts to highlight the dangers, pesticide use has continued to grow steadily, with 3.8m tonnes used in 2023, a doubling since 1990.
Dr Sheila Willis, the head of international programmes at Pesticide Action Network UK, said: “Now that the scale of suffering has been revealed, farmers must be supported to access safer alternatives to protect their health and that of their families.”
The study did not consider the impact of pesticide exposure on the estimated 84 million children working in agriculture and did not look at the long-term health impacts, with acute pesticide poisoning defined in the study as any illness or health effect experienced a short time after exposure.
Génon Jensen, the executive director of the Health and Environment Alliance, said: “We are extremely concerned about the devastating health impacts from pesticide poisonings – both the acute impacts mentioned in this study but also chronic exposures that farm workers and communities suffer.”
Hélène Nicora, the director general of Parkinson’s Europe, said there was also “overwhelming evidence” to suggest that Parkinson’s was an environmentally driven disease, with growing evidence linking pesticide exposure to the development of Parkinson’s.
Parkinson’s disease is a progressive disorder in which parts of the brain become damaged over time, affecting movement and balance. The global burden of the disease is rising, with France, Germany and Italy all recognising it as an occupational disease for farmers.
Farmers and farm workers are mainly exposed to pesticides during preparation and application, as well as when touching treated crops and contaminated equipment or clothing.
Speaking at a webinar organised by Friends of the Earth Europe earlier this year, Rendert Algra said he believed his Parkinson’s disease was linked to the pesticides he had used when working at his family farm in the Netherlands.
“Being the eldest son, I did all the spraying of pesticides in our fields for several years in a row,” he said.
Despite being the most robust study to date, the report highlights that available information on pesticide poisoning is inadequate, with the authors calling for standardised surveillance and reporting protocols so that pesticide-related poisonings become reliable and comparable.

Months after a fractured wrist had healed, a 42-year-old homemaker from Mysuru was still unable to cook or even tolerate the touch of clothing on her hand. Despite repeated investigations confirming that the fracture had healed, she continued to have severe burning pain, swelling, stiffness and changes in skin colour.
She was eventually referred to pain specialists and diagnosed with Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS), in which the nervous system continues to generate pain long after the original injury has healed. With specialised pain management, she gradually regained function and independence.
Pain specialists say such cases highlight the need to recognise chronic pain as a condition that may require specialised care.
At Victoria Hospital, attached to the Bangalore Medical College and Research Institute (BMCRI), more than 1,200 patients have undergone specialised pain-relieving procedures since its pain clinic was established in June 2023. The clinic, run by the Department of Anaesthesia, Critical Care and Pain Medicine, has also provided outpatient consultation to over 4,000 patients.
Public awareness campaign
As September is observed as Pain Awareness month, the Karnataka Chapter of the Indian Society for Study of Pain (ISSP) has launched a public awareness campaign urging people not to accept chronic pain as an unavoidable part of life, but to seek specialised care when it persists beyond the normal healing period.
“Our team led by our head of the department Nethra S.S. has performed over 1,200 advanced pain intervention procedures and has seen over 4,000 patients in the outpatient department,” said Satish Kumar M.N., associate professor, Department of Anaesthesia and Pain Medicine, BMCRI, and treasurer of the Karnataka Chapter of the ISSP.
The clinical team, comprising associate professor Nethra H.N., assistant professor Harshavardhan H.S., Satish Kumar and Dr. Nethra, treats patients with cancer pain, neuropathic pain, musculoskeletal disorders, spine-related pain, knee and shoulder pain, trigeminal neuralgia and other chronic pain conditions.
Besides image-guided nerve blocks and joint injections, the clinic performs advanced procedures such as radiofrequency ablation, which interrupts pain signals from affected nerves.
Dr. Kumar said the acquisition of a radiofrequency ablation machine had enabled the BMCRI to offer procedures that were previously available largely in corporate hospitals.
Pain is more than a symptom
Sadasivan S. Iyer, consultant and lead, Pain Medicine, Manipal Hospital, Old Airport Road, and vice-president of the Karnataka Chapter of the ISSP, said a common misconception was that patients should simply learn to live with chronic pain.
“Many patients are told to simply live with pain because investigations do not reveal an obvious cause. But persistent pain can itself be a medical condition requiring specialised evaluation and treatment,” he said.
While acute pain serves as the body’s warning signal after an injury or illness, pain lasting beyond three months can become a condition in itself, he said. The nervous system can continue to transmit pain signals even after tissues have healed. Therefore, normal scans do not necessarily mean that the pain is imaginary, while abnormalities on imaging do not always explain the severity of symptoms.
Beyond painkillers
Pain medicine is not limited to prescribing stronger painkillers. Depending on the condition, treatment may include medication optimisation, physical rehabilitation, psychological support, lifestyle modification and minimally invasive, image-guided procedures such as nerve blocks, epidural injections and radiofrequency ablation.
“The goal is not simply to reduce a patient’s pain score. It is to help them sleep better, return to work, perform daily activities and regain independence. Pain relief is ultimately about restoring quality of life,” said Murali T.S., consultant and lead, Pain Medicine, Apollo Hospitals, Bengaluru, and president of the Karnataka Chapter of the ISSP.
When should patients seek help?
According to the ISSP, millions of Indians live with persistent back and neck pain, sciatica, diabetic neuropathy, post-herpetic neuralgia, trigeminal neuralgia, cancer pain and pain that continues after surgery.
Specialists advise people to seek evaluation if pain lasts for more than three months, repeatedly returns, interferes with sleep or daily activities, persists despite treatment of the original illness, or is accompanied by burning, shooting or electric shock-like sensations.

Russian missiles struck Ukraine's capital Kyiv on Friday, with explosions heard across the city, Mayor Vitali Klitschko was quoted as saying by Reuters.
The attack comes after a Russian drone strike in the Kyiv region early on Friday morning injured five people, including three children, regional governor Tymur Tkachenko said on Telegram.
Earlier on Thursday, Russian forces continued a barrage of attacks on Ukrainian cities, including a strike on an industrial park west of Kyiv that killed one person, a local official said.

Successive rounds of US-brokered talks have failed to yield a breakthrough, while Ukraine is also seeking security guarantees from its partners as part of any deal.
US president Donald Trump said in a social media post on Monday that Russia and Ukraine had mutually agreed to stop attacking each other's energy facilities. Such strikes have caused significant supply disruptions in both countries.

When Trump and Xi meet they will discuss AI. 'Track Two' talks are already buzzing
The United States and China are locked in a cycle of fierce competition and mistrust over artificial intelligence, and experts say the chances that President Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping can change the dynamic when they meet in Washington next Thursday are dim.
In the past few weeks alone, the Trump administration has accused Chinese AI companies of stealing intellectual property by "distilling" leading U.S. AI models, and threatened sanctions. Beijing, for its part, has poured scorn on U.S. restrictions on chip exports, and accused Washington of running a "Cold War playbook" to hold Chinese AI down.
It would seem there is little room, or appetite, for compromise. But former officials and policy experts say there is a buzzing bilateral dialogue — and a growing sense of shared concern about the dangers of AI — at the sub-national level in what diplomacy wonks call "Track Two."
For decades, government-to-government interactions, sometimes called "Track One" diplomacy, have been underpinned by this sprawling network of informal private meetings and conferences, often run by think tanks or universities. Track Two discussions bring together experts from both sides, and cover a wide array of topics, from nuclear disarmament to climate change.
"I think there is no more important topic that the U.S. and China should be talking about than AI," said Sarah Beran, a former U.S. diplomat who worked on China and is the incoming president of the non-profit National Committee on U.S.-China Relations. The committee runs several Track Two discussions and has been involved in policy exchanges since 1972, when it sponsored a visit to China by U.S. ping pong players to help thaw relations.
AI is a tough topic, though, because there's so little trust in the relationship at the moment, says Beran. "The fear of chokepoints, being held back, and AI being used as a cudgel on both sides means that this is also one of the most difficult areas to talk about," she said.
The idea behind Track Two is to build understanding, and work toward policy recommendations that both sides can agree on. Sometimes, governments use them as back channels, or low-stakes ways to float ideas.
Beran said that was the case after direct military-to-military discussions between China and the U.S. were cut off following then-Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi's visit to Taiwan in 2022. At the time, Beran was the top China official on the National Security Council in the Biden administration.
"We floated some ideas in Track Two dialogues about what resumption of military-to-military communications could look like, at what level, what the topics would be. And then we took it back into the formal channels and negotiated on resuming those channels," she said.
Then-President Biden and Xi agreed at a 2023 summit in Woodside, Calif., to get the military dialogue back up and running.
Jack Shanahan, a retired Air Force general who has been involved in Track Two dialogue over military AI, said informal discussions helped tee up an agreement between the leaders a year later that any decision to use nuclear weapons should be controlled by humans, not by AI.
"That was only possible by years of quiet dialogue at the Track Two level on this very topic," he said.
Samm Sacks, an expert in Chinese tech at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies and the policy think tank New America, said she was involved in several Track Two discussions on AI in Shanghai and Beijing over the summer "that were very substantive."
"People can talk about sensitive issues more candidly and also don't feel the need to come to any consensus that would become public," she said.
Those dialogues have reinforced for her that the U.S. has a lot of common ground with China on AI, despite government friction over chip export controls and accusations that Chinese AI labs are stealing intellectual property. "So what I hear in the Track Twos I'm a part of is a sense of shared vulnerability and shared precarity created by AI," she said.
Shanahan agrees. On AI, China sees itself as an underdog, he says, but Shanahan has perceived a shift on the Chinese side as the technology advances and risks become clearer. "For the first time, I'm seeing, like, 'Look, we know we're not at parity in some of these areas, but AI is too important not to have these dialogues,'" he said.
Still, tensions over AI at the official level have been high, and the two sides have tended to focus on different concerns, with the U.S. looking at things like cyber vulnerabilities and possible loss of control of AI, and China thinking about regime stability and self-reliance for making hardware. Experts say that has an impact on the complexion of Track Two dialogues — and has tempered expectations for concrete outcomes.
The Center for Strategic and International Studies, a U.S. policy think tank, also runs Track Twos, and China specialist Scott Kennedy has been involved in a wide-ranging dialogue about economics that includes AI. He said the talks can increase awareness in policy circles of the others' red lines and how each side makes decisions on the issues.
"They provide you a sort of road map of the different points of view and the potential actions and reactions of different scenarios," he said. But he added they require a level of government support on both sides to work.
"This is the time where we need some leadership, and what we're seeing is a vacuum," he said. "Track Twos don't fill that vacuum. They can help redirect things and buy time, prepare the groundwork for new engagements, but they're not going to solve the giant problems on their own."
Sacks said the disagreements over AI between China and the United States make this a precarious moment, with the utility of Track Twos in the balance. A push this week by U.S. AI companies for a global agreement to slow down the development of cutting edge AI did not go over well in China.
"I actually think the best thing that the two governments can do is just at a high level signal [that] we both need to come together to address AI safety and cyber risk, bio risk, for example," she said, referring to the risks that people could use AI for hacking or to develop biological weapons.
Some Track Two participants say the Trump administration is less engaged with the dialogues than previous administrations, making the work more challenging. But Track Two participants will be watching the Trump-Xi meeting in Washington next week for signals that AI is a topic of concern to both sides, and one on which the two sides' experts can continue to engage in substantive talks. And Sarah Beran says that includes the National Committee.
"You need to build confidence on both sides that this is a safe space to talk about issues," she said. "Our next meeting is coming up in the next couple of months and we're trying to think about how we use whatever the two presidents say together as a way to start talking about these issues in a Track Two format."

Manchester United youngster JJ Gabriel has travelled to Barcelona as some of Europe's biggest clubs continue to vie for his signature.
The 15-year-old has told United he wants to cancel his registration with immediate effect.
BBC Sport reported on Thursday that Real Madrid have a firm interest in the forward, and Bayern Munich, Paris St-Germain and Barcelona are also known to be keen.
It is understood Gabriel left the UK on Thursday and went to France, but is now in Barcelona.
If United hold on to the Londoner's registration, it would stop him moving to another English club until the end of the season.

The Food and Drug Administration on Thursday approved a new gene therapy for Sanfilippo syndrome type A, an ultra-rare disease sometimes known as childhood Alzheimer’s.
The therapy, called Fayuvi, was developed by Ultragenyx. It is the first drug specifically approved to treat Sanfilippo. Ultragenyx did not immediately release a price.
“It’s hard to overstate what this approval would mean for everybody who is living with this really horrific disease and watching their children suffer and pass away early, and all the rest that it brings,” said Cara O’Neill, chief science officer of the Cure Sanfilippo Foundation, in an interview earlier this week. “This, gosh, would just finally mean when patients and families receive this shocking diagnosis, they wouldn’t be told to… take their kids home and love them. They would be given hope and an action plan for treatment.”

The 18th BRICS Summit was held on 12 and 13 September 2026 at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi, bringing together leaders from BRICS member countries and several partner nations. Against this backdrop, a video showing police personnel allegedly dragging a woman by her hair on a road is being widely shared (here, here), with the claim that police used force against young protesters in Delhi, dragging female protesters onto the streets while the BRICS Summit was being held nearby. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: The video shows police taking action against protesters in Delhi while the BRICS Summit 2026 was going on.
Fact: The viral video does not show police action against protesters in Delhi during the BRICS Summit. The video is from Tirupati, Andhra Pradesh, where paramedical students were protesting over unpaid stipends and mandatory 12-hour hospital shifts. Hence, the claim made in the post is MISLEADING.
A reverse image search using keyframes from the viral video led us to a video published by Deccan Herald on 13 September 2026, featuring similar visuals. According to its description, the video shows police action against paramedical students protesting in Tirupati over unpaid stipends, including footage of a male police officer allegedly dragging a female student by her hair.
Further, a relevant keyword search led us to several media reports indicating that this incident took place in Tirupati, Andhra Pradesh (here, here, here, here). According to the reports, BSc MLT and other allied health students, along with student union representatives, protested at Garuda Circle in Alipiri on 12 September 2026 over mandatory 12-hour shifts and pending monthly stipends of ₹15,000. ASI Lakshmi Kumari was accused of dragging a woman protester towards a police van and was reportedly moved to vacancy reserve (VR). Tirupati Additional SP Ravi Manoharachary clarified that the woman was pulled by her hand, while her hair covering the hand made it appear as though she was dragged by her hair.
Moreover, we found no reports of police action near the venue of the BRICS Summit.
To sum up, a video showing police action against protesters in Tirupati is being shared as visuals from Delhi during the BRICS Summit.
